Finally got around to giving this a go on the PC after all this time. I got about halfway through it on the PS3 when it first came out and just moved on to the other backlogs I had at the time. So, what do I, personally, think of this?
It's probably one of the most gorgeous games on PC available. Period. Just stunning on PC. While it doesn't have the bells and whistles of different graphic settings available there are more tweaks to do if you look them up. However, I'd say you don't really have to. The White Engine shines on PC and it is just stunning. Characters look nice, environments are gorgeous and spell effects, etc, are just amazing to behold.
Furthermore, character voice acting, while it may be "cheesy" in some parts, is still the better part of any game made in the past few years. They're believable, the voice talent shows emotions and support, you get the "Umphs" when jumping, sliding, etc. Good stuff. Surprising, weapon sounds are also on point in this game. Not something you'd expect in a FF game. Not at all. However, guns BOOM and POP, Snow's fists are your martial arts movie soundtrack slaps and even Vanille's weapon has that gracious ZING ZING going for it. It's quite immersive if you're paying attention.
A few things to gripe about. Not really downers, just minor annoyances. First, there are no graphical sliders beyond resolution and shadows. Secondly, the mouse can get a little weird sometimes. Not much, not at all. Just every once in awhile should you need to suddenly backtrack you'll notice it.
One thing I did like is that the keyboard/mouse is quite easy to use and, actually, I preferred playing it that way. Weird, I know, but even a controller wasn't as relaxing as the k/m combo was for me. So, a plus for that.
Now, the story is kind of like a MGS game. Quite convoluted and even gets a little weird sometimes, but still a great story being told. You get to play the story through multiple characters and you get a whole lotta side story to venture out and discover. While the game is quite linear up until the last part it's not a bad thing. While FF13-2 opened up the game a LOT more, I still think FF13 was nice in it's closed but slightly bigger areas.
Also, you may find some of the characters annoying. Whiny. Disturbing. I did. However, that seems to be standard fare for the FF games for some reason. You always have to have 1 or 2 really ♥♥♥♥ing annoying character actions/voices to just upset the whole balance of being awesome. Whatever, it doesn't really take anything away from the game. I just wish, and hope, that when the new FF15 comes out that Square has gone beyond that childish bs.
Catch it on sale for a worthy buy or buy full price if you're a FF fan. Either way, it's a great way to spend between 60-100 hours of playtime that never seems to get old. Not really at all.

This game is not happy. It doesn't pretend to be create a shroud of invincibility that your immortal characters stroll through leisurely; perhaps through infinite respawns or just god-like powers and abilities. It's a tale about people living in a bombshelled city during civil war. Most likely, you'll lose characters along the way. You will be faced by times where you need to choose between food, medicine and weapons to defend what little stockpile of resources you have. Do you use your last bit of scavenged fuel on feeding your hungry people, or staving off sub-zero temperatures that will inevitably result in illness. The decisions in this game feel real and they're not arbitrary. There are some moral decisions - mostly about whether or not to help neigbours with various (random?) problems which may or may not come back to help you and carry their own consequences.
That being said, this is one of the most personal games I've ever played. If you're thinking about it or are on the fence about getting this game - get it.

Basically, this game has a solid foundation - you can build your own decks with the Origins edition, you have both a Wizard and a custom deck editor, you can earn gold and therefore new boosters in an acceptable time without using real money. The AI opponents are acceptable, too.
However, numerous glitches and problems take away from the fun quite a bit - controls are sometimes difficult to use, especially when you try to pick the correct mana, daily quests only work with the decks created using the wizard (which sometimes has funny ideas about which cards are good and which aren't), animations are painfully slow (in my opinion, anyway), the sorting mechanism of the decks suck, leading you to games in which you draw the same card four times, the story quests can only be solved using premanufactured decks (some of which suck AND blow).
The community ladder system is rather unbalanced, sometimes setting Lvl 1-Players against players of a much higher level with considerably better-developed decks.
All in all, this is way better than the previous 2014-2015 versions of this game. However, do not expect wonders.

Game's good, plays like a quite frantic and technical Smash Bros. clone that mashes a little from each entry of that series into itself(obviously with major Melee emphasis in there, what with the wavedashing, fairly quick fall speeds across the board and all that stuff), while also adding its own unique spins(perhaps most notably the lack of proper shields and grabs, being replaced by parries, and the removal of ledges in favour of letting everyone cover ridiculous distance if they get to walljump off the stage). There's few characters, but they're built around unique gimmicks(that often linger on and affect the stage itself and can be used in unique ways by their characters, both to control area as well as amplifying their moves in some way) and fighting styles(many characters borrowing entire chunks of moves from different Smash characters and thus playing like odd hybrids of them) so the roster is quite diverse in spite of that.
Music and overall presentation is great, much better than any comparable game I could think off on Steam, and feels nicely polished. Singleplayer content does its job giving you something to do outside of good ol' PvP and adding some minor world building to the game's setting and characters(nothing big, don't expect an anime fighter worth of plot, just some small bits that add some context to the game beyond "funny animal people with elemental powers punch each other until one flies off the screen". It's no grand epic and it doesn't need to be).
The meat of the game is the multiplayer though, which you get to enjoy locally and online. Unfortunately the game's practice/singleplayer modes don't quite feel expansive and elaborate enough to quite get you used to the game I feel, which is a bit of a problem as it is a quite technical fighter all things considered, and due to the game's comparably low(but still acceptably sized) playerbase the majority of the online multiplayer games consist of you playing a lagtastic match with a dude on the moon or getting bodied by a guy that plays like his life depended on it. Gitting gud is a struggle because of that, and you should be prepared for that if you buy this game. That being said, finding someone you are on a somewhat even footing with(and can play with a reasonable ping) is fun, satisfying and feels like a learning experience every time.
So yeah, it's pretty dope. I'd recommend it.

I am a longtime egosoft fan starting with X: BTF, and I was among the masses more than looking forward to this game and claiming I would be disappearing from the world at launch. Sadly, this didnt happen. Launch was a disaster, crashing and save game edit requirements being among the forefront of the issues. That being said however, Egosoft seems to be working hard to bring the game in line with a true "Release" quality build and, as always, the community is hard at work to mod whatever they want into the game as well as changing what they view as needing change.
Hopefully with further support this game can come to be something closer to the anticipated game.
To elaborate on my beginning notes - what I thought while playing it:
(Just to get this out of the way) The single ship thing does bother me as I have gotten used to the previous titles ability to pilot whatever is available. However, I do like the attempt to make that single ship something worth upgrading - they just need to broaden the options beyond their simple Mk1 Mk2 Mk3 Mk4 setup.
"Player owned Ships" and their crew - Fortunately the ships are starting to respond properly (Especially with the mods available) and I do like the idea of hiring the "command" crew of the ship (I say that because i like to think the ship has more than 3 people on it, especially the bigger container ships and cruisers) and, while it does get tedious, it does play to the micromanager in me.
- Trading is a bit of a pain, and while updates have been making it easier, I have been forced to turn to the community to make this something worth doing.
-I have to say that despite any issues with control over the ships, once you get your warships into a fight its quite a sight (Given they attack what you want them to - i believe a recent update allowed for this) with the heavy beams against larger craft and chain guns against fighters.
-Building stations can be a pain, while the idea of the construction ship being able to buy from merchants to get what it needs is nice, it never seems to work - especially in Devrise. Keep in mind that I do not believe you should be able to autopilot and have a station magically appear, I do like that there are so many materials needed and you have to work for your station. I just have an issue with the apparent "WE ARE BUYING THIS AND THIS AND THIS!!" not seeming to work with the NPCs.
Now the storyline: You start off well enough. Random event leading to you getting embroiled in x and y story. However, as it progresses there are so many fragments and seeming skips in what you can tell Should be there and isnt that you get lost trying to figure out how you went from problem A to problem B and both being fixed with Solution C...yet not really. While i understand there is supposed to be an episodic nature to the game...where is the rest of the first episode?
Again i still wish there was a Maybe button. I'm recommending this title with the note that it is still a work in progress and has a lot of potential, but if you do pick this up head straight for the modding forums as there are plenty of options to make this game more appealing.

My thoughts and impressions on this game are a little split...
The game itself is - as old fashioned Saints Row fans would expect -.. gloriously stupid and over the top. Though the Story is with ~4hrs of playtime not really that deep or as good as the ones from the whole franchise. But for a legit price of 20 bucks it's justified in my opinion.
Your task is basically to play Gat / Kinzie from former Saints Row games, to save the Boss' soul  which he lost between SR IV and this game (he appears the way you created him in SR IV game if you own it), and make your way through Hell and face Satan to achieve just that (it even got short musical parts in the cutscenes which I could listen to over and over again). It's short but there are 6 different endings...which motivates (at least me) to keep on playing from time to time.
The game feels unique to me because the developers may have not put a lot of effort into story driven parts but they were damn creative concerning everything else.. 7 deadly guns (wrath, lust, sloth, etc..),
different challenges / sidequests that are easy to beat but damn fun to play and the fact that new superpowers were added since SR IV ...though some are "imported" (stomp f.e.) but all in all a nice addition.
And finally there's a Saints Row game where you are not forced to buy DLC's to get all of the achievements....some of them suffer from "standard shooter game gameplay"- grinding  (achievements for making XY kills with that weapon etc)  but even that makes fun. The others though are very creative and you actually have to do some insane tricks to achieve them...sometimes frustrating but it feels so satisfying after ;3
I loved Saints Row since Part 2 and this one might not be the best of them all but its definitely worth a shot if you are a fan of the franchise and want to play from a new perspective (Kinzie or Gat) in Hell.
What matters the very most to me in games like this is the fact that you are able to play it with friends..Saints Row has taken all that to a whole new level for me...it just makes too much fun running, driving or even flying around together and mess with everything... not that i dislike GTA but i had my early Steam days with Sr3 and 4 ..not GTA V Online...but they are all good games!

Like American Nightmare to Alan Wake, Gat out of Hell is a glorious standalone expansion to Saints Row 4 and should not be misinterpreted as anything but.
Featuring 4-5 hours of content, it is almost exactly what one would expect from Saints Row nowadays, featuring even more unnecessarily outlandish weapons, comedic dialogues and most shockingly, a most pleasant musical which awoke everyone in my home as it played.
Saints Row has always been featured heavily in regards to its activities, however Gat out of Hell takes this to an extreme. The expansion features very few actual missions and instead expects the player to repeat the same few activities on numerous different difficulties in order to progress the actual story. The activities are brilliant and most definitely do not feel grindy I may add, however, some more actual individualized missions would've been most appreciated.
The wing and powers system is mostly recycled from the main game itself, however, it still feels excellently executed, even if some powers do seem out of place for the expansions setting. You'll find yourself flooded in upgrades via "wages" and "clusters" in no time due to the games short lifespan, but alas, it still feels like a blast (hahahaha).
The characters that are introduced via this expansion have very limited progression in terms of their story and the ending seemed most blunt, however, the expansion does feature many past characters introduced in some of the older games which some veteran fans may appreciate- I sure did, put it that way.
If you like Saints Row 3 and 4, you'll like this, if not, don't bother. I personally had a blast with this short experience and hope you do to.

Did you play the original Bioshock?  Then you've played Bioshock 2, and the sound is still borked.
This sequel was actually done by a different studio, but apparently not wanting to mess with success they remade the same game.  Vita chambers are back.  The research camera is back.  Plasmids are back.  The choice to "harvest or save" a little sister is back. Fighting big daddies is back as well.  Even some of the new twists, like playing as a big daddy, don't feel that different in actual gameplay.
So, it is essentially the same game, but the novelety has worn off.  You are playing in Rapture, a city built as a Utopia but collapsed into a waring society of ugly drug addicts.  Just like you did in Bioshock.  Adam Ryan has been replaced by Sofia Lamb, who replaces Objectivism with extreme collectivisim.  The two barely seem different despite the polar opposing philosophies.
Since this game is so identical to its predecessor, that means all the problems of the first are back.  The combat still feels clunky.  Vita chambers make the game infinitely easy to beat and destroy the need for resource management.  However, the one problem I just can't look past is the broken sound effects.  Maybe this is a PC problem, maybe this is just a problem for people who use headphones.  Regardless, the game fails to do sound effects properly, with ambient noises such as splicer cries drowning out sound effects like explosions or gunfire.  It is really disconcerting.  For a more original game, like say the original Bioshock, I can work through it.  This time around, it is just inexcusable.
Good news, though.  2K recently updated Bioshock 2 to removal the atrocious Windows Live system, and add achievements.
It's like Portal in space with gravity without gravity.

(Near) Perfection.
It's a strong word so let me explain and attempt to justify it. Each idea has a place, a moment and an audience. This game is a brilliant idea, well ahead of its time, a game that works on older computers and still feels beautiful and smooth today. It feels like it was made of oil, double-cream and chocolate liqueurs. It is smooth, low on resources, easy to mod with lots of improvement with each expansion. I've had a lot of enjoyment out of it, played on run-down laptops that can't handle booting-up without groaning and it's been as smooth as on a gaming-rig.
I couldn't ask for much more from a game, hence, in completely achieving its goals I'd say it's damn near perfection.
But, the goals are a little limited. There is little back-story, most left intentionally mysterious. There is little planet development, intentionally streamlined to beautiful simplicity. Most of my quibbles are about the goals chosen and not the lack of achieving them. This game exceeds expectations, it punches above its weight and will be remembered as a classic, ticking all the right boxes and doing something unique.
Get it. (But the DLC isn't really needed, it's just there as a way to give the Devs extra money... It isn't going to revolutionise your experience).

The Last Remnant is a JRPG that can still be fun despite an overwhelming number of quirks and flaws.
As pointed by many reviewers, it's level scalling is inherently flawed, with enemies scalling to your Battle Rank, a measure of how many battles you've fought, but not of your party's strength.
The combat is turn-based, as most JRPGs, the system, however is a quirky mess, with your options for controlling unions (small parties formed with your characters) being somewhat randomized and influented by external conditions (enemy type, status, previous actions, leader class, etc.) One can adapt to the system, but it makes combat more luck-reliant than strategical.
The major gameplay problems lie, however, on the huge difficulty spikes. During the main story you'll probably never run into those, but very difficult sidequests and strong rare monsters appear way sooner than they should, making you wonder why the devs bothered including the battle rank system in the first place.
It doesn't help that the game hides to much info, such as how the class system works, character skill levels, class requirements, quest objectives, material sources, etc. Making it almost mandatory to play this game with the last remnant wikia open on the side.
Then come matters of personal preference. Being a JRPG, you pretty much know to expect flashy (and somewhat silly) character designs, oversized weapons, steriotypical characters (although a few are quite well fleshed out).
The story itself could be interesting, but it has an incredibly odd pacing, sending you back and forth between cities (your travel on the world map is instant though), walking randomly into city areas in order to trigger a scene, talking with a generic NPC nobody ever mentioned...
There are also some heavy sins such as the narration interlude at the end of part 1, interrupting a moment of tension as if nothing of importance happened thereafter. Cliches abound as well with characters fainting or dying before revealling crucial information, characters looking wide-eyed at someone outside the shot and then the scene cutting off somewhere else, antagonists leaving heroes alive just because, and the list goes on and on...
To summarize, The Last Remnant is far too quirky, unbalanced and badly written for me to recommend it, yet, it managed to make me obsess over it with a large number of sidequests and room for powergaming. If, despite such warnings you still want to play this game (seeing as it's rather cheap), do so with the last remnant wikia on the side, and study well how to keep your Battle Rank low, how to better progress characters through classes, which characters are useless, which are good, sidequests availability, weapon upgrade paths, crafting material sources, etc.

The game to melt your rig. Well, not anymore, but it still holds a level of graphical fidelity that even today puts many recently released games to shame. Not to mention that with an abundance of mods, due to the rather open nature of the game's engine, you can make it look better than ever.
The game itself is a solid shooter, an in certain regards even a really good one. Fighting the KPA on higher difficulties (with the enemies speaking Korean and no crosshair) can get really intense. And that's also the greatest thing about the game: Without being an open world game, you have all the freedom you can imagine to reach your target. Do you sneak through enemy lines? Try to find an unused path? Do you steal a vehicle? Even tanks may not be safe from you. Get the job done YOUR way! You want to do the tank mission on foot? JUST DO IT! The game rarely limits you in what you can do and what you should do.
This changes later on, when suddenly the game introduces a new set of enemies and gameplay rules. To keep it fresh, the game uses truly three dimension gameplay, although that doesn't help covering up the fact that lush open jungle with wide areas are exchanged for small, almost corridor-like levels that don't allow for the same freedom as before.
If you want more, the community got you covered: There is an unimaginable amount of mods of all kinds available, from simple texture jobs to highlights like Chrjs "Rainy Days", which reaches a whole new level of "WOW!" with intelligent companion AI (significantly better than what even Crysis Warhead offers in that regard) and excellent voice acting - and all that for free. You can of course get your own hands muddy, and dive right into the extremely easy to use "Editor" to create your own settings and missions (or just modify the maps of the single player levels to freeze every single Korean soldier with your God given freeze gun).

So you can see that I waited a good while before reviewing this game. I gave the developers time to fix the myriad of experience-killing glitches. I gave them time to fix the game-breaking bugs.
It's hopeless at this point. Even if they finally manage to fix the TERRIBLE performance issues on high-end gaming systems, and even if they fix all of the critical flaws in the game, AND even if they go so far as to fix the nearly broken interface -- it won't solve the underlying problem. What is the underlying problem? The basic gameplay is bad. It's just a bad game.
Despite some decent ideas and nice-looking visuals (that won't run past 25FPS on my high-end system no matter what I do, a known bug), the game itself just simply isn't good. No matter how much you want to enjoy that classic X3 experience, or how much you want to enjoy a modern space simulator, this isn't the game for you. If you liked X3, don't buy this game. If you like space simulators, don't buy this game. If you like video games, don't buy this game.
It has won a place in the hearts of many gamers for being their WORST GAME PURCHASE OF 2013. It is certainly, without question, the worst game purchase I've ever made. Yes, I've purchased some bad games, but never have I paid $50 for a new game and found it so utterly and completely disappointing.
Where to begin? Well, the graphics, while decent, are plagued with such terrible slow-down and framerate issues as to be nearly unplayable. The story is tepid at best, with no real attraction. Don't expect the story to pull you in. The characters and voice acting are passable at best, laughably bad at worst. Expect to see the same character models and hear the same voices over, and over, and over. Cut-and-paste characters and space stations are the norm. You'll become very familiar with the two basic layouts you'll encounter dozens upon dozens of times.
The music is quite decent, as it does what a good space combat simulator sound track should do -- it creates a nice "cosmic" atmosphere. Nothing that draws your attention too much, but makes you feel like you're in space. The sound FX are also quite decent for the most part, nothing too bad.
The gameplay... It's just bad. You can feel like there's a good game deep inside this beast somewhere, but it just can't find it's way out. An attempt to make the game controller-friendly has needlessly obfuscated the interface. Many critical and commonly used functions are buried deep in menus, and you often find that you have to go here or there within the game world just to issue a simplistic command. The "cockpit" that was so painstakingly crafted serves to do little more than just eat up system resources and obscure the screen -- it's not even a HUD integration, it's just a needless visual distraction and resource hog. Whether you use mouse or keyboard, the interface is bad -- just bad.
You want some great advice that you'd regret not following? Do not even consider buying this game. Don't look at it, don't watch videos of it, don't make any attempt to think that any amount of patching could fix this mess. It's a broken, clunky, frustrating mess of a game, but it commits the sin of looking like something decent to the uninformed. Consider yourself informed -- don't buy it. DO NOT BUY IT.

Performance issues. The game feels quite responsive and fluid until you get hit with a performance drop out of the blue.
Bug ridden. This game has so many bugs it feels like an alpha. Some of them can break your game progress forcing you to restart from the very beginning. Other bugs are quite frustrating like ships not following commands or factories not building and the like.
But finally, what was a deal breaker for me, something I couldn’t get over with no matter how many times I tried to convince myself that this was something trivial, was the fact that you CAN’T use other ships than the fugly and crappy Albion Skunk. It is also worth commenting that there are far fewer ships through out the universe that in X3 so get used to see the same ships all over the place.
There are many other annoying things that add up to the frustration of this game like the “highways”, the limited selection on weapons, multiple docking ports on the same station that you have to visit to access the wares or the people there, having to fly around stations to find the right dock, and much more that is not worth commenting anymore.
Good things that I really like about this game are the graphics (just gorgeous), the music (quite nice and relaxing) and that there may be some tinny, little, microscopic potential in this game IF (AND ONLY IF) the devs get their act together and fix all the bugs, PLUS if the modding community feel sorry enough about this excuse of a game to try and fix it. So, all in all, this game is a perfectly done turd. If you want to waste $50 bucks go for it. In fact, burning those $50 bucks right now seems like a better idea than buying this game.

If you ever wanted to know what war feels like when you're just happening to live near the battlefield, this game is for you. This War of Mine is a unique concept mixing gameplay elements from survival and management games. During a time of war, you manage a group of civilians living in a shelter who scavange at night, improve their home during the day and just try to survive through the war.
What makes this game interesting is that surviving is not as easy as it seems. Even though you manage to get a lot of materials early on to improve your shelter, the lack of wood, food, water and the cold during winter can quickly wear down a group of survivors. And when ressoures get scarce, you tend to take more risks when scavenging, which can quickly lead to the death of some of your suvivors, because in This War of Mine, combat is not only hard : it's punishing.
Overall, this game is a shining exemple of an original concept fully realised through a clever and simple design, which makes the gameplay extremely approachable and straightforward while keeping a level of depth and difficulty on par with most hardcore PC games. If you are longing for an original game with a great atmosphere and an addictive gameplay, look no further.

You survived the radioactive wasteland of Fallout. You crafted a rough-shod bunker out of dirt and leaves in 7-days to die. You managed to log off of Rust for 5 minutes without losing everything you worked so hard for, for 9 straight hours. None of that has prepared you to survive just 5 days in
.
You start the game with just a small group of survivors in the war-torn country of possibly Russia. I'm only going by what the names of the characters resemble. I didn't actually read anything. Your starting point is a bombed-out "home" (In quotes because it's a damned big home) in which you have multiple rooms to clear for the purpose of scavaging and having space to build things such as rain-water filters, beds and cook stoves. Building these items requires parts such as wood, scrap and gears(?). Some of which you will find in your shelter on day one, the rest you have to scavange from other locations.
The mechnanics of the game is simply point-and-click. The game is divided into two parts; Day and night. The daytime is when you build up your shelter (protect it with patched up holes, upgrade your cook-stove or work bench, build furniture to make people happier), cook food, apply medicine or various other things to keep your group happy/healthy. Nighttime is dedicated mostly to scavaging, but also allows to to allocate who gets rest, and who guards your shelter. The day is divied into ten-minute increments and you are allowed 12 hours per day/night. Everything happens in "real-time" but that is a bit of a misnomer as it takes ten minutes to take 5 steps or to climb a ladder. Double-clicking allows you to run to your destination, which speeds you up my a factor of two, and I have yet to see any downside to doing this (i.e. fatigue). Clicking on piles of rubbles, doors, bars, etc. allows you to perform a contextual based action such as sift through rubble, open/close doors, pick locks or pry open doors with a crowbar, saw through metal bars, etc.
Your goal, from what I have seen so far, is to simply survive. Something we have all done in countless games before. Only his time, it is brutal, gritty, real, and unforgiving. You are constantly battling hunger, exhaustion, sickness, depression, wounds and more. Balancing the act of taking care of your group, as well as sending people out to scavange (so that you CAN take care of your group) becomes an excercise of patience, frustration, and futility. You will lose people, you will get frustrated, you will die, and you will hate the game as you click "try again".
Again, just point and click. It's simple enough without taking anything away from the game.
Gritty, pencil-drawn-esque style artwork really works here.The game is a bit of a 2-D sidescroller, s don't expect a whole lot.
This is one area where I was a bit let down. The sound design leaves a lot to be desired, when using the radio. The sound is alright until then.
So what is it that makes this game unique? It's the fact that the game actually makes you FEEL the consequences of your actions. Remember that old couple who's home you raided and who's food you stole? Your group will. And they will talk about how aweful it was. Return to thier home? Now they are dead because YOU took thier food and medicine. You will not feel good about it. Niether will your group, as actions like this will affect them in a negative way. It's up to you to decide how you survive, and what kind of person you will be. Just remember: you will not survive by being the nice guy.

Story: Now in this game we continue's on from Blood money. The game begins with Agent 47 detailing his relationship with his handler Diana Burnwood whom he had trusted until she, without explanation, betrayed the International Contract Agency (ICA) by sabotaging their funding and database, using the subsequent confusion to vanish. After the ICA is reformed, 47 is tasked by his new handler, Benjamin Travis, a high level official within the ICA, to kill Diana for her betrayal and retrieve an important Agency asset named Victoria from her mansion in Chicago, Illinois. 47 sneaks into her mansion and shoots Diana. Rather than finishing her off, 47 comforts the dying Diana and asks her why she betrayed the ICA. Diana reveals everyone has their limits over the bad things they have done and she discovered hers after learning about Victoria, a teenage girl who is genetically-engineered to be an Assassin within the ICA. Not wishing to see Victoria suffer the same fate as 47, she betrayed the ICA and escape with her. As her final request, Diana ask 47 to protect Victoria, and he agrees to do so. Because 47 refuses to return Victoria to him, Travis brands 47 a traitor.
Now this story revolves around Victoria, ICA and more other great story characters. It is certainly a very good story well done to. I enjoyed it.
Game Play: The game play takes place in America e.g. The United States. Which is different that around the world like the old Hitman games. But I will try not to compare it to the old ones. Now we have the addition of the online feature called Contracts which you can compete against other players around the world doing contracts and even make your own to challenge your friends and others. Also the addition of this instinct feature. Which you can see through the walls and the enemies followed by using it to distract the enemies. Shame there is no in story weapon customization of the weapons and the load out choice to.
Controls: Controls are simple to learn as always even for the new player which is good.
The Graphics: Just amazing. Such an improvement. You can see it in the game and the cinematic's to. The detail on the weapons to and on Mr 47 even the npc's. I can not see a fault in it.
Music: It worked well with the game, it set the scenes up great even in the cinematic's to. I did not even want to turn it off which I did with the old games.
Bugs and Glitches: Well as with any new game these years there is always bugs and glitches. But there was only one or two. First would be crashing in loading sections and the other where the save file is unable to sync up. Other than that I could not come across any other. Many people have said of corrupt save files. I wounder if its connected to the failing to sync up.
Reply Value: There is certainly replay value in this game. Going through each difficulty level and there is the contracts side.
Overall: Great story as always, Game play just gets better with additions of a new skill and environments in America. Bar the loss of the weapon load out set and story mode customization's of the weapons. Controls simple to learn and use. Graphics just amazing. Music in the game adds to the game suspense. As I said there is always bugs and glitches hopefully these will be sorted. So for this next great installment to the Hitman Series. I give this game 9 paws out of 10

Well, what can I say? Sins of a Solar Empire is brilliant. 9/10
The gameplay mechanics do take experience to master, but that's all part of what makes the game so wonderful; there are so many aspects of gameplay to take into consideration when you are in a match, such as culture, research topics, and etcetera. If you think that all you have to do to prevail in a match of Sins is to build a thousand ships and spam orbital cannons, you are sorely mistaken.
One thing that appeals to me personally about Sins is the fact that, right from the beginning, you have to meticulously plan out each detail of your empire's expansion, taking into consideration events that could potentially happen hours later.
That planet with only one phase lane leading into enemy territory? Chances are your enemy will eventually try to punch through. You'll need to plan for that.
The world on the other side of the map that's just starting to produce culture? It will spread to your planets quickly. You'll need to plan for that.
That TEC Loyalist player on the other side of the map whose planet pings up for a second with a superweapon alert? You'll especially need to plan for that.
The one and only downside for me about Sins is, and I'm sure this is a common one, there's no campaign! The franchise has gone into a good deal of detail creating a backstory, seriously, there's a whole bunch of story content out there. What I would really like to see is an actual in-game campaign in which you can follow one of the three main empires on their quests within this storyline. Another little want of mine is to have a campaign constructor. That would be amazing. If these things were there, a 10/10 game.
It's pretty much impossible to get bored of Sins, each game turns out differently from the last. But if, however, you somehow manage to get bored, there's but one thing for that: mods. This game has a Star Trek mod, and subsequently has my seal of approval.
This game is amazing. I myself have had endless hours of fun with Sins, and reccommend this entirely to everybody. Get this game right now.

This game is amazing, I love it and here's why:
Before I get started, play this game with a controller! It's easier, it feels more natural and it's overall just much more fun.
Playing this game is like a magical experience. Every area you visit has unique aesthetics, completely new types of enemies and a unique soundtrack. They all feel different in a very natural way, but it never gets boring. On the contrary, they made me excited to see what else was there to be found, I wanted to explore every new area, look in every tunnel and unravel all the mysteries that seem to only be awaiting me. All the for- and background layers, the changing music and fitting enemy and battle sounds for each enemy makes this game feel so alive and such a great experience.
While it looks cute and all, it is actually quite a hard game. The game is forgiving in some ways, you have multiple lives and the more you fight, the more you can heal. Also, when you return to the place of your death you can collect the money you had. As such, the game is not only focused on exploration, but also on combat. That being said, the boss fights (and there are many) are hard. You will need to study all of their moves and attacks and try again and again. While I didn't mind having to try many times, which I instead found exciting and very rewarding when you finally make it, getting to the place the boss is at every time is very annoying, because there are very few savepoints and they can be quite far away.
Backtracking areas isn't annoying, because of the fast travel system and every time you revisit, you find the places that you previously couldn't visit, but now can because of a newly acquired ability.
I'm currently 20 hours in the game, so take my words with a grain of salt, because I'm nowhere close to finishing. That being said, the game is quite cheap for the hours of gameplay you can get out of it.
Also, what I didn't like to some extend was the mysteriousness of the game. Sometimes you find statues that just have cryptic sayings that you totally can't make sense of. And what is the point of having them in the game, if you gain nothing whatsoever from reading their inscription. Also, while I think there is a greater story in the world and some NPCs make brief mentions to the past, I'm still eagerly waiting to actually be told more of a story.

Even though it may be considered the weakest of the bioshock games, this second instalment is still a strong choice for those seeking a story-driven first person shooting experience. Although the pricetag is hefty, and the game is far from perfect, this second visit to rapture is still full of surprises and twists, and help shape the reality that was Rapture to those who enjoyed the first game. On the other hand, this should not be a person's first foray into the Bioshock universe, but rather a pleasant addition to the lore surrounding Andrew Ryan's submerged city.

This will allow you to take on pirates (or become a pirate) and loot your fallen enemies.  Trade, fight, loot, upgrade, repeat until you have enough for a bigger ship and repeat the process.  This is much what I imagine Han Solo and Chewbacca did before running into Luke and Ben in Mos Eisley.  Do you want a Han Solo simulator or a Firefly simulator?  This is pretty much it.  I also enjoy the amount of choices the devs chose to throw at the player.  For almost every mission you have multiple options of how to proceed, be it violently or non-violently.  I have yet to see how many of these choices play out, but Rebel Galaxy has made a very good impression in my first few hours of gameplay.

So. Rebel Galaxy.
If you're wondering if Rebel Galaxy is a fun game to get, well, here's three stories to help convince you.
Scenario One: Laughing at Bandits.
I took a mission to pick up a dead drop, pretty simple stuff. Fly to the location, use my tractor beam to pick up a box from the middle of nowhere, and then return it to the station I left from. Simple stuff.
Well, apparently some folks didn't take too kindly to it.
I come under attack from a wave of pirate fighters, but due to their.. ahh.. 'Lack of tactical prowess' they all come in at different points across the ice field. I start burning away, because there's no need for a fight, am I right guys? Besides, I have a small network of flak cannons (Secondary Weapon System), so these fighters can't do crap anyways.
Well, one fighter (let's call him Jim-Bob) decides to go for it anyways.
One fighter against a Corvette. Bad choice Jim-Bob. About 10 seconds later, Jim-Bob is a frozen corpse in space, and seconds before my warp drive fully kicks in, all the bandits can hear is a "suck it, nerds!" across the comms.
Scenario 2: I'm a Big D*** Hero
Not too long after that, I take a job to protect some miners. Might come under attack from some more bandits, maybe the same crew I ran into on the last job, no big deal, easy pickings. I head on out, enjoy the sights for a few seconds, before my ship tells me some unfriendly locals show up. Alright, no big deal, some fighters and a pair of gunships. Still in my old Corvette, with the flak system installed, so no big deal, they all get wiped out, I get paid, everyone's happy, the miners all lived, I got paid, played the hero, good stuff. I do my usual heading on out, accelerate to sublight, and hit the warp engine, all cool-like.
I feel the kick-back of the warp engine, and am ready to sail off towards my next job...
Except I forgot to keep an eye on the asteroid off my port side, and make it about ten feet before dropping out of warp, where I embarrasingly have to boost past the asteroid, re-accelerate, and then hit the warp drive again.
I can still hear the miners laughing...
Scenario 3: Lightning in Space. Not so Pretty
So, easy job. Eliminate this particularly nasty bandit who's been pillaging and marauding his way across the system. Easy-peasy according to my mission log, thanks to some recent upgrades after a few.. less-than-stellar performances on my next story mission. Head on out there, and as I come out of warp, I notice this beautiful blue nebula, with a bit of lightning. I think it's some really nice decoration for a pirate base, kinda fits the motif.
About three seconds later, my computer's lovely voice tells me that my port shield is down, and as a I look at the display, not only is my port shield down, so are my fore and starboard shields. Right as the enemy enters weapons range. Beautiful, simply beautiful. That easy mission turned out to be not so easy. A wave of pirate strike craft, and a Corvette greet my in my old Corvette. I've been looking to upgrade to a nice frigate, but that doesn't exactly help me right now, I'm still in this now-battered heap after fending off most of the wave as the enemy Corvette, my target, starts speeding away.
Thankfully, sublight boosters help me catch up to weapons range, which, thanks to my shiny new Proton Cannons, is about three to four times longer than my old standard probably-shooting-a-space-potato broadsides. Well, apparently he notices how my guns are about to fire on him, and he turns towards me, not that far off my starboard side, when my helpful computer notifies me of another problem
"Starboard shields down"
Well, that's just perfect. the shields I NEED to be up are down, thanks to the space-lightning the pirates conveniently chose to hide in. I'm still kind of battered, a few scorch marks and maybe a piece or two of my hull missing, but this is the one guy I positively, absolutely, have to destroy. I open up with a salvo of Proton fire, and close range to get my Scatter Turrets (run of the mill space-laser "machine gun" turrets) to fire on him, hopefully preventing a bit of shield recharge. The gambit works, and despite a few more scorch marks to my starboard side, the enemy Corvette explodes, and the people of the system are safe once more!
And I don't get caught on an asteroid this time, letting me feel like an actual good guy. Until I explode next, that is
tl;dr: Buy the thing. Seriously. I would've paid 40$ for this, and they're selling it for a sale price of 18, and a regular price of 20.

This is mostly just for the devs because if improvements are made to the game it could be a lot better. So if you don't feel like reading.  This is still your basic civ game with great new features, but why did you get rid of great existing features from the civ series?
All this game is a sci fi civilization with dumbed down gameplay.  With that said.
cons
- diplomacy is horrible.  this is a redundant comment but it needs to be fixed.  why do i need to be allies with somebody to trade anything useful? I have literally won entire games in civ V with diplomacy and trade, for example by controlling essentially the world's supply of cotton, selling it to other civs, and making 1000 gpt.
-with that said why are basic resources essentially useless now? they're tile improvements great, but no one cares.  in civ V you would start wars over luxury resources because of its economic value.  I considered that a significant part of civ and now its gone.
-The affinities are cool but shouldnt govern the game.  Just because i choose supremacy doesnt mean im a warlord.  i choose supremacy because i started next to firaxite, and any AI in the game shouldnt be hostile just because I have a different affinity.  I personally think each affinity should give you certain bonuses and thats it
-wonders are never worth the time, they're slightly better than their building counterparts but nowhere near what wonders used to be worth.  in Civ V I declared war on someone that built the eiffel tower before me.  In this game i really dont care i just build the building.  The only wonder I kind of care about is the Resurrection device which is okay.
-espionage is a waste of time.  i dont like to make excuses but its honestly impossible to do anything above tier three espionage or whatever its called.  it takes too long to perform espionage, by the time you finish something (20 turns later) the city's intrigue fell considerably so the operation ends up being unsuccessful.  In my opinion its better just to milk the headquarters bonuses.
-quests.  they're redundant and unfruitful and time consuming.  make a variety/ implement random quests that appear once every few games with better rewards or get rid of them.
same
-culture is exactly the same, bonuses are okay about what you would expect in my opinion.  the third tier should be better though. its not too motivating as it is
-health is just happiness, again the same
-energy is the same
- military strategy is very dumbed down from previous civs but personally i dont mind.  it works and you have the basics, but they compensated with some new features in affinity's military
pros
-satellites were a great improvement, their military applications are game changing
-the tech web is great and makes sense.  the affinities are scattered but you can find the different regions (satellites, computing, genetics, etc)
-speaking of the tech web if you just focus on your affinity and/or victory quests and that's it you are missing out.  the best techs with the best units and wonders in the game are affinity/victory neutral, so if you are thinking everything is too bland i think that's you're mistake.  the planet carver is a personal favorite of mine and I make damn sure I get get all the resources i need to deploy about two or three over a battlefield and keep one or two sleeping in a city for emergencies.  it's become a key part of my strategy, and I have won a couple of game changing battles this way so keep an eye open for these features/oppurtunities in this civ.
on a final note keep in mind they designed this game so you would have to relearn how to play.  you can't keep you're old strategies.  i had to play a couple of quick games on medium to figure it out and i think that investment made me find out what i like about this game.  Does this game need improvements? yes.  Is it a waste of time? no, its a completely different style civ and im glad they aren't just being redudant/milking the civ series while they can.

Honestly, this is the worst RPG I have ever played. I checked the Wiki and managed to get about halfway through the game and about 1/3 done with all side-quests. I've simply given up on this game; I was going to try to 100% it, but I simply can't. It's too bad.
For starters, the writing is incredibly bad. Rush Sykes is, by far, not only the most one-dimensional main character but also is by far the most annoying in any video game I've ever played. His only motivation is his sister; of course, it's charismatic and very noble that he wants to go so far to save his sister, but that's it. No other interests, nothing in his life. Hell, none of the other characters really have anything going on in their lives either. It's all "for Athlum" this or "for Rush's sister Irina" that. All the characters are incredibly flat and unbelievable; usually I'm able to find a character I love, but I simply couldn't here. I cared for absolutely nobody during my time playing. They all seemed to be pawn's for my battles, and that was it. Nothing more.
You have no control over any of the characters during combat - you can specify what sort of action you want them to take (heal, spells, skills, etc), but ultimately you aren't able to change the order these things happen in. This is very frustrating - for instance, I know one of my characters has an attack that can silence enemies, but I can't have him actually use that spell. It's randomized whether he'll use it or not. It's seriously moments like these that lead me to, not only dying, but getting game over over and over again. The game is punishing me for not being able to control my damn characters. You also can't customize their equipment; you're completely limited to changing the main character's equipment throughout.
To be honest, the world was fascinating at first. I enjoyed how this world did not have the standard human/elf/dwarf paradigm that many RPGs seem to have nowadays. The races constructed here are very unique and unlike anything I'd ever seen in an RPG before. It was truly a nice breath of fresh air. However, I realized that this world feels practically dead. The only real life that seems to be going on is the beasts prowling around the linearly frustrating dungeons or the vastly open, yet still dead, landscapes. NPCs in cities seem to just stand there and really don't offer anything intelligent, or exciting, to say. All the cities in the game really don't have anything going on - they're simply there for getting side quests and for buying new equipment, but really nothing is going on. It all just really felt dead, like they were simply there, which is disappointing. The point of an RPG is to escape into some sort of fantasy world (and typically to save it), but what's the point of trying to escape into a world that doesn't even remotely feel real?
All in all, I can't recommend this game. I bought it during the Steam Sale (I believe for less than $5) and didn't believe it was worth it for me. If you want a game that gives you no control over it's characters, is cumbersome, very bland, and has a good amount of content (but is only available at a limited time - after the halfway point a lot of the quests close), then this game may be for you. It, unfortunately, wasn't for me.

This game got a lot of hate when it first came out thanks to the serious issues it had with player freedom. The first 15-20 hours are spent in a series of extremely linear areas where you can't even choose your party members. First impressions aren't great.
But after the questionable opening chapters the game really opens up. It gives you lots of places to explore and vicious monsters to fight(or run away from while shouting NOPE!). The combat system is interesting as it's a combination of turn based and real time mechanics and works very well.
One advantage of the linear opening chapters is that it gives the game a chance to develop a very good story. It revolves around beings known as Fal'Cie. Imagine if the Reapers from Mass Effect were powered by magic and you're kinda on the right track. Won't go further as I'll probably cross into spoiler territory. Since this is Final Fantasy you've still got melodrama, cheesy dialogue and annoying characters but nothing unbearable. They probably could've found a better way to introduce the world and the story that didn't involve drip feeding it to you for 20 hours but there we go.
The many hours you'll have to spend to get to the "real" game will probably put a lot of people off. But if you can push through it you'll find a very entertaining game

I remember awhile back playing this game as a demo and loving the general way it worked. It was a fairly new approach to the usual physics-based puzzle genre, and with the price from the sale how could I refuse?
The game has great bits. You play as the main character named Tiny, whom inherited apparently some pants (underwear) from his grandpa. Sadly, his brother/cousin/related person Big had stolen them, and fleed to a desert with something about qualms for it's ancient power.
The game puzzles work entirely off of physics, and as such utilize a device pack that Tiny has. With it, you can cut, grapple, and rocket anything you please to complete puzzles. The music is pretty nice too, with the ability to switch BGM's with N and collect more in the game. There are a multitude of ways to complete a single puzzle usually for the more creative.
LIke a great side though, the game also has a bit of a downside or two. For one, the game is short. 6 stages to be exact (Excluding tutorial level), though fun all the way. The game also has a habit of not notifying you if you messed up a puzzle, for those puzzles that are more of a one-solution rather then a multiple.
If you find it inteesting, download the demo. It gives enough to work with to get a feel for how the laser tools work. Like it? Then buy it, it's only like...6 bucks right now isn't it? Maybe 3?

You survived the radioactive wasteland of Fallout. You crafted a rough-shod bunker out of dirt and leaves in 7-days to die. You managed to log off of Rust for 5 minutes without losing everything you worked so hard for, for 9 straight hours. None of that has prepared you to survive just 5 days in
.
You start the game with just a small group of survivors in the war-torn country of possibly Russia. I'm only going by what the names of the characters resemble. I didn't actually read anything. Your starting point is a bombed-out "home" (In quotes because it's a damned big home) in which you have multiple rooms to clear for the purpose of scavaging and having space to build things such as rain-water filters, beds and cook stoves. Building these items requires parts such as wood, scrap and gears(?). Some of which you will find in your shelter on day one, the rest you have to scavange from other locations.
The mechnanics of the game is simply point-and-click. The game is divided into two parts; Day and night. The daytime is when you build up your shelter (protect it with patched up holes, upgrade your cook-stove or work bench, build furniture to make people happier), cook food, apply medicine or various other things to keep your group happy/healthy. Nighttime is dedicated mostly to scavaging, but also allows to to allocate who gets rest, and who guards your shelter. The day is divied into ten-minute increments and you are allowed 12 hours per day/night. Everything happens in "real-time" but that is a bit of a misnomer as it takes ten minutes to take 5 steps or to climb a ladder. Double-clicking allows you to run to your destination, which speeds you up my a factor of two, and I have yet to see any downside to doing this (i.e. fatigue). Clicking on piles of rubbles, doors, bars, etc. allows you to perform a contextual based action such as sift through rubble, open/close doors, pick locks or pry open doors with a crowbar, saw through metal bars, etc.
Your goal, from what I have seen so far, is to simply survive. Something we have all done in countless games before. Only his time, it is brutal, gritty, real, and unforgiving. You are constantly battling hunger, exhaustion, sickness, depression, wounds and more. Balancing the act of taking care of your group, as well as sending people out to scavange (so that you CAN take care of your group) becomes an excercise of patience, frustration, and futility. You will lose people, you will get frustrated, you will die, and you will hate the game as you click "try again".
Again, just point and click. It's simple enough without taking anything away from the game.
Gritty, pencil-drawn-esque style artwork really works here.The game is a bit of a 2-D sidescroller, s don't expect a whole lot.
This is one area where I was a bit let down. The sound design leaves a lot to be desired, when using the radio. The sound is alright until then.
So what is it that makes this game unique? It's the fact that the game actually makes you FEEL the consequences of your actions. Remember that old couple who's home you raided and who's food you stole? Your group will. And they will talk about how aweful it was. Return to thier home? Now they are dead because YOU took thier food and medicine. You will not feel good about it. Niether will your group, as actions like this will affect them in a negative way. It's up to you to decide how you survive, and what kind of person you will be. Just remember: you will not survive by being the nice guy.

One of the most memorable momements I've had playing any video game was in Crysis.
I was on a boat, heading to an extraction point, when I heard the dooming blades of a helicopter off in the distance. Knowing I could go no further without taking care of it, I snuck onto the land, and hid behind two of the enemy in some brush. I scanned the horizion for dreaded enemy, before spotting it in the air, turning towards my direction. Now was my chance! I whipped out my trusty RPG, and fired a shot aimed directly at the cockpit. Before the two soldiers in front of me had time to comprehend that a freaking RPG was shot behind them, they were mowed down in my swarm of bullets. As the second soldier breathed his last, I saw that my rocket has found its mark. BOOM! There was just a thick black cloud of smoke where the chopper once was, I had defeated my enemy.
Or so I had thought. From the ashes, the helicopter, barely intact emerged. I went to fire anoher rocket, but I had none. Frantically, I dodged from tree to bush to tree, ignoring the hail of bullets and rockets from my enemy. I searched the small camp in and out in hopes of finding at least one RPG round, but there were none to be found. Ever so stealthily, I slowly made for a dense, small island in the distance. For what seemed like forever, I crawled to the island. As I reached sanctuary, I began to take damage. I had been spotted. Frustrated, I knew that I would hide no more, an I would face my opponent on this tiny island. I dodged from tree to tree, only firing inbetween the helicopter's bursts of fire. I was down to just my shotgun, blasting away, ready to accept my fate, when the chopper caught fire. It began to spin out of controll, and crashed into the river next to me. I had won.
If you have read all of this, hats off to you. Now go buy Crysis. It won't disappoint.

Still great graphics with GeDoSaTo, really gorgeous environments, decent English dub (better than the Japanese for my taste) and a good story, for Final Fantasy standards at least. Contrary to what you may have heard, one you can understand without looking into the in-game codex, if you have any attention span at all.
The real misstep the game makes is the glacial gameplay pacing. It is too busy telling its story and showing off its creative environments to have you stop and smell the roses for a bit. For the first 20 hours you run through linear corridors towards the next cutscene. Final Fantasy X had the same structure for the first half of the game, but it gave you a village or town to explore here and there and NPCs to talk to. Even if that was just an illusion of freedom and the game was just tapping its foot for you to get back on the railroad, it did a good job to make the leash feel not as tight as it is here.
Same issue with the combat system, it starts out barebones (and in the first 2 hours completely pointless because you don't have a progression system yet) and boring and only slowly grows more complex, engaging and challenging.
Then suddenly you're over 20 hours in and the game shrugs its shoulders and dumps you in a vast open field full with tough enemies and multiple ways to go. Exploration! Adventure! Optional bosses! It's too bad many players never made it this far. And while the game generally nails atmosphere in most places, some of the character drama is very overwrought, melodramatic and tedious, especially Hope's little arc. So I can't blame anyone for giving up out of exasperation. Still, I do think the game is underrated and suffered from people parroting the opinions of others who also haven't really played it - I was guilty of that as well for a long time.

I just got this I can already tell that it's going to be one my all time favourites.
A lot of modern games glorify this post apocalyptic existence whereas this one brings it more down to earth and adds the humanity aspect back into it. The reality is that this game actually does very little, it finds its complexity in its simplicity.
This War of Mine certainly doesn't hold your hand through, it gives you 3 people and a house and says "go." Whatever happens is random or it's because of what you've done previously.
It definitely makes you question your morals. We say that each life is as valuable as the next, but sometimes you simply can't save everybody, and surprise surprise, it's primarily your choice who lives and who doesn't. It's definitely a "hate the player not the game" scenario because ultimately, everything is down to you. Do you give your medicine to that ill kid? Do you kill the eldery couple for food? Do you trade that pistol you spent days collecting parts to build? It's all questions that you'd think to be deeply unsatisfying considering that no choice is "right." You don't get points, trophies or even a pat on the back...you get to live another day, where you'll have whole new challenges and moral dilemas thrown at you.
I highly advise anybody to get this game. What it somewhat lacks it action it makes up for in immersiveness.

Being an old Magic player, this game feels like an insult to the original card game for multiple reasons. I'm just gonna put the ones which are the worst in my opinion:
- The online is pretty much broken; many times you look for a match and the game doesn't find anything after several tries.
- A ranked system has been introduced and is one of the worst I've ever seen: every time you win or loose a match, you gain or loose 1 point, and if you win you earn 20 coins to unlock the card packs; if the opponent leaves the game / ragequits (and it happens more than often) you are either forced to play against AI, either quit the match and loose the coins and the rank point. That's just dumb. If the opponent quits, the match must be stopped, and the other player must win the game. Why should I keep playing a match against the AI if it was supposed to be an online (ranked) match? Makes no sense. And what if the AI beats me then? Cause it's not that stupid after all. What then? I end up loosing the match, the coins, the rank point, and even time I guess? Great. No seriously, there are no excuses for this.
- The game is apparently free to play, and lets the player buy the cards with the in-game coins. There's only a few problems about this.. the standard decks look bad and weak compared to the decks I was used to see and use in previous games and even in real life when I was playing this game. Another fact linked to this is that to open a pack of cards you need 150 coins; you gain 20 coins per win on online matches, and there's the option to buy the coins with real money too. Now, what's the trick about all this? They made the decks very weak to make people open as more packs as possible to always find better cards and use them; but to open them without paying real money, you need 8 wins online to open just 1 pack; and in that pack you find 6 cards, which maybe you won't even use! Or maybe you will use 1 or 2, if you are lucky.
In the end you have 2 choises: play the game tons of hours and gain tons of wins to open tons of card packs to finally build a decent deck, like we all were used at old times; or you pay, and get the cards faster, because that's what the game wants you to do. They made these decks so weak and the cards so hard to get to make people buy them and have them faster, because if you don't do like that, you are gonna be dead before you'll be able to build a good deck in this game.
Feels like these Magic videogames are getting worse every year. Oh, last thing.. Why the hell did they totally remove the previous years cards from the game? Many of them were awesome cards, and they are just disappeared. And I'm not talking about 2005 or 2006, I've not seen 1 card yet even from 2013.
This game has all the potential to be the best card game in the world.. But looks like this potential is totally being wasted.

Egosoft has still not come through with the patches they promised.  The trading is completly bugged and if one thing is done wrong it flat out does not work. It has a few very cool festures like how to scan for long range.  the station landing feels very dry and unpolished as well as the fact that your ship can be attacked while you are docked and can plainly see it on the landing pad. All in all, I wouldn't recomend this game to anyone until Egosoft fixes most, if not all of the problems with it.  Personally, I feel that I have been scammed by Egosoft and they should be ashamed of themselves for even releasing this game.

I don't usually write of reviews, but... this game has disappointed me so much.
Ok first: the history. This game is the "latest" from Egosoft, which had somewhat of a cult following by a growing community based on the X-Universe. Concept evolved a bit. At the start, you could manage only a single ship, and over the diverse iterations the game had, you could control the entire universe, pilot anything you could see in the game, board other ships, force other pilots to leave theirs so you could add them to your fleet. You could build ships, weapons, shields, food, manage the economy of the entire game... or not, if you wanted to. This was a plain good example of a sandbox.
Not that the game was any way near perfect. From what I've seen, there was little changes in the core "code" and the multiple possibilities added in the game over a period of more than a dozen year were added as time went by. Also, core "concepts" of the game remained broken, like trading, like the awful amount of submenus you had to go through for simple actions, like the amount of micro needed to manage a semi-decent sized fleet, like the awful tutorials (few games have tutorials that players complain of not even being able to start), and pathetic "early" game hell (your starting ships usually are the ones needing the most skills to pilot, a choice a load of people found dubious at best - even then, there is a load of things that need to be learned for the game to work and the game barely explains any of it). Some sell this as "good game with harsh learning curve", but it's not really learning when the game expects you to know things it does not tell you. It did get a little better with the latest iterations of the game. The game was still harsh and unforgiving, but you actually could manage somewhat.
The community was very active, modders changed and influenced the game, as with the concept of scripting nearly everything open to them, it was very much possible to rewrite most of the universe, ships, weapons, trading and so on...
What did players want for this last edition ?
Simply a rework of the engine making the game more intuitive. More beautiful graphics. An expanded universe. A decent UI. Some other "simple" stuff.
What did they get ?
(Note that I'm voluntarily ignoring the fact I spent half of my "playing time" editing xml, and other bugs.)
They got a game with less possibilities on all aspects of the game. The starting ship cannot be switched and can irrealitiscally take on the whole universe with ease. Your fleet (you can remote control other ships) currently can barely be controlled and built, but the interface for doing so is actually WORSE than before. Before, you had to move through half a dozen text sub-menus to do a simple task. Now, it's half a dozen subscreens. Your own movement : before, it was slow, painfully slow of most ships with decent firepower, but you could alleviate this somewhat by jumping around from a sector to the other side of the universe. This is not possible anymore (jumping) without lengthy micromanagement, but the ship isn't faster as a result, making the game even slower than before. Building stations was cumbersome and annoying, but with mods you could somewhat do something. Now, it's just painfully long, cumbersome, annoying, and more expensive than ever.
About the mini-games, like tailing other ships to speed on lanes... except half of the sectors in the game have no ships in them, so painfully slow at its finest. Another mini-game, each time you put on a subscreen, your copilot (which no one ever asked for) flashes her boobs at you... Bad taste at its finest, again. Yes, that's the minigame. I think. Well. Dunno. I suppose, it's written "trade" on one of the boob screens. The "conversation" minigame, which figures random (and therefore useless) rewards when you have a specific need. The "find people to pilot ship / station / build station / pilot fighter / repair systems / board ship" mini-game, which is the most time-consuming problem ever. If you fight a fleet with a cap ship and 3 fighters, and manage to board the cap ship and capture 2 fighters, you need to have 2 pilots (fighters), 1 captain (for the cap ship), 1 engineer (to repair the cap ship, otherwise you can capture it but it won't move), 1 marine officer (to start the boarding action). Except you have only 4 places in your ship. If you were doing anything like transporting a specialist to a station, finding an architect to build a station, you have even less places to use. Point is, you usually have to go though 2-3 stations and systems to get one guy...
This game was marketed as a "X-universe" game until about a day or so after it got released, after that, the community was told that this was not supposed to be a "rebirth" of the previous game, but another game. However: even forgetting all that you could do earlier and cannot do here, the game is STILL bad enough that you want to run away from it. Funny enough, a game in the same universe, with the same naming schtick, with the same motto, and named "rebirth" is supposed to be a completely different game. To illustrate, the guys from Egosoft are like trying to market Diablo 3 as a game which is not a Diablo-like. Except, they're not marketing diablo 3, they're trying to market a cheaply made copy of diablo 1 with good graphics.
Egosoft does have some history about cleaning up their own mistakes, but here, problem seems to be that the main designer of the company does not seem to have a clue of why his game was "successful" in the first place, that they still did not hire an ergonomist (or maybe they've got an incompetent one, who knows ?), that their marketing service does not understand anything about the concept of "public image", and that they still have no quality checks for bugs in the game (that's been for a dozen years).
Maybe when the company changes enough so this game series gets all this, I'll buy X-Rebirth 3.

This is a good game, but sadly it has to compete with the first game in the Bioshock series, and that's a fight this game just can't win.
Set in the same world (Rapture) as the first game, we now take the role of a prototype Big Daddy. This does not mean you are an unstoppable force, the splicers and other enemies will still make your adventure in rapture a hard one, but not as an enjoyable one. The combat, which was the weakest part of the first game, has not been improved upon. New weapons and such, but not really anything that gets the juices flowing.
The setting is the same, a leaking city under the sea, but you dont get the same feeling of isolation and hopelessness as you did in the first game. It is still a good setting and the world of rapture is nice as always, but it's just missing that magic that the first game brought.
There are some improvements thou, most notably with the hacking system, which was really teadnious in the first game. Also this time around you get a game that actually works on 16:9 monitors and also you get achievements. GFWL is gone, so you dont have that to worry about.
Is it still a recommendation? Yes, yes it is, but only if you are a big fan of the series. It's not nearly as interesting as the first game and it's really sad that they felt the need to put a 2 in the title, since it's more of an expansion than a whole new game.

My Experience:
In total it took me 19 hours to beat the final boss of this game with 65% completion. Each hour was filled with fun exploration, unique enemies and bosses, and an atmosphere that draws you in and makes you want to continue playing.
The progression is flawless, and the gameplay is extremely tight, making me never blame my deaths on anything except myself.
The game was so good that I am planning on completing the game with 100% completion because I'm sure that I missed a lot, including at least 3 full areas, around 5 true ending boss fights, 10+ charms (upgrades), and much superior abilites. This game makes you keep wanting to come back, and I would highly reccomend it to anyone who likes 2D platformers or hack-and-slash games.
Bugs/Glitches:
There are a few bugs however which could be fixed to fully polish the game however. None of them are game breaking, however if fixed it would improve the experience of the game.
First, the VSync doesn't always work properly, as there is often a line about a quarter of the way from the top of the screen if you have it on, especially during cutscenes and longer crystal heart segments. The absolute worst place is the crystal heart area in the Ancient Basin,
where the clipping on the trees is more like static noise than scenery.
Also(SPOILER - This does make the combat easier), the enemy AI gets extremely confused when it repeatedly needs to turn toward the player. If you keep hopping with down-airs on an enemy, while gliding back and forth over their central point, they will get locked turning back in forth, not attacking until you have likely killed them. Even the Hollow Knight falls into this bug.
Overall - Amazing game. The glitches are small but noticable, however both the gameplay and atmosphere quickly make you forget about them.

I remember when I was a little too young to have a job. I played the demo of this game now and then, trying to figure out what it's all about, how to 'level up' in it, where to go... this game is truly unique and separates itself from any strategy RPG I have ever played. Square Enix hit on something really good with this game, and that is the idea of strategic army-like combat. You get party members of all kinds, from simple soldiers to guild mercenaries with special traits/powers and the generals of Athlum, who are undoubtedly some of the most powerful characters I have. These characters are organized in to "unions" which are groups of units on the battlefield. Improving your characters is done through what actions are taken the most by them, so if you have a character using mystic invocations a lot, he/she will improve in his/her mystic invocations (though you can certainly have them learn more than that, depending on the character). There's no real "leveling system", Battle Rank is more of a bounty-like rating based on how well you've done in battles (except that it doesn't decrease), and will affect how tough your enemies will be from there on out. It's mostly about having your characters use what you want them to get better at, and then utilizing those growing skills on the battlefield appropriately, which I really like to grow them!
Here's the catch that separates this from your typical Strategy RPG: They don't act singly. As I mentioned with the union system, they actually act as a group, so you select from 5-6(?) battle commands which vary based on many circumstances (you can see the wiki page for this game for more on that if you're curious, I highly recommend reading up on it before buying to make sure this game is something you'd want! Even try the demo!) You might get a command that says "Attack using Combat Arts" and "Attack using Mystic Arts". Selecting the first would have all units who possess a usable Combat Art use it, unless the AP cost is too high in which case they'll do a normal attack. The second would have all units who know a mystic art (not all units can be mystic users! Your main character, Rush, however, can learn all mystic arts throughout the story... I won't spoil how, that's what the wiki is for) use the one they know that doesn't go over the AP budget for that turn; Those without mystic arts would do a normal attack. Many factors influence what option shows up the most, or with the results you want, and it's these factors on the battlefield and in the character's training that make strategy all the more important. Organizing your unions appropriately, with formations that match the role you have in mind for them, and proper battlefield wit when the tide starts turning, make this game quite insane.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for something more... unique in the genre of Strategy RPG. First of all, I recommend reading the wiki, watching some Youtube videos, and playing the demo before you buy. This game isn't for the faint of heart, but it also isn't overly punishing (unless you just try to zerg everything without any forethought at all to your foe's strengths and your own weaknesses) I can safely say, that this is the most unique Strategy RPG I have played to date, on Steam and off Steam.
