From the first riffs of the soundtrack, to the thundering broadsides in your first battle, Rebel Galaxy grabs hold of your inner "space cowboy" and never lets go.
Honestly, not many games give you the full experience of being an outlaw like Rebel Galaxy. Sure, other games has the long arm of the law chase you around, have you be loathed by the locals, and generally make life less than pleasant as it should be. So, what was missing? The soundtrack. This is hands down one in the top 20 game soundtracks I have had the pleasure of listening to while I played a game.
As for the game itself, it is pretty straightforward. Take missions, get credits, earn/lose reputation, and along the way solve the mystery of what happened to your Aunt. While it can get grindy, especially for those wanting to be outlaws and getting that initial "bad reputation" you need, there is a fair amount of variety to the missions, as well as stuff to find, kill, mine, trade, etc. You can also customize your ship in a plethora of ways, from weapons and armor, to ship class itself. From gunship to dreadnought, there's a ship for just about everyone.
Combat is pretty straightforward, you use devastating broadsides on larger ships to tear them apart, while using your turrets to add to the carnage, or use them to pop pesky fighters. With the customized loadouts, you can make your ship a straight up brawler, or make it a long range ship that deals damage from afar without having to worry about heavy plating. There are also support abilities that can further refine your battle plan, or round out a particular weakness.
The map is pretty expansive, and the economy reacts to events, so raiding a convoy or breaking a siege will also affect prices of goods that can be traded. This affords you the player lots of ways to play, from being a miner to a no guts no glory pirate.
My only gripes are that it can get grindy, but I really don't mind. The soundtrack and visuals clearly make the downtime less unpleasant, and the long warps around the map have given me lots of places to visit along the way. For someone that enjoys being a space privateer, Rebel Galaxy is a game I am glad that I did not miss out on.

Still great graphics with GeDoSaTo, really gorgeous environments, decent English dub (better than the Japanese for my taste) and a good story, for Final Fantasy standards at least. Contrary to what you may have heard, one you can understand without looking into the in-game codex, if you have any attention span at all.
The real misstep the game makes is the glacial gameplay pacing. It is too busy telling its story and showing off its creative environments to have you stop and smell the roses for a bit. For the first 20 hours you run through linear corridors towards the next cutscene. Final Fantasy X had the same structure for the first half of the game, but it gave you a village or town to explore here and there and NPCs to talk to. Even if that was just an illusion of freedom and the game was just tapping its foot for you to get back on the railroad, it did a good job to make the leash feel not as tight as it is here.
Same issue with the combat system, it starts out barebones (and in the first 2 hours completely pointless because you don't have a progression system yet) and boring and only slowly grows more complex, engaging and challenging.
Then suddenly you're over 20 hours in and the game shrugs its shoulders and dumps you in a vast open field full with tough enemies and multiple ways to go. Exploration! Adventure! Optional bosses! It's too bad many players never made it this far. And while the game generally nails atmosphere in most places, some of the character drama is very overwrought, melodramatic and tedious, especially Hope's little arc. So I can't blame anyone for giving up out of exasperation. Still, I do think the game is underrated and suffered from people parroting the opinions of others who also haven't really played it - I was guilty of that as well for a long time.

This game is getting entirely too much hate; I'm fairly certain there's a bandwagon going on here.  Personally, I quite enjoy it.
The Affinity system is excellent, in my humble opinion; the fact that the route you take through technology controls your Affinity ensures that you're probably going to see pretty big differences among factions with different Affinities, and not just in having different stats.  A Supremacy player is naturally going to have satellites coming out their ears, Purity players are going to be plowing over everything with farms and terrascapes, and any attempt to invade a Harmony player will result in choking to death in masses of Miasma.  The aesthetics are fantastic, as well, and the building tension between opposed Affinities adds a ton of flavor to the game.
The tech web is a great change from the tree.  Unlike the classic tree, with the web you can't really just shoot in a general direction.  It's entirely possible to beeline a far-away tech you REALLY want at the expense of closer techs, and the structure ties in extremely well with the Affinity system.
Virtues are basically deeper but narrower Social Policies.  While some trees (Prosperity and Industry) are objectively better, the fact of the matter is that all four are quite useful - and since you're rewarded for focusing AND for picking and choosing, it's extremely variable and once again allows a lot of options.
Sponsors - I have to give a little credit to the criticism here, if only because there are too few.  Eight?  Really?  Mods solve the problem easily, but that's no excuse to have -that- few.  One of the issues many seem to have is a lack of distinctiveness.  This, however, is simply not the case, as all the sponsors do have distinct personalities.  A large part of the problem is that, being fictional, you can't automatically look at Kozlov and go, "Hey, that guy's an expansionist jerk."  Likewise the lack of fancy backgrounds seems to be off-putting to a lot of people - hardly a major criticism, but some variety would be nice.  Despite the limitations, the leaders are believable (in stark contrast to the living stereotypes of SMAC) and interesting characters in their own right.
Trade Routes - Yes, the patch hit trade routes pretty badly, they're not game-breakingly overpowered anymore.  However, once you get out of early game, foreign trade routes will consistently benefit you and the system works quite nicely.  Also, there are stations that provide lots of unique output if you don't care for foreign trade.  There's really not much to say here, it's trade.
Aliens - People complain the aliens are not dangerous enough.  I don't understand this.  Early to early middle game, angry aliens are death incarnate (especially those freaking Sea Dragons).  Mid-game, the tougher ones are still a serious threat that need to be dealt with.  Sure, late-game you can trounce them easily, but you're packing apocalyptic firepower at that point.  The aliens are a neat addition and are frankly much more interesting than barbarians.
AI and Diplomacy - Okay, yeah, they kinda dropped the ball.  Or, more precisely, left it where it was in Civ V.  It's nothing to write home about, but at worst it's kind of annoying.  The Favors system definitely needs an overhaul, if only to get the AI to quite offering them.  Advice: if the AI offers a favor, they're probably willing to cough up energy if you make a counter-offer.  The lack of luxury resources takes away some degree of diplomacy - at the same time, the Affinity system means you may very well have buckets of a resource you aren't using.  A Supremacy player will have little use for Xenomass, so you might as well become Space Saudi Arabia and export it, after all.
Orbital layer - YES.  This was an excellent addition that opens up a lot of options.  You can add resources with Weather Controllers and Fabricators, ramp up culture with Holomatrices, remove or add Miasma with Repulsors and Condensers, and, most importantly, rain down ORBITAL LASER SPACE DEATH on your hapless opponents, among many other options.  Seriously, these things add a surprisingly huge layer of depth to the strategic game, especially since they can't share area-of-effect.  I cannot wait to see this expanded on.
Units - The upgrade system is admittedly a bit lackluster; at the same time, by the end of the game you end up with surprisingly specialized (or general-use, take your pick) units.  It does upset me that artillery does not naturally fire over terrain, but that's my only major problem.  Some of the Affinity unique units could use a bit more specialness in terms of abilities, but even as-is they're usually well worth spending resources on.  I never could find a use for the Aegis, but the LEV Tank and LEV Destroyer swiftly won a special place in my heart.
Victories - The Affinity victories are a fantastic idea with decent execution; while they can be monotonous, they still operate quite differently (Promised Land is probably going to result in some major conflict if enough land is taken up).  More importantly, they provide a -target-.  Both as a gameplay device and as flavor, this is excellent.  Instead of an abstract victory, you are presented with a very real threat to either you or your ideology.  Hutama over there isn't "winning" a "cultural victory," he's building a freaking Mind Flower to ASSIMILATE YOUR BRAIN.  You had darn well better stop him!
Tl;dr: Extremely fun game with a lot to set it apart from Civ V.  Its biggest flaws are the lack of leader variety and the AI and diplomacy problems carried over from V.  It's a diamond in the rough, but it's still a diamond.

I give it a strong 8/10, definitely worth a play if you haven't yet!

I`m sure all of us have seen anti-hype videos by the TotalBiscuits and Jim Sterlings of the world. It seems that in the modern era of games it is more important than ever to be skeptical about big budget releases. Yet despite watching all the dissapointing or just straight up broken AAA games come out over the last year or so, I couldn`t get off the hype train when it came to Bioshock "Remastered". I remember waiting anxiously on day 1 for Ryan to make his speech and reveal Rapture once more in HD... only to find out that the song used in that scene was missing.
Bioshock "Remastered" is a mess. The launch of the game was bad and while the latest patch fixed some of the major issues with it, the game still has very obvious bugs that haven`t been adressed at all. For now i`ll list what problems have been fixed so far in my playthrough. After that, i`ll list the issues i`ve found so far that haven`t been adressed. I`ll keep updating this review with the more problems I find as I go through the game.
-We finally have a proper options menu. You can now adjust your FOV from 75-130.
-Music in the intro is working
-Death animations for splicers and objects reacting to getting hit now run at 60 fps, unlike the slideshows from the original Bioshock
-Game settings don`t reset every time you launch the game anymore.
-Certain lines repeat. For example, when you get the first plasmid and you hear two splicers talk over you. Their lines play but they get repeated, which overlaps with the Little Sister`s lines shortly afterwards. Another example being when Atlas talks about the sisters for the first time. After you watch the Big Daddy kill the splicer, his line about the big daddy repeats.
-You HAVE to put on VSync. If you turn it off, the first scene with the spider splicer will be a mess of black blocks flashing in the screen. The game will also go insane once you take the elevator and reach the top. The textures will turn blurry and stretch all over the place.
-Mouse sensitivity in second Little Sister scene. For some reason, when i lowered my weapons during this encounter, my sensitivity went up like crazy. I had to turn it down from 7 to 2 just to get a decent amount of control. After that scene was over, sensitivity went back to normal.
-Oversized weapon models...? Not sure if this was intentional or just something that came with the patch (how ironic). I don`t remember the gun models being this huge before the patch so 2K might want to work on that.
But hey, you never know. It took a few weeks after the announcement of a patch for it to actually roll out and even then they missed quite a few things. Hell, plenty of people are still reporting getting crashes every hour or so. Funnily enough, my copy of the original game never EVER crashed and yet it was with this "remaster" that it finally happened. I can only hope 2K rolls out another patch but this is a big publisher we`re talking about. May Rapture help us all. Now, i`ll leave you with one of my favourite quotes from the man himself, Andrew Ryan.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

In short, everything wrong with the game (details below):
1.Boring, uninspired, repetitive puzzles
2.No proper plot
3.The games is FULL of bugs both literal and figurative to the point of being unplayable
4.Most puzzles are just a waste of time
5.Cannot save at will, also if you start another puzzle before finishing the last -> all progress lost
6.SO overpriced
Details:
1. The "puzzles" are mostly searching for specific objects in a room full of objects (example: toy animals all around the room -> find the bear, the cat and the penguin). I thought at first that this was a one-time puzzle, but apparently 80% of the "puzzles" in this game are exactly that. There are 5-6 "rearrange the squares to make a picture" puzzles and maybe 3-4 "find the differences in the images" puzzles, which were my favourite. Finally, there were 2 nearly impossible puzzles with no hints and no instructions, so it was a matter of wasting time trying to make every configuration possible to find the right one. Finally, the most frustrating puzzles were the "find 30 coconuts or cans or bottles" games where you had to run around the map for 20 minutes to find all the objects. This was by far the longest part. These puzzles felt like the game devs were just stalling to make you feel like you didn't just spend 8$ on a game that had zero effort put into it.
2. The plot was really thin. Crashed on an island, for some reason I have to complete weird puzzles, there are houses and mannequins on most of the islands for no reason.
3. Bugs....
Literal: Do not play this game if you have a fear of bugs, especially spiders. The "find these animals" searches I   mentioned include oversized bugs.
Figurative/game bugs: This games is almost unplayable. You cannot even walk up stairs, you have to sort of jump and try to make it to the top. A lot of puzzles have to be restarted because the last object is non-existant or cannot be clicked because of some strange bug in the game. You
4. Like I said, most of the puzzles are "collect 20 of these things" on a huge map where it is impossible to find everything without wasting 20-30 minutes and using several hints. It feels like the puzzles were simply made to waste the player's time.
5. Moreover, you cannot save progress except for "autosaves" in the game. If you start another puzzle without completing the first, you lose all progress in the first. That means if you collect 20/25 objects you need and accidentally or intentionally start another puzzle, the objects don't stay in your "inventory" they simply go back to where you found them and you have to restart everything.
6. Save your 8-9$ for something else. So not worth your money.

The game itself isn't bad. It's a fun action RPG in the Tolkein universe, so I was sold right away. You get to choose one of three characters, a man, a dwarf, and an elf. And you're not stuck with just that character, you can switch off in the main menu and continue from where you left off with any of the other characters. The combat is neat, but maybe a bit repetivie. The graphics are okay, but the character animation is pretty terrible. The combat animation, however, is actually great. The story isn't too compelling but you get to explore recognizable parts in the Tolkein universe as well as areas that have been mentioned but not necessarily explored in the novels or films. Basically, the plot involves the three characters banding together to fight off an evil force to the north while the Fellowship travels south towards Mordor.
I should mention the gameplay as well. It's extremely linear. Basically, you enter an area which is counted as a "Chapter", and you continue along a path in that area in Middle-earth until the end of the Chapter. So it's not open world if that's what any of you wanted to know.
If you have an Nvidia card and are a Tolkein fan, this game is good fun for its duration. No real replay value though.
7.0/10 (Nvidia cards)

I initially wrote and posted this on the official forums and had around 140,000 views and 129 replies.  But here it is for those who missed it, and I still feel this way about it.
X Rebirth - For Dummies ... Literally
My friends, developers, and our extremely tight nit community... boy where do I even start? I could start off with my prior X Series experience. I could start off with a rant. I could start off crying. I could start off being hopelessly optimistic. But the truth of the matter is, we are feeling all of those emotions.
You took the X Series and made X Rebirth: For Dummies. Literally and figuratively. Only the dummies, still feel like dummies. You accomplished 2 things with the design changes:
1.) You attempted to dumb down the existing complexity, but instead you merely convoluted everything through a new cumbersome half baked console driven UI and interaction menu system. Things that you thought took "too much effort" to display or review before, take even longer now.
2.) You took a play right out of Apple's playbook, and flat REMOVED features because you knew best. What happened to all the key bindings? Too complicated, gone. Want to target the nearest hostile? Nope, you think gamepads are the future, no bindings for that. Want to quickly spot your proximity to others on the Gravidar? Nope, gone.. you need to fly aimlessly around stations scanning for anything relevant.
Earth & Beyond
I am totally surprised nobody has mentioned this one. Maybe this shows my age, but for those of you who don't know... there once existed (emphasis there) a game studio called Westwood. OH yes, many of you know it, and if you don't.. you should. They were hugely successful. They brought us the Dune Series, Command & Conquer, and then one day, they decided they would build a space MMO called Earth & Beyond. I subscribed, and I played it up until it flopped and failed miserably.
I can't begin to tell you how similar it felt running around stations that were lifeless, only to interact with zombie NPCs who had nothing better to do but stand there. Things that could have been accomplished quicker from space and ship menus, HAD to be station oriented because "it was cool" and the developers believed in a fallacy that it's what gamers wanted. Yes, you hear players say this over and over, "Man someday it would be awesome if we could get out of our ships and walk around stations." Sounds good in theory, but has failed in practice, in every space game I have ever encountered, short of ONE game that was heavily story RPG oriented. Mass Effect.
Do you know what happened to Westwood after their Earth & Beyond debacle? They closed their doors. The company liquidated. Yes, they aren't Egosoft. But Egosoft are not immune to these kinds of failings. And I can assure you, this has an eerie resemblance.
Borderlands
To make station visiting "worth" the time sink, Egosoft decided to put in "lootable" boxes or crates in the stations. It has a striking resemblance to wandering around a zone in Borderlands opening crate after crate to get loot, or more commonly, endless amounts of nickels and quarters.
Freelancer
Not to bash Microsoft, because Freelancer was actually a hugely successful game. The only problem here is, X has never been a Freelancer game. But for some odd reason, Egosoft decided to stick you in one ship and have you wander around the galaxy, bouncing from station to station doing missions and trade runs like this was "partially" a Freelancer game now. Where are the vast control for the 100's of TS/TP ships as Sector and Universe Traders going about their trade runs you meticulously configured? It's gone, except in the form of "Squads" where your "owned" ships follow you around the lagged Universe, hoping YOU might know where everybody is actually going.
Oblivion
For those who played Bethesda's Oblivion, you will remember the god awful NPC happiness system. You would spend stupid amounts of time flirting, threatening, or joking with NPC's for a little "kickback" on prices or information. Egosoft has tried this out with their "Small Talk" dialogue options on NPCs. Sounds interesting at first, but it becomes mindless drab and not only did players hate it, but Bethesda learned their lesson and removed it from their future games. Skyrim was a huge success, because not only did Bethesda go back to the drawing board, but they learned some valuable lessons and REMEMBERED them going forward. What exactly happened at Egosoft? The whole community already knows you learned valuable lessons, but it's like you came down with an epidemic of alzheimers when you worked for 7 years on Rebirth.
X Rebirth: The True Problem
We all know Egosoft has a stellar track record to listen to the community and patch games with a plethora of fixes and new content. This is undisputed by nearly everybody who has been here long enough. But you see, the problem with Rebirth is more severe than the typical game launch issues, bugs, performance problems, broken missions, etc. No, the problem with Rebirth is the inherent DESIGN. It's 7 year design. And yes, the modding community can do a LOT of things to improve games. Even change them to a certain degree. But I can assure you, as a full time software developer in both business and video games (and enthusiast modder for many games in my life) this one is very hard to fix, IF you are looking for classic X2/X3 game mechanics. Egosoft is faced with making drastic underlining design code changes to bring their community what it wants right now. I'm sorry, but that's just the reality of this situation right now.
Graphics
The graphics are actually very pretty. In space. I wont talk about the stations. But I do enjoy the overhaul to the station exteriors. The lighting and all the effects. While in space, it is definitely a sexy looking game.
But that is all I can find, in me, that makes me want to play Rebirth. It's pretty when flying around in space. IN SPACE. Not wandering around cookie cutter stations like E&B. I like the sector/zone highways. And i'm still not sure what to think about the "Highway Leapfrog" mini-game that goes on when traveling through the highway system. In fact, I kind of hate looking straight up the tail pipe of other ships, crowding my already diminished view of space to make room for a beautiful cockpit which you can't even free-look.
Again, not to be crass here... but as an experienced software engineer, hell even in space games as an Indie, I have to ask Egosoft, what exactly did you accomplish in 7 years?
Best Regards, and good luck.

Economy balancing is at its worse.  I always find myself having too much resources so I can buy every skill and upgrade as soon as they're available, making it seem effortless, thus merely pointless.  Levelling comes at such a fast face that I often had too many available upgrades at once and I had to restrain myself from just buying everything (because I had the means to do it) just so I could get a feeling of the advantage the upgrades could give me and hopefully wish for another upgrade (which was available 5 levels ago anyways).
All in all, I like what Volition did in the past.  The few cutscenes still made me laugh like no other game can, but that doesn't make up for the rest of the experience.  This being said, I still have confidence in what the team can do.  I gave you my money, now I hope you'll use it well.

I had written a brief and unhestitatingly positive review of
a long time ago, but now that I've finally finished the game, I feel the ned to scrap it and replace it with something a little more detailed and a little less glowing.  This is a beautiful game with a great story and fascinating lore.  The game mechanics are... original at least, though I doubt everyone will appreciate having to choose from a list of not-quite-randomly generated commands in battle rather than having full control.  The game is marred, however, by the simple fact that there's so much in it... and most of what's in it is fluff.  It's a completionist's nightmare, and the only game I've played that I thought would benefit from some major streamlining.  Check my play time - that's
playthrough.  I didn't even do everything; there was a lot that I missed and some that I deliberately skipped because I just wanted the game to end already.  The many monster-hunting mini-quests quickly become a source of irritation once you realize that the monsters you're after aren't guarenteed to show up even if you're looking in the right place.  The mini-quests involving item collection and upgrading your equipment and your party's equipment aren't much better: the incredibly complicated crafting system includes hundreds of different components you may need, and the game offers no clues on where to find them - some can't be acquired at all unless you're carrying a certain unique item.  What I'm getting at is, play it if you're a Squenix fan - you won't be disappointed - but for the sake of your own enjoyment, resist the temptation to do everything, and be prepared to refer to Wikia frequently.
And now for the punchline: there's a new game plus mode.  You're hilarious, Squenix.

Having just finished it, I can say this game is interesting. Instead of playing with a party, you end up building a small army to fight. It has some peculiar ideas, but not the best execution of them in my opinion, gets very repetitive if you are going for completion. It is still a good jRPG, though far from contender to the best titles out there. I would give it a 3.5/5.
Some of the members of your army make no sense being there, and there is very little story when optional team members are concerned. Speaking of story, it makes a bit of a jump here and there, and it is not the greatest at making sense. I did find it enjoyable enough to make me sit through to the end still, though you will need to ignore a plot hole here and there eventually.
Most of the content you can see as artificial padding, in the form of the guild tasks, that make you reenter already done dungeons many, many times to find a specific random mob, hated those, and the upgrade system not allowing you to downright give items to your teammates required to upgrade their weapons, so you had to go back and farm them again and again if you care about your teams progression, very annoying. If you don't care, get ready to be pestered about it, because your team asks you for the things they need, over and over and over again, every time you go back to the world map you spend 5 minutes just skipping the dialogs of them asking.
The battle system is a nice change from normal jRPGs. You don't directly control your characters, you organize them in units, and then give the unit a general purpose, like "use mystic arts". Then, some of the unit member may use a magic, while others will just regular hit, and it is random who will do what, you can train them in different classes to increase the likelihood they will do what you want, but it is no guarantee. Also, even random battles are challenging, since after each one your party automatically recovers, so there is no excuse to not go all out. The bad side is that the toughest battles end up relying too much on RNG to win.
Instead of levels, you have a battle rating, and this is one of the bad things about the game. They give you a general battle rating, and enemies scale according to it, but each one of your characters has a BR as well, and they do not tell you what it is. Some stats are hidden like skill progression, and class changes possible and requirements, and some stuff that appear in old towns that makes you either have to use a guide to know of, or visit everywhere after each story step which is annoying and takes quite a bit.
Also you have no control over your teams skills, and sometimes they make the worst possible decisions when leveling up. For instance, I read a lot about this skill called "Cachexia" and how it is essential to kill the optional bosses, and although I had 9 members of my 18 member army capable of learning it, and with magic of it's level, just one of them chose to learn it, and only while doing the dungeon that leads to the final boss. I did grind quite a bit trying to get it, but after failing to do so I ended up having to do everything without it, making it all a lot harder.
Overall, I would say get this game during a sale and it is worth it, and give it a play, if only to check it's battle system in the very least, or try to do a quick story playthrough ignoring most sidequests. Don't get too much into micro managing though, or you will need to spend a lot of time on the wiki to try to do things right.

The gameplay is excellent and it's a lot of fun. The reason I had so much trouble following the story is that I'd spend a 1/2 hour on a story mission and then 20 hours doing other things. Just have to say this first: If you underestimate this game it will kick your butt, hard. That said, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I've played both the 360 version and the PC and found I enjoyed the PC version a little more. The ability to keep your items and dig counts from previous playthroughs makes a challenging game like The Last Remnant a little easier.
This game is incredibly complex in terms of item gathering. Just because an enemy in one area drops a type of item does not mean the same enemy elsewhere drops that item. And some enemies change what they drop once you reach a certain level. While I enjoyed the complexity, I know there are people out there that won’t.
There are a large number of side quests in the game. Some rewarding you with playable characters or new abilities for your main character, Rush. The downside is some of these quests show up for a very brief period and if you are unaware of them they are easily missed.
Then there is the leveling system. On my first run I played The Last Remnant as I would any RPG, which is power level my characters as soon as I could. That shoots you in the foot in this game. The best way to play, at least that I found, was to keep your level low. It seems counterintuitive but until you have most of the characters I wouldn’t suggest raising your level too much. The reason is if you level up early the characters you get later end up rather pathetic in their stats and skills compared your earlier characters.
The downside to the low level of course shows up when battling a boss. Expect to struggle, sometimes a lot. The bosses in this game can be ridiculously hard at times, which makes it even more rewarding when you finally beat them. This is especially true when it comes to the DLC monsters.
All of this said, The Last Remnant is incredibly in-depth game. So many of the elements are connected within the game; for example forging and guild tasks often go hand in hand. I also enjoyed the story and grew quite attached to the characters. And while you have no direct control over units other than Rush, you can direct what paths the others can take. This allows you to have them lean towards learning a specific weapon and the art that may go with it. By doing this you can make more balanced teams or have them be more inclined to magic or physical attacks. Just don’t bother forging items for your other teammates; the likelihood that the person you made it for asks for the item is usually slim.
If you’re willing to put in the time to learn the intricacies of The Last Remnant it is pretty addictive. I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a RPG that isn’t just run through the storyline and call it a day.

NOT A HERO is a tongue in cheek comedic high violence platformer starring you as one of the many assistants to an enigmatic character known as Bunnylord. Your purpose in the game is to complete various missions for BL in the hopes of helping him to win an election.
The graphics are pretty retro, but not offensively so. The music is catchy and the characters’ banter entertaining. As far as gameplay goes, the concepts are fairly simple (shoot, enter cover, reload, dash, tackle, execute) and can be picked up fairly quickly after the first tutorial mission. Depending on the character you choose, your style of run and gun will differ and some people will be easier to play on certain levels than others.
I kind of liked the limited mobility factor in that you cannot jump in this game and must instead make your way up various nearby buildings and dive through windows to progress in some areas. The slide tackle mechanic is also a nice addition and combined with execution, if timed right, it can make for a downright frantic yet rewarding experience. Some enemies in the game are immune to the aforementioned combo and must be dealt with in other ways.
Overall I think this is a nice game that yields around 7-10 hours depending on whether or not you want to get the full ending or just clear it. Some of the levels have some really hard challenges like “don’t get punched” or some sort of time-based objective, which can be kind of a drag if you manage to finally pull it off and then die or get punched right near the end of a level (this happened to me a lot). That being said, this game regularly goes on sale for less than $5 and is a total steal at that price. Worth it just for the voice acting and goofy plot.

Would I recommend this game on it's own? Yes. Absolutely. Not only does it have amazing semi-open world gameplay, but it's graphics still hold up surprisingly well today. Which is amazing when you consider that this game came out 10 years ago!
However, I cannot with any amount of seriousness recommend the Steam version. For some reason, EA completely neglected to include the latest update patches and the 64-bit version (which is the ONLY version PCs with AMD FX series CPUs like mine can run). I did manage to get the game to run without crashing on startup by manually installing the 1.21 patch and the executables for the 64-bit version myself and launching the game with a fan made .bat file but the point is, why do I HAVE to do all of that just to get the game to run? Doesn't the fact that I still had to manually patch the game myself kind of defeat the purpose of the Steam client? What's even worse is that from what I've heard, this problem isn't limited to the Steam version. The version sold on EA's own Origin service has the exact same problem!
If you want to try this game for yourself, get it on GOG. Not only does the GOG version actually have both the 1.21 patch and the 64-bit version included from the get-go, but since it's a GOG release, it also has the nice added bonus of being DRM free as well.
(Edit: In case you're wondering how I have 23.9 hours on record with this game, it's because I used to be able to run it without crashing on startup back when I ran on Windows 7 and had a quad core AMD Phenom II CPU. I didn't start having the problems described in this review until I upgraded to Windows 10 and a 4.2GHz overclocked octa core AMD FX 8320 CPU.)

Great game, took a few short games to get the learning curve.  After that it was constant decisions about what to do each day.  Do you build enough beds for everyone or board up the windows?  Do you help your neighbors, what supplies can you give up to make this or trade for that.  Should you rob from other survivors or aid groups to survive.
Your people will fight each other, over your choices.  They'll get depressed, sick, injured, hungry and you'll have to decide to provide them with their vices or trade them away for supplies and materials.
You can avoid combat for most the game, with the exception of being raided at night.  Nothing like having a safe stockpile, only to be raided and wind up losing most your food and a severly injured defender.
Combat itself could be improved a little, I only used the knife and pistol.  The knife was constant click which wasn't bad and worked out better than using a pistol.  For the pistol, it looks like there is an aim mechanic, but combat happens so quickly that I burned through six rounds, the bandit was still standing, and killed me with his shotgun.
When you start losing people, the game takes on another challenge.
When winter comes, get ready to break everything you can to keep the house warm, people fed, and fight off sickness.

Trust me when I say I've played this for a lot more than 20 hours. On disc and on console I've spent years of time with this game. Having not played it properly for a couple of years though, I decided to finish it again. Being a lot
older I found it interesting. Firstly, I have no idea how people can say this is just a tech demo or only worth it for the graphics because as a game it's 'average'. Production values are very high and it's obvious the developers were
talented and experienced in making games, not just tech. Secondly, I had no clue how goddamn fun I'd have with this game. Being so experienced with it I would've thought my opinion of it was for the most part pretty rock-solid but I
was ery much wrong. The first 2/3's of this game are exceptional. Honestly, one of the best games I've ever played... until the last third, which by no exaggeration is just utter crap.
++Game looks great. I'd say best looking game of all time by 2009, although I always thought Halo 3 didn't get nearly enough praise in comparison.
++Level design is open (absolutely not even remotely open world, stop calling it that) and has the sandbox gameplay that makes the Halo series so unique and incredible
++The nanosuit is a blast to use
+The sound design stands out massively. Some of the best I've ever heard.
+Alien origin story is cool
+Harder difficulty modes are still fair
+Driving vehicles is fun
+Different firemodes is awesome. More games need this.
+Weapon mods and weapon mod switching on the fly is pretty unique and very helpful, definitely not just a gimmick
+Movement feels great
+Decent soundtrack
+The large scale battles with allies feels closer to war than most games get
+-Body shots while shooting in semi-automatic are useless since enemies take literally 20 or so shots to kill. No exaggeration. I think it was made more for range and headshots anyway, which are one shot kills. Not a big deal.
-+AI are stupid, sure, but they're a lot of fun to fight
-Voice acting is mostly crap
-Writing is about on par with the average American drama, i.e terrible
-Needs more weapons
-The SCAR is useless since there's never any ammo for it
-The final boss fight sucks, and the first one is ridiculously easy
--The last third (the second half of missions, they're a lot shorter than the first half) of the game dips down from a solid 9/10 to a garbage 5.5/10
--Optimization is absolutely atrocious. I get frequent dips below 60fps at Very High everything at 1080p at 2x anti-aliasing on a GTX1060. I get roughly an average of 40 or so at a mix of Very High and Medium settings,
no anti-aliasing at 4K. For comparison, I get 250+ max settings on Rainbow Six Vegas 2 at 4K and that was released a year later. There is no excuse for how terribly this game runs.

Now, those who know me should know that I love dinosaurs. Always have, always will. I'm a total Dino-Nerd.
However, I can still write an unbiased review, and here it is.
This game has a very unique style of play. On one side you have the larger, more physically equipped Dinosaurs, which you play from 3rd person view. The game does a pretty good job of balancing them with the humans. You can have very few Tyrannosaurs on your team, and the frequency in which you can play some of the more powerful dinosaurs is lower than the more squishy, but agile dinosaurs. There is a great balance on the field among dinosaurs. You get a lot of satisfaction using the special abilities that the dinosaurs possess. Being able to pick people up with a Pteranodon and carry them away is great, as well as leaping onto a human with a velociraptor. The abilities are really cool, and you'll definitely enjoy the variety in play styles.
On the other side, the satisfaction comes from taking down the big dinosaurs with the humans. Concentrating your entire groups fire onto a T-Rex and finally bringing it down has a boss-battle type feeling. You get a lot of excitement out of trying to pick and choose your battles being the squishy humans. You get range on your side. For example, you can fire quite a few rounds off before a dinosaur can close on you, and you have to position yourself to make that happen in a lot of cases. Again though, the variety in play styles helps you to really find a good balance. The humans are really hard to beat as the dinosaurs, teamwork is a vital part of both sides.
I would say that the gameplay and tempo closely resembles that of Left 4 Dead, and other teamwork based, arcade-type games. You get both 1st person as the Humans, and 3rd person with the Dinosaurs, which adds a bit of variety to gameplay. A big perk is the awesome variety of skins. There are some sick dinosaur skins that you can purchase for very cheap.
Some things that really detract from the experience are the startling lack of servers. Not enough people play this game, there are only a few really active servers to choose from with good pings. That can cause problems. The game can come off as a little buggy in some situations, but its hardly noticeable most of the time.
To close, it's a very unique and fun game. In my opinion, it's a very fresh multiplayer experience with surprisingly balanced and interesting gameplay. It's a singularly satisfying experience for both factions. For an indy gaming company, they've done a very successful job at delivering a polished product for us all to enjoy.
I would definitely recommend this game, and I really look forward to what the developers will do with their next installments.

So my buddy and I finished up The Lord Of The Rings: War in the North the other day, and I have to give the entire experience a big thumbs up! It would have been nice to have played with a third human player, but the AI dwarf did pretty well for himself.
The story is that the three of you (Dúnedain Ranger, Elven Loremaster, and a Dwarf Champion) are tasked to help out the clashes going on in the North, as the One Ring is heading off to Mordor. The evil wizard Agandaûr, one of Sauron's right hand men, is raising a ruckus and we are sent off to bring him to heel, make things uncomfortable for Sauron and basically distract him while the Fellowship makes its way to Mordor.
It's a story pretty well told, although to be honest, I didn't explore all its nuances. There's a nice conversation mechanic where if you pick the default response, you get the most "cinematic" experience, which is nice. Even cooler is that once you make your way to Rivendell, you get to meet up with most of the Fellowship, and talk strategy and the like with Frodo, Aragorn, et al. That's a cool touch.
It's an action RPG, so there's plenty of fighting going on. You can mix and match all your armor and weapons and, in another real nice touch. all the in game cutscenes have you done up in your current set up. There are plenty of choices of skills to use as you go up in levels. I had fun with the Loremaster, getting some real nice area effect spells as well as a cool "dome" I could call up that gave healing and defense from missile weapons. Chris became a dual wielding killing machine by the end, so even the hated trolls went down before our onslaught. And, in fact, the final boss battle against Agandaûr wasn't really all that hard.
Speaking of difficulty, it did a pretty good job of throwing some tough battles at us. It was probably a tad on the easy side, especially as having all three characters go down really just resulted in going back to some earlier point in the battle, so not too bad. I would prefer a tougher game, but that's just me.
The slotting mechanism and the special sets for getting similar types of armor was a tad overblown, I thought. I'm not sure it really had much to do with things, at least in the first play through. They want you to:
Play through The Lord of the Rings: War in the North multiple times to fully upgrade each of your player characters.
Not really my style, though.
Also, I wish there was something to spend the money on. I almost never actually bought anything at the merchants, as recovered loot was always far more powerfull. I had almost $50,000, while Chris had over $60,000 by the end! And it was very annoying to "repair" your items, as they wore down during the campaign. You have to go through your inventory, find ones that were highlighted, and repair each one individually. As the total coast was usually less than $100, it was a drag that there was no "Repair All" option.
Another inventory annoyance was all the special potions and "cakes" that you really couldn't use. Only healing and power restoration have a hot key, so it was real hard to use the other potions, as going into your inventory during the heat of the battle didn't pause anything. So it was hard to take the time to use a handy Strength potion or Healing cake (which the Loremaster could "make").
One other glitch was that there was no way to turn off the dismal in game microphone, which made using my Teamspeak server harder than it should have been. Both Chris and I had to leave another microphone plugged in and selected as the "default" mic in Windows and then select the "right" one to use in Teamspeak. Just a stupid oversight on the programmers part.
But enough nitpicking. This was a fun game and I highly recommend it. Despite some naysayers on Steam, I thought the graphics were real nice, and not just especially for a game from 2011. There were some real nice vistas in Rivendell and the Dwarven fortress, and plenty of nice effects like water and snow. And, like I said, having the characters in the cut scenes reflect what you were actually wearing was pretty cool too. And it worked great with my Xbox controller. A pretty short game (we took about 22 hours to play it), but still two big thumbs up!

Played it for almost 100h on different accounts now. The game is quite simple actually, but you can get a lot out of that simplicity.
** Basics
- Three different characters (Ranger, Dwarf, Elf)
- Direct movement (WASD/Left Stick), direct aiming (Mouse/Right Stick)
- Always all three characters in play. Coop or NPCs.
(Many people have technical probs with coop. You might want to check that out.)
- Different levels with multiple Zones (Mirkwood part1/2 ...)
You enter at one point, exit at another one and destroy everything that moves on your way.
- Grab the loot! Obviously!
- Enter different towns between the zones. Sell/Buy/Repair/Get Quests.
- Unlimited free travel to replay visited locations. (However the many boss mobs are not there
if you revisit a location.)
** Visuals
- Not high level for current gen, but it looks decent.
- Sets and Landscapes are very well designed. Some areas felt like walking through
the cover of a classic fantasy book.
** RPG
- No real character based roleplaying. You can choose between a few conversation alternatives. But you cannot change the NPCs or your characters or the story in any meaningful way. It is about as linear as Diablo.
- Very small number of town based quest. Almost all quest are about gathering loot during the fights.
** Fighting
- Hack&Slash + Ranged Shooting. You will be using both and it is quite fun.
- Dwarf and Ranger use crossbows and bows, Elf uses magic bolts.
- Some meele weapons are also class character exclusive.
- Basic combo slashing "AAA", get a note for a critical attack, "B", knockdown/kill.
- You fight smaller groups along the way and bigger mobs/bosses in arena type areas.
** Skills
- Specific skill tree for all three characters. Kind of similar but the trees help to enhance
different playstiles or at least different feel.
- Each skill matters but might be less usefull depending on your build.
- Respec token available, so don't worry.
** Leveling
- Level 40 is max.
- Level 20 is roughly what you get after a first playthrough.
- Unlimited playthroughs. Difficulty raises up to 'legendary'.
- Attribute points are more important for equipment requirements than stat changes.
** Some Notes
- Don't go for that one ultimate item set. At least not until you approach legendary.
You will grow out of items a lot. Use that to have fun and replace them many times.
Use your elfstones, try different weapons. In the next playthrough you will laugh about the
stats of the former one.
- Helpful item boni change over time. In the beginning you want more armor, more health, more coints etc to not die. In the end you want damage multipliers and cooldown reduction to get through those puny orks fast.
- A single item with x5 coins can remove all your money worries.
- Rare items are rare! You need quite a few playthroughs to get the 'perfect' equipment.
You will be finishing the game with eyes closed by that time.
- Your item inventory is large. Keep alterantive weapons for different situations.
- Use mirrors to customize your appearance. Made the characters a lot more likeable to me.
- Switch between characters if you cannot finish some area (should not be the case) or maybe a quest requires a certain character. *wink*
- Don't stress yourself over lost items/opportunities etc. You can replay as many times as you like. Just carry on.
- Special boni carry over from weapons to special moves. A good reason to go for dual wielding.
** Suggestions
- Dwarf is considered the most powerful character. He has a broken overpowered ranged attack
that takes the whole challenge out of the game. Spare the dwarf for later, if you are interested in the other characters too. Its hard to fight big mobs and strong bosses with an axe, if you can one-shot them anyway.
- Ranger is the most 'dull' (and kinda dumb looking) character. But if you want to play a sword and bow fighter, you can have a lot of fun with that guy.
Ranger is a good start for a first playthrough and does not suffer from game ending op attacks.
- Elf is primarily written as healer/supporter for the other two. You become the nanny for them
when you play the elf. Makes the fights different and more rewarding.
** Elf tips
- You are the NPC healer. But as a player you have to look after the other guys.
That can be very frustrating when you play with two NPCs for dwarf and ranger.
Make it your challenge to keep those little dummies alive.
- When one NPC dies, the other one instantly tries to revive them. Even if they run into a mob and get killed instantly. After that you are the only target left and have the mob all to yourself. And not time to revive your buddies. Annyoing, but also challenging and a great reason to curse those stupid NPCs!!
- Yes you DO need dexterity for your magic missiles damage. But all characters get high ranged damage without dexterity anyway. Attributes don't effect damage output that much. Focus on meeting item requirements.
- A very rewarding build is to go for the Elfs AoE attack. A nova/splash attack that can later take out entire mobs of the strongest enemies. No Dex needed. Not much power (mana) upgrade needed.
- Ranged attacks have a high mana cost and don't profit from casting cost reduction.
- Elemental attacks and other modifiers take over from melee weapons to AoE attack.
- Collect the ingredients for potions and USE them. Your inventory will be full with that stuff, so at least drink it.
- You can build an AoE based Elf that kills almost any enemy with a single splash attack and does rarely need a potion for health/mana at all. VERY rewarding after all the babysitting.
- There is one boss towards the end that your gf might find very disgusting. ;)

Hollow Knight has become one of my favourite games of all time. It tells little to nothing to the player when you start your journey and every little bit of information is in the dialogue and item descriptions. That by itself may turn some players off who want a more linear storytelling - before you make the purchase decision I feel inclined to inform you that Hollow Knight doesn't hold your hand at all. Not in the slightest. It's a fantastic roguelike metroidvania that holds a candle to many other successors of the same genre. It makes nearly everything perfectly - the music, the controls, visuals, performance, story and it's mysteries, characters.. and the list goes on. This review will be divided into small sections talking about each point so it may include some spoilers, do note that you'll get the best possible experience out of Hollow Knight when you play in without knowing anything about it. If you're new to the game, I absolutely recommend it but now to the specifics!
THE STORY AND CHARACTERS:
Hollow Knight's story is very simple yet captivating, When you enter the game you see the barren Dirtmouth and the almost depressing feel that the overwold gives you. I had no clue what was behind Hallownest but soo I found it was behind its prosper and eventual downfall. The environment contrasts the story perfectly and creates this unmatched ambiance to the experience - You feel like you're in a barren and long gone peaceful place filled with enemies and newfound issues that have manifested over the years. HEAVY SPOILERS: Your basic goal of the story which progresses it is to gain access to the "Black Egg" inside of its temple. It has three seals on it, each for their own respected mask owners. I might be describing a glorified fetch quest here but hear me out - it's the main goal, yes but you never feel pressured to do them. There's so much more more and during your journey the main quest feels so well integrated into everything else that it doesn't bother you in the slightest. Only kinda nitpicky-ish problem I have with this is that it also brings one problem to the table - the pacing. Hollow Knight can feel incredibly slow at first and I was more forcing myself to play through the beginning hours. After 15 or so hours the game starts to feel incredible.
THE SOUND DESING AND SOUNDTRACK/OST:
Sound design of Hollow Knight is probably what brought me back in those affordmentioned beginning hours. Do note that in order to enhance the experience you might want to wear headphones to get every little piece of sound out of it. The way you footsteps sound of different surfaces, the ambience of Hallownest, slashes your Nail (more on that later), the composing, distinct sounds of different enemies, explosions and all that is created with perfection in mind. And it really really shows. The ost is incredible, bringing places to life and enhancing your experience into the bloody stratosphere. Greenpath, White Place (more notably Path of Pain), bossfight music (yes, all of them) bring so much into the table I cannot describe it properly. Wear headphones during this game, you won't regret it.
THE ART, ANIMATION AND PERFORMANCE:
Unity is infamous for badly animated games. Hollow Knight makes an exception on this regard because damn, it is so pretty. Everything is fluid and the backgrounds are astounding. Hollow Knight its very own distinct art design that plays very well together with the sound design. The animations are pretty basic but they fit the game, they would look out of place in my opinion if they would look super flashy. They are well animated on their own merits - abilities look good, platforming is great, combat feels fluid and just.. works well. Everything ties in together creating a very nice athmospheric experience. Hollow Knight's most notable design choises are found in the architectures and characters. Each character is an insect/a bug, yes.. even you. On one instance you're fighting mantises and on the other you're facing huge centipedes. Caverns and houses are well design on their respective areas which gives everything yet again a distict look and feel. Hollow Knight also performs well and it doesn't stutter, it has become a far nicer experience over past months due to updates and I hope it keeps improving. No complaints there, I did however run into a FPS problem when colliding with water (dropping into water) but it has been fixed well.
THE COMBAT AND GAMEPLAY + BOSSES.. + CONCLUSION
The combat in Hollow Knight is very simple which keeps evolving as you unlock more abilities and diversify your moveset. You start with the following: you can more left and right and jump up. Your attacks are slashes to left, right, up and down with a jump or fall. As I mentioned before this moveset does get wider over time with varying moves: there are three special abilities and three sword arts.
Ability 1: Forward facing projectile
Ability 2: Blast a cone shaped attack above
Ability 3: Stomp on the ground with an AOE burst
Sword Art 1: Charged slash
Sword Art 2: Spin
Sword Art 3: Dashing forward slash
All of these and your unlocked special abilities like wallclimbing will make the experience good and none of the abilities feel especially wasted or forgotten. They all contribute to the varied cast of combat abilities well and you never feel underpowered. Basic enemies usually take a certain ammount of hits to kill but you can upgrade your Nail (your weapon) as the game progresses with hidden items and a bit Geo which is this games currency. You earn geo by finding chests, killing enemies and bosses so on and so forth. Hollow Knight also spices up the combat with equipable charms that enhance your combat abilities or give you defensive force. These can be found through Hallownest and some of them are incredibly well hidden.
Bosses work like normal enemies.. except they are stronker. You hit them until they become weakened, repeat until they die or you earn an achievement. All these bosses are quite good ranging from meh to absolutely hectic and fantastic. Like Dark Souls (is that a ♥♥♥♥ing Dark Souls reference???) this game also punishes the player brutally. You leave your ghost behind upon death which carries all of your lost Geo and part of your SOUL. SOUL is the mana of this game, you use it heal (the healing system is implemented incredibly well) and use abilities.
All and all Hollow Knight is incredible and I'm tired of typing so yeah.

I wanted to love this game.  Alpha Centuari was one my favorite 4X games ever and a new version of that built on the Civ 5 engine seemed too good to go wrong.  Sadly, BE seems more or less to be nothing more than an overpriced scenario for Civ 5.  The concept behind the game is great,but it feels very threadbare.  Where AC had stereotypical, but memorable factions and leaders, BE has factions with no central identity and flat, boring leaders who make you pine for the personalities in Civ 5.  With only a handful of factions availible, if you play on large worlds you'll always have the same opponents.  Which is frustrating when you realize that there are only a handful of units availible as well.  They did add in more trade routes though; which actually hampers the game as I found myself havingto micromanage my trade routes.
Verdict: Stick to Civ 5.  This game may get better in time, but it's not worth the price or your time.

I have to recommend Beyond Earth to any TBS gamer.  While it is built on the Civ V base - a game I didn't really take to - it is truly the game we've been waiting for since Alpha Centauri.
The core factions that come with the game all have enough difference to promote a different style of play, without being wholly unbalanced, or wholly unplayable.  The different affinities really work, and the debates I've had between choosing a tech for it's own inherent value, or because it would bump the affinity I needed, are just the kind of mental challenges I look for in a TBS game.
I can't give it a 10, or even a 9, as there are bugs in the game (you can't play on a massive map for more than a couple of hundred turns before crashes become almost constant), and there are a number of interface tweaks that are absolutely essential (why, when you pop the dialogue to rename the city, didn't you have the field take focus so I can just type?)
So this is a solid 8 out of 10.

First and foremost I'm not a paid reviewer/streamer/critic or any of that. I was blessed enough to receive a key for free eventhough I will buy multiple copies of this for my family/friends. Just being upfront about it but I played in the beta and pre-release so my review is coming from all my experience with the game. Now onto the review.
Ever since the rlease of Freelancer on PC way back in 2000, I have been aching for a new space sim experience. If your like me and also have that itch then look no further. This game has pirating/trading/looting/mining/space battles.... a whole slew of things you can do in the sandbox that they have created for you.
There are several systems or galaxies in which you traverse and have jump gates to connect them. Each system has its own factions with which to either befriend or destroy. You have a main story but also space stations with side missions along with the included Trading/Mining/Mercenary guilds which also provide missions. These three factions also provide unique ships, weapons, shields, and other things to outfit your ship. The combat is likened to naval style (think Assassins Creed Black Flag ship battles) and its set on a 2d plane.
The art style, ship design, space backdrops are all top notch. The audio is also one thing that is a step above. The soundtrack alone warrants a look at this game. It gives the feel of a space fairing outlaw lol. Think Firefly, Han Solo, Cowboy Bebop, Outlaw Star vibe. The sounds of the weapons firing gives a sense of real power and gurth behind each barrage launched from your broadside cannons. The best sound to me is when your FTL drive spools up and then hits warp.
This game has been on my radar for some time now as my top 5 most anticipated games of 2015. I knew that Travis and Erich who left Runic Games to establish Double Damage wouldn't let me down. If you have any interest, what are you waiting for help these two Devs out by purchasing this amazing experience! I know I will be purchasing copies for my friends and family and for only 20$ US you can't beat that deal. The price for value is one of the best of 2015 alone. Do your self a favor and play it.

It's been a while since they made a new Hitman game, last one was blood money back in 2006, and this one does deliver quite good.
The story is centered about Agent 47 having to do one very personal contract after eliminating Rogue Agent Diana (your handler in all the previous games) after revealing classified info of the agency breaking them down, and taking away a mysterious girl named Victoria from their labs, but before her final breath Diana asks 47 to protect Victoria so they don't make her become like you, and so the game begins.
The graphics of this game are amazing and even though the game is about 3 years old they still hold up pretty good, very nice attention to detail on both enviroments and clothing.
There's a nice variety of levels and up to 5 levels of difficulty each adding more and more enemies in your mission alongside better AIs and less HUD elements.
Even on normal difficulty you will encounter a challenge if you a hardcore Hitman fan and do the classic run involving no killing innocents, only kill the mission targets, never get spotted and never change clothes.
You will be scored in each level in order to compete with online leaderboards, even though there's a lot of cheated scores, like 16m points on a 5min mission.
Can also make your own contracts replaying one of the levels unlocked and mark a target and how to kill him, in order for your friends to compete in.
The only downside of this game i would say it's the low amount of variety on the enemy patrol movements and etc, so all you have to do is study them and time your moves.

Turns out this is a pretty terrific game.
I know. I was let down when I first played it too. At one point I remember taking the disc out of my PS3, putting it back in its case, and throwing it against the wall in the next room. When I calmed down I checked to see if the disc had broken, and when I saw it was fine I sold it to Gamestop.
But as the years went by I found myself thinking about it here and there. Yeah, it's kind of a failure as a mainline Final Fantasy title. There is no exploration or traditional turn based combat, and as an old school Final Fantasy fan that had a bad taste in my mouth after XII this was not okay.
But as a game, on its own terms, accepting it for what it is and realizing that there are NO mainline Final Fantasy titles anymore, I think the game is actually pretty great. I enjoy the driven cinematic nature of the game. I love the visuals, the art design is just gorgeous. Even the combat, with an open mind and a willingness to learn the system (which the game will spend the majority of its 50 hours teaching you) is challenging and rewarding. When I originally played the game on PS3 I dismissed the combat as button mashing (changing paradigms willy nilly) but by the end of it and after defeating some of the more difficult bounties I have a deep appreciation for it while at the same time acknowledging a traditional Final Fantasy fan is probably not looking for anything of the sort.
One of my favorite things about revisiting it though, would have to be the moment I realized the plot was a twist on the old hero of light trope from the original.
Final Fantasy as we remember it is dead. Maybe that's a good thing, I don't know. What I do know is that Final Fantasy XIII doesn't really deserve the hate it's gotten over the years. And if you are like me and initially disliked it, but have found yourself thinking back to it and are able to look at it on its own terms as more of a Final Fantasy spinoff, then I definitely recommend revisiting it. Hell, I'm even going to check out the sequels.
And take the same attitude with Final Fantasy XV, because there is NO WAY that game is not a dissappointment to old school Final Fantasy fans.
EDIT - Final Fantasy XV ended up sucking balls.

I literally started this game this month in hope of it being a very good J-RPG; o boy was I disappointed. To begin with, there are way too many characters within this game. The story itself is bland and forgetable, as it kind of reminds me of FF 13 in which the story actually started becoming good after playing 30 hours of it, I can easily say the same about The Last Remnant. In terms of there being way too many characters, I mean the issue with this is the fact the game only allows a total of 5 parties with a total of 5 members in each of those parties limiting you far too much.
The battle system itself is very convoluted and never really explained. The player really has no access to what each party members do in each party. For example, the battle system tells the player that all of the party member will attack this specific enemy, either by physical damage, magical damage. Other times it lets you heal if necessary but those options are unpredicatable as when one of my party was very much injured, it would not give me the option to heal at all.
What's kind of worse about the battles in The Last Remnant is the way that they are placed. Most of the battles are ridiculous. Sometimes you go into a new area, the enemies are sometimes very easy, and then suddenly you meet this gigantic bird/ dragon and they tear you a new one because for some odd reason the developers decided to put a rare monster into the game at that specific moment. Of course even though I only died once and the auto saves in this game is very well timed, the fact is that those rare monsters are really not rewarding at all.
To keep this short, if you're thinking about buying this game, it's worth no more than 4 dollars. The problem isn't the graphics, because those are superb for a J-RPG on the PC, however the problem really has to do with the lack of story, terrible and convoluted battle system, lack of character development and in general, it really does not feel like a true J-RPG. I came into this game expecting more so something along the lines of FF 12 as my lowest expectation and my highest expectation as FF 6, but really it was nowhere near as good as even FF 12. I can truly just recommend this to players who really just want to understand the combat system by trying different things and such. However, for players who want a deep character developement, good easy to understand combat system and even easy loot system, then this is not a game for you.

Liked it very much. As an old-time fan of the series, I really enjoy this one. The style and feel of FF is still there, despite very obvious differences in the gameplay.
I like the look and the music, the general vibe of a world where magic and technology coexist, as in many previous instalments of FF. The idea of Cocoon is realized very well, in particular. Otherwise the story, characters and all the general premises are much in the common vein of the series, very operatic and deliberately not down-to-earth realistic. For those who appreciate such things it's a familiar story of that beloved kind. Not much of a novelty, but enjoyable still. An A- maybe.
The gameplay is very streamlined and action-like. You don't pick the battle commands from a staic menu, rather you pick from a menu of automatization schemes and watch your characters dance around the enemy performing their moves according to the chosen set of rules. It makes for an exciting show, but the battles are not as tactical as in many previous FFs and there is not much room for strategy.
Outside battles, I do miss puzzles and freedom of movement between locations. I'm not through the game yet, so don't know if you ever get to travel around the whole in-game planet. So overall the gameplay gets a B from me.
I can't really compare this to other Japanese style RPGs as I haven't played many, I stick to the big FF series most of the time if I play the genre. But as a beatiful story-driven over-the-top ballet♥♥♥♥♥action experience, this is very good. As a J-RPG, rather good. Can I recommend it to everyone? Probably not, but if you like FF and are in doubt or have not returned to the series a long time - this one is worth it, emotionally and visually it puts you into that right place where the earlier great FFs did put you.

Despite all of its flaws and bad press, I really enjoyed FFXII.  I played it on the 360 and now again on the PC.  I will say this to anyone who is looking into purchasing it...  Know what you are getting into first.
Final Fantasy as a series is out-dated with its gameplay.  Square -> we have powerful processors now.  We don't need to limit the number of teammates at a time or the number of enemies we face at one time.  FFXIII does a good job of overcoming its in heritance by adding the Active Time Battle which keeps the combat flowing and keeps you engaged.
The storyline is also kind of what you would expect from Square and really any JRPG.  VERY convoluted and confusing.  What makes it worse is that if you just play the game all of the way through without stopping to read the DataLog (because who reads anymore), you will miss probably 75% of what is going on.  However, if you read the logs and can follow the Shiny Object Syndrome (S.O.S.) storyline, it's very good.  It is an interesting take on racism from a society where 90% of the people have the same skin tone.
Also yes, the critism is accurate in that the tutorial will last FOREVER.  The first 3-5 hours of the game is one big tutorial.  In fact, you don't get magic or XP (you know, the things that Final Fantasy games are known for) until the 3rd level.

So the story starts with me buying this game. This is another survival game yes but it is different.
First of all you are not facing stupid zombies or some kind of mutant animals, monsters and so on instead you are facing war itself and you are just an ordinary civilian trying to survive, not a lean, mean killing machine. Space Strategy enthusiasts rejoice: real-time strategy meets 4X rules in a seamlessly zoomable universe that hasn't looked or felt this polished since the original Homeworld game. Marketed as a stand-alone expansion for Sins of a Solar Empire, Rebellion basically sums up every mechanic introduced in every expansion to date - fight off pirates and opposing empires, establish trade routes, colonize or raise every planet in your solar system... and beyond. It has the same addictiveness as Civilization, in that you feel like you're playing a board game in which your faction fights to rule the universe using various tools or domination and manipulation, every match a new iteration in the array of destinies you can forge. On top of that, the space battles are impressive in both scale and effects: tons of freaking laser beams, rockets and machine gun fire keep you at the edge of your seat when a few hundred ships in your fleet meet a few hundred of your opponents' craft and clash in a display of fireworks that is so visceral and pretty it blows your brains out and leaves you slack jawed at the display of awesomeness.
BUY it if you:
-Enjoy RTS games and civ builders alike.
-Want to engage in large-scale space battles with budget hardware (the game's zoom function works like a miracle, letting you join in on epic skirmishes or zoom out to manage your home planet in the blink of an eye).
-Always wanted to recreate the Dominion assault on Deep Space Nine or some other notoriously nerdy science fiction scene you're almost embarassed you enjoy so much.
DO NOT BUY it if you:
-Hate the pacing of RTS games (learning hotkeys, developing effective build orders and being fast in setting your bases is essential to mastering Sins of a Solar Empire, and if you need time to think things through, you might be better off waiting for Civilization: Beyond Earth for your 4X fix).
-Expect a campaign or any kind of predesigned narrative - Rebellion has none.
I would pay for a sequel.

This isn't a bad game at all. It's one of the greatest shooters of all time and 10 years later it still holds up. From what I hear this game is also used more of a tool rather than a game as a benchmark for pc gaming rigs. It even gives some modern gpus a run for their money barely passing 60 fps. High end rigs back then could barely run this, let alone at MAX. Truly a testament of it's time. But that's not why I give this game a negative review. Don't let my playtime fool you, I have the original retail copy of this game and wanted a digital copy. It's the only reason I got the Steam version. The steam version of the game is just terrible. It uses 3rd party DRM (SecuROM) that is not equipped to run on modern operating systems like Windows 8 or Windows 10. It doesn't work because it doesn't include the x64 files to work on newer windows OS, unless you own the retail copy. My retail copy works fine on Windows 7 with no problems what so ever. The Steam version works on Windows 7 however if you spend a little bit of time in the menu section or when you pause it, the game freezes. There is no need for 3rd party DRM since Steam is already the DRM. My advice, get this game on GOG instead. DO NOT bother with the Steam or Origin version of the game. The game is a 10/10 but the Steam version is a 3/10.
