The game is not fun.
If you win you will be satisfied you didn't encounter a flavor of the month champion.  You'll love having a competent, non-berating teammate.  You'll be bored because your enemies just weren't good enough for you.  You'll question hitboxes.
If you lose you'll blame the flavor of the month champion.  You'll hate having an incompetent, berating teammate.  You'll be bored and frustrated wondering why you aren't playing something fun.
The gameplay is not fun.  If the fun you can have with a game is determined by those two statements above (and it is) you cannot have fun.  Its simply not possible.  Sure you might get a rush out of killing your opponent out of a tough 1v1.  More often than not you're wondering why X skill's hitbox is so big or how Y skill has zero windup to react to it.
Characters play different only insofar that their pacing is different.  Ashka for example is slow but hard hitting with ranged attacks.  Ezmo is quick but soft hitting with ranged attacks.  There's very little differentiation between the characters compared to Bloodline Champions.  Try to think of some defining feature of each character and you really can't.  Sure you can point to a skill that nobody has (like Ezmo's straight line heal) but it exists in other paced forms.  Ashka can heal as well but again more slowly and bursty.
There's no satisfactory variety.  There's no fun that isn't determined by everything you can't influence.  The gameplay itself is not actually fun regardless of that.  You move and shoot out similar abilities against humans who do similar things ad nausem.  Its the same tedium as all other MOBAs with the fat trimmed out but the meat is rotten because MOBAs inherently are not fun.
That's why these games have grinding systems in place.  Skinner boxes are "fun" for humans.  But would they really be necessary if the game itself was fun.  Probably not.

That is one of the game series that when I hear a new Bioshock game is coming out, I get so excited.
All of the defaults of the 1st Bioshock got fixed, the enjoyment is at maximum level.
Bioshock 2 is the direct following of the first but you don't need to play it to understand the story.
You are Subject Delta, one of the first prototype of a Big Daddy protecting a Little Sister: Eleanor Lamb, the daughter of the new leader of the Ryan Industries: Sofia Lamb. However, this woman wants her daughter back, she sends a Mind Control Plasmid over the Subject Delta and pushes him to shoot his head. The story begins 10 years after, the Subject Delta revives by getting in a Vita-Chamber helped by a Little Sister and during the whole adventure you will find that you have a powerful connection with Eleanor Lamb.
When the 1st Bioshock was a little boring because you only had to save Little Sisters, here you have plenty things to do.
- A great multiplayer mode with maps of Bioshock 1 & 2 and new plasmids, but the old Windows Live server closed and it's now working by peer2peer so it's lagging pretty much with some people but still playable.
- The Big Sister, the new monster of the game, appears only when you save all the Little Sisters. She is really powerful and has the only plasmids you don't have.
- It's now possible to upgrade the weapons and use techniques of combat.
- The DLC Minerva's Den shows the end of Rapture.
Afterall, this is the most complete Bioshock ever made even though Bioshock Infinite is also good but, it all started here.
Everyone of you should have played this game, atleast once.

24 patches and still an unpolished turd.
I've been one of the people that preordered the game, fully expecting bugs to happen, same as with all the previous X series games. I've been with the series since X-BtF. I've made it through the glitchy first versions of X2 and X3:Reunion alike. I had fun.
Rebirth is different. The engine itself shows potential, but everything tacked onto it is a mess. Even completely disregarding the bugs in the economy and storyline, the game is still bad. The UI design is horrid and needs a complete overhaul. Most of the features that made the previous games great are missing entirely or dumbed down to the point of uselessness. Many of the new features that were tacked on are badly thought out or lackluster.
Yisha is the most obnoxious sidekick I ever encountered in games period. The fact that on the first days after release mods were popping up to shut her the hell up speaks volumes. Same for Ren's terribly repetitive lines every time you talk to an NPC. The entire trading/station scanning concept is a horrendous cluster♥♥♥♥. The hacking/smalltalk minigame is ridiculous.
Despite promises to the contrary, modders still don't have all the tools they need to polish this turd. The playership is hardcoded to the Skunk. The UI is all in compiled lua that is more or less impossible to modify without the sources, which the Modders still don't have. The engine itself shows great potential, but Egosoft still isn't really letting the community at it.
All that that leaves one with is a semi-decent space shooter. And there are other games that do this a lot better, for a much lower pricetag.
Scripting support aaside, it has all the marks of a rushed and terribly botched console port, despite being developed exclusively for the PC. Patches are slowly fixing this: We now get targeting hotkeys for the keyboard, for one. Ha.
There are two rays of light, though: While most of the modding community already gave up on this game, some are still working away at it, and many of the smaller annoyances have been fixed thanks to the community. Egosoft has a stellar record when it comes to supporting their games even years after release, even adding new content long after releasing a patch that completely removed DRM, both for TC and AP.
I'd say with another year or so and a solid UI revamp, this game could truly shine. Let's just hope Egosoft doesn't go bankrupt by then, and that they don't wait with opening up their Lua sources for too long.
For now, though: Very definitely not recommended. Grab it at the next WInter Sale.

Fluid combat mechanics.

Cons:

Single-player only (for now).

BioShock: Remastered or Re-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized?
What the remaster devs did right: They added new higher polygon models and higher res textures to almost everything in the game, the post processing effects are much sharper and overall better looking here than in the original, and now there's anti-aliasing for those who hate jagged edges everywhere. Furthermore, new assets were added to increase the level of detail in some scenes making the game look more modern, this is very apparent in the opening descent into Rapture, good show Blind Squirrel Games.
What they did wrong: They compressed the original's outstanding audio, meaning the game doesn't sound as crisp and haunting as it originally did. That is a big shame since audio is key to this games atmostphere, tone and a big part of the overall experience. There are also bugs in the Remaster that didn't happen in the original (enemies ignoring you, delayed reaction in animations, for example, freeze someone then have them actually stop moving more than a second after they're supposed to be frozen), audio cutting out, skipping or doubling over itself, mouse acceleration issues, graphical oddities (textures not loading properly causing blurry low res ones in their place) and an overall lack of polish on a product that was released over 9 years ago in a working state. To top this off, bugs that were in the original version of the game have not been addressed in the slightest in the remaster... oh boy.
“A man chooses, a slave obeys”. I urge you to choose to play the original and not this remaster, unless all of the issues listed above are fixed, as well as different ones other people have reported (such as numerous crashes & mouse issues) I cannot at the moment recommend this version of the game. If you already own the original BioShock and have this one as a free download, try it out and make your own conclusions, that's what I did. But for people who are considering buying this or the original, go with the original, it’s a better way to experience BioShock, the way the original developers intended.
*This review was based on my subjective experiences with the game, and your experiences may differ, for better or for worse.*

I love this game. I have played through this game once a year since it came out in 2010, although every other time I did so on the PS3, this is my first go on PC.
No doubt over the years you've heard polarizing reception over this game, lots of stuff about how it's a "long hallway simulator" and "the worst FF game ever". While I will concede that most of the game is extremely linear and that it's nothing like any of the other FF installments, I have to say that it's nothing resembling a bad game.
For one, it's got a hell of a battle system. Unlike other FF games, where player agency is minimal and you can win by holding down the confirm button after a certain point, that simply isn't possible in this game. If you don't pay attention, you will die. Battles are fast paced and demand your attention and thought to win. This fact, combined with the fact that the game consistently level caps you to keep you from ever getting overpowered (until you've beaten the game that is) makes this easily the most challenging Final Fantasy title since the 8-bit era.
The cast is pretty good, though not the best in FF history (it's hard to beat Cloud and friends, or Zidane and company). They're pretty memorable and all very well fleshed out by the end. They're mostly likable and the game does a pretty good job of letting you know who they are and what drives them.
The plot is confusing on the surface, but if you take time to pay attention and care what's going on (or just play through the game multiple times to catch everything you missed the first time around, like myself) it's a pretty well thought out tale with an impressively deep lore constructed. A good thing to keep in mind is that the story has one overarching prevailing theme throughout: Destiny Vs Free Will. If you keep this in mind the game is a lot easier to comprehend, particularly the final hours.
As far as presentation goes, this game is absolutely gorgeous. The art direction is second to none, the soundtrack is ambient and fitting, and it is one of the most polished, bug-free games you will ever play. Everything works as it should and you will never find yourself losing a battle or having to load because something in the game went awry. And yes, while the game is linear for the first 20 hours or so, there are very good, legit story reasons as to why this is, but to say anymore on that would to be going into spoiler territory. The game does a good job of constantly pushing the player forward. Think of it as an experience similar to an action/adventure game like Uncharted in JRPG form. I know that's hard to imagine but it works surprisingly well in this game.
All in all I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes beautiful story driven games with well develop characters and a deep lore with fast paced battles.

I should preface this by saying that even though I can't recommend this game, it is by no means terrible. Firstly, I will start off with what I liked:
+Flight is much more enjoyable than in Saints row IV
+Even though most of the powers are the same, they changed them up enough that combat felt different
+Cool new weapons
+Musical
+Decent Story
+Saints Row humor
Now for the sad truth. Those positives were not enough. Flight was fun, but Saints Row isn't a flight simulator. I enjoyed the new guns and powers, but I don't play Saints Row for the combat (that's why I play Dark Souls.) The story was fine, and as always I enjoyed the satirical humor of the Saints Row games, but the story was far too short (less than 4 hours froms start to finish) and so there wasn't that much humor. It's hard to have many funny moments when the game itself doesn't have very moments at all. The musical scene was fantastic, but it was just one scene with a single reference later. The missions themselves were never bad, but they didn't impress either. Saints Row has always been good at steadily building up the craziness and zaniness so that every time you think you've seen it all, something new leaves you wondering. With Gat out of Hell, it feels like they through everything they had into the setting and the single musical scene. Once you accept the fact that you're in hell and have powers, the game doesn't really have any more surprises.
If you're not like me and get your enjoyment from being a completionist, then this game may keep you interested, but I had trouble staying interested in a game that seemed terrified of trying anything new. The game is cheaper, but even with its low price, I wouldn't say it's worth it until it goes on sale for 75% off. It is being sold as a third of a Saints Row Game, but in terms of content it has less than a fifth.

Ironically, the reason why I decided to try Magic Duels again was that Hearthstone, the game I compared it to (and praised) in original review, had become a horrible experience for me. Without going too much into it, HS is filled to brim with insane powercreep, broken mechanics, horrible formats and the worst card-collection experience overrall with a forced rotation that makes your past collection useless.
So, I come back to Magic Duels with pretty optimistic expectations - I'm glad that the technical issues that plagued the game have been solved, and the exact things I want, the depth of counterplay and variety of logical mechanics are there. So why haven't I changed the review for a positive one?
The problem is, the game still feels extremely limited. While the game supports counterplay with time to react to your enemies actions, the game is still extremely casual-ized compared to its IRL counterpart. The limited card pools and rarity restrictions force decks to play on very broad strategies - and without BO3 format there's still zero reason to play tech cards over universally functional ones.
Another problem still is the card collecting system. Its really hard to actually upgrade the powerlevel of decks you're intially given since you can never craft a bunch of cards you need. Instead, you're forced to grind card packs that give you single copies of random cards until you little by little collect all the cards of specific collection (4 copies of each common, 3 of each uncommon, 2 rares, 1 mythic)
So, to sum it up - Magic Duels isn't worse than HS, but it still fails to reach the depth and competitiveness of the original product. For those interested in what I'm referring to, check out 'Cockatrice', the free community-created platform, or offical MTG online - or go outside and find your local game store!
I might have had too high expectations for this game considering it's title and genre. But when your best comparison is Heartstone, this game fails to deliver. I was really hoping for a free-to-play steam multiplayer with rules and skill ceiling as high as original MtG, but Duels is as limited in it's card/mecanic pool as Heartstone.
The latter of games also tackles the 'card gathering' part better, as you have no control over what cards you get on Duels. This resulted in that i had zero ways to even try different kinds of borderline janky tactics (that most often are the most hilarious).
I also really regret that we still have no implementation of an actual 'competitive' possibilty with BO3 and sideboards to actually give you a chance to fight against bad matchups.
BUT focusing on the Duels, it's pretty buggy by itself, with lots of visual glitches and connection problems (you need a constant internet access to do anything worthwhile in this game) and overrall bad servers. There's a lot of wrong in this game, the highest being the daily credit limits (??). Also, most of the achievements (and cards that are mandatory for them) are impossible to get without grinding this game for ages.

Do you like the idea of Hearthstone but hate all the cards that "summon a random minion" or do a random amount of damage to random targets?  Remember how Magic: The Gathering is a much better card game but never had a good free-to-play equivalent to compete with Hearthstone?  Well, this is their answer.  It doesn't trounce Hearthstone in every respect, but it does fare better in a good number of use cases.
Pros:
* Magic is a better card game than Hearthstone
* Magic Duels has a better business model; you can acquire all cards for free very quickly and easily, with no chance of getting cards that you don't need, since it won't give you more duplicates than you can use
* 1v1 duels are every bit as good as they should be, and you can play Magic with people online at any time with a deck of your own design, for free.  Finally!
Cons:
* If you lose your online connection, you won't be able to save any progress or earn any currency; this makes sense, but server uptime was a real problem for the first week of release.  It's much better now, and it hardly every disconnects.
* There's no draft or "arena" mode like Hearthstone, so you're only using custom decks.
* I haven't personally used the feature, but I hear that Two-Headed Giant mode is lacking some crucial communication features.
* There are some restrictions on deck building that go beyond the tabletop version of Magic, but it's not all that bothersome to me personally.  Instead of 4 of any card excluding Legendaries, it's 4 of any common, 3 of any uncommon, 2 of any rare, and 1 of any mythic rare.
* While this game is out on multiple platforms, you can't make a deck on one platform and play it on another, like Hearthstone allows.  This is a huge bummer, but I'd still rather have Magic in one location that Hearthstone in all of them.

A definite high point for the series. I've played all the Hitmans and love them all, but I must say Absolution is the best (yes, even better than Blood Money). First off, they replaced the garbage clone narrative with an interesting story featuring 47 protecting a young girl at his former handler, Diana's, dying wish. On top of that, the game has a good balance between stealth and full on guns-blazing action because of said story. I must say that the high point of the game for me was the Attack of the Saints mission, especially the corn field sequence. I was very pleased with the way disguses were handled in the game. I always felt that the Hitman games became way too easy after you got a disguse, but Absolution fixed it by allowing enemies/ NPCs wearing the same disguse to see through it if they look at you long enough. Another new mechanic I enjoyed was the instinct which allows you too blend in with your enemies, utilize the new point shooting mechanic (another new addition I enjoyed lots), and see points of interest, enemies, targets, etc. In conclusion, Absolution should be played by not only fans of the series, but those looking for a game that gives you freedom on how to handle things the way you want. Definitely pick it up on a sale or even at full price if you have the money.

Rivals of Aether is a Smash-esque fighting game that takes the same winning simple-but-deep systems of the game it's inspired by (Super Smash Bros. Melee) and refines them so they're both more accessible to newcomers and more integral to gameplay.
Seriously--have you tried wavedashing reliably in Smash Bros. Melee? It's pretty frigging hard! You have to practice, practice, practice, for hours or days to perform that technique reliably. Rivals walks into the room and says, "Screw that, such an integral tech shouldn't be impossible. Here's a tutorial, here are the inputs, bam. You're wavedashing. Congrats."
That's not to say the game doesn't have depth, though. Heck no. The character-specific tech in this game was lovingly built in by developers who clearly know how to make characters that are balanced and varied without sacrificing fun. The game is not fun.
If you win you will be satisfied you didn't encounter a flavor of the month champion.  You'll love having a competent, non-berating teammate.  You'll be bored because your enemies just weren't good enough for you.  You'll question hitboxes.
If you lose you'll blame the flavor of the month champion.  You'll hate having an incompetent, berating teammate.  You'll be bored and frustrated wondering why you aren't playing something fun.
The gameplay is not fun.  If the fun you can have with a game is determined by those two statements above (and it is) you cannot have fun.  Its simply not possible.  Sure you might get a rush out of killing your opponent out of a tough 1v1.  More often than not you're wondering why X skill's hitbox is so big or how Y skill has zero windup to react to it.
Characters play different only insofar that their pacing is different.  Ashka for example is slow but hard hitting with ranged attacks.  Ezmo is quick but soft hitting with ranged attacks.  There's very little differentiation between the characters compared to Bloodline Champions.  Try to think of some defining feature of each character and you really can't.  Sure you can point to a skill that nobody has (like Ezmo's straight line heal) but it exists in other paced forms.  Ashka can heal as well but again more slowly and bursty.
There's no satisfactory variety.  There's no fun that isn't determined by everything you can't influence.  The gameplay itself is not actually fun regardless of that.  You move and shoot out similar abilities against humans who do similar things ad nausem.  Its the same tedium as all other MOBAs with the fat trimmed out but the meat is rotten because MOBAs inherently are not fun.
That's why these games have grinding systems in place.  Skinner boxes are "fun" for humans.  But would they really be necessary if the game itself was fun.  Probably not.

Hollow Knight is a beautifully hand-drawn metroidvania that is equal parts fun, difficult, cute, and horrifying. All of the 100-plus characters are animated to be adorable and/or hideous, and the different areas of the humongous map each have their own art styles with some of the best use of parallax I've ever seen. One area has ghosts floating in the foreground, while others have sprawling jungles or caves with layers that move independently of each other to create much livelier levels than most 2D games can offer. After only seeing videos and screenshots of the game's first area, a dreary cave where everything is a shade of blue, I had my breath taken away the moment I got to the second area, a jungle. It was so colorful and alive.
On top of that, the soundtrack is one of the most memorable and whimsical scores I've heard in a long time. There are tracks here that I'd rank beside the music of Zelda and Star Wars. It is that damned good. Even the general sound design is great, as every enemy has different realistic scuttling sounds, and many characters speak in seemingly made-up languages I found myself quoting by the end of the game. One character you'll constantly run into is a cartographer, who can always be located by following pieces of paper found on the ground and the song he hums.
It's a real gemail and an instant buy  for me if I was you I would totally buy it and I highly recommend it to all of you reading this.

Welcome back to the castle! This game is a classic. Despite this game being released in November of 2001, it's still a 'must play' if you're a fan of classic first person shooters. Final verdict: This game is worth the buy for the price. The story is phenomenal, the game play is decent, and the level design is really impressive (for a 2001 game). Give it a go, if you have the funds!

Double Damage was kind enough to sent us a review copy of this game. We're very impressed with it. It's old school fun in a modern setting. The ships designs remind me very much of the Terran Trade Authority Handbook SPACECRAFT 2000 to 2100AD By Stewart Cowley.
The game is an open world sandbox with 14 galaxies. You fly around in big capital ships, which you can upgrade or trade in for a better/larger one. The ships can mine, collect, transport and fight. Mining is done in astroid fields scattered all over the galaxies. Each galaxy is full of spacestations, belonging to one of the 4 or 5 factions (sorry don't know for sure if it's 4 or 5). At the spacestations you can sell your mined items, but also buy and sell a lot of other commodeties. You can also upgrade and buy ships there, hire mercenaries to support you and select missions you want to play. Factions offer missions there and by doing them you will grow in popularity with them, while loosing popularity with others. The less popular you are with a faction, the more likely they will attack you when you encounter them in space. When you are really unpopular with a faction, they will not allow you to dock at their spacestations. Throughout the game you can gain or loose popularity however you see fit. Missions can be focussed on trading, mining, defending or helping others, smuggling and battling.
The ships are quite cool, all of them have a bit of an 70's - 80's scifi game to them. You can upgrade their strength, equipment, cargo space, weapons and much more. Quite some options available. To make things easy, the ships more one a 2D plane, in a 3D world. This works very well for this game. The act more like a ship then a plain. They have a main engine, sub warp enigne (booster), warp engine and a interstellar warp engine. Weapons consist of turrets and broadside cannons. You can let them fire pretty much automatic, or take control of indivual turrets. Fighting is done like sail ships do, facing sideways and firing away :D
You can fly around anywhere you like and while doing so you will encounter loot, pirates, astroid fields, others in need of assistance and more. This is all aside from the missions you can do. There are also guilds in the game, joining one or more will give you access to special equipment and ships. The ships you can fly in the game range from firefly size ships to battlestart galactica capital ships and beyond.
On top of all this, there's a full story with all kinds of missions and mystery going on. You can focus on the story, do it once in a while or even neglect it completely. Besides the main story, there are a few smaller subplots as well.
The best thing about all of this is the freedom you have. Go anywhere you like, play the way you like. Be a pirate, trader, merchant and so on. Follow a story, neglects, do side mission, explore and so on. Mix it all together. The game is really easy to get into, easy to play and offers all kinds of levels of mission, with a very low risk to a high risk. The further you fly into the universe to more hostile it gets and the more advanced upgrades and ships you discover. Easy to play and to pick, yet offering a good challenge as well. Flying is easy, just like driving a car. Battling is really done awesome, you get the whole star trek, battlestar galactica, star wars feel when doing so. No puny little fighter..... no massive firepower :D
I guess that pretty much covers it, sure I forgot a thing or two. Is it worth it? Yes, without a doubt. The whole concept is done innovative and very well. Everything blends in and just works well together. It's a very welcome break from all the massive space mmo's and all the small spaceship focussed game.

It was inevitable that a financial success like the original Bioshock would get a sequel. I wasn't overwhelmed with the first game of the series; I thought it average at best, despite some occasionally interesting architecture and some neat water effects. The second in the series is more of the same... or perhaps less.
Whereas the original Bioshock tried to be an action/RPG, the sequel disposes of most of the role-playing baggage; the game throws you into the action from the start and doesn't let up until the end. There are still some lingering remnants -you still upgrade your weapons and plasmids as choice (and collected resources) allow- but the mission structure has been much simplified. There are no branching quests; Bioshock 2 is a linear corridor shooter to the end and is the better game for it.
Better than the original, anyway; it still sometimes lets its style take precedence over story and gameplay (the final "oh my god, the place is about to explode; here are a bunch of hour-long quests you need to complete in the meanwhile" a perfect example of this). But the weapons and powers are more interesting, the architecture is still occasionally wonderful and the water effects are both neat and more plentiful. It may be damning the game with faint praise to say its a superior game to the first but given my low expectations I was pleasantly surprised. Hardly a classic, lacking innovation but competent. That's a step in the right direction, anyway.
Feeling like unimaginative leftovers cut from the original, Bioshock 2 lacks the novelty of the first game. Too many of its levels and bosses seemed to have been put in more to pad out the gameplay than to advance the plot, which was shallow enough to begin with. The only vaguely interesting bit was (spoiler?) near the end when you get to see the world through the eyes of the waif-like "Little Sisters", but even then it's too short and too limited in scope to redeem the game. The "Minerva's Den" DLC fared a bit better - at least there was some new artwork and weapons - but the gameplay remained tired and uninteresting. And I quit the "Protector Trials" - which extend the least- interesting parts of the game (the Defend the Sister battles) to tiresome lengths - mere minutes after starting.

Defy Gravity is a platformer. You might say puzzle platformer, but I’d just call it a challenging platformer in the vein of Super Meat Boy or Blood of the Werewolf, though Defy Gravity isn’t quite that infuriatingly difficult as those two. The gameplay was challenging enough to be rewarding but easy enough to be fun, I thought it was a good mix. The checkpoints were much better as well, being more frequent. If you die, you basically just start right before the last little challenge. Levels are fairly short. I think with SMB you have to start at the beginning of the level and BotW there are checkpoints but they can be pretty long at times. This game doesn’t really have any enemies either, besides some orbs, spiky orbs, and some sort of ships that shoot missiles or whatever. I don’t really remember about SMB, but BotW had more traditional enemies and super bosses. This didn’t have any of that. Mostly you are avoiding friggin laser beams on the floor or wall or ceiling. Sometimes you had to ride a platform through the level.
The way it all works is that you have a duel gravity gun. You can shoot attractive gravity and reflective gravity. Attractive obviously pulls you toward it, so you can jump, shoot that and get sucked to it and then dispel it as you approach it to give you a little jump bust. Reflective will bounce you away, like a rocket jump. You have a double jump in the air. Pretty simple. You hold the LMB or RMB until you want it to stop, aim with the mouse. Movement with A/D. I don’t think a controller would help the controls, but they didn’t work bad. I think Q dispelled the attractive gravity, though it didn’t seem I could dispel reflective. Shift put up a gravity shield so they didn’t affect you. Sometimes a level would shoot it’s own gravity wells. The more challenging levels were when you had to ride the platform, which was propelled by your gravity gun, and also avoid everything else. Problem was that the platform would continue through walls if you weren’t careful, whereas you would not. Challenging.
Presentation was pretty mediocre/cheap. It didn’t look BAD, but it was far from a pretty game too.
I would recommend the game for people that like this type of game, especially for the price. It’s normally only 2$, which isn’t bad at all and it frequently goes on sale for like 90% off. I don’t mind it, but it’s not my favorite by far. So I played until I had the first three achievements (38%) for progress and then quit. I think it was about a half hour. There was no indication of what level I was on or how many there are total. Which is annoying as you don’t know how long the game is going to be. Though I suppose most games are that way, huh?

So here's my feelings on the game in 3 catagories...
Gameplay:

The gravity gun is a very interesting mechanic, left click fires a blue ball that sucks things in and the right click was an orange ball that pushed things away. Graphics:
Not really an important part of this game as I'd have been just as happy with 8bit. The graphics are smooth and made for 1080p screens. The animations are basic with very few frames but this isnt really a con to the game. Really I think the artwork done for this game fit the theme and looked rather good for what it is.
Sound:
The music for this game is rather nice, one moment its calm and relaxing and then in some levels the music speeds up a bit for escape levels. One nice thing I'd like to note is that the sound enemies make when they bounce off of walls is there but not distracting. That I believe is very important and I'm very happy that they were careful about the volume of that ting noise they make.
Overall I can definately recomend this game to casual and hardcore gamers alike. 10/10

(Review based on preview copy provided by developers)
Rebel Galaxy is a Space Opera with some pretty legendary names behind its creation, and it definitely shows. There's no question that it's worth the asking price of $20 USD - though it does have its pros and cons worth considering if it's the perfect fit for you, as well as some gameplay aspects some people will enjoy more than others.
----
Important Notes:
- This game involves trading, mining, and most of all - combat.
- Combat is based on Naval combat, not standard 6-degree space combat, you will be using broadside cannons, ramming, and turrets for your capital ship on a horizontal plane (non capital ships use the full 6 degrees of freedom, but you don't get to fly those :P). This leads to interesting, yet still very satisfying, combat.
- You have access to a lot of control with your ship, a lot of choices, including what tools you employ and how your weapons behave in battle - and they definitely have an impact on how you play.
-You also have the ability to toy with alliances and factions, to change the system (improving/destroying your relations with different factions changes how you play the game)
- Combat, either through Bounties, Missions, or Random Encounters will be your fastest way to gather resources and progress - though Trading/Mining are definitely still somewhat viable options.
----
Pros:
- Good visuals, with satisfying explosions, weapon fire, etc. And visible damage on your ship.
- Amazing audio assets (and the ability to customize the audio if you want). Voice Acting is "good", not stellar, but the explosions, music, etc. are insanely well chosen.
- Combat caters to both the casual captain and the aggressive player ( you can hang out on the fringe of battles, letting the automated turrets do the work, or you can dive in ramming/blasting with your broadsides, while ducking and dodging through swarms of bullets)
- Solid story, while it won't win any awards, it's on par with Blizzard storylines ( "Okay" campaign story, Great universe )
- Lots of freedom of choice... and travel. Aided by procedural generation of the sectors - so no 2 playthroughs are the same.
- Fairly well optimized (sad that I have to note this, but compared to a lot of other games with similar visual fidelity lately - this one barely taxes my system at max settings)
----
Cons:
- Can get repetative after a while (go to point a, Kill stuff, get money, repeat) - but this tends to happen after the 10-20 hour mark for me. It does follow a formula similar to Diablo/Torchlight/etc. in that regard.
- Can be slow paced at times, especially when a mission spawns more than 5000-6000 sm away, there is no fast travel within a sector, and while warp is fine for medium length trips, you will sometimes run into the issue of "staring at the back of your ship twiddling your thumbs".
- "Out of Game" options menu... each time you launch you have the choice of changing the options, but you can't really change them in-game - so you might be restarting a few times to find the settings perfect for you.
----
Works well with a controller or mouse & keyboard, despite their recommendations.

It's everything you know and love about Saints Row III and IV in one affordable package. It's a direct sequel to Saints Row IV and even reads your character file so the introduction has your old Saints Row IV character intact, including the voice you selected. This actually drew me in to the story quicker and was a nice touch.
You play as Johnny Gat (and possibly other characters as you're allowed to switch with Kinzie right from the get go) I'm certain at some point you'll have your old Saints Row IV character available to you.
Either way, the game is mindless running around and slaughtering just like the previous games... nothing new here. They've adopted the "Super Hero" system from Saints IV so expect to be running up walls and flying over the map again. Run and do your fetch quests and level up Johnny to 20. Yes this time the level cap is set at 20, again this is a pocket version of Saints Row IV, so don't expect a lot of content.
Even if the game does lack in variety and content when compared to the previous entries, the creativity of the plot doesn't get cut short. It's still a hilarious franchise and keeps on finding new ways to keep it feeling fresh... despite the aforementioned similarities.

I haven't played much of it but I've already ran in to Black Beard the pirate, William Shakespere and Vlad the Impaler (Dracula) as my first batch of homies to help out. So far I'm digging it. If you enjoyed Saints Row IV, you'll probably love this as well because it's more of the same, only different. I grabbed it for a small discount price and it's definitely worth the 20 dollar tag.

Bioshock Remastered has two elements in it's name. One of these is good and the other is not. Bioshock was and is an amazing game. This remaster is bugged and lazy. I feel obliged to leave a negative review, for steam reviews are a way to send a message to developers. For PC this remaster is pointless. The issues with mouse acceleration and such could have been fixed with a patch (Not to mention that they were not fixed on release of the remaster but have been now). Not enough assets have been improved and the remaster is a technical mess.
There are numerous techical issues with the game. By far the biggest is with the audio. Sounds are all over the place. Often sounds come through walls or from the wrong side. Easiest this is to note when switching weapons: Sometimes the sound comes from left speaker, sometimes right and sometimes from both. One area seems to miss most of the ambient noises. It's really mixed up and makes it hard to play.
Another issue is that everything gets stuck to walls. Worst are the Big Daddies who are the most iconic aspect of this game. They constantly get stuck and just jitter in place. This makes defeating them really easy. Animations looks old and wonky and this hurts the atmosphere of the game. With care these could have been fixed.
The game also crashed atleast three times. All of these were in the menus which is strange.
The download is almost 4 times larger than original Bioshock, but the game looks just as i remembered Bioshock to look. I'm sure if compared side to side, the remaster has sharper textures, but polygons have not been added. This is unless you count barnacles and glowy jellyfishes here and there.
If the controller is enabled, the game switches to wrong button promps at random. Textures load with a delay or sometimes refuse to load. Mouse sensitivity goes insane in cutscenes where player has some control. Quicksaving and loading takes few seconds even on SSD. While not huge issues, these are the little touches that remasters should fix.
It's such a shame that this is the remaster we get. A lot more could and should have been done.
Real short review, The Last Remnant are one of those games where you struggle to keep playing but the pay off for finishing the game is the reward.

Did you like Bioshock? Then you'll like Bioshock 2! They're really rather similar. The biggest difference is that since you are playing as one of the first Big Daddies, instead of your options being "rescue" or "harvest" little sisters, your options are now "adopt" or "harvest", with adoption requiring you to either drop off the little sister at a port hole for a small amount of ADAM or you set them down near a corpse and defend them from splicers while they gather ADAM for you. I'm a nice guy with a thirst for ADAM so I saved all the little sisters and gathered all the ADAM that I could, so I spent a lot of time fighting off splicers.
I played on medium difficulty, and maybe I'm spoiled from recently replaying Bioshock on easy, but Bioshock 2 seems significantly more difficult. You can't carry as many health kits as you could in the first game, and I seem to remember the first one auto-using health kits when your health bottomed out until you ran out of kits. No such luck this time. The tradeoff they made here is that every weapon can be used for a melee attack, rather than having to switch to the melee weapon, which in this game is a massive drill.
Now in Bioshock, the melee weapon was traditional Irrational Games wrench. With the electric jolt plasmid (the first plasmid in the game), and the wrench (the first weapon in the game), you could almost beat it without picking up a single other weapon. It was a super effective combo that only got better with support tonics. You have no such luck in Bioshock 2. In fact, as massive drills go, it takes a couple support tonics to make it feel like it's doing some real damage. It's kind of a bummer.
The plasmids got a healthy balancing. Winter blast is far more useful than I remember it being in the first game, and even insect swarm is more fun! I didn't really use some of the less hands-on plasmids, like decoy, or scout, or hypnotize. You get the same eight slots for them as in the first game. The tonics are better handled this time too, with no distinction being made between them. You just get a number of slots and you can fill them with whatever tonics you like without regard for their purpose. A lot of them return from the first game, with a handful of new ones suited for the changes in weaponry. Wrench lurker became drill lurker, and what not.
There's another for getting all of the weapon upgrades, and towards the end I was beginning to get nervous because I had a lot of upgrades unfulfilled but I found them all regardless. Apparently you won't get every weapon up to full upgrades by the end of the game, so you should be choosy with what weapons you want to use. The game has a nasty habit of giving you a new weapon right after you've come across an upgrade station, and that kind of sucks because you can't un-upgrade a weapon and then use that upgrade station on the new gun.
Hacking has changed for the better, unless you've got slow reflexes. Instead of being a game of pipe-dream, it's a simple needle that goes back and forth and you just need to hit the A button when it's over a green section. Sometimes you need to hit a number of green slots to succeed, and if you hit a red slot you set off the security systems, and if you hit a white slot you take damage. It's easier and faster than the first game, and from the start you're given a tool to hack machines from a distance, which replaces the need from the first game to shock them with electric jolt and then run up and hack them.
If you've liked Bioshock, this one's a no-brainer. It's more of the first game, but better, with only a little cognitive dissonance from making a sequel to a game that wasn't made to have a sequel. If you didn't like Bioshock, you probably won't like Bioshock 2. It doesn't change enough from the original formula to make it a different game. If you never played the first game, I'd recommend going through it before hopping on Bioshock 2. It's a fantastic game, it's cheap, and Bioshock 2 basically assumes you played the first game and doesn't make an effort to explain the world of Rapture again.

If you can get it with the Humble Bundle 8, do so, ottherwise, wait for a sale. Now about the game itself:
It's a nifty little physics-based puzzle platform that actually has a really awesome core mechanic: The ability to slice and dice objects and then manipulate them with a grappling hook or a high-powered rocket. It's incredible fun, intuitive, and innovative. The graphics and aesthetics of the game are incredible as well, with tons and tons of work put into to giving the game a non-realistic, but consistent look. It also has a small set  of very interesting indie tracks to go along with the dry visuals of the desert.
However there are two somewhat major negatives, one of which has to do with why I said what I said in that very first sentence of this recommendation:
First, the game is very short, two hours is about the average playtime required to beat it if you look around a bit here and there for secrets, and second, I must've seriously missed something, because the "BIG CHARACTER" promised on the Steam store and GreenManGaming pages is not there at all. As much as I don't want to say this, I did not laugh a single time at any of the dialogue and the characters not much more more than text-spouting heads and plot devices.
All in all, a great little puzzle game to get if you can find a deal on it somewhere as long as you like the overall audio-visual style and don't expect or want Portal-like humor and character.

If you are a fan of the Final Fantasy style games and wanted to play them on a larger scale, then this is the game for you.
You play a guy who's sister has been kidnapped near a large war. As you help the prince in his battles he tries to help you find your missing sister. A simple plot with a good amount of storyline for several of the party members.
The game has you form groups to go into battle. On your turn, each group can do one type of move. The number of people in that group will each do that move if the have it available. If not, they will just sit there. Also, if the leader of the group is incapacitated the group cannot do any actions.
In the beginning the battles seem pretty small and not worth it. As you get further in and Flanking and Intercepting are utilized more, it becomes a very good RPG mixed with strategy. You caan easily go from winning to utter failure if flanked.
The graphics are quite good. Nothing to special but definitely not bad. There are several special moves "Summon style" that will shake things up a bit. They cannot be called at will so you have to plan accordingly.
The thing that sucks about this game is the fact that you do not have all your skills available during the fight. Depending on how much AP you have, where you are in the battle, what the status of the groups, and whether you are flanking/flanked. will determine what pops up for you to chose from. Meaning your healers may not even have the heal option show up right when you need it or as a pre-emptive tactic.
The game is long and the fights get longer. There are several special creatures that are very difficult to defeat.

I got this game for free because I owned the original. I also want to say that this is the first version I have played on the PC so my comparisons will be made from the version I played on the 360.
I loved the original BioShock. I played it on the 360 a long time ago and it was beautiful. The story was great, it scared the crap out of me at certain spots, the scenery - Rapture - was just amazing, and there was only one bug I found while trying to get an achievement. The Remastered game is not as enjoyable to play.
The Bad:
- The first bug I encountered was just after installing the game. I clicked play on steam and it crashed. No logo appeared or anything it just crashed with an error saying that something went wrong and asked me if I wanted to reset the settings to default. I clicked yes and it loaded up after I clicked play again.
- This version has one audio bug that is found multiple times throughout the game from what I've played so far. Audio will start to play then half way through it goes back to the begining of the clip and will do that usually one more time before it finishes playing the whole audio clip.
- Another bug that has shown up a few times is when I die the wall closest to me will disappear and I can see the ocean and buildings around me.
- Another issue that I've had and that has to do with the targeting while using plasmids. I have snuck up on enemies at very close range a few times and hit them with a plasmid but it goes right through them or hits them but won't do anything.
- A huge bug that irritated me was during the first time you meet a big daddy the game speeds up the mouse movement but at the same time the graphics get really choppy. I almost quit playing at that point because of how bad it was.
Those are just the bugs I've found so far and I'm not that deep into the game.
The Good:
- The audio sounds a lot better than I remember.
- The graphics look nicer.
- I like the concept museum. It has a lot of cool images and figures you can look over.
I would suggest buying the original version of this game over the Remastered. I'm surprised with how many bugs I've found during the standard play through that it was signed off as good to sell. That is really really bad on the company for pushing it out the door or just not paying attention to the issues that are there. I'm going to go back to the original on the PC and see the quality of it compared to the quality of this version. I'll post a review of it when I have time. Till then good luck and don't by this version.

I've been playing this game the entire afternoon, and I'd say that it is a pretty decent game with a lot of fun. As a expansion of Saints Row 4, the gaming style is very similar to the vanilla game, so is the ridiculous story. Now some religious element has been added into the game. If you are not offended I'd say that the game is very fun.
Story: I'll save the spoiler for here, Let's just say that this game uses a lot of lazy cutscene plot similar to the Enter of Dominatrix DLC. I'm cool with that as this is not a complete standalone game. I'm happy that the game loaded by SR4 character instead of putting a default guy as the Boss. There is a funny Disney-style musical drama. Some of the endings are pretty cool.
Environment: The New Hades is an ugly city because it is hell. Aside from the theme color issue, I'd say that the new city is a nice try. It is still somewhat similar to the virtual Steelport, but I feel that they are trying to bring Stillwater back, which is good. The civilians are all tortured souls (boring), but the city is well designed and had a variety of places.
Gameplay: The flying function is the main theme of the game. I think it is a perfect combination of SR3 skydiving and SR4 gilding. Very fun and satisfying experience once you learn how to play it. Similar to SR4, the vehicle gameplay is pretty weak. I feel like the enemy in this game is stronger than SR4 and some of the activities are challenging. HOWEVER, some of the OP upgrades from SR3 have come back, so eventually the game will be easy enough.
Long-term gameplay: the amount of data cluster is monsterous, and there are a huge bunch of challenge if you want to complete them. The city is a nice place to explore due to its complex terrain, but it's not as fun as Stilwater as the NPCs are dumb and there is no costomization in this game.
Downside: no costomization. Generally you start with Gat but can swap to Kinzie at headquarter, but they have no difference aside from some script lines. There is no clothing store and (maybe I just didn't find it?) radio. The only costomizations come from the pre-perchase DLC and do not affect any gameplay. These somehow compromise the fun of free roaming, but it's understandable since it's not a full game.
TL;DR: you will get what you paid for if you buy this cheap game, so I think it's worth it.

A unique RPG, I bought this game on sale and wasn't expecting much, but I was pleasantly surprised.
The battle system is quite complex and has little to offer in tutorials which can make even the most hardened rpg fanatics frustrated, but with a little research and perseverance, it soons becomes second nature. And the effort is very rewarding as you tactically issue commands to your unions to lead them to victory.
In all the RPGs I've played, I've found that I have the most fun when I'm levelling up and becoming more powerful. My favorite part of FFVII for example is maxing out materia. So when I play this game with the max number of units per battle capping at 18, and increasing multiple units' abilities at once, I can say that it's very satisfying.
The battle system reminds me of a few games honestly, it could use a little refinement, but that's what makes it feel so real. There's always variables involved with every situation and action, more so than other games in the JRPG genre. You'll find yourself cheering on your troops (on the inside) as they create chains and dodge enemy fire, and at other times cursing your luck as the enemies evade your attacks and hit you with criticals.
Luck is definitely a factor, but the game gives you so many options for strategy that a few good moves can put you in an advantageous position while just a few mistakes can leave you at your enemy's mercy.
The story of this game is difficult to get into, especially at first. The characters and voice acting will make you cringe, let alone some of the actions they take. The fifth time you see the main character rushing recklessly into danger, you wouldn't even be surprised anymore. Not only are a number of the situations simply unreal, but the plot will just have you asking so many questions that they wont answer until about halfway through the story, so you're left with no option other than to just give up, or to ignore it and push on through. In the end though, I believe its quite worth it. Its not the only RPG thats had a similar issue with the story after all, and it handles it a bit better than most.
The graphics, scenery, and visuals are beautiful, minus the constant pop in textures as the graphics change from low to high quality. Even with a good pc difficult to ignore. Thankfully the pc version has a minor fix if you search for it. I tried it myself and the difference is definitely noticeable.
The amount of content is unbelievable. There are dozens of side quests, recruitable team leaders, customisable weapons, formations, guild tasks, hidden weapons, rare monsters, etc, etc. And that's ignoring the fact that you could play for 100+ hours and still not have a single unit maxed out, or even with every art. I haven't beaten it yet, and I've avoided the subject for risk of spoilers, but the game has a new game+ option, and hopefully most of your equipment and stats will carry on to your next playthrough, while simultaneously allowing you to fix any mistakes youve made in a previous playthrough.
All in all I rate this game 8.5/10 and highly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the Tales series, fire emblem, FFXII, Dragon Age, or KOTOR. mostly cuz I feel that there is a little bit of each of those games in this wonderful RPG.

Rivals of Aether is a Smash-esque fighting game that takes the same winning simple-but-deep systems of the game it's inspired by (Super Smash Bros. Melee) and refines them so they're both more accessible to newcomers and more integral to gameplay.
Seriously--have you tried wavedashing reliably in Smash Bros. Melee? It's pretty frigging hard! You have to practice, practice, practice, for hours or days to perform that technique reliably. Rivals walks into the room and says, "Screw that, such an integral tech shouldn't be impossible. Here's a tutorial, here are the inputs, bam. You're wavedashing. Congrats."
That's not to say the game doesn't have depth, though. Heck no. The character-specific tech in this game was lovingly built in by developers who clearly know how to make characters that are balanced and varied without sacrificing fun. The characters are so unique and their mechanics are so cool that I can't even begin to express how awesome it is to slowly delve into each one, learning their intricate details and realizing just how much attention was put into every aspect. They all play fluidly and feel powerful.
tl;dr -- It's just the best. The developers of this game have made a fighting game experience that is built for competitive play, but remains simple and appealing enough that just about anyone who's handled a controller before can hop in and start learning without feeling overwhelmed.

One of the biggest throbbing problems I have with most games on Steam and in the indie market in general is the express desire to just make a game that's unfairly hard. It seems that every charming pixelated game has to be a roguelike with absolutely insane difficulty, like we're all collectively competing to make the hardest game possible.
NOT A HERO alleviates that problem somewhat, creating a rather casual but fast-paced little retro shoot-em-up that's very fun and easy if you just wanna shoot to the end. But much more challenge lies in the bonus objectives, which increase your score and allow you to attain higher ranks.
There's also quite a lot of diversity in the character classes, and I rather enjoy the sense of humor the game has. Full marks from me.

The combat is tedious and you basically just press Auto abilities and the game does the rest. That being said i do have this temptation to keep playing. The gorgeous visuals and incredible sound track keep me playing. Some of the Characters are quite interesting and keep you hooked. Others are dull and have the ceaseless ability to moan constantly! (looking at you Hope) The story is not too bad but confusing unless you scour through the Wiki page because it makes absolutely no sense. The background of the Game is explained in Logs you find throughout the game but that to me takes the point out of it. No one ever explains what a L'cie is, or a Fal'cie, or what Psycom is so you're just expected to know. It's not a game i'd ever have payed launch price for but for just over £10 it's a good game to kill time if you have nothing else to play.

Yes, this is yet another adaptation from Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings novel trilogy, one of the best fantasy book series of all time. It also uses characters-model from the movies...but...it's a totally different story. Kind of. In the south, war breaks between the Dark Lord Sauron and the free people of Middle Earth, as shown in the movies/books. But the game shows a "hidden" story: a fellowship composed of Eradan, a Dunedáin (man), Farin, a dwarf and Andriel, a she-elf. They too, embark in a journey to fight for the north of Middle Earth, at the same time of the LOTR trilogy battles in the south. It's an interesting idea and the plot develops really well. With the presence of beloved characters that will make a LOTR fan smile, a decent villain and some good character development for Beleram, an Eagle that helps in the journey, i liked the story. The ending is also epic and amazing with a challenging boss fight. Talking about boss fights, the game have a lot of them and they're all pretty good. The game is challenging even in the lowest difficult (normal) because of tough enemeis in high quantities. Sometimes is frustrating because of your companions AI when you die in combat, but it's pretty rewarding, as this game is about loot and there is a lot of it. You can choose one of the three characters to play, and all of them have unique skills to upgrade and purchase, that's real nice. Also they have unique abilities and usable weapons, making the variation of playing with each one of them unique. You can even play online, whick makes the game a lot more enjoyable. But while playing offline, the companions AI is pretty bad, and sometimes you die just because they messed up while trying to ressurect you. It's frustrating. The graphics are outdated, and the facial animations are bad, but the scenarios are really awesome. The combat is very cool with all aplicable skills and upgrades, use of potions and weapons, inclding ranged weapons. But it gets too repetitive. The whole game is a bit repetitive, there is no puzzles, just go and kill a thousand enemies, proceed, then do it again. It may have RPG elements, but it's pretty linear besides the fact you can travel to some places, and challenge maps in scenarios from LOTR trilogy. There is dialog system too, which have zero impact on the story and only serves to know more about events/begin side quests. There is some side quests and some of them are decent, but there is only a few. The soundtrack, as expected, is awesome and have some beautiful melodies and epic combat tracks. You can call for Beleram support, which is awesome and helps a lot. The game length is good for an action game and you can replay in higher levels of difficult with the same weapons and equipment (there is armor and other stuff in good quantity). Kind of new game+, adding replay value because you can use other characters. You can swap characters during the campaign by only going back to menu or at certain points, and giving them items mean nothing, they don't use them and you should switch at least one time to up their skills and equip the loot they found because those dumbasses don't do anything alone. The game have some bugs too, as usual.

I played this when I had a 360. I understand people not enjoying the game if it doesn't work. That is where many of the negative reviews come from. So far this game worked for me. I really enjoy it. Though I am considered a "casual" gamer so here is my expierence for it in different tabs.
THE STORY: It is kind of forgettable. I can't really remember the characters names, which should tell you something. The story is meh, it's not terrible but there is better.

GAMEPLAY: It is a good hack and slash. It feels like the origin to Shadow of Mordor. Good gameplay, comabt is fluent with swords, axes, and staves. Ranged attacks and special powers that are mapped to the 1-9 on the keyboard.
THE CONTOLS: On the keyboard are very hard for ME. That doesn't mean it is bad. It is responsive and they work well. You can remap them to make it easier. Or you can use a game pad. It helps a lot but those controls are not given. Though there may be one in the discussions area.
THE GRAPHICS: Are ok, character models aren't terrible, the locations seem different enough. The framerate is stable and it plays well. The decapatation shots in a final strike when the camera zooms in are awesome. I love watching the heads chopped off of the orcs. It looks and feels rewarding and always makes me grin.
THE PRESINTATION: It falls a little short. If you don't like LotR you may not enjoy it as it shows characters from the fellowship in the movie. Though the songs in it always make me remember the movies, and the Return of the King video game.

All in all, is it worth $20? My opinion is no, it is better off when it is a little cheaper. Wait until it's $10 or even cheaper. And if it doesn't work. That's what refunds are for.
My final verdict is a 7 out of 10. It is a great game for LotR fans, and if you never played LotR. I'd recommend it for a sale.

Worse than Civilization V.
The aesthetics are dull and the colours are not as lush as Civ V. The tech tree is confusing and hard to navigate when you want to find a specific upgrade. There is no building or trade route automation, so each turn you will be dealing with 5-10 popups you don't care about. Unit level-ups are always the same - heal or more strength. In-game lore is presented in a boring fashion. Quests are usually dull. Each time you make a new building you get to customize what it does, but the options are rather boring. Some of your upgrades are not clearly presented (for example, you can get roads maintenance dropped to zero, but the popup for creating roads will still say that you pay for upkeep), so you have to remember what you can do. Air units are dull and very limited in their capacity. Resources are a bit dull, you sometimes won't have any use for some of them through the entire game (probably tied to the affinity units).
On the plus side, the affinity system is interesting, leading to a varied game-play. You can deploy satellites which change the game dynamics a lot (from raining death upon enemies to teleporting your army across the world). Starting customization is interesting. Aliens are just glorified barbarians with a few overpowered units.
All in all, Civilization V is better.

Disclosure: I received an early Beta Copy
Simply put, I love the game. In essence for me it's Freelancer reborn, except with capital ships.
The gameplay is fantastic, although I would strongly recommend a controller. Both the 360 one, and the Steam Controller work brilliantly with the game.
One thing that separates the game from freelancer is the capital ships, and that you use Broadsides for your primary weapons. As such you need to get your sides facing the enemies.
Fear not though, it's still super intense, and you have plenty of other weaponry. Ranging from Secondary fire ones such as EMP Waves, Flak cannons and plenty of turrets.
Turrets are mostly A.I controlled, although you can set priorities for each and every one of them. Such as Fire at Any Craft, Target, Locked Targets only, or even Fighters only.
This means that you can focus all fire on a single enemy, or you can handle the capital ships while your turrets deal with the swarms of enemy fighter and gunships.
It's rather odd at first, but after a while it becomes extremely satisfying. To the point of almost feeling like you're in Battlestar Galactica fending off literal swarms of enemies.
Sadly, you're unable to be a carrier and have your own fighters, although it's not too much of an issue.
The story is very interesting, and it certainly is engaging. Although some story missions have very high requirements and as such you Have to go do other missions to get a better ship and equipment.
This is no issue at all, and extremely fun. You can do a variety of missions, or you can just do pirate bounty hunting. Doing missions however increases or decreases your reputation with various factions. This in turn unlocking newer ship hulls, and equipment.
You're also able to join some guilds, such as the Mercenaries or Merchants which give extra missions and other unique ship hulls.
I would strongly encourage you to find one you like.
Trading is not the most complex of systems, but very manageable, and slightly fun. I've never been much of a trader but each system and station has various prices and requirements. An impoverished station will pay a lot more for food and water than a well set up military one. While some might accept some contraband pirate items; ranging from Narco Cola, to Living Organs.
Ships can also be scanned so be careful carrying contraband, the Militia will scan you and will hail you to explain yourself. If you simply ignore their Hails they will go hostile and attack you. If you want to play with those items, make sure to get a Smuggler's Cargohold; They can't be scanned ;)
Graphics and performance wise the game does extremely well. It's no Star Citizen, but it looks great and runs even better. Now I might have an overkill machine with Two GTX 980Ti's, but playing at 4K with DSR I was topping out at 144FPS which is my monitor's cap, and at worst getting 80fps.
The only slight complaint I have is little lag spikes when phasing in and out of a station. Although this is most likely an engine issue that'll soon be fixed for textures loading in and out.
As for graphical options the game as plenty and they're all adjusted with through the game launcher. It also has 3 graphics APIs to choose from. DirectX 9, DirectX 11 and even OpenGL if you fancy using that.
I unfortunately only have experience running the game in DX11, but it's done exceptionally well.

Quite simply the greatest game of all time. If you choose to buy it, I thoroughly suggest the Tactical Expansion Mod you can get online for free. Adds a TON of weapons and rebalances the game somewhat. My first playthrough, I played it like a shooter with cloak. Stealth killed a bunch of dudes with silenced weapons, occassionally went rambo. But soon I realized that while that is really fun its still not the most fun way to play this game. What I started doing was turning my nanosuit to speed mode, running into enemy encampments, switching to strength mode after I've built up momentum and doing a superjump, preferably over a fence or up a balcony to deliver an absolute wrath of god punch that obliterates some poor korean. Or leaving one guy alive as you superjump from building to building and laugh as he tries to hit you. If you run at enemies at superspeed, you knock them down without dealing damage. If you jump on top of a guy trying to get up you knock him down again. If you jump on top of a guy he won't detect it. I've spent hours just trolling the NPCs, whether it be by doing that or picking up bulletproof objects and slowly walking at them while shouting "I AM BULLETPROOF" before throwing it at them in strength mode. Strapping C4 to barrels and vehicles and driving or throwing them into groups of enemies. Tactical expansion adds among a lot of other things a lot more explosives, such as like 4 or 5 nuclear grenades and explosive ammunition hidden through the levels that are incredibly op and entertaining to use. I'd buy this game for $100 and if it had 1990s graphics. The far cry series, dishonored, metro, half life, bioshock, deus ex, I've played through a lot of them, but they all pale in comparison to the brilliance and unending fun that is this game. If at any point you feel yourself getting slightly bored, try imposing a restriction on yourself. For instance, I've gotten to the aliens part using only my fists, c4 and landmines, and without using cloak.

I haven't had much technical difficulties or crashes running the game, other than I had to disable Nvidia Surround to get ingame sounds. In the end, there are probably tons of things this remaster could've done better, but as my experience so far has been mostly without trouble, there is no hesitation for me personally to give this game a positive review. Even with all of the faults reported, this still one of the best games ever made.
Although this is a remaster, the base game clearly shows its age as environment and character models or animations aren't up to today's AAA standards. That doesn't mean that game looks bad as Rapture's decaying Art Deco environments still look beautiful and have tons of details. This is also where both the original BioShock and remastered version shine as the game still delivers an unique atmosphere, a feel of utopia turned to dystopia, which is something rarely seen as succesfully made for any other FPS game. Remains of the Rapture's glory days can be seen everywhere during the gameplay, but current underwater world is full of sorrow and suffering caused by the corruption of moral values of the people. BioShock delivers this story very well.
Game's atmosphere is thus top notch and it beautifully combines horror, action and adventure themes. Where game doesn't shine is gunplay, something that IMO isn't the strongest part of any of the BioShock games. It is difficult to pinpoint why, but somehow it feels incredibly clumsy (without actually being so) and unrewarding. So, if you are looking for a fluid action shooter, BioShock isn't probably for you. If you are looking for unique atmosphere, well written and deep story, then this game is still one of the best options out there.

Two words I would use to describe this game:
.
I'm a fan of the FF series, but more specifically 6-9. After a break from JRPGs, I decided to give FF13 a try. The first about 20 hours consist of you running down a linear path. All this time I wondered when I would get to a town or some kind of hub, some place where you can interact with the characters and people in the world - but there are none of those.
What made it worse is that through out this journey, you have to watch the characters stumble about and listen to a dozen motivational talks, since the cycle of hopelessness and renewed hope seems to repeat itself. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but I found myself thinking: "Didn't we just go through a motivational talk, now you're really upset again? Why?" The setting and lore for the game seemed really interesting, but the execution was terrible. The flashbacks were particulary the worse, they felt insignificant and failed to draw any kind of emotion from me (besides boredom). I really had to push myself to complete the game.
At one point you reach a large open area, which is refreshing at first. But then I realized that there isn't much depth to it, besides grinding and making your characters stronger. I know some people enjoy mastery and combat challenges, and if you are one of these people, maybe you would like FF13. The game is also very pretty - but that's something I think that newer FF games are: beautiful graphics, but at the cost of depth and gameplay freedom.
The last negative is that if you're in Asia, you're stuck with Japanese audio. It's not a huge problem, but I would have liked to understand the battle comments the characters made...as well as have that choice to pick English audio.
So, if you're someone that's looking for a world that can fascinate and intrigue you, non-linear story and gameplay, you're better off looking somewhere else.

"This War of Mine" is one of the few games that really got me hyped for its release, and although it wasn't exactly what I imagined it to be (I expected an endless floor-by-floor apartment crawl full of random encounters and split-second decision making) the end product is still super satisfying.
And I'll tell you why. No matter how you play, you are bound to feel something. Rage-- your home gets raided for vegetables and canned sardines for the second night in a row. Desperation-- your best scavenger Boris comes home with a bullet wound and partial loot, Katia is starving and depressed, you're out of supplies and you have one night to fix everything. Regret-- you send Emilia to the sniper junction because she's the most dispensable of the group, you know she might die, and she does, she dies. And then you realize that even the most overlooked person in the room gets missed if the room is small enough.
It took me a brutal first week of failures before I finally survived the war, and boy, it felt good. I started over a couple times after that but it was never the same. Still though, it's worth it, highly recommended. Plus, it's $20. You really can't go wrong.

What a doozy. This game deserves the ultimate award for"in dire need of one more update".
So, let's boil it down to the real issue here, the BR system. There are others, but this is the main one, since it forces you to not play the game and grub around till you have the party of characters you want since if you start leveling up BR before you have them, they will never get caught up.
In short BR makes everyone stronger, but if you're smart about it, your guys will always be the bestest so no issue there. So once you've got that part set, and decide to try and change it around to accommodate new hires, you quickly realize the mistake and put back in the old guys, who have now lost a bit of their edge. There in lies, the problem. Getting further away from the start of the game makes the whole thing a tight-rope walk of using what you're handed in the first part of the game, which has some great hires btw, and excludes about 1/4 of the other talented available buddies to bring along.
So as an rpg perfectionist, it's like the long the game goes, the more dire the feeling of "maybe I'm doing this wrong" builds, till you have to restart thinking it'll be different this time, but alas, the game randomly choosing your skills means you'll never make that mystic group, or mix-tactics group your thinking up.
In short, this review is for the hardcore rpg guy. The Last Remnant offers some surface fun and excitement over the strategies you think you'll be able to construct, then just punishes you mid-late game for not specializing enough, which makes for a real drab experience of the same old "do as much damage as possible" thing, which then drags on and on.
I keep replaying thinking it'll be different, but the game sorely needs an overall with more union options to accommodate mixed tactics, or being able to multi-deadlock with one union for defensive strategies. Or just, being able to move a unit out of combat to do just long range attacks.

Beyond Earth fails a bit in terms of flavor and personality. Much of the game's visuals feel dull and uninspired. The interface is ugly, units are all mostly generic sci-fi stand-ins with pathetic customization options, and the leaders have a severe lack of presence. It also doesn't do quite enough to differentiate itself from Civilization V, nor does it really push the genre forward with any real innovation.
It is, however, a much more complete and satisfying game than Civ V's vanilla release. Of course it has bugs and balance issues that can all be addressed via patches. But it doesn't have any obvious, gaping holes in mechanics (like Civ V's complete lack of an espionage system). It's worth a purchase for any strategy fan, without having to wait for the first expansion.
I, personally, still prefer Civilization V for its historical theming, but Beyond Earth is definitely a worthwhile strategy game that strategy fans should play.
