In short, this is not a
game. It has many, many problems including an extremely convoluted battle system, a character customization and class system which is hard to manage, a world that doesn't really hold together, obviously half-implemented features, recycled monster types, and a plot that's absurd even for a JRPG. It's hard to play properly, easy to screw yourself over with bad decisions early on, and has a protagonist who's only somewhat more tolerable than Tidus.
That said: I put nearly 200 hours into this game because it's goddamn addictive to some types of players. It's clear that many of the people who worked on Final Fantasy 12 were instrumental to this game, because the art direction is extremely similar (mostly in a good way although the costumes are even more absurd), it has the same sort of "grindy" feel to it, and other similarities both obvious and subtle. There are hundreds and hundreds of different components for item creation and customizaton, a large cast of characters (many of whom have their own optional sub-plots), a guild system with huge amounts of optional tasks, and possibly most importantly, a feeling like you're commanding a small army instead of a fantasy party, since you have can up to 18 characters active at once in up to five "unions" or tactical squads.
The PC version has integrated all of the XBox DLC, which includes a bunch of optional superbosses that are pretty much pallette-swaps of existing ones, has more flexible union creation rules (so you can have squads consisting entirely of special characters instead of having to pad them with generic soldier-types), and possibly most important for the obsessive grinding addicts: a fast-forward mode for finishing battles more quickly. I cannot imagine playing the XBox version without that fast forward.
If you enjoy farming monsters for that one last rare drop because you just have to get that sword for your tank that's a little bit better than his current one, this is the game for you. If you like your RPGs to have engaging plots, skip it.

I've heard good and bad things about this game, and it was on sale for cheap so I decided to give it a whirl. It's a game that lives and dies by its battle system, which is what one does the most by far. The story is cliche and the CG segments are short and few in between. The graphics are aged by today's standards, which is fine, but the locations and dungeons are generic and uninspired.
The choices in battle you can make are random, depending on your available skills, HP, and positioning. If you have a healer unit and the game doesn't allow you to heal, too bad. If you have a full AP bar waiting to unleash hell but the game doesn't allow you to, too bad. You cannot directly control unit positioning. If a boss is dropping AOEs all around himself, you cannot order units to hang back. Extremely unpredictable and frustrating. You can't even see the HP of a boss or miniboss. The game allows you to set formations to trade off advantages and disadvantages and these are essential for boss fights, but these take very long to set up and there is no way to save different formations.
Game statistics are opaque and not explained properly. Every character has a 'unique' statistic like 'ego' but after so many years the game is out, AFAIK nobody knows what they do. You can only equip the main character directly. For the other 20 to 50 characters depending on how far you are into the game, you have to actually wait for them to ask to "borrow" a piece of equipment you already have. If they don't ask for it, you have to go out and beat up some monsters and see if they ask you again. Talk about being obtuse and beating around the bush.
You cannot see a character's skill tree so you don't know what skills he/she is going to get, and you can only level up skills by using them, making the normal attack option mostly moot. Every now and then a character asks whether to learn a new skill or not, or to focus on physical or magical skills. You cannot postpone the decision. The game doesn't explain what the skill does or who the charcter is or what kind of stats he or she has, so it might as well ask the player to pick randomly. There is no quest board, so after every story event, you find yourself wandering all the towns, pubs, and guild areas just to pick up new quests. At least quests don't get offered in dungeons so you don't actually have to check those.
Money is extremely difficult to come by, and I finished disc 1, I was wondering why the shops even bother to stock the stuff they have. You could grind money but that raises your battle rank which is essentially your level, and enemies scale up with your battle rank. Hence you find the characters who join you later on to be underpowered and generally useless. Since enemies level with you and you cannot gain gear advantage, progression feels very slow and stifled. Despite the game being entirely its battle system, its systems actually discourage you from fighting, until you hit a difficulty spike, look up a guide, and see that the recommended level is way above yours, so now it's time to actually level so you can get on with it.
If you are looking for similar previous-gen RPGs, try Star Ocean III or Final Fantasy X instead. I'm an old-school RPG gamer, but the flaws above are designed on purpose and those are unforgivable for a game released in 2008. Not recommended.

I'm not sure what I was thinking.  Civ V (W/ all DLCs, in its current state) is a much more complete and FUN game than Beyond Earth (BE) will be anytime soon.  I think I just had my expectations set far too high for this release, and because of that, I played a dozen games trying almost make myself like it.  I don't like it.  It is a stripped down version of a PC Civ game, with an attempt at new systems and intricacies that really just hide the fact that you have only a few units and a few options on how to upgrade them (compared to prior Civ games).  It also seems to lack that "just one more turn" feeling of Civ 5, and I find myself thinking instead "how many damn turns is it going to take to do _________?!"  I'd say if you are a follower of Civ games for a while, then get it -- and chances are you already got it, and you just want a new Civ game because you have already dropped hundreds of hours on Civ 5.  Otherwise, if you are new to the series, get Civ 5, and wait for BE to get patches, DLC, and everything else it needs to become a complete game.  Sigh.

I've been playing Civ V for a very, very long time, and yes, when the DLCs came out, it took me a little while to fully understand how the all tied in together, but it wasn't a big learning curve.
Compared to Civ V, this game just want in a completely different direction and not in a good way. I've only been playing for less than an hour because that is about as much as I can handle with this game.
After playing for as little as I have been, here's what I can take away from this game:
- The learning curve is you start out with the game turning on and then it just go right through the roof with the rest of it.
- It's not really clear the tech paths and how they are applied to the game.
- Yes, they do explain a few of the new features, but my issue with it is it's almost counter intutitive to what was in Civ V.
- They put too much, too soon on the game when you first start out. When we started in Civ V, a city, a unit, some hidden ruins, some state cities, and then the other AIs. All of it pretty straightforward. Here, they give you crashed space craft, aliens that seem to be able to kill you out right, AIs who seem to be able to get the upper hand faster than you, etc. and this was all on easy, are you kidding me?!
Do yourself a favor and do not buy this game. The only other game that is similar to this and more fun, IMO, is Endless Legend. It's basically like Civ V, but with a more magical theme to it along with some very interesting game play that is difficult at first, but you really get the hang of it.
I'm going to try and give Civ: BE another chance and at least try to play one game, but overall, don't buy this game. Just don't.

The game is not fun.
If you win you will be satisfied you didn't encounter a flavor of the month champion.  You'll love having a competent, non-berating teammate.  You'll be bored because your enemies just weren't good enough for you.  You'll question hitboxes.
If you lose you'll blame the flavor of the month champion.  You'll hate having an incompetent, berating teammate.  You'll be bored and frustrated wondering why you aren't playing something fun.
The gameplay is not fun.  If the fun you can have with a game is determined by those two statements above (and it is) you cannot have fun.  Its simply not possible.  Sure you might get a rush out of killing your opponent out of a tough 1v1.  More often than not you're wondering why X skill's hitbox is so big or how Y skill has zero windup to react to it.
Characters play different only insofar that their pacing is different.  Ashka for example is slow but hard hitting with ranged attacks.  Ezmo is quick but soft hitting with ranged attacks.  There's very little differentiation between the characters compared to Bloodline Champions.  Try to think of some defining feature of each character and you really can't.  Sure you can point to a skill that nobody has (like Ezmo's straight line heal) but it exists in other paced forms.  Ashka can heal as well but again more slowly and bursty.
There's no satisfactory variety.  There's no fun that isn't determined by everything you can't influence.  The gameplay itself is not actually fun regardless of that.  You move and shoot out similar abilities against humans who do similar things ad nausem.  Its the same tedium as all other MOBAs with the fat trimmed out but the meat is rotten because MOBAs inherently are not fun.
That's why these games have grinding systems in place.  Skinner boxes are "fun" for humans.  But would they really be necessary if the game itself was fun.  Probably not.

Return to Castle Wolfenstien is a simple game starting BJ "I'm special because I eat Med packs and armor and have bottomless pockets" Blazkowicz, but underneath one of the simplist and oldest game mechanics in existance, one of the best shooters of all time, In a year with the likes of Medal of Honor and Call of Duty were funneling you down corridors shouting at you with a large army, RTCW sent you on your own to fight the German might singlehandedly, no map, no sense of direction just you, alone, outnumbered but certainly not outgunned or outclassed.
Decide to be stealthy? Shock horror, you can do that, Use a silenced weapon or go for a backstab (instant kill), while listening to your enemies chat away about simple things Thief style, as a stealth shooter it does its job if its a little rough.
Decide to go loud? You have enough firepower in your arsenal, with classic WW2 weapons and a few experimental toys to play with, oh and bottomless pockets mean you can carry them all into battle and use them whever you feel like it!
Map design is a little rough but still classical old school, no arrows, no waypoint markers but designed in such a way you always knew where you were going and where you were.
Overall Return to Castle Wolfenstien is a great example of a classic shooter and should rank up for someone who wants to dive into old school shooters, people after yet another cookie cutter corridor crawler look elseware.

I suppose ill start by saying that Bioshock 2 is the most underrated sequel I have ever played.
You play subject Delta, an older model of Big Daddy that is bound to a certain little sister. The fact that you play a Big Daddy offers an array of weapons much more lethal and badass than their Bioshock 1 counterparts. Your wrench for instance is now a giant drill (with the charge ability and fully upgraded it is the most fun melee weapon I can think of this side of a gravity hammer). Now you may think that you would greatly over powered compared to splicers with you being a Big Daddy with all these great weapons but Bioshock 2 is too smart for that. This game takes place in 1968, eight years after the original game. The splicers of Rapture have had a long time to get stronger and stronger they have become.
The game play offers a bunch of improvements and tweaks from the original. Hacking minigame is now no longer time consuming and obtuse, now its quick and easy to get used to. Researching is now much easier to with a film camera you play while you fight rather than a photo camera you have to use to take photo's of your enemies while they shoot/cut you to bits. Some new enemy types also debut in this game including the hulking Brute Splicer and the spine chilling Big Sister.
The Story, Characters and locations of your second trip in Rapture though once again are top notch fall a little short of matching the brilliance of the Original Bioshock. Your little sister that you spend your time trying to rescue is Eleanor Lamb, the daughter of Sofia Lamb the games main antagonist. Sofia Lamb is a brilliant psychologist and cult leader who as seized control of Rapture in the aftermath of the ending of the Original Bioshock. As you progress through Rapture Sofia consistently throws obstacles in your way to stop you from reaching Eleanor. Helping you through Rapture this time is a very smooth talking southern man by the name of Augustus Sinclair who has an interesting relationship with Subject Delta. The secondary characters who serve as either a boss or a morality choice for each level are not as interesting or terrifying as the secondary characters were in the first game but they still do receive the signature quality mark of the Bioshock writing and acting. As you progress through Rapture you thankfully get to gain some new insight into Rapture's captivating history as well as some further insight into Atlas, Frank Fontaine and in my opinion the franchise's most interesting character Andrew Ryan.
Despite the game's short comings in its characters and story I still give it my highest recommendation, it’s about as long as the first game in terms of how long it takes to finish and you will once again be enthralled by Rapture and all its horror and brilliance.

I would recommend this to players who are both experienced, familiar, or even completely new to magick.

So, I've been delaying this review (I have about 48 hours (not 60)) because honestly, I've been too wrapped up in playing the game itself. It's very heartbreaking at times how we have to refuse people food or medicine because we have to protect our own or we don't have what they need. I would usually try to avoid killing in this game, but lately, I've been taking out the thugs who abuse others in the game because A: it gives a moral boost and B. they have a lot of materials. It's really interesting how they designed the game such that you have no choice but to take a more novice way of doings things since you're dealing with civillians.
I would suggest you get it if you're interested in learning about survival and food/time management, but it's not for everyone. If you try to take others out, you have to choose which ones who are actually hurting the other innocents or your people will be depressed. Also, you cannot just go guns blazing (limited bullets). You have to go really stealthy or have a lot of cover because it's not going to work out with just a knife or pistol with one bullet. No heatshots, Call of Duty Fans. So, just enjoy it for what it is. It is hell, essentially, but those who are willing to claw their ways through hell can be given a chance to live.

Захватывающая игра, главным плюсом которой, на мой взгляд, является рандомный разброс вещей, наполнение локаций, события, в общем, рандом - главная движущая сила игры :) Даже когда кажется, что игра становится скучноватой и однообразной - бац! и происходит что-нибудь интересное, что-нибудь кардинально меняющее привычный быт и задачи. Безусловным достоинством является и атмосфера игры: рассказы героев о своей довоенной жизни, их мысли о происходящем и надежды на лучшее, или же наоборот - переживания, депрессии и расстройства. Все смотрится очень гармонично и логично. Персонажи реагируют на каждый выбор игрока, на происходящие вокруг события и проишествия, переживают нехватку еды или сигарет, если они в таковых нуждаются, сочувствуют друг другу - одним словом, оторваться от игры бывает довольно сложно :) Жду от разработчиков новый персонажей, новые события и локации, а также не помешало бы некоторое увеличение уровня сложности, ибо, несмотря на казалось бы большое количество трудностей, с которыми сталкиваются герои, особой хардкорности у этой игры нет, а хотелось бы :D
9\10, рекомендую всем :)

Final Fantasy XIII, an extremely underrated game in my opinion.
I have never played a Final Fantasy game before (Dissidia & Chrystal Bearers don't count, do they?) getting this game on a sale after watching some gameplay. I'm very glad I did that. Now, having finished the main story and around half of the sidequests after 75 hours of playing I can say that I would defenitely pay the full price for it.
I've never been into 'round based' games or similar stuff but I fell in love with the combat of FF13 after playing the first hour of the game. The battles feel very fluid and entertaining, the bossfights tend to be rather tough and the music of the game is brilliant.
After some chapters of linearity the game opens up and gives you a rather big place to explore & grind if wanted. Talking about grind, I never had to grind to be able to continue the story, which is a huge plus in my opinion.
The weapon upgrade system is rather strange but given that you don't really need to upgrade your gear until many hours into the game, I'm fine with that. After doing some reading, the upgrade system is easy to understand.
The Eidolons could have been fleshed out better aswell, but one shouldn't summon them too often anyways.
I also liked the story quite a bit and one really starts to like certain characters one didn't like earlier.
I don't know about hardcore-FF-fans but for starters with the 'genre' I can only recommend this awesome game. Looking forward to playing 13-2 now.

I bought TWoM with the hopes of a gripping story about survival in a wartorn world. What I got was an annoying point and click adventure. It also doesn't help that I played an incredibly similar flash game to this about five bucking years ago!
Normally I don't review a game as bad
[Cue sarcastic laughter]
But really? It's a flash game posing as a real game.
"But we're a real game!" I hear the devs cry, "We have all these cool textures and mechanics!"
"Yes," I reply like I'm talking to a nutjob, "But everyone else who doesn't like beating themselves with sticks isn't going to enjoy grinding through salvage mechanics coupled with tiny character inventories. Look, I know you're shooting for realistic here, but there is a difference between 'realistic' and 'actually worth playing for more than 5 minutes. Like, if I've got 4 survivors, why can't I drag along a friend to help me carry♥♥♥♥♥♥ Why can't these desperately sleepy people share a bed? AND WHY GIVE ME ATTACK MECHANICS THAT YOU DON'T BOTHER EXPLAINING THEMSELVES UNTIL MY CHARACTER DIES!"
"But we're a survivalist game!" They reply.
No TWoM, you're not a survivalist game and you're not a simulation of a survivalist game.
What you are is a series of annoying point and click adventure puzzles. No skill, no advancement, no point.
And as for AI? What bucking AI?! I once had an uncontrolled AI character called 'Bruno' (The chef) stand in the middle of the kitchen, with the fridge to his right and the stove to his left, announce he was 'starving' but did bugger all about it. The fridge, I need not tell you, was full.
If it really wants to improve, it'll need to include a difficulty setting (Reducing material requirements and hunger would be a start), a tutorial (Or even just a journal system where the characters explain what they want and don't want) and the ability to establish resource chains (So while I'm busy poking around the city, I know the rest of the survivors aren't all in bed.)
I really want to recommend TWoM for it's visual style and it's unique 'darkness'. But really it's like being beaten with a piece of fine art. Yes, the art is expensive and pretty but that doesn't make the frame breaking your nose hurt any less.

It does not surprise me in the least that this game has won a few prizes. It's unique, a little daring, cuteiful, has good music, is good fun, ... "Tiny&Big: Grandpa's Leftovers" was the first game I ever reviewed - its greatness pushed me over the edge. The only downside is that it's quite short - only 3+ hours, but
puts the average completionist even at 12 hours.
The music tapes you can find in the game contain quite non-mainstream music by independent bands, and the music is very appealing, so you have quite the treasure-hunt incentive.
The game costs €10, and were the game not this short, I'd recommend that you rake over the full price. I've gotten it for €2.5 years ago, and it had been in bundles, too.
Get it, and give it time (30 minutes at least) to grow on you, it's well worth it. If you don't believe me, go check out the demo that's available on the store page.
Apart from running and jumping around in 3D third person and picking up the occasional stone or music tape, there are three key mechanics that you can use throughout the whole game (except intro-"mission"), all of them physics-based (and btw., the physics engine is really good):
(is our master): It's attached to a rope. You can shoot it at moveable objects and walk backwards to pull them.
You have an unlimited supply of them and can shoot them (Always only one at a time.) at moveable objects, which will attach them. Then you can ignite them for however long you hold down the button, which will propel the object away in physically believable ways. The momentum of the objects can also be used, even to transport yourself (though that's rarely the method of choice).
This one really makes the game. You can cut most of the world into pieces. Not just along predefined lines (There are none.), and not only sufficiently thin objects, no -
that is of a certain material can be cut. Technically even arbitrarily often, except once the pieces become too small, they crumble out of reality. You'll create little bridges and jump-steps, remove obstacles, etc.. But the slice-and-dice mechanic is sometimes even a source of emergent gameplay, for example when you climb that mountain or pyramid or what it is and cut down those huge wall plates and try to jump up the pile of rubble this creates - very dynamic.

This game is beatiful.  It reminds of Smash Brothers, but also has its own unique charm.  I'll cut right to the chase:
Pros:
-Extremely stylized characters with unique abilities
-Thorough tutorials for beginner, intermediate, advanced, and character specific
-Custom skin creation
-Competitive play
-Runs very smoothly (besides some latency issues somewhere along the line)
-Deep lore and story mode for each character
-4 player local play
Cons:
-Small player base leads to small matchmaking pools
-One may only compete with one other player over the internet
-Steep learning curve for those new to the genre
Overall, I really enjoy this game.  I am still new to it, but fell in love immediately.  It is a game that I can spend 3 hours dueling a friend and have a great time.  The small character pool honestly makes me more fond of the gaame because there is less to pick up.  Mechanically, I am still learning the more complex maneuvers like wavedashing, wavelanding, techs, and animation cancels, but I have a great time every time I load up the game.  Highly recommended.

Having played nearly all of Sid Meier's games, I've come to appreciate the innovation and complexity that each new release brings. However, this one falls short. All of the previews and magazine and website reviews hyped this up. While some of the additions are nice, such as the tech web, other key components of previous civ games have been neglected, or feel like they've just been ignored. There isn't enough "new" in this game to warrant it being a standalone Civ. Where the past Civ games have felt like a true step up and forward with each release, this is a half-step at best. In the end, this is a fun game, but it feels like a piece of DLC for Civ 5, not a new, standalone, breakout game. Please do not buy this game at full price, you will regret it, like I have.

Fascinating but deeply flawed, The Last Remnant is an RPG that seems almost intentionally confusing. Every system goes several layers deep and while the depth is interesting, it's a little too complicated for anyone but the most hardcore fans to enjoy.
It wasn't until about 20 hours in that I started to grasp the battle system. Even though I was reading outside information about the game it wasn't as helpful as actually playing the game and after beating the game I'm still not sure about some things. Most people on the internet suggest to keep your battle rating low, but I was constantly running into roadblocks of luck-based fights that were frustrating.
Most of the quests are fine. I liked that they take you directly to the area you need to be almost all the time, but they also make you leave right as you finish the quest as well. This isn't a problem except there are several quests that end with items in the room you finish the quest in, and then it instantly teleports you home. I'd rather talk to someone to port me home so I could get that stuff.
I completed every quest in the game and felt pretty good about the game going up to the last boss. Completing all the quests screwed me, since the final boss was simply too strong for my team and required way too much grinding to get by. Although it's cool that the game changes depending on how you play almost none of it is obvious at any time.
In fact, almost none of the game's systems are surfaced. From some quest parameters to learning skills to equipping friends with items, there is no information at all about the game. The extremely limited tutorial only covers union attacks from different directions. In the Xbox 360 version there are loading screens with tips, but these were taken out of the PC version. Most of the time I resorted to the helpful wiki and an external program that hooks into the game to display things like enemy health and what the heck a class like an "Expert Swashbuckler" does.
I found the environments to be boring. So many corridors and caves with few paths that usually just lead to items. A few scenes were pretty, but the majority of the game made me feel claustrophobic.
Despite all that, there's something to this game's battle system that is fun and feels good to play with after learning its intricacies. Breaking this game was a joy, learning new spells and training familiar ones is good (though complex) and fighting requires tactics that I rarely see in RPGs. I just wish that stuff was surfaced a lot more in the game.
There's a reason that this game still has an active community - this game probably has thousands of ways to play it and no two playthroughs will be the same. If you can get past the massive hurdles that are required to play this, The Last Remnant is a perfectly average RPG that offers a ton of depth in its battle system.

Beyond Earth is fun and interesting.  Main cons are that it can take a long time to reach the parts of the game where Beyond Earth's personality begins to show.  Once it does, the game's science fiction flavor starts to show.  Prior to that point, it can feel like a rehash of civilization V with poorly defined leader abilities.  It will also become apparent (again, perhaps too late into the game) that each civilization is not defined by what they brought with them in their loadout, but rather by the choices that they made after planetfall.  Endgame units and technologies are cool and fun and actually feel like non-nerfed endgame units.  The climax of the game is not anticlimatic and genuinely allows for different victories that all feel worthy of a victory.
I highly recommend this game based on its flavor and the long games where a lot can happen as well as its general fun factor.  I would not recommend if you like fast paced strategy games or Call of Duty or if you have a job/better things to do than spend Saturday night playing 1/2 a game of civ.

I've bought this game in Early Access in December 2016 and I have played it regularly so far, and I do not see myself stop playing it anytime soon.
While the core concept of the game is rather simple (Arena Brawler), it's one of the most challenging and satisfing PvP games I have ever played. The game relies entirely on skill. There are no lock-on skills or anything like that. Nearly every ability is a skillshot and you need to manage you cooldowns properly.
While some argue that the game doesn't offer much depth because all you really do is fight each other without other objectives (like destroying towers in other MOBAs) or any items that could be purchased, I'd argue this is what makes Battlerite one of the purest compettive games out there. There is no such thing as level or item advantage, snowballing or winning due to any other circumstances other than your own skill.
Heroes are by and large very well balanced and even though one or two might be especially pesky to play against, once you switch sides you'll see that every heroe indeed dows have it's strengths and weaknesses and that sometimes you find yourself killed by what many people would assume to be an underpowered hero. In the right hands, every single hero on the roster is a viable pick.
The game will go Free to Play in Nov 2017. If you are looking for a great competitve game that you can play in snack sized bites or spend a whole day roasting faces, I can't recommend it enough.
For more in-depth info on this game, check out this Deep Dive on Battlerite by PodcastHeroes:
Recommended.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice.
The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing. It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again.
Final Decision: 7:10

When Final Fantasy XIII was announced and over the months it was spoiled, I was very excited by the prospect of having a large, expansive RPG set in the FF multiverse, after all, what could be better than getting to experience all the thrills of exploration, political intrigue and vast wealth of content its predecessor provided, but this time on next gen hardware, right?
As further details emerged sooner to release, of the return of battle transitions/arenas and constricted, linear level design, I began to worry and it was this that ultimately saw me leaving off of pre-ordering or buying at release, waiting instead to see what the reviews had to say about it all.
When I read the reviews, my heart sunk and such was my disappointment with the direction in which they had decided to take this iteration in the series, that I did not buy it. I decided instead that if I were to play this game, then it would have to be long after my disappointment had subsided and I could experience and judge the game on its own merits and flaws.
Fast forward 6 years and here I am, doing just that, unfortunately to find that my apprehension was fully justified.
In judging this game on the basis that it is an action RPG, it's difficult to know where to begin cataloging it's problems, because they are truly numerous :-
I have never played a video game featuring such uninspired, dull, unimaginative, unimmersive, constricted and down right lazy level design as this. In order for an RPG to consume me, I have to be able to explore it, get lost in it and become a part of it, I have to be in awe of it; overwhelmed by it, in order to enjoy playing within it.
Where are the towns and villages? Where are the quirky shops and their vendors? Where are the townsfolk, all with their own stories to tell about the world they live in, thus providing you with a deeper, more empathetic understanding of the world you're to spend 100s of hours in?
Thus far in my play through there aren't any, not a shop, not a village, not a single individual anywhere that has anything to say about what's going on, who you are, who you've been, who you might become, war and peace, personal intrigue, nothing... Outside perhaps of the FMV cut-scenes.
The only story quest this game has, is the main story, there is "literally" nothing else to do in this game, no other paths to follow, nothing to do in order to enjoy the process of leveling up to face more difficult adversaries, or get over a skill plateau along the main story path. When you hit a road block, the only thing you can do about it, is aimlessly wander around, often just back and forth between save points along the "corridor" you're in, going through pointless battle after pointless battle in order to earn experience points.
I have never known a game; an RPG no less, so utterly devoid of content as this one.
The Crystarium system in itself, is not bad, it's a pretty much run of the mill RPG leveling system, it works, there's little more to say beyond that. But that's where the positives end :-
This game insists on continually putting you into parties of 2 along the way, leaving you utterly unable to designate and commit roles for characters without potentially crippling your ability to overcome obstacles, the espers/eidolons can be particularly troublesome in this respect, but hey that's fine right? Just leave off the main story path for a while and wander off to find some other interesting, immersive quests to fulfill, in order to level up in preparation for the task ahead? Nope, see the previous paragraph, this game has no other content in it, there is nothing else to do, anywhere, ever!
The area leveling is absurdly unbalanced, you can enter into and overcome an easy battle, only to move less than 10 seconds along and then be confronted by a roadblock enemy 5 levels above your party. This leaves you completely unable to gauge which conflicts to enter into and which to avoid anywhere in the game and irrespective of what level your party is at. The roadblock enemies in this game plunge you into horrendously long battles that aren't boss battles, provide you with absolutely no pay off when you win them and half the time are completely inconsequential, they seem to exist solely to frustrate the player, push them back and siphon off huge wads of time out of your existence for no reason than the drag the game out.
When you come up against any of several dozen of these roadblocks throughout the game, all you can do is just run backwards and forwards along whichever "corridor" you're in, repeating battles you've already won several dozen times over to earn experience and level up in order to progress and you can forget out doing anything else, as I've been keen to point out in this review, there just isn't anything, there's nowhere to explore, nobody to talk to, no story quests to undertake, there aren't even more than 1 or 2 (that I've found so far @63 hours in) radiant quests and when an RPG actually makes you feel like you need MORE radiant quests in it, that's a sure sign that the publisher has really dropped the ball.
I'm a big fan of nostalgia, but in this day and age, expectations have evolved somewhat with regards to how much freedom players expect an RPG to provide them with. Transitions were necessary in the 80s and 90s, because the hardware those golden RPGs of old ran on, had technical limitations that recent hardware does not. These transitions: being locked into doing something the game insists you must do, whether you want to or not, are annoying and intrusive. They were best left in the past, where they could be gazed back upon fondly, along with random encounters and any other "roadblock mechanic" that the hardware of yesteryear rendered necessary.
How a VG publisher with an RPG heritage as rich as SE, could demonstrate such a dire lack of understanding of what makes an RPG enjoyable, memorable and rewarding is completely beyond reason.
Do I have anything good to say about Final Fantasy XIII? Well yes, a few things, but each with a downside at least as significant :-

If you've seen any other reviews of FF13 you already got an idea what this game is like - linear, corridors everywhere, wasted potential in characters, but nice artwork and soundtrack and enjoyable fights. I do not disagree.
Story is very legthy and it was very difficult for me to keep attention, especially with massive amount of fights between cutscenes. It's like you'd be watching a movie, but every 5 minutes you'd have to pick up a button and press it for 30 minutes to get next 5 minutes of the movie.
Sadly, pressing one button for fights is reality for two thirds of the game. (With few exceptions of like 3 boss fights) Some call it 25 hours tutorial, I call it boring bs. For those 25 hours you have no power over your battle team and thus have to play as every character in the game, no matter how much you dislike them. (Feels really bad if you bought the game specially to play as Lightning)
Another point I'd like to make is that in no point of the story I felt like I want to know what happens next. And that's bad for any game... Basically if you are able to play through the game in one or two days, it could be okay, but when I left the game for a week or so, I had to really push myself to click that FF13 icon again and progress further...
On the positive side, once you endure through the first 10 chapters, you are greeted by beautiful open world with lots of side missions, combat challenges and achievements for completionists.
Design of the locations is also very nice, unfortunately now I realize that I didn't really care where I was as long as I was making progress. And it's of course not possible to return to places from chapters 1-10. Welcomed feature would be unlockable mode that would allow you to play again from chapter 1, but with a) fully upgraded characters so that you can easily tear any enemy apart and quickly go for the story or b) without enemies at all.
I really want to recommend this game, but as I went through this review, it proved to be unrealistic to click thumbs up at the end of this, so no, don't buy. Go watch FF13 all cutscenes movie on Youtube. It's faster, cheaper and it'll still deliver the most important part of the game.
EDIT: I realized I forgot to mention one very important thing; I ran the game on an ancient laptop, having 7-10 fps all the way. I imagine the combat and exploration are much more fun if you can react to enemies' action and actually run, not hobble like my 80 yrs old grandma... So, if you have good machine to play this on, consider this review to give thumbs up...

This type of thing happens a lot in this game, but it is so absurd that it really doesn't matter.

Is it cheating to write a review for a game with your name in the credits? Maybe I don't know. What I DO know is that When It Hits the Fan is a fantastic return to top down 90s arcade shooters. Playing this game will make you feel like you're playing a real arcade game, which is supported considering that the game actually does have an arcade port.
The game is fast paced and difficult. It's also very fair, the camera makes sure nothing ever sneaks up on you that you couldn't expect. The replayability is probably the best part of them game. I've played through the game a countless number of times and not once did I ever get bored with the game. The game's branching paths, secrets, extras, and fun to learn level design keep you on your feet even through 10-20 playthroughs. This is very much the game that is fun to learn and master. Achievments are another positive that this game has going for it.
The game sets achievements in a really smart way. While you have some that are grindy like your "kill a brazillan* enemies with the laser cannon" are present. However, most of the achievments are stepping stones to help the player learn and master the game. By giving increasingly difficult goals, players who are hoping to 100% the game are going to improve dramatically because of these set goals.
All in all, When It Hits the Fan is not only a fantastic blast to the past, but it has a leg to stand on its own. I am glad to have been able to beta test for When It Hits the Fan and be involved in the development.

I was looking forward to this game for a long time and it didn't disappoint.
I wasn't quite sure what I was expecting, but I knew the devs intention was to show war from a civilian point of view.
I managed to complete the game on my second playthrough (I quit my first one thinking things were too far gone) and while it was difficult, it wasn't quite as punishing as I thought it would be.
The game is essentially a rogue-like resource management game by day mixed with stealth exploration at night. The stealth sections are very tense, so much so that in one of my first encounters with other survivors I panicked and before I knew I was swinging a crowbar and there were two dead bodies on the ground. While I got plenty of salvage this caused a depression within the shelter and the inhabitants began to argue amongst themselves. You will get the chance to do some good though when people visit the shelter and ask for help from your team. Sometimes they ask for items, other times they'll ask you to accompany them for the night (you won't actually see or control your character during these expeditions). When you're successful you'll generally get a morale boost as well as possibly some salvage. The risk / reward factor can be quite important here. A morale boost can be incredibly useful, but can you afford you lose any of your group?
I found it a little difficult to connect with some of the characters using their backstory. There didn't seem to be enough of it for me to empathise with them. However the longer they survived and the more valuable they became the more I missed them when they didn't make it back after venturing out of the shelter. It's quite shocking how sudden and violently you can be killed by well armed strangers. On my second playthrough I was taking a pacifist approach and doing my best not to steal or hurt anyone. One of my group was murdered for walking into a room while a soldier attempted to assault a female scavenger. It's fair to say that the next time I went out I shot first and asked questions later.
I don't really want to give away any more than I already have, so if you fancy something bleak and at times "unforgiving" then give this a go. For me this is what Indie games are all about.

This is an intricate game that is a lot of fun to play, and rewards the careful planner and strategist.  Union formation requires planning beforehand, but is still quite versatile with plenty of options.  Each turn in battle requires careful consideration.  The battles are challenging but enjoyable (for the most part).  Outside of battles, there's plenty to keep a completionist player occupied: sidequesting, collecting, crafting, guild tasks, fighting rare monsters and superbosses.  There's a bit of everything here, and I think The Last Remnant puts it together quite well.
The main storyline is serviceable but nothing spectacular.  The party members (ie. leaders) are a nice variety with their own distinct stories and related quests.  The cinematics are pretty, but voice-acting could definitely be better.  I'm usually big for a good story, but I was too busy crafting, questing, etc, to notice how ordinary this story was.
I didn't find it too hard to pick up and grasp the basics of the battle system, and I think you can play the game without needing the Wikia website.  But there's so much content and detail that is easy to miss, and if you're a completionist like me, you'd want to use the Wikia.
Apart from battles and following the main campaign, I had a lot of fun just running around, looking at things, exploring the world.  I recommend The Last Remnant if you like a TBS that rewards careful planning before and during a battle.

Hitman: Absolution is a fantastic game! It has interesting story, visuals, characters as well as gameplay.
There are two modes in this game, the single player mode named absolution and contract mode.
The single player mode features a great story in which we play as agent 47 to carry out assassinations on targets in beautiful and immersive environmental set pieces. There are around 20 levels which takes place mostly in Chigaco and Hope town. Levels are broken down into several sections in order to make gameplay much more digestible as they are served in bite-size portions.
Players are also scored for almost every mission and with the inclusion of the leaderboard, it makes the game highly replayable for me as I would want to replay every mission in order to beat the scores of my friends and be at the top of the leaderboards.
Lists of collectables in each level are also featured at the end which enable the player to know which collectables they have collected and the ones that they have not. This give players who are completionist an additional task of replaying that particular level and finding the rest of the collectables.
Although you are able to complete each mission on a variety of ways, this game highly emphasizes on stealth as you are given more points for being stealthy such as hiding bodies and remaining unseen, while going in guns blazing would give you a low score as you are given negative points for every NPC you killed that is not the targets.
Contract mode enable players to create their own contracts by marking any target in any of the single player levels and playing it in order to prove that it can be completed before other players are able to attempt their contracts. This help extends the game replayability as I am able to play through other player's contract and attempt to kill their mark target in the same fashion that they did and vice versa. Completing contracts award players with money which they could use to unlock disguises, weapons or weapon parts.
The only major gripe in this game would be that it could be extremely frustrating and challenging to play through in the higher difficulty levels such as expert and purist mode. There are also minor bugs in this game such as character's clipping issues with clothing which is very obvious in a level called blackwater park with the character Layla as you can see some patches of the clothes clipping into the skin.
To summarise:
PROS:
+Great Gameplay
+Great Visuals
+Memorable Characters
+High replayability
+Cool looking disguises!
+Contract Mode
+Great voice acting
+Score System and leaderboard
CONS:
-Bugs like Clipping issues
-Ridiculously challenging in higher difficulty level
Overall I would give this game a 8/10 which is a fantastic game!

Overall, I give the game a "thumbs up", but it will ultimately split players based on its quirky leveling and combat system.  There are a couple other design decisions that I thought were odd, but they did not detract from my enjoyment of this title.
The core of this game is all about the fighting, and you will do a lot of it.  The battle system takes some getting used to.  First of all, your characters fight in small groups called unions.  As you progress through the game, you unlock more characters, formations, skills, etc.  The bit that takes some getting used to is that the player does not necessarily give orders to individual characters, but only to the unions.  For the most part I did not have any issues with this system once I got used to it.  However, there were times when I needed to heal up and that option just was not available.  It was also a little frustrating when my super skills that can be used by some of the main characters would not come up during boss battles but would come up while fighting some weak creature.
The game itself does a horrible job of giving any real details about this battle system.  So much is really out of the player's hands.  Other than giving high level commands to your unions, the actual skills that are performed are up to the individual characters and can change based on the situation.  This seemed to work fairly well other than a few critical times when I needed to heal up a downed union, but this will drive some players bonkers.  Another odd bit about the battle system is the area of the fight.  You get to decide which enemy union your unions will be fighting against.  Sounds great until you see that the positioning itself makes no real tactical sense.  AOE skills may completely miss or hit all the enemy unions.  Unfortunately, the player really has no control over specific placement.
The other major leveling portion is weapons and crafting.  There are literally hundreds and hundreds of components, upgrade materials, crafting elements, etc.  The actual inventory system is terrible.  Keep that WIKI handy as it is crucial to find that one oddly-named item you need to upgrade your weapon.  Your party characters will also ask for items at times and it is satisfying to see their weapons change from low level into deadly works of art later in the game.  Be aware that for some items you need to first have to complete a quest to get the ability to farm that needed item off of a monster.
Story is overall fairly good and kept me interested.  Know that my time with the core quest was only about a quarter to third of my gametime.  The rest was doing optional content and we aren't just talking about a couple of zones.  There are whole areas and cities which can be missed.  Even some party characters will give quests which can be satisfying.  Graphics during the fight scenes are excellent with fluid movements.  On the other hand, characters moved stiffly during some of the cutscenes.
Completionists can expect a lot to do with all of the items to upgrade and quests to complete.  Most of this is good, but one of the most annoying aspects of the game for me was trying to get certain monsters to spawn for certain guild quests.  Monsters in the various zones spawn off of a set table (check WIKI) and this includes rares.  The issue is having to zone to the overworld and then back again just to get the desired monster to spawn.  It really gets tedious when the needed monster is deep in a labrynth.  It just takes away from the whole immersion and it made some of my play sessions tedious.
I realize I gave some negative items in the review above but for the most part I really liked this game.  I would strongly recommend the demo first so you can see for yourself if it is something you would want to spend 100+ hours on.

Your wreathe making is your classic give the AI enough stuff until they like you enough to let you win the game blah blah blah. The game's strongpoint, however, is it's grand strategy. Do you like strategy? Do you like mass allocating loads of units thinking you're just gonna steam roll an enemy position only to find out it's fortified with an equal amount of units and a starbase? No? Wassat? usaidno? Too bad! Cause now it's time to switch into fleet combat. Yes, this is one of the few games I've seen successfully pull off both 4x Grand Strategy and small scale combat successfully. Sure you can do what I do and just go look at how much Culture you're producing while the fight is happening and come back to find your entire fleet has been decimated. But that's not how Empires are built, my friend. This is a game that is both long lasting and fast paced. Carrying with it the feeling of a streamlined Endless Space level of 4x and an intense and in depth fleet combat, you'll simply find a difficult time finding a better game to eat your weekends up with hours of fleet combat and long as hell real-time campaigns.
There are some downsides, of course. The game is widely builts around culture and military strategy (Which, is there really any other reason to play an RTS other than Military victory? Come now.) The Diplomacy is just as boring as any other game "Here's 15,000,000 Crystals and Metal, now love me". The fleet combat is made overly hectic by the fact that you have to actually tell every last ship to preform every single ability that isn't passive. And, no, you can't mass select your frigates and corvettes and tell them to all do the one ability, you have to go through the list of the ships and click the ability on each. But, with how long fleet fights can last, it's not apocolyptically bad.
Overall, this is game is a classic in my opinion. It's real time grand strategy with tactics mixed together in an expertly crafted cocktail.  Should you buy it?

I assume Civ:BE is going to be compared to its predecessors, mainly Civ5 and its expansions.
On its own, it is quite a decent game.
But compared to Civ 5, it feels much too like a very well-made, but still a mod.
Civ 5 had quite a winning formula with its hexagonal turn-based combat, sense of history unfolding and variety of ways to victory.
It did frequently seem to have too long an endgame, rudimentary spying abilities, and not much in modern combat beyond stealth bombers and nukes.
All of these shortcomings are addressed in a way, in BE.
Spying is revamped and made more interesting and satisfying: you can now, in certain ways again steal technologies, incite unrest and even get combat troops from your opponents.
Combat has not changed much, but the added orbital layer and its use both for combat and peaceful purposes has been implemented quite well. The new science tree means that you will only be able to access orbital layer for combat more towards endgame, giving plenty of opportunity to utilize conventional troops, too.
Troops themselves are now much less individual. They still gain xp, but it is only used for adding certain percentage of attack/defense to the unit, not selecting unique abilities. The unique abilities and troop upgrades now happen automatically and are applied to all existing units upon researching specific technologies and completing certain quests.
One can feel this as beneficial, so you don't have to retro-upgrade ALL your archers ALL the way to the gunships. The associated cost of less individuality might be rather disappointing for many a civ5 fan, such as me, though.
The game itself is much shorter; while the paths to victory are supposedly several, they all (apart from standard domination victory) follow the same routine: research, build a specific wonder associated with your chosen Affinity, be the first to submit X resources (depending on wonder, either troops, or energy (which replaces gold) or some other thing, to the wonder = win.
City states are revamped as "Stations" and work somewhat differently, but still provide a nice trading option.
Trading itself has been limited to only 2 trade routes per city, with the option of acquiring several more in specific cases.
Diplomacy has been improved with the options of Alliances in which the partner automatically attacks your enemy, when you declare war on him(or vice versa) and the option to gain favours with the other civilization. I, however, had not much to do with diplomacy and not much to do with other civs at all. Perhaps, it is possible to intimidate them better, or do some other nifty things, which we missed in Civ5. if so, they do not appear to be required in lower difficulty levels.
There are a number of notable differences, but these are the ones which struck me most.
I haven't played BE much yet, but I feel I would have very much preferred BE to be an expansion to CIV5 concentrating on endgame. All the spying, diplomacy and orbital layer improvements would seem to me to be so much more fun there than they are on their own here.
BE is very new. I wonder, if it will have some significant retweaks, but whatever is going to be added BEYOND Earth, I still hope there will be some of the good new things ported back as expansion or something to CIV5, or maybe CIV6, which will include the abovementioned improvements, but would still provide the richness of CIV5.
In the end, I suppose I will play BE maybe a bit more, but I feel I am rather longing for my Civ5: Brave New World copy instead.  And that is saying much.

Even though every aspect of the cards is spelled out, it is done so through a rather ugly menu interface. A simple mouseover would serve much better for quick explanations.
That being said, if you are an experienced MTG player, it is free MTG, which is good. The lack of good cards will be painful to cope with, but they couldn't exactly stick the power nine into the game without everyone going ballistic. Deck variety is also a pet peeve, with very few tricks that can make your deck "you". However, my biggest issue is the quests, most of which require you to use the archetypes set in the game. All of the archetypes make you take bad cards and the decks are broken from the archetype mold if you change anything beyond the initial build. The archetype decks aren't bad for beginners, but experienced players will be left gritting their teeth at the lousy choices they're forced to make.
Final score 7/10
Complex...but worthy.

CONS:
- Save/travel system is very frustrating. At first you won't get it, but later you'll be moving same place MANY times, and only way to do it - move from rarely placed save points. Later you'll be screaming, after each death, because sometime save points placed in very far and difficult to reach points. And getting back from there to your corpse can be not the easiest thing.
- Many things are unclear. So many times I was walking around whole map again and again - just to get any progress. Game doesn't guide you.
- Most sad part, upgrades don't make your life easier. They only let you visit most hard and very-ftustrating-to-reach places.
NEUTRAL:
- Game has no mercy. Getting back from save point sometimes can take 10-15 minutes and can end by another death. If  you like such style, then enjoy!
OVERALL:
- Game is frustrating and difficult. But beautiful.

Well, I can see the reason why people don't like this game. It is without doubt, linear. The characters aren't that memorable, and they are all a bit childish. There is an average story. Combat can be extremely annoying, obtuse, and vague. However, I enjoyed my time playing the game (the majority of hours played were offline).
The game is gorgeous. The character designs (while flawed) are good. I found myself taking time to pause and just look at the scenery.
I never had problems with the port. A lot of people did and still do. Everything ran perfectly, even using an old laptop with a 650m.
I enjoyed this game, because it is a step out of the normal FF mold. It was a breath of fresh air. I didn't need to spend hours wandering in circles trying to get one forlorn character in a forest. Any customization ws focused more on combat than otherwise. I didn't need to experiment with weapon customization.
Note, there are some really annoying features.
1. Partial Controller support.
2. Combat is more of a test of patience than anything. You can kill it, but it might take forever.
3. Only 99 saves.
4. There is all this stuff to upgrade with, but after reading a FAQ I discovered there were only two or three useful items.
Pros:
1. Graphics
2. Music (amazing)
3. It's  different FF experience (I liked the linear movement of the game).
Cons:
1. Combat can be about strategy, but I found it to be more about patience.
2. Drags on at certain parts.
3. Split into multiple games.
I recommend this game, but I also think you should watch some videos before making the jump.

The Stanley Parable is a narrative story that stars, you guessed it, Stanley. Stanley works in a dead end job carrying out mindless tasks; and the story is told by one of the best narratives I have ever heard. Graphics isn't an important feature here, but that being said, it looks really nice.
The design of the world is very well done, you are essentially in an office building, but it does a very clever thing where you can sometimes be walking around in a circle, and then all of a sudden the world changes, and you are somewhere else. This made the experience feel more real to me. You can make this game as easy or as difficult as you want. There is fifteen different stories and endings to the Stanley Parable, each of them is amazingly written, probably one of, if not the best story in gaming I've experienced and well worth playing. It has taken me almost seven hours to play through all of the endings, and do all but one of the achievements. After you have played all of the endings though, there is probably no need to go replay any of the game again.
Final Decision: 7:10

Newer: EDIT!:
I have since completed the campaign and it was a brutal grind at times (Most of the X games had that at some point). And I must say there are some systems in the game that once they have been fine tuned and you understand them completely its... pretty damned impressive compared to the earlier games. The automated trade system is absolutely lovely, manual trade was the one thing that always turned me into nothing but a hitman in the other X-Games as the combat was really the only rewarding thing. The boarding system is much more interactive and challenging however it can be very difficult to get going initially as marines are sold only as recruits and even with a decent commander they can still get wiped out in seconds of reaching the inside of a craft. Combat against larger targets is much more interesting as they have soft points that can get blown off individually (Turrets, Jump Drive, Engines). The new missle system is short but not very sweet, as they are very cookie cutter (3 different types for fighters, 3 different types for scouts/interceptors, 3 different types for capital ships and stations) also there is NO missle defense system, once the thing is launched there is no getting rid of it unless it hits you or self detonates due to range. Drones have had a huge overhaul, there are hacking drones, automated interceptor/defense drones, missle drones, and manual control combat drones.
Crew: Yeah these actually exist now, mechanics, marine captains, captains, defense officers, architechs, pilots and they can all be trained and have thier own skills.
The game its self is unique in its own way from its predecesors and it expands on its idea as its own and I dont think it should be compared to the other X-games because it is so different from them as there is no comparion really. However those crappy highways need to go away and they need to bring back the Singularity Engine Time Accelerator (SETA)
If Egosoft did the following:
Took Terran Conflict/Albion Prelude and put the many systems that X Rebirth had into games like that then they would indeed have a title well worth their time, X3TC/AP with automated trading, indepth combat/boarding, Crews, Automated Station Administration, Adaptive Drones and took the complexity and diversity of the Terran Conflict/Albion Prelude and that would be something I would gawk at.
However the game its self doesn't stand very well on its own and its so mediocre that I still would skip it.

This game is brutal, unforgiving, and ruthless.  10/10 would buy again.
My three survivors are trying to live in a shelled out building. Katia, Bruno, and Pavel.
Day 5. An older man knocks on the door of my building, asking for refuge. I agree to let him in as I figure another addition to the crew is always welcome and we have resources to spare.
Night 5. Katia goes out on a trade mission to the soldiers in the Northern part of town. She trades moonshine, coffee and smokes in return for building supplies. The only weapon the group owns - A small kitchen knife - is left with the remaining refugees in case of an attack. Pavel guards the door while Anton the new guy and Bruno the cook sleep.
Day 6. Katia returns home to find bandits raided it. Pavel didn't stand much of a chance, he was wounded. All their food is lost. The group is sad, Bruno hasn't had a smoke in six days and the wear of withdraw is creeping up on him.

Night 6. Anton goes on a raid. Nothing of worth is found except a shotgun, some shells, and a few herbs.
Day 7. The lack of food is hitting the group hard. Pavel is recovering slowly from his wounds, Bruno is becoming sick and depressed from withdraw. Katia and Anton are tired from having to take shifts sleeping and clearing out the building because Pavel is recovering in the other bed.
Night 7. Katia goes on a raid to a small apartment complex owned by an eldery couple and their son. She knows the building is locked and the man probably has a gun for looters, so she takes the shotgun hoping she can just take enough food and not have to use it. She's up the side, in through a window and halfway to the kitchen when she hears the old woman scream for help. Katia panics and fires on the old woman, killing her. The woman's husband hears the shots and  runs. She fires again, injuring him. The young man yells in horiffic surprise, his parents gunned down. He's running up the stairs with his own shotgun. Katia fires twice, killing the man and taking his gun. She pulls out a crowbar and kills the old man so he can't run for help.
Before the shock of what has happend  hits her, Katia has 4 cans of meat, 5 bits of raw meat, and enough medical herbs and bullets for her compatriots to last until next week.
Day 8. Katia returns home. She opens the door to the building and collapses to her knees. "How can I live with myself. I killed those innocent people." she cries. Bruno comes up and tries to comfort her but he fails. She's "broken". On the verge of suicide over her actions, and the consequences have effected the whole group. Their all "sad" and it affects the way they act. Bruno makes hot food for the group. They may all die, but it won't be of hunger.
Day 15. Katia finally gets over the worst of the depression, and the group is back to normal. They haven't gone hungry thanks to the moonshine stills upstairs which provide enough alcohol to trade to the soldiers for food and bullets, but the house still has a long way to go to become defensible.
Night 15. Katia raids "sniper's junction". Intel says it's completely safe, but other refugees say otherwise. Arriving, two things greet her; A refugee's wounded screams and sniper fire in the distance. She makes her way to the wounded man, taking cover behind blown out cars. In between sniper shots and the man's cries of agony he begs for his help. Several sniper bullets and a few minutes later and she opens a sewer grate for the man. His relief and gratitude is shown as he asks her to follow him back to his flat. She escorts the now hobbling man back to his home. They enter to the sound of a screaming baby "I'm home Jacob" cries the man, hugging the infant. "I have everything we need and I promise I won't leave you again"  He tells her he wishes he could do more for her, but she is welcome to all the contents of the box under the bed in the next room. Katia enters the bedroom and opens the box - filled with jewlry. "Thank you again, I don't know how I would have survived without you" the man says as Katia heads home.
This is not a story, these are actual events within the game. Killing innocents has effects on your survivors, they aren't soldiers after all and sometimes they can't cope with killing. Sometimes refugees become sad, or depressed. They can become suicidal or become prone to fits of rage against their fellows. They can freeze to death, get killed on raids, starve or die of sickness. But they can also become happy, even if only for a short while. They can build gardens, stills, read books and help other people and families. Every action has a reaction.

I assume Civ:BE is going to be compared to its predecessors, mainly Civ5 and its expansions.
On its own, it is quite a decent game.
But compared to Civ 5, it feels much too like a very well-made, but still a mod.
Civ 5 had quite a winning formula with its hexagonal turn-based combat, sense of history unfolding and variety of ways to victory.
It did frequently seem to have too long an endgame, rudimentary spying abilities, and not much in modern combat beyond stealth bombers and nukes.
All of these shortcomings are addressed in a way, in BE.
Spying is revamped and made more interesting and satisfying: you can now, in certain ways again steal technologies, incite unrest and even get combat troops from your opponents.
Combat has not changed much, but the added orbital layer and its use both for combat and peaceful purposes has been implemented quite well. The new science tree means that you will only be able to access orbital layer for combat more towards endgame, giving plenty of opportunity to utilize conventional troops, too.
Troops themselves are now much less individual. They still gain xp, but it is only used for adding certain percentage of attack/defense to the unit, not selecting unique abilities. The unique abilities and troop upgrades now happen automatically and are applied to all existing units upon researching specific technologies and completing certain quests.
One can feel this as beneficial, so you don't have to retro-upgrade ALL your archers ALL the way to the gunships. The associated cost of less individuality might be rather disappointing for many a civ5 fan, such as me, though.
The game itself is much shorter; while the paths to victory are supposedly several, they all (apart from standard domination victory) follow the same routine: research, build a specific wonder associated with your chosen Affinity, be the first to submit X resources (depending on wonder, either troops, or energy (which replaces gold) or some other thing, to the wonder = win.
City states are revamped as "Stations" and work somewhat differently, but still provide a nice trading option.
Trading itself has been limited to only 2 trade routes per city, with the option of acquiring several more in specific cases.
Diplomacy has been improved with the options of Alliances in which the partner automatically attacks your enemy, when you declare war on him(or vice versa) and the option to gain favours with the other civilization. I, however, had not much to do with diplomacy and not much to do with other civs at all. Perhaps, it is possible to intimidate them better, or do some other nifty things, which we missed in Civ5. if so, they do not appear to be required in lower difficulty levels.
There are a number of notable differences, but these are the ones which struck me most.
I haven't played BE much yet, but I feel I would have very much preferred BE to be an expansion to CIV5 concentrating on endgame. All the spying, diplomacy and orbital layer improvements would seem to me to be so much more fun there than they are on their own here.
BE is very new. I wonder, if it will have some significant retweaks, but whatever is going to be added BEYOND Earth, I still hope there will be some of the good new things ported back as expansion or something to CIV5, or maybe CIV6, which will include the abovementioned improvements, but would still provide the richness of CIV5.
In the end, I suppose I will play BE maybe a bit more, but I feel I am rather longing for my Civ5: Brave New World copy instead.  And that is saying much.

Okay, This game is a combination of awesome and terrible.  If you go into this game expecting it to outdo Civ V or similar games, you may be disappointed, because it isn't a historically based game.  It is fun, which is the main point, but unfortunately, it suffers from a number of game-breaking bugs.  A few patches have come out to address this, but I encountered a few horrible ones after the patch was implemented.  The game is still really cool, and it has a lot of replay value, but don't be surprised if you are 90% of the way toward a victory, and a glitch prevents you from winning.  For example, Covert Operations (which is a neat element to the game) might completely black out so that you can only press "accept" or "cancel" without knowing what is going on.  A game victory called "the beacon" does not work right now (they might fix it), and a few other interesting things take place.  The multiplayer is fun, but good luck finding other people to get together with and play on a regular basis.  Single player is fun as well, but the computer cannot outplay a human being.  To compensate for this, the developers allowed the computer to cheat a little bit by not having to worry about health (happiness) or other elements and having extra energy (money) at the game start.

One of the most underatted games of all time, and one of my favorite rpg's ever.
Originally released on Xbox 360 to mediocre reviews, yet if you played through the
terrible frame rate and texture issues then a true gem was waiting.
On the PC version you can enjoy the game with most of the technical issues resolved.
The battle system in this game is simply amazing, if you truly get into the game and face
some of the later bosses the wealth of depth and tactical choice is awesome. The
fighs are turn based but instaed of controlling individual characters you control different
squads consisting of numerous soldiers recrutted on your journey. As the game progresses
the squad limit rises with your level (Battle Rank) which means battles get bigger and better
the further you get. This leads to some epic, amazing and huge encounters.
The progression, story and side quests all fit into one of square enix's darker tales. While the
story isn't the greatest I've experienced in  a JRPG it's still very good. I love the lore and history
of the game world. If you want to do all of the side quests there is well over 100 hrs of gameplay
(I must have at least 500 hrs on Xbox). It starts slow but stay with it.
To put into perspective how highly I rate this game here is my top 5 JRPG's (in no order 'top 5' was hard enough)
The Last Remnant
Dagon Quest - The Journey of the Cursed King (say no more)
Final Fantasy XII (yes 12, a masterpiece and way ahead of it's time in my humble opinion)
Grandia (my word what a game)
Persona 4 (sweeeeeet)
As you can see it joins some pretty good games on that list.
Word of advise if you are just starting the game- grind for an hour or so early on or the first true boss will
own you.

- Combat is simple, but fun with a few different ways to change up how you play with charms
- The world is vast, and full of hidden secrets
- Challenging boss fights
- Fantastic soundtrack
- Progression of your character makes you feel more powerful as the game goes on
- Artstyle, this is my opinion obviously but I adore the cutesy look to the game, even though it can be hard as hell
- Price. It's hard to find an indie game of this quality for $15
- Free DLC, and support from the developer. The game continues to improve
Cons:
- The backtracking in the game can get quite tedious at times, although it has improved slightly with some of the updates
- Some people may find the death penalty too brutal for their tastes. If you have played Dark Souls, it is similar to that.(I personally do not think it is a big deal, but I have seen many posts disliking it)
Overall, I highly recommend Hollow Knight if you enjoy Metroidvania esque games. I personally think Hollow Knight is a 2D Dark Souls. The game has length, exploration, progression, challenge, and great gameplay all for a cheap price tag.
You won't regret your purchase!

Despite everything that has been said about it, "BioShock 2" still manages to be a great sequel.
Indeed, there is truth in the claims that the world is more 'empty' in terms of storytelling. The story itself is much more linear and personal, but that's what made the game special to me. Feeling that a Big Daddy feels was not only interesting, but oddly emotional. A lot of great moments are to be heard and seen in this game.
The biggest upgrade has been recieved by the combat system. Here, it's significantly more fluid and rich, to the point of being insanely fun, in drastic contrast to the first game.
This game does absolutely not deserve the hate it has been given. It's not to be disregarded in any way. And if you let go of expectations and comparisons, try to experience it as a standalone story in the same setting. That's the best mindset to go with.
It's absolutely not as philosophical as the first game. But it's much more fun, intuitive and not at all less emotional.
I recommend "BioShock 2" to everyone. And I will say this: different is not always bad. And new sometimes contains the "good" and the "bad". Some say the perfect blend of the two reasults in perfection. "BioShock 2" is not perfect, but it ain't that far either.

Recommended if you can get it on sale, this is a fairly truncated RPG, not just in length, but in terms of the amount of narrative expressed over the course of the game. There are other short RPGs out there which pack more story and/or character development into a similar amount of time. But Machina of the Planet Tree still delivers a solid gameplay experience, and may be worth checking out even if RPGMaker games which try to evoke the feeling of classic RPGs rarely meet your standards.
Pros:
-Visually impressive, fast-paced combat system with enough strategic depth to not wear out its welcome over the course of the game.
-Dialogue is competently written and reasonably entertaining.
-Characters and setting are, if not groundbreaking, at least outside the realms of cliche.
-Good original music.
Cons:
-Crunched pacing.
-Poorly developed setting. The characters visit several dungeons over the course of the game, but almost none of them have any significance other than as waypoints, and they aren't used to flesh out the game's setting.
-Barely any character or relationship development over the course of the game.
Overall, the game manages to be pleasant, but not exciting. If the screenshots make it look appealing to you, it's worth checking out. If they don't already have you sold, it's unlikely to offer any surprises to pull you in.
