I'm going to have to go against the grain on this one, disagree with the average folk, and say this game is kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's graphics are amazing, and the destructible terrain is great. Gameplay, at least as far as how it handles, it good. But here's where the budget ran out. The NPC's are broken. They'll get stuck on walls, and at times will just walk one by one into a building for headshots like sheep, but they have very peculiar cones of vision at times and incredibly sharp eyes if you happen to be in that cone. Brush and rocks sometimes help keep you hidden, but overall the vegetation feels like it's more for looks than cover.
And don't get me started on helicopters. If the AI doesn't decide the helicopter should leave on a whim, you can't run away. Find a missile launcher or get really good at using your grenade launcher, because there's no such thing as hiding from one. You could speed away and hide beneath a cliff wall, and the helicopter will magically, on a whim fly directly over you to see if you're over there, regardless of distance. Helicopters are fight or die and do not take damage from small arms fire or machine guns.
The mechanics of the game are "cool" but quickly become a handicap when you realize just how many NPC's with pinpoint accuracy you're up against. Managing your energy becomes a chore, as your energy reserves are just too goddamn low.
You know what? Screw EVERYTHING I just said. You want to know why this game really fails? Because I don't really feel like a super soldier. Sure I have cool abilities and can take a few hits, but most FPS games are like that when you get down to it. This game fails on the simple notion that it doesn't make you feel like a super soldier. It's just meant to be visually pleasing as hell and have entertaining enough gameplay to keep the graphics obsessed players happy while the rest shrug and move on.

The most interesting thing I've found about This War of Mine is that it forces you to plan ahead. You're not going to hit a point where you think you've got a good handle on your current situation, and that you're comfortable knowing nothing is going to go wrong. You always have to think about what the next problem is going to be, and how you're going to plan for it. The game is well balanced, and the different elements (food, meds, weapons, trade..) that you have to manage are well balanced and each have a significant role to play in your planning for survival.
Each new game has fairly randomized events and locations, though as you get to a second or third play through you start noticing a pattern and that some of the events are scripted, for example,
. This doesn't take away from the experience though, and will be mitigated with new content.
My first play through lasted 39 days, which isn't all that great, and it ended with the shooting death of one character, another lost to illness, one fleeing my shelter, and the last committing suicide.
Overall, definite purchase for anyone who likes strategizing in games, and a great addition to anyone's library.

I wrote a “mixed” review of this game a while back that through repeated consideration and recently going back to play other Final Fantasy games I realized that my complaints regarding it's linearity were and are unwarranted. I do however wish that Square Enix had broken away somewhat from this formulaic approach.
I absolutely loved the battle system, it's so fluid and dynamic. It's one of the best I've ever dealt with.
This game is linear... really linear, almost literally the entire game is in a hallway. Connected by more hallways. This is true while it does open up in the late game, the VERY late game but that area still feels like filler material.
Mechanics :
The battle system is extremely chaotic at first glance. It's essentially a meter management sim. However it sure feels good when you manage those meters well. The battle system is almost completely automated, you have 6 characters and 6 roles they could play.
Quick summation of each role
You take either two or three of these roles depending on where you are at in the narrative. And form Paradigms or strategies (up to six) Essentially you control the leader of the pack while the other party members fulfill their role they have been assigned in the current paradigm. Effectively you as the leader switch paradigms to best fit the situation at hand. With most battles objective to get the enemy stagger meter all the way up, allowing their turns to be interrupted and take more damage. All battles essentially go on like this for the duration of the game. (Building chains essentially is the stagger meter, as in when the meter drops to zero you must restart “the chain” to get the enemy staggered once again)
There are a few exceptions such as the gestalt Eidolon battles. Which have you perform the same sorts of tactics under a timer. THE DOOM TIMER. Spooky. You end the battle by getting the gestalt meter to the top and pushing a button. A sort of manifestation of consciousness as I understand. Which leads me to the other part of battles which is known as TP or technical points. You can summon your Eidolon or do other moves unlocked through the various roles. Which in my experience were only useful in the end game. The Summons however where almost completely useless. A sort of fan service if I may borrow the term.
In Chapter 9, you gain the ability to select your party and assign them any role. However it seems slightly counter productive to have your characters spec down a completely different path then what you've been doing for the past 20+ hours. In Chapter 11, the infamous open world comes to fruition. Sort of. You're no longer traversing an extremely linear actual hallway. You now have open fields to explore. You do have the option to take side missions but they are just crystal way-points. There is some loose narrative in that you are fulfilling the focus of a l'cie turned Cei'th but what it really feels like is monster hunting to disguise level grinding. All that being said, they are not all easy fights. I had to adopt new strategies rather quickly to survive.
The game is in fact rather easy until you are suddenly dropped into the wild fields of chapter 11 leading you into ten's possibly triple digits (if you're a completionist) of additional hours of fighting enemy after enemy. It can be a bit grind-y sure. But in this genre that is too be expected.
It's just missing that special something. There isn't any HUB world. No replenishing stock with your favorite vendor and establishing a rapport after a long grind of killing beasts in the forests. Just inanimate kiosks that bring you goods should you ever need to actually purchase something. And that's another issue. Other-worldly precious Gil is almost a total non factor. Complete let down.
The story is fine. It's nothing to write home about. Lightning is a cool character. I like her better than Liara T'Soni (same voice actor which is a strange comparison to bring up to be honest) Although some obvious character tropes drag on a little long in my opinion.

Keep in mind that I will be treating this game as its own standalone game, rather than part of a series. Comparisons to previous games will just turn this into a lengthy review with too much complaining.
Hitman Absolution created by IO Interactive and published by SquareEnix, is a stealth based 3rd person shooter. Now this isn’t a typical action game with cover based combat and massacre mentality gameplay. Absolution encourages taking a stealthy approach and punishes your gaming score if you take out enemies who were not targets or get spotted while trying to sneak around. Unlike other games, you don’t get an automatic game over for getting spotted. If you get seen by a guard or evil accomplice, you need to find your own way to solve the situation. There are several modes of the enemy being on high alert for you: Suspicious, Hostile, Cautious, Searching and Hunting.
This game takes a brutally realistic approach how easily enemies will see you and how they’ll attack you when it all goes to hell. Firefights are a challenge with these guys and gives you all the more reason to be stealthy. No regenerating health and very few health stations make avoiding combat seem ideal.
However, even with the realistic reactions from the enemy AI, there is a problem with the disguise mechanic; most of the time, the disguise mechanic only really gives you a five second head start during trespass sections. Pretty much everyone can see through your disguise, you won’t even get ten seconds in a hostile area if you don’t have instinct. I’m pretty sure that not every cop, construction worker, guard or engineer knows each other by heart. It’s a hindrance but it wasn’t enough to ruin the game.
This game is very story driven, and I feel that is one of the bigger disappointments of the game. The story starts off very strong and interesting and ends in a satisfying way, but the journey from point A to point B is a bit lacking. This story lacks many interesting characters. Almost none of the people you are hunting have an interesting backstory or motivation. All they really become are faceless NPCs that just had some really small part in the overall evil scheme. It really feels like Agent 47 is just trying to get rid of everything associated with Victoria and tie up all loose ends. That motivation is fine, but you can’t really feel 47’s drive to eliminate these individuals because the reasons are just so simple and open ended. You just don’t get the same satisfaction as killing someone like Handsome Jack from Borderlands 2, who was interesting and easy to despise.
Another problem with the story is that I don’t think the gameplay designers and the writers were on the same page, or really communicating with each other. There are some parts in the late game where Agent 47 seems to know things that he shouldn’t, like when a certain target will be in the area. How did he even know that this person needed to die? Some of the main antagonists were people that Agent 47 knew nothing about or even met, so him knowing things about them even when his information broker Birdie was gone is a bit illogical. Some explanations during those lengthy cut scenes would have been appreciated; otherwise the story will sound rushed and lacking.
Again, that aspect was annoying but it didn’t ruin the game for me.
Gameplay is where Absolution shines and the ways that you can approach any situation is very fun and satisfying. Using your environment and your critical thinking skills make this game fun and addicting. If you care about score, then this game will cause you to have mental masochistic perfectionism. The only part I can really criticize when it comes to the scoring system is that it’s used for an upgrade system that really doesn’t feel helpful at all. Every time I got an upgrade, I didn’t feel any different and I didn’t feel like my experience and approach to the levels evolved at all. Being able to choose your upgrades would have been ideal.
Overall, I found Hitman Absolution to be a very fun game that, despite the somewhat unfair mechanics and lackluster story, I still found myself playing through levels over and over just to get that satisfying feeling of doing well.

Action games in general take themselves rather seriously these days, but Not A Hero isn't one of them. From the get go you're told by a giant talking purple rabbit from the future to shoot gang members so the British public will elect him as ruler of England and prevent the world from ending. From there on you're sent on 21 missions set in various warehouses and tower blocks, all filled with various thugs and criminals to shoot your way through.
The gameplay is simple enough: you run through a series of 2D buildings fighting enemies in short, fast-paced battles, using a basic cover mechanic to avoid being shot along the way and regenerate health when necessary. The same cover button can be used to tackle and trip over enemies, leaving them incapacitated for a short while and vulnerable for a stylish execution move. Fallen enemies can occasionally drop special ammo types that last until the next time you reload your weapon. Sometimes these effects are useful, and sometimes they just add a brief special effect to your ammunition, such as flame ammo or disintegration beams. There are also special weapons found in certain places, offering you powerful, limited use attacks for the more difficult sections.
Successfully completing missions (and the optional objectives in each one) increases BunnyLord's approval rating. High ratings result in more characters being unlocked, and they're all fun to use and have their own styles of play. For instance, Clive can shoot in both directions at once as a special attack and kick down doors, and Kimmy has an instant kill katana that charges up with every execution she makes. You'll generally end up experimenting with the characters to find your own favourite because they're all effective at getting the job done in the end. The music is also great, having a certain 8-bit chiptune charm to it. Sometimes having a great track in the background helps to relieve the frustation when a ninja manages to slice you in half for the thirtieth run in a row.
The game does have a few problems though. As likable as the cast is, they aren't particularly well balanced. As mentioned earlier, they're all effective at beating the levels, but some characters are better suited for 100% completion than others. Basically, early characters all have their own special attributes, but a few of the later unlockables have too many strengths and few weaknesses. Mike is especially guilty of this due to his rapid movement speed, powerful shotgun and instant knife execution, which generally allows you to slide tackle entire floors and run back down the corridor stabbing everyone up until the third chapter.
The humour is also a bit hit and miss. I thought the playable characters had some genuinely funny lines, especially in the character select screen, but BunnyLord himself is too reliant on spouting random things and jamming various words together. In all fairness, his dialogue is randomly generated in places to begin with, but it's sometimes more annoying than amusing because of this. Finally, the game is a bit short. I managed to reach 100% completion in roughly 9 hours of play, although I really enjoyed the time I had with it in the end.
In short, Not A Hero is a fun, fast paced game that doesn't take itself seriously and is definitely worth a look if its on sale. It has a few issues, but if you're looking for a good action game you could do a lot worse than voting BunnyLord.

Not a hero is an excellent action game with an outstanding retro soundtrack and tight controls. Each level is like the setup for an action movie and you control a bunch of hitmen out to help a purple bunny win an election by taking out all the criminals in the city to save the future. Yes, the story is quite ridiculous but it is told in a suitably tongue in cheek manner and is still entertaining. The action itself is smooth and enables a lot of cinematic moments as you crash through windows and doors and use your chosen character's special abilities (run and reload, slide and shoot, etc) to clear the levels. The animations are excellent and the level layouts really up the intensity. Each mission has optional objectives used to help determine a perfect clear and achieving them turns the levels into an almost action puzzle-like setup where you have to carefully plan and execute your moves while carefully exploiting all the opportunities presented to you. It's fast, intense and funny (with the occasionaly gratuitious violence and dark humour which may not be to everyone's taste). The 8-bit style pixel art is fantastic too, very detailed with nice little touches everywhere to set the atmosphere. All in all, a strong recommendation if you like action games, shooters in particular and skill-based yet accessible to everyone progression in a game.

From someone who's not a "diehard" fan this game has it's ups and downs. Keep in mind this is all coming from someone who's only played this and Civ 5. To be honest the game is pretty broken in a lot of aspects and doesn't have many redeeming factors... Why a recommended? The game does it's job which is to hold your attention. This is evident when you look at all the reviews. All the negative reviews with 200+ hours of gameplay. I feel like this game could become something great if patches and DLC are worked correctly.
Anywhozzle.
Pros:
The Barbarian alternatives. (Won't say too much here other than that they definitely improved on the randoms of the game. Almost feels like you're defending against another civilization while holding off the hoards.)
The Story. Most people in the reviews don't seem to give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about the games lore but the game transitions small aspects into the gameplay. Just enough to where you can piece together a little of whats happening while building your civilization.
The aggressiveness. I felt like in Civ 5 every other leader was just waiting for a chance to denounce or declare war on some random fellow on the map. In BE the gameplay (single player) seems to be toned down a lot which makes it seem more realistic for what it is. No one seems to declare war on you unless you downright deserve it.
Tech Tree and policies. These I felt were done much better in BE. As opposed to unlocking each previous tier of the trees before being able to move to future tech, like in the previous game, here you can jump around by unlocking certain techs before others. This can allow you to make many different decisions throughout the game and allow much more replayability.
Cons:
Simplistic design. Lots can be improved on here. I feel like I've landed in South America + Aliens on each map I load. Not much variety as to what you can find in the maps. It's about the same as Civ 5 dispite being on distant planets. I was hoping for more cool unique alien related biomes.
Leaders don't seem like leaders. Every leader in the game seems like some random pulled off the street and told "Here ya go be generic for this game"
Lack of Units. The goodness of the tech tree can be counted against it as well. If you make a few early game mistakes and don't start leveling the right tech up you'll be left with a serious lack of units in the game. I've also noticed in general that you can't build very many military units either. The units you unlock seem to relate to farming, mining, production and such more as opposed to firepower. On one playthrough where I focused on a certain victory type I made it to turn 350 with only 4 available miltary units but something like 15 to 20 random units. Every unit serves it's own purpose and none of them are useless really but I don't feel like so many PvE related units were necessary.
Too much going on. Going from above the massive amount of PvE units make every turn a constant click around. To get to your 2 soldiers you have to go through about 30 unit prompts just bringing random♥♥♥♥♥♥up while you had them asleep. I found it hard to understand the early game even with the tutorials just due to the massive amount of different dialaog boxes being thrown at me every turn. Seems like building a simple monument comes with 3 yes or no questions and a survay.
All in all not a bad game. Would give it a 6/10 as of now but major potential.

Do you like grinding?
Do you like minimal control over your characters?
Do you like almost no customization options for party members?
Do you like a cringe-worthy story with cutscenes playing out like a complete amateur scripted them?
Do you like poorly ported controls and optimization?
Then The Last Remnant is the game for you.
Almost every part of the game requires some degree of grinding. Let me elaborate. You are advancing in the story. You just unlocked a new place to visit. But wait! If you do not re-visit the previously visited stories and kill every single enemy 3 times, you are not going to have a chance against the enemies in the new area!
What is that? You just did that and are no longer having problems with fighting enemies in the new area, even if you aggro 5 groups at a time?
I guess that means you can go fight the boss, right? Whoops, he instakilled you because your level is too low. If you exit the area and clear all its enemies 3 more times, the boss will actually only deal about half as much damage! That works every time!
Coincidentally, the only parts that are not grindy or fetch-quests are essentially the tutorials and early side-quests, because they automatically teleport you to the area you are goign to, initiate the thing you are supposed to do, and teleport you back to the quest NPC to give you a reward, all automatically. Which is not really that good at teaching you anything, but at least you do not have to grind.

Every action you have in a fight will have a pre-determined combination of actions, depending on how many action points you have. Half the time, there is no option for ranged attacks, even if you are able to do them. When you are healing yourself with white majykks, all non-healers will stand by. If you use the option that allows you to attack AND heal, your characters will prioritize using items, unless they have no item skills, even if their magic is stronger. If you let them play by ear, which is supposed to let each character in a squad attack the way they want to, they'll just auto-attack without using skills most of the time, even if you have 100+ AP and their skills cost 7.
The only way you can customize any character except the MC (Rush Sykes) is by deciding whether you will let them take your loot to upgrade their weapons or not. Other than that, you can only tug them in the right direction by spamming commands that will increase a certain skill or attribute if used a lot, but that will unbalance your entire party and make them less efficient, since Legions normally have a mix of melee and caster characters.
The rest of my points speak for themselves.

I am now going to write some things about a video game.
This video game is called "The Last Remnant." Like many Japanese RPGs, the MC is a young child (called Rush) who is  estranged from his parents, and naturally this is a key plot point and one of the driving forces behind the story. This is generic and loathsome and not something I enjoy. However, the detestable MC, who is probably named after his tendencies to act brashly and without thought (Very subtle, game.) is one of the few characters I found myself disliking. I rather quickly grew fond of David and his 4 generals, for instance, despite their lack of any given motive other than to serve their leader. In fact, David's motives are perhaps the most confusing of all. I found myself playing on to try and discover what they were.
However, along the way, I was swept away by my love for the combat. It's highly detailed and strategy based; you create squads of soldiers and have them perform commands as a group. It's an interesting style and quickly captured my attention. However, it quickly lost it again once I realised how grindy the game is. It's also needlessly complex for newer players, not teaching anything more than "Attack enemies! Heal allies! Win fights! Don't lose!" The character progression system is overly complex, and is never quite explained, to my knowledge. I've done a fair bit of research, and the gist of it is that the more a unit uses a specific type of command, the better it becomes with that type of command (e.g magic, physical attacks, healing spells) and will learn more powerful abilities of that type. However, managing the equipment of your allies is hopelessly complex and grindy and this is where the game falls down. It's painfully slow in the early to mid game, and that's about as far as I got before getting bored and giving up.
It pains me to say that I don't recommend the game. It's an interesting game with a fairly nice range of characters, and there is some kind of ridiculously complex yet... existing plot. It features magic, so you know it's good. But the monotony, repetitive battles and grindy nature make it far too slow to enjoy. And this is coming from a guy who loves a good grind.

LOVING THE GAME SO FAR.
There's just a different appeal for this game compared to the rest of RPG maker games that makes it so enjoyable.
- The characters are amazing, something you'd find in a typical Anime.
Their dialogs are nicely written, and they interact with each other fairly frequently.
Voices fit the characters really well too.
THERE'S EVEN VOICE ACTING FOR BATTLES AND THE AFTER BATTLE DIALOG. ;^)
Typical teenage, deepish voice for Cram, a high pitched, cheery voice for Relta, A calm, Kuudere sounding voice for Esty.
Can't forget the mid 20's sounding roboting voice for Cronos too.
- The story is pretty decent, it's somewhat comprehensible.
The characters explain a good of the background information time to time, and there are also three books in the library that can help you understand what the hell a "Machina" or a "Planet tree" is.
- The combat system is really nice too. It's similar to FF's style of combat. (Turn based, picking skills) But, presents you with an Action point system that allows you to choose your skills based on how many points you're able to expend during your turn. There is a multiplier to the amount of damage you deal as well. The more combos you chain, the stronger the next attack will be. If the monster is weak to that certain attack/element, then that will also increase your damage multiplier.
This gives a very nice diverse combat feel to experiment with, allowing you to find out which combinations are strong or weak against certain enemies or bosses, which can be used to your advantage.
- The upgrading system for weapons includes finding items through excavation or monster drops and collecting the quantity required for a weapon enhancement. There aren't that many upgrades for each weapon, and the weapon balance in the game isn't too perfect. You may find yourself selling weapons more often rather than equiping.
- The difficult of the game varies, but is also quite balanced. You may find yourself losing a few battles, due to ineffective elements against bosses/monsters or an error during combo chains. As stated before, creating the optimal skill set for battles is the key to victory. If the four skils you assign to your characters in the battle aren't effective against the current enemy you are battling, it may prove to be more difficult. But having the right elements/attacks in each battle will give you an upper hand. Mainly trial and error.
- The art is the strongest part of the game. God, those visuals look amazing.
Something different from other RPG maker games. This uses VN styled character animations that show the characters emotions and body gestures as their dialog is displayed.
- OVERALL, 11/10. AMAZING RPG MAKER GAME, PICK THIS UP WHENEVER IT GOES ON SALE. IT'S A PRETTY PRICEY GAME FOR 12.99, BUT A DAMN STEAL FOR $3.24.
(TIP : Make sure you extract multiple times from each attribute slate too.)

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a borderline Recommend (call it 3 stars out of 5).  First, the good:  the story that drives the game is a good one and, for a game initially released back in 2001, the graphics are pretty good.   The cut-scenes and voice acting are also pretty good.   The initial key-binding are awful, but with a little effort they can be made to approximate current bindings.
Now, for the less-than-good:  there's nothing really wrong with the game, but the fact that the player can't affect the outcome in any way drags it down for me.  Specifically, most levels have Secret Areas (SAs) and Treasures.  But, whether or not you enter those SAs or pick up any Treasures is irrelevant.  You get nothing useful outside of the box saying you've found all the SAs/Treasures when you leave the level (and maybe some additional health, ammo, or armor).  Also, even though I used "Return to Castle Wolfenstein Single Player v1.42c Unofficial Patch" to fix various bugs and allow me to use my standard 1920x1200 resolution, I still ran across a few glitches associated with those SAs.  Specifically, in one case, even though I found, opened and looted a certain SA, the game refused to give me the credit for it.  In another case, when I entered one SA, I couldn't manage to leave it.  Also, in every level, you can go back to search for the SAs once you've cleared the it of enemies.  Except for one level.  But, again, that means nothing to how the game plays out.
So, all-in-all, it's an OK game.  If you favor straight shooters over more quest-driven action games, you'll probably like this better than I did.  It's currently listing for about $10 and is on sale for $5.  At $5, it's a buy.  At $10, you might want to think about it a bit.

Although Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion lacks a campaign that so many gamers love and look for, it more than makes up for this by atmosphere, scale, and depth. Sins of a Solar Empire is one of those games balanced in such a way that there's no clear balance. That doesn't mean it's bad, it just means that each race (the Vasari, the TEC, and the Advent) have different playing styles.
In contrast to games such as StarCraft, where everone knows the three races have their own triangle of defeat (Zerg beats Protoss, Protoss beats Terran, and Terran beats Zerg), Sins of a Solar Empire is all about your strategy. Will you expand your space outwards, take planets and conquer the enemy, or will you lie in wait until the time is right?
The scale of the game is truely marvelous, but often goes overlooked. The zoom function is really helpful, as it shows that even the tiniest of battles are absurdly dramatic: If you're zoomed out enough, you see two little ship icons, and perhaps some fire in between them, Zoom in more and you see stunning 3D models, complete with thrusters, blinking lights, etc, and you can see exactly what they're firing. Zoom in until one fills your screen and suddenly you notice that it's on fire, sparks are flying, and the enemy's fire is devastating the hull with massive explosions.
If you love strategy games, space games, or just want to watch ships burn, you'll probably like this game.

Man has long yearned to fly among the stars. To be in space. The final frontier. There's all kinds of cool things up there, all of which could kill everyone on our planet in the blink of an eye. We've obviously never really been in space though, or on the moon. That's a conspiracy perpetuated by Richard Nixon and the Disney Channel. You don't want to believe the lies, but it makes people happy. Just like the tooth fairy or the concept of chivalry. You can believe whatever you like, but really all they want is to get in your mouth and leave some money on your nightstand.
While humanity will probably never REALLY be in space, because space is actually also a conspiracy that Disney Channel likes to keep going for their "special interests", we can imagine what this fictitious place called outer space is like through video games. Yeah!
According to the legends, people can float in space. There's a force that pulls things towards planets, but there's none of it in space. "Gravity", they call it. It's apparently what holds us onto Earth. Even though everyone knows that we're actually held to the Earth's surface by the natural paste on our feet and shoes. If you ever sprayed non-stick cooking spray on your feet, you'd float into the sun and die.

Defy Gravity is a little budget puzzle platformer. Nothing too fancy. I probably bought it for a quarter. But definitely a quarter well-spent. It's short, sweet, fun, and surprisingly smart.

Defy Gravity packs a lot of punch for a simple game. I can count the amount of stage hazards on my fingers. And yet the way they're combined is never dull. It's a short, compact game. Most puzzle games need to be this huge♥♥♥♥♥Rube Goldberg type of thing. I wrote a “mixed” review of this game a while back that through repeated consideration and recently going back to play other Final Fantasy games I realized that my complaints regarding it's linearity were and are unwarranted. I do however wish that Square Enix had broken away somewhat from this formulaic approach.
I absolutely loved the battle system, it's so fluid and dynamic. It's one of the best I've ever dealt with.
This game is linear... really linear, almost literally the entire game is in a hallway. Connected by more hallways. This is true while it does open up in the late game, the VERY late game but that area still feels like filler material.
Mechanics :
The battle system is extremely chaotic at first glance. It's essentially a meter management sim. However it sure feels good when you manage those meters well. The battle system is almost completely automated, you have 6 characters and 6 roles they could play.
Quick summation of each role
You take either two or three of these roles depending on where you are at in the narrative. And form Paradigms or strategies (up to six) Essentially you control the leader of the pack while the other party members fulfill their role they have been assigned in the current paradigm. Effectively you as the leader switch paradigms to best fit the situation at hand. With most battles objective to get the enemy stagger meter all the way up, allowing their turns to be interrupted and take more damage. All battles essentially go on like this for the duration of the game. (Building chains essentially is the stagger meter, as in when the meter drops to zero you must restart “the chain” to get the enemy staggered once again)
There are a few exceptions such as the gestalt Eidolon battles. Which have you perform the same sorts of tactics under a timer. THE DOOM TIMER. Spooky. You end the battle by getting the gestalt meter to the top and pushing a button. A sort of manifestation of consciousness as I understand. Which leads me to the other part of battles which is known as TP or technical points. You can summon your Eidolon or do other moves unlocked through the various roles. Which in my experience were only useful in the end game. The Summons however where almost completely useless. A sort of fan service if I may borrow the term.
In Chapter 9, you gain the ability to select your party and assign them any role. However it seems slightly counter productive to have your characters spec down a completely different path then what you've been doing for the past 20+ hours. In Chapter 11, the infamous open world comes to fruition. Sort of. You're no longer traversing an extremely linear actual hallway. You now have open fields to explore. You do have the option to take side missions but they are just crystal way-points. There is some loose narrative in that you are fulfilling the focus of a l'cie turned Cei'th but what it really feels like is monster hunting to disguise level grinding. All that being said, they are not all easy fights. I had to adopt new strategies rather quickly to survive.
The game is in fact rather easy until you are suddenly dropped into the wild fields of chapter 11 leading you into ten's possibly triple digits (if you're a completionist) of additional hours of fighting enemy after enemy. It can be a bit grind-y sure. But in this genre that is too be expected.
It's just missing that special something. There isn't any HUB world. No replenishing stock with your favorite vendor and establishing a rapport after a long grind of killing beasts in the forests. Just inanimate kiosks that bring you goods should you ever need to actually purchase something. And that's another issue. Other-worldly precious Gil is almost a total non factor. Complete let down.
The story is fine. It's nothing to write home about. Lightning is a cool character. I like her better than Liara T'Soni (same voice actor which is a strange comparison to bring up to be honest) Although some obvious character tropes drag on a little long in my opinion.

: I really wanted to like Crysis. Like REALLY. I've waited years to play this game, to make sure my system could handle it at max settings. While the graphics still look great even 10 years later, everything - and I mean EVERYTHING - else in this game is a broken afterthought, as if the devs built a great benchmarking tool and then said, "Wait, isn't this supposed to be a GAME?"
If you want to play a spec ops game, Crysis ain't one. Not even close. You can't play this as a stealth game, nor can you play it as a shoot-em-up FPS. Enemies (without NVGs!) can see you a mile away at night, when you are
. Does that sound fun? They go on alert when you kill with a silencer a hundred feet away, yet remain completely unfazed when coming across a fresh body on the ground. Melee combat is a joke and you have no knife or any other instant takedown ability, except for grabbing an enemy and punching the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out of him or throwing him like a ragdoll, alerting the whole base in the process.
If you choose open combat, you will die A LOT - even on normal difficulty. You move slowly (or
fast for 5 seconds at a time); cover is useless, and you cannot suppress enemies even with a machine gun or a goddam MINIGUN. Using mounted machine guns, you have no cover and become a bullet sponge. Grenades have a ridiculous delay and can't be cooked, and enemies ALWAYS know when you throw one. Enemies on boats are EXTREMELY hard to kill, and any enemy on a machine gun will take you out if you go head-on.
You are supposed to be fighting a highly trained KPA force, but they act nothing like an organized military. Think of enemies in Far Cry 1 - these are just as dumb. They have no concept of tactical movement, flanking, suppression, air support, mortars (what mortars?) or artillery fire - except for superficial artillery fire towards the end of the game. You can spray and pray with a machine gun and enemies will literally stare at the ground where your shots land (I kid you not), instead of taking cover and flanking and/or calling in air support.
. It has less battery time than your iphone before it needs a re-charge. You can only use one mode at a time and they are all useless. Armor is weak, you can't shoot in cloak mode (whaaa?), speed is slow and ineffective, and strength mode isn't much to write home about, either. Stealth and speed run out faster than your bank account in Vegas, too.
There is no gore in this game. So much for "realism." The blood setting is off by default and does nothing but create small, disappearing blood sprites when you first shoot an enemy. No pools of blood, no bullet holes, no corpse damage from explosions or point-blank shotgun blasts. Nothing. You can't even move a dead enemy.
I just don't get how this game got such high reviews for being as broken as it is. Crytek has failed at game design in Crysis 1. Am I ten years too late on this review? Maybe. But this is just my $0.02.

Alright after about a month I can't recommend this game to anyone.
This game is way more grindy than the previous ones. This should be somewhat expected, given most free-to-play models; but the grindiness is compounded by a variety of issues.
1. Packs cost 150 gold and give you six cards. A game against the medium AI (minimum difficulty to work quests) gives you ten gold. Quests seem to be worth about 10 gold per game. So it takes five or six games for each pack, if you play optimally. This is about one card per game, which would be okay, except...
2. There are many hidden requirements in quests. I've learned the hard way that you must use the Deck Wizard to complete any archetypal quests. Also you can't play against the Easy AI. For the current community quest, I don't actually know what it wants me to do, and I don't want to spend the time on the trial and error.
3. The Deck Wizard is outstandingly bad. If you want to use your newest cards, then you have to go through the Deck Wizard before most quests and re-build a deck from scratch, and you have to HOPE that it lets you select your new/good cards. If you're building a tribal deck, then it still presents you with strictly worse off-tribe creatures. The same goes for any type of theme.
4. The server is still down quite frequently. I just attempted to play this game again after almost a week-long hiatus (I can't get motivated to play it any more; it feels like work), and I had to sit here for ten minutes trying to reconnect to the server so that it would log my single game win toward my quests.
This is all just from my experience playing against the AI on my own. I've heard lots of complaints about multiplayer.
tl;dr: It's a bad game and it's not fun. I only play because I want the cards.

Hello, first I'd like to say that this review is coming from a player which does not enjoy the Final Fantasy series' that features the random-battle feature and has played this game continously and various platforms.
The first point I'd like to highlight is the presentation of this game. Even if you're a major fan of the old-style gameplay of the final fantasy series you can atleast appreciate the artistry of the game. It's a beautifully constructed game with 4k graphics and a stunning soundtrack but this doesn't remove your focus from the game itself. The story is deeply routed in the game-play. Hell, at one point a character uses a heal OUT OF BATTLE during a cutscene just for added realism. The story follows the main protagonist Lightning, who becomes a L'Cie (bad guy) after trying to save her sister (Sarah) after she became a L'Cie and fulfilled her focus (a job which otherwise turns you into an ugly golem, thing). The story follows these characters through the realities of becoming something you hate while trying to fulfilled your focus without deterring from your morals.
The battle system isn't turn based like the older titles in the FF series but can easily be enjoyable if you play with an open mind. Instead of you having to calculate how many turns are needed to kill an enemy, you need to work out the fastest way to kill an enemy before they hit you - as they will, trust me. Enemies attack as if they have a ATB bar just like you, so expect to be constantly aware of your battles. The battle system itself is a pain, though. It features a tree-like leveling up system which honestly doesn't give you any indication of how to use it. It just says to level it up and level it up until eventually you have no idea if you should've gone down one path or the other.
I'd have to say the main feature of the game that I ADORE is the character development and storyline throughout the first game. While Lightning herself has the most character development all characters undergo their own personal battles which are seen through the story. These battles and mishaps aren't unrelated to the story, either. Every action that an emotionally unstable character makes has an inpact on the story and can turn it in a direction and these directions are justified. If you're looking for a gorgeously animated, well written, gripping story with a really fun (and I mean fun as in play for 10 hours straight) game engine then play this game, seriously.
P.S - If you don't want to kill Snow for shouting "SARAHHHH!" a bazzilion times by the end of it; you haven't played it enough.

In my opinion much better than Magic 2012 and Magic 2013 on Xbox, which I have previously played. There's a vibrant multiplayer community, you can build custom decks using a starting pool, plus Magic Origins cards that you can buy by earning or purchasing in-game coins. A perfect way to get acquainted with the new Magic Origins cards, and the way they function. Also perfect for total beginners, as the game rules are explained in the tutorials. Going through the tutorials is also beneficial because you earn a few boosters right away by doing so.
Deck building is fun, and it's nice that you can test play against the AI with your custom decks, and even earn some coins by doing so. The AI sometimes makes clear errors and mistakes, and even when it doesn't, is not too hard to beat on the hardest setting. The real catch is playing your friends, and random opponent in ranked 1 vs. 1 matches. Also, there's 2-headed giant! The single player campaign is also nice in that it tells the story behind each planeswalker in Magic Origins.
I play using an Xbox controller, and the only thing I'm missing from the older (Magic 2012 and 2013) games is "LT: Zoom into the last played card". Other than that, the controls are smooth, and you can always switch ot the mouse when you really need to do some card viewing or complicated selections.
Also, incomplete decks sometimes disappear completely when you go back and forth editing them, so I have to keep a separate record of my decks. This will hopefully be patched, but we'll see. Overall, a very good Mtg game, and free to play. Also you get boosters for free, just earn coins by winning and completing quests.

What an incredible disappointment.  I loved the X Series, and this one promised to get away from the menu micromanagement that dominated the previous games and be more immersive, which was about my only complaint.  So I am excited to start playing this, and I was amazed at how true it was.  I start out roaming an asteroid field looking for this concept ship that was space's equivalent to Gran Turismo's X-Racer, a ship so ridiculously outperforming and expensive that only the one was ever made and no fleet could afford it.
But then the first disappointment.  The devs, for reasons I will never understand, decided to call the ship the Albion Skunk...  They wrote in storyline that you catch during load screens that the name was the Albion Pride but someone hacked the ship's registry and changed it's name, which is pretty weak to me.  And of course, your character sticks with the name because nothing boosts a guy's pride in his super rare, super powerful ship like naming it after an animal synonymous with garbage heaps.  And then while he's trying to get the ship working, he is boarded and his new copilot is introduced.
Bad storyline out of the way, I'm ready to rock and roll, and thank god this new lady is some genius engineer because after a few console commands and slaps to the console, we've got engines, boosters, weapons, and other basic functionality.  After a quick "getting your feet wet" dogfight, we land at a station and I once again get to awe at the scope they tried to achieve. Flying around the outer portion of this station are hundreds upon hundreds of ships in line to dock at the numerous facilities the station has to offer. Thankfully, everyone realizes that I am the player, and damnit my time is important, because my slipping through to the front of the line does not get anyone all frisky with the trigger.  Even the cops are all, "Carry on, dude!" as they fly by.
I dock and am rewarded with the ability to get out of my ship and wander the space station, various little junk sellable pickups everywhere to make things interesting, and dozens of occupants buying and selling, offering to become pilots or other crew for your ship, or ships you will eventually get.  I do my business and take off, continuing on the storyline mission.  More shooting, and I get to dock at an old frieghter.  Again I get to get out of my ship and explore, and I'm wandering the cargo area of this frieghter.  I can see out the airlock forcefield in the back to space and watch the ship as it moves.  At this point I am floored by how great this game is.
Fast forward through a few missions, I am already growing bored.  Docking with a ship gives you one "wander area" with one of something like 4 backdrops.  Even the little loot boxes are all in the same spots. And contain usually the same things.  Junk that'll sell for a couple credits, nothing that will get you anywhere financially, though, if you can even find the guy to sell it.  Space stations are not much better.  It looks like they took the same few space station building modules in a level editor and plugged them together in 3 or 4 different configurations, and after about an hour of work, they called it good.
Another gameplay aspect is scanning the space station exterior, ostensibly to find out how the whole thing functions.  And when you get the whole thing scanned, you get a pretty decent stationwide discount and bonus to what you sell.  But this becomes extremely tedious as you are looking for the last module that you can see with your scanners that you haven't scanned, but the little question mark you need to get close to won't appear until you look at it from a very specific angle. Ahh frustration, hell with it, moving on.  You can also get these little hacker drones that you remotely pilot to various points around a station or ship within a certain time to hack them and supposedly take control of the ship, force it to dump its cargo, force better deals at the stations, etc.  It doesn't do any of that.  It is a neat stealth gameplay that forces you to hide from patrolling cops but there is no benefit.  You finish the hack and the game tells you you've completed it.  That is it.  No reward whatsoever.  It was like they planned to have it but never got around to finishing it.
Short version:
The game started out pretty good but quickly devolved into a game that looked like it was rushed out the door months before it should have been.  I did not cover all of the different things you can do in the game, but the review was long enough as it is.  I recommend staying away from this game, though.  The amount of time I spent in it before getting bored, several hours actually, is way above par.  Most people I talk to gave it about 15 minutes and called it quits.

Have you ever had that moment when you've been pinching all the custard creams from the biscuit tin, only to come back some time later to find that there's only a half one left, a single half with a bit of cream left on it? Well, this is sort of like that.
Gat Out Of Hell is a standalone expansion for IV, with your custom US President (if you have made one) being abducted by Satan and forced into marriage, and so Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kensington must go in to rescue them!
I remember playing this for about an hour or so at first, getting some of the main mechanics in the game first hand, and somehow not being fully drawn in as I thought I would. Yes, there are some missions, albeit a few. Yes, there are activities for you to do, but the game sadly relies heavily on them to stretch out the gameplay. YES, I have completed the takeover of New Hades and have collected a wealthy amount of collectibles, but it somehow didn't satisfy me as much as the special weaponry.
I'll come on to my good points: The special 7 Sins weapons are fun to use, though can be tedious to unlock, particularly Wrath. Those who have played the game will know what I mean. Yes, I did get a kick out of creating a complete massacre whilst relaxing in my heavy calibre armchair. But, that's pretty much it.
It just somehow feels lacklustre. Most of the humour only cropped up briefly, and most good bits were spoilt by being in cutscenes. And even after doing so much to get the 7 Sins, I'm not sure what else could draw me back.
If you enjoyed the Saints Row series and want something small and silly to pass the time, then do get this game. If you're fussed about the pre-order DLC, don't be. It's not much. But like Saints Row IV, I will say this. The game itself is fine. Looks good, plays fairly well, and recommend giving it a go. Unless you're looking in the biscuit tin again to try and pinch my last bourbon.

Not many games made me change my mind so much like this one.
Originally I gave this game a negative review. I liked the combat but the over-the-top difficulty made the game incredibly frustrating and forced me to rage quit several times.
But...
I always came back after a few days. I call it The Dark Souls Effect: Yes, the game is incredibly hard but not impossible and when you finally succeed it feels very rewarding. And the combat itself is entertaining enough to keep me in.
So I tried and tried and tried... and got better. I learned to do the executions properly, I discovered enemy powers and weaknesses, I started counting ammo in my head instead of always looking on the counter. And here I am now, all chalenges completed, global megalord status achieved.
So yes, I recommend the game but be prepared. And patient.
Update 9/28: The GLOBAL MEGALORD EDITION added three more levels which ramp up the difficulty to the point where I can't be bothered anymore. Especially the third level. This is no longer about skill, it's just about dozens and dozens and DOZENS of attempts, running through enemies, hoping to dodge bullets and to avoid the brutal time limit represented by The Killinator. Replay a hundred times until you finally get lucky.
Also a few impossible achievements were added, destroying my 100% completion. ♥♥♥♥ this game.

Tiny and Big? Well, that title is half-right.
I'd probably replace "Big" with "Mediocre", though!
Tiny and Big is a game that has a lot of good ideas, a really solid engine with some great physics functions and not much else. The gameplay ranges from mildly enjoyable to downright repetitive and quickly grows old. Luckily, it doesn't have much time to stay boring because it ends after a mere two and a half hours.
The story is nonsensical, full of exposition, and bland while the characters are bland and not well fleshed out. That doesn't really matter, though, because by the time you've decided which of the three main characters you hate more, it's over.
The writing is awful and full of spelling mistakes and the graphics are one of the few redeeming qualities of this game. The game itself breaks often, leaving you stuck post-checkpoint with no option but to restart the level. The "boss fight(s)" is repeated two or three times identically and only really gets enjoyable the last time... and then ends.
I paid $2.50 for this and it (just barely) managed to make my $1/hour ratio. I would not advise paying more than $2.50 for this game, as I feel I pretty much wasted my time with this game overall.
If they had fleshed it out, gave it better pacing, and ditched the story entirely, it could have been great.

Now that we got the "graphics part" out of the way.
Let's get to the actual review:
I played this game 9 years ago when it came out and I loved it. The Physics are some of the best I've seen in any game to date. You can destroy entire huts. Without having them collapse in a predetermined way. but instead theyll actually react physicly correct to how you interacted with them.
There are 10 Levels in the game. That are all pretty big. So there is no pre-determined way to go like in call of duty. Each of the levels are several square kilometers big that you can actually walk on. And there aren't really any areas that feel empty.
The AI is pretty smart for the most part. On the highest difficulty they are pretty hard to beat at times. However they aren't perfect ofcourse either. For instance in the 1st level there is a guy in a toilet. and 8/10 times when he gets alert to you he runs into the wall of the toilet instead of out through the door.
The Story is probably the games weakest feature, which doesn't say it's bad. It's just nothing particularly special either. That beeing said, as a little side note: The story in Crysis 2 is actually quiet an improvement over the one in Crysis 1.
And now the most important gameplay element: The nanosuit. For me this made it for one super cool, cause you are some super hero kind badass (with a slightly more grounded background lore to how the powers work than most comic book super heroes). And also I think it makes for some very fun options gameplay wise. You have great mobility with speed and strength mode. you can choose to fight as a tank with armor mode (although you still die very quick on delta difficulty so its not crazy overpowered) and you can play very stealthy with the cloak mode (which makes you almost but not completly invisible).
All those abilities use the suit's energy, so they can not be used indefinitly.
And the best thing is you can switch in between the diffrent suitmodes at any time, so you can adapt your playstyle to the situation at any given time.
Last: The Multiplayer:
So appereantly the multiplayer doesn't work anymore due to the service it used (gamespy) shutting down. However there may be workarounds to still play online. And the LAN mode still works ofcourse.
I personally didn't bother much with the multiplayer in crysis 1. Back when I tried it it seemed alright, but I don't think it lived auiet up to the potential of multiplayer fun there could have been with the nanosuit. crysis 2 was an improvement in that regard in my opinion.
So all in all Crysis 1(and I'm mainly referring to the singleplayer here) in my opinion is one of the best shooters ever made. And I'd recommend it to anyone who hasn't played it yet. (9/10) (10/10 if you choose to ignore the slightly weaker story)

The Stanley Parable is not really a game, then again it is.
Then again its not. Oh, look, now its pretending to be an alltogether different game.
But all in all, it is just what it is: The Stanley Parable
Theres nothing quite like this again on steam, so this is a dangerous affair for your dollars.
Lets start by being mean to the game, as seldom people are.
I honestly dont think that this is a game as good as the combined review-score puts it, and I honestly dont think its a game that has a large variety of people that would really >get< where the enjoyment lies.
What rescues the stanley parable from being a weird outsider in the games playground is its very witty yet completely relateable approach of humor and its coherent way of telling (or not telling, or corrupting) a storyline.
That I think is the one reason really everyone could give it a shot if its on sale.
With regards to the mechanics: You can walk, you can interact or choose to not interact, that all. Its clean, it works, it has no bugs that I know of, and theres nothing that needs to be added to it, theres no missing part, everything makes sense. The Stanley Parable will be as challenging for you as your mind bends it to be. The biggest mechanic of this game are your own thoughts, and its very controversial to which degree it even could be called a game. This is not a casual buy like its advertised in my opinion, because the fun part happens outside of the screen.
In some way you will get exactly of what you dont know you will get.
Which absolutely seems like another plus, because buying this game now sounds like poetry.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
So the only question that really counts and remains is: Do I recommend it for whatever it is, having played the whole game?
It somewhat depends:
- If you want it for the fun joyride you maybe have seen elsewhere, I dont recommend buying it except on sale. Not because its bad, but because I think 11,99 is too much for just the fun parts of the dialogue and the running around. You will have seen a fair bit of the game after playing 5 hours. (A more casual comparison to movies of course makes this worth it, but im comparing it to games, ultimately its your call.)
- But, and the reason theres ultimately a thumbs up on this review: If you actually aspire to enter the whole brute force of the stanley parable, engage in its problems and think about just what the heck it all could mean. And If you want to explore in the empty office building of the entity named stanley and face the crisis of not knowing whats fake or real anymore, then its the time to stop reading this review right now, butcher your funds and start playing the game.
For everyone that has the time and lust to wonder on his hands, this is what you would want to buy.

As a long time JPRG Fan and lover of such titles as Breath of Fire, Grandia, Chrono Trigger, Seiken Densetsu etc. I always mounred the direction that Final Fantasy took after the 10th iteration. During the Steam sale I thought I'd give the game a chance anyway and overcome my presumptions because the price wasn't that high.
After 10 hours of gameplays I feel like I have a general impression of the game where it is going. And I came to the conclusion I will no longer waste any time on it and here is why.
I must admit the presentation of the game is stellar. The graphis are gorgous even though the game by now is already a few years old. The soundtrack is fitting and the overall design is more than solid. But that is it. The game is a shiny object and lacks any substance from what I have seen so far.
- The characters are laughably shallow and stereotyped. Only Lighting seems to have any sort of genuine emotional impact. All the others feel remote to what is actually happening to them.
- The pacing of the game is horrible so far. It just throws set piece after set piece at you without any breathing room other than pointless enemy encounters. The story feels extremely contrived and unnatural with lots of unnecessary lore but no emotional investment on the side of characters as of yet.
- The game mechanics are insultingly simple and repetitive. Only to give a brief example, there are 2 types of gear a character can be equiped with and the customization is limited to throwing random items at them for XP to level up which has little to no effect on the weapons or armor.
- The fact that you can not switch partymembers (which is only unlocked shortly before the endgame) leads to cheaply contrived reasons within the storyline in order for the party composition to change every 15 minuntes.
- The battle system is the worst I have played so far in any JRPG - it's mere button mashing and the battles aren't even that short. The ATB has almost no control or strategic depth. I know it may get more complex over time - but so far I have been getting by using only 2 methods against any enemy and from what I've read it doesn't get any better in the later stages.
- There is no exploration or overworld.
These reasons were enough for me to stop playing the game and regretting having bought it - leading to Square making money with these games instead of having to reevalutate on the core elements of their games and what made them so great back in the day. And I am not only rambling out of nostalgia. I've played some RPGs in recent times which were way better than this convoluted mess.
Guess here's to waiting for Square not to mess up the FFVII remake.

As a long time mtg player I was thrilled to see Wizards of the Coast finally move to this format. After a rocky start rife with bugs and network problems the dust seems to have settled and I think people can finally begin giving origins a chance.
If I were new to Magic I believe Origins would be a great place to start getting into it; the tutorials are great (and skippable if you already know how to play) and there's a fantastic single player campaign to help you get used to all the concepts of mtg and prepare you for online play. I also think the business model is also very fair, you get daily quests and a nice amount of starting gold to buy boosters. You also can't get more than 4 of any single card so you don't have extra useless copies and will therefore eventually fill out your collection. As to how long that will take I can't be sure, someone else can do the math.
However if you're coming from an experienced background, like myself, you may find Magic Duels somewhat lacking. Of course I don't expect to gain access to a huge collection of cards, that would be too daunting for new players and I can respect that, I really don't believe Wizards chose a star line up of cards for their first venture into this format. There is almost no duo colour support (one of my personal favourite parts of Magic itself) and the online meta seems to have got stale rather quickly; running into the same archetypes ad nauseum.
I don't presume to know that this is how everyone else finds the game or that things won't change as people start to fill out their collections and experiment more with the cards. I hold out hope that Wizards will be open minded enough to keep updating Origins and not be too dissuaded by the cold reception. Until the sets get varied enough to grasp my interest I'm going to keep playing another certain online card game owned by a company that rhymes with Wizard.

This will be my first review of a game on steam, actually, first review ever.
English isn’t my first language, so I will apologize in advanced about any grammar and spelling mistakes.
My opinion about this game varies from day to day and from event to event. I will try to make this review as consistent as possible. I’ve been thinking of doing  this review for a long time now. I kept putting it off because I find it very difficult to get my opinion on paper.
For those who think this review is too long to read, I’ve put a list of pros and cons at the bottom of this review. The current version of this game is 1.22. a lot of bugs and issues have been addressed by Egosoft at this time. I won’t be writing about earlier issues in this review. There will be issues of course that I haven’t encountered or don’t find annoying or broken. These will not be mentioned either.
As you all might know by now, the game is riddled with “major” bugs and flaws. Many of them are annoying, but to say the break the game? I think not. I will try to explain why I think that is. To do this as correctly as possible I’ve divided everything in three categories, bugs, flaws and  wants. But before I do this, I want to stress the fact that Egosoft has been working hard to solve the issues the community has pointed out to them.
Bugs:
-	Capital ships sometimes fly through stations, this bug isn’t game breaking at all, but it does kill the emersion quite a lot. I’ve encountered this bug at a solar energy plant, where the ship kept flying  through most of the solar panels of the station. It then proceeded to crash into an array of smaller ship which catapulted in to space. Which was cool to see.
-	The game sometimes slows down for no apparent reason. For me using the alt-tab keys to go back to Windows and then back to the games, solves this issue. Or else restarting the game entirely.
-	Enemies getting stuck inside the station building. Sometimes, enemy drones / fighters fly into or spawn in a solid block of a station. They are then impervious to attack and they don’t go despawn. Missions can’t be completed then because not all enemies are destroyed. When you abort said mission and accept a new one in the same zone, the enemy inside the station gets activated again and you can’t finish the new mission either.
Flaws:
-	Enemy NPC’s and the police patrols act as they have been trained by monkeys and not very bright ones at that. AI combat and manoeuvring in space should be improved greatly. This will affect the emersion a player can have with the game.
-	The game economy is based on trade ships, the trade ships however don’t leave the station. They just fly around it in circles. There are however capital ships that jump between stations and systems to trade.
-	Using the jumpdrive of a capital ship should be made easier and more clearer. Look at EVE online for a good way to jump capital ships.
Wants:
-	Either redo the entire station walking  side of the game or make it so the player doesn’t have to get out of the ship anymore. Trade and talk to people remotely. This however means there has to be a way to make more money in space. Since when you avoid going on to stations you can’t rob said station of its goodies.
-	Better galaxy, system, zone, etc. maps. Navigating through these is a pain which, when resolved improves the gameplay drastically.
-	Third person view in space! I really want to see what my ship looks like when flying around and blasting stuff.
-	Modular ship design of the player ship. It should be possible to remake the ship into a fighter / trader / miner or something else. Now you can only get upgrades, but you aren’t able to trade with energy cells or other materials. You need specialized remote controlled ships for that. For example I should be able to make my ship be able to mine asteroids, but the trade-off should be that my ship is slower and not as well armed. This will al so eliminate the need to crawl around mostly empty stations and robbing them.
-	Bring back automated commands on the other player owned ships! Building an empire should be about delegating and getting other people to work for you. Not ordering around brainless monkeys!
Stations:
Stations are constructed out of modular blocks, which is logical. They have been put together into massive city like  structures which you can fly through / scan  and destroy with your ship. So far so good. On the outside the station look great and they really give off the immense scale of the game.
On the inside however they are very underpopulated and at the same time feel very cramped and small. The immenseness is completely lost.
AI:
The general AI used by the NPC pilots is poor at best. Capital ships tend to fly through stations and bump traffic circling said station. Pirates attacking stations actually bump against it and sit on its outer hull. Fighters / drones defending a target only react when tacking direct fire.
Emersion:
I find the emersion to be great when flying the ship in space, but completely lost when existing the said and entering the station. Docking in capital ships and such is a great feature. But the walking around needs a lot of work. I am betting the community is making mods as we speak to greatly improve or disable this feature completely. If not, Egosoft should be doing something about this.
The space environments are wonderfully made and really get you in a sci-fi mood.
Pros:
-	Awesome space vista’s, the stations look great, despite the fact they are modular and the asteroid field and the backgrounds simply look great!
-	Flying the “Albion Skunk” (the player ship) is as smooth as a baby’s bottom. Especially when the engines have been upgraded a bit.
-	Great emersion when flying around in space. Exploring the stations and the asteroid fields in all their details is quite captivating.
-	Being an X game, it’s quite challenging, a lot of stuff to figure out. This can be fun, but all so frustrating at times.
-	There seems enough to do in the game so people won’t get bored easily. It takes a lot of time to figure out how everything works, but that is a reward in itself, at least for me It is.
Cons:
-	In station walking is a failure. All the stations are exactly the same on the inside, including the rubbish people leave around. Stations are only populated by 10 – 15 people, which is strange since they are as huge as cities! Rooms and bars are empty and I as a player lose my emersion when walking in a station. Furthermore not many items can be interacted with. When a station is damaged, the internal damage seems massive and the people in it simply don’t care!
-	In early game, you will spend a lot of time crawling through stations in search for loot. More simply put, you need to rob the stations blind to get enough stuff to sell back to the few people who live in those stations. Ships that you can buy to start building, shooting, trading or mining your way across the universe are too expensive to get with just simple mission running or doing other stuff in space.
-	The voice acting of NPC’s is terrible, they only have a few lines they keep repeating over and over. (I only tested the English voices.)
-	The textures for people
-	 Bugs, the game doesn’t run as good as it could be, some people still have performance issues and the game does have some odd behaviour now and again.
Conclusion:
Reading back on this review I can see that it has been somewhat negative and there is indeed much room left in the game for improvement. But the feeling of flying around in that ship and skimming the surface of stations, asteroids and capital ships alike, is just too damn great. So I will recommend this game. When Egosoft (maybe with the help of the community) fix most of the bugs and the whole station walking debacle, they will have made space simulator gold.

Got a remastered version along with the original Bioshock.

I did not set my expectations high, but 2K managed to make me furious either way.
This list of issues is written after a long-expected patch, so at least for now all my fury and anger still stands.
1) Game configuration bug is still present. While Blind Squirrel team managed to fix the black screen issue due to default video resolution, and partially eliminate full reset of the game config after crash, the game still has an annoying bug of constantly resetting the resolution to 1024x768 (even on proper exit).
2) The game still crashes
3) The game still looks like a ghost of a past decade (aesthetically there is zero improvement over the original game).
4) In addition to the game engine bugs there are also many AI bugs that were never present in the original Bioshock (enemies freeze w/ their hands raised).
5) UI issues with the camera never got fixed
6) Difficulty still resets, because it is stored with game config, and not a save file.
So, unless you already have it, or you are a devoted fan of the Bioshock series - do not buy it. Wait until it goes on Christmas sale for $2-$3, and only if somewhere along the way 2K releases a second patch.

Not a Hero is a 2D shooter with minor platforming elements. It has a couple of unique mechanics revolving around cover and slide tackling/executions. As well as a handful of unique characters all with their own abilities, strengths, and weaknesses.
On the technical side their are only a couple of faults. Firstly it has pretty non existent technical settings. As such, when it launches windowed it can be confusing how to get it into fullscreen (Press ALT + Enter). Also, you can slide tackle enemies which knocks them to the ground allowing an execution (insta-kill). However, shooting your gun and executions are tied to the same button so sometimes when you try to execute your character instead shoots their gun. Executions should really be tied to a seperate input from shooting.
It's also on the shorter side which I actually consider a positive. A lot of indie games that don't really have a narrative and instead revolve around completing levels (like Not a Hero) often pad out the game with 100 levels in order to justify the cost by having a lot of content despite few mechanics/narrative. However, that just tends to make those games tedious to finish. Not a Hero is the perfect length to leave me wanting more without overstaying it's welcome.
If you enjoyed Hotline Miami, Gunpoint, Mark of the Ninja, or Broforce you'll like Not a Hero.

I cannot in good faith recommend this game right now, even if I do enjoy it. Much like Civ 5 upon release, this game is not finished. I have no doubt it will be improved upon with the future expansions as there are some great ideas in here that could be amazing with a little bit of TLC.
Right now, this is very much a spin-off of Civ 5 as opposed to a sequel. Many assets from 5 were reused (mainly the hill and ice tiles). The biggest problem though, is the lack of strong civilizations. Being set in the future, all the leaders are fictional and not memorable at all. The only one I ever remember is "that guy who looks like John C. Reilly". The civs abilities aren't very memorable either, as the "create your own" civilization at the beginning of a game just makes it feel like everything is homogenized.
There are a few positives though, the new tech tree is very fun once you get used to it. The need to constantly upgrade your militairy units is gone thanks to a new affinity based unit promotion tree. This leaves you with just the basic unit types which you can specialize as the game progresses. The new policy trees are great too, incentivizing both branching across multiple trees and focusing on one.
I think the most important fault of BE is the victories. Other than the Domination-esque victory of capturing all capitals, the others are just sitting around and waiting, making for a really boring Next-Turn button simulator.
In conclusion, wait till the expansions come out. BNW and G&K really improved Civ 5, and I have high hopes that the same will happen for BE. Until then, just buy the complete addition of 5 if you want some Civ.

It's exaclty what I wanted - more weapons, more excellent writing, and more overall insanity.
The powers are greatly improved over Saint's Row IV, with way less to do between collecting all of them (sprint and flight are given to you right as you start the game, and the other four are gotten through basically the next mission). I found myself switching between them much more often than I did in the previous game, too. Flying around the city is fun, sprinting around the city is hilarious (cars have little durability and will explode if you barely touch them), and there are lots of weird buildings to parkour all over.
I kind of wish there were more activities to do, or at least a way to repeat completed objectives once you finish the main story. You've got Hellblazing (Trailblazing), Fraud, and Salvation (flying around catching bodies as they fall into Hell), but everything else is a one-time deal and that leaves little to do once you've completed taking over the city. There also doesn't seem to be any hourly income, making money a hard thing to come by once you've cleared everything.
I can definitely see how this is a sort of self-contained expansion, and I'm really glad they released it as its own game rather than be a DLC for Saint's Row IV. It is its own thing, really.
