So I've been meaning to pick this game up for a while, finally got around to it. It's pretty damn good.
At this point, you probably know what it is. It's a Smash-Like game with some nice pixel art, catchy
music, and elemental animal-like characters instead of guest characters like Smash.
What's good?
-It looks awesome.
-The music is pretty catchy.
-All the characters are fun and interesting to play, and feel relatively well balanced.
-Gameplay is enough like Smash to feel familiar, but unique enough to feel refreshing.
The combos in this particular game are very fun and solid feeling to string together, and
there's a good enough balance between power and speed to make each character feel like
they have a good variety of options. Plus, there are a few major differences to Smash, namely,
no blocking, but instead you can parry, to temporarily slow your enemy for counter attacks.
-Though it's nothing major, there's a little story for each character with some nice artwork to boot,
an Abyss mode to challenge for fun that you can do with a friend, and local multiplayer of course
is always a blast with a good friend or two.
-Nice little features such as custom colour palettes for each character.
What's eh?
-The roster is not huge like the recent Smash titles. At present, we see 8 playable characters, which is fine, because it means each character has a good variety of ways to play and there isn't many balance issues from a normal players perspective. However, for those who like large character
rosters, this isn't the title, even with two more characters coming.
-The story mode won't last you long (I beat the entire thing casually in around half an hour), and the Abyss Mode gets stale after a bit because it's a lot of the same repeated challenges. These
aside, you have your standard normal and online matches, which are fun, but not particularly deep for those looking for variety.
-For whatever reason, you now need to buy non-base characters with an easy to obtain in-game
currency. This presents no challenge as the money comes from practically every mode and is plentiful, but it seems unneccessary, and some of the alternate stages you can buy feel unneccessarily barred.
-Online play is kinda hit or miss. To my understanding, it's a p2p connection, so sometimes it's great, other times it's terrible, and apperantely it's hard to find matches sometimes with just random searches.
Overall?
An awesome game, in my opinion, the best Smash like game on PC emulation. It's an absolute blast
to play once you get the hang of it, with satisfying combos and cool characters. It's best played with friends locally, and though the single player isn't particularly big, it's a bit of fun for a short while.
Overall, 8.3/10, very solid and fun game, can't wait to play Greninja. I mean Zenyatta. I mean FROGGO

You just browsed onto a farming simulator.  I know the reaction that's coming.
"Wow farming?  How boring."
Save yourself trouble and move along.
For those looking for something like this, or might be on the fence wondering who would buy this.
I'll sum this up in a nutshell.
'Relaxing'.
The appeal of a game like farming simulator isn't in action, it's in relaxation and looking at the neat machines while they work.  If you ever found yourself stopping and staring at a combine in action, you may want to consider this.
Farming Simulator is an open-ended tractor sandbox of a game.  Your only real goal is to sow, harvest, and sell crops (and trees and livestock products) for a profit.  So you can buy more, better machines, sow more crops, and get more money.
As far as gameplay goes, it's solid.  Your game avatar is apparently an unstoppable cyborg super farmer (run forever, never eat, never sleep, jump off silos without injury, etc...) that can instantly teleport to any vehicle with the tap of a key.  But I digress, Ultimate Cyborg Farmer aside, the game doesn't bog you down with life bars, fatigue, or anything associated with any kind of player survival mechanism.  You just get in your tractor, and farm.
Graphically, the game is smooth and pretty.  The environments aren't overly complicated, and they don't look bad.  You'll notice some minor things having to do with draw distances, but that's not really a bother.
From an audio standpoint, machines sound good.  If you're fine listening to diesel engines all the time.  Overall, the ambience is simple and has nothing noteworthy of report.  No news is good news, so to speak.
Controls are complicated for more complex machines and knowing some of the common key command groups is important for overall gameplay.  Luckily, the game keeps an ever present 'available key commands' window in the corner to help remind you of the main functions.  Subtle functions like lamps and horns might require a quick lookup.  Controls are also remappable to your desired configuration.
Game settings also allow for playing your way.  If you want to make the game challenging, the settings can be set to make you work hard and carefully.  If you desire to just fire up your tractor and set it loose on a field, you can set the settings to the point that the farm is ALMOST a screen saver.  There is even a key press that automatically 'hires' a fine indentured servant for a chunk of your earnings to automatically drive your tractor or combine back and forth through the fields.  His english isn't so good though...  Can't seem to understand 'don't run into that tree line' very well.  Also available in the game are a few 'plop down' items you can purchase that can further easy any burdens.  Want to completely ignore money concerns?  You don't need to cheat.  Just earn enough to drop a wind mill or ten down.  The income from one of those can outpace the automatic daily expenses of your equipment, meaning you don't have to technically DO anything to maintain a profit margin.  (I call this more or less 'set it and forget it mode.)
Equipment also includes utilizing tractor components with complex hydraulic controls and articulation.  From front loaders to grapling arms and even that Scorpion King (that thing that looks like a crane on treads, but is a tree cutting BEAST) in the store page screenshots.  You get to play with those.
Be advised, you can't damage anything or kill Super Robo Farmer, but physics does get a little upset when you do weird things.  That's to be expected when you do something that would normally wrap you around a telephone pole or launch a tractor trailer over a house.   (By the way, feel free to go crazy like that.  Nothing in this game can be 'hurt').
Overall, FS is a simple, solidly built farm tractor simulator.   If your forte' is playing with complex machines doing simple tasks to relax, this is for you.  There's enough to keep you busy, if mildly so, and plenty to work for in terms of earning your way up to larger, heavier machines.  It'll eat away the hours without you feeling your have to watch it like a hawk.
Just, don't expect it to be twisted metal, country edition if you tune it to be challenging.  It's just tractors and plants.

This War of Mine is my new answer to the question, "Are Video Games a Legitimate Art Form?" In This War of Mine, you play an every day group of survivors, making tough, brutal decisions on how to survive. Battling sickness, injuries, looters, and the ever looming threat of death, your main goal in each of the Day/Night phases is making it just one more day.
Good: EXTREMELY atmospheric. The visuals, music, and even the UI evokes a sense of desperation and despair. The characters just FEEL real. Their daily diaries do a good job of putting you in the shoes of desperate survivors. The choices in this game, the ones that hit you in the gut, are all natural and emergent. There's never a popup asking you if you want to steal for survival, there's just an unarmed old man asking, "Why are you doing this?" while you take meat for your two friends who haven't eaten in two days. The art style is... just beautiful. With the gameplay in "This War of Mine", they could have easily settled with 2D graphics, but instead they created a moving and engrossing setting with very real feeling characters. I LOVE 2D games, don't get me wrong, but I felt their treatment of the set pieces in this story really added to the experience for me.
Bad: Sometimes the characters are a little hard to control. I found myself unable to make one of my characters do something for an entire day. Only happened once though, and that's about all I have to say negatively about this game.
Ugly: War.

This is my first-ever review. I normally don’t use my time to talk about games, but I had to do it because this game is great and I think that everybody should play it.
– Excellent, very well developed, the texts are short (for the people who doesn’t like to read too much). This game really tells a great human Story.
– Good characters, it’s easy to get emotionally attached to them, you really don’t want them to die or suffer.
– Great environment sounds: dogs barking, screams, people crying, gunshots, car engines and explosions. It really helps with the immersion.
– Not many, but good. The soundtrack is very atmospheric.
– Well balanced strategy game, not too many options and not too little. It has an addictive (in a good way) gameplay. It’s hard to stop playing.
– Many objects to craft.  It’s a well developed crafting system.
– There is no money in this game; you have to negotiate and trade your items. It’s fun trying to get the best deals. It demands strategy too.
– Good graphics for an indie game. They use this gray color pallet that fits very well with the sad war theme of the game. The art is excellent.
– I finished the game in 15hs. The total time of the game is programmed to be random (you never know when the war will be over). I believe that you can play from some weeks to months (in game days).
– You can start the game in a different house, with other characters, in the summer or winter, with many other places to go and distinct loot. So the replay value of this game is nice.
– Is simplified because you play as a survivor, not a soldier. It’s always tense since is really easy to die in this game. The stealth approach works far better than fighting.

Let me tell you a story of a man named Stanley. Every day, Stanley reports to work, doing the same boring job in his same boring office. But then, one day, everyone simply disappears. Will Stanley uncover the dastardly plot at work? Will he get hopelessly lost and wander to his death? Or, perhaps, will he simply close his door and pretend everything is okay? It's a big, scary world out there after all. Regardless though, the decision is entirely in your hands.
Seriously though, this is a game that's not a game. It's an experience, with tons of easter eggs, many different endings to discover, and which defies all the standard rules of gameplay. Will you heed the wise advice of your all-knowing narrator? Will you go your own way and see what secrets there are to be found? You set the rules and decide how you want to play. And, best of all, can find a different experience waiting for you every time. Not to mention, even the achievements are a lot of fun and creative to obtain.

DO NOT PLAY THIS GAME.  ANY POSITIVE EXPECTATIONS WILL BE DESTROYED.  It is clear that the developers didn't do any testing at all, since every aspect of the game is buggy and poorly-designed.
I would describe this as less of a game and more of a prison.  Installing it is slightly confusing, as it's listed under "Demos" rather than "Games".  However, it's only once you get into the game that you realize just how much the developers, Stainless Games, hate you, and you realize how low their opinion of you must be.
First, there's the tutorial, which is required before you play a single game.  Even if multiplayer weren't locked, it would still be required, as it rewards gold to get more cards.  So, you play through the five missions of the five planeswalkers.  These missions range from easy to impossible, entirely depending on your opening hand.  You have no control over your deck and can't even see what cards are in it, so you just have to mulligan until you get a start that beats your opponent.  This basically boils down to luck:  If the computer gets a good hand and you get a bad one, you have no way of turning that around.  There is very little room for correct or savvy play, rather you just grind until you get a better opener, get an unsatisfying win, and collect your gold.  A couple of the missions are kind of fun, but overall it feels like a chore that you have to take care of before you can play the game.
Actually, I lied.  VERY first, you hear the opening music at max volume, then click Play! and hear a resounding BOOM, again at max volume, no matter what your volume settings are in the game.  A minor but all-too-telling error.
Now that you have some cards, you can build a deck.  So, let's say you're a total newb and you use the Deck Wizard, which gives you a range of archetypes to try.  You pick a feisty, red-white aggro deck, planning to chip away at your opponent a little at a time with your early creatures, burning a path for them with red spells.  Unfortunately, the Deck Wizard doesn't understand that you want your "All-Out Assault! " theme deck to be mostly made of things you can play with less than 3 mana, so when it chooses what cards you can pick between (you get 5 options at a time), it will most likely be full of 4-drops.  Furthermore, even if you do get low-drops, it's entirely possible that they will require a heavy commitment to the wrong color, e.g., you're building a mostly-red deck and the options are all cards with WW in the casting cost.  Finally, when it comes to adding mana to the deck, you have no control over what lands are added, and the game always adds the same number of lands, in the same format.  In this example, 18 Mountains/Plains (appropriately portioned), 2 dual lands that don't come into play tapped, 4 guildgates that do come into play tapped.  So, 24 lands, 4 of which come into play tapped, into every deck.  This is a serious hindrance to an aggressive deck that wants to draw maybe 3-4 lands tops for the whole game.  To avoid this, you can build your own deck, but I'll get into that later.
So you have a deck now, and you're ready to face an opponent.  You have two choices:  play against humans, or play against the AI.  Both of these guarantee gold when you win, with humans giving slightly more gold than a Hard AI.  So you decide to pit yourself against another real opponent.  You click the button, choose your deck, and hop into the queue.  But, your connection drops and you're back at the main screen.  "The session was full", says an error.  So you try again.  No dice, same error.  Well, so the game was just released, it's a little buggy, alright.  You try again, this time it says "The server timed out".  You keep trying, and on the fourth or fifth try, you manage to find a real opponent.  Great!  Time to play some magic.
You draw your opening seven, you're missing one of your colors but hey, no problem!  You get a free redraw of seven cards (which I like)!  That hand works out and you're ready to lay the beatdown.  You play your 1-drop.  Your opponent plays a land.  You play your two-drop and SWING!  Your opponent loses a life, they play their land and a 2-drop, go.  You burn the two-drop out of the way, hit face again, and so on.  After a couple more burn spells, your opponent's out of real plays, and you still have a couple cards in hand, so they concede.  Woohoo! you've won your first game of Magic Duels Origins!  NOT SO FAST.  "PlayerX has been replaced by the AI", the game tells you.
Even if your opponent concedes, you still don't win.  Again, it's all-too-telling.
Okay, well, by now you've gotten your toes wet, so you're ready to dive in, build your own deck, and start cranking out that sweet, sweet gold.  You check your Daily Quests, which you know exist because they're presented to you on log-in.  You have two "Archetypal" quests:  "Win 2 duels with a RW or GW archetype deck", and "Win 4 duels with a UB or UW archetype deck".  They both reward 40 gold.  Well, 2>4, and they both reward the same amount of gold, so... time to make a rushy white-blue aggro deck with lots of fliers.  It goes well enough, you don't have that much beat-down but you also have some bigger threats for when the game goes long.  You don't have cheap countermagic, but all-in-all that's probably for the best.
So you slog through the matchmaking process and find yourself a match.  You beat your opponent (woohoo! +20 gold!) but your quest doesn't update.  Why not?  Well, it doesn't clarify in-game, but when you go to the reddit you find out that "archetype deck" means "Deck Wizard deck".  So basically every day, you're required to play with what is almost certainly a worse version of a deck you could create.  Since it's a requirement in order to progress, this means that you waste no less than half an hour of play-time every day throwing together an archetype deck that is as aggressive as possible and then zerging down the AI, because you're never going to win a game if you play that deck against other people, and it'll take your ranking down if you lose.
I should spend a few words on the ranking system.  Here's how it works:  When you win a game, you go up a rank; when you lose a game, you go down a rank.  Your rank caps at 40, no matter how good you are.  Rank barely matters anyway, because you're liable to face anyone within 10-15 ranks of you anyway.
Whatever.  You keep playing, because you're optimistic that, once you get more cards, you'll actually be able to build some pretty fun, pretty powerful decks.  Six cards at a time, you're completing your collection.  (I do like the way this is handled, by the way:  Once you have the maximum playable number of a given card, you can no longer receive that card in a booster.  This means that if you play long enough you are guaranteed to have a complete collection.)  You've been at it for a few hours, rising in rank, when suddenly you finish a game and don't receive any gold for it!  This is because you've hit your gold cap for the day.  You can no longer earn any gold, except from daily quests.
That pretty well puts a damper on your ladder aspirations.  If you're not earning anything by doing it, what's the point?  If you rise in rank you'll theoretically be facing harder opponents, making winning more difficult, so you're shooting yourself in the foot a little bit by continuing to ladder.
It's as if the game is saying, "Stop playing me!  Go away, do something else with your time!"  Fine.  You decide to play some funsies 2v2's with your buddy.
By the way, it's a little strange that playing vs. the AI earns you gold while playing with real players, in 2v2, does not.  After all, the games aren't any shorter or easier than playing 1v1, certainly not shorter or easier than 1v1'ing AI.  It certainly makes me want to play the game less, since 2HG is the funnest game mode.

Well, they did it again.  Somehow year after year, magic's digital analogue to their card game comes out, and each year, almost amazingly, it seems the previous edition.  All the work seems to go into how to make the game profitable, with no thought into making a game worth the money.

Honestly, wizards, I'm fine with paying for a game, as long as it provides value equal to the costs.  I've never been a fan of microtransations, but I'll even go that route, purposely buying things I don't need, if I feel the game deserves the support.  If the game is money grab, forget it.  Trying to force my hand by making the game extra grindy just made me lose interest faster.
While all the features are being added, did anyone take the time to actually make the game better?  Each edition runs worse the the last one.  This current one has loading screens that take forever, which is doubly annoying when you are restarting a duel because you can't pull land, and you can's skip these loading screens.  Then the game itself is exceedingly sluggish.  Every action seems to take forever to resolve.  And what did we get in return?  Someone better graphics?  Some cut scenes that would be embarrassing if they were done in the late 90's?
After the main story, which consists of you piloting the 5 planeswalkers through their backstories, in 5 duels, the gameplay is mostly grinding out coins fighting bots.  It takes 150 to get a pack containing 8 cards.  A medium level fight gives you 10.  So it takes 15 of those to get you one pack.  That's 15 fights before even have a shot at getting more cards, and in all likelihood, none of them will fit my deck.  I could build another, but I probably only have the cards for one decent deck until I grind out enough for another.  There is also a limit to how many coins you can earn a day.  Luckily, the game is so bad, reaching the limit means you've probably gone insane.  All this so magic can get you to buy virtual coins - like the booster packs in the last game.  Only worse, since at least those had a premium card guaranteed.
In the end, I find that I played this one even less then the previous ones, and bought even less as well. Where I made some purchases to support the game previously, this time I quit just after doing the storyline, and I probably will never play this or any other game they produce again.  I'm thoroughly dissappointed in the direction magic has headed in their video games, and they should be equally ashamed of the garbage they've created.

tl;dr - pretty good story and lore and fairly lengthy, but slightly grinding and obscure
Similar to: Castlevania, Metroid, Dark Souls
==
Major Pros
==
- Excellent story, characters and use of the Dark Souls style of piecemeal lore with minimal exposition, as well as visual and gameplay-based lore cues. It is simple but effective, and the main plot has impact while still leaving some aspects open to interpretation. You have to bust your♥♥♥♥♥for the Best Ending, but it's worth it.
- Wonderful interconnected world design with a great variety of locales that all have their own unique feel. Some of it may seem a bit old hat, especially for FromSoft fans, but it has enough of its own charm and originality that it really sticks. The urge to explore is also used very well, as the elements of gameplay as well as the style of storytelling encourage you to poke in every dark corner and search towards the ends of the earth to find whatever it is you're looking for.
==
Pros
==
- Soundtrack is good, at least as mood music. It does sound a little dry out of context, but so do the large majority of actually good video game OSTs as well. The standout "ear-worm" piece would be City of Tears, and the final boss is also good.
- Pretty long game for an Indie priced title. I clocked 50 hours with an initial completion of 94% (not including expansion content), though I also tend to take things fairly slowly, leave no stone unturned and try and get the maximum amount of dialogue out of every character.
- Lots of interesting enemy designs and bosses, and it's nice to feel that satisfaction of being initially intimidated but then learning the moves and being able to breeze through it. Same goes for the platoforming sections.
==
Neutral
==
- The fairly intense thematic similarity to Dark Souls 1 may or may not dull the anticipation of certain plot points depending on your mood towards copypasting in art. But of course, FromSoftware isn't a plagiarism-free zone either. That said, like I mentioned above, the most important parts - the setting, characters and final ending - are all original, so no need to think about it too much.
==
Minor Cons
==
- Can sometimes be obtuse just for the sake of it. Breakable walls are fine since they are easy to miss but you can still notice if you are careful, but I think the walk-through illusory walls are a bit too much. Nail-pogo as a mechanic I think should have been explained. Some mechanics and areas are extremely easy to miss as well.
- Some bosses feel spammy and uninteresting, both on the boss side and player side. Sometimes I felt like I just got ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t RNG'd with the right (or wrong) combo of screen fillers, but on the other hand, with the right combo of charms, you can basically just stand next to certain bosses and facetank mash X your way to victory.
- The game can get pretty tedious if you're a completionist. There is immense backtracking and some areas feel like they go on for too long. You unlock new spells and a few special moves, but for the most part you use the same weapon throughout the entire game
==
Major Cons
==
- None

I've tried twice now to like this game. The first was years ago on my Xbox, and now on the PC. The story is appealing and involved, but the main character is a cringeworthy blockhead. I understand at the beginning of the game he's meant to be lovably obtuse; a character meant to have room to grow. But it'll leave you gnashing your teeth at his sheer density more often than not.
Additionally, the game's scaled-down version of Dynasty Warriors it calls a battle system is a hot mess touted as being unique. There are so many things going on at once you're left guessing who's attacking what at any given time. You are encouraged to attack multiple enemies at once due to additional reward drops, but this can be unfair at times. If an NPC-controlled unit contends a player-controlled one, the enemy NPCs usually get a first swing, and rightly so. But I have found, much to my dismay/frustration, that this is STILL the norm even when a player-controlled unit starts a skirmish. Enemies will get to attack you first whether you're on offense/defense, and it has bequeathed me with a Game Over more times than I can count. And if ever you wish to heal your units, you have to break off fighting any enemy units you're currently skirmishing. And you know what that does? You guessed it; it provides the enemy with another chance to attack you.
The game also suffers from an error many of its predecessors have made: level-scaled enemies. No matter how strong your characters get, you're no stronger comparitively to NPCs than you were at level 1. You just dish out bigger numbers against bigger health pools.
Worse still, if you don't have a character in your party, they will not receive XP. Couple this with scaled enemies, and you will have a very, VERY tough time trying to level-up any neglected party members later in the game.
Another minor nit-pick is that the camera controls while using a keyboard do not lock while navigating dialogue or game menus. You will often see the camera pan/jitter while moving up/down/left/right through menu screens, and yes this does happen during battle as well. Again, minor annoyance, but it is pervasive, and for this reason I had to complete the game on my Xbox instead (notice the 1.5 game hours on record).
I feel this game's story was a solid pitch, but then poor dialogue and (english) acting, as well as an experimental battle system gone awry have left it collecting dust. It's unfortunate, considering an epic story is only 1/3 of the formula that makes this genre great--the other 2/3 being story delivery and battle system, where this game falls horribly short.
Can't a guy dream for the return of the original turn-based encounter system? Tried and true, it's what put this genre on its feet. What on earth was so wrong with it? Don't fix something that isn't broken.

LOTR: WITN: 7.9/10
War in the North is an adventure RPG game based in the LOTR universe. You can choose to play as three different classes - The Dwarf, The Elven Wizard, and the Ranger. The Dwarf is a slow but sturdy fighter, the Elf is a weak but powerful alternative, and the Ranger is a balanced knight. All of them are fun to play in their own ways. Now on to the review...
This game is quite fun, and if you like fantasy, this is surely not to disappoint. The graphics, all though slightly dated, still look good. The atmosphere of Middle Earth is very much present, in some areas more than others. You can collect different weapons, armor, treasure, and other loot along the way. This makes the game feel large.
Sadly, this wouldn't be at the top of the list for Best Fantasty RPGs. This game executes flawlessly but the final product is bland.
The fighting is based around clicking your mouse and Num. Pad buttons, similar to the Arkham games and how you can just mash your Left Mouse button to take down swarms of enemies. That being said, the further you go, it tends to get difficult.
Single Player in this game has the classic campaign feel to it, and it can be a blast to go through the story, but it is clear from the start that this is meant to be a Multiplayer game. You and you two teammates are constantly side-by-side, and while that isn't a bad thing at all, it tends to get bothersome to always have to get to your AI friends to revive them and get them back to the fighting. And for me they go down a lot. I end up just leaving them to the 20 Goblins surrounding them while I hastily defeat everybody alone. Luckily for me this isn't very challenging, though intense.
Going back to mulitplayer, it is impossible to find a game online. Which means that you'll be going through the Single Player with your computer cohorts, plowing through the orcs on your own with the somewhat useful help of your team.
Overrall, this game isn't asking much for $19.99. If you love RPGS, or love LOTR, I'd suggest buying this game: you'll like it. If you have a gut feeling not to purchase this, don't. But if you're sure you'll like it, I think you'll have a fun time playing this. But don't expect a Skyrim adventure in this; it's anything but. I hope you liked this review, and please, check out the game!

I'll have to give this a down.  I love the Saint's Row series for the sheer insanity that comes to pass in an open world sandbox style game.  It's like the GTA series without the bad gangsta story lines and stupid moralizing - like the original GTA series in fact.  But this stand-alone isn't a very good look at it.
The setting is, uhm, unique.  Having a Judeo-Christian hell theme was a bold choice and I fully support it.  The mythology of modern religions is very evocative and has some very interesting characters.  But the actual hell-scape is rather small and lacks some of the variability of, say, Dante's Divine Comedy.  Flames are all fine and dandy but give us an ice-scape or an eternal desert, eh?  The very basic demonic soldiery and denizens are also a tad disappointing but they're effective for what they are - just wish it would be more creative in this realm.
The combat is too frantic for me, as well.  Sorry but I was one of those types to invest heavily in Notoriety decomposition upgrades.  I prefer a more relaxed combat pace where I can approach things in a methodical manner.  Having swarms of demonic enemies every two steps put me off on actually doing anything in-game.  And the size of the game world is telling.  Because there is only one type of purchasable good (weapons) that is bought from a vending machine (usually out in the open where demons will gleefully pick you off with cars), there's no easy and ready way of clearing Notoriety.  Which - for me - made combat a chore to slog through instead of something fun to do.
The powers are a retread of Saints Row IV pretty much.  They are quickly gained but it takes a long time to upgrade them and the collectathon to do so isn't as fun as SRIV in my opinion.  It felt like I was just doing the same thing in a smaller space.
Now here's the kicker and what really made me go from 'so-so' to a firm downvote: character customization.  Hey, hey.  Hey Volition?  No one cares about Gat.  Not really.  We care about the Boss.  You know, the player stand-in?  Gat might be your big wet dream but not ours.  If I want to play as Doctor Manhatten with a rocket launcher, well damn it - that's what I want to do.  And throwing the female players a bone in the form of Kinzie only works if SHE IS MENTIONED IN THE CUTSCENES.  Or is playable at the end boss.  Or, well, anything takes into account her existence.
So, this is a 'not recommended' on my end.  It's fun but that fun is tempered with a huge helping of 'same old' from SRIV, the lack of anything really pulling me back to the game, lack of customization and too-frantic and not much fun constant combat - as well as a bit of a missed opportunity in the setting.  Wait till the price drops by half or more and then give it a go.

OK, so! There are a lot of bad reviews for this game, and probably well deserved. People had problems, and still have them to be honest, but the game is playable now imo. I think at this point the only thing that really bothers most people is a sense of missing functional capabilities for a more comfortable feel. Now, with that said you know you will love the way this game looks, you'll love the way piloting feels which is nice and fluid. Something that could be added would be to constantly drift (because its space) and there are substantial physics in this game to make that available I think.
The Dev's have been working tirelessly to accomodate to the vast amount of potential hardware differences and the way the game reacts when you have additional programs opened, I reccomend not to have anything running in the back ground at all for full performance. Also, this is no hardware friendly game, you need some serious serious serious hardware to get it to perform smoothly. There has been major performance increases as the Dev's have been working to improve the overall optimization of the game.
The critics are harsh, the X game veterans are even more so when it comes to talking about the game. In my opinion its because this is a game that has 10 times more potential to enjoy and immerse yourself in that seems to be missing, BUT is most likely going to be added over time.
In conclusion, you won't find a better space sim with an A.I. active enviroment and living economy like this game. Sure you could go back to playing X3 and all the other previous X games, but those games are  horrible to look at in comparison, and the learning curve is rediculous with all of the sub menus you have to sift through. If you have a decent rig and have been looking for an immersive Space sim with a living AI economy, get this game!

As my first review, I'm happy to put it on such a wonderful game. Defy Gravity Extended is perhaps one of the best platformers I have played in my life. The challenging levels and the great music makes a great experience to play. The levels go from super easy, teaching the mechanics to difficult levels that require split-second decisions. The graphics aren't Skyrim-esque, however, they fit the simplicity of the game. The gravity wells and anti-wells allow you  to float, hover, and boost yourself across levels. The gravity based platforming really makes this game a wonderful thing to play. I do think the player model can be improved, as it doesn't have much to write home about. I also found a glitch that if you put both a gravity well and antiwell in a corner, and walk straight into the corner, you won't be able to control your character. To fix this, you have to use your gravity shield(makes you immune to the effects of the gravity wells you place down), or place a new well. Overall, I rate this game a 9.5/10, and it would be a 10/10 if the devs could improve the player model and the glitch I have found. I really recommend this game if you want a calming experience, or a challenging game. I think the devs should add in a level-creator, so players can make and share their creations. Once again buy this game, its very nearly perfect.

i can tell you as a huge Sid Meiers fan having 1,000+ hours into Civilization V and playing Civ Rev on console,  that this game was just a build-up of excitment, and then a huge let down.
FIRST- The  AI have no personality. If any of you are Civilization V players, we all can agree that Ghandi was a *****, but in a good way, and made you want to keep on playing for the anticipation and the excitment of interactive AI's. However, you will not get that in this game. The only sort of AI activity you will encounter is Declaration of Friendship, and having them do Covert Operations against you (spying). That is pretty much it. No AI have a significant "Label" (Ghandi being with nukes and Gengis Khan a warmongerer, etc.) All of them act the same and are completely non-interactive. They are just NOT FUN TO PLAY WITH.
SECOND- This games feels like a overpriced DLC or mod in the Steam Workshop. Its a fairly nice game, but it did not need to be a stand-alone game. It had a starting prce tag of $49.99 and i  bought it on sale for 50% off. I'm glad i didn't throw out an extra $25 for this game.
OVERALL- This game was a let down to me. Sure the affinities are fun and the tech web is very complex but overall, for all of you die-hard Civ Series fans, just stick to Civ V or SMAC. Unfortunately, this game was not worth the money and i do not recommend buying this game at full price. If you plan on buying it, wait for a sale of at least 50% off, maybe even more (holiday sale or summer sale).
I'm not sure what 2K can do to fix this, other then to just impress me on another Civ game, the last one was in 2010, expect to wait another 4 years.
Upgrading units is very fun and picking affinites and interacting with the alien species is enjoyable, but there is nothing else to it, especially how the screwed up on the latest patch that messed up everything it was supposed to "fix".
I'm sorry for all of you reading who were expecting a good review. you will expect to find similar reviews down below. Sorry for the bad news but long story short, wait for this game to be on sale, otherwise, go spend that good money somewhere else.....

There are some games I like, this is not one of them. There are other games that I hate; this is not one of them. There are few games which I will defend to the grave – Final Fantasy XIII is not one of them. This game falls into an unusual category. It is a game which I feel I am not allowed to love. Why you may ask? Well it is simple, and it explains why I must write this review with a huge amount of caution.
The reason I have to make such a drastic statement before getting to the heart of the actual review is because I am 100% aware of the criticism this games receive, and I won’t disagree with most of these criticisms. In other words, there are very valid reasons for criticising the game, but It is for you to decide whether you view these criticisms as actual criticisms or strengths of the game. What I must point out is that this game is not fundamentally flawed or broken in its game design.
Large amounts of the game’s criticism surround three main areas: story, characters and gameplay. I’ll tackle each in turn. There is a brief separate comment to be said about the quality of the port itself: essentially what I can say is that there have been reported framerate issues and stuttering. However, I experienced very few noticeable problems, especially considering I played the game when it was originally released for the Xbox 360. What I would say is to double check that your PC is close to the recommended rather than minimum system requirements.
*No spoilers*
There are two main types of story driven games: those which take the player through a chronological journey from start to finish with very few disturbances in the ordinary sequence of events. This is a safe route to use, particularly for a JRPG which relies on using more creative conventions and methods of storytelling. The second main type throws the gamer in the middle of things. Instead of showing the player the background information leading up to the main events within the story, the game throws the player in the middle of an already chaotic situation. Final Fantasy 13 takes the second form. The game begins in the middle of conflict between several conflicting sides of society: The oppressive government known as the Sanctum on the one hand and the ordinary citizens on the other who are being purged by the Sanctum for coming into contact with a Pulse Fal’Cie. Final Fantasy 13 is the kind of game which requires you to be willingly engaged and interested in the story. Not being so will result in you as a player losing the plot (and I mean that literally). Playing this kind of game requires attention to detail which typically is not present in the majority of Final Fantasy games which take the standard beginning-middle-end format. Whilst the game may be linear, it does not hold your hand with its story.
Lightning: Not one to bring to parties…
One of the criticisms of the game is that the main protagonist, Lightning, lacks character and personality. It’s easy to understand why people would have that view. My cat expresses more emotion than Lightning ever does across the three games in the series – and my cat sleeps all day. Ironically I argue that her cold-heartedness, the monotone aggression, the bitterness she
expresses against Snow all add to her character, and that character is a seemingly fearless woman who ends up being overcome by the one thing she lacks… her emotion. Dramatic monologue aside, the supporting cast are quite varied in personality, Sazh being one of my favourites and Vanille being… Have you ever heard the sound of a young child trying to play the violin for the very first time? Well that sound describes Vanille's character... Okay I confess I liked her by the end of the series.
The final criticism that the game has been flooded with is fundamental issues with the game itself. A huge criticism is that the game is largely linear. This is a fair criticism if the defining feature of Final Fantasy games in your opinion is the open world and the focus on exploration, or if you dislike linear games in general. Personally, my attraction to the characters and my enjoyment of other things such as the music and the gameplay enabled me to overlook this criticism, but again, I understand and accept this to be a valid criticism of a game within a franchise which is so reliant on freedom and adventure. It worked for Final Fantasy 10, but 10 had a certain humility about it which 13 admittedly lacked. I personally felt that 13 was too adamant on expressing the huge cinematics and beautiful graphics which Final Fantasy games have never really been so dependent upon.
I often hear arguments that the turn based battle system is dying. I actually felt 13 attempted to reinvigorate and give the system a fresh look. I would even go as far to say that it has kept the turn based system alive. Whilst it may not have been as complex as previous systems, it had its own uniqueness. In short, 13’s paradigm system involves switching between different combinations of magic that you can freely alter throughout the game. As the game progresses, character’s gradually unlock stronger magic and various stat upgrades. It is a far simpler method of levelling up character stats and abilities, but requires some planning in order to overcome difficult bosses.
Say what you want about the quality of the game itself. If you argue that the character’s sucked, I’ll accept it; if you argue that the story sucked, I’ll accept it, but if you argue that the music sucked… Well I’ll have to unleash the Behemoth within me. Whilst the soundtrack was not composed by my beloved Nobuo Uematsu, for once it honestly did not matter. Masashi Hamauzu did an incredible job of capturing the sense of isolation, oppression and the emotional complexity of characters such as Lightning in a diverse soundtrack. Whilst there were pieces which were played incredibly frequently, the quality of the soundtrack made up for this. The battle theme ‘Blinded by Light’ was particularly able to recreate the intensity maintained throughout the game whilst continuing the bass motif’s found in every battle theme in the franchise. Other incredible pieces include: ‘The Promise,’ ‘Sazh’s Theme,’ ‘March of the Dreadnoughts,’ ‘Hope’s Theme’ and ‘Vanille’s Theme (not to give any credit to Vanille by the way).’
Final Fantasy 13 is one of those rare games which I still struggle to explain why I love so much. Whilst it would fail to reach my favourite Final Fantasy games, that does not retract from the genuine enjoyment I experienced playing this game 3 times over. I’m in the process of doing a Final Fantasy marathon (FF1 – 13) and I am looking forward to replaying the 13 series. Even if you didn’t enjoy 13 itself, the sequels are amazing games in their own right but I’ll save those reviews for another time. In summary, I do love this game. Perhaps I was literally blinded by the light of a franchise which I adore, but as I mentioned, there are genuine reasons to love this game, just as there are reasons to despise it. I do believe the game receives way too much criticism than it actually deserves but those criticisms aren’t found on some imaginary basis. I once honestly believed I was the only person who actually liked this game at one point. The ultimate question however is should you buy this game? For the first time, I will copout and leave the decision up to you, the reader, taking into account what you like in a Final Fantasy game and what you dislike. If I attempted to score this game, I fear I would be giving some arbitrary number which does not actually represent anything at all.

I don't think I've ever gotten 100% of a game's Steam achievements before but I enjoyed this one so much that getting them all was a happy byproduct of playing it.
The gameplay is fast 2D shooting with different characters catering to different playstyles. Each character also represents a British stereotype, often ones that you don't get to see much in any media, let alone in games. I don't think I'll ever play another game where my favourite character sounds like they're from St Helens and if you're not from Northern England you'll probably have no idea where that is. The stereotypes are funny and weird without being nasty which is great.
There's about twenty levels split into three sections (Downtown, Council Estate and Chinatown) with slightly different enemy types in each section. The basic mission objectives are varied and there's decent replayability provided by bonus objectives which amp up the difficulty or force you to change up your playstyle. Nothing groundbreaking but it is all done very well.
Bunny Lord, the main character and your boss,
a random "crazy" character but as in the best farce/absurd comedies while what Bunny Lord is trying to achieve (winning a Mayoral Election via a literal war on crime so that he can save the future (which he is from) from disaster) is crazy he presents a twisted logic behind it that makes it compelling. For instance, in one mission you have to escort an old lady (don't worry she's invulnerable) through a council estate full of heavily armed gangsters. After the mission Bunny Lord acknowledges this seems like a waste of time but, he reasons, old people love to talk and are very likely to vote thus this act of kindness is likely to win him votes. Very silly but it almost makes sense if you squint at it. The game has enough awareness and wit that it remains very funny throughout.
I highly recommend this game.

This is a pretty fun expansion of the Saints Row universe. While not being particularly extensive, the game builds on the "super powers" engine from SR4, to create an awesome and memorable atmosphere in hell. Angelic flight was a ton of fun to play with, although I was disappointed at how labored the controls were to get used to, particularly when maneuverability in the previous installment was so buttery smooth and natural.
The side activities are EXTREMELY enjoyable, in particular hijacking armored vehicles and searching for the coveted "Seven Deadly weapons", were a ton of fun. The story and cutscenes themselves are more than worthy of the Saints Row moniker, by way of pure absurdist hilarity alone. But overall I found myself wishing for a bit more in terms of exploration and discovery. While finally being able to play as fan favorite, Johnny Gat was a fantastic treat, I must admit to some of the flavor being lost in not taking on the legions of darkness as my own unique character, or being able to roam hell's streets decked out in all manner of hellish armors and crazy getups (hell mascot suit, anyone?). Perhaps a "Game+" expansion, allowing players to design or import their own characters from SR4 upon completion is in order?
Still,I found 'Gat Out Of Hell' to be a fun and thoroughly enjoyable ride, worth the price of admission. 7/10.

For the multiplayer version, however, could have met it's potential. There are many problems with it. First thing is that it uses peer 2 peer technology for connection with players around the world. There is no option whatsoever to host a dedicated server. You just find a room with the type of game, and that's it. Second, there are a lot of disrespectful people that come online. TL;DR. Single Player is awesome. Multiplayer is good, but with too many problems.

This War of Mine is a fantastic survival sim with rogue-like elements and a moderate difficulty curve.  What makes the game great is the overall atmosphere.  It is very bleak and depressing in a thought provoking way and it really draws you into the setting.  Unlike in most games, the moral choices you will be making here have real consequences to them, and you may find yourself making morally questionable decisions that make you (and your survivors) feel guilty.
The rogue-like elements include a significant amount of RNG that keep the experience fresh when playing through a handful of times after your previous attempts end poorly.  You should expect to lose your entire group of survivors a few times while you are getting a hang of the game, but the process of figuring things out is a rewarding one as you manage to keep your survivors in good health longer.  Sometimes the RNG can cause uneven difficulty, however, as starting in the middle of a cold spell or without any characters with large backpacks can make the game significantly harder.
The gameplay is split into day and night cycles.  During the day you use what resources you have gathered to feed your survivors and craft things that will keep them alive and in good spirits.  During the night you can send one survivor out to scavenge from a variety of places utilizing side scrolling stealth/combat gameplay that is fairly barebones but is well polished with no bugs or glitches that I encountered.  The entire game is very well done and it would be nice if this level of polish was standard in the industry instead of an unexpected surprise.

Note that the game is still being worked on, so any negatives that I mention could very well be remedied in the near-to-distant future.
The point of the game is to show you the other side of all the war games that are so popular these days. You've almost surely been a soldier, invading enemy territory and mowing down waves of 'bad guys,' but I personally have yet to see another game that lets you get a glimpse of the effects of war on the people living in the area where it happens. This game does that, and very well. You have to decide what you're willing to direct your survivors to do to keep on living, whether you'd rather let them starve than stroll into a defenseless elderly couples' home and raid their refridgerator and leave them with nothing, or risk sneaking into a military compound to grab what you can and (attempt) to sneak out in one piece. It's very difficult and it should be, in both the decisions you have to make and the game in and of itself.
It is depressing. You get to know the characters you control better throughout the game by reading their war journals, you slowly learn bits of their history and personality, some of them you may like, others may seem to be generally bad people, but it's your job to keep them alive. If the game ends with the deaths of all of your survivors, you're treated to something reminiscient of an obituary; did their parents learn about their death and visit their grave? Did anyone ever hear about the relative they were so worried about? Etcetera.
It does a fantastic job at what it sets out to do.
On the downside, some more variety in the game itself and the areas you visit would be a huge plus and greatly increase replayability. I don't know if it's in the works, but randomly generated characters with unique backstories, along with the locations that become available, would be great. As it is now, after playing for a certain amount of time you'll see and become familiar with most of the survivors that it's possible to start with or recruit.
Another welcome addition (to me) would be the introduction of a couple different game modes. As it stands now, your goal is to survive until the war comes to an end. I would like to see an endurance mode, where at no point will the war end, and you get a score based on how long you manage to keep at least one survivor going. This could feasibly go on for as long as you wanted if you were skilled enough, with old cleared out buildings disappearing after enough time without being visited and being replaced by newly generated ones.
All in all it is absolutely a solid game in the state it's in now, and I'm excited to see any improvements they make, regardless of whether or not they're any of the ones I mentioned here. It makes you think, and it does something that a lot of games can't quite hope to do- it can make you regret the actions you take to survive, if you really let yourself get immersed in the game world and think of the fact that real people have lived, -are- living, in conditions like this. If you're a fan of any kind of simulation, you would be doing yourself a disservice not to try this at some point.

You will run out of resources. You will get injured.  You will become clinically depressed. You will be raided. You will become desperate. And your desperation you will consider despicable actions. This is the crux of This War of Mine: how much of your humanity are you willing to sacrifice for survival. Will you give your neighbours your hard-earned medications to save their sick mother? Ranks on the top of frustrating games. For some good, and some bad reasons. I'll provide only the main reasons.
TL;DR version: Enjoyable stealth game if played on 'normal'. Aggravating (challenging) game on expert/purist (good luck without prior gameplay experience or guides - still doable, but you will get to know levels quite intimately for the number of times you play).
The good:
Very challenging without previous experience. Yea, it was a doozie. Satisfying to have finished the game and there was a reasonable storyline. Lots of quirky characters. Most of which you kill. Yay! Oh, and headshots.
I have never played a Hitman game before and I like playing my games on difficult settings. I did not run purist because that appeared to need some familiarity with the game to play. However, so did Expert. I am glad I played Expert and not Purist. I found it difficult to catch on to what 'deaths' could be setup, what mechanics to use and how they could be used. This isn't necessarily bad... Except that you will probably miss a lot of cool setup deaths such as an individual peeing on a wire you have exposed that leads to their electrocuted demise. It was not intuitive that these types of kills could be done. Decent story. I cursed many times as I was caught in many awkward situations. Also, I did not realize you could upgrade weapons until I finished the game. To have more freedom to 'enjoy' these tidbits in the game I recommend that you play on Normal unless you want the Absolution achievement, then play on Hard,
Headshots.. Headshots are rewarding and make you feel good. 99.9% of occasions 1 headshot = 1 kill. So for those of you who have good accuracy and hate games like GOW for the reason that no person/monster should take a sniper round to the noodle and survive, this game is for you.
The bad:
Melee, lack of checkpoints for higher difficulties, some complete BS detection.
Melee has got to be the most frustrating aspect in the higher difficulties (replaying normal for achievements, melee is a joke because it is so easy in comparison). I did not know for the longest time, until rage level exceeded maximum and I looked up a guide that you are better off watching the animations to know what buttons to press than to actually wait for the QTE event (which gave you a window of what seemed to be less than a second and required inhuman reaction times). FYI: 'Space' if they are attacking you; 'Q' for first hit; 'W' if 47 knocks them in the face backwards; 'E' if 47 knocks them towards the ground.
Checkpoints... Oh dear. Having no familiarity with this game and playing it on Expert lead to a long time of trial and error trying to figure out how the hell to beat some levels. Admittedly I looked up a guide in two circumstances: One of the first levels (can't remember which), and the courthouse. Other than that, no guides... But I can see why people would instantly go to guides after 3...4...10.. 20 failed attempts at a level haha.
Detection.. Silenced weapons are not so silent. I always loved how shooting a target with a silenced weapon would result in being spotted first, then being awarded for the kill (the game awards score based on activity and so it shows, in order, the events that occur and the points associated). Albeit, the circumstances in which I was shooting a silenced weapon (from afar) and being detected were somewhat reasonable, but annoying all the same. So expect to be detected frequenly and die frequently if you play higher difficulties. Especially under circusmtances of choking a guy out only for one of the teammates to 'happen' to turn around and see you. I felt like the game was just trolling me for the number of times people turned around for no reason, not because I made noise, but just because this is Hitman and you need to be demoralized a few times.
There were also many instances where throwing something to distract an individual never worked. The NPC refused to move at all. So you were forced to find some way arouund these stonewall NPCs. On most occasions I emptied a clip into them out of frustration and had to restart the level because A) No checkpoints in expert, and B) I would be detected even if my weapon was silenced.
Alas, time to finish the achievements and move on... Probably never to play this game again.

Free to play Magic: The Gathering presented in the style of the earlier 'Duels of the Planeswalkers' games.  No exclusive content that can't be earned with in game currency. The game uses a selection of cards from the latest 'Origins' set.
Magic Duels is plagued with bugs, ranging from inexplicable launch errors preventing many from playing the game, to infinite loading screens and some instances of cards not following the rules.  There is also an unreasonable DX 11 hardware requirement which is plain sloppy programming, Duels could easily be software rendered.
Playing Duels online can really push my patience to its limits sometimes.  Matchmaking fails most of the time, I often have to search 5+ times before finding an opponent, and getting into a match of 2HG has been 100% impossible.  Players can avoid losing rank from losses very easily, making the whole mode a joke.  Also, people playing this better enjoy battling poor AI opponents, since whenever you play a person in any mode, if there's a slight connection hiccup of any kind or the server acts up, your opponent gets replaced with the AI.
I can't in good conscience recommend the game to anyone in its current state, it is simply not release ready and I'd strongly discourage anyone from spending real money in the game until drastic measures are taken by the developers to improve just about all aspects of the game.  Those desperate for a decent F2P MtG experience (such as myself) may be willing to forgive a lot of the shortcomings and problems this game suffers.  It is frustrating, there's potential for a lot of good MtG cardslinging with this release, but it needs SO much work to be considered a good game.
Unfortunately I have little faith of Magic Duels recieving any of these much needed improvements simply because of the track record of the developer, Stainless Games, which despite imaginative boasts on their website are responsible for a lot of bad releases, from the recently released Carmageddon game which is a complete wreck (in all the wrong ways) to all the previous 'DotP' iterations, which ALL have had bugs and problems of varying magnitude that were never fixed.  The amateurish online functionality in particular is something that has plagued all the earlier versions of 'DotP' and never seen improvements.

I will have to unfortunately echo the other sentiments.  This game had a lot of promise, but falls flat on it's face once the excitement of the first few games are done.  It feels very much like an incomplete game.
* The factions have a lot promise, but mechanically, there's nothing to distinguish them.
* Even the traits aren't really unique enough.  The units still do basically the same thing as civ units.  Orbital units show promise, but are ultimately weak and easily countered by conventional units.
* Diplomacy and the station system is unfinished and imbalanced.  Rival AI, for example, can attack the Stations you are trading with and there's virtually nothing you can do about it.
* The end-game is even more flat, uninspired, and anti-climactic as Civ 5.  The hardest part about achieving the victory conditions is actually figuring out what you have to do, as the game provides very little clues.
* Certain problems in Civ 5, e.g. the clunky trade routes UI, haven't been fixed and have just been copy-pasted in.

Wonderful game.   Almost everything I've found addictive about the whole Civ series and more.   Yes, late-game turns are a bit long.  But being able to blend faction perks with user customized perks pre-game and then guiding your civilization toward one of three different philosophies (with associated not-just-cosmetic perks) adds a depth I haven't seen in the series before.   I was quite frankly getting tired of reliving history with the other Civ games.  The affinity-based units are different enough to enjoy and add replay value.  Everythign is an improvement in my opinion until the very end.
Now, the bad:  At first I had a worse review, because at the end of the game there wasn't a bunch of stats and graphs and playable timeline of how my civilization progressed.   I later found that at least the charts were available for any save game under the options menu off of the main menu.  Still, I miss the playable timeline showing when I built what wonders, etc.
So - kudos for thinking outside the box and having rich gameplay mechanics and customization ability.   Boo-hiss for the mildly dissatisfying post-game.  Still, it's at least replayable 3 or 4 times after you win.

Hollow Knight is a metroidvania platformer which I will lead by noting that this is not my preferred genre nor is it a genre I am extremely familiar with. I've played some of the older Castlevania games and enjoyed them a lot but on the whole I don't love the genre. Please if you read this review keep that in mind because many of the points of the review that lead to me not recommending this game are subjective. Another point to consider is that I played this game for barely over two hours and refunded it at which point I was about 4-5 bosses in and had only a few abilities.
I'll lead with some observations which I believe were objective. So firstly the aesthetic of this game is interesting and pretty unique in the current market; you won't play many games that are similar visually to this one and I believe that's a good thing. I enjoyed the characters who appeared during my brief time playing the game and the atmosphere was quite appropriate. This category in particular among friends of mine seems to appreciate the presentation and sounds of games so this is a big plus for people in that camp. As far as gameplay is concerned the game contains multiple enemies from the start that are unique if not extremely interesting. Fighting the grunt enemies is quite simple at first with a small difficulty hike in about the 3rd area (obviously this depends on the order in which you explore areas since they're relatively open.) Enemies don't really have a unique character of their own but they're only grunts so I would'nt consider that a downside. Boss enemies are interesting to fight but often not particularly rewarding; many of them feel like a grunt enemy from the later game that has been presented earlier which is pretty common in games so not a huge concern however the lack of interesting early bosses leads to a detraction of the story since you are spending a few hours (unless you're quite a bit faster than me) working your way through these bosses without actually developing the game's story. As far as strictly gameplay criticisms are concerned I have few issues; enemy placement feels deliberate and interesting as well as apropriate to the areas which you move through. Getting hit in the air knocks back further than on ground (at least in the forested area which was where I noticed this most) which leads to interesting situations that force you into tricky spots unless you adapt quickly. I liked this element of the game that made enemies more interesting to fight and breaks up what could otherwise be monotonous grinding. The main reason I stopped playing this game is that for me it simply wasn't fun to play. The game could've been extremely interesting to watch but playing didn't produce satisfaction at all comparable to the effort I put in. I felt every time I accomplished something that all I was doing was what was expected and not really anything impressive and each time I died it felt like I had really failed at something that should've been easy. Note that these are all my feelings and not universal.
The game just wasn't satisfying for me is the bottom line for why I don't want to play it and can't recommend it. However if you know you like games like this there's no reason not to play it in my review. I think that objectively this is a great game that just missed something I can't quite grasp which resulted in my personal lack of enjoyment. So in short I don't like the game when I play it but the game looks quite good as long as I'm not the one playing it.

The first half of this game is more of an interactive movie than a game. That's not such a bad thing, I like interactive movies, but I can see how it would turn most people off.
The story is even pretty good, at first. It's an interesting exploration of loss and grief. In first few hours of the game, a group of people is granted tremendous magical powers, but at a terrible price. They lose their freedom, their family, their future, and their place in society. They become outcasts and pariahs, and the military/police have orders to shoot them on sight.
Sounds like a pretty compelling setup, right? I thought so. I got sucked in. Even though the areas were all linear and the battle system was dull, I got sucked in. I regret it now, because the story eventually fell apart. Most of the characters' arcs and key moments were bungled. Sazh is an exception, but he wasn't enough to carry the others' dead weight. In true anime fashion, the world made less sense as more of it was revealed, and the twist at the final battle was just idiotic.
Eventually, the interactive movie takes a break, and you are dumped into an open world. Neat, right? Except there isn't anything all that compelling to DO out there, and the story kind of takes a break as well. It's boring as hell. It's the section everyone touts as the game's saving grace, and I didn't enjoy it at all. Maybe if I liked the battle system, it would have been a different story, but I really didn't.
The battle system works differently than most other RPGs. It doesn't really concern itself with the minutia of players attacking. You can micromanage their actions if you really want to, but you quickly learn that the best results are achieved by mashing the auto-battle and letting the computer sort it out. The paradigm (mode) a character is in determines what attacks are available. So your job is to assemble characters with the right combination of abilities and switch their paradigms at key moments.
Again, this could have been interesting, but it wasn't. Most battles are easily won with a simple pattern of paradigms, all the while mashing A as fast as the menu animations allowed. Worse, the equipment system is unorthodox and not at all explained, and it doesn't seem to matter for most of the game. Only certain boss fights and monsters in the open world were even challenging, making equipment upgrades unnecessary for most of the game.
Even the visuals were a mixed bag. Some were gorgeous, and some were blah. The one bright spot is the prerendered cut scenes, which are very pretty and quite entertaining. The music is also a mixed bag, sometimes amazing and sometimes unremarkable.
So, yeah. This game stinks. Save your money and your time.

I am very picky when it comes to the Metroidvania genre.
Too many times have I seen uninspired Super Metroid clones that don't do anything interesting with the formula.
Get red upgrade, destroy red block. Get blue upgrade, destroy blue block. (Yes, Guacamelee, I hate you.)
Others try desperately to break up it up with interesting mechanics, just to lose themselves in a mess of mediocre level design and other terrible decisions (Looking at you pre-DE Ori.)
Hollow Knight is not one of those.
Rather than laying it on thick, the game is presented in a rather humble and somber manner.
This ends up working very well, because all it has to do is accentuate little things here and there in order to make certain moments stand out - and it does so beautifully.
For example:
There is an area called "The City of Tears", a place of constant rain.
That, by itself, is not what makes it special. It's the way the developers lead you through it.
Right at the beginning of said area, you come across a bench. Since sitting on benches (or dying) is the only way to save your progress, you will immediately decide to sit down. It's only a short moment, but suddenly you feel like you could just sit there for a couple more seconds, as you take in the ambience created by the visuals, the rain, and the music.
It's moments like these that elevate videogames from mere entertainment to pure works of art, and that is something I will always gush about. Anyone can make a game nowadays, but it's only a select few people that are talented and educated enough to craft something truly special. Team Cherry belong to those select few, and as harsh and trollish as my reviews tend to be, I consider my opinions fair and grounded on actual evidence - and Hollow Knight provides me with a large amount of evidence that leads to nothing but praise.
In terms of gameplay, there are your standard upgrades like health, "ammo", and damage, but also more interesting ones like charms. These allow for some individual customization, at the cost of not having access to every single upgrade at any given time.
Want to know where exactly you are located on the map? There's a charm for that, but it will take up one of your pins (slots for charms). Want more reach for your melee attack? Too bad, you don't have enough pins. Maybe you'll want to remove that map location pin and use the melee pin instead.
It's decisions like these that make the game more interesting and offer a more personalized experience.
All of this is rounded off by challenging combat encounters, fairly interesting NPCs (some of which have their own adventures parallel to yours) and an incredibly well-done soundtrack that couldn't be any more fitting.
There is a certain beauty to be found in loneliness and sorrow. Hollow Knight manages to tap into that beauty and use it to its advantage - and to great effect. The result is a fantastic Metroidvania that was very clearly crafted with a lot of love and care. This is videogames done right, and that's why Hollow Knight deserves a big, blue thumbs up.

I like some metroidvania games (Ori and the Blind Forest and SteamWorld Dig 2 are great), but Hollow Knight just doesn't work for me. It just not fun, rather it feels a dull grind.
Positives:
Music, vocals and sounds are great and the controls are spot-on, there is no (or very little) inertia, the jumping and movement is precise and you don't get damage from falling.
Negatives:
Visually it starts quite atmospheric with muted blue colours but it seems that this melancholic dullness doesn't give way to more vibrant colours (maybe in later stages?), the green colour in Greenpath area is just a variation of the same murkiness and it just gets monotonous and boring.
Mapping is not available from the beginning, instead you have to kill a bunch of enemies to get in-game currency to buy an area map from the cartographer (in each area you need to find him to buy that area's map) and then you have to kill a bunch of enemies to get money to be able to buy an ability to update the map yourself (which you can only update on save benches) and if you want the map to show hot springs (healing), stag stations (fast travel) and so on, you need to grind for more currency to buy each ability separately. It doesn't take that long to get your maps to show all the essentials, but it's an unnecessary chore.
There is no difficulty selection (that's a BIG negative) and after grinding past the False Knight and Hornet, I didn't care to continue playing Hollow Knight. My idea of fun isn't to battle the boss for 10+ times, each time I die, walking and jumping from the save bench to the boss through a couple of platforms and hallways. Save benches are fairly close by to the bosses (well, the first two anyway) but a 30 second jaunt to get back to the boss battle is as stupid as an unskippable animation before a bossfight.
I hope the developer considers adding an easier mode, otherwise I can't recommend the game unless you like difficult games or the colour palette is to your liking.

This game could quite easily be called "The Lost Final Fantasy". It Shares a lot of similarities to final fantasy 12, it builds on and expands the freedom of exploration, merchant crafting system, monster hunting system and combat system.
The story you will either like it or you wont. I liked the overall story but I really didnt like a couple of the main characters, enough to skip cutscenes with them. a bit like Hope in FF13.
The combat takes things to a completely new level. You start out with your standard 2-3 person party to learn the ropes with and progress naturally over the course of the game to 18 party members spead over up to 5 squads. Thankfully its turn based so you can plan out your attacks. Although you dont see it, there is an underlying battle grid that the fights take place on. The relative positions of you and your enemy play the main role in determining what attack/skill options you have available, which get learnt over time. You can either take it at face value and charge in, or learn the intricacies to take full control of the battles and play at a tactical level.
Character progression has been done very well, most of the micromanagement has been taken out, instead of having to craft/individually gear 18+ party members they just chime in when they want something. Skill progression is handled equally well on the PC version, you can either direct them in a specific combat direction or you can allow them to develop organically by enabling/disabling skill trees, which also determines their overall class.
overall i'd give it:
6/10 story
9/10 battle system
8/10 character development
8/10 game world

This game's okay. There's a few problems:
First off: lack of content. There's not a lot to do, and the gameplay, while fun at first, gets rather old in a short amount of time. You unlock characters as you complete more objectives in levels (approval rating) and once you unlock a few characters there's no reason to use any of the others ever again. Mike is by far one of the best characters, and it's really odd that they'd have so many characters and make two of them a lot better than the rest. This game isn't difficult, and most of the difficulty I would say is a battle against the controls, so the content's duration is "padded" with a little bit of frustration. More on that later.
The content that is there is somewhat... repetitive. There are three zones with 7 levels and some secret levels. Different zones have different enemies and themes. but only the enemies are really at all different, some marginally so. It took me about 5.5 hours to complete everything in the game, including achievements. Honestly, if you don't go for all the objectives, it'd probably take you around 1 or 2 hours. I think the asking price is a little high for this amount of content. A full completion would take less time if it wasn't for the next issue.
The controls are pretty bad, especially on keyboard. The analog stick control is terrible, and I ended up using my Steam controller to try to compensate for it (the default controls are... mushy). Maybe it's better with an Xbox/PS controller dpad, but I can't imagine it would be. There's a button to reload, for special weapons, shooting and dodging/cover. I REALLY wish cover/dodge were on separate buttons, as most of the issues I had with completing challenges was because of context issues; sometime's I'd be rolling when I wanted to take cover, sometimes I'd take cover when I needed to roll. It's also worth mentioning that you
rebind keyboard controls, so gamepad is the way to go.
Honestly, this game isn't "bad", but it's not something I'd recommend that you "must play". In fact, most people could skip this game. The premise is interesting, but the execution just sort of fizzles out by the end. I think that if controls were tighter, if there were more actions or some sort of weapon system, or if there were bosses or something it would be more interesting. I'd wait until it's 3-5 bucks.
