I am almost halfway through the game and I must say - I really enjoy it so far. The graphics style may be pixelated and simple, but they are so comical and always fit the scenario. The visuals are appealing and full of humour. The antihero Bunnylord explains us, who to kill...while having a spear through his head. He calls it headwear. But don't forget, this guy also uses crayons to paint his posters. Humor and artstyle all perfect but this is not the main part of the game. The gameplay is spot on. It is fast and it is so fun. You can slide, you can go in cover and the cool thing is - your skill improves. You get faster and with each level you feel more and more ruthless. And you know what? You are. The sound may be simple, but it doesn't feel misplaced. An elevator jingle after a rampage? Why not. I highly recommend this game to any person interested in a Hotline Miami-ish game experience. It is not easy but I really wouldn't call it hard, if you are familiar with videogames in general.
EDIT: I am now through it, took me almost 5 hours. I could 100% it...but I won't, at least in the near future. I really enjoyed the game and especially the style and humour. Games aren't often that funny and solid in execution and I really hope that we get some more Bunnylord, but with a bit more refined gameplay and gamedesign, even though I really like the gameplay. But sometimes it is kind of unfair...especially the last 2 levels were a TOTAL pain the butt, the last one the most. Maybe I just wanted to complete the game and help Bunnylord to become a mayor, but still - I would rather have it skipped or altered. Anyway, I do recommend the game to anyone who enjoys some great gameplay, nice pixel art and of course the really clever and funny writing - both dialogoue, story and the characters. You may want to get it on sale, if you don't plan on 100% completing it. It is "only" 5 hours afterall and I didn't really think it was that repetetive, but I didn't play it in one sitting...more like 3-5.

Intro music for our band of stalwart heroes, a human ranger, a dwarf fighter and an elven wizard(the only woman of course), who set out from the Prancing Pony at Bree, a place cursed with being drenched in perpetual rainy nights, after receiving instructions from non other than stapper, which is the Dutch translation for the nickname for Aragorn, who in this game looks remarkably like an actor called Viggo Mortensen.
The going is pretty unidirectional from the start. Stop the main bad guy Agandaûr from intervening with the rest of the world by killing him dead until he is. Easy enough. In between Bree and Agandaûr's grave you meet some critters that are in the way, but that is how this game should be. They consists of nasty orcs and goblins, undead, biggers orcs, very big trolls, a huge giant even, humans in all shapes and sizes, spiders small, large and very large and that is about it really.
At various moments you get helped by token people you can do well without. At least they don't die on you most of the time, which saves you from that headache. The coolest thing around is however the giant eagle friend your team gains, which gives a nice air asset that you can throw against some of the bigger nasties, provided they are in the open and you didn't waste your limited supply of airstrikes on something smaller.
Somewhere in between you make a stopover at Rivendell where you are briefed by someone who looks remarkably like the actor Hugo Weaving. Incidently Hugo doesn't even hush up the fact that Frodo has a powerful ring that needs to be destroyed. So far for secrecy.
You get to speak to other actors too, like Orlando Bloom, Ian Holm, John Rhys-Davies, Elijah Wood and Liv Tyler and yes by now you know the game takes its cues from the Peter Jackson movies. It isn't bad but it isn't very original either.
And that might be the overall theme of this game. It isn't really bad, but it isn't really good either.. It is okayies. A word I just invented for this purpose. For instance; to lengthen your game experience they threw in a truckload of containers for you to plunder. You have to loot them all cause that is the only way to get neat new gear and what you find is pretty random. So there you are, hero of the war of the north, defeater of many a container...for you destroy or open more caskets, caches, barrels and other containers than you ever want too, because you will not only need to find loot for your own character, but also for your ai buddies, who might have no use at all for that stuff as far as can be told, but maybe they do or at least you can sell the stuff so you buy better stuff for you own, but most of all because this game is meant to be a co-op and can't quite figure out that you play it as a single player or as a co-op.
Your ai buddies require some hand-holding for them not to be killed and if you are the elven maiden wizard it is doubly up to you to make sure that your ai buddies don't get killed, for the wizard biggest task is preventing the other two from turning into pin cushions.
The overwhelming sensation you get when proceeding through this game is: if they just had.. If they just had added some more variety. If they just had added some more ways to do the quests.. If they just had added some more options in character development. If they just had added some interesting side quests. If they had just added some meaning full conversations.
The biggest surprise is at the end when you discover that after all is said and done and the dead are buried and the living celebrate, you still are only halfway developed. And why? Cause you can then redo the whole game again on a higher difficulty level and gain more levels. Oh wow..
War in the North is amusing enough to do once, but it totally lacks the charm to play once more, even as a different character. It is after all only okayies

Right, we all have games that we would show other people to play as our "No, seriously, games are an art form". Next to Spec Ops: The Line, P.T., Metal Gear Solid 3 and Portal, welcome to the club, This War of Mine.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Katia's Dairy
Day 1:
I began my dairy. We cleaned out the house and put together a rota. Pavle was an ex-footballer and he felt he was the most fit to go and scavenge. Bruno was a bit ill, so after he made food, he had to rest. I decided to stay up and write this dairy. Once the war is over, I'll sell it and be rich. We built a bed and rebuilt a cooker, and Bruno is sleeping. I am standing guard, listening to the sounds of the artillery in the distance.
Pavle returned later, carrying a lot of wood, food and random, useful looking crap. I wasn't particularly impressed.
Day 2:
So I spent most of the day asleep on the bed. Bruno was better and made food, and Pavle began to patch up the holes in the building. Again, I am standing guard. Things are going well.
Day 10:
We were raided. While Pavle was out and I was asleep, men snuck into our house, stole our food and medicine, and now Bruno is hurt. We patched him up as best we could, and let him have the bed. We built another one for Pavle.
Pavle began to discuss us getting weapons, but I argued against it. We just need to fix up this house and stay on guard at night, and sleep during the day. The house was coming together, and we began to make some cigarettes for Bruno and we found myself some coffee. The music on the radio helps to block the noise of the war... block the silence...
Day 11:
Our neighbours came to the door. I wanted to hide but Bruno just answered (but he is over 6ft tall, so I can't imagine him too scared) and asked what they wanted. They gave us food, and he left to help them fix up their house like we did for ours. Pavle cooked that day.
Pavle was forbidden to cook again. We don't have enough food to waste.
Day 13:
Pavle didn't come back from Sniper's Junction. They say the military aims for civilians now.
Day 14:
I went to the military base with some moonshine Pavle had been making in the basement. I stood in that flashlights glare, and I hoped to God they wouldn't kill me. They took most of our food, and our alcohol, and some cigarettes, but I walked away with an AK47 and some bullets. We will never be victims again.
Bruno saw it and looked away, but understood the necessity. He keeps trying to give me pep-talks, but all I want is some time to myself. We sleep during the day. He will be on guard tomorrow, he'd better get to like the gun.
Day 17:
A schoolteacher came to us today, asking to stay. Honestly, in the sadness of Pavle, we accepted. We needed the extra hands, and we had the food (we'd set up some cages in the basement to catch... I don't want to know, and I don't ask Bruno what it is) to feed her... And a spare bed from Pavle. She immediately began to help with the water. I began to go out at nights. Bruno was a big guy, but nowadays, big simply means a bigger target.
Day 19:
I began to get a collection of contacts with whom I could bargain. We didn't ask names and we didn't need to. I found a talent for bargaining, and we began to more precisely fix up our house. I also began to look around these houses, and take whatever junk was around. They wouldn't need it.
Day 20:
I came back from bargaining to find that Cveta was bleeding heavily, and that we had been raided. Bruno managed to protect our food, but they simply went for the vulnerable middle-aged women. We fed her, and began to make her rest. A part of me hated her for the burden we now faced, and quietly wished she may die in the night. I once sat in her room and wept for my lost humanity. She stroked my hair. I vowed I would rob a hospital to save her.
Day 22:
Cveta was beginning to circle the drain, and even her upbeat talks were becoming weak. Me and Bruno faced losing the heart of our morale and another member in less than two weeks. Another teacher, hearing of her plight, came to stay with us. I quickly greeted him (Anton, apparently), and then left the house. I knew what I had to do for her.
The hospital has been completely destroyed. I walked in, offering to help find medicine. And I found it in the office of the doctor. Bandages and medicine, enough to save Cveta. But if I take them, patients will die.
Day 23:
I bandaged Cveta. Today was quiet. No one wanted to ask where I found such clean materials. Everyone already knew. Bruno gave me a respectful nod and a warm meal. The teachers didn't even look at me.
Day 25:
I found more bandages. The husband asked me not to take them. I had a shovel in my hand but didn't need to use it. I didn't meet his wife's eyes as I took them out of her bedroom and walked out of the house. Cveta is healing, but will not even look at me.
Day 27:
I do not deserve to live.
Day 33:
Bruno had carried me to bed at some point, and fed me. Cveta would sit in silence with me. Anton left books at my bedside table, and cups of coffee. I do not deserve them.
Day 34:
I am a burden.
Day 36:
I decided to help them again. If I can steal from the helpless, I can steal from anyone. I began to steal from a couple as they spoke with their son, while I walked in their basement taking their food.
I would walk into their house, take their medicine and food, and then trade it back, sympathetically offering them a better deal to help with the constant thievery they suffered.
The group didn't know; they didn't need to know. Morale didn't suffer. After the couple, no one care. I stole a guitar from someone's basement, and Anton fixed it up. Only I can play it though. I give little performances for the group. We are... for a while, happy.
Day 38:
Winter has come. Anton built another heater. This house is now too hot, because Cveta is constantly cold. Bruno uses snow to make water, because everything has frozen. Cigarettes and alcohol have become rare, yet we continue to produce them. Bruno is fine with a few per day, the rest we trade for food and medicine, everything else we find or steal. And by we, I mean me. The teachers are too kind and Bruno is... well, he's a big lad.
Day 41:
The militia have asked me if my neighbours have been stealing. As they have been constantly giving us food, probably. However, they have saved us a few times, and Anton had stayed with them while the husband was sick and bandits were circling. Bruno wanted the reward, but I denied it. I then informed Bruno to keep in line and make me some food.
Day 45:
The war has ended. The teachers thanked us. Bruno went to find his friend. I am sitting here, playing this guitar and writing this book. I wonder if the owner of the house will come and find me? Find my dairy? My story?

Let me first say that I am an X series fan. I am not a veteran of the series, since I just started playing X3 Albion Prelude less than a year ago (it being my first X game). I absolutely love the lore of the series and the core gameplay mechanics. This would have been a perfect addition to the series if it had just did the following simple things:
1) Add a few more graphics effects to X3AP, like SSAO and the new anti-aliasing techniques such as FXAA and MLAA.
2) Add good tutorials for the X3AP UI. (Don't make a silly radial UI; it makes the same quantity of data harder to read, makes complex functions harder to access by requiring the player to dig through menus, etc.)
3) Improve AI decision-making
4) Add in-game access to an extremely detailed encyclopedia about everything, especially the history of the Albion System and information about weapon systems and ships. This exists in X Rebirth, but much of the potential combat depth of X3AP is missing in X Rebirth.
5) Build the rest of the game around it.
Admittedly, it would have run worse and not looked at good as X Rebirth does now, but at least the gameplay would have been better.
The biggest reason that this game is so buggy and broken is that Egosoft developed an entirely new game engine. That's right, this is NOT running on an older CryEngine. They spent a huge chunk of their development costs on creating an entirely new engine for the sake of graphics. This game will stand as a testament against the philosophy that graphics are the primary contributor to the quality of a game.
Final Notes: In X3AP, you could captain or pilot every ship in the game - including capital ships - yourself. You could create fleets of numerous types of ships all supporting each other in various ways, according to your specifications. For instance, you could purchase a carrier and dock dozens of fighters to it. If the fighters needed to rearm with missiles, you could stock the carrier with missiles. You could outfit one destroyer to support your fighter wing with anti-fighter and anti-frigate capabilities, or the destroyer might attack other destroyers while protecting a missile frigate (probably piloted by the player) that barrages fighters and frigates with swarm missiles and capital ships with torpedoes.
In X Rebirth, the tatical options have been limited for the sake of simplicity, rather than explained. Honestly, why couldn't they just make in-game tutorial videos for all the already-existing, complex functions? Change and improvement are often two different things.
Do not buy this game, even if it's on sale for five dollars, unless it's drastically patched.

Large battles are not a massive click fest and you do not have to micromanage the hell out of everything like Total War or Starcraft, and the wait times for building,resource gathering, researching ect. are miniscule compared to stuff like early game Civ. Sins of a Solar Empire is a blast to play with your friends or even on your own. It occupies the same niche in my gaming heart as Civilization 5 and Rise of Nations. All three games are about capturing territory, and exerting your cultural and military might to uproot the locals, eventually to dominate (in Sins' case) the universe.
The game is excellent on several levels:
-A huge variety of levels makes for a truly unique play experience every time.
-Thoughtful expansions add a lot of replay value.
-The speed of game elements can be customized individually. Want fast income but slow ship movement? Great. Want lightning quick income but sluggish research? Can be done. This means you can set the game to what you're comfortable with and really enjoy it.
-It's just really fun.
Where it doesn't excel:
-I don't like how hard it is on my mouse scroll wheel. Because of the huge scope of the game (multiple planets, multiple galaxies) I find it can be a lot of in and out.
-Normal enemies can be easily defeated by paying off pirates. I feel like this system can be tweaked a bit.
-Games can take a long time to finish (good or bad depending on your perspective).
-If you don't engage in combat relatively quickly, it can get to a point where you will hit total deadlock with your computer foes.
-If you lose your connection during a multiplayer game, you can't get back in. This is a huge pain when playing with friends.
Overall a really fun RTS with lots of replay value, balanced teams. 8.5/10

This is the third game in the Wolfenstein FPS series and fifth overall, released in 2001 and still playable even today, especially when compared with its preceding titles. (Not that they were bad, but they are considerably more dated.) Notably, it was developed by Gray Matter Studios, the same people behind Call of Duty's expansion pack United Offensive, with help from Nerve Software. iD only published it.
You play as Agent B.J. Blazkowicz, allied saboteur/spy/killing machine sent behind Nazi lines in World War II to...spy on the Nazis, specifically their paranormal activities. Unfortunately, you and your fellow agent-in-arms are captured and sent to the ubiquitous Castle Wolfenstein, where you must make your escape from the retrofitted dungeon.
The gameplay consists of making your way through levels and fulfilling objectives in any available manner you see fit - there's little hand-holding here. The levels are designed well and realistically, and even when they are linear it does a good job of convincing you otherwise, like in Half-Life.
Obviously there are Nazis in your way, and the number of weapons you get to choose from to kill them grow in accordance with the types you'll face. RTCW starts out akin to Call of Duty: World at War, but starts to resemble something more like that game's zombie mode pretty quickly and gets hairier from there.
The gunplay is great. Most of your weapons are generally useful, and you'll go from blasting troopers with a pilfered MP40 to silencing enemies with a silenced Sten that is both accurate and great fun to use, to roasting all manner of monsters with flamethrowers, Panzerschrecks and other big guns.
Interactivity isn't something you might expect from a game like this, but there's a good amount of it here. If an enemy sets off an alarm, you are capable of switching it off or simply destroying it to silence the alarm. You have a dedicated kick button, which lets you kick down doors and destroy objects with your mighty boot such as pictures of Hitler. Sometimes you must do things like destroying walls to continue. There are also secrets to be found in the levels, containing health, ammunition and sometimes Nazi treasure, akin to Wolf3D. The treasure does nothing but increase your treasure counter at the end-of-level score screen, but it's nice to grab it anyway.
There are two stealth levels that are nice ideas in theory but can prove frustrating and sometimes nonsensical in practice. Expect them to take a few tries, and don't be afraid to save. There are also ways to take stealthy approaches to the other missions, which are much more enjoyable.
The game has 3 difficulty settings, which are basically akin to the three hardest from Wolfenstein 3-D, the easiest setting from that game being removed. Playing on the middle difficulty, by the time you're nearing the end of the game it will prove rather challenging, with health and armor (especially armor) in short supply and a good amount of tough enemies...and those are just the regular mooks. There is no shame in quicksaving at certain points, or really ever but that's another matter. The AI is generally good, but not perfect (elite troops barrel rolling into walls come to mind), and while the final boss has the distiction of being easier than the levels preceding it you still need to watch yourself.
I have not played the multiplayer, but as far as I know it still has a relatively small amount of players. It primarily revolves around Axis players defending installations from Allied attackers, and is class-based. There is also a free multiplayer-only title out there called Enemy Territory that contains more features.
Overall I'd place RTCW as a slightly below-average length game, but with how atmospheric and difficult it can be you'll likely spend a decent chunk of time during your first playthrough.
RTCW runs off the Quake III Arena engine, which means fast default movement speeds and strafejumping when the levels permit it, but you can change it to a slower walk if you wish for a more realistic/difficult game. I'm sure this accounts for the graphics, as well, because when you max it out (and it's easy to do), the game looks very good, especially for a 2001 title! There is a
to increase resolution sizes beyond 1028x760 and enable widescreen, but I personally couldn't get it to work and I didn't feel a need for it.
The plot, as befitting a Wolfenstein game of this period in the series, revolves around sci-fi/occult Nazi meddling with a bit of camp and a portion of horror. It can get outlandish at times, but the atmosphere the game presents only serves to complement it. If you're at all interested in secret Nazi stuff and alternate history, or blowing up secret Nazi stuff - especially with their own
- you'll probably like it.
Tony Jay is a voice actor here, and he's good as usual. That's worth quite a bit, at least.
While the game is good, I'm not sure about the Elite Guards. They're an all-woman enemy force, and while it's nice to see women taking action-oriented roles I could do without them wearing revealing outfits that I'm not sure are entirely practical. They serve as challenging enemies at least, but that's about it.
For me that's the best stealth game.

The developers sense of achievement from people buying the game, based on an impressive marketing Wonder is important, however I believe the gamers experience should come first.

+ A true open-world Metroidvania with an incredible feeling of freedom regarding how you choose to explore the world.

+ A fascinating story.

- Some achievements are beyond the reach of standard human beings.
An absolute masterpiece. Original, unique, fascinating, the game will invite you to dive deeper and deeper into the ruins of Hallownest, a fallen underground Kingdoms full of dark secrets and strange enemies. The atmosphere is beautiful and profound, and the gameplay is top-notch. Each fight is enjoyable as such and the exploration feeling is incredible. The price tag is more than honest, and the game is a bargain even out of sale.
I couldn't recommend a game more.
Now let's discuss some of the main issues that might help you to decide whether or not this is a game for you!
Many people have pointed out the high amount of backtracking. They are right to do so, even though, the game being a Metroidvania, backtracking is encoded in the DNA of the genre. Backtracking is an issue insofar some bosses are located in an area which takes time and effort to reach (it might because of a high number of enemies, because of hard platforming elements, or just because of the distance). Given the amount of times you need to restart some boss fights so as to learn the attack patterns and adjust your strategy, this can indeed be an issue.
However, if you explore thoroughly enough your surroundings, you might find a lot of secret passways which will allow you to reach bosses more easily. This is not always true, but very often, exploration is much rewarded. Also, if a boss is to hard to beat, it might be because you need to grow stronger. Some bosses become ridiculously easy once you have upgraded enough your abilities.
It is also true that both checkpoints and transport stations are far-between, and this might be annoying. There is a total of ten or eleven "teleporters" in the whole map. It might seem a lot, but the map is truly immense, so really it's a few. One may argue in this regard that the game has been exactly designed that way. There is a real "rogue-like" feel in the game, and sometimes you wander for a very long time in dark mazes surrounded by dangerous foes, trying to get as far as possible. Adding teleporters and checkpoints would only betray the overall game feel of the game.
In the end, backtracking is an issue only if you don't like the game too much. The graphics are so beautiful, the fights so well-done, that I never minded go through an area I already visited. Each time you can find new secrets and, even if you are just bored, you can race through the area without trouble. One should also point out that, very often, you open new passways once you have gone through some harder than usual platform bit, so that the more you explore, the faster you can get from one location to another.
The game IS difficult. But, thanks to the 'healing' system, you are allowed to make mistakes, as long as you can repair them. You have a 'soul' reservoir which fills up any time you strike a foe. This soul reservoir can be used to heal yourself (and perform a few attack spells, but the swordfight is to me much more interesting). There is no instakill strikes from enemies, so if you fail to dodge one strike, it's fine. What matters is that you must be able to dodge in average, so that you must pattern all the dodging patterns. Also, some enemies can be hard to beat and, once you have understood how they work, you can crush them without loosing one single hitpoint. This is always a satisfying feeling.
There are, overall, two kinds of difficulty. The first kind is the rogue-like type of difficulty that I mentioned earlier. You need sometimes to survive for a very long time in a very inhospitable environment, in which you don't know when you will be able to rest, to restore your health, to find a checkpoint -these three or one and the same thing-, or simply to leave the location. There are some cheap peak of difficulties when, once you are about to find a checkpoint (indicated by some rusted panels), there is suddenly a very hard obstacle on your way. If you were desperate to rest, then it will certainly be your doom. Fortunately, it doesn't happen very often.
The second kind of difficulty are the boss fights. Some of them are very hard. They require you to stay focus for a very long time so as to correctly dodge all the different attack patterns and strike when the opportunity presents itself. So be warned. A good thing is that you can tweak yourself with charms which are little bonuses, that you can reconfigure entirely at each checkpoint. This allows you to adapt your strategy, or to give you an edge according to your own playstyle. Another good thing is that, apart from that Hornet fight (see below), there is almost no bossfight which you cannot try later once you would have grown stronger. So, you can't really get stuck in the game.
Overall, the most difficult part of the game is the beginning: your weapon is weak, so that each foe is its own little challenge, you have very few hitpoints, and you don't know yet how the game actually works. The first serious boss, Hornet, took me literally fifty trials. People will tell you it's an easy fight, and surely it is, but not when you have only played for three/four hours and you don't know yet how the game works; plus, you cannot dodge. The game truly starts and unfolds after this fight.
So, be strong! Life in Hallownest can be harsh, but a true Knight never renounces.

LotR: War in the North is an underrated gem. I put off playing it for a long time, as I'd heard very average things that told me the game wasn't worth it. How I wish I hadn't listened, because I had an absolute blast.
You play as three characters: Eradan, a Ranger of the North; Andriel, an Elven Loremaster of Rivendell; and Farin, a Dwarven Champion of Erebor. Their story takes place parallel to the Lord of the Rings trilogy, and ties in nicely as you battle to prevent Sauron's dominion over the North while the Fellowship trek South-East to Mordor. Although none of the new characters are particularly interesting, and the story isn't particularly gripping, together they serve as an excellent excuse to spend 14 hours hacking and slashing through hoards of goblins, orcs, spiders, trolls, undead, and the Men of Carn Dûm.
Combat is pure hack and slash, and makes up just about the entire game. It plays well with your standard light and heavy attacks, as well as the abilities to block, roll, fire a ranged weapon and learn and upgrade a number of different attacks and spells. Though fighting can be monotonous when you're faced with dozens of weak enemies, leaving you with nothing to do but repeat a single attack, it really shines when you're up against large, tough foes that force you to carefully watch their movements and react accordingly. I only wish there'd been combo attacks similar to Return of the King.
Between slicing and dicing Sauron's minions, you spend time recuperating in areas like Bree or Rivendell, where you'll repair your armor and weapons and have the opportunity to spend time conversing with characters like Elrond, Bilbo, Gloin, Arwen, Gandalf, and best of all, Barliman Butterbur. There's also a hobbit in Bree who'll challenge you to a game of riddles. If you love Middle-earth as much as I do, you'll get a lot out of engaging with these characters. If you don't care and are just there to kill stuff, skip through all the conversations to receive side quests.
The downside to this game is that it's designed to be played cooperatively with two other people. I tried to get a friend in with me, but both of us disconnected constantly, so we gave up and I played with AI partners. They did their job fairly well at the beginning, but grew progressively worse over the course of the game. I didn't have a problem with this, for the most part, as they provided a good distraction while I got to do all the killing, and Andriel is good at knowing when to cast a healing spell, but there were times when I'd find them around a corner, aiming ranged weapons at a wall, and when enemies got really tough, they were pretty useless. Then there was the time when one of them disappeared completely, forcing a checkpoint reload after a brutal battle. That wasn't cool.
AI parters also won't reveal secrets, which can only be found with specific characters, and since you can only swap between characters every so often when loading into a new area, you're gonna miss a lot of hidden loot, but it doesn't really matter. I was also confused at first as to how the AI level up and equip items, as when I switched back to one of them after a few hours, I saw that they were still level 1, but it's all taken care of independently when you're not in control of them.
Long story short, this is an excellent game, but if you're after anything more than walking from area to area, slaying orc after orc, you're gonna grow bored quickly. Fans of Tolkein's work will get more out of this than anyone else, as it offers the opportunity to play through different regions of Middle-earth and interact with its characters while referencing the ongoing events surrounding the Fellowship.
And lasty, I've got to give props to the writers for including a section of dialogue with Gandalf in which he explains why the eagles can't simply fly everyone straight to Mordor. I'm always hearing that stupid argument, and it was fantastic to finally see it addressed. You go, Gandalf.

If you like J-RPG’s, you must have this. The Last Remnant was one of the first genre releases by Square Enix back then in the early days of the X-Box 360 and long before Final Fantasy XIII got criticised for its linearity and lack of freedom, this game remembered the classics strengths of the genre and despite some of the typical flaws will always be one of my all-time favorites.
The story uses the most common of tropes, when teenage hero Rush starts on a journey to save his kidnapped sister and stumbles into a larger narrative about the war of nations and ultimately the fate of the world. Despite the characters following archetypes we all have seen before in similar games, they are all fleshed out enough to be relatable. You will not just handle a small party of 3-4 heroes, but a small army of up to 18 characters. These can be recruited out of a much larger pool during the course of the adventure and lots of them are rewards for optional side quests or hidden missions.
This is where the main fun lies, building and optimizing your army, you will have to arrange them into different groups, that will act as unit on the battlefield. That means a lot of actual gameplay happens in the menus before you actually engage an enemy. If you are fond of this kind of fumbling, you will love this game, if you however prefer a more action oriented approach, this might be frustrating. The battles themselves won’t give you too specific control over your team’s actions, but are still full of important decisions based on relative positioning and timing. Downside is, when your army is fully staffed everyone’s attack will be displayed individually, dragging even random encounters quite a bit (at least 1 minute per fight).
Worth mentioning is, that you probably want to use a gamepad (ideally the X-box 360 controller) since the mouse keyboard optimization is horrible. You will also run into some brick walls along the way, where you will need to think carefully on how to approach. Specifically there is a very challenging sequence of 3 consecutive boss battles in the middle of the game, that you can get trapped in between. But again all this will shake things up and you have to do some work in the menus, re-shuffle your unions, re-align your formations and things might look brighter the next try.
The general freedom between story progress and rewarding exploration will keep you playing for a long time if can muster the patience for the drawn out random encounters and the time spend in menus. The overall world structure, character design and storytelling is close to Final Fantasy XII while the battle system draws more from Final Fantasy Tactics. Not the worst references and therefore a must pay for any JRPG fan.
Pros:
- deep tactical combat
- large amount of optional content
- lovable characters
- strong story with a great villain
Cons:
- uneven difficulty curve
- long duration of random encounters
Edit: I want to clarify one point that I see frequently brought up in negative reviews. Yes, the finer mechanics of leveling are not explained well in game and external lecture is recommended, but if you normally play, follow the story and do side quests when they become available, you will encounter a smooth difficult curve. However, if you want to min-max and if you want to brute force encounters (that normally would scale) by keeping enemies weak (at a low Battle Rank) while your party is high, then you need to avoid fighting as much as possible early on. So yes, getting the most powerful party possible can be achieved by manipulating the systems and you need to read-up the internet to know how. But again for regular play this is not necessary, the game wants you to overcome difficult encounters by optimizing your tactic and setup, which works perfectly fine.

I have been looking forward to this remaster of one of my all time favorites.
Unfortunately, there are quite a few issues on a very basic compatibility level even after the recent patch.
Further, the remaster introduced its own interpretation of the original's art direction, which is deviating quite a bit from the original.
While it managed to implement high-res textures quite successfully, the added detail to the setting such as star- and jellyfish sometimes looks out of place to me and has a kind of a hit-and-miss result atmospherewise.
While comparing the opening scene side by side, I also noticed that the fire effects right after the crash landing aren't working as well as in the original, which is especially noticable when the fire spreads on the left side of the screen. Also, water effects don't seem to work properly or haven't been implemented sufficiently, e.g. when walking through water-"curtains" in rapture. These kinds of effects were a huge part of the immersive experience of the original and seeing them missing in the remaster kind of ruins the experience for me.
All of the above plus current issues regarding game stability and missing settings caused me to stick to the original, which is still looking surprisingly fresh due to its fantastic art direction.

NOT A HERO is the kind of game that you feel should be a lot more popular than it is. The action is great and so is the humor. It keeps track of various stats for each level and the things that Bunnylord tells you are determined by a sort of Mad Libs system, so you have multiple reasons to replay levels.
My objections are few, but I think that the player can come to terms with them and still find the game to be incredibly enjoyable. Objection #1 is that the 3 out of 4 secret levels (the 4th secret level is meant to be a joke that's next to impossible NOT to beat) that the game keeps stats for are not acknowledged in the order that they are discovered in. To elaborate, each of the 3 districts has 1 secret level that you can view stats for, but the 1st district's secret level stats are shown as "SECRET 3", the 2nd district's secret level stats are shown as "SECRET 1" and the 3rd district's secret level stats are shown as "SECRET 2". Objection #2 is that it seems that each character that you can play as will not necessarily be able to complete all 3 extra objectives for certain levels. Objection #3 is that it can be very difficult to understand the spoken dialogue due to the thick British accents and terminology. The 4th and final objection is that Xbox One will be getting a Super Snazzy Edition of this game with 3 extra levels where you can play as Bunnylord, but it doesn't seem like they'll be offering the same courtesy to PC users.
As I said, I believe that once you come to terms with these objections, then you can truly enjoy this game. Do I recommend this game? Well, I see no "Hell, yeah!" button to press, so I'm going to have to settle for "Yes". You'll feel like a badass as you off bad guys and then laugh that newly-acquired badass off at its humor. This game deserves an entire friggin' FRANCHISE! Spread the awesome word of Bunnylord!

Bioshock Remastered has had a rough time, so far. When it launched it was a pretty mediocre port job, to the point that it was arguably worse than the original game from what I hear. It's since been patched, but it's still got a bit of the plasmid blues. The graphics are upgraded, but from what I've been able to tell they've also been downgraded in some ways, primarily in the realm of water, fire, and other environmental effects. The audio mixing also seems to be suffering a bit. These aren't things that I noticed while playing, though; if you've never played Bioshock or just haven't played it in a long time, you probably won't ever notice. What you will notice, however, is that the game has a strong tendency to crash when doing anything menu-based, and the game loves to shuffle your plasmids and even weapons when you upgrade them, usually forcing you to edit the keybinds simply to get your plasmids to work with the right keys.
I'm sure there are also other issues that I didn't personally experience, but overall it's still Bioshock, and even though Remastered still isn't perfect it's at least now a safer bet than getting the old original to work with the same functionality. I'm not enough of an authority on Bioshock to say which version you should play if it's your first time, but this version is at least playable now, so there's that.

I was a a late adopter to the last version of this game, Bloodline Champions (BLC), and thoroughly enjoyed it while it lasted. The mechanics of Battlerite are basically identical, with an array of playable hero characters and all abilities being skillshots. The maps are markedly different though. Sadly the community is small and is still shrinking. I will continue to play, support, and evangelize about this game because it deserves much more attention than it has. Gameplay-wise it is solid and the format is fun both for short bursts and playing for hours. No pay-to-win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t here either!
I was generously gifted a 'Lite' key for this game from a friend so I didn't have to pay anything. I am considering upgrading to the full edition to support the developers and unlock all current and future characters. EDIT: I've since purchased the full game and am fully confident in my purchase. I have played most of the characters in the game; I think it is valuable to be able to use them to gather intelligence and understand matchups. There are characters I have unlocked since buying the game that I wouldn't have otherwise attained through the grind.
Some criticisms of the game:
- Queueing times can be longer depending on your region. I don't have too much trouble in 2v2 on the west coast but YMMV. The game has more players in EU apparently.
- Maps are not very different from each other. You don't have to change your strategy at all in the different maps; the prevailing strategy is to control the center where the orb spawns which is the same in every map. There is a center area, there are some walls arranged around the center area. True of every map.
- Like any competitive game, the players can be toxic but I have found this to be less of an issue than in much more popular games e.g. Dota, CS, Siege, OW. It remains to be see how this will change when the game goes F2P and inevitably gains more players. The community being small, you end up running into the same people, often teaming up with and battling against the same people so you kind of find kindred spirits occasionally.
- For better or worse, voice chat is not a native feature of this game (unlike BLC) but is most likely forthcoming. There is an active Discord server for this game featuring players who are willing to party up on VOIP and queue into competitive together.
If anyone who purchases this game is looking for someone to play with, feel free to contact me.

The Stanley Parable is a first person exploration game made by Galactic Cafe and released on October 17, 2013. It is based off a pre-exisiting Source mod of the same name, where a man named Stanley has a boring job, and finds one day that all his collegues are missing, and goes to find them. Since this review will be spoiling the game, I will say that this game is a good time waster for 3 or 4 hours, and maybe even more (like me.) Whether or not that is worth 15 dollars is entirely based off whether or not you like 4th wall breaking humor. I will be going over the story, graphics, sound, and gameplay.
Story:
As stated above, there is a man named Stanley who works at an office building, and he eventually finds that all his co-workers are no longer in the building. This prompts him to go out and search for them through the sprawling office. This game is entirely based off 4th wall breaking humor, and that is presented by The Narrator. Voiced by the imaculately spoken Kevin Brighting, he basically tells you what you should be doing, and whether or not you do what you are told is completely up to you. This results in there being multiple paths, kind of like a choose-your-own-adventure book, except it can do so much more than just a book. The game's selling point is it's multiple endings, which are mostly funny, and provide, in the narrator's words, "insightful and witty commentary on the nature of video games, and structural narritive tropes," my favorite of which being the "Not Stanley Ending." This game is just downright hillarious at points. If you enjoy 4th wall breaking writing in your games, you will love this game.
Presentation:
If you played the original Source mod Stanley Parable, then you would know how... stock the game looked. Blocky, reused assets from Half Life 2, and kind of boring where it should be very interesting and large scale. The remake though, looks very clean. It is still very blocky, but in a refined sort of way, and it also has new textures made specifically for the game. The mind control facility especially looks very large and bright, giving it a unique look to anything else in the game, or even any other game.
Sound:
The few tracks found in the game are very well used. Anyone who has played the game can sing you the entire adventure line theme, or the disco secret, or even the elevator which can appear randomly plays the bossa nova elevator music, which is a very fitting song, and you can hear The Narrator in the background humming along to it. The music that lets itself be good is really good. The other music is more situational, like the music in the insane ending, or the true ending. That's not to say it's bad. It is actually very good, but it's not something I would listen to on it's own.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very dry. You get six forms of input, WASD, left mouse or E for interaction, and mouse for looking around.  This is what some would call a "Walking Simulator." While I'm not very fond of the term, I can definitely see where they are coming from. It really isn't what the game excells at, which is the comedy and the story.
The Stanley Parable is a wonderfully hillarous game that I come back to time and time again to play a few endings and have a good laugh. There is also a demo for this game, and without spoiling anything, it does a very good job at showing what the game is all about without showing one bit of gameplay from the actual game. The writer of this game, Davey Wreden, also went on to write The Beginner's Guide, which is a very different game to The Stanley Parable, in that it focuses more on being sad, rather than getting a laugh out of the player. I recommend this game to any fan of video games as a visual art form.

This War of Mine is a fantastic survival sim with rogue-like elements and a moderate difficulty curve.  What makes the game great is the overall atmosphere.  It is very bleak and depressing in a thought provoking way and it really draws you into the setting.  Unlike in most games, the moral choices you will be making here have real consequences to them, and you may find yourself making morally questionable decisions that make you (and your survivors) feel guilty.
The rogue-like elements include a significant amount of RNG that keep the experience fresh when playing through a handful of times after your previous attempts end poorly.  You should expect to lose your entire group of survivors a few times while you are getting a hang of the game, but the process of figuring things out is a rewarding one as you manage to keep your survivors in good health longer.  Sometimes the RNG can cause uneven difficulty, however, as starting in the middle of a cold spell or without any characters with large backpacks can make the game significantly harder.
The gameplay is split into day and night cycles.  During the day you use what resources you have gathered to feed your survivors and craft things that will keep them alive and in good spirits.  During the night you can send one survivor out to scavenge from a variety of places utilizing side scrolling stealth/combat gameplay that is fairly barebones but is well polished with no bugs or glitches that I encountered.  The entire game is very well done and it would be nice if this level of polish was standard in the industry instead of an unexpected surprise.

Note that the game is still being worked on, so any negatives that I mention could very well be remedied in the near-to-distant future.
The point of the game is to show you the other side of all the war games that are so popular these days. You've almost surely been a soldier, invading enemy territory and mowing down waves of 'bad guys,' but I personally have yet to see another game that lets you get a glimpse of the effects of war on the people living in the area where it happens. This game does that, and very well. You have to decide what you're willing to direct your survivors to do to keep on living, whether you'd rather let them starve than stroll into a defenseless elderly couples' home and raid their refridgerator and leave them with nothing, or risk sneaking into a military compound to grab what you can and (attempt) to sneak out in one piece. It's very difficult and it should be, in both the decisions you have to make and the game in and of itself.
It is depressing. You get to know the characters you control better throughout the game by reading their war journals, you slowly learn bits of their history and personality, some of them you may like, others may seem to be generally bad people, but it's your job to keep them alive. If the game ends with the deaths of all of your survivors, you're treated to something reminiscient of an obituary; did their parents learn about their death and visit their grave? Did anyone ever hear about the relative they were so worried about? Etcetera.
It does a fantastic job at what it sets out to do.
On the downside, some more variety in the game itself and the areas you visit would be a huge plus and greatly increase replayability. I don't know if it's in the works, but randomly generated characters with unique backstories, along with the locations that become available, would be great. As it is now, after playing for a certain amount of time you'll see and become familiar with most of the survivors that it's possible to start with or recruit.
Another welcome addition (to me) would be the introduction of a couple different game modes. As it stands now, your goal is to survive until the war comes to an end. I would like to see an endurance mode, where at no point will the war end, and you get a score based on how long you manage to keep at least one survivor going. This could feasibly go on for as long as you wanted if you were skilled enough, with old cleared out buildings disappearing after enough time without being visited and being replaced by newly generated ones.
All in all it is absolutely a solid game in the state it's in now, and I'm excited to see any improvements they make, regardless of whether or not they're any of the ones I mentioned here. It makes you think, and it does something that a lot of games can't quite hope to do- it can make you regret the actions you take to survive, if you really let yourself get immersed in the game world and think of the fact that real people have lived, -are- living, in conditions like this. If you're a fan of any kind of simulation, you would be doing yourself a disservice not to try this at some point.

This is a 2D point and click survival game that asks some tough questions not unlike Papers, Please. I highly recommend This War of Mine, especially if you liked Papers, Please.

As a fan of the Sci-Fi genre I love everything that involves massive starship battles, and Sins of a Solar Empire have always delivered on that front, Rebellion brings diffrant factions to the table, it splits the three main factions into six factions, one loyal and one radical faction. The gameplay is much like in the old games, a real time strategy where the goal is to fight it out among the diffrant maps and planets. the maps are usally split up into a number of solar systems, on some maps they are connected by wormholes or you can reach each of the solar systems by traveling by your local Star. each solar system consist of a number off planets that you can colonise, some reqiure a bit of research to anable them to be colonised, while astroid belts can't be colonised at all.
Each planet ( depending on the kind of planet, and the ammount of research made) will allow you to produce a number of buildings, such as two kinds of tech labs, one to research defensive and offensive tech for your empire, while the other lab focuses on the economic and diplomatic side of your empire, this will allow for diffrant strategies and a bit on empire planning. then you have the standard Ship factories, one will produce small to medium ships while the other one will construct your capital ships, the core of any armada. These Ships will need research to unlock while the capital ships will require you to research fleet logistics, a sort of supply system were every level of research will unlock more ship supplies and more captains for your capital ships. After these two we have the largest ship your faction can construct, these are faction and race specified, meaning that every faction have their own "Titan" as they are called, while the capitalships and lesser ships are race based. These titans require lots of research and will take quite some time to construct, that said, these ships will more then often decide the outcome of any battle. There is also the possiblity to construct "Trade ports", "media huts" and "refineries" to generate credits or influense the planets around your solar system and generate extra amounts of crystal and metal. Of course the game also allow you to bunker up your planets with large amounts of diffrant defences, all from large Starports, Mines, turrets, Warp disrupters and a special race super weapon.
Now moving on to resurses, there are three resurses that are used in the game, Credits that are generated from your planets and ammount of people you have living on the actuall planets, then you have crystals and metal, these two will require you to construct asteroid mines where ever you might find them, some planets might only contain crystal while others only contain Metal so deciding what planet to colonise is again quite important.
The game also futures a bit of rouge covert bits, were you can send pirates ( that said, this is a game optiuon that can be turned off before the start of the game) to harrass the planets of your enemy, these will grow in strenght over time and can be quite hard to take out early in the game because of the ammount of defences around their base. There is also a black market where you can trade crystal and metal for credits and vice verse, this works with supply and demand and some times the market for metal can crash because of the ammount of people trying to sell their large amount of metal for a bit of credits.
The factions in the game are just as in the old games TEC, Advent and the Vasari Empire. These are then spilt up into two diffrant factions within the Race, each of them have their special Titan and each also have special powers that the other faction and race can't research. For example the Vasari loyalists can research a special upgrade so that their warp gates ( that allow them to move around to other warp gates constructed around the solar system) can summon the Vasari dark fleet that will assist the defence of their planet.
The game is to me a balanced strategy game that in my opinion futures a large amount of content, that said, this game is made for multiplayer as the campaign is non existing. That said this game is at its best when you can gather a group of friends and just battle it out across a large space battlefield. I give it a 10/10 for a very polished and fun strategy game and one of the best space real time strategy games on the market.

In a word, Hollow Knight can be described as unintuitive. Unintuitive mechanics, unintuitive map design, unintuitive progression all make for an unintuitive game.
There are a sleu of frustrating features and mechanics in Hollow Knight, but one that most immediately comes to mind is the game's failure to provide the player with a map upon entering a new area. It's astoundingly bad, and it's something you won't realize is so bad until you actually try playing the game without one. Instead of just giving the player a map, you have to hunt down someone named Cornelius who is just stuck somewhere randomly in the zone. It's incredibly easy to just pass him, seeing as how each zone has an incredible amount of branching, and if you do, you are guaranteed to get lost. If you get lucky and find him, he still doesn't give you the map, you actually have to fork over a pretty sizeable amount of your money (called Geos) in order to get the map. If you can't afford it (at some point, you most likely won't be able to), you're completely out of luck. You're going to have to farm Geos from enemies until you get enough to actually get the map, which is incredibly annoying and completely halts gameplay.
Mechanically, exploration is totally inane and wildly inconsistent. When you explore a new part of an area, it doesn't update your map straight away. In order to actually get the map to update, you need to find a bench, which functions as a sort of rest area, which will update your map, except for the times when it doesn't. There are some parts of the map that just don't get revealed. This is an incredibly annoying and completely unjustifiable approach to exploration, and you have to put up with this while exploring the zone except for when the map magically updates on its own sometimes.
There's been a tendency in the world of game development to construct a mechanically full and complete game, and then strip said mechanics away to be unlocked later on. This is passed off as progression, and it's a lazy development tactic. Hollow Knight suffers tremendously because so many fundamentals for a good platformer aren't introduced until later in the game. Hollow Knight begins as an incredibly barebones platformer where you can only jump, and then slowly introduces more and more platformer mechanics. Want to double jump? You need to unlock that. Want to dash? You need to unlock that. Want to wall jump? That's also an unlock. This is just plain bad game design.
So combine bad exploration mechanics with a failure to introduce all fundamental platforming mechanics and you end up with one of the most painfully tedious and headache-inducing spans of backtracking in a game to date. I played three hours of this game and at least 75% of my time was spent backtracking. When you enter a new part of an area, you will run into occasions where progression is impossible without having unlocked one of the platforming abilities mentioned above. The vast majority of the time, you won't receive credit for having explored the room, meaning that at any given time, there are at least ten places strewn out all across the map that remain unexplored, and you very frequently will end up having to visit each unexplored area on the map again at least once to confirm that it is, in fact, not the place you need to go in order to progress through the game, since the developers offered absolutely no insight at all as to where you should be at any given time. The time I wasted backtracking in this game to find out where I needed to go to progress made for what is probably my worst gaming experience to date.
All this is really just scratching the surface of how unintuitive this game is, but it's enough to tell you that you should save yourself a headache and avoid playing Hollow Knight entirely. Not even the beautiful art, wondrous soundtrack, and thoughtful worldbuilding and creative characters could provide a saving grace under the burden of gameplay flaws with which this game struggles.
(It's also worth mentioning that Hollow Knight is very frequently seen as difficult, which is just something I can't understand. If you feel like this is a selling point to the game, dismiss it. After about two or three hits, you're given the ability to heal for a full heart of damage. If you can land at least three hits without getting hurt, you are literally invulnerable. The most difficult part about this game is trying to figure out where you're supposed to go.)

Do you enjoy turning creatures sideways? You'll love this game. Because of the very limited card pool, the game skews heavily toward aggro decks. In fact, aggro is the only win condition available in this game. Unlike in previous DotP (Duel of the Planeswalker) games, every deck here feels like variation on aggro. There's no lifegain deck, there's no mill deck, no janky ramp deck, no full on control deck, no token swarm deck, no... anything. Everything just feels the same. And boring.
Currently the game is limited to cards from Origins. Although, not all of Origins is there. They've decided to cut some cards out. A lot of cards in fact. About 100 cards are missing from the Origins set. Those cards were replaced with cards from other sets. Most of the cards they cut were perfectly playable cards like Clash of Wills, Nivix Barrier, and Touch of Moonglove. It baffles me why they would remove them. I can understand Infinite Obliteration and Day's Undoing, one for technical reasons and the other because of how annoying it would be, but perfectly playable cards? I'm stumped.
Unlocking cards is tedious. There's a limit of 400g per day that you can earn. Boosters cost 150g a pack. Each booster contains six random cards. Want a specific card for your deck? Too bad. Not even spending real money will definitely get it for you. It's strange. I understand it from a cash grab perspective, but as someone who actually plays magic I can't remember the lat time I straight up bought a booster pack. I just buy singles or draft. I wish there was a way to buy specific cards, say like 25g per card. You have to ask yourself, do you enjoy playing a deck you hate to grind up gold to possibly play a deck you may enjoy? I really didn't.
At the end of the day this game is strictly worse than any of the other DotP games based entirely off of the lack of variation. Sure, DotP doesn't let you build your own deck from scratch, but at least you can play something other than aggro. There are other problems with the game such as the lack of priority holding, bugs, more bugs, and general connection issues, but strictly speaking, as a game, Magic Duels is incredibly lackluster.
**Note: This game is actually really good at teaching you the basics of Magic. It goes over the mechanics and is pretty easy to follow. The AI has been improved from previous games, so you can learn some pretty simple combat tricks from them. Still, once you learn how to play either find a FNM near you or try one of the DotP games.

Civ 5 - 236 hours played on steam (probably more like 300 if including off-line play)
Civ BE - 33 hours (been 4 weeks since I last played it.)
It's not a terrible game on its own, but after playing Civ 5 w/ all their factions, special units and buildings and unique faction perks it honestly kind of feels like im playing a civ game made for a cell phone. I loved this game when it came out... I played it for probably 20 hours in the first week alone, but for me, the replayability of the game was just not there. (one of the greatest achievements of civ5 imo)
There are no factions like in civ 5... just starting perks you can choose.
There are no special units that only you can get because of your chosen starting perks... Every player can get EVERY unit w/ the required research and resources. There are the 3 branches of tech which kind of makes the appearance of race/faction... but I think this system is just a few steps down from Civ 5.
There is alien life!!! But they are simply barbarians ie: unintelligent cattle with chitinous armor, sharp teeth and the occasional acid spitter.
There is no challenge!!! Even with the difficulty on higher diff's it is extremely easy to maintain peaceful relations with every other NPC faction on the planet for the duration of the entire game.
I could go on, but its basically a list of things I would have wanted to see or things done differently.
My bottom line is:
It just gets boring really quick, and after a handful of games (33 hours played), I find little reason to launch the game again, which in my opinion is the polar opposite of the last couple civ games (sorry didn't play very much of the earlier civs so I can't comment on those)

If you're bored of typical RPGs and want something different and fairly unique, give this a try. From its "union" based combat and the two way morale system and the semi auto skill execution and the "critical timing", there are many things in the game that feels special compare to other games out there.
The most prominent aspect is the union group system, where you assign characters into a squad and have their HP combined to one unit. You can have up to 18 characters in up to 5 unions with up to 5 cahracters each. This sounds generic although quite unheard of in an RPG, until you get to the formation system, where each placement has different bonuses (and weakpoints) so where your squad stands can matter, and the bonuses can actually increase if the "right" type of character stands on the right spot. The formation system is properly trick and is one of the most complex out there and most players won't even bother learning it, but those that do will have an easier time, as certain formations, besides the bonuses, also features different style of placement that can really help against certain AOE spells.
There are typically two types of RPG, those that don't need movement to attack (old FF style), and those that has a battlefield and grids where units battle. This game sits in the middle, or rather sits in neither. Unions move automatically to attack enemy groups, so initially you assume that it is essentially a 3D version of FF's style, until one fine day you notice a "too far away" or "move towards the enemy" and be brutally awaken to the fact that there is a real sense of range. Although the game handles movement automatically, there is real strategy involved in WHEN you move, as most enemies (and your squads) can only engage one group at a time, and selecting an enemy to attack involves real battlefield senses, as in is there a clear path and is the enemy too far away that you risk being attacked by another nearer enemy. To intercept (and be intercept) is all part of the game.
So is morale. This game's morale system is pretty drastic and can turn the tide by as much as a mind boggling 400%, so its safe to say that morale management is key to every battle, no matter how strong your unions are (or how strong the enemies are). Even if your unions are weak, if you manage to have high morale, you can hold your own against seemingly impossible enemies, like fighting dragons early game.
At first glance, fighting seem pretty normal in itself, with each character attacking one at a time, until all of a sudden a "quick time event" comes up and you're caught off guard. If you played Assassin's Creed 3, you'll note the similarities, only this is much harder as the timing much be exact. Successful timing upon evade will result in a counter much stronger than usual, while successful timing upon parry will stun the enemy. Seems easy enough, until you realise that if you're successful the first time, all the characters in the union that attack afterwards all earned a quick time event as well, so you're caught off guard again, until the first time you did a successful chain and witness the final character in the chain gaining an unavoidable +500% critical attack. No other RPG gets even close to this.
Sure, you're thinking that having 18 characters in an RPG, this should be properly easy right? Except that the enemy side can have up to 50 in one long, multi stage, large scale battle, and in most cases, enemies can heal as well. Large battles like this gets properly intoxicating as you witness your support group gets ganged by 3 enemy squads, or you managed to gang up on an enemy squad who just decimated yours, or you managed to slaughter 3 groups with one well placed spell, or you endured and endured the relentless bombardment from 7 enemy squads until you managed to activate your battlefield-decimating skill and watch the resulting destruction. Again, no other RPG gets close to this.
Sure, it's not perfect, for example the class system, which the game auto-selects, is quite mind-numbing if you want some control of it (trying to get the class you want is never easy). Fortunately, the class system is purely bonus based and doesn't affect the skills you can use, although each character you can hire has different skills. The story isn't anything special and the game isn't exactly "open world" so the world map isn't explorable. Leveling up your skills can take some micromanaging too as the game auto selects what skill your character uses depending on the circumstances (again, unheard of in an RPG), but you can restrict what it can select by disabling skills.
This game has a charm that's not found in any RPG to date, and i suspect ever. It's a future classic, and certainly a must have.

In a market saturated with indie platformers this game brings something refreshing to the table.
Defy Gravity is probably best described as a physics based puzzle platformer;
You play as an astronaut in outer space equipped with a single use jetpack, gravity gun & shield.
The gameplay relies on requiring the player to shoot positively & negatively charged balls of gravity across each stage to aid their travel. Players will be navigating the astronaut through short levels of increasing difficulty, avoiding deadly laser beams and robotic enemies to reach the end goal.
This title has no loading times between levels or deaths which results in seemless addictive gameplay.
You may die instantly upon impact with a laser or enemy; but there are infinite lives and a clever checkpoint system has been implemented which means you will never be taken too far back, if you happen to fail any part of a level.
Overall, I was pleasantly surprised by something so simple but different from the 2D puzzle/platformer genre.
The game features Steam Trading Cards, Achievements & Xbox controller support as a bonus.
I purchased this game on sale for a matter of pennies, however after playing it I probably would've paid full price.
8/10
Non-stop physics based fun in 2D space but I wish there was a bit more variation in design.
EDIT 6/Nov/15: The game appears to only support Xbox 360 controllers as it wouldn't recognise my unbranded PS2 style USB controller, which is a shame as it works in most of my other games.

Very, very fun! It is an impressive game for the price, and I absolutely love the feel of this game: basically survive Jurassic Park, lol. The core game is great, and the interactions between human and dinosaurs can lead to some dramatic one-on-one moments. During my first play-through as a human, running along alone, my screen began to shake, thumping with the rythmic beating of ever-closer foot falls. I quickly ducked into a side alley, turning in time to see the leg of a Tyrannosaurus, another live player, running past. After a moment it returned, roaring and thrashing, trying to reach me at the back of the alcove. My gun rang out shot after show along with my screams of equal terror and delight. The beast retreated, returned at an angle anew. My gun clicked out of ammo just as the great reptile's head burst deep into the alcove, pulling me screaming out into the light where it finished me off with one swift gulp. Simply awesome. Its one of those games where you can really find yourself immersed in the action...or sometimes, lack there of. I spawned during one playthrough, again as a human, deep in the dense woods, far from my other team members. As I treked aimlessly through the for forest in search of someone, anyone, my mind raced with thoughts of what foul things may be stalking me from behind or even above. It's moments like this that make this game great. It is not without its flaws however, including some rendering issues from time to time and other assorted bugs, but overall, I am well pleased and would whole-heartedly recommend it.

NOT A HERO is a very fast paced tactical shooter. I greatly enjoyed this game; at the time of this review, I have played about 14hr and I have completed all achievements.
STRENGHTS
- Beautiful pixel art. Enemies are highly recognizable despite being stylized, and the sceneries are pleasant to look at.
- Good soundtrack.
- Solid fast paced gameplay, which rewards both skill and creativity.
- The several playable characters all offer something different, which means more gameplay options.
- Humorous, although your mileage may vary on this one.
WEAKNESSES
- No video options, to go fullscreen you may need to press Alt+Enter on your keyboard.
- The game is relatively short, unless you are going for completion. Moreover, most of the extra time will be spent of the final level, the other levels are all pretty easy to 100%.
To sum it up, NOT A HERO is a very enjoyable game, that suffers from some minor defects. Gamplay is fun and addictive, shame there isn't a lot of replay value. User made levels would improve the longevity a lot, but it seems unlikely to happen.
I definitely recommend picking this up, maybe wait for a sale if you are concerned about the longevity of the game.

For the past year I avoided this game like a plague, seeing that most reviews were either bad or ridiculously bad.
Finally after giving it the pass for so many times (it's summer sales anyway), I finally bought this copy and gave it a try.
I'm a total idiot. I've just realised:
1.  I've missed this game all for naught for the past 2 years.
2.  Whomever wrote all those junk review, do you even FF?  Linear? Boring? Really?
3.  I'm not going to take reviews seriously anymore.  Especially on FF titles.
On the bright side, I have you *********s to thank for, since I have the whole trilogy to binge through this year!
The first 10 chapters is akin to an interactive story, where you're guided through the background story and character development.  The pace is slower than previous FF titles, but it also paces the player into gradually learning the game's system.  You will notice that there are more and more things to fiddle with as you progress into the game.  It won't take long before you find yourself into the routine of building up stats, leveling up weapons, running from point A to point B, and tapping the 'ok' button through every battle.
You're looking for more challenge and control over the story line from Chapters 1 - 10.  However, you will still get to develop your characters and weapons.  Boss fights are surprisingly challenging.
You're here for the JRPG element of FF series - particularly the storyline.  You will realise that considerable effort has been invested into this aspect, at the risk of oversimplifying interaction at the player's part.  Nevertheless, I enjoy sitting back with a 6-pack of ice-cold beer after a hard day's work, hitting the same button while looking at the battle scenes. Doesn't tax the brain too much but gives just the right amount of entertainment. Oh and did I mention that sight seeing it great too, it's like Skyrim except you don't get to jump off the cliff.
You will find a significant change of experience on Chapter 11, where you are presented with a sizeable 'open' map, and the freedom to complete missions at will.  Will update my impression again once I clock more hours into the game.
A lot of critics (starting the raging bitter ones) compare FFXIII with other FF titles. This is probably what stopped a lot of genuine buyers from buying this title, myself included. While most arguments are valid, being judged as ♥♥♥♥♥♥ compared to other FF titles doesn't make it ♥♥♥♥♥♥ compared to all other games available on Steam.  If you're into JRPG and don't hate FF games in general, chances are you're happier buying and playing this than some other random title on Steam.

This game is an amazingly immersive experience. I got totally shrecked the first 4-5 times I played it before I started to become more familiar with the mechanics and how to survive. I made it through the winter and into the spring time when the war finally came to a close around about 60 days in or so. I was absolutely hooked on this game, I didn't want to stop playing it until I'd beaten it. And to be honest, when I finally did beat it I was a little bit sad that it was over. But at the same time, I was happy for my fictional in-game characters. They wouldn't have to do those despicable things to survive anymore. The♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder, and pilaging was over. And then I sat in my desk chair for several minutes contemplating everything I'd done in those 60 days to survive. Thinking about how those things really happened to REAL people back in the seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian war in the 90's. I've never played a video game that made me think about real life(...and death) such as This War of Mine.
10 out of 10, would recommend. To anyone. Play this game now, before you forget about it. Also, don't be put off by the difficulty at first. After an hour or two of playing you will be a lot better at surviving guaranteed.
Shout outs to all who had to go through the seige of Sarajevo. I know This War of Mine is just a game, but it's a game that gave me a MUCH MUCH greater respect for ANYONE who's gone through such a terrible war and had to get their hands dirty to survive. And to those who did all that they could to help other innocent civilians while putting their own lives at risk.

The second entry in the BioShock series is set in Rapture as the first game was and, yet again, is bloody brilliant.
Most people who haven't/hadn't played the game (including myself) looked at BioShock 2 as the video game equivalent of a direct to video release. If this is what you thought, I urge you to give it a try.
If you've played through the first BioShock, the setting and atmosphere will be very familiar, though set in an entirely different part of the city. This time around, Rapture doesn't feel quite as new and exciting as the first game, however the story and characters are still really compelling.
There have been a few gameplay improvements, including hacking, general controls and a few weapon mechanics. The enemies are familiar, however a ton of new baddies are introduced.
There may be a bit of trepidation going in initially as the original BioShock was so well crafted in story and characters, but I can assure you that you'll meet some very interesting and well written characters, as well as getting a more in depth look at the origins of the city and Andrew Ryan himself through audio logs.
If you've beaten the first game and you're looking for more Rapture, you can't go wrong with BioShock 2.
