BLUF (Bottom line up Front): This game is one of the better resource gathering games with few bugs so far.  I do not know how the game will end, but I would recommend this to strategic gamers and non violent survivalists.
This is a great variation on the resource gathering genre of games.  This game will delight and frustrate perfect gatherers at the same time (those gamers who, no matter how something of little value, they pick it up and put it in one of their many caches).  While I would like the game to feature other scavengers who may take the stuff that you leave behind, if you try to gather all the resources from one place night after night, you will find yourself starving or trapped in a vicious circle of living day to day.
I do not have enough time in the game to evaluate the end of game scenarios (if there is one) as i was hoping to hear news on international relief on day 14.   For the "good" players, this game does force you to question the value of your ethics versus survival.  My team was starving, so one of my stronger players simply walked into someone’s home and took their food, leaving them to starve.
If you are looking for a resource gathering type game with a twist, this is your game.  If you want a linear story line game with obvious choices given to you, this is not your game.

The game is also relatively fun to play. Well at least for the first half of it. You don't really have a great variety of weapons but at least you can approach your objectives in different ways. You can play it stealthy, though on easier difficulties there is no real benefit to do so.
The second half of the game is the part where it completely falls apart. The gameplay becomes very linear and you just follow along as the games drags you from setpiece to setpiece. The problem is, it becomes less and less an FPS. There is a pointles Helicopter mission, A pointles floating through an alien ship mission, a pointless escort mission and finally a pretty anticlimatic final bossfight mission. If the game would have stayed a stealth shooter the whole time I probably would recommend it. But due to the extremly weak second half I can't.
I also can't recommend it, because it doesn't run very well. It crashed multiple times. At one point i couldn't progress in a level. And one time the objective marker wouldn't show up, so I had to watch a let's play, to see where I needed to go. At least I could finish the mission. But it still was pretty frustrating.
I can't recommend this game because nowadays there is nothing, that makes this game special. If you can get it for two or three bucks you could play just the first half, where it is a competent shooter and not some on rails sci-fi shlock

This game put itself in a terrible position. A position where, if it's easy, it's boring &, if it's hard, it's tedious. What I mean is that a metroidvania that punishes you so heavily for death is incapable of being a fun game because dying just twice in this game is unacceptable due to the harsh consequences but never dying would be boring.
The annoying death mechanic was a minor annoyance in Demon's Souls that brough nothing good to the table but it was far from a deal breaker. Here, it contradicts the entire draw of the genre. The point of a metroidvania is exploration & progression. I'm not eploring & progressing if I'm following a map marker to return to a place I've already been to get money I already had.
I know the game has to send me back somewhere so dying matters but sending me back to a checkpoint would've been enough. No one has ever died in a game & sighed in disappointment at the fact that the game didn't kick them completely out of the level, weaken them, & take all of their money.
Worse is the fact that I died with over 200 money but killing my specter only gave me back 20. When I played a much harder metroidvania called Rabi-Ribi & I died to a boss that took 20 minutes, I loved it. It was my favorite boss in any game ever. The key difference there is that I could immediately try again & I didn't get weaker & lose money every time I died. I was fighting her for hours & loving nearly every second of it but this game killed all of my enthusiasm in only 2 deaths.
Edit: After some people told me it gets better later, I tried it for 2 more hours & it got worse in every regard. The things they mentioned were mostly true so I'm not accusing them of lying but it's just too little too late since it's all badnaids instead of solutions.
For example, rancid eggs can be bought & used to summon your specter & get your stuff back but it doesn't fix the terrible checkpoint system or the tedious combat. The fanbase mostly responded to the fact that I think the game is bad by calling me stupid, telling me to git gud, & rooting through my profile for things to publicly judge out of context.

It's probably worth my while mentioning the reason I first purchased this game (on Xbox, originally): some of the best slash writers in my reading list were writing really interesting stuff about the characters, and I wanted to get the original context.
Basically, this game is best played for the story and the interplay between the characters.  The animation, frankly, is as clunky as all get-out - it's best played after playing something like Final Fantasy VII or VIII (the original PS versions if you can get them) as something of a palate cleanser if you're a real graphics junkie (or you could go the whole hog and just play Angband or a similar text-based RPG as a starter).  The battle system is different - it's turn-based (as with the Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest series), but instead of making decisions about each individual fighter's actions, you're issuing commands to groups of fighters (and they will perform their actions based on your command).  You don't get access to every possible command - instead, you're choosing from a limited list - between six to eight options most of the time, narrowing down to about two or three when things get really nasty.  If you're a gameplay or a graphics fan, this probably isn't the game for you.
If, like me, you're interested in story and worldbuilding, however, this game is *brilliant*.  The world is complex and well-realised, and it's fun to be sitting down and figuring out the back-story and the background politics.  The story is fascinating, and if you're a slash fan, it is a hoot how slashtastic the interaction between Rush and David (pronounced Dah-veed) turns out to be at times - and the slashtastic moments start very early on in the game.  The art is marvellously detailed, the backgrounds are glorious, and the characters are wonderfully created.  In many ways, I get the sense they spent so much time and effort on creating the story and the artwork that when it came time to add the animation and the gameplay, they'd almost run through the budget.  This resulted in very unrealistic movement (it's almost as though their animation models were puppets on strings - it is *very* Thunderbirds movement at times) and a lot of skimped details in the FMV scenes (the one which sticks in my head is one scene where Rush is sitting on a bed... and because the bed isn't animated at all, it stays a rigid rectangular shape.  All I could think is "that has to be hell on the back").
It's almost a pity, in a way, they didn't put the same amount of time and effort into animating their artwork that they did into crafting it.  The voice actors do their best (although if you're familiar with British accents at all, you'll notice Lord David's accent keeps sneaking off toward Sarf Lunnon when he isn't watching) but really, given they're trying to effectively make wooden dolls live, their best has a limited effect.
As I said earlier: if you really need good animation and good gameplay to make a storyline live for you, this probably isn't the game for you.  If, on the other hand, you're a big fan of complex worldbuilding, interesting characters, and a fascinating plot, you'll probably be able to find enjoyment in the game despite the rather wooden movement.

I'll preface this with admitting I bought this game while it was on sale for just under $6. However I wouldn't recommend buying this game at its current price of $21.99.
I’ve completed a single play through of the game in 21 hours and I don’t see myself playing it again in the foreseeable future. The Lord of the Rings: War in the North is a hack-n-slash adventure game with RPG elements. It accomplishes staying within the confines of its genre labels but just barely and by the most generic means that quickly get stale and familiar. There’s little to no variety in combat, customization, “quests” and other mechanics. The inventory system works but I noticed it will automatically sort things for you in an unintuitive way and is shared across by all of the 3 playable characters, if you choose to play single player (as I did). The AI of your allies is in a word; functional, but don’t expect them to go above and beyond so if you do end up playing, it would probably be best to play with others. However, you’d have to know 2 other people who play the game as well as there are no public servers online anymore (the game being released in 2011). The acting is really subpar (even with Nolan North), but it does the job. The game has a dialogue system similar to the Mass Effect series but without the usual consequence of action save for one special instance in mind.
Now if you’re a fan of LOTR lore this will be a bit of a WTF to you. The game takes place during the Third Age and even starts at the beginning events of the LOTR trilogy. It introduces a major antagonist, Agandaûr, which is apparently so competent that Sauron is tasking him with waging war on the entire North of Middle-Earth. You’d think someone of such notoriety would’ve been mentioned at least once by other major characters such as Gandalf or Elrond. Major characters that you happen to meet, as these newly created protagonists who also eventually gain their own fanfare through their deeds, and seem to be seldom mentioned by anyone else. The game will take you through locations such as Bree where you get to visit The Prancing Pony all the way to Rivendell and Grey Mountains before climaxing at the capital of Angmar, Carn Dûm. There are other made for game elements that don’t quite fit with the lore thrown in for story purposes, but hopefully by now you get the idea. Thankfully it’s non-canon.
So in conclusion, if you’re bored and happen to see it on sale for something like $6, it’s not bad for a time killer. However, you won’t get your money’s worth at full price (at this moment $21.99)

Danmaku Unlimited 3 is a vertically-scrolling shoot'em'up made by Doragon. It takes inspiration from eastern bullet hell shooters and is accessible to newer players thanks to its multiple difficulty options and modes of play.
What's good:
+ Crisp and clean sprites, the game looks rather streamlined
+ Backgrounds look pretty cool, bullets don't blend in with them
+ Soundtrack by the Blankfield doujin circle. Impression: very heroic djent.
+ Player ship's movement speed and firepower feel just right. General gameplay feels either like a mix of Touhou and Dodonpachi or how it's like to escape from responsibilities and expectations life throws at you.
+ Patterns are some of the most creative ones I've seen yet
+ Two modes of play - Spirit and Graze, with the latter providing a real challenge
+ Autobombing is there and can be turned off. In Spirit mode it functions by draining one bomb each time you get hit (like in DDP DFK 1.5), in Graze mode it drains your entire bomb stock (like in DDP Saidaioujou, DFK BL)
What's bad:
- Enemies aren't too varied
- Bombs are weak and aesthetically unappealing
- Practice mode is unpolished, but at least it's there
- Lack of resourses may encourage credit-feeding
Neutral (?):
+/- The scoring system's rather unforgiving.
+/- Resourses are limited - you get 2 score-based extends per run and a bomb after every stage. (This mostly applies to Graze mode. In Spirit mode bombs essentially function as extra lives)
+/- Boss battles are long.
+/- Trance meter is completely depleted upon death.
+/- Not enough special effects and explosions (now i'm just nitpicking)
Scoring 101:
Graze a lot, don't drop your graze chain. Cancel as many bullets (preferably lasers) as possible via timed Trance mode activations.
Feedback and personal wishes
- The homing shot type is useless.
- Bosses take too long to spawn in practice mode. Please fix.
- The space whales found in one of the sprite sheets aren't used in the game. Disappointing.
- DU2 customization system was more interesting, albeit lacking in shot option variety.
I didn't manage a Graze mode clear (it's hard), but I'll give it a shot later.

After playing through every affinity and most victories, I feel this game is a fresh take on a beaten idea. The victories are innovative and having so many can allow for you to adapt to your situation with 1 affinity victory and domination + contact victory for anyone. Unit upgrades are a bit bland, but overall well designed and well thought. Covert ops no longer require dlc and give you a wider range of options, and make unused agents buff ones in the field. I don't feel the removal of religion or world congress (Until later dlc possibly) were bad, world congress was a pain anyway and religion's buffs were miniscule without lots of cities. The unique units are similar to each other, with affinity based diffrences that go beyond design, making no affinity a nessesarily bad option. Strategic resources are plentiful, making these units not very hard to make either. Affinitys themselves are a fresh take on ideologies but hardly are copies. While each come with special buffs and buildings, they now have a much larger impact on your cities and even units, with Supremacy even negating road/magrail maintanance, and Harmony lvl 6 giving a 5hp heal in miasma, while tech only negates the damage. Aliens are nothing like barbarians, being neutral to start and even becoming somewhat of an ally in the right circumstances. My only complaints about the game is the aliens are insensitive when it comes to angering them, ranged units can fire twice if they don't move, and unit graphic overlays in several panels, noteably the upgrade screen. Overall, apart from a few minor glitches, this is a charming addition to Firaxis' otherwise old, beaten series.

Whenever friends asked why I played the X series I always told them that buried under all the sh*t was a diamond and it was only a matter of time before enough patches and community content wiped all the crap away and exposed the games for the gems I really believed they were. They didn't believe me - they knew Egosoft's reputation for DOA game delivery (as did I) - but I kept the hope alive. And while far, FAR from perfect X3:R and X3:TC with substantial modding proved to be decent experiences in the end. We have to take what we can get in this genre - It feels like there will never be another Freespace 2.
I guess hope died when X was reborn. All the problems I had hoped resolved in this game - horrible AI, ships colliding constantly, UI that can only be explained as having been designed to annoy and torment - were still present and accounted for. And then some. A lot of some. Yes, it's pretty to be sure but not pretty enough to justify the sheer terror it will run your CPU and GPU through. The campaign is nothing more than a broken tutorial. Combat with other ships is akin to a special-needs jousting contest. I could go on and on but others have done my job for me. Lamentably, Egosoft doesn't appear to be listening.
I don't know why this keeps happening with Egosoft's releases. A more naive soul might blame the developers but as a developer myself I have to believe that the product management and sales of Ego's games are driving them straight into the ground. Much like what you'll be doing with the Albion Skunk should you deign to pilot her.
Pass on this one. Check back again in 3 years. And don't make the mistake of buying Egosoft before the community has had a chance to find something redeeming and shiny under all this sh*t.

This game is an amazingly immersive experience. I got totally shrecked the first 4-5 times I played it before I started to become more familiar with the mechanics and how to survive. I made it through the winter and into the spring time when the war finally came to a close around about 60 days in or so. I was absolutely hooked on this game, I didn't want to stop playing it until I'd beaten it. And to be honest, when I finally did beat it I was a little bit sad that it was over. But at the same time, I was happy for my fictional in-game characters. They wouldn't have to do those despicable things to survive anymore. The♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder, and pilaging was over. And then I sat in my desk chair for several minutes contemplating everything I'd done in those 60 days to survive. Thinking about how those things really happened to REAL people back in the seige of Sarajevo during the Bosnian war in the 90's. I've never played a video game that made me think about real life(...and death) such as This War of Mine.
10 out of 10, would recommend. To anyone. Play this game now, before you forget about it. Also, don't be put off by the difficulty at first. After an hour or two of playing you will be a lot better at surviving guaranteed.
Shout outs to all who had to go through the seige of Sarajevo. I know This War of Mine is just a game, but it's a game that gave me a MUCH MUCH greater respect for ANYONE who's gone through such a terrible war and had to get their hands dirty to survive. And to those who did all that they could to help other innocent civilians while putting their own lives at risk.

BLUF (Bottom line up Front): This game is one of the better resource gathering games with few bugs so far.  I do not know how the game will end, but I would recommend this to strategic gamers and non violent survivalists.
This is a great variation on the resource gathering genre of games.  This game will delight and frustrate perfect gatherers at the same time (those gamers who, no matter how something of little value, they pick it up and put it in one of their many caches).  While I would like the game to feature other scavengers who may take the stuff that you leave behind, if you try to gather all the resources from one place night after night, you will find yourself starving or trapped in a vicious circle of living day to day.
I do not have enough time in the game to evaluate the end of game scenarios (if there is one) as i was hoping to hear news on international relief on day 14.   For the "good" players, this game does force you to question the value of your ethics versus survival.  My team was starving, so one of my stronger players simply walked into someone’s home and took their food, leaving them to starve.
If you are looking for a resource gathering type game with a twist, this is your game.  If you want a linear story line game with obvious choices given to you, this is not your game.

Pros:
- Excellent graphics. Seriously, almost a decade old, and it holds up very well.
- The macho military dialog is groan-worthy, but it's fun. "You want guarantees? Get a toaster!"
- Some really cool level designs. It's generally very clear which direction you need to move in; there are a lot of visual cues that help guide you through some of the busier environments. There were quite a few instances where I found that I knew where to go without really *knowing* that I knew it, and that's always a good sign.
- A variety of ways to move through the level, especially in the early going. A recent review called it more of a "wide corridor" than a true open-world, but it feels open enough.
Cons:
- Gunplay isn't bad, but I never felt like weapons were varied enough - or had enough ammo - to really make me like one over any other. I tended to just grab whatever was lying around.
- Some overly long missions without much variety. I can only be entertained by moving into a new room and killing the three identical enemies contained therein for so long.
- And the big one - it feels needlessly frustrating in some places. Dark Souls is frustrating but feels fair, for the most part. Crysis is frustrating and feels capricious. There's a tank level partway through, and I figured, hey, this'll be sweet. But it's not. You get one tank for the first half, a second tank for the second half. Every enemy has RPGs. Something kept falling from the sky and killing me. Enemy tanks hit hard. You can't repair your tank. If you lose your tank, that's it - you have a huge field to slog through, and you better hope you don't run up against an enemy vehicle, because you're screwed if you do. It should feel cool; it should make you feel powerful. But it doesn't.
The other big moment like this is at the end of the game. I won't spoil anything, but let me advise you to look around your environment and find the box of infinite rockets that the game, helpfully, does not tell you about, or the minigun which is wisely hidden amidst flaming wreckage. Can't just hand out that kind of power.
If it weren't for the atrocious design of the final level, I would still recommend Crysis. But in my opinion, it's too frustrating, and diminishes the entire experience.

Is it a game? Is it an experience? No, it’s The Stanley Parable.
Superficially a first-person walking simulator, The Stanley Parable has the player wandering around their abandoned office building – where is everyone? While exploring, a voiceover addresses what the player’s avatar is doing or thinking, often in a humorous manner. This narrative is key, as it examines what it means to play games and what exactly it means to be a player in such a designed environment. It is intended to be played many times and has multiple endings, but a couple of hours play will uncover most of them. Well-made, thought-provoking and funny; The Stanley Parable is closer to an interactive art experience than a game (in my opinion).
I dare you to find a better game.

I see a lot of Magic die-hards have left negative reviews here, that's understandable.
For me, as a player of the game for over 20 years, I have suffered (and paid for) several online and offline versions of our beloved CCG. This revamp of both the core set and UI are long overdue.
It feels new yet familiar and owes a lot to the cohesiveness and accessibility of Hearthstone.
The UI, whilst supporting keyboard and mouse is centred around the controller which makes sense as this rolls out to PS4 and XBone however the timer bar can be threatening when you're trying to highlight a card to take a closer look. The faint white highlight around the selected card amongst others outlined in red is counterintuitive and take some getting used to. Several mis-sacrificed creature later, I'm getting used to it. I think the mouse would be better for accuracy but I just like playing this on a big TV while slumped on the couch, controller in hand.
Magic is still broken. There's no changing that. Lands and their RNG placement in your deck are still the major bane of the game's fluidity. A victory just because your opp Mulliganed himself to one card is a hollow victory indeed.
It's early days and the wife and I had a lot of fun playing through the Story mode and "making" a limited deck with the first few boosters earned. I still prefer paper magic, something much more rewarding about being face-to-face with a real person.
WoTC have pulled off a coup though: 3 days before Hearthstone's Grand Tournament release I am suddenly distracted and playing more Magic.
The lure is still there. I still want this to work and I imagine I'll get disinterested once the expansions kick in and it becomes impossible to keep up with the Pay-to-Win crowd.
Like with Hearthstone, I am strictly free-to-play on this. I've spent enough money on Magic cards down the years both digital and paper and I know that collections can be lost as soon as another platform comes out.

This game starts off pretty fantastic. the freedom initially to approach skirmishes as you please provides some great emergent gameplay; use your super strength to jump up to higher ground and rain holy vengance from above, cloak yourself to get into an enemys face choke the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and throw him at one of his comrades, or just go in all guns blazing. However your room for creativity is stifled later in the campaign as it becomes increasingly more linear, more of a coridoor shooter and starts to take away what makes the game so compelling.
In my opinion the super suit is really underpowered. I played it on easy as I wanted to feel like a god going through small villages smashing them apart with my fists but quickly found I couldn't be that stupid. You have to approach each fight tactically, and although that has it's own merit I feel like this limits what is possible. The game is fairly sanboxy when you're on the island so with the awesome physics you kinda want to play around, sneak into an enemy camp and throw a grenade watch the roofs fly off and enemies go flying, but that's sometimes easier said than done because your suits cloak lasts about 10 seconds. The super strength is completely neutered, it doesn't seem as if throwing things whilst super strength is activated makes a difference to how far things actually remain in the air, which is a real shame. I want to grab a guy and watch his lifeless corpse go flying for miles off a corpse. It kills enemies much quicker whilst using melee but that's pretty pointless as you very rarely get time to get that close to enemies as you die really quickly. I was suprised how easy it was to get murdered initially, and although I got used to it and adapted, I was a bit upset that you couldn't truly feel like an immortal super weapon whilst armour was activated. I appreciate taking a more thoughtful approach whilst engaging enemies, scouting out camps and using your different powers and grenades when applicable, but there is a difficulty setting built for trying to survive. This setting gets rid of UI hints such as grenade indicators, forces you to use true iron sights and changes the enemies language to korean which is an awesome feature for people who want to truly be challenged but again, I was playing on easy and expected to live out a power fantasy of the most kitted out advanced super soldier. The enemies will actively engage me, they never seem to run away and can see me from miles away through vegetation and hit me with pinpoint accuracy before I've even been made aware of their existence. Having said that the AI can sometimes be quite dumb, I'm not sure whether that's because the difficulty setting but occasionally I'd catch an enemy unawares, start shooting at him and he'd continue to do nothing not even turn around to see where the bullets are coming from!
The lack of power also comes into play with the super speed too unfortunately, which can be frustrating at times if you don't have a vehicle as the normal run speed seems slow to me. When speed is engaged and you start running it feels fantastic but again your energy runs out in a few seconds which is really dissapointing. Also the super jump is mapped to the strength suit setting, whilst that does make sense I suppose it can make navagating a bit annoying when you're constantly switching between powers, would have made more sense to have the speed suit control just bundled in with the strength if the logic is that it gives more power to the legs? I don't know if that's an improvement that was fixed with the later series, I feel having just armour strength and cloak modes of the suit would be a much more compelling way to play.
The game looks.... ok. I mean it's actually 9 years old which is incredible, the foilage tearing up, tin roofs flying off when grenades explode, people flying everywhere. The phsyics can be kinda awesome and make it seem like you're really involved in some serious warfare. But some of the textures such as grounds and rocks are seriously gnarly. I put all the settings up to very high, stuck the highest amount of AA the in game menu would allow but some things still looked seriously jaggy and I was quite suprised. Again I know it's a 9 year old game, and back then I would have been absolutely blown away with how this looks but it's a shame how sharp everything seems. Who knows maybe my aliasing wasn't working properly for some reason. But at certain points of the game, when you climb up a hill and overlook the lush palm trees and beautiful seas, you can't help but appreciate that it still does a pretty good job at holding up to this day.
However as I mentioned before, half way through the game it gets really linear and then it just becomes a really generic shooter where most of your powers are completely pointless (use strength to break down a door! yay!) and the story is definitely not enough to carry it, generic military rubbish, random characters that just get introduced and then suddenly become important for some reason. Literally nothing matters in this game, so once you get through the first half just stop playing. I almost gave this game a negative review because I've literally just finished it and the last 6 hours of gameplay have really left an uninspiredly bland taste in my mouth.
So yeah. Buy it on sale, spend some time picking up turtles and blowing fools away with the awesome shotgun, and once you get inside the alien space ship just stop playing because you'll find yourself wanting it to end and there's absolutely no pay off.

FINAL FANTASY XIII is a turn-based RPG that tells the story of 6 individuals, who are branded enemies of Cocoon, being hunted and chased down by a corrupt government. They run away for the most part and eventually had enough and decided to challenge their fate.
FF13 brings a whole new feel to the ATB system from previous games. You only play as one character out of a battle party of 3. This leader decides on the paradigm (or strategy) that everybody employs. Per exemple, I can set my leader to attack physically while team member #2 heals and tem member #3 debuffs the enemy. It's important to learn how to switch paradigms mid combat to adjust to the situation. You mostly sit back and react to any change while the Auto-Battle does it work. Having a strategy is important because of the new Staggering system. To put it simple, a magic user attacking the enemy fills its stagger bar while a physical attacker prevents the bar from depleting rapidly. Once that bar is full, the enemy becomes weak and for a set amount of time, you can deal a lot of damage.
Other new mechanics is a Crystarium system that takes care of leveling up your stats. It's really similar to the FFX Sphere Grid. Unlike FFX, grinding is really limited in FFXIII and decisions like leveling up as a healer or as a physical attacker are not as important as they look. The game is really linear making sure that the next enemy (visible on the map, no random encounters) is always a little bit stronger. This is more to see if you understand the mechanics properly than if you are strong enough.
Weapon upgrades are shallow and uninteresting. You spend money on components to upgrade your weapon for better attack power. It never seems to do that much of a difference and it's only relevant comes the aftergame. The ultimate weapons are simply a fully upgraded weapon.
The point of FFXIII new and odd design is to put emphasis on its story and it's a good one. It's linear because you are being chased down (you're not going to explore and grind in these situations). The game features many skippable tutorials that are really helpful but sometime a little redundant. Ironically, it's emphasis on strategy is putting a line of enemy between cutscenes and mashing Auto-Battle until a harder enemy or a boss shows up. Eidolons (or summons) are a pain to battle against or with (and are never necessary). The story starts out as a confusing mess as it's throwing you unknown names and terms left and right but it quickly settles down to explain them little by little.
The game only features one big sidequest near the end of the game and it's an amazing one. This is where you finally understand the point of an extensible Crystarium and weapons and accessories upgrades. It's basically a 64 bosses you got to beat and get a perfect rating on. This comes with some superbosses. This is to really test out the complex combat system that doesn't reach half its potential during the story.
The cast is enjoyable with many characters having little to no experince in combat. They feel a lot more real than the other games. They all go through their personnal feelings of hope and despair. Each have a reason to fight. The game does a great job to somehow connect them all together.
Production is amazing. Graphics are astonishing. Voice acting is great. Music fits well but isn't the best in the series. Cool battle themes though (regular, bosses, eidolons, etc.).
+Story-oriented game (around 50 hours long).
+Great cast.
+Superb production (voice acting, graphics, music, art)
+Fun customizable paradigm system.
+Amazing and long end-game sidequest that makes you feel as you truly mastered the game (extra 20 to 40 hours of content).
+Good price (for a story).
~Confusing story at first, it's lore is a good but complicated one.
~Story makes the game linear which is okay but might throw people off.
~Too many accessories, most of them really situational and useless without good upgrading (Poison resist, Fire resist, etc)
-Combat against regular enemies are really boring. (Auto-battle mashing).
-Poor weapon upgrade system.
-Eidolons are a pain to battle and to use.
-Obvious treasure chests (every dead-end that branch off your linear path).
You'll either love it or hate FINAL FANTASY XIII. Those looking for deep and fun combat are only really going to get satisfied at the end-game sidequest where everything opens up (after many, many hours of story...). Those looking for a good story will easily be able to bear the combat as long as they enjoy the story. I enjoyed my time with FFXIII and I do recommend it but at your own risk. Wait for a sale.

Oh boy, here we go: Final. Fantasy. X. I. I. I. Ahem. Originally released back in 2009, this was the first entry of Square's juggernaut franchise on the PS3 and Xbox 360. This was also one of the most (if not the most) controversial title; fans and critics were heavily divided. The game itself spawned two direct sequels, FFXIII-2 and Lightning Returns, as part of the "Nova Crystallis" series. Honestly, I'm still conflicted about this game but let's get into the details:
This is easily the game's weakest point. It's a colossal mess of unnecessary jargon and convoluted narration. Seriously, get ready to face a barrage of terms such as cie, fal'cie, l'cie, ci'eth, and etc. The characters try their hardest to explain everything but it just falls flat. The gist of the story is that a group of people becomes "tainted" and labeled as "enemies of the state" so now they must elude capture while overturning the status quo by taking down storm troopers, a guy who looks like the pope, a Gundam Wing reject, and a giant Picasso painting? Um, yeah.
The main playable characters are okay.  Nobody stands out as being super annoying or unlikable, but nobody stands out as being well developed with deep personalities either. Everyone is just kind of bland. They are there to move the story along and that's pretty much it.
If the story is the weakest part of this game, then the gameplay is the second weakest. There is one saving grace that I will get to shortly. Anyway, the game is 90% corridors and hallways. If you're claustrophobic I highly recommend you stay away from playing this. You go from point A to point B  and are interrupted by cutscenes at various checkpoints. You can also expect boss fights and the such. Treasure chests are plainly in view and you'll never get lost. The game is almost entirely devoid of puzzles. Sounds like boring and lazy dungeon design? Well, it is.
The saving grace for this game is the battle system. Square implemented an interesting and engaging battle system that takes the classic ATB system and morphs it into something refreshing. Your ATB gauge fills up and the total "length" determines the number of actions you can take. For example, I can choose to "Attack" use "Flamestrike" and then follow it up with three casts of "Ruin". There is no MP in this game; all actions are limited based on how many commands you input in the ATB bar. The stronger the attack, the more space it will require.
Furthermore, there are the paradigm and stagger mechanics as well. Paradigms allow you to quickly switch the roles of your characters. There are six roles: Commando, Ravager, Medic, Sentinel, Saboteur, and Synergist. I'm not going to go over what each one does, but you do need to understand when and how to use each of these roles to get through the tougher fights. This also plays into the "stagger mechanism". Every enemy has a "chain gauge" and you fill this up by attacking it. Once it reaches its limit the enemy will "stagger" and for a limited amount of time your attacks will do massive amounts of damage. This is absolutely key because most bosses and regular enemies have very healthy life pools. In fact, if you don't quickly learn how to balance staggering enemies and keeping your characters alive, you will be defeated in many boss fights.
Indeed, the battle system is both refreshing and challenging. At first things will be easy, but by the later chapters the difficulty ramps up and even normal mobs can wipe you with ease if you're not paying attention. This makes the game engaging to play and overcoming a tough boss very satisfying.
Another plus for this game are the graphics. Despite this being a seven year old game, it looks quite nice. Square clearly spared no expense in this department. The character models and facial expressions are very well done along with enemy design and special effects. The only issue is the background environments, but that's mostly because of the boring design (all the corridors and hallways kind of blend in) and not technical faults.
The music is very "meh". Nobuo Uematsu's scores are no where to be found and there wasn't anything memorable. (I believe Uematsu's final work for Square was in FFXII). I mean the music is not terrible by any means but it just doesn't do the game justice, especially a flagship FF title. The voice acting ranges from average to above-average so no real complaints there. I just wish the characters were actually interesting though.
Come for the battle system and pretty graphics and try not to get bogged down by everything else. If you can get over the abysmal story and dungeon design then you'll enjoy this game for sure. And if you're into achievement hunting look up a guide for "Treasure Hunter". It's notoriously grindy :)

Final Fantasy XIII is, as the name implies, the 13th main-line Final fantasy title. And much like previous titles, the game has very little to do with the rest of the series, apart from some minor reoccurring elements, like the Chocobos (a kind of large bird that some people ride on).
Let's get the most glaring issue with this game out of the way. The port is terrible. Slowdown for no obvious reason was quite common, but what was worse is that the game has really bad keyboard controls, yet there's a common bug that causes the save menu to freeze if you have an Xinput controller plugged in, and it does not play nice with a DirectInput controller. It recognizes DirectInput controllers, just not all buttons on it.
Final Fantasy XIII is a really nice looking game. It keeps a mostly consistent art style, with interesting looking  enemies and beautiful environments. Animations leave a bit to desire, but they're not terrible.
The soundtrack is a disappointment. The Final Fantasy series is known for its great music, but here it just felt flat and uninteresting. Thinking back on the game, I don't actually remember any of the songs, yet I remember songs from the FF games I played in the 90's. Voice acting is mostly good, but not outstanding. The voice actors do a good job with the material they're given, even if there's no standout performances, but it feels like they are hampered more by the script than with any lack of talent.
The story always plays an important role in the Final Fantasy series, and 13 is no exception. There are a lot of cutscenes and a lot of dialogue.
The game takes place in a place called Cocoon, which is led by a fal'Cie. There's the l'Cie from pulse that are the enemy to Cocoon, and if you have no idea what a fal'Cie or a l'Cie is, then you've just experienced one of the major issues with the writing in this game. It loves to throw in-universe terms at you without explaining them. After a while you will figure out what a fal'Cie or a l'Cie is, but it's something that the writers seem to have expected you to know getting into the game.
The fal'Cie are supernatural beings of great power, who more or less rule the world. The l'Cie are humans branded by the fal'Cie, who need to fulfill a task given to them, or else they'll be transformed into monsters. The branding also gives them special powers.
The game throws you right into the story, some people who were near a pulse fal'Cie (the enemy of the l'Cie of Cocoon, where the main characters  are from) getting deported, due to fear of them being marked and dangerous. The main characters want to stop the deportation, which is protected by the soldiers of Cocoon. And it's boring. You're not really given any motivation for why you should care about anyone at this point, and the game does a terrible job at actually explaining what's going on, who the people are, it just expects you to be engaged in the story already. The characters are also introduced as 1 dimensional stereotypes with little in the way of personality outside of their one dominant trait. This goes on for nearly 3 hours.
Then the characters reach the Pulse Fal'Cie and get branded, and this is where the game actually gets started. Now you're given some motivation, and the characters start showing some emotion (though it still takes a while before they really evolve into something relatable9. In terms of story pacing, this is terrible, you should not have to sit through nearly 3 hours of made up words that the game just refuses to explain and drip fed story before it gets anywhere, at least not in a game that tries to put the story in focus. Once the story really gets going, it actually turns into something that's relatively good, and moves along at a mostly good pace, up until the last 3rd of the game, where it starts to feel drawn out and padded once more. Overall, in the hands of better writers and with a better pacing, this story could have been quite good.
Final Fantasy XIII uses a real time combat system, unlike most previous games in the series. You only control one character, who you can give direct orders to. The rest of the characters are just given "stances", and they'll do whatever they want to do that fits into this stance. It works, but much like the story taking 3h to get started, so does the gameplay. Until you've become l'Cie all you can do is attack and use items, and there's really no skill or decision-making involved. You just attack. You won't get experience until you've become a l'Cie either.
Once you've become l'Cie, you can start earning levels, and leveling up is handled in a less direct way than most Final Fantasy titles. You have skill paths for each stance, and you invest points into them to get stronger. Some give new abilities (but just for that stance), while other improve your stats. It's not a very complex system, all you really do is move along mostly linear progression paths, but you at least get to chose which path you want to invest your skillpoints in at any given them.
Level navigation is more or less entirely linear. You move through long corridors with enemies. No chance to deviate from the path, other than possibly take 2 steps to one side to open a chest at certain points. Most FF games are linear, but none are as linear as this one. This makes for rather monotonous gameplay.
Most enemies are easy enough to take down, and you don't really need to worry about stances and such all that much. Bosses though, those are at the same time almost always really easy and really frustrating to face. The game developers figured that by just giving the bosses huge health pools, they would make them harder,. Most bosses during the second half of the game are just damage sponges with some special attacks you need to watch out for. My advice is to just play the game on easy, they have smaller health pools if you do (an advice I wish had been given to me before I started playing, as I played through the entire thing on normal, apart from the last 3 bosses).
Final Fantasy XIII is a deeply flawed game. The main story is actually rather interesting, but it's ruined by poor writing and pacing. The port is really bad, and you might have to play through the game with really awkward keyboard controls. The gameplay is also a bit monotonous, but were it not for the damage sponge bosses, it would have been alright at least. Overall, this is a game that can, and probably should, be skipped. You won't have a terrible time playing it, after the first 3 hours at least (which were the most boring 3 first hours I've ever seen in a JRPG), but there are so many better games out there that deserve your time and money instead. Games like Tales of Zestiria or most previous Final Fantasy titles.

First off, this game is AMAZING.
Let me start with the bad, just to get it out of the way.
--The animation can use some improvement BUT it does NOT effect how well your gameplay may be. In fact, it might even be seen as comic relief, esp. with how the units ragdoll when terminated in battle.
--The story could be executed WAY better; not to say that it's completely poor, but there are some cutscenes that are lacking in specific reactions and some relationship development that could've been included to bring about a far more emotional pull.
--They don't really give you too much information about the connections in the plot and the background.
--In my own personal opinion, it lacks a couple that probably would've been amazing if they made it canon.
Now, onto the AMAZING:
--AMAZING plot/story with AMAZING characters. They're all dorks, seriously. While relationship development and animation could've been better, they are all unique in their own right. Even the ones you can hire to be as a part of your own union have their own personalities, and some of them come with their own sidequest to get into. The plot itself could have been explained a bit better but it is DEFINITELY worthwhile with a type of ending that tends to be unique among games and even stories themselves.
--The bosses, while incredibly difficult and ragequit-worthy, are CHALLENGING. You really need to think and strategize how you sort out your unions and how you use each character and especially what moves you make. Each boss has their own style of being beaten, and it's really awesome to get into how exactly to defeat them. Their moves are unique to them, so you have to think of ways to get around it if you die repeatedly the first twenty times. It isn't easy, and THAT'S what makes it so fun. It can be considered near IMPOSSIBLE because one of the bosses you encounter in this game, The Gates of Hell, is just lkmifowmfoIAMOIAmf rage everywhere BUT I /thoroughly/ enjoyed each battle, no matter how hard I did rage.
--The OST is to DIE for. Every single piece is AMAZING.The battle themes? They REALLY get you pumped and it IS download worthy. And you remember that boss I just mentioned? The Gates of Hell? The music that plays during that fight is absolutely SPECTACULAR; it's one of the reasons why I didn't give up straight away.
The battle system seriously needs it own paragraphs because of how UNIQUE it is and how PERFECTLY it's set out.
--It's kind of like chess, except more elaborate and you operate in what they term 'unions'. The formation and the leader and the units in them are customizable; the unit limit allowed in battle as well as the number of unions is small atfirst but as you go through the game, it increases. The units themselves, unfortunately, are not customizable but the main character certainly is.
--The commands are tailored specifically to what abilities the leader has, and to an extent the rest of the union. They are also dependent on situation and the items in your inventory as well as where your unions are position on the battlefield, which makes it realistic.
--When you launch your commands, the sequence itself that plays out gets you on the edge of your seat and it's actually REALLY mesmerizing to watch. It's not boring at all and there's the option to get involved in helping your unions attack because there's a live trigger that appears sometimes (I tend to put it on automatic but if you like getting immersed in the game then there it is!).
--No character operates individually unless you specifically assign only one character to a single union (which is probably a straight ticket to them dying). Each character works together and it's REALLY charming, in my opinion, because you can really see their teamwork (especially when they're allowed consecutive turns due to the live triggers) buuuut I digress. What I'm trying to say is that this battle system isn't like any other, simply because the way you command them is not as individuals, but as a whole. This means that they attack as a whole, they heal as a whole, and they, well, /die/ as a whole. I'm not sure what other game exists out there that has kind of the same system (except maybe Warcraft and Dawn of War but they aren't exactly turn-based), but nothing else really comes to mind so The Last Remnant REALLY takes the cake on unique battle system.
I've probably just rambled really badly in this review but I REALLY REALLY REALLY recommend this game!! I'm actually REALLY surprised that it isn't popular because I would've thought that the story and gameplay would hook people in despite the downsides. All the same, this deserves a FAR bigger fanbase so I really encourage anyone that happens across this review to try it out. Just pleeeaaasee aahhhh. Not even this review can express how amazing I think this game is.

3rd person, hack and slash, story driven, action RPG in Lord of the Rings universe, that follows the story of the Lord of the Rings books / movies, yet is presented from a different angle, where you play as one of the three heroes set on a quest to eliminate Sauron's mysterious ally in the north.
Story is very similar to the movies, and you meet many known characters throughout your journey, like Gandalf, Frodo, Bilbo, Aragorn, Legolas and many more. Most of the time you can only interact with them in "safe" hubs like towns and scripted cut-scenes.
Even if you didn't watch the movies, there's fair amount of lore available through dialogues if you chose investigate dialogue options. I didn't encounter choice and consequence in dialogues, so probably they are straight forward and just there for information, lore and story.
Combat is mostly hack and slash, with melee weapons as well as ranged ones, depending on hero. You defeat enemies, find loot in linear levels with some hidden passages and secrets here and there. After leveling up you get skill points you can spec into 3 trees, and stats points you can increase stats with, so your basic RPG elements.
You can find, buy or get as a reward different kinds of armor pieces and weapons. I have no clue if you can equip your AI controlled allies, but you can trade with them, and if you play in co-op, it's a good idea to trade and offer items you don't use to party members, as you often find items not wearable by your hero.
Co-op is strongest aspect of this game, it's really fun and enjoyable, with great synergy between heroes. Dwarf can be tank or tanky melee warrior, Elf has healing, shields and support spells, and Human is basically archer or rogue damage dealer. All heroes have some sort of ranged attacks and require some aiming to successfully hit enemies.
Game offers some side quests and challenge locations besides the main story. You can revisit almost any level for additional loot and XP. Dwarf can collect ore and bash through weak walls to uncover secret areas. Elf can gather herbs and brew potions as well as dispel magically sealed areas. Human however can only gather hidden cashes of supplies, and is a bit dull compared to other heroes.
There's decent variety of enemies in the game, orcs, trolls, spiders, humans, wyrms, dragons, just to name a few. AI is straight forward, usually rushing you head on as melee or shooting from range with ranged attacks, bigger creatures and bosses have special attacks and require careful positioning or dodging to not get hit. You can easily fall in battle after couple direct hits, unless you dodge or block the attacks.
Environments look good yet lack detail, texture quality on characters is decent with somewhat low quality on environments. Visually game looks similar to "Game of Thrones" game. Voice acting and facial animations are decent enough and sound similar to the characters from the movies, yet I doubt there's any line from the actual actors in the game.
For a game made in 2011 it doesn't look that good, and could be much better with serious polish, never the less the story and 3 player co-op makes this game very enjoyable 12 hour experience. With hero switching and story replay on harder difficulties, this game will give you up to 30 hours of "content". I experienced some disconnects while playing in co-op, so it has some network issues, make sure if someone disconnect to not advance in story, and just remake the lobby.
Enjoy.

I found it funny and unlike SR4 (which I played a week prior), I 100%ed this in the end. It even has a few extra epilogues for you if you decide to clear a district or complete all activities (nothing for challenges, though). There's an achievement for playing 20 hours - I full-cleared it with 13 hours on the in-game clock. That ain't bad for the discount price. Have some fun, see some sights in Hell. I cannot recommend this enough, despite my crippling OCD.

With one playthrough under my belt I feel that I have a right to write a few words on this game. And, in all honesty, I enjoyed it greatly. It is very lore friendly, more so, than PJ's movies, it has amazing art style, the characters are vivid, even if not particularly deep, and it is nice that each has different, suitable to their race dialogue options. Story-wise the game is certainly passable, offering enough plot content to satify the RPG fans in most people, and surprisingly not single-minded, with detours and side stories which tie in to the main arc, but standing well on their own, too.
As far as gameplay is concerned, it is good. Combat could have used more variation in available combos, because as is, it's just button mashing with occasional "strike when the arrow shines for a crit hit". I miss all the different combos from the old Return of the King games. Still, fighting hordes of enemies is fun, even more so, when you play with friends, as AI is wonky at best and in some sections you are definitely at a disadvantage (I look at you, mounted crossbow parts). There is a good variation, though, between characters. The dwarven champion is a heavy hitter, ranger is quick and slick DPS, loremaster is a support. All three work very well together and if you play with other humans, the slaughter you can do together is wonderful. Interestingly, each character has access to different kinds of secrets, with loremaster also being able to make potions for use of the team.
All in all, I recommend the game to people enjoying the world created by JRR Tolkien and to people enjoying nice and simple hack'n'slash games. It is definitely worth buying at a discount, and a worthy item to consider buying without it, too.

Rivals of Aether is a technical platform fighter, with the kind of gameplay you might see in a tournament set of Super Smash Bros. Melee or the competitive Brawl-mod Project M. There are no random items in this game.
What I really like about Rivals of Aether is that instead of being some kind of blind copy of Melee's physics and quirks, it reimagines this technical fast-paced gameplay that's unique to Melee (and PM) as something intentional. Melee's competitive scene is a result of a decade's worth of discarding parts of the game that make the game a bad competitive game, finding ways to exploit the game's physics engine to do cool stuff, and grinding tech skill way past what the developers ever expected.
You have a game about two (or more) players fighting to knock each other off a small stage with some platforms, using only their character's unique moveset and their own skill. The game's physics, character controls, and hitboxes make it possible to move around the stage quickly and effectively, letting you chain attacks together to defeat the other player in a satisfying and rewarding way. But you also have the tools to escape combos and recover back on stage, and when you play another player you're always trying to get in each other's head. Melee's competitive play is unique and interesting, but it's not what the developers had in mind when they made the game.
Rivals of Aether on the other hand has this kind of competitive play as its vision, a reimagining where everything is designed from the ground up with intent and purpose. And it shows.
-Characters were constantly tweaked and the game was patched according to player feedback to keep the game balanced.
-The game's singleplayer offerings complement the multiplayer by teaching you how to play and building on your fundamentals. Getting good at Abyss, the most arcadey mode, still involves learning how to move your character quickly and learning the other characters' attacks
-Inputs are streamlined, customizeable, and buffered. You don't have to do frame perfect hand-breaking button presses to move around the stage and do what you want, and this makes the game a lot easier to get into at any level of play, and is one of the big reasons I play this instead of Melee. The fact that you can use whatever controller you want and customize your controls helps, but the main factor is intentional design.
-You can play solo, play locally with friends, or play online. Though its ranked and random online modes aren't very useful outside of the US until the playerbase goes up, joining a discord or a steam group or whatever lets you jump in and play another player online at any time through Steam.
RoA manages to preserve the genre's depth while rejecting the artificial difficulty you get from frame perfect button presses and unintentional game design, and I'm a big fan of that. If you ever watched Evo and thought "wow Melee looks cool, but there's no way I can play like that" then you really need to check this out. The fact that it's a lightweight indie game for a fraction of the price of an old nintendo console with an old nintendo game controller and an old nintendo game helps.
Obviously this isn't just "Melee: the indie game" and I think there's a lot in this game that appeals to people who just can't relate to Melee's appeal, I just wrote this from a competitive Smash point of view.
Finally, I'd just like to say that the characters are cool and I like the art a lot and the music's really good too. Kragg is cute. That's all.

Day 5,
We're out of food (we have been for a day already).  There was a night raid, and one of the team was wounded.  We used up our last bandage already, and there's no way to make more.  One of our people went out to help two children with a sick parent, and will not be back until tomorrow.  We're going to have to make our wounded fellow stay awake and guard, while our scavenger hunts for food.  All of the nearby places have been looted already, so we have to try an occupied location.
Day 6,
Our man returned from helping the children, content, but also exhausted and starving.  Our wounded man isn't getting better.  Tragedy, our scavenger was set upon by armed men while trying to bring home food and medicine, and died before he could make it back.  We're out of options, and out of time.
Above is a pretty accurate excerpt of what this game is like.  It's a powerful tragedy.
Gameplay is made tougher by a single save slot, with no way to go back if you mess up -- that's intentional.  It's rough, and you're quickly forced to choose between doing what's right, and doing what's required.
To date I've managed up to 8 days without doing anything bad, then it all quickly falls apart.  That's the point though -- it's a game with only hard choices available.  If you don't own this, you should buy it, even if it's not your usual game style.
I think the developers should offer an option to transcribe the events as they occur into story form.

Is it a game? Is it an experience? No, it’s The Stanley Parable.
Superficially a first-person walking simulator, The Stanley Parable has the player wandering around their abandoned office building – where is everyone? While exploring, a voiceover addresses what the player’s avatar is doing or thinking, often in a humorous manner. This narrative is key, as it examines what it means to play games and what exactly it means to be a player in such a designed environment. It is intended to be played many times and has multiple endings, but a couple of hours play will uncover most of them. Well-made, thought-provoking and funny; The Stanley Parable is closer to an interactive art experience than a game (in my opinion).

While this game does pay some homage to the infamous Smash Bros, this game has done something that most smash clones haven't done, stand from the shadows of its master. Rivals of Aether is a game that I feel like is the game that does all of the right things and I can say doesn't feel like a Smash Bros game.
With all of that said, I can definitely say that this game has a high learning curve for beginners and people familiar with smash bros. If you're going in thinking you can do all of the stuff you think you can do in this game, well this game will glady and swiftly send you flying into the blast zones upon thinking like that. This game optimizes combos and character familiarization to its prime. Yes, it doesn't have a crazy 58 roster like Smash Bros for the Wii U, but with 8 characters that have its own strengths and weaknesses, I found it easier to learn about every character's strengths and weaknesses with it coming down to putting in the time to play the game. DON'T GET DISCOURAGED, keep it up and you'll do fine.
Anything that I was messing up on or need some clarity helps out in Local mode where there's a tutorial, story mode and abyss mode that can help you improve. Online allows you to push yourself to the next level. There's so many small things included in this game that makes playing each match enjoyable. From controller calibration, color customization, to ranked matches, and playing your friends online. For a clone, this game is amazing. With Ori coming out this summer, hopefully this will attract more people to play this game.
I would say for its for price, I think its worth it. With 8 characters, online mode, story, training and small subtle things in the game, there's no reason not to pick this up if it appeals to you. If you do, prepare yourself, competition is rough!

It could be said it was a game looking to try something new and/or capture new comers to the genre and/or franchise... but the gameplay is more "interesting" to seasoned RPG players who want something different, while newcomers would likely just be put off by it.
It looks great, even with limited enemy models (which is probably an FF fan point of acceptance), but that initial hallway grinding is seriously a dozen or so hours too long... granted, it did more than get me in tune with the combat mechanics and role strategizing in advance of being let loose into a fairly tough world (which is what they had claimed it would be the entire point up to then)... I could see that initial grind fest putting off A LOT of non-fans of the series... as well as fans of the series.
For Final Fantasy Fan Points:
-it's a JRPG where you assign roles [as opposed to classes like in past games, which are also roles but  with micromanaged actions].
-From a game/story design standpoint, the experiences you have in the opposing worlds have interesting parallel values to the playing experience. It starts off repressive, linear, seemingly easy yet aggrevating, expected, etc... and as you learn things and you approach your sort of exile, as you learn your focus, things become more complex and tougher, but you also become more free... eventually leaving that bleak world for a more expansive open one with a lot more freedom but also some pretty tough obstacles along the way also.
-great looking animations, IMO
-I like the music
-in terms of a game in an RPG collection, it's IMO a unique game to have in a collection and once your far enough along, further grinding towards a goal is a lot more enjoyable .
Not so Fan Friendly points-
-grinding in various hallways for dozens of hours
-not being able to make your preferred group for dozens of hours
-not being able to earn gil AND exp for upgrading for dozens of hours (its one or the other)
-not being able to change into new classes for dozens of hours
-sometimes aggrevating wasted efforts by certain group characters in certain roles who could/should clearly be doing a different action in their assigned role (for dozens of hours, till you can change into their place and execute the proper actions)
-Seems like story events could have had more impact with just a little more effort. (at least in terms of the trilogy)

After and Intro Sequence which is a BEAUTIFUL but nonsensical movie, which you can literally read up on later to understand what happend, as the entire story and worldbuilding happens in a kind of encyclopedia which you can read in the pause-menu, your sword-weilding protagonist and black companion exit a train - stop me if that sounds familiar to players of the 7th installment.
Please note that I dont mention him being black as an actual racial thing but as a stereotypical thing, meaning he's the kind of weirdly insensitve uber-black that only japanese games seem to see, where any moment you expect him to ask for melon and KFC and start a rap battle.
The next few hours you will find yourself in a city embroiled in revolution where young, heroic rebels fight the corrupt regime to stop the deportation of people thats happening for some reason. Or at least thats what the game claims. Because actually you appear to be on some kind of... highway? Its a ~4m wide strip of street that appears to float hundreds of meters over what the game claims is a city, no-really, and run along this steet. Theres no real gameplay. The combat consists of forming combos, but youll find theres always a "best" combo, and  theres an auto feature that does find it automatically so youll end up just using that. This means you run down a 4m wide one way street pressing "auto" from time to time.... exciting
After what felt like an eternity, and probably was like 4 hours real time, something happens that Ill just spoiler here - a woman dies and Snow, the male lead, at this point gets as the first character for the first time in the game some kind of character-building where as any other character just "has a personallity" which you can read up in the childishly-written encyclopedia. However the death felt very very wrong. - You see if you have the kind of gameplay where every character constantly gets shot, impaled, exploded, eaten, hit with swords a.s.o. and just brushes it off with a shrug and a potion, it feels weird when in a cutscene, a character being somewhat close to an explosion dies in a weirdly "tragic" way as in written by someone who never experienced a real feeling. If you want us to feel sorry about a characters death, please show us that character more than twice before. Also Snow is very sad about this woman he just met dying, but then becomes heroic for no reason and a few hours later he rides a motorcycle made of women to save his girlfriend or something so you know.... yeah...
Anyway after your highwayadventures are done you will go to some sort of temple, where a ~4m wide corridor will lead you, in another excrutiating 4 hours of walking forward, to some sort of bossmonster, everyone knows we cant defeat but we go there anyway to.... not defeat it.
After all this excitement the group leaves the City, defeated and hopless to go to the outside world, a dystopian Ice-desert with no Idea what to do next. Luckily for the Group, a convenient ~4m wide trail leads them to their next probably amazing adventure.
After walking down the icepath for a couple of hours with nothing happening besides people screaming their names a lot and doing random things I was almost 10hours in and just coudnt stomach it anymore, so I stopped.
You see the older games had, in my opinion, never good gameplay. The combatsystems were always overdone, the random encounters annoying and the layout of some of the places confusion. The grind later on just brought the story to a screeching halt.
This game seems to understand the problems, but each of its solutions made it worse. The one-way levels with one-action combat are boring and while I appreciate that theres no grinding, a leveling system that just makes your attacks stronger, in a game with predefined amounts of enemies means there basically is no levelling system, as the enemies get stronger at the very same pace always.
Also the game forgets that while gameplay was always weak, the BIG strength of Final Fantasy games were always their worlds, their worldbuilding, their characters, their story.
But theres no worldbuilding, as you never see interesting things but only corridors, and everything happens off-screen for you to read in the encyclopedia later! And the Characters are TERRIBLE! Besides them not being "build" as in previous games but just existing, they are incredibly bland and inconsistent! You have Snow, the Rebel, who is shown as a all-talk showoff "Bro" just looking for a fight, but then constantly does the most heroic things. You have a Boy, who everyone "protects" in the cutscenes and is scared for, but who smacks the monsters in combat as hard as anyone else. You have a Girl that appears to be mentally handicaped, as she is constantly oblivious to any danger or things happening around her and the main lead "Lightning" whos "mysterious" and broody. And these are her ONLY characterfeatures so she constantly doesnt answer questions, walks away from conversations or says things like "you wouldnt understand" or "ill tell you later, theres no time" before walking next to the person she said that to, silently, for the next few hours.

Danmaku unlimited as a series is great. Don't get me wrong. It really is. But it suffers the curse of being put in with a field on Steam that is made up of even greater company. Bug Princess by Cave has the brutal difficulty angle sewn up, Ikaruga has the absolute classic angle nailed, Jamestown has the glorious pixel-art sorted. In order to stand out in this genre, you absolutely have to bring something new to the table.
As good as Danmaku Unlimited is, it does not bring anything new to the table. It brings a lot of -good-, but nothing -new-. The greatest sin here is that if you've played a lot of bullet hells, this is going to feel immensely familiar, and you're going to blast through it fast, nothing is prone to catch you out. At all. Now that may be a plus point, if that's what you're after, but if you're seeking something to change up the formula? Yeeeeee-no.
Mechanically, it works great. You have a ship with a teeny tiny hitbox, same as most "Eastern" BHell games, you have anywhere between "Mildly offensive" and "Absolutely terrifying" levels of hostile fire coming toward you, and you pump out similarly scary levels of fire back, with your only choice generally being "Do I spam the screen with lots of little beams or do I fire ONE BIG BEAM at something that needs cracking open like a walnut."
It has good Bullet Hell music, albeit not outstanding music, it has good graphics, albeit not outstanding graphics, you see a pattern here? If a game could ever nail what I'd define as the absolute essence of an "8 out of 10", this would be it. The problem is there's games out there such as Revolver360 Re:Actor that do -better-.
The problem is that for all the good it does, it's been beaten to it by other games, maybe not in every field, but in each area I can name at least two or three games that stand above it. The one area it does win out on is bang for the buck. It's kinda hard to argue with this kind of quality at this kind of price point. It's a very, very solid return on investment, particularly if you're a bullet hell fan.
Does that make this a "Do not buy"? Far from it. If you're a fan of bullet hells, chances are you already own it. If you don't, eventually you should, but I'd genuinely suggest you look around first, there's a decent market now on Steam for this genre, and there's more innovative and interesting options around. If however you've already consumed them and you need a fix of something fairly solid and fairly entertaining, then sure, this works, it will scratch the itch quite nicely.

The game is well made. Graphics are good, sound is good, soundtrack is excellent although it gets old fast, hit boxes are accurate and gameplay is smooth, and bullet patterns are good but a little unbalanced at some difficulties. The game is also well optimized and runs without any hitches, and menues are well designed and easy to use. The game also gives plenty of gameplay options and shot types.
The only problem that brings the game down and ruins the whole experience is the gimmick mechanic. Get super close to bullets even when it's unnecessary to build up the boost mode meter. When the meter fills, you clear the screen of bullets and get a massive power boost to your shots and a bit wider shot range for a limited time. The idea of giving the player an incentive to get near bullets is not good when you are learning how to play these games. It's actually counterintuitive. The way to learn these games is to gradually and incrementally improve your strategies and instincts as you continue to play. The way this mechanic works does not allow for that type of learning curve to exist. When the game incentivises to get close to bullets, it breaks your process of improvement through survival instincts and reflexes. It teaches you to be reckless and mindless, which is counterintuitive.
This is made even worse in the more casual mode called "spirit mode". Whenever you kill an enemy, their bullet paths stay on screen, but their bullets become harmless. This allows the player to build the boost meter without harming themselves in the process. This causes its own problems as you tend to throw yourself straight into bullet paths you anticipate becoming nullified, but don't. It also becomes a confusing clutter of bullets that are real and fake. It even made me nauseous a few times.
There's no doubt that the idea of challenging yourself by playing dangerously sounds like a cool, hardcore idea on paper, and it might actually be for those who have already played bullet hell games for years and gotten to that point. For anyone who wants to improve rather than just show off, stay the ♥♥♥♥ away.
