If you played SR4 but thought "this game would be way better with no story missions, customization, or music", then Gat Out Of Hell is the perfect game for you, because it has none of those things.
This isn't to say that I didn't enjoy the game, just know what you are getting: a SR game consisting almost entirely of side activities. The sandbox elements of SR have always been fun, but the brilliant campaign missions (think Murderbowl, the freefall firefight at the beginning of SR3, and the MGS inspired stealth mission in SR4) are what really make me love the series. So in that regard, GooH falls a bit short.
But at a much cheaper price tag than a full game, it does a lot of things really well. Hell is a well made environment with some nice touches. The new weapons are as creative, fun, and devastating as ever. If you want to run around just destroying hundreds of demons, they definitely give you the right tools. The powers are also a nice improvement from SR4. Flying is especially of note as an improvement. It genuinely feels good to soar around hell on the wings, especially when they are full upgraded. The other powers are pretty familiar if you played SR4, but have some creative and useful improvements. But seriously, I can't stress it enough, the flying is probably the best part. It just handles so well...
For a $20 game, I completely enjoyed the 8ish hour experience of completing all of the activities. But here's where I have a major problem with GooH. I've 100%'d the rest of the series (in the case of SR3, I've done it twice), and I'm going to 100% this game as well. The challenges have always been fairly grindy in past releases, but it's a little absurd in GooH. Unfortunately, the challenges weren't scaled down at all from SR3 or 4, so it takes way longer to complete them all after you've completed the rest of the game. Killing 1000 enemies with super powers wasn't a huge deal in the 30ish hour SR4, but is just hours of post game grinding in the 8 hour GooH. I have already more than doubled my "story" playtime just doing challenges, and I still have 1 left, which will take me at least an hour or two. It honestly lost a lot of it's fun about 6 hours of grinding kills ago. Obviously this will only be a problem for completionists, but it has certainly annoyed me.
I also had a bug with the upgrade all powers achievement not unlocking (possibly due to me playing connected to my friend's game). Achievement bugs are always annoying, but this one is especially so as I'm going to have to start a new game, play my way back up to the max level (20), and go around collecting all 940 souls again. Hours of getting the same collectables for the second time is not exactly how I want to end my game play experience, but at least you can collect most of them while flying, so at least I can enjoy that.
All in all, you should play GooH if you enjoyed SR3 and 4. Don't expect the same full experience as either of those, but does  feature the same kind of wacky fun. I definitely wouldn't recommend GooH to anyone who hasn't played (or enjoyed) either of the 2 previous releases, but there's plenty to love here for any Saint looking for some more murder time fun time.

- Surrendering Players get AI'd, so you can still lose the match or you don't feel to have won a match against a human. So the key element (PvP) is obsolete since the AI-matches give you almost the same amount of gold (15 vs. 20) while beeing so much easier.

Review:
This game came out in 2007, and it feels like it. The graphics are still amazing, and look better than some of the games now, but the overall mechanics feel dated.
The story so far is a bit generic. Aliens.
The enemy AI is laughable. They have no problem finding loud noises or seeing you. They're even blind if you're standing in tall grass, which is something games now can learn from. Where the AI really fails is finding you when you're using a silencer. If you shoot a wall, they will predictably, look toward where you fired. But, if you get them with a body shot, they will still frantically look around trying to find you. I hit you in the body!! How do you not know where I’m shooting from!?! Likewise, if you kill an enemy next to another, that enemy will have trouble finding you as well. This makes the silencer rather overpowered, and takes the difficulty down to a minimum.
The game tries to emphasize stealth, alerting the enemies to your presence will usually result in many more enemies herding to your location. Unfortunately, stealth kills weren’t a standard mechanic at the time. You can however pick up your enemy and use them like a shield, though they die fairly quickly.
The cloaking ability itself is rather overpowered as well. You can easily switch back and forth between cloak and armor, using a small amount of cover to regenerate your energy.
Where the game shines most is in the minor features that games now really should have.
Highly destructible environments. You can throw a grenade into a building, and the thing will collapse down, killing anyone inside. You can also chop down a tree with your gun, then proceed to chop that tree into several pieces.
Weapon customization is done during the missions, and by picking up other weapons, you can add their mods to your repertoire. This allows you to change your style according to the situation that you’re about to enter.
The overall style of this game is great, with amazing art. Very good immersion.
And… It’s just fun. The level designs allow you to approach an area however you want and play in your own style. The weapon customizations allow you to tweak based on your current situation. The gameplay is just fun.

I bought this game almost a month after release so I'll write about its current state (as it should be). I don't care if it was not ideal before patches because it's a pretty amazing game as it currently stands, and people should update their reviews.
In short, I'll list the pros and cons of it as a sequel in the Civ series.
Pros:
- Those that like domination victory will rejoice, it is now more viable then it has ever been before. Units now get upgraded globally without additional costs, which eliminates the awkward situations where (in the previous titles) you'd send a knight across the continent only to have it arrive at it's destination when it was already 1 or 2 tiers behind. Which essentially meant that you could only *properly* wage war in the final stages of the game.
- Those that despise domination have more than just their forces to defend them (even though your own forces are still the best defense) Miasmas, orbital lasers and communication arrays, absurdly long canyons, numerous defensive upgrades that make your cities unconquerable and even covert agents are now cheap and effective ways to subdue warmongering players.
- Stations are not "minor civs". They are very useful and a lot less annoying. You even get to pick which resources some of them will offer. Think of them as stand-alone corporations (trading partners) that only defend themselves within their single tile.
- Aliens combined with miasma are an amazing feature. You won't get that feeling unless you try sending a unit anywhere outside of your base (even across the ocean) and contending with its many denizens.
Mixed:
- The new tech tree is terribly confusing for beginners and amazing for people who know that they're doing. Thankfully they allowed players to filter research based on their needs. For example, if you colonized too quickly you'll need
Cons:
- Not all affinities are easy to get (some need dozens of turns more to acquire) It makes those that aim for harmony a lot weaker in the beginning. The ability to mix affinities helps but it comes with its own set of problems.
- A few minor UI bugs here and there. I can't imagine it being a problem if you get the message that the person who is losing the war is getting dangerously close to a domination victory :D
-If you go all the way up in the Supremacy tree (and I mean ALL the way) your entire population will be cybernetic, yet they still need to watch out for their health and get bonuses from genetic engineering. Spolier:
I think this shows that they still need to work out some of the finer attributes to immersion in future sequels.
More info:
Happiness is no more, health is the new standard and it can be sky high even during times of war if you deeply care about your citizens not-starving and hopefully tapping into their gene pool.
Health is a lot easier to manage and it provides constant bonuses (or penalties if below zero) instead of providing golden ages in hard-to-sync intervals.
Victories are now straightforward because everything else isn't. The terrain is now more interesting then ever and overcoming its difficulties (unpassable tiles, alien swarms, miasma) is leads to fun and engaging projects.
Also, don't let the fact that you can mix affinities and virtues let you think that every game will be the same. Unless you're playing on the lowest difficulties you won't have time to research half of it before the game ends which makes the number of viable builds immense.
Finally, fighting miasma and aliens across the globe is a very expensive effort requiring an astounding amount of forces. This makes landmass an even more important resource than in any of the previous titles.
If this still seems like a Civ V reskin (as I'm sure it does to many people) then go and try out the free demo. I've personally come to the conclusion that only the grid layout and model shading are similar.

No, this is not just a re-skinning of Civilization V!  I am sure this is the first question that everyone has about this game, and it was definitely my deepest worry when I purchased it.
I've played through the game several times now and I have to say I am extremely impressed by the thought that went into the changes to the way the technology web and culture expansions work, as well as the new way that upgrades are applied to units.  Speaking of units, this game has some of the most incredible and fun units of any 4X type game I have ever played, and there are SO many of them!  The music and art are fantastic, the journal entries by the leaders lend a lot of character to them, and the AI seems to have pretty good strategization capabilities.  Possibly the best improvement over Civ V and Civ IV though is the espionage, it is finally a great blend of being useful/necessary, but simple to manage and not tedious.  Lots of fun stuff you can do with spies now, and the city intrigue modifier is interesting also.
I am very impressed with the game overall, and thrilled that they kept their word on the Linux release which runs flawlessly.  I would recommend this game to any fan of the genre, you won't be disappointed.

The Stanley Parable is kind of like Jim Carey in the film The Truman Show (1998). There was a particular scene where he's about to go to work. And as he walks into the revolving door, he gives it a bit of thought and chooses not to enter instead.
You may like this game... you may not like this game. But the one thing you will love about it is the narrator. He's somewhat reminiscent of Wheatley from Portal 2, except the narrator is a voice in Stanley's mind.
The game play is a walking simulator with about 17 different endings. In about a 4 hour period you will more than likely discover half of those without the aid of a guide. I'm not a big fan of multiple endings, but there were some variations with each restart to make the game play seem non-annoyingly repetitive. But the variations do seem random, so annoying repetitiveness will be inevitable. To save anyone reading this one of the many pains ... there is an "Escape" ending. In which a female narrator will tell you to go to main menu and "Quit" before it's too late. Pressing quit as opposed to letting yourself be crushed by some machine yields the same result. For some reason I can't recall anymore I ended up doing this about four times because I thought I had missed something.
Perhaps the most interesting thing about the game is not the game itself. Rather the community and how they went about solving how to get some achievements like "Unachievable" and "Commitment" which was about playing The Stanley Parable for the entire duration of a Tuesday. I really thank those who figured it out, because like hell I'm going to leave my PC on for 24 hours on a Tuesday just to get a silly achievement. The jokes on you devs ;P
It really makes me wonder though. Were the binds for "Unachievable" leaked by the devs? If not, how was it figured out? What's the story of the people who figured out how to get to some non-straight forward endings? Did someone really play The Baby Game for 4 hours? Did they use a macro at least?
Do tell.

All in all, it's not the worst little game I've played. But that's just it... it's little.
Small of scope, if you will.
What this is, make no mistake about it, is just a reskin of Civ-V minus half, if not more,
of the (expansion driven) depth.  Quests? More like "pick your perk", no depth, no feeling
of actually being on an alien planet. In fact, this feels like "Earth Invasion 2035" or some
modpack of like name, since this could have been done (and I can't help to repeat myself)
as a mod.
Sure, sure. "How dare you compare it to something like Alpha Centauri?! You shouldn't,
it's not meant to be a clone."
Duh, really, nobody expected a clone, we expected better.
But let's test that "This aint SMAC" theory shall we?
In the past Civilization added something called Colonization to it's stable. And somewhat
later they added something called  Alpha Centauri which was about the remnants of mankind
or some such fleeing the Earth to establish colonies on an alien planet, hopefully to prosper.
Does this ring a bell?
Noticed that pattern repeating itself lately?
Colonization then ... ?
(Yes, I am aware of the period of time that passed between many of these games... but they
still are part and parcel of SM's brand.)
Years have run their course since SMAC first appeared, the tools and resources for
making incredible games have become more amazing, more streamlined (to some extent)
and the pool of creativity has increased god knows how much.
How the hell do you make a game STEP BACK in quality and depth, not just from its "ancient" predecessor but also from a base game that was released not long before? I mean this sucks even compared to CIV V, the base game of which at least kept me interested in it for the amount of
turns it took to research everything and take over most of the map.
Perhaps next time we spend a little less money and time on cut scenes and promo video clips and more on gameplay development.
I pray and I hope they take an inordinate amount of time and effort with the expansions (if any) to flesh out this "game". But somehow I get the feeling the mod community will have to nurture this poor pup to its potential. If not, well then perhaps it is best to let nature do what she does best.

The next part of what is probably the more beloved indie shmup series to grace Steam is here, and it's fiercer than ever.
retains the core premise of being the fastest and flashiest shoot'emup offering around while offering an accessible and easy to manage experience for newcomers. It once again offers the most dazzling of bullet patterns with the most intuitive and accessible of controls for easy and gratifying swoops between the bursts of colorful shrapnel, while upping the ante with an engaging new mechanic that rewards your most daring and tricky maneuvers. It's been a long wait since 2, but the monumental leap in quality has made it more than worth the wait.
's visuals have evolved from its very indie predecessors to a point of pure polish and bright, arcade bliss. The designs of ships are much clearer and the animations of their movement much smoother, the backgrounds are layers deep and have an attractive sci-fi complexity that just wasn't present in 2, and all around the whole package just feels much more professional. The screen is constantly alive with flashes of light and bursts of color, and breaking into a well-time Trance mode has the overwhelming assault on the senses that gives the transformation an impactful satisfaction.
Any fan will be excited to hear BLANKFIELD makes a return for more powerful and heavy themes to your score-chasing destruction. The same fast, pulse-driving, almost math rock-y heavy guitar riffage is here with an extra layer of blissful headbanging melody. Just like the game itself, BLANKFIELD seems to have only grown in talent and musical ambition with a much cleaner and more experienced sound than before. It drives the frenetic pace of the game more than well, but I do miss the lower-quality grit of the older and more appropriately indie sound. Fans of the genre, however, will not be the least bit disappointed.
The newly introduced Graze and Spirit systems in place are fun and easy to grasp, while being incredibly deep in the long-run for seasoned players who play dangerously and want a higher skill ceiling. Your inner daredevil is rewarded as every bullet that comes close to contact with your core sparks against your ship and adds to the powerful Trance meter, bringing you closer to a satisfying power trip. This gives talented pilots even more reason to play recklessly, weaving in and out of the spinning streams of bright bullets to graze closely and collect energy for a satisfying burst of power.
still excels at what it does best; making you feel like an utter and complete arcade bad♥♥♥♥♥even when you might not necessarily be one. The satisfying screen clear of bullets when neutralizing enemies, the flash of your Trance meter filling and the intense overdrive of power thereafter, and the fluid, pinpoint control of your ship as you dance between the mesmerizing patterns of bullets make
the most refreshing shmup offering around, and a perfect entry point for newcomers and curious shooters alike. For the longest time
was the one of the best shoot'emup series you could find on Steam, and 3 re-validates that entirely for a new generation.

The Last Remnant is my favorite JRPG of all time, and definitely holds a place of my top 10 games of all time. Here's why.
This game is wholly unique. Usually, when one says "JRPG", you have a good sense of what you're getting into. Cliched characters (whether you like those cliches or not), quirky personalities, a turn-based battle system, a long convoluted story with plenty of twists, and be prepared to roll your eyes or shake your fist at the screen for some character antics or story twists you saw coming from early on. In The Last Remnant, little of this is true. The story is unique, the art style and characters are unique, some of the twists and story archs are surprising, and the battle system is so unlike anything else you've ever played, somewhere between a JRPG and a large scale strategy game with army simulation elements.
This game is known to be quite challenging. I bought the Xbox 360 version on the game's release date, and have beat the game a few times and put a couple hundred hours into it. After completing my first PC playthrough tonight after about 90 hours, I can say for certain the PC version is about 3000% easier. An update was made to the game that made a few changes that made the PC version exponentially easier, though it is still more challenging than the average RPG. So if you happened to try the 360 version and were turned off by its difficulty, I urge you to try the PC version.
The Last Remnant needs to be commended for its ability to have realistic and relatable characters, and multiple characters you care about and will remember forever. In this game, you are able to literally build up a small army to take into battles with you, where enemies and your people are separated into "unions" rather than each person being separate from one another. It is here where the game brings in large-scale strategy type battles, allowing the unions to act as one unit. Strategy fans will delight in the ability to hire soldiers and characters for their army, picking and choosing people based on their unique skill sets and abilities. You are able to hire people you've perhaps done quests with, or people you've never met that happen to have a skill you've never heard of, just because you want to see it in action. You then pick and choose which people to put with whom, how to set up your unions, etc., giving limitless possibilities for your army. Also, your followers will often ask for certain items, ingredients, etc. throughout the game, which they'll use to upgrade their equipment and become even more badass. (And trust me, this game is full of badass characters.) You can also dictate how your soldiers level up, as they ask you from time to time if you want them to delve into a different skill set or art style.
Even if the game had a terrible story and cliched characters, the battle system would keep me crawling back. Battles are by far the best part of this game. While some will say that some boss battles can be "cheap" or "unfair," I'd argue that your characters also unlock plenty of abilities and special moves that are just as if not more cheap or unfair to the enemy (Blackout is ridiculously powerful, for example, and that's a move my unions ended up using frequently). In summary, fights can be nail-biting, because you are constantly reminded that you are fighting enemies that are just as skilled and able as you. Will you still scream at the game in frustration? Sometimes, yes. But I've personally also nearly broken things with excitement when a single decision or a stroke of luck turned the tide of battle. Also, I'll let it be known that I find games that are hard just to BE hard quite annoying and to be little to no fun. This is not a game that is consistently cheap or unfair. It can be extremely challenging, and you'll call BS on a fight from time to time, but with strategy, that same fight on your next try could be immensely rewarding and much simpler.
The Last Remnant is a refreshing game in a genre that is usually predictable. It has a gritty realism that is usually reserved for western RPGs. It also respects its characters. You'll find no little girls with parasols fighting in battle, nor will you have a guy insist on being shirtless while on the battlefield (seriously...whenever I see that, I think about how easy it'd be to take them out). The characters--while they can be quirky and humorous at times--are never walking cliches. Each woman or man has her or his own personality, back story, goals and motivations--and YOU get to decide whether or not to add them to your army and help them grow over time.
This game is a true gem. It is nothing less than a crime that a game of such originality is not mentioned in conversations of JRPGs more often. This is the JRPG that I hold every other JRPG up to--and until we get another game in this universe, I see no other game coming close. I cannot recommend this game enough.

This game is definitely one of my favourites that I own. It isn't exactly amazing, but it isn't bad at all. The story is pretty good, nothing too exciting however. You don't really get any sort of connection with the characters. You're kinda just an elf, dwarf and a human who are tossed together, it feels. Throughout the game you get to visit places such as Fornost, the Barrow-downs, Rivendell and even Carn Dum, the capitol of the old Angmar empire.
As far as pros go, the story is alright, and you can tell the devs did put a bit of research into things. There's a few nice name drops here and there as well. The soundtrack is pretty good, and none of the levels are exactly impossible, though in some cases it can get that way pretty easily. Combat is alright, consists mainly of LMB for light attacks and RMB for heavier attacks, or a critical attack when the enemy has a yellow arrow over their head. You also have 3 abilities for melee and 3 for ranged, used with the 1, 2 and 3 buttons. You also have a handy eagle to call with the fourth. Combat isn't exactly amazing however, I'll admit, though it's pretty simple to get the hang of. Isn't slippery or hard to adapt to whatsoever. You and your companions are, in a way, tied in with that of the Fellowship, and several things that occur in the movies happen because of things you did, which is pretty neat.
Now to the cons. This game is pretty well known to have a LOT of bugs. There's a few quests in particular that are very buggy, and you can easily screw yourself over with them. If you're focusing on whether this is canon, I've seen mostly people saying that it is not canon. The achievements aren't very bad at all, either, though the "strength of our alliance" achievement is extremely tedious to get in my experience, and is very buggy as well. There is a lot of issues when it comes to balance. As Farin, the dwarf, unlocking the explosive bolt can do up to 150k damage from what I've seen personally. Which can instant-kill trolls and usually 2-3 shot a boss. Took around 8 shots or so to kill the final boss with it. Now, what I said earlier about the levels sometimes being crazy hard comes down to you. If you run out of health potions, you do NOT have the option to save manually. So, if you go into a level, run out of potions and can't leave (example being a later stage of Nordinbad) you're pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed, and you have to do it on your own. Ended up doing this myself and trying to do it with no health potions, which isn't too easy.
To 100% complete the game there's a minimum of 3 playthroughs to get the achievement for beating the Legendary mode. This is a little bit of a con as well, in that there isn't really any sense of a challenge. Mobs do a little more damage and take some more as well, but it never really is an issue.
Now, be warned, two levels in particular, the Barrow-downs and Carn Dum are very well known for crashing computers. I run the game flawlessly on ultra settings, but I crash constantly in these spots. I read that it has something to do with AMD drivers or something along the lines, but I don't know much about that. Just be warned that it does have some crashing issues.
In the end, the game is pretty good, has a good bit of replayability, it isn't boring or stretched thin, and it's pretty well rounded. It does have a lot of bugs and isn't the greatest with balance in the second and third playthroughs, (being in your favour as opposed to being in the enemy's favour) but there isn't really any game breaking issues. This is a real gem, a very thoughtfully crafted game. Even as late as 2014, I might call it the best game since Civ4 came out in 2005. The basic setup is almost cliche: three factions, three types of resources, spend those resources on tech/buildings/units, kill enemy. However, it distinguishes itself in several ways to become a truly great game. First, you play at both a macro and micro level and everything between, and the game somehow makes this seemingly incompatible mix of scales work unbelievably well. Second, unlike many RTS it is not all about APM, as it proceeds at a pace where deliberative thought is possible. It is an RTS that might appeal to TBS players. Third, despite the slower pace there's still plenty to do, because it does a great job in presenting the user with interesting meaningful and situationally appropriate choices, from where and how to spend resources, how aggressively to push, and with what ships. You're constantly making choices, and the game somehow manages that precise balance only the greatest games do of making you never quite comfortable with that choice.
One flaw: The learning curve is steep without a campaign. It's not a complex game, really. It's easily playable with nothing more than a mouse, after all. However, it takes a while to appreciate that and let the true depth of the game shine through. I understand things more or less well now, but it was a hard slog. (To save time: Read GoaFan77's guide, every last word of it. I didn't have that advantage when I started.)

My first play through was difficult both in game dynamics and mentally for me, the gamer. I lasted three hours. Then Anton, one of my team of three got sick. The second, his name was Bruce, he got stabbed in a raid. They took our medicine, food and bandages and left our friend hurt. Paulo tried to go out and get medicine and bandages, but eventually Anton succumbed to his illness. The two remaining survivors were sad and mourned his death, spending an entire day grieving. That night, Bruce left. No note, no goodbye. Paulo spent that third day sitting alone in the empty house. He wouldn't eat the food, wouldn't sleep in the bed, he just sat there. Crying about the loss of his friends, wondering if he'd ever see his little boy again. I told him, "Just hold on one more day, maybe things will get better. Maybe tomorrow will be ok." That night Paulo committed suicide. Then I had to sit there, staring blankly at the screen, grieving for three character's I had become so attached to as their 'final words' came across the screen. The first, Bruce, he died from his illness, there was nothing we could do, there was no medicine to be found, it was all taken in the raid. Bruce, well, he left in the middle of the night to go into the city to try and find his family but was betrayed by a trader and killed. He died alone in the city, killed like a dog. And Paulo, he hung himself in the attic because he had lost hope of ever finding his son after the war.
That was three hours of game play, I felt like it was a life-time of heart ache.
My next play-through I made it and we survived the war, no one died, not a single character, but it cost us. Paulo stole from the elderly couple, because we needed medicine for Anton. We left them some medicine, but we took what we needed while the elderly couple cried and hid in the bathroom, begging Paulo to leave. Anton spent the next three days distrusting Paulo, doubting him. "Is this what we've become?" The others, they spent those days wondering if the sickly elderly woman would survive. If WE really needed the medicine more then her. We stole, we killed, we offered aid and we survived, and in the end what did we get? Meek stories, stories that felt real. There were no happy endings. Anton was ruined by the war, Paulo? He's still trying to find his son.
This game is amazing, and you need it in your life.

Crysis is the best and worst of gaming.
The best is it's got all this emergent gameplay based around simulation, where there is a giant map you can seemingly go anywhere in, can accomplish objectives however you want. Blow up all the buildings, drive all of the vehicles.
Your suit has a great mechanic to it where you can select between "modes" like strength, speed, or armor, and run around
The game is surprisingly low budget as well, but uses every dollar spent to maximum effectiveness, because it's not about the "guided cinematic experience" but rather the actual gameplay.
The bad is the gameplay isn't all that great.
All of the randomness in the gameplay systems makes for a frustrating experience. Mostly this takes the place of weapon accuracy where you are forver at the mercy of RNGesus. Sometimes you can waltz into the middle of a crowd of enemies and one shot them all to the face. Sometimes you can shoot into a wall and the enemies still die. Other times RNGeus will dictate your shotgun blasts all miss and the AI gets headshots at the same time and you die instantly. Sometimes enemies take 3 seconds to react to you standing directy in front of them. Other times you get insantly killed by a mounted machine gun on a boat 1 km away while you are hiding in the bushes.
Other games with recoil, even in 2007, usually make it feel good by making the camera shake so the weapon always shoots where it points, in a semi-random pattern you can learn to control. In this game the bullets spray out in a random pattern around the reticle, in addition to randomly rotating your camera to simulate unsteady aim, in addition to randomly rotating your reticle because of screen space "cinematic" effects.
The audio sounds good sometimes, and bad other times. There is an issue with prioritizing effects here. Stuff like distant explosions has no audio at all, because the game doesn't know that is more important than a nearby ambient sound.
Something with the rendering pipeline seems to be adding significant display lag to things. This is often done when people want to really push graphics, as you can parallelize things better if you can delay processing of graphics stages by several frames so the CPU isn't spent waiting. Unfortunately in this case it seems to mean where you shoot isn't where the graphics is rendering you will shoot, but rather where you are in the simulated world. This is just too much lag for a FPS game that asks for precision. RNGesus may be here to try and mask this issue.
The end result is the gameplay loop is reduced to this: save often.
This may have been the norm in 2007, but playing it in 2016... yeah it's not worth finishing IMO.

Well, this was kind of disappointing.  I love Saints Row!  The consistent original style and fun gameplay of the entire franchise has been nothing short of astonishing and ironically. in some ways even surpasses the Grand Theft Auto franchise (the series that Saints Row was initially dismissed by many for it's similarities), despite Saints Row significantly smaller budget and development timeframe.  Saints Row IV was my second favorite in the franchise, behind Saints Row II and Kinzie Kenzington (my favorite character in the franchise) is a playable character in this game, which picks up after the events of Saints Row IV, so I had some high hopes for this game, while also remaining cautious in my expectations due to it's mere $20 price tag.  I wasn't expecting anything spectacular and yet I was still disappointed.
I've played Saints Row IV to death and I was eager to play a brand new entry in the franchise, what I found was basically the same game, playing like a total conversion mod but with half of the features in IV removed.  Why the hell is there absolutely no radio in this game?  Why are no clothing stores or customizable outfits of any kind?  Why is the map so much smaller than it has ever been in any other Saints Row game?  Why giving the game a plot when almost the entire game consists of "city takeover" side quests that have absolutely nothing to do with the plot?  These are only some of the many questions you'll end up asking yourself as you play this game.
Many fans were initially skeptical of SRIV's quality before it was released after news broke that it was originally supposed to be DLC for Saints Row III, and they were eventually proven wrong when SRIV turned out to written and developed well enough to actually justify it's status as a stand-alone title; But be warned, this is the real deal!  A stand-alone Saints Row game that really should have been DLC for Saints Row IV!  Even with it's $20 price tag, it's still lacking enough content and plot to justify it as a stand-alone title in the franchise.
In short, if you're new to Saints Row or you're not a die-hard fan, don't buy it.  However, if you're a Saints Row fanatic like me, I'd recommend it, but wait until it's on sale for $5 or lower, because that's what most DLC should be worth and this is just DLC pretending to be it's own game.

First and foremost this isn't like MTG 2014 or 2015, it's a free 2 play version based on the Origins set from MTG. There's a base set consisting of 256 cards which include lands and they will be adding new sets just like the regular version of MTG does. The free 2 play model is pretty good and similar to the model Hearthstone has. You can unlock everything without paying a dime. If you choose to buy packs you can though. The game isn't pay 2 win, it's pay for convenience. The gold is currently capped at 400 gold per day, however this doesn't apply to the story mode, quests, tutorials or the 20 gold bonus you receive for your first pvp match of the day. There is an option to buy packs, however it's only an option.
There are cunnrelty 4 game modes.. Story Mode, Solo Battle Mode, Versus Battle Mode, and Two-Headed Giant. There's no chat so you might want to add the person you team up with on steam or use a voice server so you can communicate with your teammate since there's no chat in game. The game has a full deck creator and you can create up to 30 decks.
If you played MTG you kinda know what to expect. For those that haven't and are coming from games like Hearthstone, this game requires more skill and is a lot deeper than Hearthstone is. Like many fans, I was really hyped for this game, having played the crap out of Civ 5. Unfortunately, it feels like an inferior Civ 5. Cities, units, combat, and geography are mostly the same. That's fine, but what's not similar to Civ 5 is typically worse.
IMO, the tech web is a mess. I understand that it's now non-linear, and you can't research everything, but it's so clunky and disorganized that I often feel like I'm just researching random things that I don't even need. I see something I want but it's 5 techs away, with 100+ turns of research required, so instead I research some smaller thing that doesn't help me at all.
Aliens replaced barbarians, but again it feels clunky. Befriending them seems great, but more than anything they simply get in your way. They keep spawning infinitely, and so if you don't kill them off they overrun your space, especially on a small space like an island. If you do kill them, then AI players hate you, just for defending your space. Civ is a game about expanding and placing cities, is it not? Barbarians worked in 5 because they were annoying but rewarding too, whereas aliens are annoying, take up space, and get you denounced by AI players.
The interface is crap as well IMO. It's designed in a "futuristic" style, but it just comes off as busy and user-unfriendly. Hell, for the first two games I couldn't even find the Trade Overview screen because they did such a good job of hiding things instead of having everything displayed at once (but still cleanly) like in Civ 5. Some things are too big or too small, and like I said, things aren't clear, they're hidden for some reason.
Altogether, it just feels like a less interesting Civ 5 in space. For me, I can sink hours at a time into a Civ 5 game because the tech race is so fun, competing for wonders and grabbing that good area before your neighbour does. In BE, there's no tech race, because everyone does their own thing, except on top of that, tech in BE seems quite disorganized. Instead of racing players for space, you're racing annoying aliens that don't stop spawning, and also get you known as the BE equivalent of a "warmonger". Not enjoyable.
TLDR, if you haven't played Civ 5 (with the DLCs), then do that instead. If you have, well maybe you should just play it more. That's what I've been doing.

This remaster had an extremely rough and badly executed launch. Bug ridden and lacking basic features necessary to play it on a PC, such as the possibility of disabling the awful mouse acceleration, graphical configurations and, on top of this, ridden with bugs and constantly crashing. It took the devs a month after the release to provide a patch which fixed, at least in my case, the majority of the bugs and crashes which plagued this and added the necessary basic configurations/options to call this a PC game.
Graphics in this version were revised and hold well to 2016 standards, giving the original Bioshock a facelift for a next-gen console release gave me reason enough to re-play through it. The core gameplay is unchanged.
As to Bioshock itself, this is one of those stories that you simply must play through. The setting and level design is breathtaking at times, the characters are interesting, the and the story is extremely well put together. The various voice recordings will tell you the tale of what Rapture was and what eventually brought it down, be it stubborn ideals of it's ruler or the manipulative political play of an extremely influential powermongering faction leader in the middle of this free market society, and of a few characters, both pertaining to the plot and context of Rapture and the player's.
The gameplay is that of your typical FPS with a currency and power system, in the form of money/adam and plasmids, respectively. The gunplay is fun and challenging at points. The progression you go through is noticeable and entertaining and the 'bosses' are pretty good aswell.
All in all, I'd give it an 8/10. If you've never played through Bioshock, you should. As soon as possible. This is a must. If you already played through the original game at some point, try the remaster eventually.

First of all, I really appreciate the intent and work of the developers in order to bring back Bioshock game for us, and for blowed down the dust from this great game with a remastered version.
I've decided to wait with my review until the first Patch is released.
Therefore I will not take into account the issues at the beginning, which were solved in the meantime.
BUT
God, I'm still quite dissapointed with the technical background of this game.
I've played through the original Bioshock game many times, long before I bought it on steam.
The game's atmosphere was very great with the underwater environment, where everything is collapsing and - at some places, where the water found it's place inside the buildings - the walls and floors gone wet.
The Remastered version simply not reflecting this back.
Yes, It's visible that some new models and meshes added, and the textures are much better as well, but what about the lightning and the wet environmental effects? Where are those just gone in the meantime?

When I took the first steps on the stairs of the light-house at the beginning of the game, I've realized that the lights of the vibrating lamps, and the wet effects from the stairs are completely missing in the new version. Later, I looked out from the window of the batisphere, I saw some sea-plants and medusas were added, that's great, but what happened with the whale? It looks like completely dry under the water! Where are the ripples, and underwater bubbles? Everything is covered with sharper textures, while those effects which made the whole environment complete are actually missing, or maybe not visible because of some technical issues.
(I just checked at this point that all effects are switched on in the graphics menu and yes they were set on.)
Later, I've realized that - even if some meshes are changed -  they are not loaded correctly.
When I come closer to some statues, the engine is loading some low-res meshes and textures.
Not to mention that I still experiencing some strange mouse issues during and after cutscenes.
The crashes were solved when I installed the latest GTX 970 Nvidia driver and updated Windows 10 to the latest version, but for me, the game lost it's atmosphre. You can find better Shooter experience, but not this atmosphere. I've tried to play with the Gamma settings, and look into .ini files, without success.
To make sure that my memories are not just playing with me, I have installed the original game, and went through on the first part again and I've felt: Yes, this is the game I like so much. Somehow the environment feels more wet, more ruined and creepy.
I'm sorry if someone is not on the same point, or disagree with my opinion, but I've always looked the ART behind this game.

Bioshock is one of my favorite games ever.
I was pleasantly surprised when this remaster appeared in my library, as I recieved it for free from owning the original. I immediatly installed it and played it and it felt brand new again.
As a game: Bioshock is incredible. It's setting and story fascinate me, and it's singleplayer FPS gameplay/progression is well done.
But this is a remaster, and as others have said, the game is not without its bugs. Personally, I experienced no bugs or crashes when playing through the entire game, but because of the bugs so many others complain about, I would recommend purchasing with caution.
But as a fan of Bioshock, I would recommend this remaster, as it makes the game feel new again. The new, higher resolution textures look great, and the lighting system looks so much better than the original. The game also includes developer commentary that dives into the process behind the creation of the game, coupled with a concept art and scrapped ideas museum that you can walk through and see much more of what the game could have been, if not for time and budget constraints. Other than that, the game is exactly the same as the original, but with a nice polish. I appreciate the effort the devs put in to one of my favorite games.
Should you purchase this game?
The answer resolves to a resounding: maybe. I am biased, as I recieved the game for free and I encountered no bugs, so take what I say with a grain of salt. I do, however, recommend it, as it was, and still is, a great game. If you already own the original game, and did not recieve it for free, however; I would say to save your money, as you really aren't missing out on much.

Last Remnant is a JRPG with some good production values and it is worth buying cheap on that count alone. The 'thing' with Last Remnant is the combat system that lets you put up to an army of characters into battle for you. To do this however the game engine has a lot of complexity and much is this is shielded from the player by automation. If you let the automation do everything then you're not involved much and your characters won't improve. However the problems come when you naturally try to understand what's happening and manage the automaton. Unfortunately, it's just difficult to get past the automation and the manual doesn't help you to do it at all. For example there massive amount of detailed itemization in the game and it is important to equip your characters well, however you can't give them items unless they ask for it. They typically won't ask for stuff you want them to have, but if they do they ask for the wrong item, the wrong person asks for it, the same person asks for everything, and even if they take something they might discard it for something worse later. That's just one side of the itemisation problems as well.
So anyway, there are a lot of good things in just playing Last Remnant but it encourages you look into the complexity and disappoints when it is frequently opaque.

Bioshock 2 doesn't quite excel as much as the first one did at a viscerally innovative experience and unexpected journey, but nonetheless does a great job of constructing a fun and interesting second foray into the underwater city of Rapture.
The simultaneous use of weapons and plasmids is welcome, and the game is still plenty challenging, provided you pick a normal difficulty level. It doesn't come with an equal share of memorable moments to the first Bioshock, but the story of the search of Johnny Topside for Eleanor is peppered with the same gripping atmosphere that made the first game so haunting, with only slightly less of a punch, but nonetheless draws the game to a memorable finale.
Considering Bioshock 2 takes place 8 years after the first one, I scratched my head over what the still sane and human denizens of Rapture had done all those 8 years in Rapture, considering it was in more or less an identical state in the first iteration of the series, but if you ignore that, the game had a great story and the gameplay, with its numerous weapons and plasmids, and chances to upgrade both, and similar moral dilemmas that the first one presented, I think it's a very competent follow-up to the first Bioshock.

Someone gifted this game to me. I was curious, intrigued by the art style. I'm a fan of Metroidvania games. This... I'm sad to say... is something of a letdown.
The manner of animation makes the game feel choppy and unresponsive; it's not that the game is choppy and unresponsive, it's how the action is animated. Literally. So many times I've run across a platform and gone to jump off the other side, just to run off and fall down because where I wanted to jump from was between the places the game would let me. I get stuck mid-animation when I need to change tactics (mid-attack when I need to jump, for instance), and this is letting the only fightable "boss" I've encountered (big club, shockwaves) kill me repeatedly.
You literally have to be frame-aware and frame-responsive. Or, if I had to guess at the problem another way, I'd suspect the game only checks controller input at a relatively slow rate. The game itself runs fine; control responsiveness is just that choppy.
The only save point I've reached so far (in the town) is far removed from this boss; death means going all the way back, trying to build soul power (I think?) I can't safely use mid-fight from the intervening monsters and probably getting hit by them in the process (again: mid-action when a change is needed... I need to move when I'm stuck mid-swing, and they'll hit me between swings. If I try to change my swing frequency, then I'm between swings and they hit me anyways.) and THEN I have to kill my shadow to get my coins back, while the boss is right there.
No map. There's a key for it, but no map. If I die exploring and I'm not sure where I died, how do I get my shadow and coins back?
All and all, I LOVE the style, but the poor responsiveness breaks it for me. I could look past the lack of map (and subsequent boring re-farming of coins it likely leads to if you can't find your shadow), but the unresponsive, choppy control design just wrecks it for me. Breaks my heart.

The Hitman series has continually challenged players with tracking and assassinating various targets across the world, while providing multiple routes in which to accomplish the particular tasks at hand. Absolution marks the first true entry in the current generation of games built upon its powerful, in-house built Glacier 2 graphics engine. In addition, the gameplay has been altered with the introduction of new features associated with the Instinct and Contracts modes.
Set directly after the events of the previous game, Hitman: Blood Money, Absolution tasks Agent 47 with tracking down his series handler Diana Burnwood after she goes rogue and reveals the agency's identity to the public. The new Agency director Benjamin Travis orders Agent 47 to kill Diana and capture a teenage girl by the name of Victoria that has been under her care. Upon reading a letter left from Diana, the narrative spirals into a chaotic set of events interwoven with Agent 47 being hunted by both the police and a cast of villains that aim to capture the mysterious Victoria from him. The majority of levels are set in various exterior and interior locales in Chicago and a small town in South Dakota.
A major contrast from past games in the series is the addition of entire level sequences that focus on evading the police while reaching a designated exit. In these particular sequences, players aren't even provided with particular targets to assassinate that results in the gameplay resembling a generic shooter versus a Hitman game. Some sections feel eerily similar to the gameplay of IO Interactive's past Kane and Lynch series of games. The levels that do offer particular targets to assassinate and multiple routes in which to accomplish that task are the most memorable of the narrative and beg for multiple playthroughs.
Each playthrough of a level is continually scored based on each action taken by the player from killing civilians to being detected by patrolling enemies. The game has a way in which it wants the player to complete each level and any deviations result in the loss of points. Compared with recent games in the Hitman series, Absolution includes far too many linear paths and evade the police scenarios that result in an overall more restrictive experience.
The major change in the Hitman gameplay formula in Absolution revolves around the addition of the Instinct mode. Instinct in the game is displayed through a meter that regenerates overtime through various actions taken. There are a variety of uses that involve Instinct mode from scanning the environment for enemies and their movement, which is similar to the detective mode in Batman Arkham Asylum, to a quick shot kill system, which is similar to the mark and execute feature in Splinter Cell: Conviction. While both are not original concepts, they work exceptionally well in surveying the environment and when in difficult situations that require a quick takedown of multiple enemies.
The major aspect of Instinct mode that will cause some frustration with players is how it handles disguises. NPCs in the game can detect that the player is lying about their identity if wearing the same disguise, with the example that other police officers would be able to spot someone new in their ranks. To counter this, Agent 47 can either wear disguises that aren't of the same group of NPCs or use Instinct mode to hide their true identity. Unfortunately, Instinct mode when used for disguises drains at an alarmingly quick rate that makes it useful for only brief scenarios. In later levels, disguises feel completely useless when nearly all of the NPCs are of the same group and can quickly discover Agent 47.
Aside from the new Instinct mode and cover system, nearly all of the Hitman series basics return with the infamous fiber wire and dual Silverballer pistols. Along with a host of other weaponry from pistols and shotguns to rifles and explosives, Agent 47 has the ability to utilize various weapons and staged accidents located throughout levels. Makeshift weapons appear in the form of small objects like knives, hammers, and even bongs. While some of them aren't the most practical to use in combat situations, they serve as great alternatives to when a more specialized approach is required for a certain situation.
Following with the tradition of past games in the series, Agent 47 has the ability to utilize conveniently-placed staged accidents around the level that range from a hoisted car on a lift to food items that are ripe for poisoning. While some staged accidents are simple to put in motion, others require carefully-planned timing and execution to perform the perfect assassination. Absolution stays true to the Hitman series by continually providing players with a near endless amount of options in assassinating targets from going completely Rambo style to a more subtle approach with a knife stab in the back.
Levels completed in the campaign mode can later be played through in the Contracts mode that has players setting their own targets and selecting loadouts of unlocked disguises/weapons. The points earned in the both modes can be used to unlock additional disguises, weapons, and gun modifications ranging from silencers to extended clips. Contracts mode introduces the Hitman series first online feature in that the scenarios that players devise can be uploaded online for others to download and play. When creating a custom contract, players walk through a level and assassinate whom they wish and with what disguise and weapon they feel is right for the particular task. When the target eliminated, players then rush to an exit point to complete the level. With the level complete and statistics tracked for the time taken for both assassinating the target and reaching the exit, players can then proceed with uploading the contract for other players to compete in beating their score. Players that use the particular disguise and weapon that the creator did in their original playthrough will earn additional points when completing the contract.
Contracts mode seems to be the developer's answer to the restrictive campaign levels and escape from the police sections. The Contracts mode is clearly not the perfect solution for fans that were looking for similar gameplay from the previous Hitman game, but it's a step in the right direction considering that players can select their own disguise and weapon loadout. Contracts mode will be interesting to watch as more players upload their specialized combination of levels, targets, disguises, and weapon loadouts.
IO Interactive's Glacier 2 engine can be summarized with 1 word: stunning. From the massively-rendered crowds to the detailed interior/exterior environments, Absolution never ceases to amaze with visuals that beg to be set to max. Absolution debuts as the first real entry of the Hitman series in the high-definition era of gaming and succeeds at trumping nearly all of the current game releases. The sound effects and most notably the music succeed at impressing with loud and bold gunfire and mesmerizing classical scores. The soundtrack composed by Thomas Bärtschi fits the atmosphere of Absolution perfectly whether it may be a hectic gun battle or silent takedown.
Absolution marks a bold new direction for the Hitman series that focuses less on player freedom and more on telling a defined narrative. While the levels and poorly-implemented Instinct mode are sure to anger and frustrate fans of the series, Absolution still succeeds at providing an entertaining and most importantly, engaging gameplay experience that is difficult to put down until the credits roll. Both the expansive Contracts mode and stunning graphical overhaul help in overcoming the issues associated with the restrictive campaign levels.

A standalone expansion for SR IV, Gat out of Hell lets you make the Devil's playground your own.  Satan has kidnapped the President and the player as Johnny Gat or Kinzie Kensington are going to hell to get him back.  What is Gat's plan to get the boss back? -- Simple! Shoot the Devil in the face!
If you enjoyed Saints Row IV then you should enjoy this game.  Gat out of Hell is a trimmed-down version of SR IV with a hellish theme.  You get a new city with New Hades that weighs-in approximately half the size of the Steelport map.  Super powers make a return but have different elements to reflect the new setting.  A new flight mechanic is introduced and it feels real good.  Many existing weapons also make a comeback, but new weapons reflecting the 7 deadly sins are introduced, which are very amusing and fun to use.
Mission structure is somewhat different than previous games.  There are no scripted story missions.  You are introduced to 4 allies which you gain favor by completing side activities.  Finishing all of the activities for an ally will usually grant a new weapon.  The completion of side activities will also leave a trail of destruction that will gain the attention of the big red man himself.  A progress meter will fill as the player completes more activities, and once the meter is full, Satan himself will finally show-up and confront the player.  There are some good cutscenes as the player is introduced to allies and completes their tasks.  Story specific cutscenes also play at certain points as the progress meter fills which includes an amazing musical score.  So the game mainly plays as an open world sandbox where the story ends after completing a certain amount of side activities.  Surprisingly enough, once the game ends the player gets a choice of 5 different endings.  This is merely a choice that results in a cutscene and none of the actions during the game will influence the outcome.
There is a lot to do as I spent about 20 hours completing the game to 100%, but one can actually complete the main story in 5 to 10 hours.  Additional time can be spent attempting to complete all of the numerous challenges in the game so the $20 price tag seems fair.  The numerous side activities are a lot like those from SR IV but with a twist to fit the theme.  A few new activities are also introduced to mix things up a little.
There are a few downsides that may disappoint fans of the series though...
You get to play as Gat or Kinzie, which is fantastic, but there is no customization for these characters at all.  There is also no weapon skin customization (though you can thankfully still upgrade weapons and powers).  In fact the only customization that you get in this game is the ability to import your unique "boss" from SR IV, but you only get to see the boss in a select few cutscenes.
There is no licensed soundtrack like in the other games.  There is also no special celebrity guest appearance this time.  I guess the $20 price point made these features prohibitive but it would have been awesome to see something like Ozzy Osbourne show up in hell as one of the four allies and some heavy metal from Black Sabbath blaring in the background.
Other features cut are vehicle upgrades and garages.  The player can still hijack vehicles, but the variety of those are few, and vehicles cannot be stored for retrieval or upgrade later.  I suppose these were lesser used features anyway since the super powers rendered them mostly useless.
Another minor quibble is that there is little difference between playing Gat or Kinzie other than mainly appearance.  The player may easily switch between either at the Ultor building and there is no separate upgrade path.  So the choice is mainly a cosmetic one.  Although both Gat and Kinzie has their own set of 30 audio collectibles and the player has to be playing as the respective character to find those collectibles.
I found the game to be rather entertaining as a SR IV expansion.  Definitely worth a look if you are a fan of Saints Row IV and want a little more of that kind of craziness.

Pavle never came home from his run last night.
No one said anything when he didnt return, but it was understood. Pavle was never late, he always returned just as the morning light crept over the ruins of our dear city.  But not this morning, this morning he never came back, and it was understood. A deep meloncholy had washed over the survivors safe house, for with Pavle died their last chance for survival. The others were too sick, too battered and broken to move. They would die here. Death was preferable, Marko thought as he lay bleeding on the couch. The deep wound in his side had opened over night, and without bandages, he would be dead before night came again.
"I never should have gone", he thought to himself.
Two nights prior Marko had made a run to a small apartment building just south of the survivors safe house. He knew an elderly couple and their son were still living there, but he figured he could be in and out with enough food to last his group a few days. But his plan was flawed. The elderly woman had seen him and called to her son, who swiftly charged at Marco with a knife.  Before he could react, the son was on him, the knife sunk into his side. But Marko was strong, and his flight from that apartment proved as much.
When he arrived back at their decrepid domicile, the others rushed to his aide. "Sleep my friend, we dont need to make a run tonight". Pavle had always been a kind man. A football player before the war, he had a rough exterior that hid the kindness in his heart. He was a good man. But it was cold, and they were hungry. So as night fell, Pavle took the handgun they had managed to steal from the military base, and made his way back to the small apartment.
"Im not going to hurt anyone", Pavle thought to himself as he crept along the ruined city streets. "In and out, if they see me, ill threaten them with this."
He held the gun close to himself. It was his dearest companion, his lone friend in what was to come.
The apartment was quiet as he crept inside. Perhaps, he thought, the family had fled after the scare they got from Marko last night. As he made his way into the kitchen, he noticed a picture on the wall. The family that lived here; the picture showed happier times. Pavle missed his own family, who had been seperated from him in the early days of the siege. He planned to find them just as soon as he could, and he felt great pangs of regret as he wondered what they would think if they saw him now. He was lost in thought, so much so that he didnt hear the soft footsteps behind him. All he heard was a shrill scream, and the shots being fired from his own gun.
The old woman lie dead before him, shot 3 times in the chest. Pavle was shocked, he hadnt meant to do it, he was startled and afraid.
"MOM!?!?"
The sound of footsteps grew louder, but Pavle couldnt move. He had to explain himself, had to make things right. The son entered the kitchen, staring at his mothers corpse. Pavle tried to speak, but only dull murmers escaped him. "Im sorry...Im sorry..." The son shook his head, tears streaming down his face. He closed his eyes and raised the shotgun he was carrying, leveling it with Pavles heart.
"Im sorry..."
Pavle never came home last night. No one saw him leave, but it was understood. He had taken the survivors only gun, and returned to the small apartment to take what he could. He was gone now though, it was understood. Marko could hear Bruno weeping upstairs. He had spoken earlier of taking his own life, and Marko no longer had the energy to stop him. So he lay there bleeding; waiting for whatever came next. "At least", he thought to himself,"I have some time to think." This war had ruined them, just as it had ruined their dear city. They were broken, desperate, and soon they would be dead. Why had Pavle taken the gun? What did he intend to do? He had to have known what would happen if he went back there. How did it come to this, how did they fall so far? They were good men, Pavle was a good man.
Right?

First off, I have been playing the X series since day one, so my judgement is naturally influenced by what i have seen before and what improvements i would have expected to see now. I have played 40+ hours on this one. So here goes my first impressions:
PRO:
The universe is beautiful. Actually perfect. Best I have seen in space games so far and probably exactly how I would have done it with the technical means of today. Full of life. I love exploring it and this is a big part of X. I don't mind the fact that you can only fly one ship as long as you can do a lot of upgrades with it and at some point feel like a boss. I have the feeling it's a bit to easy to get there though (which is a pro for some ppl who would just like to explore). I like that they moved to controller support but more on that in the CONS. And last but not least X Rebirth supports Mods, which are very easy to install/deinstall via Nexus Mod Manager.
CONS:
Game breaking bugs everywhere. Which has been covered to a huge extend in many forums, so I will not go into details, but as I was playing in the beginning I didn't notice them at all. Only later when you have to manage your first trade freighters you will realize the problems with Bugs, the UI or just the plain misunderstanding of how things work.
The main story serves more like a tutorial than an actual story and does a very bad job at that. Most important things that one need to know are not explained properly by your co-pilot. The voice acting btw is horrible. Very often I thought I witnessed another bug and later found out it was a misunderstood feature.
It's funny how many of the new features made a nice impression at first, but then you get annoyed by them. Here are some examples...
You can walk around stations, but sooner or later you will switch that feature off via mods, because the stations are so sterile and boring. The characters are animated poorly and the "smalltalk" minigame gets so much on my nerves, that i prefer to pay the normal price instead of going through it for a discount.
You can travel via highways, which is a brilliant idea to not cut immersion when going from one sector/system to the next, but you will switch off the lame lane mini-game via a mod pretty soon, i promise you that!
The controller support is nice to lean back and control everything on a big screen from the couch, but the UI is a torture. On one screen you have to press A to confirm, on the following screen you have to press X to confirm. The radial menu is very unresponsive to navigate through it fast enough to be comfortable and many of the details on your ships for example you have to reach not by the normal axis you use for the radial menu but with your digital cross. a few filters you can only select with the mouse and very common tasks are hidden way deep in some sub-sub-sub-menu. X was always known for horrible UI but they improved it with every iteration of the series. Now with the controller support it feels like we are back at day 1.
You cannot rename your ships, nor is all their status broadcast to you. If one of your ships gets attacked, you would like to rush over there to help them out, right? Bad luck, because the captain will tell you that he is about to unload freight, but not that they are under attack. In fact, you will only realize when you want to give a new trade order and find out that your freighter does not exist anymore. Thats one of those moments, where I assumed it was a bug.
You know those indicators, pointing to objects that are outside of your vision? Yeah, you don't have a radar (which is fine by me) but those triangles and circles on the borders of your screen. Wait a second, they are at the border of your window of the ship, so you have to scan with your eyes an uneven area around the window for your enemies red triangles, which by the way are sometimes hidden behind the cockpit metal thingy. Although I like the cockpit, it just blocks too much space. I like the fact that you can switch it off, but then you also switch of all the holographic displays and menus.
I would have prefered to see a three-degree-switch: cockpit on, holographic only, off.
Also I would have prefered to have items that are outside of my vision to be indicated around my crosshair and not at the edges of the cockpit window. Or at least at the edges of my screen, because then i would have a clear idea about where to look for my enemy in a dogfight.
CONCLUSION:
I am sure that I would find more annoyances if I would continue thinking about them long enough. But I won't. All in all I really see the potential of this game becoming great and I am quite impressed what a game studio with only around 20 people is able to produce. But unfortunately this one is just a beta quality at best. I have no clue why it got released in this state. And I really hope it's not going to be the end of Egosoft, but I think it very well could be. However, they always released games with bugs and were able to fix them. It was just never that bad as far as I remember it.
All in all, I would really like to recommend the game, especially because of its atmosphere, but without mods and savegame editing its nearly unplayable beyond the first 10h. I am sure they are going to fix that though, so just wait a while and watch the forums for messages talking about how it improved... i hope sooner than later!

Even though I'm not the best player at this game, at least not yet, I can most likely say without a shadow of a doubt that Rivals of Aether is probably going to be the best Steam game I have played in 2017 thus far. A fleshed out and equally balanced pool of characters to choose from, 8 almost balanced stages to choose from (except Tempest Peak, god I hate that stage) coupled with an OST that I can listen to for hours on end, and it's safe to say that nothing is going to top my Rivals experience, at least not this year.
There are so many hidden secrets and techniques about every character's moveset that I honestly could be spending hundreds of hours on the game and I would probably still not fully master it. With Ori coming out shortly, I can see a bright future ahead of Rivals of Aether and I will definitely be playing it for quite some time from now.
Honestly the only two complains I can give this game are:
- Exhibition and ranked online modes barely ever matches me with other Australian players, although that issue can be easily bypassed by getting games from the Australian RoA Discord server.
- The character and map pool is a little too small, but honestly, I'll take a balanced and fleshed out character and map pool over massive but mostly unplayable ones every day of the week. Plus, with Ori on the rise to shake up the game, I don't think this would be that much more of an issue moving foward.
Overall, if I had to give a score for the game, I'd give it a 8.5/10. Solid gameplay in every aspect, amazing OST, and I cannot recommend this game enough to anyone from competitive players from other Smash games (especially Melee, since this game's mechanics borrow greatly from that game) to casual players who just likes a fun game to play against friend(s) on Saturday night. Go buy it.

I love this game.
is what happens when you take competetive Super Smash Bros. Melee and make it accessible to everyone.
is a competetive Platform Fighter ("PlatFighter") which places extreme emphasis on movement and aggression. Many of the defensive maneuvers from Nintendo's Super Smash Brothers series are absent: you cannot grab ledges, and shields have been replaced with ridiculously strict (1/20th of a second) parries that leave opponents vulnerable. There is virtually NO defense in this game, so professional Smash 4 players need not apply (#ShotsFired).
As of this writing, the game contains eight playable characters, with an additional five to be added to the game before the year is out. They're all extremely different in playstyle, with each character posessing a unique gimmick that can affect the field of battle in some way. Zetterburn ignites his enemies to deal damage over time, Forsburn uses smokescreen and fake copies of himself, Wrastor lives and dies by his combo ability, Etalus can encase himself in ice armor, Kragg is
for a heavyweight character, so on and so forth.
If you're going to play this game online - and you really ought to, as the game's A.I. is garbage - then you will need to accept that you're going to get bodied. Like, a lot. I just got bodied three times in a row earlier today.
is NOT an easy game, and you will need to sink a lot of time into practicing the game if you want to start playing in the online tournaments and earning tournament-exclusive character skins.
Thankfully, the game's online community is generally non-toxic (most of the time), and I've met several incredibly nice people who have helped me improve my Etalus game immensely. There are myriad useful learning resources, such as the
, among others. Learning to play competetively can be a long journey, but you won't be alone for any of it.
The game's presentation is... mixed; and I'm not just referring to my personal vendetta against pixel art. Some characters seem to be lacking in animation frames when other characters have plenty of animation frames. The pixel resolution is at least consistient, and very rarely are any of the pixels 'rotated' like in games such as... well, 90% of all pixel art games.
The game's soundtrack is mostly excellent, though it's obvious which tracks were the first tracks composed, as they are only ~45 seconds long compared to later tracks which can be three times as long. My personal favorite track belongs to the Tempest Peak stage:
.
The game's Story Mode is... uh... well, it certainly exists. The real meat of the single player content is Abyss Mode, where you can customize your character with overpowered enhancements and take on waves of unique enemies and challenges. It's great fun once your character is fully decked out. There is also a toggleable Developer Mode which lets you customize the game's characters as you see fit.
The game has two major flaws. The first is that the grind to unlock all of the unlockable stages and the second custom color slot for each character is unbearably long, so much so that I resorted to save file editing just to spare myself the grief. The second is the aforementioned character Kragg, who is genuinely far too heavy for a character with the most versatile moveset in the entire game bar none.
So, in conclusion, even though the game is far from perfect, it is nontheless a rewarding experience with a surprisingly level-headed community surrounding it.
If nothing else, at least it's a better fighting game than Street Fighter V.
