One of many many re-iterations of the MTG trading card game.  I usually like these games, I also rarely write reviews, and when I do it is purely for reccomendations.  This game... however, has caused me to make a exception to that trend.  Most MTG games are fairly straigth forward, and as with most of the games, an eventual purchase is expected to fully enjoy the game.  Either you need to pay intially to play the games, or you will have to purchase some cards/booster packs to play beyond the standard pre-made packs.  This game... however, advertises itself as truly free, and then berates you with annoying totorials, oddly placed buttons that often result in misclicks, and a very liberal use of language.  I began playing and went through the very lengthy, and quite tedius tutorial/story mode because it provides you with enough ingame currency to purchase a few booster packs.  This tutorial is the epitomy of "well duh" and takes you through some rediculously obvious and self explanatory game mechanics in a fashion that requires you to constantly load and swap out of your main tutorial into a secondary tutorial scenario that forcefeeds you mechanics as simplistic as casting an instant spell, using a creature ability, using a "tap creature" ability... and many other things that truly shouldn't need clarification.  In fact, there are a couple abilities that could do with a bit of explaining, but they actually seemed to have changed the rules (you can now tap a tapped creature.. which doesn't seem relavent, but it used to come into play a lot) and leave out those tutorials until you coincidentally run into them during an actual match..  but back to the main issues.  The starter pack is quite possibly one of the worst starters you could possibly get.  I'm actually wondering if it is truly random, but many of the other reviews back up the fact that it just seems horrible.  You get virtually no cards with any form of synergy with each other and then must grind very slowly against AI opponents with incredibly simple but well synergized decks in order to get enough coins to buy more boosters in hopes that you'll get some of the missing pieces to form a real starter deck to then farm for an actual PvP deck over what I am assuming is the better part of a half millenia.  You will generally win 1 out of every 5-10 duels vs these AI decks simply due to the fact that you have a random assortment of low strength spells and monsters with abilities that do not work well together (I.E. A card that boosts its effects for every creature of that type in play, and they only give you 1, or a card combo that allows you to farm up all of your enchant spells, which would be incredibly powerful IF you actually had any enchants that would impact the outcome of the game or provided more than a +1 +2 bonus)  Then we get to the quests...  There are player base quests where all players of the game work towards a goal such as beating the final tutorial opponent 5,000,000 times (last I saw we were at 5,004,531 although there was no actual payout yet for some reason) which would be cool only it doesn't seem to work...  and then you get individual quests which request very specific color types or goals to be carried out in "Duels."  Now personally I'm still trying to figure out WTF a "Duel" is to the makers of this game, because the AI battles are actually called duels.. and yet they don't seem to give you credit for them for your individual quests.  I found this odd because the 5,000,000 win quest also specifically mentioned winning "Duels" only in that instance it WAS against an AI opponent.  I guess this could mean that you have to win vs another player, but this is completely impossible without spending about $80-120 on the in-game boosters, which are roughly $7-8 a piece.  I can't fathom why they would sell them for so much in a game that has no actual card or re-sell value, especially when their largest Free-To-Play MTG game actually sells them for about the same price AND has the added value of allowing you to exchange these cards for the real life physical copies should you gather an entire set of them...  Plus that game has every MTG card in existence in it and also allows you to play reasonably against other players for free, or pay a small fee to get a workable set of pre-chosen cards from which you can assemble your own deck from.  If you want to spend some time on a free MTG game I highly suggest looking elsewhere at the far more successful iterations of this franchise.  Wizards apparently gave this project to the crackheads of their company that chose to follow the tradition FTP model of making the game terrible unless you pay, and just barely fun if you do.
Steer clear!

From what I have gathered, this game is somewhat controversial. I have 3 playthroughs now, looking forward to a 4th, and I would like to bring up a few points and offer my opinions, that potential players might have a better perspective on the game beforehand. This review will be quite lengthy, for there is a lot to cover, even scratching the surface as I am. I assure you there are no story spoilers.
Journey - The game is very linear. The first 80% of the story takes you on a singular path from one locale to the next, with little deviation, before it opens up into the main side-questing hub. (Firsttime players: at this point, I strongly advise following the map and pressing on with the main story for the best experience; there will be plenty of time later to complete this content, and you will be much better prepared.) Those of you looking for a cohesive, story-driven rpg that will keep you glued to your controller for 40 hours before you even get to the endgame, look no further.
Story - An intricate and well-developed plot replete with heroism, hope, despair, and intrigue. Consciously make sure you develop a firm understanding of the terms being used (l'Cie, fal'cie, etc.), or you will find yourself a bit confused often. The game introduces the story in a very logical way, and if you diligently read the journal entries, you may find yourself thoroughly immersed. The characters are very human (if sometimes melodramatic), and the overall experience was satisfying and complete.
Presentation - The polish in this game is quite astounding. The graphical style of the characters seems to deviate just enough from photorealism to avoid the uncanny valley, yet be very believeable; and I found myself often taking time away from the story to just stare at the environments for a bit. The soundtrack is phenomenal, sound design is very pleasing, and the voice acting is absurdly well done. If there was such a thing as a quadruple A title, this would be one.
Combat - Combat starts almost insultingly simple, but evolves into an extremely tactical and customizable aspect of the game. The systems used are quite novel, and somewhat difficult to describe. Your party maximum is 3 members, but you only control the party leader, and the commands you select are executed when your command queue (called ATB gauge, which charges within seconds at a set rate over time) finishes charging. This makes combat a much faster and action oriented experience than the customary Final Fantasy turn-based combat. Another aspect of combat is the paradigm system, wherein you save up to 6 builds (called paradigms in the game) for your party (out of combat) by specifying each member's role. These paradigms can then be cycled through (called paradigm shift) on-the-fly in combat to fit the given situation. There are 6 different role types. Put simply: tank, healing, damage, damage multiplier increasing, debuffing, and buffing. There is a ton of potential for diversity here. In order to survive many battles post-game, careful timing, thoughtful planning, and equipment tailored to the situation will all be required.
Progression - This is one of my favorite things about the game. While the system for leveling up is arguably as linear as the story to a certain degree, it simply cannot be denied that there is a vast and satisfying journey to be had in regards to increasing your party's strength. The game's EXP is used to purchase abilities and stat upgrades from giant role 'skill/stat trees' (for lack of a better term). All 6 roles have their own trees, and eventually become accessible to everyone, but each character is 'native' to specific roles, meaning that progression with EXP through their native trees is much cheaper. This essentially means that your characters will be limited in their individual role capabilities until you are well past the end of the story. Maxing out each tree is possible, but it is an extremely daunting goal that will take many hours of post-game play to achieve, so there is a certain definite replayability in the way you level up your characters. At a certain point, you can also decide which 3 of 6 party members you utilize as your active party, and who you use as party leader (all of which can be changed at any time, once available). The role trees will be your primary source of progression, but upgrading weapons will increase their damage stat (there are 2 damage stats: strength and magic) boosts, and earlier in the game you will also find it useful to use accessories to boost your stats.
Endgame - As mentioned earlier, some of the endgame content is actually accessible before you finish the story. The trick here is that most of the encounters in this area will either leave you sweating by the end, or simply have you die within the first 10 seconds from a single blow. There are 64 side quests in the game, with some of them actually being woven into and required to complete for the main story. Each quest is essentially a boss enemy you are tasked with hunting down, and the 'quest givers' (term used to avoid plot details) are spread throughout a great portion of the game. To offset this, there is a fast travel network you unlock as you complete certain quests. Generally, the higher the quest number, the more difficult the boss and the better the item and EXP rewards. The fact that there are enemies that can simply wipe the floor with you by hardly trying is one of the things that makes this such a fun experience for me. Because eventually, if you do enough side quests, farm some of the more lucrative quests (quests are repeatable), and obtain the right equipment, you will eventually be more than a match for that enemy. And those groups you were sweating to beat when the quest hub unlocked will die in seconds. Other activities aside from questing include working at completing a robust set of achievements, upgrading your weapons to their ultimate forms (very expensive), upgrading your accessories, and maxing out role trees.
Replayability - As mentioned earlier, there is some replayability value in the design of the role tree system, and which 3 characters you choose to have your experience with when the feature is unlocked. There is also a choice to make for each character: that is if you are specializing them for strength or magic or both, in regards to weapon choice. Some characters may be more naturally inclined to one stat over the other, but it's still your choice. Personally, I think that perhaps the story itself is one of the greatest advocates for replayability. Despite its extreme linearity, it was an amazing and intense journey that I look back fondly on.
Beginner Tips - 1.Once you start gaining experience, don't rush the game and skip encounters. Doing so will leave you much weaker once you near the end of the story, and you will really just be making the game uncomfortably difficult for yourself. 2.Best defense is a good offense here most of the time. 3.Paradigm shift. A lot. 4.Grab ATB and accessory upgrades from the role trees asap.
Other opinions - As far as hearsay regarding this game in comparison to FFXIII-2 and FFXIII-3: The second and third games seemed little more than truly terrible fan fiction to me, and featured some awful game mechanic and interface changes/additions. I simply can't understand why anyone would claim that they were an improvement over this game in any way whatsoever. Unfortunately, I found that the only way to preserve the memory of the wonderful characters I came to know and love in this game was to pretend that the second and third games do not even exist. Story and mechanics aside, they are absolutely abysmal ports, with the first game being BY FAR the best optimized port of the three. FFXIII is the masterpiece, people.
Closing - If you've taken the time to read this entire review, I hope you've gained a better understanding of what to expect from this game, and wish you a very enjoyable experience.

Rating: 6.5/10
Overview: Turn Based JRPG
The Good:
+In any JRPG you will spend the majority of time in combat, so it's important that you enjoy it or else you probably won't enjoy the game. Luckily this game has an enjoyable and strategic combat system. Rather than control single units you command groups of units called unions. You can have a max of 5 party members per union and a total of 18 party members. Thus one of the first strategic decisions you make is whether  or not you should have a few large unions or many smaller unions. Each one comes with its own pros and cons. Within each union you can also set the formation which also grants certain benefits and weaknesses. I.e Higher strength vs lower magic.
In combat each union is given a list of commands depending on which party members you grouped together. When you engage with an enemy union "deadlock" occurs. Deadlock means you have to kill the enemy union before you can target someone else. However, you can break deadlock to heal/revive another union, however this  will mean the enemy will get an extra attack. Thus, it becomes very important to only break deadlock when necessary. In addition to this, there is also flank attacks, rear attacks, interference/interceptions,...terms the game does a decent job of explaining.  Who you attack and how many unions you send to attack is a large part of the strategy involve. Do you gang up on a single enemy union causing more damage but leaves you more vulnerable to flank attacks or do you target multiple enemy unions and hopes your party is strong enough to handle each one? These are some of decision you make during some of the tougher battles.
There is also a morale meter in combat. The more you kill enemy unions, flank attack, interfere, and in general the better you do in combat, the higher the morale. A higher morale means more damage given and less damage taken. Conversely, the better the enemy does the lower the moral meter. Lower morale means more damage taken and less given. During some of the easier battles, moral doesn't play that big of a role, but when you start fighting boss enemies it's important to keep the morale as high as possible as it could be the difference between surviving an attack or having an entire union wiped out in a single blow.

You put this all together and you have a fun, fast and engaging combat system that can easily hold up throughout the course of the game.
+ Turbo mode option doubles the speed of battle. A great feature that speeds up gameplay.
+ An option that turns off quick time events in battle and makes them automatic. During battle there are times when you have QTE granting you higher damage.  Again, a great feature to have. The only downside to this is that it has roughly  80% success rate.
+ The game auto saves after every battle and every time you enter an area. I know it's not exactly a big thing but this feature saved me a lot of trouble during the course of the game.
+The game is filled with interesting locations and characters. Each city feels different based on the geographical location. The areas you explore are varied, from subterranean caverns, sandy deserts to forests and swamps. Artistically they all feel great and fun to explore.
+ The game is filled with plenty of side quests and optional areas. Completing many of these side quests allow you to hire specific characters for your party so it provides a good incentive for completing them. If you just stick to the main story you will probably miss over 50% of the game.
+This is more than just a straight port to the PC. The game makes a variety of gameplay and balance changes throughout the entire game and Square-Enix should be commended for taking the time and effort to make the game better on PC.
+Loved the music
The Bad:
-The biggest downside is the game does such a poor job of explaining some of the more important game mechanics. For example, the game gives a brief 2 line description about the type of formation you want to use but does not mention how specific of a bonus or weakness it will give your party. The game desperately needed an codex within the game detailing monsters and where to find items to upgrade your equipment. Having to go online to search for this information is an indication of poor design.
-One of the more important mechanics the game fails to explain is Battle Rank. As you win battles your Battle Rank goes up which is dependent on how many monsters you fight, how hard the battle is, how many unions died in battle etc. You would think the higher the Battle Rank the better your doing. In fact the higher the rank, the harder the enemies. If your Battle Rank grows higher than the rate in which your stats increase you could find the enemies very difficult to defeat and find yourself stuck. Granted, this is one feature they improved upon the PC version however it's still a problem and it is poorly explained in the game.  In theory, it is a good system to have to prevent grinding, however this system can also be exploited.
- The game has some ludicrous difficulty spikes. I almost stopped playing the game early on because of how frustrating the battles became, especially boss battles.  Normally you can just can grind it out, however because of Battle Rank you have to be a bit more careful how you improve your stats.
-I am not a fan of JRPG's stories and this game is no exception. The story feels stereotypical of all JRPG's before it. The dialogue is embarrassingly bad and the voice acting is just as terrible. The characters are one dimensional and the main character is annoying.
-Significant texture pop in.
Conclusion
I enjoyed the game but its flaws really dragged the game down. What should have been a more enjoyable experience ultimately felt more frustrating. Despite the  score I still recommend the game because if you like JRPGs and like learning new game systems  and getting really immersed in the game this is a game you should check out. Everybody else should expect an average JRPG.

Quite possibly the worst videogame I've ever played in my life and a mortal threat for epileptics.

I don't know another person who owns this game luckily but at least I got a good glimpse of the nice textures that were flashing white and stretching into the sky all across the map.
There are seven weapons, none of which feel satisfying or fun to use on any of the bullet-sponge enemy varieties (there are two; the big dudes who take about three times too many bullets or punches to kill and have awful hitboxes and then there are the armoured kind of those guys). Some weapons lack the functionality they are described as having (looking at you, "Radio Frier"). The single-player campaign ends in an unwaranted cliffhanger and has three maps in total, all of which are near-impossible to navigate because everything looks the same and it's like the developers went out of their way to make sure that the way you're supposed to go is placed in the LEAST intuitive place possible.
The voice-acting is atrocious, the story is awful, the graphics are admittedly not terrible (aside from character models and character animations) but they're buggy instead. The framerate is horrible and inconsistent. The game crashes both regularly and irregularly.
There are maybe four songs in total that repeat throughout the entire game (when it isn't being completely silent aside from that one enemy that fell through the floor and is now shooting you from outside of the map) and yet if you asked me to hum one of them, I couldn't. Many things in the game lack sound effects entirely and the existing sound effects will only play at random occasions. An enemy can walk up to you from behind and start beating/shooting you in your back and you will have no idea until your screen turns red because no sound is playing at all.
Don't buy this game for any reason except maybe if you're a hardcore masochist, in which case you'd still have more fun wedging hot needles under your thumbnails.

Bioshock 2 is a commendable sequel to its predecessor. Best of all, the combat system is much better this time around: all weapons are effective; you can use a primary weapon and a plasmid concurrently; upgrading plasmids yields noticeable improvements in their power and usefulness; and the combat simply feels better and more polished. Unfortunately, this time around Rapture is no longer the mystery it had been in the first game. We know the gist of the city, who built it, and what enemies to expect. The story is pretty well done (better pacing than Bioshock 1 IMO), and a few scattered moral choices fit well with the games heavy themes such as medical ethics, the human condition, and morality. The environments also take a leap of regression: they are less varied, less unique, and less iconic than in the first game. Overall, Bioshock 2 is a great sequel to a great game!

So, i tried Magic out after I played Hearthstone for quite a while and I directly want to compare these games due to their general popularity and (almost) being the only popular strategic card games.
GENERAL CONCEPT: First off, i quit Hearthstone because of the ridiculousness of collecting cards. I think it's simply unfair to not give a new player all the opportunities that an advanced player has. After all, skill (and the RNG, of course :D ) should make the difference of winning or losing and not the time spent to collect all the possible means to play the game. In League of Legends, for example, you can't (really) directly influence your performance by spending money on the game, but instead the developers offer "skins" for real money to make your character look better/different, which turns out be working pretty well and I think this concept is absolutely great! (You still have to unlock almost everything though ;_; )
The thing is that people of western society have the need to be rewarded for their commitment, so the game developers abuse this attribute to actually make the game more attractive and keep them playing, which is absurd. They give you the game bit by bit and most players don't even question that and some even argue that it's a good thing because of their feeling of being rewarded.
GAMEPLAY: Magic is more complex than Hearthstone and offers a lot of interesting options in tactics and deck building due to the tremendous variety of cards and the more precise turn-based combat system (instant spells, playing minions at the end of turn, etc.), which is awesome! Some may say it's more boring like that, but I think it's what makes strategic card games so fun.
Unfortunally you may only use the bad/mediocre/not synergizing cards from the beginning, so most of what I called great can be thrown into the trash again.
In general, there's too many "Continue" buttons to be pressed in this game in general, but especially while playing and that makes it UNBEARABLE because it's too goddamn slow. If the AI doesn't have something to counter or whatever your land card on turn one, the waiting time becomes just wasted life time and it adds up for sure. And if I don't have anything to play instantly, I should also have the ability to skip the waiting time.
STORY MODE: The concept was cool and I enjoyed to play these different characters and their improving decks, but it's just these decks, man... The third story had such a terrible deck that I just got mad at the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t I had to deal with and it made me quit. It's like not just having an opponent to play against, but also playing against your own deck because your early game is okay, but your late game doesn't even exist, so you just keep drawing one bad card after another.
CREATIVE DESIGN: I'm kind of a nerd when it comes to things like these, but someone has to talk about optics and music as well, right? I loved all the artwork, they surely put some effort in these and they got my props. It's just too bad that the game boards were blank and dull, which is just boring, just like the lack of music.
CONCLUSION: The game has big potential to be great and attract some players, but in its current state it's unplayable due to the slowness of the game (continue pls) and the lack of diverse gameplay because of the cards your have to unlock and a lot of minor flaws. I would also be willing to pay like five euros/dollars to have a complete game like this instead of playing for free and being♥♥♥♥♥♥on by my own cards, which hurts the gameplay enormously.

A huge emphasis today is one what a game brings to the table in ways of innovation. Is Gat out of Hell anything new? Hell no. It's Saints Row IV, but in hell. That being said, it is so much fun it's insane. Almost sinful.
+Flying. Probably the best ever.
A new edition (though similar to gliding in IV) is the ability to fly. The flying is extremely intuitive, and it's exhilarating to fly at break neck speeds through narrow gaps. The game really excels here, especially in the two new diversions the game offers. Flying through rings in a race against time is intense, and racing to catch souls falling to the ground is exciting to say the least.
+Guns. Hysterical, destructive guns.
The new guns are also a reason to get this game. Without spoiling the surprises (unless you watched the video on the store page), there is a gun based off of each of the 7 deadly sins. These are just as epic and hysterical as you would expect them to be, and really do make running around hell a... well a hell of a good time.
+Comedy. H-A-H-A-H-A
C'mon people, it's Saints Row. It's pretty damn funny and absurd. I would argue that Gat has some of the best one-liners in the series, and he does not disappoint here. A lot of the humor is also subtly done through advertising and buildings around the open world, which is always fun to stumble across. Even the audio logs (A Damned Souls Orientation Guide) are funny to listen to.
+Collectibles. So many. So worth it.
Speaking of the D.S.O.G. (see above bullet), all of the collectibles have a purpose. Whether it's to give you more lore on this version of hell (which is a fairly unique and funny one at that), giving you exposition on some of the characters you meet, or allowing you to make your super powers more powerful, it's worth the neurotic completionism. Plus the game lets you buy a radar to reveal them all so... that was a break from my rage of scouring the corners of the map for that last one.
+Powers. Super even.
While a lot of them are reskinned from IV, it is still fun to turn an enemy into stone, or steal his soul, or vacuum everything in a wide radius toward you. Summoning demons is also a nice addition, from the tiny imps to significantly more foreboding allies.
+Co-op. Gat and Kinzie double trouble
What's more fun than ripping hell a new one? Doing it with a friend. Phrasing, boom. But seriously, need I say more?
+The Verdict?
Get it. Have Fun. Blow stuff up. Laugh. Blow more stuff up. Laugh again. Kill things. More fun.
: Remember it is an expansion. It's not going to be a super long game. That being said I've almost reached 30 hours and I haven't quite finished everything yet.
tl;dr
It's an extremely fun game that improves on (slightly) and changes the formula of IV just enough that people who played IV will love it, and people who haven't played IV will want to. A great standalone expansion.

X Rebirth has provided a few gaming firsts for me in this genre. First: Buying a ship and watching it being built from the railing of the shipyard. Second: Being docked on a ship and ordering the captain to take me where I want to go, all while watching some of the best space scenery pass by while standing in the hangar of said ship. Now, I've played a lot of games with space and space travel being the premise and never have I seen this kind of vision or ambition in a game. Of course, perhaps Egosoft was too ambitious. A lot of the systems that are implemented are prone to failure, some of them gamebreaking. But I've played X2: Beyond and X3:TC and AP, I can say that this company never stops working on their games, the FANS never stop working on their games. Most people who have played this game get down on it for being buggy. Try to picture it this way, all of you have played betas, bought into kickstarter games, etc. and these games will have their problems, I've got friends who have plunked down 200 clams on Star Citizen to simply get a hangar and explore their ship. My point being, don't jump on the bandwagon of bashing Egosoft simply because their game came out about the same time the Steam Review system did. Think about it for a minute. Any basement-virgin-internet-punk can bash a game. And destroy the english language in the process, but my respect goes to the articulate. Thanks to Steam, we can play this game any time after purchase, and thanks to Egosoft, this game will be perfect given enough time, I'm excited to see where it's at a year from now.

Defy Gravity follows a similar road with some other platformers we've seen lately, using space as a foundation for the game, as you take control of one of the Gravitymancers who came to the Gauntlet, the ultimate test, in order to prove themselves. However, where other platformers with a similar pattern such as The Swapper manage to tell an interesting and unique story using the darkness and emptiness of space, Defy Gravity only introduces you to the Gauntlet, without actually telling you what it really is, what purpose does it serve and why would anyone risk their lives just to prove that they can get to the end. It is quite obvious that story isn't the main focus here, but even so it's hard not to notice the missed opportunity, since The Gauntlet itself could've been filled with messages from others who tried and were defeated by The Gauntlet or pretty much anything at all to justify your desire to finish it; instead you're left with a left to right Mario-style platformer without any princess at the end.
The gameplay is based around the use of gravity wells, which can be created using your gun, in addition to the ones that are already placed on the map and cannot be moved; using those wells properly and learning how they influence other objects is key in Defy Gravity, as almost every puzzle is based on how well you manage to use the gravity wells depending on position, as well as timing. There are two types of gravity wells: positive and negative; the positive wells will attract objects towards them, including yourself, while the negative ones will repel them, and combining those wells with your anti-gravity shield that makes you immune to all wells is what makes the gameplay unique and interesting. The whole concept does wear out by the end of the game, as there won't be any new ideas introduced into the game later on, leaving you mostly with more bouncing objects to avoid in order to make the game harder, something that does happen once you finish the game and Hard mode is unlocked, disabling negative gravity wells and changing a few things in each level in order to make it more challenging.
The first thing you will probably notice are the backgrounds, which look amazing and change from level to level, but what on the other hand, the levels themselves are designed using the same monotone, gray blocks and the only thing that differentiates them one from another is the layout of those gray blocks and the bouncing objects between them. The visual effects are basic and nothing stands out, mostly because no beam or ray of light can move your eyes away from the galaxies in the background.
The tunes are okay, but since there is no story or momentum to what is happening, this is probably one of those titles you'll play with your own music in the background. The sound effects feel absent most times, as they are either too quiet or not in total sync with the action, but then again you probably won't need those anyway.
For its 3€ price tag, Defy Gravity offers enough to justify the purchase, even if you can finish the game in less than two hours, adding 2-3 more hours to that time if you're down for the Hard mode, but if you are looking for anything extra, there is nothing more to the game than the adventure itself.
Defy Gravity is an okay platformer if you only care about the gameplay, as it does introduce a new concept even if it only lasts for a short time, but for anything else you might expect from this game, you will probably be disappointed.

I absolutely love this game and stand by it. I have put probably about 300-400 hours into this game (not on steam, but mostly on xbox). I bought it on PC because it is a superior version which does allow more specific choices for characters and doesn't punish you for grinding.
I Think the battle system and character progression system is great, but not for everybpdy. Your characters will grow depending on the commands you give in battle, the commands you get to choose from in battle are limited, but are always swayed by the choices you have made for that group of characters previously. Instead of having 6 focused characters, which you make specific choices for growth, like in the usual JRPG fare, you have 20 characters and make general choices in combat that indirectly affect the character's growth. It means that all the choices you make will have an impact, so you have to be mindful of what abilities you want a group to have.
The battles are both challenging and engaging and unlike other JRPGs I've played. The fact they are large scale is really enjoyable, and you can also speed past them if you'd like. If you really want to enjoy it, you will need to use the wiki for it. There are details which appear as random in this game, but are really a number of complex factors that create a coherent, if unclear, system.
The game's content is mostly sidequests and completely optional, and are amongst the most rewarding challenges I have faced in most JRPGs. I always feel like there is more I could do and more progression I could make, creating powerful and interesting combinations of characters.
I thik this title is greatly misunderstood and underrated because of the sub-par Xbox release, but is really a unique JRPG gem and will shine through if you have the time and interest.

This problem, however, hasn't stopped me from more than doubling my play time in the past two weeks. Despite a few flaws, Rivals is a very fun game and I would recomend it if you want to play in a 1v1 format.

The Last Remnant is a great JRPG, and while the Xbox version had some issues, they all seem to have been resolved in the PC version. Battle Rank (a leveling system that scales up enemy strength the higher your Battle Rank is) is a bit more balanced than it was in the Xbox version, so the penalty for grinding isn't as great. The framerate has been greatly improved, and you are now able to make unions entirely out of general units instead of having to hire the free generic soldiers to fill in gaps, which makes the game much more fun and interesting.
The story is well written overall, though I wouldn't say that it's the best point of the game. It's interesting, but what really makes the game shine is the combat and the sidequests. There are tons of sidequests to complete and guilds to visit all across the world and the rewards are all genearlly very useful and valuable, ranging from general units to recruit to components to unique weapons. The battle system itself may seem really confusing and complex at first, and then it may seem a bit basic and boring once you get through the first scene, but very quickly it expands and becomes much more exciting and interesting. It is honestly one of my favorite battle systems out of any RPG that I've played.
I'd definitely reccomend this game to anyone who is a fan of JRPGs and intricate battle systems. The game is a blast to play, it has a great soundtrack, and the atmosphere and visuals are amazing.

Bioshock (1) is one of my favorite games of all time. Even over Team Fortess the Bioshock Series has surpast my intrest in Team Fortress. This sequel was ok, it still had the same feel as a Bioshock game but I felt it was not quite as strong as the first. Bioshock 2 is what you could call the Little Brother of the franchise; an attempt at multiplayer mode, the off-key continuation of what has digressed sense Jack's visit to Rapture. But it just wasn't as strong I feel than the first Bioshock. It is for sure a good game though, just not as good as Bioshock 1. Here and now, as I type this, Bioshock Infinite is just beyond the next 2 weeks and know it will be better than this. I'm kind of sad they left Rapture behind. When this game is all said and done, the story of the underwater city (Rapture) seems incomplete, Dr. Tenenbaum mentions at the beginning that she must go and "...help 'others' before the city drowns" I cant help but wonder who these "others" are.

The game feels as if they're just using the IP of Middle-earth for the sake of it (much like Shadow of Mordor). It's as generic as it comes for a game. It might as well have been a Dragon Age game and nobody would notice a difference.
The gameplay itself gets fairly repetitive. You take control of one of three characters and do the same thing over and over until the level is finished. You level up as you progress and get better gear (though it feels like they've taken a generic RPG element and just thrown it in). But the other two characters you don't play as also level up alongside you. So eventually they're completely outmatched by the enemies and you need to gear them up. This requires you to actually log out and log back in as the new character... you can't just switch between them or gear them from one character.
There is also a part where the game just decides to ramp up the difficulty for no reason. It's a random spike of difficulty out of nowhere. You have to protect a gate from two trolls, who can take it out in about 15 - 20 seconds. Problem is, they just ignore you and run right past you, even when you're stabbing at them. I had to wait until the game glitched and the trolls froze on the spot before I could beat it, because the DPS you'd need to take them out before they reach the door only a few feet away is way beyond what you'd be expected to have by that point.
There is no way to save manually, so sometimes you'll waste a lot of time fighting a load of enemies, want to save but you can't until the end of that section, which could be anywhere, you don't know. And if the game crashes (more on that further down), you've wasted all of your time.
AI is pretty stupid. If you get taken out, you get a chance for your teammates to help you back up. But half of the enemies interrupt them before they can get you up fully, so you have to wait. Instead of them killing the enemy then trying again, they just keep going in a loop of try to help, get interrupted, try to help, get interrupted, and then eventually die. Sometimes they'll just run into the enemies that killed you, get trapped in them and just keep trying to run at you with no success.
But the reason it gets a solid 'no' recommendation is just because of all of the graphical problems. Some levels (like the Barrow-downs) are so glitchy that the game will crash all the time. My own PC is high-end and takes punishment from any other game without issue, it just puts out some heat. But even on the lowest settings, this game creates graphical glitches (weird glowing and static-looking graphical elements) or just crashes to desktop. It's not the sort of thing you expect from a game.
Overall, a buggy game that feels like it's just been given a LotR coat of paint and brings nothing to the table that other games of the same type don't do already. A cash-grab that relies on Middle-earth fans (who, ironically, will cringe at the lore-breaking elements, like American accents, a dragon, and constant use of eagles).
Edit: I recently just found this in my "Unfinished" section. After loading it up, I remember why. I'm currently stuck in a part called "Carn Dum". It's basically a load of blood-filled sewers. However, the game is not coded well enough to run properly. It crashes every single time you try to just walk through the game. That's all. Just walking will crash it. It can even crash your entire PC, not just the graphics driver, so watch out when playing this game. It's a damn liberty.

I was content with what was given to me, but a game shouldn't leave me content- it should leave me throwing my money at the screen asking for the next one. This Hitman game didn't do that. But what we need is more Blood Money gameplay. So many of the features in this game exist to make it casual friendly- anyone can clear this game, and that's OK. This is what is going to sell, and I fully understand that- but I also understand that this doesn't make the game good.

Absolution had some mighty big shoes to fill after the glory that was 2006's Blood Money, which is one of those games that is on a 'you must play this before you leave this terrible planet' list, and dosen't match up at all when compared side-by-side. Absolution is far more concerned with telling you a (really bad, silly, nonsense and kind of enjoyable at the same time) ~*cinematic epic*~ story as opposed to Blood Money's sequential contracts that tie into a bigger overarching plot.
however, all is not lost. Absolution is still really fun to play, it's great to look at (seriously, even in 2015 this game looks damn good and it's hyping me up for the next Deus Ex which is going to use it's engine) and the missions, when you aren't trying to get perfect silent assassin runs and scores, are super fun to play through and plan out. although, some of the later missions get a bit confusing with what exactly you are supposed to be doing, but that's just imo.
there is a *lot* of replay value here too, especially for the score-obsessed. Absolution's one big contribution to the Hitman franchise is the contracts mode, which allows people to play through maps, make challenges where you mark certain targets, kill them with certain weapons or in certain ways and escape sucessfully. the other big addition is the constant scoring system and leaderboards that is always measuring you up to your friends, which of course stimulates that competitive side of all of us.
all that being said, i do recommend it if you are willing to not measure it up to Blood Money. it's a fun game!

Lets get two things out of the way:
1) my main issue with this game is a price tag. If i got in on sale for, say, a buck, i wouldn't write this.
2) it just so happens that i measure roguelike expenience against the industry standard, the one, the only!.. FTL!
First - the game mechanics. It's simplified to the point of feeling little to no involvement in combat. You bump your head into a goblin and hope for the best. Sure, technically every decision you've made up to the head-bumping point has some significance in a form of percentages, but actual _decisions_ are rare - most gear is either obviously better or obviously worse then the one you have, so it feels like more of a luck thing then a decision, and the relative combat success does not feel dependent on your skill but rather then on "was i lucky enough to be ahead of the curve with my gear?" thing. Compared to the enormous difference the same FTL ship can have depending on the player input - not even close.
Second - the replayability factor.
a) New outfit options and perks. I just don't see what i'm fighting in a current playthrough for, when the difference between playthroughs is the minor gear option that you would have gotten anyway. Some upgrades are not contigient on your achievements but rather on the time spent in the game. You shouldn't reward people for playing, you should reward hem for being good at it.
b) New classes - well, these are better. Would prefer not being able to see everything about them before i even unlocked one, but that's nitpicking.
c) Beating the game on a higher difficulty - basically this is the main thing: is the game involving enough for you to percieve beating it on a higher difficulty an achievement? No. See 1 - you don't feel like you contribute much, difficulty defines the curve, luck defines your position in relation to said curve.
In conclusion,  this is just not a ten-buck game. Something like FTL has insane replayability, something like Invisible Inc. posesses production values, so the price tag feels justified one or the other way. Here? I just don't see it.

This Game engine is flawed with performance issues for High-end gaming PC's but according to other reports seems to work best with low end CPU's and Video card combo.'s.
End results For Higher end gaming PC's: (AMD 6-core @ 4GHz; 8GB-RAM + ATI HD R2-290)
> The game can become very laggy due to very, and I do mean very low FPS (5-10 FPS) depending on which area you are in.
> Player experience is worse when in larger, big Space Ports with very busy traffic from many ships coming and going.
> Player experience is best when in deep space staring into nothingness.
> A flurry of patches/fixes are coming in from Egosoft but so far, very few of them have nothing to due with performance gains.
> Player experience for Patches/fixes that do address performance gains, range from negligible at worst, to mediocre at best. Still, for many players the game remains unplayable.
Conclusion:
> This game is for you if you do not mind viewing this more as a "turn based strategy game."
>  If not; wait for the patches to fix the game "The Way It's Meant To Be Played". But lets face it; if it were that simple to fix, it would already have been fixed long ago and real performance gains may only be realized incrementally over a very, very long time. This, maybe even mores so if they have to port this over from Directx-9.0c to Directx 11.0 to fully fix the problem.
I believe the reason they chose Directx 9.0c is because they thought they could use their experience with it as leverage for a  reduced development time but when the code never gets "Locked" due to continuing feature adaptations then this just stretched the development even more so. (7-years and counting).
And of course Directx 9.0c is probably much cheaper to licence per game sold than Directx-11.

Back when this game was first released, I remember how my PC at the time refused to even start it, giving me a screen of noisy colors and a crash to the desktop instead. Once I finally upgraded, I spent quite a few hours playing the demo, but I never ended up purchasing the full game. I noticed it on a Steam sale one day, and decided I'd finally finish the first-person shooter that gave me so many options, even with only one level.
When Crysis was first released, it was groundbreaking. It pushed every graphical limit known at the time, and the result was one of the most detailed and greatest looking first-person shooter games ever created. Post processing was used tastefully, almost every part of the environment is on the same high level of detail, and though some newer games have since left it in the dust, Crysis still holds up nicely, showing up games like Far Cry 3 or Arma 3 Apex thanks to the beautifully crafted levels of the Ling Shan islands. The only faults that Crysis has in the graphical department pertain to two vastly different ends of the spectrum. Terrain detail suffers the closer you get to the map boundaries, and character models - more specifically, face models - could definitely be better. With that said, if you want something nice to look at, Crysis will still give you that.
Audio design in Crysis is similarly high quality on most fronts. Weapons all sound punchy and satisfying, and the environmental effects are fantastic. The soundtrack, while not especially noteworthy, does contain some very nice orchestral tracks, and the game was scored well. The only major flaw with audio design is the voice acting and writing. The writing itself was like something out of a B-movie, and the voice acting quality matched it accordingly. One nice consolation about the voice acting is that all KPA troops will speak Korean on the highest difficulty level.
When this game was first released, it was often criticized for its performance. The question in many people's minds about PC gaming became,
and often times, the answer would be no. But thankfully, as hardware has evolved, most people will have little trouble running this game now. My system runs Crysis on maximum settings and maintains a nice 60 frames per second at almost all times. There aren't many bugs that I've found, and although I did encounter a handful during my play-through, none of them were game-breaking.
At first glance, Crysis probably looks like a run-of-the-mill first-person shooter. Taking a deeper look reveals, however, what makes it so unique. The player is equipped with an experimental Nanosuit, a wonderful piece of technology that allows for them to switch into different enhanced modes: Maximum strength, speed, armor, or a cloaking system. This allows for situations to be tackled in almost any way imaginable, with either a focus on stealth and guerrilla tactics or pure shock and awe. There is also an on-the-fly weapon customization system, allowing the player to swap out attachments on every weapon to suit whatever situation they're faced with. This all leads to an immense amount of freedom in both single- and multiplayer environments, and is one of the things that makes Crysis so fun to play.
The singleplayer campaign of Crysis places the player into the boots of Jake Dunn, a member of the futuristic Delta Force team Raptor, assigned to the Ling Shan islands in the Philippines. Raptor team was sent to locate an archaeologist who was taken hostage by a task force of the Korean People's Army, though they soon discover there are far deadlier things at play than just the KPA forces on the ground. Each level is sequential and allows the player to carry over their items from the last, and each one presents the player with one goal or another, typically miles away from where they start. This means that the player is free to reach their objective however they want; some might opt to steal a vehicle and blast through KPA checkpoints, while others might stealthily creep through the jungle undetected. There are eleven levels in the campaign, each taking place in a different part of the islands, and the campaign itself will take most players between eight and twelve hours to complete, depending on the difficulty level and their tactics. Most complaints stem from the latter third or so of Crysis's singleplayer campaign; it becomes more focused and the pace completely changes - though explaining how would spoil it.
The multiplayer component of Crysis featured two primary gamemodes; Power Struggle and Instant Action. The latter was a run-of-the-mill deathmatch gamemode, made more unique by equipping every player with Nanosuits. The more unique and popular gamemode was Power Struggle, which at first glance resembled Conquest from the Battlefield series. The biggest divergence from Conquest was how a team would win; a specialized 'TAC' heavy tank would have to fire a tactical nuclear warhead at the other team's main base, obliterating it. Larger maps also featured factories in addition to normal objectives, which would produce vehicles over time, rather than simply spawning vehicles when an objective was controlled like in Battlefield. Unfortunately, I describe all of this in the past tense because the multiplayer was run through GameSpy, and Crysis did not receive a multiplayer patch after GameSpy shut down. As a result, there is, to my knowledge, no multiplayer community left in Crysis.
Crysis redeems itself for its lackluster multiplayer component here. It features a terrain editor known as Sandbox which allows for the creation of both single- and multiplayer maps, and also supports user modifications. These modifications are unfortunately (mostly) limited to new weapons and vehicles, but you'll still probably be able to get a few more hours out of Crysis thanks to its support for community content.
The Crysis franchise is a bit of a tragic tale in my mind. The first game was so unique, and yet its developers threw away nearly all of what made it unique in favor of two scripted corridor shooter sequels which are, if you will, "all looks and no brains." Crysis certainly isn't a thinking man's game like the Arma series can be, but if you're looking an interesting and entertaining semi-open world first-person shooter and you see Crysis on sale, I would definitely endorse it. Just, consider using a mod to unlock the weapon slots so you can rampage through it while carrying a full armory like in Wolfenstein or Doom. It feels more appropriate that way, I have to say.

Rivals of Aether is a Smash Brothers-esque fighting game (more similar to Melee than the others) that delivers what it sets out to accomplish - follow in the steps of Melee while standing on its own two feet as a unique game.As you would expect in a game like this, the main kicker of this game is the gameplay. With shielding gone, grabs are no longer in the game. These are the two main differences, although you'll find more minor differences as you play. In general, controlling your character feels extremely smooth and polishes. There were little to no issues with controller regarding input. The game also features a story more which is very simple but also includes a time trial like system and gives you a chance to experiment with 6 characters against each other. The game also features an online matching system which is very well built. Even though the game only features 8 characters (but more to come!) they are all extremely different from each other and all enjoyable to play as and against. Overall I can't recommend this game enough to just about anyone. I can say that even beginners to the fighting game genre will love this game.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

If you're learning how to play Magic or if you want a more casual experience, this game can be helpful. It's informative to new players and has a lot of built-in guides like the previous installments, and the story mode can give new players a feel for each deck color. For veteran players, it's more frustrating due to quality of the starter set (full playsets of commons, but zero rares aside from lands) and lack of decent synergy within the card sets. Unlocking cards with in-game coins is a slow process (10 wins against a Hard computer opponent generates enough coins for a pack), and each pack is 6 cards (3 commons, 2 uncommons, 1 rare). The gameplay has been smooth so far, with the only hiccups being the somewhat odd timer amounts (you only have 2 or 3 seconds to play an instant or stop the timer except during your main phases). Three of the campaigns have had a decent difficulty level, but Jace and Liliana's campaigns have fairly difficult match-ups, with the first match in each campaign being played against much better deck. Overall, I would recommend this as a learning tool first and an actual Magic game second, due to the low quality of starting cards and story mode decks. Open deckbuilding is a plus, but previous installments were overall much more fun to play due to good cards and deck synergy. Experienced players may want to skip this.

"7.0/10"
+ Rich graphics, memorable symphony music, unique/massive scale fights
- Zero character growth, battle commands are random, sidequests are grindfests
A beautiful mechanically sound game that brings in an interesting battle system into an otherwise predictable jrpg plot. The Last Remnant caught my eye from the get-go with its visuals but dulled me back to real life with its  nuanse of storytelling and smaller-than-it-looks worlds. You play as Rush, a stubborn and small-minded individual out to save his sister and the world from destruction (How different!). What saves the narrative is a union-based system that gives you a commander-shouting experience. Rather than control each member, you're giving directions to the union as a whole and letting them decide.
It gives the game a unique flair and really, Steam should list "Strategy" as its 2nd or 3rd tag. Without a proper setup; having a healer, disabler, tank, area of effect abilities, you'll be left scratching your head, getting smashed from some of the more formidable story bosses. Thankfully Steam gives you an emulator-esque experience, letting you save at any point in the game as long as you're not presently in a battle. This means you can rewind and plan accordingly. Thin your numbers out with more unions and flank the enemy? Bolster two-three unions for a direct assault? Focus on moral boosting units and leader special abilities?
Acquiring more party members is also a treat as you'll be entering towns and recruiting people from various guilds. Getting the better party members requires you to do sidequests... and boy are some of them lengthy. Despite an engaging battle system that keeps you interested, it also has flaws. For one the commands are random. If you want a unit to do something specific, chances are it may not show up. Heal this union? No, sorry, I'll heal this other one. Use our special union ability even though we have enough mana? Maybe next turn. It's discouraging as well as prolongs otherwise 20-30 seconds fights into 2-3 minute charades.
Buy:  For the gameplay
Don't buy: For the plot

text:
An interesting follow-up to Civ 5.
I started the series with Civ 5 and many players said it was more simple and the AI was much easier. The DLC for Civ 5 expanded the gameplay a bit and I found it a fun game. After I played Civ:BE for a few hours I don't really want to go back to Civ 5. Likes people said about Civ 5, BE has even more simple AI and the gameplay is a little more simple. Not always a bad thing, I like how the tech web and purity is set up. Trade routes add a new dynamic to the gameplay but can also be frustrating to manage in a large empire. One of my favorite changes is when you level up your purity and get a unit upgrade, any unit you have gets upgraded. At the same time, once you've gotten a unit upgrade you can not produce the previous versions, which can lead problems if you don't have the production.
All in all, it's the same but different. I really do love the Sci-Fi theme and I can't wait to see what more mods and DLC will add.
Story continue and contribute to the meaning of city of Rapture, but Bioshock 1 atmosfere is in the end, gameplay is same good. Must for fans.

If you are a fan of the Lord of the Rings, or you are looking for a fun co-op game to play with friends, look no further.
Lord of the Rings: War in the North offers hours of fun especially as a multiplayer co-op game. The roles of the three characters you choose from are diverse and allow for each player to find their own rhythm and role in the gameplay. This is a typical third person action adventure RPG, offering the usual inventory micro management and looting.

This game is overrated.  There's literally nothing to do but walk and listen to see what the narrator says.  I get the point of it, but I don't find it particularly amusing or fun.  It also seems to prey on conventional perceptions of "depth" when in reality the tree of choices for this game is actually pretty small.
I get that it's supposed to be an indie game and it's not meant to be a crazy complicated game, but if you've seen somebody play this on a youtube video, you've experienced pretty much all it has to offer.  It's also not set up in a way that's particularly expansive, so don't expect the game to grow down the road.  It's essentially a well-done student game, and not something that keeps my attention for long.

That said, the story part of FF XIII (20-30h IIRC) is basically a huge cutscene with some bossfights in between. If you're the type of player that skips conversations and can't be bothered reading log entries, this is the wrong game for you. The post-game awaits with grind, optimization and crazy hard super bosses.
Story is okay. Cast is okay (Lightning is great, Sazh is dank and Hope annoying as ♥♥♥♥). Music is great.
BUT it is a bad port. You have to do some system tweaking to get it to run smoothly:
- plug in a controller
- disable as many HID-Compliant devices as possible in the device manager
- create an application-specific profile for your video driver
- download RivaTuner Statistics Server and limit the game to 30 fps
- exit any Logitech software that's running
- run the game in window mode

Surpisingly fun, despite the ridiculous concept behind the game.  Its simple, addicting, and entertaining.
The human teams feel like something out of an Alien vs Predator game, with the player never knowing if there's something leaping at him from behind, or scoping them out from above.  And there's always the general feel of hopelessness as you notice a T-Rex coming your way.
The dinosaur teams are entertainingly diverse, with each one serving a purpose.  The Novraptors are entertaining, and feel like the general soldiers of the team, as they're fast, do a lot of damage, and in plenty.  However, flying with the pternadon is a chore with its semi-buggy flying mechanics, and not very rewarding unless you like being helpful to your team, or just enjoy picking people up to drop them from the skybox.  The dilophosaurus are a bit underwhelming as well, being extremely underplayed because their only skills are utility, with their blinding/poison abilities.  And good luck trying to snatch a T-Rex role, but goddamn does it look ♥♥♥♥ing fun.
All in all, I'm extremely happy with the game, but I have no illusions that is anything but arcadey fun.  Its not deep, and probably won't snag a thousand hours by anything, but it is entertaining, and something to quickly pick up and play.

First time I tried this game I really didn't like it, even after investing 40+ hours into it. It's very different from other Final Fantasy games, which I found immensely disappointing, and that put me in a mood where I couldn't appreciate anything the game had to offer because none of it is what I was looking to get out of it. It also annoyed me that the game launched with some performance/graphics issues.
So, why recommend it? I came back to this game a year later with a totally different set of expectations. Instead of treating this as a typical Final Fantasy game, and thus expecting things like towns, an overworld, the attack/magic/item combat, leveling, Cid, Biggs and Wedge references, etc. (none of which this game has), I chose to approach this as if it were an interactive visual novel with a light Final Fantasy flavor. With all the chatty cutscenes and linearity, that's exactly what it feels like, and if you come in expecting it then this game is actually quite satisfying.
tl;dr: Very nice game if you're looking for a visual novel with a heavy focus on combat and some light Final Fantasy themes. Very bad game if you're looking for anything that resembles the usual Final Fantasy experience.

The short version of this review is this: They didn't even bother to give us the little video at the end of the game that shows the growth of all the civs. That's pure laziness right there, and was the final straw on the giant haystack that broke this camel's back.
This game is just so obviously incomplete, it's kind of a joke. It wouldn't run on my desktop for the first 2 months (it ran great on my laptop, but it doesn't have the power to have the graphics turned up), until they released the major patch a couple weeks ago. But the major patch didn't really fix any of the issues I had with it except making it take a lot longer to crash.
The biggest issue I have with the game is that it's the Civ V engine, but while Civ V had an amazingly simple but effective interface, BE has a neutered, confusing UI, and beyond that, it's missing a lot of the informational tools from Civ V. Like, all of them. There are no advisors, there's no way to see how you're doing compared to the other players beyond score, which is a fairly useless metric. Trade Routes are completely jumbled, with no way to sort them properly to see which ones are best. And the thought of being able to combine the various starting benefits to make your own civ turns out to be much better in theory than in fact. I have no idea what civ I am in any given game, because I really don't care. The benefits don't really change the way you play the game at all.
On top of all of that, some of the stuff that Civ V didn't do as well as Civ IV, like diplomacy, is even worse in BE. Most of the time, I forget entirely about the other Civs. There aren't any "luxury resources" to give you some motivatoin to trade with them. I have no idea what Favors might be able to do, but I've never been able to get one anyway, so that doesn't matter. Wonders are utterly useless. Not only are most of them no better than a regular building, but you also have to research a tech that does nothing but let you build the wonder in order to do so.
The one thing they did that's way better is improve the espionage stuff. But even that wasn't perfect, as it seems to be impossible to get a city to have an intrigue level higher than 2.
Still a fun game with friends no matter what people say.

Ok so it wasn't 'just like' the previous Hitman titles that we know and love to death.
Ok so it was absurd that you could be wearing a disguise and have collected some nice new weapons and then went through a door to the next section of the level and you'd be back in your Agent 47 outfit and the weapons would be gone.
Ok so it was even more absurd that you could cause so much havok in one room having a huge gun fight with 10 or bad guys and then go through a door and the people on the other side of that door are utterly unaware of anything. Like they didn't hear the screaming or gunshots, or bullets belting off the door they were behind.
Ok so when the part comes that those female hitmen ('hitwomen'? surely you wouldn't?) who were dressed in shiney nuns outfits, it made the game feel weird and like i wasn't even playing a Hitman title, it was just so odd to see that. I couldn't take it serious at all.
Ok so at one level where the bad guys killed a bunch of real nuns in real nun sort of clothing, i really got annoyed that i was being penalized for killing those bad guys. I mean they just killed some nuns who were looking after orphans, c'mon, the bad guys really did deserve to be wiped out for that.
Ok so this Hitman felt more like it wanted you to NOT kill anyone who got in your way, actually, it felt more like it wanted you to ONLY kill the target(s) even when at times you have no option but to do so because you were unable to get close enough to them to knock them out so you had to shoot them. I didn't like that aspect either. If they are bad guys, but not the target, who cares if you kill them as long as you are tidy about it?
Ok so i really missed having the safe house feature, this would be great to have back in the next Hitman game in a large sandbox world, like GTA type of thing. I was a bit let down as well that i couldn't select my own gear then take the next contract in the story mode. Unless I'm missing something?
Ok so the maps are very small on average as well, something which was a bit of a downer because it meant less options for how to do you job.
Now despite those clearly messed up parts I've mentioned here, it still felt like a Hitman game. I still enjoyed it as a Hitman game. I still got to poison, snipe, strangle, drag bodies and dump them in the gutter where no one would find them. I still got those Silverballers, i still got into those tight heart pounding Hitman situations when i was either desperately trying not to be spotted or desperately trying to find a way out of trouble before i got wiped out. I still got to shoot lights out and stand in a dark corner and then grab a bad guy when he was walking past and strangle him.
Yes, some things COULD have been different, better? perhaps so, but isn't that what we all say about EVERY single game out there?
Some things i want to say about what ever next Hitman game comes out - DO NOT EVEN PANDER TO FEMINISTS OR POLITICAL CORRECTNESS.
We want a Hitman game, and Hitman games have to be dark, gory, and show the gritty and sickening side of real life. Absolution had some of those elements, perhaps not in the same dose as previous Hitman games did, but they were there in any case.
As for the online part of Hitman Absolution, I'm just glad that it wasn't some PvP or Co-Op gig. It's actually really good the way it's implimented as well.
I can say that i enjoyed the experience of Hitman Absolution, the gameplay was fluid and deep enough to get immersed in, just about. The graphics were very good as well as was the voice acting and environment sounds and even the dialogue between NPCs was wuite funny and even interesting at times.
Too much BLOOOOM though haha luckily we on the PC can actually do something about that!
So for anyone who reads this and is unsure about getting Hitman Absolution, don't be put off by websites out there saying bad things about it, or the 800+ downvotes here on Steam. Just buy it, because you'll certainly enjoy it enough to warrent a purchase. Anyone saying this is trash is out of their tiny minds. It's far from it, it's just NOT as good as some previous Hitman titles. That's all.
Despite many people disliking this sequel, I still believe its a brilliant game and well worth checking out.

This is one of the first games i got on steam, if not the first.
This game can be so simple or advanced, which ever you want. if you want a simple game just do a smaller map with fleet size, resources max. if you want an advanced game do a huge map with normal or low bonuses.
One of my favorite parts of this game is the diversity. 3 races with unique bonuses and 2 factions with race, both having more specific strategies. like the tec. there are the tec rebels and loyalists. the loyalists want to stay by themselves and have huge defensive bonuses. But the rebels are very aggressive and have aggressive bonuses, like being allies with pirates. This huge diversity causes each game to be different and random.
The combat system is good, the only complaint i have is how easy it is to spam, especially in the start. There are regular ships, capital ships and then titans. each race gets unique capital ships and each faction gets a unique titan, further increasing the diversity. You get your first cap free so you have to decide with one suits you best, rushing to your enemies with a heavy or settling the planets around you with a colony capital ship, the choice is yours. The leveling up of the titans and capital ships is another thumbs up. It allows each capital ship to take a certain roll in the fleet by unlocking and upgrading skills. Like the Advent colony ship able to restore shields of friendly ships around it.
The research trees i find amazing. there is so much research options, each race having a unique one that can suit a number of strategies. you guessed it, each factions get certain unique research options, like the tec rebels able to research nearly every tec weapon with tec loyalists can increase armor in friendly planets or having two starbases around a planet. Very well done.
Overall i give this game a 9/10 only for the huge learning curve and some balancing issues. Warning, if you do get this game there IS a huge learning curve, just be patient with it and it gets SOO much better. If any newbies have any questions i would be glad to help!

I started out doing very well. Too well and got sloppy. While going through a church I came upon some survivors. They seemed friendly enough so I ignored their suspicious stares and kept exploring until I opened a door to a room that happened to have their wives and children in. They shouted at the kids to run and then attacked me. They were just terrified innocent people so I decided to run instead of fighting them. They overwhelmed me. Stabbed me with knives and Marko died.
My other survivors were saddened at the loss of Marko, but it also seemed to harden them. Where before they would be glad to help someone else now they were glad not to.
A new survivor arrived a few days later. Roman who had soldier training. I started using him more for the dirty jobs. He became somewhat of a hero. In the supermarket he killed a soldier that was about to♥♥♥♥♥♥an innocent girl. At the construction site he took out two snipers that were using civilians as target practice. In another house he killed an entire gang of thugs without alerting any of them. Silent. Deadly. He freed a hostage from another bunch of thugs. In this war torn city Roman was the hero looking out for the innocent survivors. The one who got his hands dirty when it needed to be done.
Then one night while sneaking through a house one of the occupants heard a noise and ran to investigate. He had a shotgun so I hid Roman in the shadows and killed the person with a knife when he got near. Someone else in the house had seen this and screamed and came running towards Roman. I panicked, remembered what happened to Marko so I pulled out Romans gun and shot the women. Two more came running after that. Also screaming and crying. Running towards the dead bodies. Still not taking chances and this all happening too fast I killed them as well. Only afterwards while searching the bodies did I realise that only the 1st person, probably the dad, was armed. The others which I suspect was his wife and daughters, they were unarmed.
I have never felt so bad for the actions I took in a game. Roman the hero, the protector of the innocent had just become a murderer. A thug like all those he had killed before.

This is a truly brilliant RTS game, and a brilliant edition to the Sins of a Solar Empire franchise. It combines incredibly large-scale battles with micro-management of superb levels. The game is beautiful, and expertly made. Even in some of my largest battles there has been little lag if any, and I have a mid-range PC. Fleet sizes can reach HUGE sizes. And that is not all. The game comes with mod support, and if you can think of a sci-fi franchise, there is undoubtedly a mod for it. I've been able to recreate Wolf 359 in Star Trek Armada 3 (one of the mods) and fight the Clone Wars in Sins of a Galactic Empire (another mod) all for the price of one game. It is fantastic.
However, if you do not like long-drawn out battles over star systems, then this is probably not for you. A typical match in Sins can last hours and hours. I have sixty something hours logged into the game, and I think I have only played seven major matches. Also, if you have played other Sins titles then this is not going to bring that much more for you except a few new ship types, better graphics and - from what I can tell - an improved research system. And if you are not very good at RTS games, don't worry as there is a tutorial which will run through the basics and give you a headstart.
In conclusion, I would definetely recommened this to any person who is either a fan of RTS games, sci-fi shows or explosions, and if you are not a huge fan of any of these things I would still ask you to go and buy it. Honestly, it is worth it.

By far the best RTS I've ever played. Because of its unique economy and supply systems this is one of the few RTSs that doesn't devolve into muscle memory and "build patterns" online. As such you actually get to enjoy strategy instead of dance-dance remix for your fingers when playing.
At first the 3 races (6 factions in rebellion) will seem very similar, but as you play the game you'll discover each of their strengths and weaknesses. These strengths evolve into unique strategies in themselves (rather than just unique unit graphics). Do you want to wall in and let your superweapons slowly take out your opponents? Will you focus on overpowering your enemies with the largest army? Will you focus on spreading your culture so your enemies' planets rebel against them? The various options and paths you can focus on is so refreshing in a world where everyone else is all about "build lots of units and kill the everything."
Along with that, you don't have to waste time micro-managing  every unit in this game as your "troops" actually have decent AI. This makes you feel more like a commander, and less like you're controlling mindless hordes. So you can focus on the wide scale war, and have massive, epic scale battles.
On top of all that, my low-power laptop (that's always running every game in low graphics with lag), can run this at medium-high graphics just fine. That's quite a feat considering it runs a huge map with thousands of ships (once you factor in all the trade ships and builder ships) at once. Their graphics engine has been masterfully optimized. Once again, very refreshing in a world where many game companies seem to think that modern computers can run anything thrown at them, so optimizing is a waste of time (either that or lazy programming).
So pick it up and try it!

I just wanna say I really enjoyed this game but man is it short. I mean I have 12 hours in according to steam but that includes picking up every collectible and getting gold in all the missions on hard difficulty. They include side objectives such as kill x amount of this enemy, kill x amount of enemies with this gun, kill x amount of enemies with this power, and on and on..
