As you all know now there are only a few actual story missions and the rest is side missions and side objectives. To try and explain a little better I'm separating what I refer to as side missions as being the usual fraud and destruction missions where you're given a bronze, silver or gold rating and the side objectives as being kill x number of this type of enemies. I finished all the side missions which are much fewer in number compared to SR4 with a gold rating. TL;DR Fans of real Roguelikes like ADoM, NetHack(and its variants) *Angband, ToME, CoD, Stone Soup ect will find this one very shallow. For long time Roguelike fans, Cardinal Quest 2 is entirely lacking in the depth and variety that makes those games interesting and the reason they've been played for 25+ years. For those just getting their feet wet in the genre, it may provide a good introduction to how a Roguelike works without overwhelming the player. The unlockables are nice, and I like the pixel art and music, but as it stands the game is way too bare bones to recommend it to any but an absolute beginner to the genre.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
To start, I'd like to say this is a Roguelike incredibly light. And when I say Roguelike, I mean a *real* Roguelike. Not "any game with permadeath and procedural generation" which seems to be what Roguelike means to a lot of people nowdays.
But a turn based (as in, every step you take causes the enemies to act)RPG in randomly generated maps where you make your way through the levels, killing enemies, collecting randomly generated items and levelling up similar to the old ASCII game Rogue. The base mechanics are like any roguelike. Turn based, top down map where you go around killing enemies and finding loot to proceed through the levels.
Compared to most real Roguelikes out there, Cardinal Quest 2 is very shallow. Theres no identification that I can see, and no negative/cursed items(theres no BUC status at all). There isnt even any diagonal movement. You have 5 item slots, 5 spell slots, and your standard "armor/boots/cap/gauntlet/magic item/weapon" (No shield that Ive seen) equipment. Beyond that, there doesnt seem to be any inventory - you dont seem to be able to carry anything beyond what you have equipped and your 5 spells and 5 items. When you find an item, you have the option to "trash" it for gold, or wear it, replacing what you have currently equipped. Theres no shops, but sometimes on a map theres a "scavenger" who has 3 different items to offer you.
Go around a map, collect pre identified items, go to the next screen when you find the exit. Level up on occassion with a tiny 9-skill skill tree. Thats it. There are 7 classes, only 3 of which are unlocked to start, and no races. You cant even name your character from what I can see. (if there is a way, let me know and I'll remove this line)
There is also unlockable perks and gear for each class that you can get by fulfilling certain conditions (like Rogue's Tale). Thats the main draw, and unfortunately appears to be one of the only draws.
Thing is, if there was stuff added it this game across the board it'd be a pretty good lightweight Roguelike. It has decent music and pixel art, unlockables, a global leaderboard and seems like a good foundation to build a deeper game on. As it stands, though, its bare bones. I really can't recommend it to anyone but the most absolute beginner to Roguelikes. Even in that case, theres way better lightweight Roguelikes out there (like Sproggiwood) for the beginner who's just learning the genre. For a longtime player of NetHack, ToME, and ADoM like myself theres not much here to keep you interested.

In preparation for playing this game, I replayed the entirety of SR3 & SR4 (including DLCs). That might've been a bad idea after all. You see, compared to the previous two games, Gat out of Hell is not up to par. It has no real story missions. The story progresses along after you've beaten a set number of side missions. That number isn't a lot and the final boss sort of just sneaks up on you. It also isn't very nice that the final boss (Satan) is just so easy to beat (Pro Tip: Fully Upgraded "Gallows Dodger" pistol, unlimited ammo, & instant pistol reload is key to the rest of the game being♥♥♥♥♥♥easy). Seriously though, the Gallows Dodger might be the most overpowered gun in the series and it doesn't help that the requirements for obtaining it are also easy. After obtaining the aforementioned weapon, I ceased to use my abilities entirely except for the summon minion spell (Pro Tip #2: Fully upgraded summon ability, & fully upgraded summon titan along with the Gallows Dodger makes the game easy as fudge).
The big gimmick of this edition of Saints Row is the fly ability. For its credit, flying is incredibly fun and out of it comes two new activities that take advantage of this new way to travel. But it seems that every new incarnation of Saints Row makes the previous form of travel obsolete. SR4 made vehicles obsolete by giving you super sprinting that had you running faster that any vehicle. And this game makes super sprinting obsolete by giving you flight. It still gives you super sprint in this game, not that I've ever used it.
I feel like there was so much room for potential here. Really Gat Out of Hell should have been its own full fledged game. Hell, SR4 started out as DLC before becoming a full game, so I don't really know what happened here. Perhaps they spent their entire budget on the musical sequence.
If you are a fan of Saints Row games, it's still hard for me to recommend it. It's 20 dollars and going through the missions without doing any side stuff will bring you about 3-4 hours of entertainment. So not a lot. For what its worth, the writing is still spot on Saints Row humor but there's a lot less dialog overall. It's such a shallow experience that I would place the DLC missions from SR3 & SR4 higher than this game.

08-Aug-2016 :  Finished main story
Equipment : MSI GT80-2QE Notebook
REVIEW :
I never had a chance to play this game back in 2007 because I didn't have the hardware strong enough to run it. Now that I have, boy, the graphics quality still doesn't show it's age. Technically, I didn't have any problem running this with newer hardware in Windows 10 environment, but I have problems with the gameplay aspects.
First, the difficulty. I play this on Normal setting but I felt like playing on Hard. The nano-suit energy battery drained really quick. The ammo is scarce. The enemies are everywhere. The stealth and tactical approach are broken. I tried going Predator when infiltrating an enemy base and the cloaking device auto-disabled before I even had a chance to do any stealth kill because the battery already drained. The sniper rifle doesn't have suppresor and really hard to aim enemy from far away, so tactical approach by cloaking and sniping almost always ended with direct combat. Second, although the game is a sandbox, you really don't have any reason to exploring the island. Third, some of the level are frustrating because the game doesn't give  clear explanation on what to do. The final mission for example, you have to survive swarm of enemies and kill the boss using a special gun, but no explanation given on how to use it (you can't just shoot it). So between shooting the swarm of enemies, salvaging ammo, dodging deadly flames and attacks, you have to figure out yourself how to use this new special gun and keep dying in the process. Really annoying.
The story is mediocre, little bit boring for my taste. The multiplayer doesn't work anymore because the servers were closed in 2014. Overall, a really good and innovative game back in 2007, but for today, I suggest save your time and play newer games instead.
CONCLUSION :
Recommended on sale price.

I can't recommend this game, even though I'm probably one of the most patient guys, when it comes to bugs and slow grinding, micromanage demanding games.
The release version was awful, the campaign completely broken and unplayable and the framerate unacceptable. I have an iCore5 Haswell  CPU with 8GB of gaming RAM and an ATI 7700 Series graphics cards. I could barely muster 15 frame per second, which made me feel like being in the 90s, the only kid stuck with an 5 year old Pentium and can't play any latest games.
This is not the case here. I can't actually find a game, that would bring my computer down so much. Not even Crysis 3. And Rebirth isn't even that great looking to begin with.
As of this review, the game is patched to 1.21 and the framerate has improved and some bugs have been corrected.

Regardless of patches, there are much much deeper problems with this game. I doubt they ever gonna be fixed, since they are "features".
Appearantly, the dev team thought, that everyone wants to navigate a space trading/fighting simulator with an XBOX controller, where there are multiple menus and submenus and sub-sub-sub menus to deal with, instead of giving a simple keyboard shortcut.
Appearantly, they forgot, that PC games have 101 keys + at least 3 mouse buttons. I won't even mention people, who got joysticks.

Here is an awful example to compare: Battlefield or Call of Duty both are heavily console-aimed (now), and yet I got shortcut keys for everything, even joystick support for flight.  And we are talking about a simple shooter on a comparabily small map to play on, unlike Rebirth, which has numerous sectors, zones, systems and stations.
I could go on with the menu system starmap, which I have never even heard of.  Dumb down games like Mass Effect has a starmap for crying out loud, even though the space part of game is just some visual  addition, not really required.
Here is the deal.
You may have fun looking at the space stations and flying around for a bit. Heck...you may even have some fun successfully trading or pirating a freighter from the enemy faction.  But I can almost guarantee, that this game will go stale on you, once you realize , that after the first space station built with tremendous amount of work to be done, you'll be doing the same thing for the rest of the time you play. It's not getting easier, it's not getting harder, because you could have billions of credits if the raw materials needed are not there, or you have to travel for 1 hour all around in the sectors to find a cargo freighter carrying the right stuff.
By the time you get to that cargo ship, you'll realize, that your traders are stuck somewhere or being destroyed, without your knowledge,  or your trading computer "forgot" where things are bought and sold and the sectors you have already scanned are showing up again as unscanned.
You are going to get sick of this game real fast and only the most patient will go ahead to continue for a while, possibly install 10s or 20s of mods just to get by or constantly edit his save file to make it someone bearable.
Avoid it...wait for some great space games coming out next  year (Elite: Dangerous, Star Citizen), which are already probably in a better state as alphas, than this "release" version of a giant mess called Rebirth.

This game is fantastic, the art is gorgeous, the music will get your heart pumping in no time, and the controls are spot on. There's a lot of depth here to explore like all the different ways Kragg can use his neutral special to wall off his opponent or all the insane ways Orcane can use his puddles to power up his smash attacks. If you like Smash Bros but want original characters, this is definitely the game for you.
But four warnings for those who want to pick it up:
1. There is no ledge grab. This seems small but it's definitely something to get used to for players who are just coming off smash and expect it to play similarly. Also expect to eat a few lives because your recovery came just short. No items too, but that's up to you if it's a good or bad thing.
2. Online has nothing stopping a pro from stomping a newbie. If you go online and you're not ready for it, prepare to be destroyed by someone three times your skill level.
3. Blast zones are a hell of a lot closer than you think they are, just in general. The game wants you in the center to duke it out or on the side bars sparingly to style on an opponent, you go off screen, you're dead for the most part. No negotiating. The sky hitboxes tend to have the most leeway, but chances are if you're already up there from a juggle, you're not coming back down.
4. If you're fresh off Smash controls, be sure to hit the wrench icon on the character profiles. It can be very jarring to need a seperate button for strong attacks verses tilts or a seperate button to jump. Thankfully before you even hit start there's a great "test play" option to make sure everything's in working order before a match.

This game is a blast and I've enjoyed the hell out of it.
Let me start off my review of the game by stating that this is clearly just a stand-in title until SRV comes out.  It's not meant to be a full game, and it could have, very well, just been released as a DLC for SRIV.  The primary reason that this is not simply a DLC is (in my opinion obviously) because you will not be playing the character that you were using in SRIV.  You are playing as either Gat or Kinzie.  Likewise, you will not be using the same powers as you did from SRIV.  While some of the powers are very similar to what they are in IV, they are very different from them in most regards.
So, here are the things that I liked.  Running around as Kinzie or Gat is fun, simply put.  They have interesting quips they spout as you play through the game; they are always characters that have interested me.  The powers are also really well done and allow you a lot of diversity in how you can play.  Unlike SRIV where I question why they bothered putting some powers in the game at all, none of these feel like they are useless.  I have found a purpose for every power in the game and I like that.  The array of weapons you can choose from is also very interesting.  Unlocking the 7 deadly sins weapons was fun and now they are pretty much my favourite weapons in most cases.  If you are familiar with the gameplay of SRIV, you'll find a lot of the same here, though the ability to fly for as long as you want once you max out the flight powers is really nice.  Lastly, the game is only twenty freaking dollars.  Anyone complaining about a AAA title at this price is an idiot, quite frankly.  The game is very well done and is well worth the price.
Moving on from the things I like, I'll now cover the things that I think could have been done better but didn't really mind.  The dialogue and story for this game is, understandably, short of SRIV.  The reason for that, I believe, would be because SRIV set a really high bar and it would be difficult to reach that again without a good bit of effort.  While some effort clearly could have been spared, I wouldn't say the dialogue is terrible.  A little bit of a spoiler, there is a musical scene in the game that is fantastic and I really wish that they'd done more with that.  It was a really welcomed break from the usual blatantly foul language that persists through the franchise.  The lack of music in the game to listen to while driving around is disappointing, but I have plenty of music of my own to listen to and this does, actually spare me from having to listen to the same songs over and over again, or just listening to one radio station because I don't like the music on the rest.  While it would have been really nice to customize Gat and Kinzie's clothes, I think that would have distracted from the game and I'm fine with it not being in the game.  It would have really been nice to get to use more of the characters as you progressed through the game, such as being able to take the war on Satan as the DeWintre sisters or even Jezebel.  DLC perhaps?  No homies to join your cause, but they'd be more of a burden since you can freely fly around and they wouldn't be able to keep up.  I'm pretty sure a lot of the dead Saints are down there, though.
Things I didn't like about the game.  Really, there's not much.  I didn't like that you couldn't do any sort of vehicle customization, though you'll rarely want to touch a car anyway since you can fly around at will.  No garage or headquarters was kind of annoying as well.  Starting locations were arbitrary when you died, either at the Ultor building or some spot on a different island that wasn't always clear as to why you started there. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the forces of hell is entirely too easy and in the early stages of a (hardcore) game, you are super squishy and very likely to die before accomplishing anything signficant.  There are only 20 character levels, so the stuff you can level up ramps from really weak in the lower levels to really strong later one.  The price jump between levels of abilities is hefty enough that you most likely won't have bought everything by time you finish the storyline unless you are just grinding for cash.  Just playing through the story and doing the loyalty missions, I reached level 20 long before the end of the game, but not before dying a whole lot before I reached level 8, where many of the better abilities start to unlock.
Hope you find this review helpful.  I did enjoy the game, and the shortcomings of this title weren't significant enough to make me unable to have fun, just not as much or engaging as it could have been.  Was I disappointed?  Mildly so.  It could have been more, but it wasn't.  I don't regret making this purchase though and hope that it will be expanded favourably with good and affordable DLC.

Oh, and there's daily quests to get coins! Yay.. or not. Because it requires ARCHETYPES deck - so you can customize it A BIT.

THE BAD
- Still not getting the right gold amounts from daily quests, or it simply erases what i had saved up to now and gives me the ''correct'' amount. Must have lost like 600 gold this way up to now.

I can't believe such bugs still exists many months after the game's launch. Seriously.
THE GOOD

- That's it.

For all the hate this game received, it's pretty amazing.
Now, I will admit that it has a few flaws ; it's far from being a perfect game, and if you start playing, expecting a typical Final Fantasy 7-type game, you will be disappointed. Even if it is a Final Fantasy, it is pretty linear for the first half of the storyline, and the battle system doesn't offer as much freedom as other turn-based RPGs. To finish up the flaws, I'd say it lacks in comparison to other PC games on some otherwise basic features ; for example, a lot of missing customization functions (you can't even change the sound of the game), framerate dropping a little in certain parts of the game, etc.
Those flaws aren't too bothersome, and honestly aren't enough to ruin your experience ; the performance issues aren't that annoying (and even common nowadays because of the poor PC ports that keep being made), the battle system, even if slightly automated, isn't boring at all (thanks to the paradigm system), and, well... Whether you like the linear story or not is up to you ; I personally liked being immersed in a story as incredible as FF XIII's, so it didn't bother me.
Talking about qualities, this game has plenty. As I said, the story of this game is beautiful and complex, with some cutscenes that have truly left a mark in my memory as a gamer and the OST contains tons of songs that fit the game perfectly. The characters all have a deep story and personnality, if you're willing to look past their first impression, which is exactly what the game wants you to do, and which is exactly what many people DIDN'T do. Sure there's a "cutesy" kind of girl, sure there's the stereotype of the stubborn hero, but there's so much more than just that to their character. All these elements that were criticized separately, actually complement each other very well to create a unique experience.
Also, a small but important detail : there is a ton of post game content with very hard superbosses, at the cost of a lot of farming. Farming isn't too hard in this game however, so just hang out with a friend in a skype call, grab something to munch on while you put your brain on autopilot, and it will become more relaxing than annoying.
To finish up my review, I'll repeat what I've said earlier ; if you expect a good old turned-based RPG in an open world to explore, you're going to be disappointed. If you want your game to run perfectly, you're going to be a little annoyed. But look past that, and you have a game with an immersive and amazing story, charismatic characters, a fast-paced combat system, and plenty to do even with a somewhat linear story.
By the way, the game IS very long, and IS very hard. Expect a tough challenge if you play on normal mode! (but well, there's always an easy mode if you just want to enjoy the story)

Egosoft, or rather the lead designer, apparently succumbed to their own arrogance and chose to ignore every bit of feedback from their loyal customers and chose instead to develop a mediocre arcade shooter.  I was alarmed when I read that there would be only one pilotable ship, but was assured that it would be wildly customizable.  They lied, there is virtually zero customization...  which primarily revolves around which of a half-dozen weapons to equip.
They touted on-foot exploration as a groundbreaking feature where we could explore space stations and factories that actually had working machines producing physical goods using physical resources.  They lied...  there are ~4 layouts of space stations with a minimal amount of space to "adventure".  Hallways are blocked off via doors painted on walls and piles of janitorial refuse.  None of them appear to actually serve any real function, although one was obviously intended to be a jail.  I guess some genius figured that nobody would question why 1/4 of the space stations in the game used to be prisons.
They got rid of the time acceleration feature, claiming that their usage of space highways would make the game faster.  Unfortunately it just means that your cargo ships now take hours of real time to get anywhere since they don't use the highways.  And you end up staring at the♥♥♥♥♥end of the 34th century's equivalent of a Honda Civic while traversing the wonders of space.

This game was very poorly received upon release; frame rate issues made this game practically unplayable on even the most powerful systems with a serious degradation in visual quality at playable visual settings. This is no longer an issue for many modern GPUs however and we can begin to get the experience originally intended. The last remnant is a fun jrpg, it's not a big departure from square enix's typical offerings and but the combat is functional and the environments and the world is well realised. I had a lot of  fun playing this game, the world is an interesting enough place I was happy to  spend time exploring it and there are plenty of side missions to aid procrastination if you find the main quest moving by a little too quickly.
In short, if you like Square Enix's other rpgs you'll probably find yourself enjoying this one; fantastical worlds, winding plot lines and outlandish villains are all in place, together with weapons so massive it'd give even Cloud Strife an inferiority complex.

On the surface, Rivals is a really fun game. I got it during the summer sale so I could play with my friends and luckily I was able to do that the day I got it. I jumped straight into the story mode to get used to the game. Despite it being blatantly tacked on, the story mode was a good challenge for me who has never owned a Smash Bros game but has played it countless times at friends' and reletives' houses for maybe 10 years. After story mode, I played with a friend who came over to my house and I introduced him to the game and he picked it up pretty quick, given that he plays Smash semi-regularly at home. After an enjoyable couple hours another friend of mine joined online, the friend who suggested I get this game. Strangely we found that you can't actually do a free-for-all online. Luckily you are able to damage your teamates so that worked out fine but the online features lack clarity (like how no one had any clue as to what was going on when picking a stage). Not having game setting customization is fine (to my knowledge; so no fun gamemodes like sudden death) but not having a free-for-all mode or being able to pick your teams is unexcuseable. At this point, I was still having fun but still was learning and decided to actually try the tutorial. Surprisingly, I found the tutorial very helpful and very in-depth even going so far as to tell you how many frames something lasts or needs to be done by and practice mode can show you the hitboxes of you and your attacks. But the more advanced tutorials show how the game wants to be played and I can't deal with that. The game not only teaches you how to play compettitvely like a pro; it expects it and the skill of some randoms I fought online compared to mine or my friends reinforces that idea for me. The tutorials teach you exactly how the game mechanics work and then immediately task you with abusing them before being alowed to continue. The edgeguarding tutorial alone took me around 30 minutes. Whether its true or not, you have to play dirty in this game in order to compete; you can't just get someone to 100% damage, hit them with a power attack, and expect them to die becuase few attacks have any real knockback on them and even then it's kept to a minimum. If you want kills, you have to push them over the edge and pummel them into the abyss yourself until they finally die. I like to fight a fair fight on the stage and I don't edgeguard becuase I'll either feel like a♥♥♥♥♥♥or be dead afterwards but this game doesn't facilitate that. There is no honor in this style of fighting. If your in to that, I highly recomend this game, otherwise, don't pick it up unless you are exclusively playing with friends you are comfortable with fighting. I'll still play this game with my friends, but I can't take it seriously anymore.

If the content is your issue, maybe you want to wait for the DLC and buy the completed edition, but I love this game and would recommend playing it. Quests in game can vary, but can bring benefits, for example, your citizens can be split on something, but you have the option to change it so that you get extra production, or maybe the other option gives you more science. if you enjoy the base version of Civ 5 I can almost guarantee that you will enjoy this game. But I really encourage that you give this game a chance, and I also think that the mixed ratings are a little unfair to the game.

A worthy follow-up to one of my favorite games. There is more Rapture and it looks gorgeous as ever. This game you play as a Big Daddy and you get the sweet drill. I found myself using the drill more than anything after getting various power-ups and tonics for it. This game is more emotional than the first and I will admit that I cried when I finished it for the first time with the "good ending". This game adds multiplayer, and while a lot of people felt that it was not needed for a game of this type, I personally enjoy this multiplayer more than most games that have a strong single-player portion. Hollow Knight is such a great game.
To start off, the soundtrack and art style are both refined and captivating. The soundtrack helps immerse the player with the scenery and fights contained within the game. It is quite diverse, as I haven't gotten bored with any song in this game. The art style also makes the game unique and creates a distinct atmosphere. However, every room still feels special. Hollow Knight's art style separates the background and foreground quite well, which causes the platforming to be apparent.
Another solid attribute is the platforming. Each room has difficult platforming that isn't completely unfair, but it still provides a challenge. Also, every room doesn't feel repetitive and new concepts are introduced frequently. If you die, you have to run back from your savepoint to where you die and kill a 'ghost' version of yourself. This concept is quite fair, as long as you don't lose your patience. If you die another time, without killing your ghost, you lose all of your money. This shouldn't scare anyone, since you already know how to pass each room. There are also some ways around that issue.
Hollow Knight also provides the player with a varied of enemies, powerups, strategies, and paths. Without spoiling, every section in the extensive world that you play in has a themed variety of enemies. These enemies never feel dry or pointless and are always placed in well-thought-out spots. I have heard people calling the enemies too strong, but they often have a weakness that you can take advantage of. Also, there are many bosses to fight and overcome. In order to overcome these enemies, the developers have put in many powerups for whatever your playstyle is. The main way they do this is by adding charms. Each charm has an exclusive ability that can be used to make certain builds. There never seemed to be one completely overpowered charm, but some builds can be very strong against certain bosses/enemies. There are also upgrades to your weapons and 'magic'. The final thing I would like to talk about in this tumor of a paragraph is the paths/choices. When you start off the game, these paths may overwhelm you, but do not be weary. Eventually, you will get the hang of the massive world and begin to conquer it. Even I enjoyed the different routes. (Usually, I only like linear games.)

One of my favorite parts of the game is the problem-solving aspect. Each boss and enemy, as said before has a certain Achilles Heel. The bosses, however, are my favorites to figure out. The player needs to identify the different 'tells' for each attack, along with a way to dodge it and captitalize on it. There are some random aspects that don't make the game too predictable, but still doesn't make any attack unfair. If you are stuck, try to fight the boss a couple times, not to do damage, but instead, to figure out their attack patterns.

Now it is time to talk about the glitches that I experienced. I am going to start off with the glitches. One glitch that I experienced is when my character started floating and could never touch the ground. This can be helpful, but it can also be annoying, as it is harder to go to different rooms. This is solved when you go to another room, however. Within my current game time of 40 hours, I have encountered this glitch thrice. Another glitch is when my character won't put away the map or the map stays on screen. This glitch is also solved by going to the next room. I only encountered these two glitches, but I have heard of more. These glitches didn't bother me too much, but I still wanted to mention them.
Finally, I will move on to the cons of the game. One problem that I have has to do with the save points. These save points usually have convenient locations, but some of them have terrible locations and make walking back to your body an annoyance. Another problem I have with this game is when some stages have offscreen platforms. These are just frustrating, although it happened only a few times. If you ever get overly frustrated, just take a break. (it really helps in those situations)
Final Thoughts:
-The new DLCs are nice
-This game has some extensive lore (I just didn't talk about it because I don't really care for lore.)
-Great platformer with various content and enemies
-Only 15$ when not on sale
-Too much Zote sex appeal

X rebirth is what you get when you take past X games, arguably take the best parts of those games and add a full body avatar to them. The game starts off good but you will find that there are a ton of bugs present in the initial launch game.
The game is a pretty good space sim, and extremely detailed. Lots of ships are flying about, space cities and stations that span several kilometers and have intricate workings. Lots to see and lots to do. the same can be said for fights with capital ships, no longer are these behemoths large bludgions that will kill your ship when they as much as take a right turn if you happen to be in their way. And instead of just attacking them to dwindle down their HP, they now have actual hard-points on board that can be destroyed, often after you get past the shield generator that protects them. Destroy the engines, jump drive and docking bay ports can render a ship incapable of defending itsself. But get too close or in line of sight with its AA batteries and there will be hell to pay. Large scale battles between multiple capital ships can be a sight to behold. Small ships on the other hand will swoop around larger objects and seek you out, through they can be easy to kill with the right weaponry.
It is certain to say that the combat mechanics of X-rebirth are certainly an improvement.
Unfortunately this can not be said about some of its other main mechanics, and this is mostly due to bugs... Lots and lots of bugs...
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Minor bugs that take you out of the game:
Like crouching characters and falling through the floor when spawning.
- Annoying bugs & behaviour such as:
Icons and triggers not loading for at least half a minute after undocking, or the fact that you often need perfect line of sight to see missions. Or being unable to buy items at discount because you can't afford the the item at full price.
- Major game breaking bugs such as:
Ships that were impounded not being returned to you after a mission is complete, deleting them from the game. Trade ships not functioning like they should, getting stuck.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Another problem is both the games strength and weakness, SATA, (the time skipping feature used to speed up the game) has been removed. Instead, you will now find highways, high speed routes that cross entire sectors. These highways function great for getting around, (as long as there is traffic on them, otherwise you're still very slow). When off the highways you now have a boost feature (partially to replace SATA) this boost allows you to rapidly accelerate, but in exchange it drains your shields. Its a great feature, but shouldn't be used too much in combat.
Initially and AFAIK there is no fast travel to speak of. I suspect you'll be able to hitch a ride later on a capital ship with a jump drive, but I can't say for sure if this is player controled, or just a part of specific missions.
Unfortunatly, capital ships seem to lack the boost feature. Meaning that you will often have to wait several minutes for your trade ship to complete its docking procedure after it jumps into the area, something SATA in previous games so nicely circumvented.
This is compounded by the sheer size of the game world. Finding a character that sells you something can be a chore or even worse, and this is all because even though the game world is suppose to be defined, the merchants and NPC's, besides the terminals you buy and sell bulk goods from are all randomly generated.
So if a character gives you a recommendation for a certain mechanic (npc) with very good stats, that npc won't be there the next time you dock.
Characters, like any other installment of the X series, look like they are either 70 years old, or had a serious cosmetic accident. And the voice acting, while not terrible, has some of the worst writing I've ever heard. Don't even get me started on the small talk feature.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In conclusion, I guess the campaign is decent, if somewhat stale.
Most of the tasks you are asked to do are default sandbox cookie cutter missions such as, Find NPC, Buy/Sell, Deliver, Kill, Scan, Mine, etc. Unfortunately, the few that I found that are unique and contain story telling tend to be quite buggy. The first 5 hours are spend teaching you the ropes on how to play the game. This makes the campaign just a tutorial for the sandbox mode.
My advice to people who are considering this game, WAIT.
The game is fun to play, if it works... but right now there are too many things broken.
Luckily, if EGOSOFT has one saving grace, its that they are pretty good at patching their games. At this time they have already released 20 patches. Give it half a year to a year, pick it up during a steam sale and have the experience this game was suppose to have at launch...

Thanks to its working Steam achievements, actual (yet simple) story, more memorable and eventful levels, and faster paced gameplay, Rescue Team 7 is one of the high points of this time management series.
Since this is the seventh entry in a series of time management games where the core gameplay has not changed since its creation, most players probably know the drill by now: in Rescue Team 7, we use rescue workers, doctors, firemen, policemen, dogs, and vehicles to collect resources, fix buildings, and save civilians.
Despite looking like a copy-paste job of Rescue Team 6, this game hides quite a few surprises, chiefly in level design. Thanks to careful object placement, all stages feel a lot faster and busier, so gameplay is tighter and more fun—but it also requires more attention from the player, especially to meet some of the time requirements.
The puzzle levels also received a large overhaul: they now feature cavern exploration, where the goals require less guesswork and more focus on proper resource management.
For the first time since the third game, we also have an actual story. It is just a very simple romance between two workers, but its presence alone is enough to consider Rescue Team 7 a fun and memorable time management game, one of the best in its series.

- The rest of the bad reviews are from the long term fans of the game. The game is lacking a large amount of the functionality from X2/X3 and has regressed to be more like the first game in the series and as a result you have less control and freedom in the game than the previous two titles.
Although I'm judging the game as its own title, it needs to be said that the game is an attempt at a reboot. Egosoft were for a time not going to make any more "X" series games and were going to work on something else. Due to fan feedback they decided to make their next title an X game after all (I beleive they just slapped the X label on what they were working on, this timing would have been very early in development so wouldn't have caused them much issue). While as its own game, it is a nice little diversion while I wait for better games comming out over the next 2 years (primarily Star Citizen and Elite: Dangerous) the previous games (X3/X2) are better overall.
This game is like all X games, they start out buggy though not unplayable and over time the bugs are quickly resolved. If you've played an X game before you will expect this. Be warned however there is alot more under the hood besides the graphics this time around meaning you need a beefy PC to run it. The system requirements on the store page are not accurate and were probably written early in the games development though noone has thought to recheck.
The story is pretty terrible but lets face it, X games never have a good story. The game world is interesting and detailed, with lots of background history that is interesting. The gameplay isn't so different from previous X games though the interface is different in both good and bad ways meaning it is improved in some areas though worse in others evening out over all.

Quick and fun side-scrolling shooter with a great soundtrack and a simple but very effective cover mechanic. Characters (9 of them) are distinct and provide very different game experiences, although one or two are unfortunately rendered obsolete by even more specialised later unlocks (looking at you Cletus). Enough levels to keep you interested, and difficult enough (especially with optional side objectives) to keep the shortish levels playable. There's no checkpoint system, but very rarely does dying in the final stretch of a level seem like any more a punishment than dying in the opening corridor. You're never more than a second or two away from the next playthrough, in any case.
Comparison have been drawn to Hotline Miami, due to the pace, twitchy skills and the ease with which everything on screen dies, but NOT A HERO does a number of things differently. Infinite ammo, cover, the occasional defenestration-based platforming section and a (very small) pool of regenerating health turn the central challenge from one of 'how do I make sure I'm the only thing left alive' to 'how do i move quick enough through these enemies to reach that payphone in the next building'.
Overall, if ever you'e after an arcadey, gratifying experience without any of the drama of a real storyline, and the idea of a main character voiced by a squeaky airing cupboard door (no really) appeals to you, this is the game for you.

Before I start this review, I'd like to note that I had absolutely no idea that this game existed prior to blindly purchasing it over the Steam Summer Sale. With that said, I'll begin.
The Last Remnant is certainly a unique Square Enix RPG. As opposed to following the formulaic "3-4 party members in an HP and MP driven turn based battle" system, this game tries to implement an original and somewhat unique battle system. The basic elements of a Square Enix RPG are there, but the new features in battle are also very important factors. These new features, however, can be very confusing and overwhelming upon first playing. The battle system still functions, though, and it's enjoyability boils down to the player's understanding of it. The writing is as you'd expect from a Square RPG: Over the top, and very anime esque. This causes the writing on some characters (Most notably, the protagonist) to be very cliche and predictable at times. The graphics are somewhat primitive, but aren't distracting in any way. From what I've heard, the soundtrack ranges from being stale and bland, to awe inspiring. It's really an open bag. My biggest complaint with the game is that it anticipates that the player uses an Xbox 360 controller. So much so, that the tutorial commands use 360 button inputs. However, this can be remedied with a very brief visit to the main screen settings menu.
Overall, The Last Remnant is a game that I would recommend. I realize that I've been somewhat down on it in this review, but it really is not a bad game by any stretch of the imagination. If you're a fan of JRPG's and Square Enix, this is a game for you.

As someone who does not have the time nor the money to get heavily involved with actual Magic cards I found Magic Duels to be a great way to scratch that itch.
Let me put this simply:
If you are looking for a digital Magic experience that is as rich as playing the actual cardboard version of Magic and you adamantly refuse to settle for anything less, then Magic Duels is not for you.
Why?
You will likely find the truncated card selection irritating and will miss many of the social aspects of real life playing that is not present in Magic Duels at the moment. In truth I doubt any digital version of Magic will ever completely replicate all the nuances that people enjoy about the physical version
However,
If you are like me and are looking for a fun way to get into (or back into) playing Magic with out the hassle and expense of cardboard magic then look no further.
Why?
While the card selection is not 100% complete, it is certainly more than decent enough for many interesting deck building possibilities and the F2P business model for acquiring the cards seems very generous relative to other digital cardgames *cough*Hearthstone*cough*.
There are guides on the forums which can help newbies create viable starter decks out of the free cards that are initially granted after the first set of tutorials and the rest of the card selection can be unlocked at a fair pace for free by playing the AI and other players (I probably got the currency for half my boosters just by testing the various decks I've built against the AI). Still, don't expect to unlock all the cards in one day with out laying down some cash; though it can be done in about a month completely for free if you are an avid player.
A few notes:
-The game has had server issues, though they seem mostly cleared up at this point. I haven't run into any trouble playing in the past week or so.
-Some people report bugs with certain hardware configurations, I've had none. Your mileage may vary.
-Some complain about the lack of features, I agree. More features are always better however the developers have said they are committed to adding more cards/features and refining the interface in the future. Specifically, new cards are suppose to be added on the same time table as they are released for the physical card game, so that is cool.
-Some people complain about a lack of in-game chat and other interface qualms, personally I can do without it during matches. Though an in-game lobby would be cool to discuss the current metagame and strats etc...
If the devs and Wizards tend to the investment they have in this piece of software then I am sure things like this are on the horizon as they would better flesh out the already enjoyable experience that this game offers.
-Personally I wish there were more cosmetic things available to purchase in the store (avatar pictures, card table backdrops and stuff like that.) As of right now it is just booster packs and it seems like a waste to me to spend more than a few actual dollars on them as if you play regularly you will eventually unlock them all in pretty short order anyways. *shrug*
Its a really good game with good graphics and good interface and the campagin is good from my expericance and a good story. Would recommend

It seems that SquareEnix tries to re-live the thriumph of its golden era but not so succesfully i suppose. Here is The Last Remnant a jrpg with turn based battles that feature some RTS elements. More in depth we have:
GAMEPLAY:

In TLR you get to control a youth named Rush. You venture in 3D invironments in towns and dungeons while the city and wolrd maps are simple images (kinda .. "Naaaaahh" to me). The enemies are visible on the screen and you can ambush them avoid them or get ambushed (you dont wanna do that). Well here comes the sad part! The battle system thought it seems quite promising it ends to be very boring one sided and soooo automated! Well its seems like the developers would like to make it extremely simple yet strangely difficult to win a battle. What do i mean? Here is the thing. When you enter the battle there is no option of escape!! The player has to choose between some automated commands like "attack", or "back em up" or "attack with combat arts". Seriously? All you have to be careful about is not to get flanked (amonst enemies) and all is great! i mean come on?! what happened to equipping magic or using items manually and stuff like that!? Many will say that TLR differs cos it is more like strategy when it comes to the battle part but i disagree! Even if it is that way its quite noobish! Unfortunately gameplay isnt its strong part!
PLOT:
The plot is quite classic yet very enjoyable with the classic fantasy world and its kingdoms. In the first intro we see Rush rushing into a battlefield while he searches for his freshly kidnapped sister! i wont do any more spoilers. Play it yourselves!
MUSIC:
The music part is one of its strong points i guess where its plave has its own music. It is very pompous and magnificent at parts and get you quite well in the mood
GRAPHICS:
Graphics are wuite detailed and "clean" with lots of colors and drawn and designed with creativity and talent! The only thing is that sometimes it gives me the impression that there is so much symmetry especially in towns!
OVERALL:
In general terms TLR is a game worthy of your time and money that every jrpg games must at least once experience!

I've played this game extensively and only recently bought it on Steam, so my real hours are probably more like 30-40 hours.
This game is one of my favorite as far as allowing players to basically create their own mechanics goes.
It honestly gives you some of the best tools to work with. AI that have semi predictable, but also somewhat realistic behaviours. There's a large array of tools at your disposal, from the firepower that you possess, to the main focus point of this game, that being the super suit that allows you to choose between speed, strength, invisibility and increased armor. And tying all this together, is a large open world enviroment that is designed specifically with directed, but branching pathways that allow players to approach any situation in any way they desire.
This alone is why you should buy the game.
True, it has beautiful graphics, and an amazing physics engine, the story is actually honestly interesting. Plus the gameplay manages to change as the enemies get tougher, the challenges change, and new approaches to situations arise as vehicles get worked into the campaign.
The single player is amazing, but lets get to one of the biggest drawbacks to this game as is.
Even when it was functional, the multi player was never quite there. The biggest drawback to this game was how high the system requirements were to play this game, only around 5-7 years after the game released was the average computer actually able to play it. So the multiplayer, while bloody amazing in my opinion, never got traction. At best there were ten people or so actually in a server.
But anymore, its impossible to play it because the gamespy servers shut down. Maybe there are ways to still play it, but the game you specifically buy doesn't have a way to play multiplayer.
There are also complications with running the 64bit version of the game, there are some things you need to patch in if it doesn't work on 64 bit, just to be aware. So this game does have its issues, but its still very much so a worthwhile buy.

The Last Remnant is a random-soup of a jrpg with funny moments/references, serious situations, (I think?!?) and deep gameplay, with the amount action seasoned to taste just right. You play as a character named rush out to save your sister. Combat has lots of ins and outs so reading a guide or the manual is helpful, BUT having just jumped in myself when I played on the XBOX360 there's no harm in trial and error.
I'm just gonna keep it simple. Imagine you are a commander on a battle field, with a REALLY big megaphone. You can control units, having them engage enemies, retreat,and heal themselves or others. Depending on class/weapon choice and style/character you get different abilites to use in combat, and the more often you use them the more powerful they/you become.  Formations also change the way your members stats have an effect on the group as a whole and they also get stronger with use. (I think I may have accidently got carried away and over explained combat o.o #hypocrite)
And for the crafter in you, enemies and their bits n pieces, along with mining (not gonna spoil what tool you use!!), Provide components with which you can create and upgrade current gear, and you can later disassemble said gear for MORE goodies.
I do suggest you do quests though, they help with making REALLY shiny gear...speaking of...
The abundance of side quest/ lore material is lovely, and reading a statue that later reveals deep meaning in a conversation with a random npc is always a great experience, dots connecting YO! Very important I think in making a world believable. And they aren't just fluff either quests unlock new areas, items, customizations, characters, AND more. So doing them, although not  mandatory, is helpful and fun indeed.
The map is very huge and filled, though their are lots of loading screens between areas. Although you better be used to it after the Zelda series >.> The areas you visit are unique. I find this to be important when conveying personality of an area in a game and the little details are important as previously stated, SO SEARCH AND YOU SHALT BE REWARED!!!
And lastly the story is very interesting, and deep if you dig into the game you realize there's a lot more to it then if you just ran through and even then its nice. The character designs are multi-faceted/ They can be serious, and are sometimes caricatured versions of personalities they represent. I think the overexaggeration is a nice touch, a change to all these people in games who aren't awkward at times, seemingly perfect. Also it's very common in jrpgs for the personalites to be more pronounced, so if you aren't used to it, watch some foriegn films from places like japan or korea etc. or read some novels from there (Ex. I have always been a big civ fan and started playing in the early 90's. First Civ, then Civ2 (big fan), 3, 4 and 5. Also Alpha Centauri, Colonization and Civ4 Colonization (bah).
Despite all the mixed reviews, I really enjoy this a lot more than Civ 5. Played two games so far and have not encountered any major issues/bugs.
Some of the things I like:
- The new tech tree is really innovative, you can research anything you want.
- Military has been simplified with just a few units to choose from.
- Spying is a lot easier to understand.
- Cities don't revolt, but you do suffer certain penalties.
- Really unique ways to win the game.
- Doing away with the stacking makes warfare a lot cleaner and easier. I generally don't like going to war, so this helps.
- You don't pick one country with perks, you pick a combination of perks you want at the start of the game.
- Games on a standard map with standard time take about 10 hours to finish.
- You really don't need to build a huge amount of cities to do well, I think having 7-8 cities is plenty.
- Really enjoy the concept of Affinity. You want to leave in harmony with the planet or fight it?
Some of the thing I feel mixed about:
- A lot of wonders don't have a little movie.
- Diplomacy feels somewhat limited. You can't trade technologies. Then again that might hurt the computer even more.
Things I don't like:
- During diplomacy you can't see how many resources you have, making it hard to determine if you want to trade or not.
- You can't tell your opponents to not settle or start an expedition near your cities, but they can.
- Computer AI can go from friendly to neutral to declaring war on you in just a few turns.
- Computer AI will tell you to remove your expedition while the expedition is already finished. Can't do too much then...
All in all, a fun game and a more simplified Civ experience. I think if you felt that thing needlessly got more and more complicated after Civ 2, you might want to give this a try.

Opinions on FF XIII are either strongly for or strongly against.
I fall under the former category.
In short I strongly recommend this game to all fans of jRPGs, those who do not put freedom of exploration before the story and are alright with being steered by the narrative instead of shaping it. The story is only hard to understand if you are unwilling to read the additional information provided in the codex which offers further explanation, but if you spend some additional time reading it, I believe you'll find it quite enjoyable.
It is a tale of coming to terms with one's circumstances, challenging onself and then facing a seemingly hopless situation head on and learning the machination behind what might seem a random plot at a glance.
Narrative is placed in a world that is a mixture of sci-fi and fantasy, focused on the struggle of each of the 6 main characters learning to deal with the situation they have been thrown into and their growth into people which will try to change their fate however improbable the odds may be. It is set in a time of unexpected war and starts off by throwing the player into the middle of the things, ensuring the player is as every bit as confused with the entire situation as the protagonists  are.
While the story unfolds, it offers some additional insight into the protagonists minds by means of flashbacks mixed with some read-through material in the form of a codex.
It is also being told for the majority of the game through the points of view of the specific characters until, quite late in the game, it gets unified into one generic point of view of all the characters joined together in one goal.
The initial pace the story unfolds in is slow, however, mixed with a sort of prolonged introduction into the battle system. It picks up the pace after around 7-8 hours into the story.
Hands down one of my favorite OST ever created for a video game. Love it, is all I am going to say.
I find this game to be beautiful, with detailed settings, interesting character design, but not something you would not expect in a jRPG, and interesting monsters design. All is kept in a clearly defined style which adds to the story as one can see everything is a part of the same universe. Nothing in this game seems out of place.
The battle system is sort of turn based with its own twist, but it really takes its time to give the player full control.
I agree that the tutorial is way too long for no apparent reason, limiting the player choices to very few options in the early game. The introduction of class switching and the intricacies of this system are explained and then make for some very spectacular and interesting battles, but I do feel it has been weirdly dumbed down in its execution. The complexity of this system and the need to really plan one's tactics comes up in only a couple of battles.
The entire game can be beaten quite fast, but in order to complete all of the side quests, all of which involve running somewhere and killing a monster, and get all of the achievements griding for experience becomes necessary and quite tedious. Especially since the sidequests are not really that creative and forcing player into a lot of running through all of the locations only for the sake of prolonging the time the player spends with this game.
Thankfully the beauty of the game somewhat makes up for the need to revisit the locations and the amount of running one's does, nonetheless, I could have done without it and would have still loved the game.
If you want to obtain all of the achievements you're looking into around 80 to 100 hours, depending on how willing you are to truly understand the mechanics of the battle system to ensure you can beat the most difficult enemies to receive the most experience points.

I'll start this review with a very important point:
This is "Sid Meier's CiVilization: Beyond Earth" (SMC:BE), NOT "Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri 2" (SMAC2?).
When I read the announcement for Beyond Earth I was so happy. Finally, I thought, a new SMAC game! How I had waited for this day! Wrong. SMC:BE is not SMAC2. Never has been, never will be.
Obviously, the backbone of SMC:BE is based on Sid Meier's Civilization V, which is a good thing if you liked SMCV. This is also a bit of a flaw, the game is a bit too much like SMCV, and occasionally feels as a DLC rather than a game on its own. The game includes some rather neat mechanics, though, like minor civs spawning during the game (as compared to CiV, where they were as ancient as the major civilizations) and an "affinity" system. I really wanted to make a simple pros/cons list here for prospective buyers to look at, but oddly enough realized that many of the features I like is also in some way (in my opinion) flawed.
+Hexagons
I think this is a vast improvement to the squares of Civ I-IV. It might seem like a minor issue, but I like them hexagons!
+/- One unit per tile
This is a difficult one... the stacks of doom from Civ I-IV (and SMAC), was definitely annoying, but maybe it would have been better with two or three units/tile? Artillery becomes very vulnerable, and it does seem weird that you combine your units a bit better. And seriously, how many soldiers do you have in each unit if you can't fit two in one tile? Either the units should be more abstract (artillery as a promotion on a base infantry or mechanized chassis maybe?) or it should be possible with more units on a single tile (although some kind of limit is probably good).
+/- User interface
Ok, although a bit messy at times. Not bad, but Firaxis is a studio with plenty of experience, so I had expected better.
++/- Affinity system
Your colony is defined by the way you treat the planet and your citizens. This is a really neat feature, but mechanically it falls a bit short. You just can't feel how your choices affect the colony, I would have liked to see something more dramatic, seeing the terrain becoming more earthlike for a Purity-type colony would be great. Similarly, getting improved yields from pristine, unchanged, terrain for harmony-type colonies would be cool. Sure, it is a nice feature as implemented, but it could have been better. Your opponents choices also alter their leader appearance in a (too) minor way, which is nice, but it is a bit unfortunate that you can't (as far as I know) look at your own leader.
- Leaders
Not much personality on the leaders, and the factions don't really differ that much. The factions (or sponsors) are tied to geographic regions rather than ideologies (although in-game quotes do point at ideological differences). I would have preferred leaders with a more apparent ideology, but since this is partly decided by player choices along the affinity track it isn't too much of a problem. And if factions are geographic; why is there no North European or Middle East faction? Planned DLCs?
(+) Diplomacy
Somewhat improved from SMCV with the "favor" system.
+/- AI
Seems pretty good. Haven't tried too much on the higher difficulties though. A bit annoying when the AI leaders proposes trades that they themself don't accept, but that will probably be solved with a patch.
+/- Minor civs
Minor colonies appearing during the game is a really nice feature. Unfortunately, the only thing these minor civs are used for is to destroy or trade with. More personality would have been nice.
- Trade
Awfully implemented. Too much unnecessary micromanaging.
- Terraforming
Ok... seriously, why can't I do this? Is the "Terrascope" improvement as good as it gets? At least being able to plant forests would be nice... which brings about another issue: why do forests suck?
+ Graphics
Nice. Not in any way spectacular, but still nice.
+/- Tilesets and terrain
The game comes with three different tilesets for the planets: "lush", "fungal" and "desert". Some complaints have been raised that within each tileset there is not enough difference between terrain types (e.g. grassland or tundra), and I concur with this, but that is not a major issue. The fact that there are different tilesets is something I find really neat, but just like the affinity system it falls a bit flat. I would have liked each tileset to be a completely different experience, possibly along with different taxa of aliens and different resources. As it is now it stops at nice, but implemented fully it would have been awesome.
- Game ending
In one word: underwhelming. In my first game I won the Supremacy victory. I'm not going to spoil the story, but the after effects should be rather profound, and a short movie prelude to show this would have been nice.
+ Overall playability
While the review might seem a tad negative I still have played 28.8 hours, and must say that I enjoyed it. I'll probably spend at least as many hours again before I'm fed up. Having paid about 30€, I can't really regret my purchase. 30€ for 60h of entertainment isn't bad. The game is OK and I do recommend it, at least if you can get it at a reduced price. It is a bit disappointing that it plays so similar to Civilization V, though, some groundbreaking new feature would have been nice. The affinity system is nice, but Firaxis could have given more depth to it.
With a DLC or two it will probably be really good. Which is a bit tragic, I guess, but that is how most of the gaming companies work today. Some more so than others.
What is the deal with the low user scores then?
Well... the main reason, as I see it, has to do with the point I began the review with. SMAC is awesome, way better than Civ 2 from which it spawned. Way better than CIv 3, 4 and 5 for that matter. And SMAC is... different. It has a well-written world with plenty of personality, leaders you can love or hate (or love to hate). I have spent a hideous amount of hours on SMAC. The bar was set so tremendously high by SMAC (way back in 1999) so the expectations on SMC:BE by the community has been ridiculous. And I think that SMAC has a rather vocal fanbase in the 4x community.
But this is not a review of SMAC2, there is no such game.
If you would like to play a new, modern Civilization game, with a few rather neat features, go ahead: buy SMC:BE, you won't regret it. Compared to SMCV (which I liked), SMC:BE is a good game. Compared to SMAC, well... it is kind of mediocre, but still ok. If you haven't played SMAC, it is available at
for a meager 4.79€, if you like Sci-fi and Civ-type games you'll love it. Sure, graphics are a bit dated, and the AI is a bit weird at times, but it is still the best 4x game to date.

As crazy as any game you will purchase. You have no doubt heard the hype about this game. For this game is nothing but hype. Why? People say "play this game". "Why?" you respond. "I can't tell you. Just play it." I'm sure you've had that conversation. The reason people want you to play it is that the game is very very funny and to tell you anything about it would spoil the comedy. So rather than say specific things about it I'll just loosely describe it. Firstly it isn't a game yet it uses a game engine...the source engine from Half Life 2 to be exact. This game followed on the heels of Portal 2 and it pretty much owes that game for its popularity as well as its sarcastic and passive aggressive sense of humor. I guess calling this a cross between an adventure game and a digital interactive novel would be the best fit. You have a character and you wander around in this game world. You can click on things. The point is not what you can accomplish, the point is to enjoy the story...or rather the attempts to get to the story. There are many many games now, mostly in the anime game world that exist just as stories where you make choices and the main point is to enjoy the story and especially to experience all the different endings you can. Things like Hatoful Boyfriend and Long LIve the Queen, and a little bit of the Skauras and things like that. Not much game but choices you make in the narrative affect what story path you take. Well THIS is kind of the opposite. You don't make choices in the narrative. YOu make choices in the game world by your actions and the narrative follows you. However, the narrator is not always keen on the choices you make. So as far as the gameplay goes, if you like roaming around in a portal worldthen sure you'll be okay with that part of it. I do feelit gets a bit resource hoggy and the frequent loadscreens at times just kinda take over until they are finished. The story here is less of the point. This is a comedy game. And you willdefinitely see several points where you are laughing your hiney off. One thing that should be said is that yes you should keep playing and peel away every little shell of this game. It is not very clear of the amount of content that is here and you may think that when you get to the end ...and go...."That's it??" Well that's not it. There's a lot here. Now aside from the comedy there lies another layer beyond that will go over many people's heads. This is quite an existential philosophy game. It is a satire. It is social commentary about gaming and gamers as a whole. IT is a spoof or parody of adventure and action games. Yet it IS one itself. Like the movie Scream was a parody and commentary of horror movies while being one itself. Primal Carnage is an excellent game!
Dinosaur games have had a very rough history. Most were either "meh" or just bad. However, a few of them were gems; and Primal Carnage is one of them. This game succeeds what many games failed at creating: fun, cool, playable dinosaur gameplay.
Playing as the dinosaurs is in third-person and is solid, though they could use a bit more polish. Playing as the larger dinos, such as the T-Rex & Carnotaurus may seem a bit slow to respond to turning, but it doesn't deter them, or the other dinosaurs from being fun to play as a whole. Each dinosaur plays similarly, but each brings their own unique class abilities to the table.
The design & animation of the dinosaurs are amazing & life-like, and the DLC includes a ton of beautiful, high quality skins to use for your favorite dinosaur classes.
Playing as the humans is also surprisingly fun. The control is fluid and reminiscent of more classic forms of first-person shooters like Halo & Team Fortress 2, having no ironsights for guns other then the sniper rifle. The classes have some creative members on their team, such as the Trapper who wields net gun and dual handguns.
There is no form of progression system such as perks or upgrades. Though some may think the game lacking in that respect, it fits the game's simple approach to making a fun, easy to pick-up humans vs. dinosaurs multiplayer game. Though skins for the humans is still lacking compared to the number of dinosaur skins, the human DLC skins are fully remodeled and not simple reskins like as in many other games.
Graphics are also top notch, rivaling many other higher budget games while at the same time not sacrificing natrual lighting and colorful environments for the filtered, cinematic atmosphere that many games today have.
The classes are fairly balanced and the gameplay relies on teamwork like in the Left 4 Dead games rather than players running off on their own and doing their own thing like in most other online multiplayer games. The game is also constently updated and is driven by community feedback via the game's website.
This game is definitely worth its price, especially as the game is still growing with more maps, gametypes, DLC, and more in the future.

This is by far and away the greatest game I have ever played. From the very beginning exploration is put at the forefront with the opening area to be freely explored until culminating in a spectacular boss fight and the first of many powerups. The combat and platforming mechanics are also used to their full potential as the game has some fights that require considerable mastery to beat. The game does not ape Dark Souls, however, and so the standard end of the game can be reached by those do not have as much skill or time to put into the game through use of the upgrade system and charm system. The controls are also incredibly tight with instantaneous acceleration upon movement and the "super mario" style controlable jumping mechanics. As the game progresses the character's moveset increases and map traversal becomes even more of a joy.

And you will be traversing the map a lot, crawling back and forth through the areas. No one's playthrough is quite the same. At its most basic level the world may be your completely standard Metroid-Vania fare, but it's so enjoyable and polished that it stands out from other titles. When I finished my first ~30 hr playthrough I knew the layout of HallowNest better than my own house. And that's saying something considering the enormous scale of the map. There's something incredibly satisfying about crawling through what looks like just some short dead-end crack in the wall and coming out the other side in a completely new area. The world kept expanding long after I expected it to stop and when it did stop I was saddened it didn't keep going farther. The world is vast and complex, but it certainly doesn't overstay its welcome.
The areas themselves are also stellar. Each has its own unique set of themes tweaking the flavor of the combat, platforming and exploration mechanics. And the game rarlely repeats itself. Some programmer had the thankless task of scripting how the conveyer belts interact with every platforming mechanic only for the convey belts to be used in only one area, but the backtracking ensures that you will get to experience every area to the fullest before you finish the game. Not every area is quite so memorable, but those areas shined more upon my second playthrough since I had not quite mastered their mechanics or layout and so still had exploration and discovery left to do.
If this was all there was to say about the game it would still be a masterpiece: but no. When I went into this game I though that the most important part of a game was, of course, its mechanics, but this game may be changing my mind because the visuals and audio are some of the best I have ever experienced. They may not seem that outstanding in the trailers (or maybe they do), but the artstyle and soundtrack go a long way in selling the experience of this game: that of a small bug exploring an ancient decrepit world far bigger than itself. The artstyle, despite its slightly horrifying mind-contol imagery, is very cute and can soften the large uncaring world it depicts into a place I feel happy being in.  The music in the base game is largely moody atmospheric tracks played on what sounds like the viola, cello, and piano, but the game also knows how to use its large bombastic orchestral tracks when the mood calls for them.
Hollow Knight exemplifies everything that a Metroid-Vania should be and everyone should play this game even if they have no interest in Metroid-Vania platformers, or even video games in general. This game is the perfect Christmas / Birthday present. As for the cost, this game would not be unreasonable at $60. The $15 pricetag (and $10 sale price at time of writing) feels like highway robbery. If there really isn't room in your budget for this game you need to make room as soon as humanly possible. This game is well worth your money and will not dissapoint.

For those of you who have played the original Bioshock, you will be right at home in Bioshock 2. For the rest of you, go play the original Bioshock first; if you don't you will be more than a little confused.
A little background first: both games take place in a city called Rapture located on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean. It was created as a utopia where you could choose your own destiny without the interference of governments or organized religion. As you can imagine this didn't last, and by the time you show up in the first game Rapture has deteriorated into a big free-for-all. The man who created Rapture, Andrew Ryan, serves as the main antagonist in the first game.
The second game takes place eight years after the first one, which is surprising because I can't believe that the city continued to function for that long. You play as a Big Daddy who has been gone from Rapture for ten years.
The city is now under the control of a psychiatrist named Sofia Lamb, and you have plenty of reasons to hate her. In direct contrast to Ryan's exaltation of the individual, Lamb is all about everyone working together. I find it interesting that all of these people who came to Rapture specifically for self-determination are suddenly working for Lamb.
In Bioshock the end cutscene depended on what you did to the Little Sisters you found: did you save them or harvest them? In Bioshock 2 there was more to it. In addition to the Little Sisters, there were several characters who you could decide to spare or kill; different situations surround each choice. I have heard that there are something like 12 different endings to the game depending on what you decide to do. This is one of the significant things that they improved over the original game in my opinion.
Other than that though I felt that the story wasn't quite as good as the original. While it wasn't too difficult to understand where Andrew Ryan was coming from when he went on his rants, I really couldn't understand the reasoning behind Sofia Lamb's plan to create a perfect society. Speaking of Ryan, many of the characters and recordings talked about him and their opinions of how he ran things; clearly Rapture was still living in his shadow 8 years later. I felt like Bioshock 2 was similarly living in its predecessor's shadow, especially because the creative minds behind the first game (read: Ken Levine) weren't directly involved in the second.
The area that Bioshock 2 made huge improvements in was the gameplay. In the original game you had to switch between your weapon and plasmid, but in the second you always had both available to you. This alone made battles much more fast-paced and hectic. There was also more variety in enemy types; the splicers are a lot more deformed, presumable due to the extra years since the first game, and there are now brute splicers. They aren't quite as tough as Big Daddies but they fill in the gap between weak foes and really tough ones. The scariest enemy that they added was the Big Sister. They come after you sometimes after you have rescued a Little Sister, and they are tough. They use plasmids and melee attacks, and they are extremely nimble. I couldn't get a screenshot of them while they were alive because I was too busy trying to shoot them, but here is a dead one.
There were new weapons as well: the metal pipe you wielded in the original game is replaced by the Big Daddy's Drill, and I took malicious pleasure in pinning enemies to walls from afar with the new spear gun.
raphically Bioshock 2 is beautiful. The environment was almost identical to the original, but you can immediately tell the difference when you look at character models from the two games.

Defy Gravity Extended is a puzzle platformer game where you play as Kara, a gravitymancer. You will use a gun that places gravity wells and anti-gravity wells. You will use them often to solve various puzzles throughout the game. Gravity well pulls you into its center, while anti-gravity wells repels you from its center.
Defy Gravity Extended has a very unique game mechanic, it is quite different than most puzzle platformer games I've played. The soundtrack for this game is very nice and relaxing too. You can get 100% achievements just by finishing the game. I like that the game doesn't make you finish a level in a particular time so you won't be pressured while playing. The game has 24 levels and certainly doesn't lack in challenge. There is also a checkpoint system in the game, so if you die, you won't start from the beginning which is nice.
However, for me, it is more frustrating than It is to enjoy while playing this game. The controls are a little bit difficult. I don't like the animation. The game looks very unappealing to me. The game lacks on the options menu. You can't adjust the game's volume at all, so you will need to change it from Windows or your speaker. It also lacks in resolution options too. The game at one point crashes, but it wasn't in a middle of a level. The story is pretty much non-existent.
In conclusion, Defy Gravity Extended is a unique and very challenging game. But it is very frustrating to play. I don't enjoy this game very much, maybe because this game isn't for me. The price seems a little fair though. But I do not recommend buying this full price since it goes on sale quite often. I do recommend purchasing this game on sale because it's usually on sale for 90% off or more.
