If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Hehe~ I've actually played about 55 hours of the game, but Steam was offline at the time... so they're all lost.
Truly an Awesome JRPG with a good mix of characters, masses of quests to do and a compelling storyline, it just makes me want to play more. I hear people worrying about Battle Ranks and being unable to beat certain bosses, yes I have come across that issue slightly... but like any other JRPG I just resolved it by ignoring it and doing the other quests, grinding and getting items as such. Aka playing the game thorough... I certainly don't think this is a game you can play through in 5 minutes, not now or never, just make sure you save regularly because the game will punish you otherwise; the level of difficulty is quite punishing for new players and can spike very quickly which may catch some people out.
The weapons available are all pretty unique but at the same time not particularly easy to get, which encourages actually looking for the components and getting the funds to purchase them. Some of the best weapons can be purchased straight from shop, but for the real awesome weapons you'll have to upgrade existing or craft from scratch. There's a pretty huge choice available which is nice. The enemies can vary from very weak to extreme challenging, all depends on what area you are venturing; you'll often stumble across something considerably stronger than you... and meet the game over screen... but it wouldn't be a game without challenge. ;)
Unreal Engine is pretty okay with this game... it looks good on the relatively low settings I have, but the thing is ridiculously demanding if I turn anything up higher... which is kinda odd seeing as I can play games like Hitman Absolution and JC2 without too many problems. Its not like its a latest game or anything (2-3 years older than Absolution), so running it on borderline low is kinda meh, and the only reason I'll put it down a little.
The last thing I'll say is the Musical score is downright impressive... and whilst the standard battle theme can get a little repetitive, the boss music is incredible; it feels completely and utterly epic when you get that incredulously hard boss fight that will punish every mistake you make, it makes what would be a frustating boss fight for me, actually feel like I'm fighting something that is waaaay stronger than what I can handle.
Even the way the game consists of Unions makes the scenarios of battles epic, there's nothing more unique than fighting with a huge onslaught of 25 people versus a single extremely strong monster with rocking battle music playing; a pretty awesome experience.
I completely recommend this game to anyone, but only if you have the patience and knowing that ultimately you will lose battles a few times; this game does NOT hold your hand. However, if you're wanting a truly unique RPG with a good storyline, strategic battle system, a decent amount of game hours and awesome music... you've come to the right game. ;)

Whoever said this was a glorified tech demo had their head buried in a hole.
Crysis is a truly open world first person shooter. Nothing before nor after (at least at the time of writing this) has matched its prowess of being able to almost literally do anything you can think of to complete a task or objective.
You're given an experimental special ops nanosuit. A suit that has the ability to infuse strength, provide protection, increase speed as well as provide a stealth cloak. Limited only by the suits energy levels, these functions can be swapped on the fly. Aside from the suit you have a extremely modifiable weapon not to mention weapon pick ups that are additionally modifiable; from silencers, stocks, sights and auto/semi fire type can be exchanged at a whims notice. As well as vehicles and gun mounts to use, any play-style is immediately within your grasp.
There is nothing quite like punching through a wall and blasting the occupants close range with a shotgun with full armor going “H.A.M.” and tanking it. With the dichotomy of attaching a scope, applying strength to steady scope sway and using a silencer to drop enemies from afar and then go in closer using your cloak and take them out with a pistol or however else you may desire.
With all of these options at the ready constantly, you are truly only limited by your suits given power at the moment, your imagination and I suppose the edge of the map if you want to be that guy.
It's not going to win any awards, its certainly a big blockbuster summer movie thriller. But its got that primal visceral gumption to effectively pull at your heart strings and asks you to defend humanity from certain doom and annihilation during an alien invasion. A very, very minor spoiler warning; There are some very well done sequences involving the loss of power and the absence of heat that will really test your resourcefulness of the games mechanics.

If BEyond Earth were a mod for Civ5, I would be singing its praises for the ingenuity of the changes made to its underlying engine, the amount of work that went into revamping the graphics, and the willingness to venture beyond Civ's historical framework out into the unknowns of science fiction.
But I have to consider that Beyond Earth is in fact not a fan-made modification of Civ5, but a release by Firaxis themselves, and billed as a complete standalone game valued at a release price no less than that of its "parent". In this light, the game feels lackluster and incomplete. It has none of the boldness that characterized the changes made in the step from Civ4 to Civ5, and most changes are superficial in nature. Worse yet, despite being so evidently a spin-off of a larger, more developed game (because let's not forget that Civ5 has two expansions under its belt by now, which hugely improved its scope and depth), Beyond Earth adds too little of its own to the Civ formula besides aforementioned superficial changes. Affinities are merely a replacement for Civ5's late-game Ideologies; the tech-web is structurally different and at first glance the most intriguing change, but navigating it devolves into a race for affinity points. The unit customization feels tacked on, barely even replacing Civ5's more complex promotion system.
For something that can count Alpha Centauri among its forebears, which remains the benchmark for the 4X genre in science fiction, Beyond Earth simply falls short of achieving orbit.

It's basically everything I read in other reviews, so I'll sum it up in 3 lines;
*Races all feel the same, it's hard to notice any defining traits.
*Looks/feels like a Mod produced by fans.
*Quickly becomes extremely repetitive.
Now an expansion on my impressions in-case, by some miracle, the Developers weren't actually trying to milk cash from their fan base by using Civ's good name to flog off the most expensive DLC I've ever purchased.
*************
The intro was standard for Civ games, though it did feel like it was missing something ...... almost like the animator said they needed 15 mins to give a good into and the bean counters responded "have it done in one or your sacked!".
After the intro the game took about 10 minutes to bring up the "click to continue", followed by the menu - I honestly started believe the game had locked up since I run a high spec machine. Since that first run it's been quite fast, it appears the issue only happens on the initial load.
I started out with a random game, by strange chance I got Poly-Australia. I'll admit I got lost in the world for the first 100 turns or so, it's Civ after all, but I quickly started realising the races all look the same. With Earth it's easy, Ghandi is famous, so is Khan, and it's for that reason the defining traits of each Beyond Earth group has should have been exaggerated.
After 150 odd turns I was well past the learning stage and had time to take in the scenery. This was when I really noticed it was Civ5 with a new skin and a couple of Mod's. The real difference is that this game feels like it cripples you in order to make the game last longer. The Tech tree looks like canvas someone messed up with a few paint-ball guns, expansion is slow, and quests are basically just city-state missions a player is forced to complete so they can keep up with the competition.
After 300 turns I was fighting sleep, I could resist a few elephant tranq's more successfully. The repetition of endlessly dealing with trade routes, putting up with various AI's asking for vast resources in exchange for their utterly useless favours, and watching advanced workers take longer than a man with a stone-age pick has finally driven me to exit the game and leave my thoughts.
The game lacks soul. It's like purchasing a Gold Plated iPhone, pretty to look at for the first few hours but ultimately ends up been an expensive piece of crap once the novelty wears thin.
p.s. It's also sent my G19 Keyboard ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Trust me, I know. I had a 1090t and an 8320E both overclocked to over 4GHz and it could barely maintain a stable 30fps. Skyrocketed to pretty stable (but still not 100% always) 60 once I got a 4690K. It supports high resolutions and if you can meet its ludicrous requirements, it'll run well, without technical issues and with proper X-Input controller support.
Given the at times unbelievably good visuals and aesthetic design, the unique combat system and the very engaging narrative (despite its linearity), I'd say you're in for a ride.

I have ahicived all 4 difficulties on all 3 charachters, many long hours doing so, I can honestly say that War in the North is a wonderfull experieince. It certainly was shadowed by Skyrim's release in November, so it didn't get the recognition it deserves.
Each combat method of Magic, Range, and Melee work expectionally well in various situations. The lack of feshed out charchter customization is made up with the sheer abundance of loot and rewards. You can certainly find a mirror (most likeley in resupply areas on the map like the rangers camp) to change your character's face and hair, but I think the sotry was meant to focus on the 3 protaganists rather tan the RPG element like skyrim or Dragon age.
The over all story is quite well done, adressing what is going on in the North at the time when the fellowship is doing it's thing in the south (across all 3 books or movies) so you meet alot of the charachters such as Aragorn, Gandalf, and Frodo  and the gang along the way. Along with that, there are many beautifully done enviroments you play throuh, but you can feel boxed in at times, which is disspointing. It is not an 'open world RPG' it is like Dragon Age: Origins in a sense; you may go back to all the locations if you like, but once you start a new playthrough you cannot visit locations until you unlock them.
The combat and skill trees are very fluid and well structured, but it can be repetitive at times. It's very satisfieing to see your enemies skull break open in slow motion. Their limbs also break off, ofcourse there is also tons of blood and gore, and settings to remove it. The combat style is based of of which charachter you choose, all of which have a range weapon. Magic for Elf (swords as well), axes and crossbows for Dwarf while the Human uses longsowrds, clasymores, and somewhat of a vanguard suit using sword/axe and shield. It is pretty mcuh what you'd expect them to use.
Multiplayer works alright, but is best for friends. Multiplayer only works for 3 players with each player using one of the protaganists. In the game, there are 2 locations that use a wave-based setup. One in Ministirith, and the other in some undead elf area. Both areas are quite small and poorly executed.
Overall I rate this game a solid 8.5/10  Interesting story (if you are familiar with the Trilogy Definetly worth a buy.

I had fun playing it but it only took me 7.5 hours to beat the story, complete all side activities, fully power up my character, and find all collectables, which is actually pretty good. TL;DR Game is short but good, I had lots of fun playing it and highly recommend it.

Alrighty, as a hardcore enthusiast of RTS and similar strategy games, this worked it's way into my top 3. The online scene is a little dead, but that doesnt take away from the fact that this is a fantastic game.
There are 3 things that set this apart from most other RTS's I have played:
1) The diplomacy is challenging as you have to build a relationship with a faction. Unlike other games with diplomacy mechanics, you really have to work at it.
2) The resources are scarce. It's not like Starcraft where you can just start mass-producing probes/drones/scvs to boost your economy intake. You need to manage resources and take advantage of the refining boosts you get through research.
3) The research tree. This is probably one of the most standard mechanic of any good RTS, and because of that I have seen some terrible tech trees. This game however has a balanced tech tree that allows for a little variability in expanding and is grouped into nice little sections for easier maintenance. I like this a LOT.
Aside from these three things, the game is also visually appealing, with an interesting (if a bit cliche) backstory and lots of available strategies for play. The only true downsides are the somewhat annoying and repetitive unit voices, the rather repetitive soundtrack, and the steep, steep learning curve.
In any case, I give this a 9/10. Excellent game to pick up if you dont mind spending an hour or 2 per match.

The world is headed into a doomed future! Our ray of hope is Bunnylord, an anthropomorphic purple rabbit that needs the help of a very peculiar group of misfits to help him get elected as mayor, by obliterating the current crime wave in the city, using a more "hands on" approach than usual, since voters need to see quick and effective results to insure those votes!
Not a Hero can be described as an arcade-style, run-and-gun shooter with simple covert mechanics (pretty much feels like a combination between Bonanza Bros & Broforce). There is a pattern on most missions: funny intro that overviews the situation at hand, disposal of pretty much every enemy you come across and fulfillment of a side objective such as rescuing hostages, plastering posters, collecting random stuff (truly random stuff if I may add!), etc.
The game features a solid pixel styled appearance, an awesome chiptune soundtrack and some hillarious voicework. The characters at your disposal feature some variations in their gameplay mechanics so its easy to find someone that suits you best. Although the game can be finished in less than 8 hours, fulfilling all of the missions requests and finding the secret missions can give this game more playtime. All in all, this is a really fun action title that anyone who likes arcade-style action should give a try!

The Last Remnant is a game I'd recommend, however, only to a certain type of player. In this review I'll try to go over what I liked and what frustrated me, to try and give a clearer picture for those looking to buy.
I should note, I finished with 95 hours played at BR45. This was also completing most of the side quests as well as recruiting all major leaders, I also did a small amount of rare monster hunting.
I also edited files to give the game a larger FOV and reduced texture pop in, I high recommend doing the same before playing, you can find a guide detailing how here on Steam.
Here's what I liked:
The graphics, this game looks fantastic. The remnants are wonderful to view and the small areas of the citys you can visit are well detailed (this does not include the bland dungeons).
The large amount of items, drops and weapons. If resource gathering, crafting and mining is your thing, TLR's got you covered. The game contains tons of different items and components. You can go down many different weapon tree's, crafting better version of each weapons, turning them into more deadly looking tools. There's a fair amount of rare and boss weapon drops in the game too.
The variation of combat arts and mystic arts. These's are the ability's your characters will learn and perform. There's a huge amount, most look fairly wonderful to watch. It's also nice to assign certain Leader's to specialize in these area's.
The music. This game has some fantastic music, tracks like Swirling Sands from the Great Sand Sea are a favourite.
The menu's and IU. It's a fairly important part of an RPG, this game nails it. It's clean, slick and easy to use.
Here's some things I didn't like:
You can't manually select what a character cast during battle. I see what Square Enix was trying to do here, but it simply ended up with you turn different move's on and off before battle, just so your desired move was forced to come up during battle. It ended up becoming annoying more than anythign else.
When you most need a certain command during battle, it won't show. Let's say I only have one Union left, I want to revive my other downed Unions, the game will at times, only give me attack commands rather than showing me something I really need.
Poor character development. Firstly, Rush is out right annoying and the few characters who have likable personalities aren't explored, they're left to occational one liners.
Battle's a boring at first. TLR is a hard game. Until you open up the better moves and are able to create more interesting Unions the battles feel alot like pressing the same button and watching a short cutscene until it's over. Now this changes somewhat later on. Anyone who's played Final Fantasy 13 will understand this very problem.
I would say The Last Remnant is an aquired taste. The more I played it, the better and more interesting it's mechanic's and features got. Anyone who's interested in a challenging JRPG will want to give this a go. If you're looking for something more traditional, this may not be for you.
If you're unsure my advise would be to YouTube some gameplay videos, flick over the different mechanic's on this game wonderful Wiki.

I wanted to get into Magic the Gathering. I really did. I read up on the rules, watched tournament play and numerous Youtube videos and thought I'd give it a shot.
Totally disappointed.
Two general categories. First MtG as a game and Duels Origins as an online product.
I liked the concept of a mana base of different colors. However in practice getting too many creatures/spells or too many lands. I ran the probabilities for various starting hands and initial draws and more importantly the variances and was disgusted with the results. Too variable, even for monocolor decks unless you have a large card collection to build a decent deck from which I didn't. Even using the recommended lands suggest by the program, I often had issues. I also tried deck simulators and had the same issues.
Second, Origins Online is a poor product for me. The interface was designed with touch hardware in mind. I prefer the larger size and benefits of playing on a PC. Like other games this was designed first with non-PC/Macs in mind and then adapted.
Then I always seemed to lose connections when I completed a quest. This happened to me three times before I finally had enough and wiped this program from my drive. Even after spending money to buy more cards in game, I still found many of the decks I needed to build for quests were quite weak.

Lured into buying it by a decent MetaCritics score, I could not actually play this for very long.  I simply found no entry into this game. The decent in-game video sequences were providing a very japanese RPG feel, and I guess one could view this as mix between RPG and tactical/skirmish combat. However, from the graphics to the controls everything cried out "console port", and IMHO not at very good one at that.
This may have been a decent console game some years ago, but trying to play this on a PC keyboard was pretty frustrating, the visuals were sometimes a mix between decent and annoying (e.g. not showing your party when moving around, very basic tactical environments), and the "unique" turn-based tactical combat system was pretty lame, IMHO. E.g. no tactical movement of your party members, but just a selection of attack options from a list, "combined" Hit Points for entire groups, etc. Still, there are the typical RPG elements such as character building, item drops, etc., but nothing like crafting, enchanting, etc. known from more complex RPGs (at least not as far as I went into it). There is a strong feeling that this game almost plays itself, and while some may consider it to have a deep or compelling storyline (though not compared to e.g. BG2:SoA I'd say), I just couldn't stand the gameply between the video sequences which seemed mainly about depicting some asian kids saving the world...
This type of Japanese RPG game with simplified turn-based tactical battles may have it's fans, but I am not among them. If you like JRPGs you may love this one. If, like me, you prefer Divinity 2 or old-school BG2:SoA type RPGs with tons of "fetch this, kill that" type side quests, then this is most probably not for you.
Depth: Immersive (?)
Setting: Fantasy
Type: RPG/Tactical
My Rating: 4 out of 10 (you may rate this 8 of 10 if you are into JRPGs)...

This game is basically an indie smash bros., if the trailer and pictures didn't make that obvious.
Pros
- Gamplay: It's very smooth and each character is very unique in almost every single attack.
- Music: The retro feel is clearly there to pair up with the pixel graphics, but it doesn't get annoying. In fact, the main theme is still stuck in my head.
- Graphics: While it is pixel graphics, they're not annoyingly big pixels and it gives the game an authentic retro feel to me.
- Characters: Each character's design helps hint at what their playstyle is, and the color customization is awesome and cool.
- Abyss Mode: While this isn't a 'never-before-seen' mode, it really adds more gameplay to the game. I also thought it was cool how it was implimented with the story, but I won't spoil anything.
Cons:
- Story: The only issue I had with this is that some of the character's stories (cough* Wrastor cough*) felt stretched and short. But the ending makes me feel that there will be more story.
- Characters: I know that this is an indie game, and each character is really unique, but 8 characters for some reason feels too small, especially how you start with only 6 and the other two are paid with in-game currency. (And yes I do know that more characters are coming in updates)
- Stages: Again, I know that it's indie and there is a creative stage for each character, but the paid unlockables take 5 times the amount for a character, and I feel like it should be the other way around since character's typically provide more gameplay time than a stage.
Overall, this title is a great indie game and, in a lot of ways, almost better than smash bros itself.  I highly recommend it, even if the online mode sucks right now.

The new battle system using the crystarium and paradigms was a great change to the series. The battles are very exciting and fast-paced now with this new combat system. However, you only ever have control of one of your party members in battles, and the use of "auto-battle" is often necessary, so the battles are quite automated. Therefore, while the battles are more exciting with the graphics and visual aspects, the battles usually consist of you just pressing the enter button 5 times and watching.
Other than the great battle system, the rest of the game is pretty disappointing. Compared to FF7 or 8, the story is very short and simple, with few, if any, cliffhangers or twists that make you want to keep playing. I enjoyed the interactions between the characters, but only a couple of the characters themselves were likable. Unlike the freedom you have in previous titles in the FF series (the world maps, ability to explore the world throughout the game, finding hidden items, completing side quests) this game has none. You have no freedom to explore the world or go back to areas you were in previously, no hidden items, no side quests, no mini-games, and the list goes on, It is completely linear. You literally run down one long hallway for the entire game and fight the same 10 monsters repeatedly for the whole 30 hours of game play. A huge drawback to the boss battles is that if your "leader" dies, it does not matter if your other two party members are alive, it is game over. And when you die, you have to rewatch the longer-than-necessary cut scenes before you can retry the battle.
Many of the cut scenes run at over 5 minutes, and are not very entertaining. With the automation of the battles, excessive number of cut scenes, and complete linearity and  lack of mobility freedom, the game is essentially a 30-hour movie where you have very little control over anything.
Strengths of this game:
1. Crystarium/paradigm battle system
2. Character development and interactions
3. Visual appeal and graphics
Weaknesses of this game:
1. Battles are extremely repetitive with high HP monsters
2. Battles are highly automated with control over only one party member
3. Story line, lack of plot depth
4. Linearity
5. No world map or ability to explore other places or regions
6. Inability to revisit places you were in previously
7. Excessive number of cut scenes
8. Having to re-watch cut scenes if your party leader died in battle
9. Game over if your party leader dies in battle, even if your other two party members are still alive

This installation in the Civ series is rather different from it's predecessors.  Civ Beyond Earth is focused on the future, while most other games are focused on the past.  I find the tech web a very interesting part of the game, as it allows a player to min-max, as opposed to the tech tree, which results into a race toward the end of the tree.  The orbital layer is another welcome addition to the game, as it adds another interesting layer to military and industrial strategy.  While some have complained of crashes, I have experienced no such problems, and my recomendation is a reflection of my own experiences.  Alien units may initially be dismissed as mere reskinned barbarians, though they in fact behave differently.  Alien units don't constantly attack your units unless provoked, but some are very much stronger than barbarian units, with an example being the siege worm, capable of easily devastating any early game unit, and with only moderate difficulty any early to mid city.  In addition to all that, there is additional customization of the early game, allowing for differences in civilization beyond mere civilization bonuses, a much needed feature due to the comparitivly low amount of different civilizations in the game.  To conclude, I believe that Civilization Beyond Earth diffentiates itself from Civilization V enough to justify buying it, particularly if there is a sale currently ongoing.

This game has a wildly incoherent story, uninteresting characters, and humor that simply falls flat. Rather than respect the player, it mocks the player by intentionally frustrating them.
The game asks nothing of the player. Aside from a few endings which require, for example, clicking on a button repeatedly for four hours, everything in the game can be seen by following the clear paths that the game gives you. That, and the choices are almost all boring things like "do I go through this door or this other door"?
Accordingly, the game gives very little to the player. Right off the bat, the game presents questions such as "Where did Stanley's coworkers go?" or "Who is the narrator, exactly?" that are meant to drive the player forward. But after a couple hours of completely irrelevant endings, the only question that drove me forward was "What exactly is in this game that made it get such good reviews?". This game has a slow start. You're given rather basic options to explore a boring-looking area, and the little town and that friendly explorer in the temple kinda ruin the oppressive atmosphere the dark ruins might otherwise have. Even the first real upgrade is underwhelming. Luckily, the second area is much more vibrant and full of wildlife trying to kill you, and really probably should have been the first area.
It doesn't help that both the controls and the map system are weird at first, but the controls are actually very precise, they just take getting used to, and the map became part of the fun for me.
Once past the initial low, the game will only get better from there. I'm not the most strongly-versed in metroidvanias (especially on the Castlevania side of things), but the exploration in this game definitely got more open-ended than any I've played. The underground kingdom is bigger than Planet Zebes and encourages you to return to areas much more than Planet SR-388. The combat and platforming sections are quite precise - reflexes aren't necessarily needed except for maybe the hardest moments. It's one of the most satisfying fundamental systems I've ever played.
I have over 30 hours in my save file and haven't 100%ed the game yet. Some permanent choices involving side characters also require you to play the game twice if you want to get
and I'll gladly do that to see how it goes with experience.
There are a couple minor QoL issues.
-The dash can't be canceled at all, combine this with every enemy having hitboxes instead of collision boxes and it makes it impossible to dash in from anywhere closer than the full dash distance. It works adequately, but for the great fundamental system, this seems out of place.
-The map doesn't have manually-placeable pins, which matters for one or two things. This will be added in a future update!

Lord of the Rings: War in the North is a hack-and-slash game. That's... it.
You control one of three characters with no personality or character development trying to chain as many finishers as possible, until you unlock Farin's Explosive Arrow and trivialize the game. Even the only vaguely challenging sections, which are the optional horde challenge maps. Along the way you will meet other fan-favorite characters such as the Fellowship, but then you will discover they have about as much relevance to you as this game does to Tolkein's legendarium. Sorry, Lord of the Rings fans.
Your mission is to go kill the leader of Sauron's forces in the North, Agandaur. He is pathetically easy, but it's worth it (?) to see the CGI animation that probably ate up 70% of the budget for this game.
The only way this game becomes decent is if you somehow game one, preferably two, friends into playing it with you. The time commitment shouldn't be that bad because the game is both easy and short. Playing with friends helps disguise some of the game's more egregious single-player faults, such as an incredibly limited inventory system, no ability to switch between characters on the fly (this requires you to completely reload the game), and the fact that some parts of the game are straight-up inaccessible without two or more players.
Fortunately the game isn't super glitchy (there are some glitches but reloading usually fixes it) or unplayable, and you'll probably unlock 95% of the achievements without even trying.
Sadly, War in the North failed to live up to any of its promise. It's not a HORRIBLE game by any means, but there are way better uses of your time.

As crazy as any game you will purchase. You have no doubt heard the hype about this game. For this game is nothing but hype. Why? People say "play this game". "Why?" you respond. "I can't tell you. Just play it." I'm sure you've had that conversation. The reason people want you to play it is that the game is very very funny and to tell you anything about it would spoil the comedy. So rather than say specific things about it I'll just loosely describe it. Firstly it isn't a game yet it uses a game engine...the source engine from Half Life 2 to be exact. This game followed on the heels of Portal 2 and it pretty much owes that game for its popularity as well as its sarcastic and passive aggressive sense of humor. I guess calling this a cross between an adventure game and a digital interactive novel would be the best fit. You have a character and you wander around in this game world. You can click on things. The point is not what you can accomplish, the point is to enjoy the story...or rather the attempts to get to the story. There are many many games now, mostly in the anime game world that exist just as stories where you make choices and the main point is to enjoy the story and especially to experience all the different endings you can. Things like Hatoful Boyfriend and Long LIve the Queen, and a little bit of the Skauras and things like that. Not much game but choices you make in the narrative affect what story path you take. Well THIS is kind of the opposite. You don't make choices in the narrative. YOu make choices in the game world by your actions and the narrative follows you. However, the narrator is not always keen on the choices you make. So as far as the gameplay goes, if you like roaming around in a portal worldthen sure you'll be okay with that part of it. I do feelit gets a bit resource hoggy and the frequent loadscreens at times just kinda take over until they are finished. The story here is less of the point. This is a comedy game. And you willdefinitely see several points where you are laughing your hiney off. One thing that should be said is that yes you should keep playing and peel away every little shell of this game. It is not very clear of the amount of content that is here and you may think that when you get to the end ...and go...."That's it??" Well that's not it. There's a lot here. Now aside from the comedy there lies another layer beyond that will go over many people's heads. This is quite an existential philosophy game. It is a satire. It is social commentary about gaming and gamers as a whole. IT is a spoof or parody of adventure and action games. Yet it IS one itself. Like the movie Scream was a parody and commentary of horror movies while being one itself. LIke Shakespeare in Love told the tale of Shakepeare writing plays while having a complete structure of a shakepeare play. That's the genius of this game. If you are looking for an actual STORY. Well there really isn't one. If you're looking for an actual game....well there really ISN'T one of those either. But this is definitely worth experiencing on the level of binging your favorite comedy series on netflix. The replayability however...well you can put it down and pick it up in a few years once you've forgotten some of it. But there isn't much. YOu can try the achievements which are equially satirical of achievements. The game basically boils down to "Find all of the game" and enjoy every bit of it. Does that justify the price? Not one iota. I've never liked interactive novels , whatever they are called having prices over 10 dollars. They usually aren't worth more than 5. Sales didn't really take this down to what it should have been priced. However...like I said with the Portal and Source names behind it and following after those...it had its acceptable pricetag. Now however, you'd think they would have lowered the price. There just isn't enough content to justify it. Just very very little replayability. Would you pay netflix 15 dollars to binge watch one season of one show? That's the equivalent here. Still it's very funny and worth experiencing on sale.

Introduced as a standalone expansion to Saints Row IV (SR4), Gat Out of Hell (GOH) is a remix of SR4's gameplay. It is interesting that the Boss of SR4 is also seen in GOH.
GRAPHICS
The graphics are less pretty than one from SR3 or SR4, but it only used 66% from GTX 770 clocked at 1135MHz, and 33% from i7 4770k clock at the stock at 3.50GHz. There are no stutters except from taking screenshots. I wish it was better though.

SOUND
The soundtrack used is fine for a short game. I have a little bit over 17 hours from playing, but playing only the main story only took around 5 hours. The diversions and achievement hunting took more game time.
GAMEPLAY
Everything in the gameplay is copied from SR4. But rather than gliding, GOH lets you fly. You only get a maximum of flaps out of your wings per jump, but that will cover a lot of ground.
OVERALL
Good fun, but the lack of story telling bogged down the experience. Many parts are told through illustrations and narration, and the 5 minute musical tries to make up for it. If you loved Saints Row IV, you will love Gat Out of Hell. Otherwise, this remix will bore you. This is somewhat a "for fans only" game.

The main tag line of this game is tasteful, nice and surprisingly well shoutable in many situation.
But really what is Not a HERO about?
The totally rad BunnyLord came from the future to be elected mayor of your city because if he's not there will be like a totally unrad doom explosion and so in order to be elected BunnyLord and his Fun Club will eliminate all crime... by shooting it in it's ugly face.
And so we come to the gameplay:
Now Not a HERO is technically speaking a 2d “cover based” shooter but if you’re like me then it’s more like a run and melee/shotgun enemies down and before you know it, you’ve fell in love with Mike and are on a 30 Killstreak through a five story building and only 35 seconds into the mission.
That sounds like a lot? It’s not really because most of the game is designed around the idea of constantly switching between always moving and using the cover mechanic to plan ahead. X is your slide which does two things, slide you into cover and knock enemies over. C is your fire button and if someone is knock over to assassinate them. Your V is for special weapons which can be found in the levels and the rest are your arrow keys. Quite simply mechanics, right? What ties it all together are the characters, which there are plenty of and different enough to be enjoyable. Mike, the one I mentioned earlier, for example has a shotgun and a machete. He is a fast character which can silently assassinate enemies and has a powerful shotgun, but it only has two shots and the reload is very long. So most of the time you will be tackling enemies left and right and just slicing through their necks like a extremely hot knife through warm butter… for BunnyLord’s election of course, not because you enjoy killing all these hopeless meatbags.
So it’s a game with simplistic controls? Nothing new, there are plenty like that out there and the idea for the core gameplay isn’t neither. But most levels will force you to pick your battles. Sure you can just murder your way through a level, that’s easy, but completing the additional goals for extra glory to BunnyLord can be quite challenging. Even more you can’t complete all 3 additional task in separate runs of one level. It all needs to be done in one try which becomes especially hard if you’re asked to rush through a level in 30 seconds to find a ♥♥♥♥ing phone which is hidden somewhere in that ♥♥♥♥ing level and there are like 5 ♥♥♥♥ers which can’t be knock down for assassinating so you just have to ♥♥♥♥ing murder them and waste your ♥♥♥♥ing precious time… On the other hand the soundtrack really helped me let my rage flow into Mike and the vicious killing rampages I have. The 8bit style of music feels good and smooth and even after trying a level several times doesn’t become annoying.
To sum it all up: Not a HERO is a fast paced game about a time traveling bunny who wants to become the mayor and gets a bunch of assassin to do his campaigning. The gameplay, art style and soundtrack fit wonderfully together, they are lots of milkshakes in it and it’s even political.
And really what is a little bit of violence for a better tomorrow?

As much love as I have for this game, I can clearly say this is one of the games that I will pull up when a friend asks me why I never tell them about obscure games made by high end companies. You should experience it. But if it's your last couple of bucks or you do not want to be cruelly punished for trying to defeat rare game as much as this. Stay away. This seems to be targeted to people who liked everything about final fantasy 12 but the gambit system and having full control over everyone. You have almost no control here, You're pretty much trusting the ai to use from a skillset you create for them to use, though those skills you can turn off, probably need to be on to grow. Go figure. Happy sails to figuring it out, or go find a guide that works, play the game in a linear fashion, or get trolled by the levelling system wondering why enemies aren't dying when they were when you left it. Let me give you a glimpse of what to expect.... Ever played dissidia? got to a high level and turned down your level and watched as everything became easier to do? That's how this gets, But you can't go back, and trading for a weaker party may not help.
I say this, because it is comparable to copying answers on the wrong test. Everything that square excels at is pure gold here. And what they do not do well gets caught through the filter and is easy to spot. Most strategy games will have you building perfect moves and ideas to make the best attacks possible and use them in battle to your own benefit. This does exist, but there is no explanation whatsoever to how this works, and looking it up online takes away from the flavor of playing the game on your own, and it seems very futile without it.
Strategy... Is and isn't here. Obvious options like strike from afar and stay back is normal for most strategy games, but they do not last here. You will end up putting them in the fray or getting them ambushed by using waiting as a strategy. This game is sheer punishment and one wrong turn or missed action could doom you, Autosave exists. Thank the PC gods.
As far as strategy games go, this is comparable to why most games force you to select a loadout before you do anything, you can do this here, but since there is no clear sign to if your unselected skills will grow or not, I leave them on in sheer faith that they will do what is needed, and that leads you to counting mp and tracking commands to predict what moves will show, which works. Another thing that delves from strategy is how often certain individuals reassess the situation and with who and under what limits, Certain groups with high holds of hp will not see danger in not maxing out health and will get you killed. While others who may be useless in battle or offensively grief your unit, will always know when to reassess and who to heal to keep things fresh and alive. Furthermore, the system shines at learning as you go at times, as when you're on the ropes healing just over what you're getting damaged, you'll learn a new skill, and you'll get better at it or beat the opposition afterward.
But the problem is that the game knows what it has to offer, and it does anything it can to ruin it for you. On overpowered bosses? part of the strategy is to die to preserve your unit hp without having enough available units to be overwhelmed by a per unit attack. That is beyond realistic, and is almost impossible to do if you have or learn a revive skill. So you turn it off. Hope the curse kills off one or more of your units, it'll kill the leader and everyone on the team will turn vegetable no matter their own individual rank or standing. So the Marquis will literally just sit there and die, not join a unit or anything, ironically they will last the longest because they retain the group's health pool. Keep all party members and take a critical group attack? Game Over. Take small groups into battle? A direct attack will kill you. Normally you would think, hey, I probably need to gain a few levels and learn some attacks. No, the game has a tiered level system less brutal than xbox, but is more rampant on you developing a strategy closely to luck and hopeful reassessment. You will not notice this until much later, or instantly if you are the thickheaded type to never put down a challenge, which is wholly enabled by a perfect auto save system.
In its entirety, I can compare it to a fighting game, People watching you play will clearly see the holes and imbalances in the strategy and delivery in the game, and call how cheap it is at a constant beat, but when they ask why you still play it... my answer is more of wanting to see how much more obscene the curve balls are going to be, and when they're going to stop tearing holes through groups without fair reason. I'm sure anyone else looking for balance in the game will quickly pick up a guide and follow their lead to a balanced game and read through everything, spoilers included, to see when and where are the best times to defeat and complete enemies and quests. And I can safely say what a shame it is they weren't more introductive to newcomers to the genre as final fantasy is the normal mainstay of square, and even they made gambits a fair and eventually obvious system of priority and functionality.

When you get how this game works or when luck favors you, you will save over your game and have a breath of relief, because it's finally over and You won't have to sit curiously staring at the majestic enemy that can and did raze your team at every moment for no favorable reason at all.

So yet again, Wizards of the Coast has decided to grace us with another installment to their yearly Online Magic the Gathering experiences, and oh boy is this one a real kick in the pants to all the fans of Magic the Gathering everywhere. If you thought Magic 2015 was a real failure, you will love to hear about this. Im going to be honest, I was extremely excited to see this game after the reveal trailer was shown, and I was eager to see what magical journies would await me as i clicked the promising download now button and awaited for the game's arrival on to my laptop. As I opened the game I was met with the familiar logo traditional to the Wizards of the Coast , along with the new logo that had joined with them, Stainless Games. I was then met with a loading screen typical of many games, and then i Loaded into the game. Upon my loading in to the game, I was met with an unfortunate error message- "Could not connect to the server, please retry." I did not think much about this as i pressed the retry button, but oh boy was I wrong. as i continued to press the retry button, my hopes dimmed, and i realized what was happening. Day 1 connectivity issues. Normally, for games with a single player mode I  would not mind this as much, but here is the real kicker. Any, and I mean, ANY progress made in the single player campaign or in single player duels would be lost. I will never forget the feeling of dread that arose while playing the Jace campaign and finishing a duel that took 40 minutes due to the dreadfully slow nature of his deck, only to realize the progress and in game currency was lost due to a connectivity issue. Even after the initial release, there have been connectivity issues, which have caused myself to be quite dissapointed with the creators of the game. If that was not bad enough, the game only features cards from the most recent set, Magic Origins, which, with all due respect, was a pretty terrible set aside from the mythic legendary planeswalker cards found within the set. The gameplay present within the game is not awful, but with clunky controls, awful combat damage designation, and an infuriating timer button that causes you to often be unable to react to what is happening, and ultimately lose the duel.
This brings up another issue present in many online trading card games, that was started infamously by the outrageously popular trading card game Hearthstone. while the game remains free to play, it is certainly not free to win. the in-game currency can often take a long time to acquire after finishing the campaigns, and with your 6 card boosters (which are pathetic compared to the 15 card boosters present in real Magic.) costing 150 a piece, and daily quests being 40 gold a piece, it will on average take you about 3 days to buy one measly booster pack. Have you ever had that feeling of hopelessness that arises when playing a game and realizing that despite your best efforts, you were doomed from the start? that is exactly what the online environment treats you like. You will play against people with outrageously better decks, which will make you feel like garbage afterwards due to the high variety of rare cards they possess that would take a large chunk out of your wallet to acquire. This would not be so bad if your starting card pool was at least somewhat decent, but unfortunately, just like Hearthstone, you are stuck with some of the most horridly bad cards Wizards of the Coast has to offer. Dont get me wrong, I Love Magic the Gathering, and I have spent a large amount of real world money on the game to have an amazing deck for Standard that I could call my own, but this cheap imitation of the real game leaves much to be desired, and I would not recommend this game to anyone unless it is your only available option of playing MTG with real people.

Don't listen to what everyone else says, I say that this is a successful new entry into the Civilization series.
PROS:
-Affinity System: This is a great system when you can really define who your faction is. Each affinity has specific bonuses which are very helpful such as units, and buildings.
-Unit Upgrades: Much better than in Civ V where you had to spend gold to upgrade units. The units automatically upgrade and the upgrades are all different depending on the affinity you have chosen.
-Combat: THANK YOU! WE CAN NOW DO COMBAT WITH MULTIPLE UNITS AT THE ONE TIME! This speeds up combat a lot.
-Tech Web: A large improvement over the tech tree from previous games, you can choose what to reasearch and when. The 'leaf' techs add even more depth.
-Covert Ops: The concept of spies from Civ V has been greatly expanded, you can now steal science, energy (the equivalent of gold), destroy their orbital units, send a seige worm on the city or take the city over in a coup. The list goes on.
-Explorers: A better version of the Civ V scout, can create expeditions and recieve large bonuses, orbital units, science, affinity points, etc but they are much weaker combat wise than the scout.
-Victories: The victories are very diverse in this game, there are three tied to each affinity, the contact victory, and domintation (which we all know). All of the victories require you to build a planetary wonder, which occupies a tile of land in your territory. After you have built it you either wait, which is fairly boring, or with two of the victories (Promised Land and Emancipation) you have to either bring humans to the new world via warp gate or send in powerful units into the warp gate.
-Orbital Layer: A great addition. Can be used to create miasma, clear it, destory the enemy, give you a combat bonus, or an increase in energy, culture, science and food.
-Health: Health is the equivalent of happiness and it is more dynamic, not only does it have the usual penalties for being unhealthy, there are now bonuses for having high healthiness! However having positive healthiness can be quite hard to achieve if you have many cities, and wonders don't give happiness/heathiness.
CONS:
-Factions: There are only eight factions in this game which causes the game to become less dynamic as you can usually expect the same leaders in every game. (But there's finally Australia, Woo!)
-Demographics: The problem with this is that there is none, I can't check who is leading in what areas (population, techs, energy production). But there is the graphs you can check at the end of the game (by going into 'Other' then 'Replays') like you could in Civ V.
-Tech Web: This is also a con becuase is can be very confusing to know what to research, it can also be hard to navigate (but thankfully there's a filter features and a search bar). After playing through the game for a bit it has become easier to navigate (at least at the start)
-Buildings and Wonders: This is probably an early game problem but the icons for building and wonders are very confusing, I have to mouse over the building to see what it is before I reasearch it. The wonders are also more 'nerfed' and don't seem to provide as good bonuses as in Civ V, I personally can't find them in the tech web.
-Combat: Again, this is a pro and a con as the whole combat system depends on the affinty level everyone has as the units upgrade depending on your affinity level, if you have a low affinity level and the person who you are at war against has a high one, you know who will lose.
-Achievements: There's just a lack of them, Civ V had 287 achievements, Civ BE only has 64 and they aren't as dynamic as the ones in Civ V, this decreases its replay value.
Overall this is a great game. I give it an 8.75/10

I am astonished by the volume of negative reviews of this game. Before you dismiss this one, let me say that while the first couple of playthroughs had me condemning the game as a Civ 5 skin, but my persistent attempts to like the game have paid off in spades. I recommend it, and here's why:
1) Simplicity and Continuity with the Series . . .
As many point out, the form of the game is very similar to Civ 5. Some who expected novelty and more complexity complain about this, but the plus is that if you're experienced at all with its predecessors, you can jump right into this game and be familiar with the mechanics.  I would also say that this game has a lower learning curve for newbies than its predecessors as some mechanics have been streamlined. For instance, the research interface is much more transparent, lending itself to premediated and careful play without having to play 100 hours just to get a firm grip on how the research tree works.
2) . . . But Still a Refreshing Twist
Although heavily criticized for being a Civ 5 skin comprising just a few tweaks, IMO the relatively minor changes done were very clever and the combined effect of them has an emergent, significant affect on the gameplay. After numerous playthroughs, these games feel significantly different than Civ 5. For instance there are more opportunities for combat—as well as opportunities to avoid it, should the player choose. The player's relationship to the alien presence is much more nuanced and compelling than barbarian spawning, and the decisions one makes about aliens has a huge impact on relations with other civilizations, which in turn affects how one treats the alien presence, and so on. Furthermore, the affinity system allows for much more fluid development of a civilization based on circumstance and events, and I've found that the outcome of games is much less predictable and more exciting than Civ 5. One can no longer assume what sort of victory another player will shoot for based on the civ they chose. Espionage is constant threat and can really create some sudden gamechanging events. I can go on about other gameplay elements, but suffice to say there are enough changes to make this feel like a new experience. One hundred hours in and I have hardly scratched the surface of orbital coverage gameplay.
3) This Game Is Art
One thing I have always loved about the Civ franchise is drawing parallels to history and current events. One can always analogize the game theory behind Civ to real life statecraft. In adding a speculative fiction/sci-fi element into the mix, Firaxis has masterfully created a universe that is both fantastic and plausible. The alien world is harsh and civilizations must must adapt to thrive there. Adaptation is a key theme in this game, and the three affinities are believable extensions of how our current values would survive and transform in space. There are no moral judgments regarding the affinity choices; there is no right or wrong—only surviving and ensuring victory for your civilization. Because the game does not supply these judgments, the player is inevitably left to value their own decisions and contemplate the most desireable fate for a spacefaring humanity in the not-so-distant future.
4) Ripe for New Content
As mentioned in #1, many of the elements of the franchise have been streamlined and simplified. Some diehard fans have denounced this, but sometimes you need to demolish a house before you build a new one. That said, I see lots of room for exciting DLC additions to this game and earnestly look forward to them. After purchasing every Civ 5 expansion, IMO that game became indundated with needless complexity and added bells & whistles but not a substantially different gameplay experience. With a blank slate in Beyond Earth, Firaxis is in a great position to develop this on a tangent from the rest of the franchise—I hope they take some bold moves in doing so. I get the sense that these have been in the works well before Beyond Earth's release. Or maybe I will regret this whole review.
Either way, I agree with a number of complaints, including: 1) very poor explanation of victory conditions and the paths to victory, 2) victories feel sudden and underwhelming—comeon guys,, I just won a 10-hour match, let's have a little more ceremony, 3) the leaders, inspirational quotes, etc. can feel pretty corny sometimes and kill the immersion; 4) lack of variety in structure and unit design/style, etc. (I expect this will be remedied with DLC).

It's a fantastic game. There are several aspects of play that have gained in depth, although there are some that have diminished in depth. Over all, it's a very well structured game. More than with any other Civ -from 1 to 5- the activity level of the game is MUCH higher in the early part of the game.
I would recommend this to anyone new to Civ. Well, okay, maybe CivRev would be an even better start if you've never played Civ before. But on the other hand, CivBE is not just great for someone new to Civ - it absolutely stands up to its predecessors. It's not *just* faster in the early game. The late game is satisfying as well.
All in all, I love it. Everyone who says it lacks personality, I feel, is focusing on the wrong parts. To me, it has more personality than ever. The characterization of the worlds has simply been lifted out of the encyclopedia. That's right - you don't have to spend an hour reading all the flavor text to get a feel for the game's character. The world types behave differently, the 'barbarians' are ten times as rich and interesting, the Orbital layer adds a whole new side to territorial control, the oceanic-aliens especially are really cool, and the way your affinity transforms your units and structures if wonderful.
Not to say it's perfect. There are some valid criticism, and there are SOME ways in which the leader and nation's personality has declined. For example, there's no narrated intro to your nation anymore - instead on ever save load you get a paragraph "log" entry (although there are several for each nation) - which I don't think serves as well. And yeah, if you loved constructing your own religion - there's no parallel to that. But I still loved the game. And I think most gamers would, tool.

My score: 7.5/10
Pros:
-Solid combat. Going from ranged to melee is quick and smooth, and the ranged combat is properly balanced so as to be over-powered compared to close-combat.
-Skills. Each of the three characters has small skill trees. They give passives and castable abilities from magical defense to explosive crossbow bolts (my personal favorite).
-Many regions. The Barrow Downs are present in this game, something we haven't seen much of. Also, parts of the NORTH, as the titles suggests, though this game is not solely bound in the North (you're in Rivendell at one point).
-Character asthetics. You can actually change the face, beard, and hair of each of the three characters. I foudd this very nice, especially since the dwarf's beards are amazing.
-Enemies. I actually enjoyed the diversity of the enemies, as they all have different tctics to defeating. The Uruk-hai are especially fun to deal with, as they just take damage like it's nothing.
-Loot. Lots of items to use, with armor sets and other effects on them. There are also potions and food rations to be used (with varying effects), though there is no UI to use them besides opening your inventory and eating/drinking them.
-Good group dynamic. The classes work well with one another and can revive eachother if one or two should fall in battle.
-Some Choice. There are some RPG choice elements in the game, one of which you encounter in Bree very early.
-EAGLES. You befriend the Eagles, and one of them fights with you in a few zones.
Cons:
-Strange voice-acting. The voicework isn't bad, but it isn't on-par with Shadow of Mordor or the films. Some of the characters sound as if they're reading a script.
-Cinematic animation. The converstaional animations are rather stiff and not life-like in some instances. This is easily ignored, and if you've played Mass Effect 1, then this game isn't as bad as that in regards to sub-par cutscenes.
-Color. A lot of the zones could be improved with a special filter or lighting. Gray is not the prettiest color (as a guard in Fable would have you believe). Even Mirkwood's green could have been a bit more vibrant.
-Radagast. Just because his dialogue is strange to me. And because the Hobbit version is better in my own opinion.
Neutral:
-Nolan North voices the Ranger character. I liked it, you may not.
Also, make sure you've read the Hobbit, because this game has characters from the book in it who will give away some plot details.

So now we have this standalone expansion for SR IV... I'd rate it as "mixed" but unfortunately Steam doesn't have this kind of rating so I must give it thumbs down. It's fun to play, I must admit, but it takes only 10 hours to complete and there's absolutely NOTHING to do later. It lacks a lot of basic SR features and for me it's really big dissapointent.
PROS:
+ Crazy idea and concept.
+ Musical.
+ Well done new city.
+ The weather is different depending on the district.
+ Activities (most of them are copied from SR IV but still, they're fun).
+ Upgrade system.
+ Really good optimization.
+ Awesome weapons and superpowers.
+ Audio logs and commentary.
+ Historical characters.
+ Lots of references to previous SR games.
+ Very few bugs.
+ Modding.
CONS:
- Really primitive storyline.
- 5 storyline missions. (!)
- Lack of Boss appearance.
- Very few characters overall.
- No radio stations.
- Small amount of weapons.
- No vehicle storage.
- No customization of ANY kind.
- No minigames nor text adventures (it wouldn't be too hard to put something like that, come on).
- Lack of easter eggs.
- Only ONE type of pedestrian. (!)
- No homies.
- They finally put Dex but it's done really sh*tty.
- There are five endings but only two of them actually don't suck.
- No weapon skins.
- Outro includes more storyline than the whole game.
- Kinzie and Gat don't have any differences except model and voice lines (also, you can't complete the final mission as Kinzie for some reason),
- Again, no mission nor cutscene replay.
- Again, no cribs (except Ultor Building).
- Again, pretty weak car damage system.
- Again, there's no way to toggle upgrades.
- The whole game looks like a poor overlay for SR IV.
- Literally nothing to do in the freeroam.
I rate it 5,5 out of 10. I find this game fun but way too short and unfinished. I know it's just a standalone expansion but for real, just take a look on Episodes from Liberty City. It shows that you can do a standalone expansion without cutting out literally everything. I just hope they'll put some effort in Saints Row V.

While many reviewers are saying not to purchase it because it does not work in 64-bit systems, there is a way that allows it to work (though it is
that these steps are necessary). This is tested and working in Windows 10 Pro.
What I did was to follow two different suggestions found here:
and here:
Step 1:
Download the Bin64 files from the first link then extract and copy the entire folder into the Crysis program directory.
Rename the Bin32 folder found in the same directory to Bin32.BAK. Then rename the Bin64 folder you just copied to Bin32.
Step 2:
From the second link, download the Crysis.exe file found in the video description. In the newly renamed Bin32 folder (the one that was Bin64), rename the Crysis.exe file to Crysis.BAK. Next, copy the Crysis.exe file you downloaded from the Youtube link into the same Bin32 folder.
Step 3:
While still in the Bin32 folder, right-click on the Crysis.exe file you just copied and select Properties. In the Compatibility tab, check the box next to "Run this program in compatibility mode for:" and then select "Windows Vista (Service Pack 2)" from the drop down menu. Click Apply then OK. You're finished!
Now the game can be launched from within Steam.

There are many reasons to hate this game, as you may read in other reviews both here on Steam and elsewhere. The thing is that, if you are a Final Fantasy fan like me, you won't care about that. You'll still feel the need to try it out yourself. Just make sure to waste your money when it is on sale.
If you are still unsure about the purchase these two points may help you in you decission:
- Many who like the game claim that it gets better after a while (e.g. the awful linear gameplay) and it does. It doesn't make that much of a difference, though, since there isn't much of the story left after that. Sure there are other things still to be done; missions to be completed and achievements to be unlocked - but it will mostly be grinding. Take that from someone who spent ~300 hours completing every aspect of this game (just to be able to say I really did do everything), which is about as much time as I spent on TES: Oblivion, where I did every quest, visited every location, heck I even collected every book in that game.  Out of the 300 FF XIII hours played, 50 - 100 hours were related to the storyline. The rest were leveling and farming the same items from the same enemies over and over again.
- This game stays true to the FF "lore". It is a genuine Final Fantasy game. The story is one where your party fights forces of evil to save the world; the backstories of the characters are cliché and the dialog is so simple and naïve that is seems out of place; it's semi-turn-based; you level your characters to get all the usual spells such as "Life" and "Quake"; you get to fight against the same unimaginative "slime"-enemies as you did in the first installments and the bosses are epicly designed to the point where you don't know what's the face and what's the rear; you get to summon powerful beings to your aid; and you get to ride chocobos.
Finally, I will warn you that this game will require a lot of patience - the wrong kind. I hardly enjoyed any of it. This could be the worst game I've ever played but, considering that I played many weird console games back in the 90's, that is unlikely.

Alrighty then...well, this is the continuing saga of "how many people can we get to buy THIS iteration of Civ?"
Apparently quite a few. I caught it on sale and I'm glad I did.
Preface: I love the Civ games.
Okay: So now you're on "alien" planets. What's that mean? The "Barbarian Hordes" are now differing aliens with strengths and weaknesses and varying attacks, I guess. Other than that...zippo. Your total interaction with "aliens" during the game is ZERO.
So, why bother having aliens at all? I dunno. Maybe someone can ask?
Here's how a game goes: you choose "Massive" for map size. Then half the NPC players drop onto the planet within 15-20 hexes of your starting position. Seriously. They're contacting you on like Turn 2. "Hi! We're here! Let's be friends!"
The Tech Tree is cool. You can slide it all around and see what hooks onto what and you can click on the Tech you want and the game defaults to the Tech you need before you qualify for the one you want.
There are random "supply drops" that give you mostly resources but occassionally some Tech help. I haven't seen a "Free Tech" yet, so I don't know if they're in the game anymore. What I have seen are, I guess, "Theory" points, which lower the turn cost of some expensive, down-the-line bit of Tech. There are Primary Techs and then Secondary Techs. To research a secondary, you have to research the Primary Tech that governs it. This is what gets reduced: the Primary. Which is cool.
There are also random "Relic" sites you can send your explorers to and deploy them to search for goodies, which turn out to be mostly more resources or again, some bonus to a Tech you haven't researched yet.
All the buildings have been renamed to be cool and all xenomorphic/alien like. You have three resouces: "Energy" which is cash, then "Nuts" which are production and "Health" which is happiness, sort of. They're all affected the same way they always are...size of population, number of cities, time between building cities, etc. No surprises here.
Unless you disable them, the game is all about the Victory Conditions. So, of course, the game will always win, unless you play like the game and do the same thing over and over and over again...which is why I don't get why people play these Civ games. It's always the same thing over and over and over again. Nothing changes except the maps. So there's that.
Yet I have thousands of hours on the series.
Oh well. At least I'm not playing World of Warcraft.

I was personally alittle disappointed with the final outcome of the game when comparing it to the other hitman games out there (Especially Hitman: Blood Money) but I would still rate it a good 7.5/10. Below Ill put the pro's and con's
Storyline - 7/10
+ Interesting Plot
+ Alot of missions to play through
- Linear storyline
- No real replayability aside from getting a higher score
Characters - 8/10
+ Interesting and Unusual characters
+ characters have different personalities
+ Interesting conversations between characters, some would talk about the current mission you where on and may give you clues on what to expect and others where just random and funny.
- The main character you play (Agent 47) has empathy all of a sudden, in the older hitman games he had no real empathy for anyone so why all of a sudden make him betray his own agency, endangering his own life just to follow through with the request of someone he knew?
GamePlay - 6/10
+ Good fighting animations
+ Sneaking around works quite well
+ Can tackle levels in different way's
+ Challenges and play styles which can be unlocked through how you play the game, does not really do much.
- Disguise system does not work well. This is because they changed the way on how disguises worked in order to make the game harder so the player just cant walk past anyone without ever getting caught but they shot themselves in the foot with this new mechanic. The disguise overhall has made choosing a disguise almost worthless as when the instict bar runs out the player will almost surely get spotted and will end up either running away or (in most cases) end up having to kill everyone which causes points to be lost.
- You lose points when attacking someone who is not your target. this could restrict players freedom
- Instinct made the game too easy allowing the player to see people through walls and allow for predictions of movement in enemies but then again this is my personal opinion.
Graphics 10/10
+ Great Graphics. Some of the best graphics I have seen in awhile.
Map Design - 7/10
+ Lots of different themed locations
+ Many ledges and windows that could be used for different ways to tackle the mission
- The maps seemed to be quite small compared to the other hitman games but this could be because sometimes the missions would cut the map into small segments.
- The maps are dont have much to offer for those who want to adventure around the map.

I've played Contracts and Blood Money -- Absolution doesn't disappoint. I appreciated the more story driven progression of the game compared to the earlier games in the series. Prior to and at release, I think there was a bit of controversy over the "instinct" meter and how the game may be tailored to consoles or "dumbed down". I saw none of that here.
The game plays very much like a modern Contracts or Blood Money. You do not lose any of the core gameplay that existed in previous game at all. They added onto the series with Absolution if anything. AI works great or just as well as it always had. Disguise/anonymity mechanics have improved. Weapons are neat and varied for the most part.
The inclusion of the "Contracts" portion of the game makes it worthwhile playing again and provides some entertainment with other people if they are into the game as much as you are. I purchased the game quite some time after release and I still had people across the internet playing and rating contracts I made and I see tons of new contracts being created.
If I had anything negative to say about the game it may have been the slightly anti-climactic ending (it doesn't compare to the end level(s) of Blood Money, for instance). A couple small nitpick things I thought could have been improved were some more exotic level designs (though they were varied and all fun) and perhaps more weapons/choices of assassination.
Definitely a buy whether or not you've played a Hitman game before.
