Heavenly battle is a Shoot 'Em Up that looks and feels like it belongs on an Atari 2600, with a couple of more modern touches.
Gameplay is very simple. Lots of planes fly straight down the screen, with occasional special planes and powerups mixed in to liven things up. Kill 100 guys, face a boss. Do that three times, and you beat the game. Get hit once (mostly) and start over.
After killing a few guys you can upgrade your gun so it doesn't fire so darn slow, and after a few more, you can have extra shots.
Difficulty is low, normal enemies aren't a huge threat and boss patterns are easy to learn. I completed the game in 20 minutes total with 2 upgrades. After that, there is a hard mode, which makes enemy planes fire bullets randomly. This does make the game more challenging, but due to bullets being unpredictable and too fast to avoid easily if your happen to be in the wrong place, which means cheap deaths.
Technical issues:
Hard to click on menu options, possibly due to curved TV effect.
After completing the game, you get a "victory lap" which is basically the first level with some credits overlayed. but after killing 100 enemies, no more spawn. And then I realised there was no quit button, so I had to alt-F4 the game. After starting the game again, I did have hard mode, but didn't get the upgrade points from that run.
Overall, the game is okay for a few minutes. If you have nostalgia for a simpler time of gaming, you might get some enjoyment out of this, but for the majority, there's nothing here worth seeing.

In brief: I loved most of this game but it has issues that drag it down. Therefore, I can only give it a cautious recommendation.
In details,
The visual design is superb. It's clean, varied, appropriate for the desired atmosphere of the moment, and effectively simplistic/detailed where needed.
I played this game both with an XBox 360 controller and a Logitech F310 and had no issues. The controls are responsive and very accurate. No complaints.
Then there's the incredible value you get for your money. This game is HUGE. Both in its  varied areas and the amount of different enemies, NPCS, and platforming challenges you'll see. I'm at around 50 hours in and I just recently got close to 106%'ing the whole thing (Yeah, it's pulling an "Over 100%" stunt). Yeah, you might not be the type of a gamer who likes to explore every nook and cranny and collect everything, but keep this in mind: The lowest time for the quickest speedrun achievement of this game is FIVE hours. Also, the lowest time for speedrunning AND 100%'ing the game is TWENTY HOURS. One single playthrough will get you your money's worth. Oh, and did I mention there are 3 free DLC updates?
And there are many other oros that you'll easily find in the other reviews that recommend this game. Therefore I'll focus on...
With everything I just said you might think "He LOVES this game. What could he possibly be complaining about?". Well...
First, the combat. It's not that it's bad, but that it's a bit underwhelming. By that I mean your abilities are relatively limited. You only have one weapon through the whole game, the nail, and the upgrades you can perform on it only increase it's damage output. There are 3 nail skills you can acquire by finding certain NPCs which let you perform a spin attack, a "strong" slash with a longer range, and a dash-into-slash "strong" attack with an even longer range. There are also 3 spells which allow you to fire a straight projectile, "ignite" the space right above, and do a descending ground pound attack. All three spells can be upgraded once to increase their damage. There is also a short dash and later down the line a double jump.
That's nice and all, but I really think there was potential for a more versatile skillset. The variety of the enemies will make you approach things from different angles though so you will be using all of your available skills to their fullest potential without any of them feeling unnecessary so I won't say it's a deal breaker. I will however say that something as simple as the regular dash should have been available from the start.
I should not, I say I should NOT need a charm (that I have to buy first by the way) JUST TO KNOW WHERE I CURRENTLY AM ON THE MAP!  And speaking of maps, the map system is busted. You start every unexplored area without a map of the place until you find the map charter  and buy it from him. And he can be so deep into the region that you'll lose your way trying to find him. Even then, the map you buy is not complete and you have to explore the rest of the area and fill it out yourself.
On the other hand, there's one particular thing that shouldn't have been implemented to begin with. You see, if you die, a "Shade" of your player character spawns in the room you died or right outside it. What's the problem? Your "Soul" (basically mana) meter gets cut down by a third and ALL, I repeat, ALL your money is lost until you track it down, kill it, and absorb it. And if you think you can quit the game before you do so and return later, well buddy, you lose all your money forever and need to start literally from zilch. This is so bad on many levels. For one, why such inconvenience to begin with?! Who came up with it? It doesn't even make sense lore-wise so you can't give me any "It's symbolic" excuse. Also, there are times when the shade will spawn inside a boss room which SHUTS DOWN once you enter meaning you absolutely need to reach said boss (through arduous trips in some cases), kill your shade, and make it out alive which will probably take many frustrating tries. Otherwise, you lose your money for good. Admittedly, there's a certain merchant NPC at the "hub" town who will teleport your shade to your location so that you don't need to track it down, but even said NPC can only be reached by unlocking a door using a key you find somewhere or buy from a rip off merchant who overcharges for his merch.
Now let's talk about charms. They are items you can equip. There are also charm "notches" which are vacant spots that determine how many you can equip. Different charms have different "loads" ranging from 1 to 4. Now here are the problems. Many charms have high loads compared to their effects that they're usually not worth it. There's even a useful charm which went up from 2 notches to 3 after an update (Just why?!). Why would I give up 4 notches for a charm that only increases the amount of Soul I get out of hitting enemies? Why would I give up 4 for a charm that slows the already slow healing time just to heal 2 HP instead of 1? Why give up 3 for one that barely speeds up that process? Why give up 4 for a charm that SLOWLY regenerates the last, and ONLY the last damaged HP? And why on earth do I have to give up a notch (Yes, one notch matters) just to increase the running speed a little bit, something which should have been there by default in such a huge game area-wise? Keep in mind, you start with ONLY 3 notches and possibly max out at 11.
Now to my most detested thing, the occasionally cheap combat.
First, touch damage is a wretched archaic mechanic that we're clamoring to remove from games like Sonic and Mega Man let alone the so called 2D Dark Souls. The fact that all enemies (including passive critters that mind their business) can damage you by superficial contact is annoying and is only made several magnitudes worse when combined with other factors. Then there's the long time needed to heal and the fact it can only be done while standing still. This is a death sentence with certain bosses and gauntlets of mooks who will leave you little to no time to heal even one HP especially since there's a delay between you releasing the healing button and the knight starting to move again. The scarce and far in between save points will also make you rage with certain bosses whom you'll most definitely die to at least a few times. Furthermore, I could understand that you're supposed to memorize the patterns of enemies and bosses in order to dodge and counterattack, but there's a point where the game shoots this concept in the face by having enemies that teleport all over the place with no pattern if you get close to them. Furthermore, they have energy orbs that orbit them as shields which will damage you upon contact (touch damage can go kill itself). Furthermore, there's a LOT of them on a LONG way to a difficult boss meaning there's a high chance you'll start the fight in sub-par condition.
Then there's the abundance of backtracking due to scarce spaced out transient stations.
In conclusion, it's a very good game overall. But I won't recommend it unless you can handle the downs.

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is a stand alone DLC following the events of Saints Row IV. Sadly it doesn't live up to the hype, nor is it worth the $20 price tag.
Let's get the good out of the way first:
Flying is friggin awesome.  I can't wait for it to be ported into SR:IV
The musical cutscene.
The bad: (There is a LOT)
The game takes away your ability to easily fly rather early in the form of anti-air towers.  You can destroy these, but it's a pain.
Kinzie. She only has a few dozen lines of dialog and the game always refers to her as Gat during the missions and cutscenes.
The mission system. Doing ANY mission advances the story bar.  Once it reaches the end you have free roam back again, but if you're in the middle of a mission and trigger it a cutscene immediately plays. I was going to call it a fluke but it happened with EVERY transition.
No music. In a SR game.
All of the events are boring rehashes of main series events.  And since you can trigger the endgame without doing many of them, they are pretty pointless filler.
Finally, the ending. It's a freaking "Choose the ending" choice that plays 20 second clips of the aftermath and the game is over.
So do I recommend it? Not at $20. $5 is completely acceptable and if you wait long enough it sure to drop to the 80%-90% range during a sale.  I had a couple really good laughs with the game, but a couple good laughs to an otherwise boring game don't save it.

This War of Mine is a strategy game where you control a group of civilians trying to survive in a civil war. Who and how will you survive is up to you.
It is hard to write a review for this game without spoiling what This War of Mine has to offer because having the unpredictability and uncertainty element is part of the game. Knowing that going to a location could spell death for your character or killing a human being for canned goods is justifiable. This game will test your morale. An instant buy for anyone who wants a break from current trend of games. If your are still on the fence about this game, here is a review:
GRAPHICS: The characters are well detailed and the backgrounds show the horrors of war. The black and white tones with the pencil shades give the game the perfect look and mood.
SOUNDS: Excellent from the sounds of shellings at the background to the sound of stabbing. The music also fits the mood of the game
STORY: What makes this game have a high replay value is that you start off with different set of characters in new games and you learn their stories as the game progresses. You also develop your own dailogue with the choices you made and it can affect you characters.
GAMEPLAY: There is no tutorial which should be applauded because it adds more to the tension where you have no idea what is going to happen. Point and click from scavenging to backstabbing bandits. You have a home base which has an ant-hill set up where you can build the necessities to survive (e.g. stove, heater). You spend the day improving your shelter and tend to the needs of your characters. During the night you select a location to scavenge and be sure to read the description because it tells you what you will find and what to expect from the said location. If a character dies, he/she is dead for the entire playthrough.
SCORE 9/10

This review is rated P, for Positive.
While many reviewers of this game have given it a giant negative review, for various reasons, I have found the game to be an absolute delight.
While the game certainly carries on the "passive" feeling of Final Fantasy 12's combat system, the paradigm shifting add-on feels kind of like "Dress sphere changing" without the needlessly long cameos.
The "leveling" system, rather than going by character levels, involves leveling up individual classes, which you then slot in to Paradigms, to get access to their abilities.
The graphics in this game are decidedly breathtaking, with but few exceptions, and in contrast to a great many Final Fantasy games, all of the characters are not only well written in to the story, but even the whiney one, who has a vaguely Vaan/Tidus/Zidane feel to him, is neither useless, nor feeling particularly unnecessary to the story(Vaan).
While some of the characters do borrow elements of their dress style(Lightning - Ashe + Squall), or general attitude(Hope - Zidane + Squall + Vaan), they aren't a direct one to one rip-off, and all have interesting motivations for being part of your story.
Snow's punch-punch-punch battle style gets over-rated, eventually(As most monk-esque characters do, late game), and I would definitely nominate him for the most unnecessary feeling character in the game, but that doesn't mean his parts of the storyline aren't interesting; just his combat style is vanilla-monk feeling.
Overall, this game is not as overrated as most of the reviews seem to make it out to be; though it is linear, and doesn't "Open up much" for most of the early game, the same arguments could be made for FFX. Perhaps the only major drawback that I would offer this game is this:
If you are on a metered bandwidth, I suggest buying the disc for your game console.

Welcome to the best Magic: The Gathering Game by far. Wizards should have been doing it this way right from the start. It offers new players a very fundamental introduction to the game. It walks them through a lot of basic things they need to know. Combined with the fact that it's free, it's possible the best way of learning the game out there right now.
The campaigns are nice to play. Very creative ideas, however there were better games and a better feeling of being entangled in the wolrd in former DOTP-Games. I especially liked how Magic 2014 played out. The Single-Player-Campaign is nowhere close to that in density. I finished everything in one evening. You have to play with the Decks you are handed out (Similar to the Garruk campaign in Magic 2014). That's also a little unfortunate though I understand that they did it for flavour reasons. I miss the puzzles a little though that's not a huge loss.
The game per se in multiplayer can get quite grindy. At the beginning, you are given a pool of cards that's the same for everyone and a few boosters. From this you basically can build only one very mediocre Deck. Every 150 coins (one win nets you 20 coins) you can "Upgrade" and "buy" a booster containing 6 cards (1 rare, 2 uncommon, 3 common). It's compeltely random if these cards fit and it's very likely that you are stuck with the same kinds of cards for a very long time unless you spend some money on coins. That's basically the way they make money. Pay to progress. If you want to see something else, pay a little (or a lot of) money. As of now, I have spent 22,50 € on the game for a pack of coins. I don't intend to go any futher. I wanted to support a solid game. The game is free to play but not pay to win, UNLESS you start spending huge amounts of money (I'd say it starts at about 50-70 € to get really unfair) to get ridiculous tournament-like Decks. However, the matchmaking probably won't pair you against opponents like that anyway.
Now to the bad part: The game is bugged as hell. I had multiple games in which I couldn't activate activated abilities of my cards. Sometimes the timer won't stop because of lag, which is very unfortunate when you had been playing a control-deck and you just threw the game away. If your opponent choses to quit the game while you were agonizing over taking a mulligan, you never get to decide if you actually wanted to. The opponent is replaced by a computer who plays his deck, you have to keep your hand and the (still rated) game starts for you with a crappy hand. You can now chose to let the computers battle it out or you try playing it on your own. If you lose, you lose a point in the rating.
I also don't really get why I don't get the bonus of winning with a certain kind of deck even though I did. That's probably not a bug but just not explained properly. Honorable mentions: Cards tapping in the wrong direction, animations that display me being milled even though the opponent got milled, strange graphical displays on cards (i. e. lines).
I hope the developers are working on this. I can suggest the game but only if you can stomach a little bit of unnecessary frustration. Play it until you stumble over the bugs, give it a rest and try again later when they finally finished this contraption. :)

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Running through the jungle, you feel the ground shake. Something is catching up to you. You try to dodge between the trees, the ground shakes even more as an ear-splitting roar sounds just behind you. You turn around and bring up your rifle just as a gigantic head swings down and crushes you in its jaws.
You have just been T-Rex'ed. Next turn you'll get to chase the humans down. Welcome to Primal Carnage!
Pro:
*Awesome setting, dinosaurs and humans always makes for good fun. The screams, the adrenaline...
*Both sides are playable.
*Active development.
*Good graphics (not everyone agrees on this apparently. Well, I like it at least)
*The best organised team tends to win...mostly (see below)
Con:
*The most clunky fix to an (supposedly) overpowered class ever; the Pyro now slows to a crawl when he fires his weapon.
*Given two equally matched teams, the dino's tend to win. As the teams alternate constantly, this is not too much of a problem, and a good human team will win against the dino's without much trouble.
Pro or Con, depending on your views:
*The T-Rex will flatten any human team that fails to work together.
*The playerbase is not nearly as large as the game deserves.
Summary:
A FPS / TPS game that features dinosaurs and humans. Carnage ensues, much fun is had despite some imbalances and the worst "OP Class"-fix in history. 7/10 -Recomended.

Final Fantasy XIII is quite frankly, boring. I played 45 hrs before I realised that the gameplay was unlikely to open up enough to make up for the time spent on it. I stopped playing it for several reasons:
1: This game runs like a turd, with an fps that goes up and down with more vigor than your favourite pornstar, terrible issues with stuttering ( it seems to be the in thing these days ) and very few settings to change.
2: The linear maps. I went through chapter after chapter in a straight line. No joke. There was a few obstacles to "auto-leap" over. Seriously? Most likely you will keep moving forward, come accross a very obvious floating orb, you cant miss it, open it to find loot, move forward and face an ememy and do it again.
3. No side quests, no dungeons to get lost in, little to no customization, a level up system that is a straight line and the most challenging puzzle I played ammounted to turning 4 switches on which were only guarded by enemies that I had been defeating for the last 4 hrs - that's it. There is some upgrading to weapons and accessories, but it's overly complicated and not worth the hassle. You discover weird things like a microchip, electronic this and that but what it boils down to in the end is converting it to exp to level up your weapon in microscopic ammounts. I did this for a while only to find a better weapon in those very easy to access orbs. And by the way, the orbs are the only thing that have loot besides enemies.
That being said the game does have some positives. Despite the issues, the game is very pretty and the cut scenes are epic. The story line is pretty epic, though I didn't want to finish it because the gameplay ruined that aspect. I think the only reason I put up with this game for so many hours was because of the interesting story line. I think I might just watch all the cutscenes on youtube or something.
The combat system is moderately fun, and there is an element of trying to figure out what moves work and don't, and learning to chain with paradigm shifts is somewhat satisfying. Unfortunately, it's all you do... all the time.
I have never really played Final Fantasy before, so unfortunately, this seems like a bad place to start. I'm not sure I can handle the graphics of Final Fantasy 7. So I guess I'll wait till 15 comes out.

As a fan of side-scrollers I can definitely say I've played my far share of metroidvanias.  Hollow Knight makes a clearly unique mark for itself in this genre filled with classics.  Two of the things that stand out the most about this game is it's length and difficulty.  Hollow Knight can be anywhere between 24 to 30 hours depending on if you just play through the main story-line or go for more of a completionist run.  Much of the challenge in this game can be compared to Dark Souls; e.g. requiring the player to go back the place of their death if they doesn't want to lose all the money they had on them.  The moderate difficulty combined with a massive map to explore goes to show why this is such a lengthy and fulfilling experience.  If everything so far has your interested piqued lets dive into the finer details.
For those who aren't familiar with metroidvanias this genre is based in exploration.  There are over twelve different zones each with unique enemies, obstacles, and layouts.  As you explore you'll find many areas blocked off or unreachable that you must come back to later in the game after unlocking certain powers.  Your knight will continue becoming more and more mobile while continuously learning a series of new attacks and spells.  You will also find around 40 different charms that will have an array of different effects that change or enhance your abilities.  Each charm requires so many notches to equip with more powerful charms requiring more space.  Charm notches can be found and bought thought-out the game letting you equip a greater number of and/or more powerful charms.
Your knight can only take so many hits but as you play you'll find mask fragments which will eventually make him tougher.  The same goes for your soul meter which allows you to heal and cast spells.  Usually you can only recover soul by damaging the enemies.  Being able to heal is incredibly important since you'll drop your ever valuable Geo if you die.  Geo is the currency you get as you defeat monsters and it is necessary for buying charms, opening shortcuts, and purchasing maps.  As mentioned earlier you can go back to the place of your death and defeat your ghost to get all your Geo back.
The fact that this is a fairly lengthy game makes for very smooth progression not only of the story-line but of your own abilities.  As you progress you will often find yourself exploring stages and encountering bosses that force you to use new abilities or specific tactics.  The bosses often have specific patterns to learn that will usually go through three or so stages of increasing difficulty before they are defeated.  By the time you get to the late game content you'll be amazed at how far your reflexes have developed.  I myself was amazed that I was able to overcome some of the incredibly challenging content needed for the best ending.  However, after playing for over 25 hours I had been training myself the whole time to take on these most extreme obstacles.
Anyone who enjoys overcoming challenges along with those with an itch for exploration are really in for a treat.  Although this game is fairly though don't let that discourage you.  Most of the really brutal stuff isn't necessary for completing the game.  That being said the standard ending is a little haunting and won't leave you satisfied.  Since you'll nearly get two hours of entertainment (maybe a little frustration too) for every dollar you spend you know you'll definitely at least be getting great value for your money.  I almost forgot to mention too just how beautiful this game is.  The simple color scheme combined with the detailed creatures and backgrounds is utterly enthralling.  There isn't much else to say, the array of quality content in Hollow Knight speaks for itself.

I wish I could recommend this game. It has a lot of great things about it but IMO the bad outweighs the good. I finished the game with 90% completion BTW.
PROS:
-unique character design
-challenging platforming
-LONG game. definitely get your money's worth
CONS:
-terrible map system. you'll spend hours and hours getting lost and double/triple/quadruple checking areas.
-terrible pacing at times. what you need to do next isn't always clear and when you finally aquire one of the abilities you need at a certain point, everything snowballs from there and is quite easy to aquire.
-unnecessary difficulty at points. Honestly, it gets stupid hard for the sake of being hard and when you beat it, the reward isn't often worth it.
-areas of the game look too much the same except Greenpath and The Abyss. There are no sloping inclines, everything is a flat platform and the game can get dull because of this.
-the music isn't terrible but it most certainly isn't memorable. if fits each area somewhat (one track sounded like the one from Alien before they land on the planet and another sounded very similar to Interstellar) but it's not great.
All in all, the game is good but I don't see much people finishing it and most certainly never completing some of the extra challenges (White Knight area platforming). If you like Castlevania SotN, you won't necessarily like this game. The music isn't catchy, the platforms and different areas are almost identical, most enemies aren't interesting and the extra characters's voices sometimes don't match their body types (quite odd). If you're a masochist, you'll like it.

I've played SR2,3,4, and now GooH.  Each has bright spots for me.  SR2 had solid gameplay, great voice actors, and a pretty good story.  I thought the gameplay for SR3 was very good, and I found it to be the most "fun."  SR4 went in a different direction, and while I wasn't always a fan of the gameplay, I really loved the story, which had a stronger emotional impact than I expected.  GooH, thus far, has flight and an interesting concept.  It has "superpowers" like SR4, And the biggest plus for me, it lets you be Kinzie, who is far and away my favorite SR character.
My biggest problem is the lack of length combined with the lack of true need to upgrade most weapons and powers (aside from flight).   As with SR 3 and 4, you can upgrade your weaponry, health, etc.  I beat the final boss after upgrading all of my weapons one notch, on "normal" difficulty.  I'm really not that great a player, so I'm not quite sure why greatly underpowered weapons should have done the trick.  Despite beating the final boss, I still have many, many missions and challenges to go, which means a lot of money to be made to upgrade more.  In a way , it's good, in that I can play the rest of the game without thinking about the storyline.  But it would have made more sense to progressively increase the difficulty so it's necessary to do more missions, get more money, and upgrade more weapons, to challenge the big boss.  What I'm basically saying is the storyline game is too short, not because of lack of content, but because of the way progress is measured.  It's a bit anticlimactic, as I'll get stronger and stronger without a looming challenge to put it to the test.
There are a few other downsides.  Vehicles are still largely pointless, and there isn't much in the way of variety.  There are no flying vehicles (it's understandable, but still).  There are no garages.  There is no soundtrack.  Thee's no "call a homie/call a vehicle" etc., so there's no clever talk between your homies.  There's no customization of your character or vehicles.  They messed up with the voicework a bit, in the sense that more variety was needed both for random comments, and for in-mission comments.  For example, when you hit the checkpoints in the flying mission/diversion, Kinzie says one of three or four things.  But she says one at pretty much each checkpoint.  It gets a bit annoying when there are 15 checkpoints.
All that said, the game isn't meant to be the equivalent of SR 3 or 4, or a GTA 5.  It's a third the price for more than a third the content, so it's proportionally fine, if not very good.  It is a new map, the enemies are new, the weapons are new, flying is new, playing as Kinzie or Gat is new,   It's legitimately fun to play.
If you approach the game with reasonable expectations, especially given the price, you'll likely be satisfied.  If you go in expecting a fleshed-out AAA title, you're going to be disappointed.  You'll likewise be disappointed if you start thinking about the missed opportunities in the game.  I'm far from the first to reach that conclusion.
When all is said and done, I'll likely get more than 20 hours of play out of the game, which for $20, isn't bad at all.  I'm still on the Saints Row bandwagon, and I'm looking forward to SR 5 or whatever the next iteration is.

I'm sure many would disagree that HK is so, but this isn't their review.
Something just feels off about this game, little things. The jump descends too fast, hit boxes are mystifying, enemy tells and attacks get lost against the intricate scenery. Combine that with stingy power-ups and infrequent save spots, and it's a nasty brew. It feels like a misapplication of the Souls games formula in the same way Galak-Z wasn't necessarily improved by its Rogue-like elements.
I want so much to like it and I plan to keep playing but at the moment it's mostly making me angry. The combat just isn't fun or varied enough to justify the time investment. Getting good doesn't seem appealing, as I'd just be better at a system I don't think is fun to start with.
That said, Team Cherry are clearly very talented and I'll be interested to see whatever they so next, whether I play much more Hollow Knight or not.

This War of Mine is a strategy game where you control a group of civilians trying to survive in a civil war. Who and how will you survive is up to you.
It is hard to write a review for this game without spoiling what This War of Mine has to offer because having the unpredictability and uncertainty element is part of the game. Knowing that going to a location could spell death for your character or killing a human being for canned goods is justifiable. This game will test your morale. An instant buy for anyone who wants a break from current trend of games. If your are still on the fence about this game, here is a review:
GRAPHICS: The characters are well detailed and the backgrounds show the horrors of war. The black and white tones with the pencil shades give the game the perfect look and mood.
SOUNDS: Excellent from the sounds of shellings at the background to the sound of stabbing. The music also fits the mood of the game
STORY: What makes this game have a high replay value is that you start off with different set of characters in new games and you learn their stories as the game progresses. You also develop your own dailogue with the choices you made and it can affect you characters.
GAMEPLAY: There is no tutorial which should be applauded because it adds more to the tension where you have no idea what is going to happen. Point and click from scavenging to backstabbing bandits. You have a home base which has an ant-hill set up where you can build the necessities to survive (e.g. stove, heater). You spend the day improving your shelter and tend to the needs of your characters. During the night you select a location to scavenge and be sure to read the description because it tells you what you will find and what to expect from the said location. If a character dies, he/she is dead for the entire playthrough.
SCORE 9/10

Oh the Saints. How far you have come since your gangster origins. From Stillwater, to Steelport, Whitehouse, to Outer Space, the Saints have seen it all. But now comes there greatest challenge, Satan himself. Yes it would seem Lucifer has actually taken interest in the "The Boss" (Generally YOU in every other Saints Row game) due to his ability to cause mayhem, fight for power, and still get the job done at the end of the day. Due to this interest, Satan ends up kidnapping The Boss after the gang decides to play with a Ouija board, thus opening a rift to hell pulling The Boss into his certain doom. Sounds ridiculous right? Well it is!!! That being said, I absolutely loved this game, and here is why!
[Pros]
- Play as Johnny Gat or Kinzie Kensington whenever you desire.
-Tons of weapons unique to hell and a few classics, including the 7 Deady Weapons, one for each of the 7 Deadly Sins.
-The Glide Ability from SR4 is replaced with the Winged Flight ability, a much more maneuverable means of travel.
-Team up with the likes of Vlad the Impaler, Blackbeard the Pirate, and William Shakespeare.
-Meet up with old cast members such as The Twins from SR3, Dex from SR1, and even Dane from SR2.
-All of the "Super Powers" have been replaced with "Arcane Abilities" which act similiar, but have unique differences.
-Tons of collectables filled with lore, and lots of side challenges to help keep you busy.
-Up to five different endings, some serious, some silly, some very random.
-Tons of upgrades between your character, weapons, and powers.
-Great dialogue with equally as great voice acting. You can tell the whole cast has fun filming their lines.
-Possible cliffhangers hinting at Saints Row 5.
-Co-Op available through the whole game. Whats better then one person beating up Satan? Two people!
[Cons]
-Very few vehicles to drive around in, tho you will likely spend most of your time flying or running.
-No radio stations, this stinks because things can get quiet at times.
-Very short (Only took 4 hours to complete the story), tho this is ment to be a standalone DLC at a $20 price so that kind of was expected.
-Once you finish all of the quests, side missions, and challenges, you really have nothing else to do but run around.
-Some side missions are recycled versions of missions from other games, just renamed and slightly reskinned.
-You cannot use your phone to call any holmies, this is replaced with the ability to summon creatures.
-You cannot change the custom skin of your weapons, a feature that was refreshing to see in SR4.
[Neutral Thoughts]
-This game is NOT for everyone, especially for die hard fans of Saints Row 2 and prior. This is not the Saints Row game you remember, back when it was all about forming a gang and running the streets. I would recomend it to people with a good sense of humor and who can handle a game that doesen't take itself too seriously. This game is alot of light hearted fun, and does a great job at making references to all Saints games prior this one.
[Final Thoughts]
Contrary to popular belief, the Saints Row series stopped being relatable to the GTA series ever since midway through Saints Row 3. This is NOT GTA. If you want a serious, more realistic experience, then this is NOT the game for you. If you want an open world, gun slinging, super ability whipping, wing flapping HELL of a good time (PUN INTENDED) then I would definetly recommend this game to you. If you enjoyed the whackiness of Saints Row 4, and maybe even Saints Row 3, I would highly suggest giving this game a try. It has a great price, a great cast, and great fun all around.

Welcome to the best Magic: The Gathering Game by far. Wizards should have been doing it this way right from the start. It offers new players a very fundamental introduction to the game. It walks them through a lot of basic things they need to know. Combined with the fact that it's free, it's possible the best way of learning the game out there right now.
The campaigns are nice to play. Very creative ideas, however there were better games and a better feeling of being entangled in the wolrd in former DOTP-Games. I especially liked how Magic 2014 played out. The Single-Player-Campaign is nowhere close to that in density. I finished everything in one evening. You have to play with the Decks you are handed out (Similar to the Garruk campaign in Magic 2014). That's also a little unfortunate though I understand that they did it for flavour reasons. I miss the puzzles a little though that's not a huge loss.
The game per se in multiplayer can get quite grindy. At the beginning, you are given a pool of cards that's the same for everyone and a few boosters. From this you basically can build only one very mediocre Deck. Every 150 coins (one win nets you 20 coins) you can "Upgrade" and "buy" a booster containing 6 cards (1 rare, 2 uncommon, 3 common). It's compeltely random if these cards fit and it's very likely that you are stuck with the same kinds of cards for a very long time unless you spend some money on coins. That's basically the way they make money. Pay to progress. If you want to see something else, pay a little (or a lot of) money. As of now, I have spent 22,50 € on the game for a pack of coins. I don't intend to go any futher. I wanted to support a solid game. The game is free to play but not pay to win, UNLESS you start spending huge amounts of money (I'd say it starts at about 50-70 € to get really unfair) to get ridiculous tournament-like Decks. However, the matchmaking probably won't pair you against opponents like that anyway.
Now to the bad part: The game is bugged as hell. I had multiple games in which I couldn't activate activated abilities of my cards. Sometimes the timer won't stop because of lag, which is very unfortunate when you had been playing a control-deck and you just threw the game away. If your opponent choses to quit the game while you were agonizing over taking a mulligan, you never get to decide if you actually wanted to. The opponent is replaced by a computer who plays his deck, you have to keep your hand and the (still rated) game starts for you with a crappy hand. You can now chose to let the computers battle it out or you try playing it on your own. If you lose, you lose a point in the rating.
I also don't really get why I don't get the bonus of winning with a certain kind of deck even though I did. That's probably not a bug but just not explained properly. Honorable mentions: Cards tapping in the wrong direction, animations that display me being milled even though the opponent got milled, strange graphical displays on cards (i. e. lines).
I hope the developers are working on this. I can suggest the game but only if you can stomach a little bit of unnecessary frustration. Play it until you stumble over the bugs, give it a rest and try again later when they finally finished this contraption. :)

If you have not played Magic before, this game have the tools required to learn Magic (one of the worlds first TCG's), it features a tutorial that teaches you all the basic stuff, and a campain of around 25 missions if you need some more practice (also gives you gold for progressing and getting more cards). It also have good bots that play random generated, but good decks. It have a deckbuilder to help you get started building decks.
If you played magic before, I think you will like this game.
Good implementation of magics ruleset. Gives you a decent cardpool to start with. Have some technical problems, but nothing game breaking. Progression is a carbon copy of heartstone, but a lot faster. Have better starting cardpool then heartstone, and gives more for duels than heartstone.
Pros
+ good starting cardpool, you get an amount of cards in the beginning of the game that is sufficent to build some different good decks.
+ bot's, this game uses them for a lot of things, for example dealing with disconnects
+ populated match making, you get into games quickly, agains fairly even opponents.
+ commitment, it seems like magic duel will feature all upcomming magic sets, (around 500 card names/year), and while they might be delayed compared to the paper reseases, they will get here, and there are already a lot of cards
+ rarity deckbuilding change, they have done a change, compared to paper magic, which is that you can't play more then 2 of each rare card, this means that the impact of planeswalkers and mass removal is way lower in this metagame. (If that wen't over your head, don't worry)
Cons
- Technical issues, there are no game breaking bugs in the game, but there are time when the matchmaker does kick you back to the main menu, and times when a dayly quest does not cach in directly. Mostly small things like that.
- Reading issues, on laptop resolutions (might also happen on other resolutions), you might have a hard time reading the cards outside of games, as there is no zoom functionality while out of the game.
- Land taping. The automatic land taping works most of the time, but for some strange cases you want to tap lands manualy, and sometimes when you do that, the game does not drain all mana from your pool, but tap lands instead. This is mostly an issue with some of the zendicar cards, like when you have man-lands and want to cast awaken spells.

Certainly is underrated. Story is alright for a JRPG. Its full of traditional JRPG tropes so not too much new there. The protagonist is a sis-con/etc. However, where it becomes more unique is in party formations. This is like an RPG game with a heavier emphasis on setting up your parties to handle all threats. It is a different and welcome approach. Because of this, some fights can be much harder than they need be.
You'll likely find lots of people complaining about the difficulty. But here is probably the greatest tip of all and it didn't take much to figure out. Yes some are hard, but they all have optimal strategies to make them work. It isn't luck of the draw. Luck only comes in when it comes to damage/resist totals. Overall instead of simple luck, it usually involves who you target first. If you are having trouble, try other combinations. I've had some tough ones become insanely easy because instead of focusing down one enemy, I focused another. Or instead of splitting up, I focused.
The other big factor for this game is do a search on it for how to manually set the graphics/etc. Square - Enix did a pretty poor job. But there are wikis out there which will quickly tell you how to set the game up to look much better. It literally is a must do for anyone who buys this game. Read the sites, hack the ini, enjoy the game.
It is a shame this title didn't get more refinement or better support from Square. Certainly is one of the more unique JRPGs out there. Play it in the Japanese dub if possible. This game was torture to play, but I had to see it through to the end to really understand.  The most frustrating thing about it is, all of the necessary parts to have made a very passable and enjoyable Final Fantasy game are here, but any gems were sunk deep into an ocean of bad design decisions and poor storytelling.  The gameplay is a complete mess driven primarily by random luck and twitch reflexes, and the game primarily plays itself.  Battles are needlessly and frustratingly long, and because the vast majority of control and configuration are taken OUT of your hands, you don't even feel like victories are the result of your actions.  Yes, Final Fantasy games have always had battle systems where you did the same thing over and over again and very rarely needed to change your strategy up, but once you've removed even THAT gameplay, you're left with nothing.  But in "streamlining" away the actual gameplay, Square-Enix didn't bother to REDUCE the amount of it.  In fact, they doubled down on making all of the post-game content entirely combat based.  Well, scratch that... half combat, half WALKING.  Out of my 40+ hour save file, easily 5 hours was spent watching Lightning's butt run across meadows.  And none of that was "exploration", it was needless backtracking.  There's a point in the game where there's a circle of stones that give you quests.  It is a 3 minute run across an open field away from the closest fast travel point, every single one of the missions it gives you is a 20 minute run away (or 6-8 minutes with fast travel you need to run ALL the way back to), and you can only accept one of the missions at at time, and they HAVE to be set from the stones.  They'll get added to your list of missions alright, but if you want to change your active one, you have to WALK to the stone you got it from.  This game has more senseless padding than a dozen freshman term papers.  If they'd pared down the crappy gameplay and tightened this to a 20-30 hour experience, spread out the exploration instead of trying to cram an unimpressive Monster Hunter clone into the middle, and fleshed out the story and characterization more with writers instead of character designers, they could've had something to be proud of.   Instead it's an incoherent padded mess that just frustrates you with squandered potential.

TL;DR at bottom. Only recommend for particular kinda of use.
First of all, I haven't experienced any of the technical issues reported by many other users. (GTX 970, 4th generation i5 and 16GB RAM on Windows 7.)
Now, on the good bits: they've finally got the interface to work well, unlike in previous renditions. It's clean, easy to use and easy to understand. (Both with and without a lot of the gameplay automation.) The tutorial system is excellent, and its monetization system is very fair (10 wins per pack just playing hard Bots + loads of money from story mode and skill quests.)
BUT: the card pool is VERY limited, and the options you're given in the story mode are kind of misleading. A lot of fairly simple cards, like Lightning Bolt (3 damage to player or creature for a red) which appear in skill quests and story mode, don't appear in the game itself. This makes a lot of archetypes rather difficult to play, and restricts deck building options to the point where there seems to be little point in playing quite yet.
TL;DR Overall, I wouldn't recommend this for longterm players, or anyone who already plays MTG. I would, however, recommend it as a free learning tool to get newbies into Magic. Might be worth another look in a year's time.

Very straightforward shoot 'em up that, unfortunately, doesn't do anything different or even better than any other game. Instead, it's very lacking in almost every respect...
The only designed piece of this game is the Boss Fights, of which there are 3. They're not spectacular bosses, but at least there's something to them.
Here's a rundown of the game:
Ship Upgrades: 1 damage upgrade, 2x 1 front shot, 2x 1 lateral shot.
Game Progression: Periodical spawning of enemies that simply fly downwards until you kill 100 of them, then a Boss fight. This happens 3 times. After each boss, the enemies get a stronger version spawning.
That's about it. Yeah. There are occasional enemies that spawn form the sides or that shoot, but nothing game changing.
There's a Hardmode, in which every enemy shoots, instead of the basic ones simply flying downwards.
There isn't even a scoring system to the game! The only score "mechanic" is that each enemy killed increases it by one. Different enemy types (with different HP, or that shoot or w/e) increase the score by one as well. Not differentiation there.
... There's also the fact the gamepad and keyboard controls are different. Keyboard has default Unity physics, while the Gamepad has a more "digital" movement (for lack of a better word... no physics, move directly left/right).
There are powerups, but they're redundant after you get the ship upgrades. With the exception of "lives".
Speaking of which... You have one shot. If you get hit, you'll have to restart. Unless you have additional lives that occasionally drop. That's ... annoying, but okay. The bigger problem is that there is absolutely no feedback when you're hit. And there's apparently a 3 lives limit, even after you collect more.
It's just... so barebones. Doesn't do anything that I'd consider surprising or good. And doesn't compensate in being somewhat compelling in variety or good design. So yeah, I wouldn't recommend this one.

Civilization Beyond Earth has completely failed to grasp my attention for longer than one playing hour and has me very dissapointed in so many facets of the game. Since buying the game on release, I can't bring myself to play this game anymore because of how unoriginal and terrible the AI and gameplay is. Unfortunately this is even with the added steam workshop content that is 'recommended' after downloading the game, another area requiring work. I've tried my hardest to like this game, but I can't.
If you want some really healthy advice, buy Civilization V and download a whole heap of mods from the Civ Fanatics website and don't pay for any upcoming DLC from this game. By assisting this game in sales, you will not be teaching the developing team a lesson. It's also easy to say that you'll suffer the same fate like many others if you make that very risky jump.
Shame Shame Shame.

"Bioshock: Remastered"
An un-review by Richard Valkinsenn.
DISCLAIMER: I did receive this for free, but only because I own the original.
"Oh, boy! This is not good."
This will be an open letter to AAA publishers out there who read this "review." Since this game is not an actual remaster, this will not be an actual review. Well, at least it won't be too in-depth. Let's be clear: I loved the original Bioshock, and, by extension, Bioshock 2. It's a great game with an amazing story that deserves to be remembered and cherished as an important landmark of videogaming history. Everything from the writing of the characters to the bizarre, but memorable atmosphere, and even the game's soundtrack made the game one of the best I've ever played. Yes, Bioshock indeed sits next to such games as Doom, Halo, Call of Duty 4, and many other classics I've had the pleasure of experiencing, so far.
Bioshock: Remastered, on the other hand... is an abomination. One that spits in the faces of fans of the original game, for a number of reasons. It's a technical, buggy mess lacking much-needed options. And the technical problems aren't just the only problems this thing faces. Nothing in this game has really been "remastered" at all. There is no real discernable difference between this game and the original to speak of. Maybe the textures are sharper or the lighting's been reworked somewhat? Honestly, I couldn't tell the difference. Visually, it's exactly the same as I remember it from the original, something that also extends to the gameplay, of which there is also no discernable difference.
But the bottom line is simple: this... "thing" is not a remaster, but a resale. Nothing really new or interesting has been added into it, save for bugs that should've been squashed before the game launched. And overall, this so-called "remaster" is an insult to fans of the original looking for an augmented and redone version of the game they loved.
So, let's make this abundantly clear, shall we? The original game STILL EXISTS and it runs JUST FINE on modern hardware. It didn't need a half-baked touch-up, and it didn't need a casual resale as a buggy, technical abomination, either. Triple-A publishers, READ THIS CAREFULLY: if you're gonna remaster a game like this, THEN YOU NEED TO FULLY REMASTER IT. From the ground-up. Redo and spice up the art direction, change up and streamline the gameplay, and add surprises for the fans of the original game to discover as they run through it. Do NOT, and I repeat:
DO
NOT
RESELL
YOUR GAME
AS IS.
And do not attempt to pass off a resale as a remaster. You will only hurt your own reputation in doing so.
Final Verdict:
I loved the original.
I hated this quote-un-quote "remaster."

Signing off.

This War of Mine is a strategy game where you control a group of civilians trying to survive in a civil war. Who and how will you survive is up to you.
It is hard to write a review for this game without spoiling what This War of Mine has to offer because having the unpredictability and uncertainty element is part of the game. Knowing that going to a location could spell death for your character or killing a human being for canned goods is justifiable. This game will test your morale. An instant buy for anyone who wants a break from current trend of games. If your are still on the fence about this game, here is a review:
GRAPHICS: The characters are well detailed and the backgrounds show the horrors of war. The black and white tones with the pencil shades give the game the perfect look and mood.
SOUNDS: Excellent from the sounds of shellings at the background to the sound of stabbing. The music also fits the mood of the game
STORY: What makes this game have a high replay value is that you start off with different set of characters in new games and you learn their stories as the game progresses. You also develop your own dailogue with the choices you made and it can affect you characters.
GAMEPLAY: There is no tutorial which should be applauded because it adds more to the tension where you have no idea what is going to happen. Point and click from scavenging to backstabbing bandits. You have a home base which has an ant-hill set up where you can build the necessities to survive (e.g. stove, heater). You spend the day improving your shelter and tend to the needs of your characters. During the night you select a location to scavenge and be sure to read the description because it tells you what you will find and what to expect from the said location. If a character dies, he/she is dead for the entire playthrough.
SCORE 9/10

Gat out of Hell is a game that's difficult to list as recommend or not.
Although it is Stand-Alone, it's really an expansion pack for Saints Row IV. It's the same idea as expansion packs for other open-world games that take place after the main story and are shorter, take place in just part of the main map (or a new smaller map) and after the main story but still offer fun game play and a decent, albeit short story. The difference here is that it's Stand-Alone as opposed to launching it from within Saints Row IV.
While short, this is still a fun game. Even in the small(er) world (at least compared to SR IV) in which the expansion takes place, there is still plenty to see, do and collect.
However, because of the structure of the missions (i.e., there are only a few main ones and you do side activities to build up Satan's anger enough to fight him), you will likely find yourself able to fight the last battle with much of the world still left for you to discover and play. You may well find yourself feeling a sense a disappointment as it only takes about four hours of play to reach this point.
There however still will be plenty left for you to do and collect. Couple this with the last battle being one you can repeatedly fight and the expansion can last well beyond those initial four hours.
The activities themselves are sadly mostly just Saints Row 4 activities in slightly different clothing. The exception being the two based on the new flying ability. That's not to say they're not fun. It's more that they feel like more of the same.
Speaking of which, flying is a lot of fun, especially once you've purchased upgrades. You may well find yourself wondering how you were ever happy without it.
The collectibles are more or less the same as in Saints Row IV but again, in slightly different clothing. I don't want to spoil too much. However, I will say that listening to them did give me the feeling that the team put a lot of thought and effort into this game. It does feel as though there could have been much more of a story here. I.e., that though they could (or perhaps even should) have expanded this from an expansion into a full game with a full set of missions.
Gat out of Hell ends up being a game that is fun and it is good to have another adventure with the Saints, albeit only a couple of them and a short one. It feels like a game that could have been a lot more and does suffer more then a little from feeling like a re-skin of Saints Row 4. However, when it does have new things, it does a great or at least decent job with them. The team did a lot with what they had to work with.
While Gat out Hell may seem to be missing something (maybe even a lot), I think it's important that we remember that (iirc) they did advertise this as a stand alone expansion rather then a whole new game. Could it have been more? Yes. On the other hand, it wasn't as though they were claiming it was going to be.

First off before I get started with my review of this excellent game, you have to take into consideration  that "This War of Mine" is not a typical 3rd or 1st person shooter. Where you normally play a gung ho elite soldier,  who has the ability  to murder dozens of  NPC's, without facing both the  physically and physiologically consequence's of taking another persons life.
But rather, in the  war of mine you play a group ordinary people  just like you and I, who once had Jobs, responsiblitys and families. That have now been destroyed in the face of a poltical war, in this game every action has a consequence that impacts both on the player and the characters  and it ultimately paints a very real and a  very scary picture of what people will do to overcome certain death.
Let me give you an example,  during one incident  my character was looting a house for supplies that my group desperately needed, during this time i found the medical locker of a family who's mother was sadly sick and without the meds she would surely die, now this is where the game really stands out as it places you in situations that make you question your own moral code, do you take the supplies for yourself in the hope that your group may need them in the near future, or do you leave them in the belief that the mother will recover and see her children though to adulthood. This is the real goal of the game, for the player to battle their own judgements and question themselves.
Finally, this war of mine is a must buy for any gamer, that wants to see an alternative angle on the far reaching conqences of  war because as one highly successful game said.
War, War never changes.

A great game with an even greater message, based on a real life event from the 90's.
It's basically the sims, with starvation and murder.  The premise is that you are already three years into the siege and have taken refuge in a neighborhood that has a military sniper preventing your movement.  Other sections of the town are doing better, but yours is deseperate.
You're never quite 'good enough' to survive and the atmosphere of the game will trigger a response if you are forced to do something 'bad'.  You are given three random survivors out of a dozen or so, each with a single advantage and several disadvantages (in the form of addictions, being overly apathetic / emotional, or physical drawbacks).  The game also randomizes when major events like winter, crime waves, and the end of the war arrive.
Those three starting survivors shape what kind of game you will have, adding replay value.  One batch may be emotionally cold and able to take from others, another may be very self-sufficient but their addictions smoke and drink your currency away.
The soundtrack is also very good if you are into that... check out #5 No Good Choice.
The only complaint I have is that the mechanics are opaque.  You wouldn't know that hunger ticks every other day without googling it, for example or that vegetables need THAT MANY!? fertilizer.

A lengthy, sci-fi FPS game that was capable of melting age-old graphics cards? Crysis, coming up!
The graphics in this game were the draw in the day, and even in 2016, 9 years later, they still hold up pretty damn well for their age.  The colors are a bit saturated, and obviously the textures are a bit flat, but for it's age, this looks good.  Another draw was the intense use of physics in the game.  This is yet another thing to add to the list of reasons your new GPU probably still can't max the game out and run at a smooth 60 FPS.  The explosions really blow things up and launch stuff everywhere and the amount of work going into the realistix physics emulation, really takes a toll on your hardware.  Overall the physics and graphics have aged well, and aren't something to worry about when deciding to try this out.
The vehicle mechanics are clunky and hard to handle sometimes, but not unbearable (think early Halo), and you'll need them, as the map is a pretty damn big island, and you'll see almost all of it before you've finished.
The gunplay mechanics are well done.  Not as polished as newer FPS games, but definitely nothing to be worried about.  Stuff shoots well, animations look clear and fluid and the gameplay itself feels fluid.
The gameplay is also semi-linear.  You're given you're objective, and some suggestions, but no direct requirement on how you go about accomplishing it.
The story is also pretty original and interesting, and has some length to it, so that's a nice touch for an FPS.  Something FPS' these days could learn a thing about.
All-in-all the game is great.  The graphics are still good 9 years after release, the sound effects are great, the physics are awesome, the story is interesting and unique and the gameplay is fun and as exciting as you want to make it.

This game is basically just a 3D version of any Final Fantasy game, not everything about it is great including the linear feel of it, it feels like you're definitely forced to move in one direction and the game also has an interesting difficulty spike, even as I'd been increasing my characters abilities throughout the game, there were still points where it was near impossible to kill simple enemies but all in all the game is fun for what it is, it has a nice little story to go with each character and every character has a use including Vanille (who is adorable and useful). I can see why this is a disliked game by the FF community but personally, I enjoyed the game and story and I'd recommend giving it a shot.
Something I certainly suggest doing, however, is cloud saving, this is something that I hadn't started doing until recently and it's an extremely useful feature if you're somebody like me because I've had to restart this game 4 or 5 times purely because I lost saves (computers breaking or upgrading), I'd certainly suggest cloud saving so you don't have to do what I did and restart 4 or 5 times. Another thing I'd suggest is possibly changing around the exit and "go back" keys, this is something that I often found frustrating because I'm used to using ESC for going back in menus etc. and every time I'd accidentally tap it and the game would ask if I wanted to quit, that's just a suggestion however and if you're used to the default setup of backspace being go back then I'd say keep it as is.
From what I've played so far of FF13, I'd definitely suggest giving it a shot because it can be quite a fun game and if you can get past the first section it tends to become very fun and interesting, especially with the summoning aspect that's added when you meet the Shiva Sisters, The game is stunning graphically and the humour in it is brilliant from what I've seen so far, it also has that FF combat system that we all know and love and a nice little tree for upgrading abilities which I personally love. The story isn't the best and the soundtrack is always drowned out by game-play but all in all I'd suggest giving it a shot because in my personal opinion it's quite a fun game and worth the money I spent on it, even if I did have to restart a few times, I'm still enjoying the game and trying to get further in to get a full opinion on story and character development, from what I've seen so far, the story is okay and the characters are all quite interesting, Vanille is especially a nice little character in this game.

This is the first Final Fantasy I have completed, I had FFX on the PS2 but got stuck at the blitzball tournament and never went back to it. FFXIII seems to be a divisive game for people, with a lot of fans of the old games hating the linearity of this one, and some or all of the characters in 13.
Regarding the linearity, it is incredibly linear for most of the game, with you just running along straight paths fighting enemies. Once you get to chapter 11 it opens up and you can explore and run around in this massive field (you even get a chocobo to ride to get around faster), with these huge dinosaur turtle creatures and sh*t you can fight. This is a really cool area, but if you really don’t like the linearity of the game I wouldn’t recommend you buy it and persevere till you get to that part. There are 13 chapters in the game and that is the 11th, which is more than 30 hours through the game! You are close to the end at that point, I honestly wondered why they even had an open section at all, I was used to the linear paths.
I don’t usually play turn based RPG’s so I have nothing to compare the combat system in this to, but it does a good job of easing you into it, at first it’s a cake walk, I had no issues for the first 10 hours. There are 6 main characters you get to play as, but in battles you can only equip 3, but at the beginning as the characters split up, you go between fighting with 3 equipped to only being able to use 2 at some points for story reasons. This gave me some trouble early on, with one or two boss fights, like most RPG’s grinding would make those encounters a lot easier.
I had to use a guide to defeat some bosses later on, there really seemed to be only 1 or 2 methods that worked on them and if you don’t know what you’re doing you could be there hours without a guide, but most of the time I had no problem, though I did grind for a few hours to level my characters up (also with a guides help to find the best places to grind).
There is a ton of secondary boss fight missions you can attempt once you get to chapter 11 (63 in total I think) so there is plenty here for you to do, I put in 70 hours at the time of writing this and I still have about 5 missions left to do. If you don’t feel like doing those then you should be able to complete the main story in 55 – 60 hours.
I bought this game for the story more than the combat, and this is the other area people have a problem with. I liked the characters, but some people had issues with Lightning being stoic through the whole story, but the other 5 characters all have different personalities, and each of them has their own story and arc through the game, so even if you don’t like Lightning or find her boring, the story is always shifting between all 6. This is really an ensemble cast of characters, even though they heavily promoted Lightning in all the marketing/trailers and covers for the game. In the first game it's an ensemble anyway, in the second one you might only get to play as her sister, and in the third you may only get to play as lightning (though they do feature the other 5 characters in the story still).
This should go without saying but the game looks visually amazing, and the architecture and creature design is unique to a Japanese mindset, so as a westerner I enjoyed it. There are many CGI cut scenes throughout, which I enjoyed because I got the game for the story, but if you only want gameplay and minimal story that could be an issue for you.
The port has some issues, outside of combat I would get 60fps if I turned off the mini map, in combat it dropped to 30, I noticed it dropped as low as 24fps once or twice. I tried a few different methods to try and fix it and none of them worked. This wasn’t an issue for me because the game’s turn based, so the camera is in a semi fixed position when fighting, it didn’t really bother me when playing. NOTE: my pc is pretty good (I7,R9 290), if you have a mid or low range PC it might not run as well for you.

Secret in Story is a true surprise for me. I did not expect that kind of game at all. Actually I was not expecting anything since I didn’t really understand what kind of game it was before starting it. And I certainly did not expect to nearly break my keyboard playing it...
I would say it is more of a game of speed and memorization. Each playthrough takes around 10-15min at first then around 5min once you have figured out what you have to do.
The story is short. Memories of a love story, nothing exciting or mind-blowing.
The graphics are cute, manga-like. Black and white. Except the writings that are a little blurred. The music is nice.

The goal is to take the story further by clicking in specific places. You have to guess them, or have memorized the clues that were given to you earlier. Furthermore, you have limited time to click on each image. If you click in the wrong place, you "die".
Some scenes require skill and speed. Some objects are also placed randomly, which adds difficulty from one playthrough to the other.
It is easy to finish at least one playthrough. I succeeded after 5 attempts.
This proves more complicated if you are looking to get all achievements. One requests to complete the game in less than 5 minutes, the other to click less than 150 times, and another one, not to die. It was these sadistic little challenges that made me nearly break my keyboard.
I think it is possible to complete this game 100% in less than 3 hours.
In summary, I recommend this very nice surprise to all players who are looking for a short game that will give them a little bit of trouble.
Considering the price, it is totally worth it.

Lastly. Story. I'll admit, at this time I haven't finsished the game. But I have found the story to be pretty good. Though not as good as many other games in the Final Fantasy series. My favourites, FF X and FF IX, grabbed me and held me tight with vast and diffrent charechters with many diffrent reasons, and while it was all fantastical, it was beliveable and felt smoth. TLDR: Third Person hack/slash RPG similar to Dragon Age 2, but set in Tolkien’s Middle-Earth. Melee combat has a similar feel as the first Witcher game where you kind of need to flow from one hit to the next to build up strike power. The game appears to be built around multiplayer co-op, but I’ve only played single-player thus far. WARNING: If you have an ATI/AMD video card you will probably have technical trouble with this game. Big thumbs down for the game breaking bug (near the very end) - 2/10. Would have been 6/10 if the game actually worked.
If you liked Dragon Age 2 more than you liked Dragon Age Origins (not many people do) you might want to give Lord of the Rings: War in the North a try. The game is more linear and focused on combat than world-building. This might have to do with the fact that the “main story” is happening elsewhere (Fellowship of the Ring) and you’re just the distraction to help Frodo sneak into Mordor.
You play one member of a trio of adventurers at around the start of the first Lord of the Rings novel. Before Frodo, Aragorn, and their buddies start their journey to Mount Doom, Farin the dwarf (melee fighter), Eradan the ranger (archer), and Andriel the elf (mage) are fighting the good fight against the servants of the dark lord Sauron, who are led by a bad dude named Agandaur. Since Agandaur is Sauron’s right hand man fighting the bad fight in the north, your goal is to smash him and draw Sauron’s attention away from the south, where the Fellowship of the Ring are making their way into enemy territory.
The game is played in the third person perspective and while you can only play as one of the three characters at a time, you get opportunities to switch which character you’re playing between game chapters. Really though, you should probably stick with one character per playthrough because the game will auto assign the stats and skills of the characters you aren’t using when they level up, and you won’t get much opportunity to customize if you keep switching around. Unlike the Dragon Age games, you don’t control the whole team, just the guy you’re playing. Also, you’re controlling all your character’s attacks as well, not just designating a target.
Like many hack and slash action RPG’s you run into a lot of loot and equipment in the game. You pretty much have as many equipment slots as Diablo 2, but most of the gear you find is “non-magical” and can be easily compared to similar pieces. This means there isn’t much in the way of randomly generated loot stats, and you don’t need to spend much time grinding for items. In fact, you probably shouldn’t even buy weapons from the vendors because chances are you’ll just find something better in about 10 minutes.
Pros:
+Co-op gameplay available so you can go through the single player campaign with a friend or two. Each character has a unique “secret finding” skill that can only be used when a human is controlling the character (in single player, you only find secrets that your character can “see”) so if you have a full team of human players you can find all the secrets in a level. Also, bear in mind that like many squad based games, you can revive your allies if they’re knocked out. So you don’t need to spend too many healing potions if you know your buddy can just bring you back to life at full health.
+Decent story that takes you all over Middle Earth (well, a lot of it) and involves some of the characters from the Lord of the Rings books/movies. Why don’t the eagles just fly everyone everywhere? Play the game and find out!
Cons:
-This is the big one. If you have an AMD video card like I do (Radeon 7850) you will find the game has extremely poor frame rate at many places. I was unable to finish because at the last chapter, the game slowed to a crawl and would crash out repeatedly at the same place. Searching online, this seems to be a problem for a lot of people. My friend has an nVidia GPU and didn’t have this issue.
-The “critical hit” system of the game can be fun sometimes but after a while it gets really repetitive. You built up power by continuously hitting a single enemy uninterrupted and eventually you can use a power attack with a chance of instantly killing them. Problem is, this means it takes like 2 minutes to kill many of the more powerful enemies, especially near the end of the game. Also, you only hit one enemy at a time no matter how wide your swings look, so attacking large groups of bad guys is really annoying (the little ankle-biters keep interrupting your combos against the big guys).
-Despite how linear the game plays, it’s still possible to miss side quests because many of the quest items are randomly dropped. Cleared the whole area and didn’t find the special quest rock? Too bad for you, play through it again.
-You can’t see the enemy’s life (except for bosses) and most bad guys seem to have a ton of life. This is probably intentional to force players to use the critical hit system more, but it means every fight seems artificially prolonged. Should it really take 50 hits to kill an orc?
Overall, the game is fun (when it’s working) if you enjoy hack and slash and want to dive once again into Lord of the Rings lore, but there’s a lot of room for improvement. The fact that there are 3 playable character classes is reason for replay, but from what I’m told they’re mostly the same. If this game is in your backlog you should push it back in favor of something better, but it’s worth playing eventually: IF you have an nVidia graphics card. The game’s developers have abandoned the project so the crashing/low frame rate issues will not be fixed. The 90% of the game that I got to experience was sort of fun.

A really fun game to waste time on. However theres not much indept tactics during a battle. There's basic strategy, choosing how to move your fleet and ships around, but during actual combat it basically comes down to how many commaning ships and titans you have. Theres almost no line of defense as an enemy fleet can warp to your planet then just rush to warp to your next planet before your ships even get to them. Theres a mode where if you lose your capital you lose the game, it mostly involved how many turrets i can put around the thing and actually being able to leave it alone.
Strategy games need to have two things during combat- strategic fighting and tactical fighting.
Strategic involves placement of buildings, moving fleets to critical locations, and being able to interact with the enviremont to decide your decisions. At this rate it doesn't matter where anything is because theres really no way of defending it unless you wrap your planet with turrets, the enviremont is basically point to point and doesn't have much change.
Strategy gets a 5/10 for me.
Tactical involves micro management. You have unit of army fighting against the other fleet. You should have multiple amounts of tactics to choose from, different angles to come at, just dozens of ways of approaching an enemy to create endless battle tactics. In this its quantity over quality, and based on how many titans, commander ships, and frigates you can squeeze together. Every time i want to micromanage the ship stops outputing damage and takes a while to move as the enemy is still shooting you. This is common because it makes sense- but then what. I've moved my ship but it didn't do any good, it doesn't accomplish anything other then, "oh look i moved it." The only tactic that really works is just put the fleet in let them auto target the enemy- if I try doing anything else there's not much of a bother. I even tried pinceriing or moving my ships around the fleet- it doesn't stop them from retreating or does more flank damage. I would give tactical a 2/10.
I won't go into the tech tree, pirate buying, or even the market (because no matter what or how long you wait the market will always be expensive). That stuff is basic research and buy. The economy handling is rudimentary (like all games).
Really I've seen nothing special from this game. It's move army, fight other army, and hope you have better tech and more troops than they do.
Despite the crap I've been giving it- the graphics and art design are legit. I hooked my pc to a HDMI cable to my flat screen TV, put the game in theater mode, and watched a massive battle. It's like seeing that space battle scene in Ender's Game towards the end. 10/10.
My overall quote on this is probably a 6/10. The graphics really saves it, and I still enjoy the game- even though it'll get boring and repitive after an hour. If I were to buy it again I probably would, but I don't see myself playing it for long periods of time. It's that one game you use to video the scenes or play if you run out of other games to play.
Hope this helped to anyone bothering reading it and considering buying the game.
