Over 450 hours. That's how much time I have on Civilization V. So, needless to say: I'm a big fan of the series, especially the predecessor to Beyond Earth. That said, I'm still not fatigued by the game, and I still can go back to Civ V and have a lot of fun on it. So, when Beyond Earth came out I was very excited to see what they'd do now that they're changing the setting to the future rather than the past and present.
I'm going to be blunt: this is a massive letdown. This game is Civilization V if you sucked out all of its soul. This game has absolutely no personality, you don't get any of the old Ghandi and his nukes, or the backstabbing of Napoleon, or the wonder-stealing of Ramses. I've clocked up a good few hours on this game, and the leaders from this game are still yet to show any personality or do anything even remotely memorable.
This is a big problem, as in Civ V: part of what made it fun was the fact that each Civilization had a unique AI, as well as unique abilities. The abilities of those Civilizations would mean that every game would feel different, not only based on the Civilization that you choose: but the AI you're pitted against, your starting location, and sometimes just plain luck would play huge a part in how the game plays out. In Civilization V, each Civilization got its own unique ability, unit, and/or building. But, in Beyond Earth, when you're choosing your Civ, you get one stat boost, and then you pick three more bonuses. These bonuses lack any depth, it's stuff like "Get a free worker" or "Reveal minerals on the map" or "+2 culture for every city", and it's all just either boring stat bonuses or getting certain abilities or units a little bit early. In Civ V, you would get things that no other Civilization gets, and you could build a strategy around that. For example, the fact that Venice can buy City-States makes them a truly unique civ to play, and offers a unique experience. Beyond Earth lacks that depth and personality, and it really feels like hardly any real effort went into its design. The bonuses that these new Civilizations get are more akin to the bonuses you'd get from religion in Civ V. It's nice that they're there, but they're hardly game-changing. I'd also like to point out that Civilization V has a total of 43 civilizations, whereas Beyond Earth has only 8. You'd expect that those 8 would be really detailed this time, given that they have considerably less things to work on but: no. They feel like the type of Civilization someone would make if they'd just started modding Civilization V.
Also, the bonuses that you get from wonders are not very impressive. It's actually kind of hard to tell what is an isn't a wonder when looking at the technology tree, and their bonuses are so lacklustre you could easily mistake them for a standard building. On top of this, there are only 4 culture trees in this game, as opposed to the 13 that were in Civ V, and again: these trees are very boring and they offer things like "+2 production when healthy" and just really boring thoughtless things like that.
The graphics in this game are ugly, frankly. The actual models look great, better than Civilization V, in fact. But, the UI is absolutely hideous. It uses blue: exclusively. This just adds to the lack of personality here, and it also kind of makes it hard to understand what's going on on the minimap. I played as Franco-Iberia in my first game, and their territory on the map is represented with a pale blue. This made it so that on the mini-map, my territory was light blue, land was a darker blue, and the sea was an even darker blue. It was kind of confusing to look at, and it made the landmasses (as well as my land) look highly amorphous. On top of that, it looked genuinely ugly. The game's UI is like an Apple store: just a cold colourless environment. Well, colourless apart from blue.
Also, every victory type is the technology victory from Civ V. I mean, the exact same. No matter what Civilization you play as, no matter what you do, you are always doing it on behalf of advancing your technology. True, you can declare war and kill everyone, but whether or not you win is entirely based on who has the best technology: nothing else. There are a total of five victory types, but 4 of them are based on reaching the end of a technology tree. This is incredibly dull, because again, in Civilization V, you'd need different strategies to get different victory types. I could use the same strategy for every victory type in Beyond Earth. Why was there no cultural or diplomatic victory? Nope, all of the victory types in this game rely on you reaching the end of the technology tree that you've chosen.
The aliens are better than the barbarians from Civilization V, but only by a bit. They're still a massive nuisance, but there are ways to avoid them, and even use them to your advantage. For example, I built a city on a one-tile-island very close to an alien nest in the sea, and I managed to use the aliens as a defence. But, they're still mostly a nuisance, so it's not a massive improvement. They also feel kind of unfinished, as a lot of buildings seem to make it sound as though you can tame the aliens and turn them to your side, but you really can't: they will always be either hostile or neutral.
Another good feature is that the planets now have three different types of landscapes: terrain, fungal, and arid. They kind of shake up the atmosphere a bit, and it gives the illusion of variation quite well, which is a good thing. I'm unsure if they effect the resources or actual tile types, but it's quite nice playing on them (except fungal which is a nightmare because it is YET MORE BLUE).
Just going back to the factions for a second, I'd just like to say that I highly object to there being no British civilization. In Civilization V I very much enjoyed playing as England and the Celts simply because I'm British and it's kind of cool to build places that you're very familiar with. Do Firaxis really believe that their European fanbase is entirely composed of French and Spanish people? There are more countries that have been completely excluded but it would take me far too long to list them all. In Civ V, they at least gave each country some kind of representation or another. For example, Italy wasn't in the game, but they instead included Rome and Venice, so they still had some representation in the game.
It's not a terrible game, but it just doesn't have the personality or replayability of the earlier Civ games. Some of the changes it makes are for the better, like the removal of barbarians in favour of aliens, and the ability to choose to start with a worker rather than a warrior. But, the idea of letting the players create their own civilizations has just made the game feel very thoughtless and rushed.
Pick it up only if you've somehow exhausted Civilization V and it is at a significantly reduced price.

Imagine if "cover-based shooting game" didn't have a stigma of "rehashed terrible bog game play"?
"Not a Hero" is a frenzied paced cover-based sidescroller with very simple core mechanics that are modified by situation, making it easy to learn but ramps up the difficulty by throwing a lot of situations at you simutanelously.
It also has excellent replay value - each member of the cast plays vastly different and will require a different strategy for every stage.  Even characters who are similar will have a key difference that changes the experience entirely, such as an ability that replaces using special weapons.
On top of the unique characters, each stage had 3 special challenges that aren't required to unlock the next stage but are required to see the true ending of the game.
The game itself is challenging without ever being unfair.  There are random power-ups that can make a stage much easier but your success is far more skill based than luck based, as no matter how good the power-up you find is, it won't last long and it won't replace ability.  The difficulty scaling is beatiful, from a breeze in the first few stages to brutally hard at the finale, but the pacing matches your skill -- if you're doing very well no stage will last long and it goes well within the madcap world the game presents.
Finally, its characters rival Team Fortress 2 in terms of being unique and colourful and their banter is spot on as they scream and swear in unique ways when things go wrong and have different ways of expressing their satisfaction when things go right.
This is a game that I'd love to see more of and I'd automatically snap up a sequel.

If you missed out on the magic of Rapture back in 2007 there is no better time to jump in. Despite the little bugs, a crash or lack of options in the current version, the additional features make up for the shortcomings, which should be patched in due time. BioShock Remastered is my third time in Rapture and the first time the game opened itself up to me. While the world was always immersive, lousy physics aside, I found the gameplay clunky and repetitive. As an immersive world, Rapture is a joy to explore though, so I was not surprised that this time I had missed only one Audio Diary.
BioShock now has achievements. Thankee-sai! That wasn't the case back in 2007, which was a different time, obviously. As someone who likes achievements in my single player games, they are often the best way to learn about every aspect of a game on your journey to a 100% and this was no different. The Research Camera, for example, was something I didn't fully understand at the time or the various tonics with their bonuses, but now I realize they're an ally for harder difficulty levels. I've only ever played it on Medium.
I haven't tried the Challenge Rooms yet, but one thing I enjoyed immensely and not found in the original, are the developer commentary film reels scattered throughout the game. The video commentary, hosted by Geoff Keighley, gave me a newfound respect for BioShock and what that small team had pulled off almost 10 years ago. BioShock owes so much to its voice acting talent, which I guess is a passive aggressive way of saying the writing wasn't all that compelling, but that's only partly true for me. Another thing that holds back the writing in this case are outdated character models. I mostly attribute the success of the writing to bringing the world to life, than to its twists and turns and conclusion. I can tell you the names of the main characters, but none of them have cemented their presence over the years.
BioShock is an amalgam of genres and with successful results, something I can finally agree with being a modern classic. I often envy the connection fans have with certain games, games I don't click with at all, like F.E.A.R., Far Cry or Crysis, but if BioShock Remastered has taught me anything, it's worth giving a game another shot, especially when so much effort has gone into bringing a game world to life. An art style not found in many games and ultimately it's a period piece with the appropriate music and use of language and all in the form of an FPS. That is rare and something I always respected about BioShock. The terrible physics are still there, but at least it doesn't look as plastic anymore, once the textures have popped into place. I hope a grumpy "BioShock is meh" person is reading this, cos here's to you having a good time.

I recommend this to people who get addicted to trying to puzzle their way through challenging pizelated violent scenarios. You know, Hotline Miami (which I'm sure pops up in these reviews a lot). It's got some fun voice acting, music, visuals and the gameplay is pretty solid, too. But often I couldn't tell if it wanted me to play fast or cautious. Neither seemed to 'fit', whereas a game that supports both options, I'd want both to feel right. When found a playstyle that worked, it was the one that boiled all the game's nuance to sliding at people and doing a ground takedown over and over again with the fastest guy. Now I feel like i'm playing the game right but I'm having a lot less fun. I am racking up all the objectives, though.
The controls can bugger off. We have a million buttons on any modern controller, why is it the same button to run at an enemy AND jump into cover? These are opposite actions, and the game often confuses the two. Same goes for ground takedowns and just regular firing. It's infuriating in the wrong ways most of the time. When it's infuriating in the right ways is when it really shines, and that happens just often enough. Completing a level with all objectives is often rewarded, and the flow of levels seems pretty well thought out, too. I wish it would use these objectives to encourage changes in playstyle, but sticking to the fast guy is usually the way to go, once you have him.
Also the writing is pants. They seem to have a wonderful handle on joke structure but not joke content. It's just random crap they thought up and giggled at, when they could have sat down for 10 more minutes and made something way funnier if they just put time and thought into it. and they even have art accompanying some of these jokes, which makes it seem even worse. If you're having someone animate a joke, put the effort into making it worth animating. There were times when jokes really landed, at least on a basic level, but it wasn't frequent. And their use of dark humour seemed unearned and uncomfortable. "Look, we beat this guy to death" isn't a joke. It's weak. The writing is what bothers me the most about this game.
Anyway, this has been a fairly negative review, but it's far from a bad game. Just the ways it needs improvement seem basic, like they just needed to put more thought into it or another pair of eyes on it during production. It's a good game. I just really wish it could have been great.

Not A Hero is an interesting game involving fever pitch combat mixed with nonsensical but on target humor where you do things that are fitting of the title.
Basically, run through identical buildings with different layouts, shoot lots of baddies, be awesome, die a lot. Simple.
Death comes fast (towards you and your foes) but most of the time the levels are short enough that a single death won't put you back too much. The longest of the 25 levels is about 4 or 5 minutes even if you're rushing through, and a lot of these happen towards the end of your heroic murderspree. Which is an aggrivating issue especially when you reach a point where some enemies can one hit kill you.
That said, the game is very well balanced. Each of the nine playable characters are unique and have enough quirks between them to justify playing starter characters even in later levels. Each level of the game highlights what our cast can do well whether it be attack enemies from both sides, move fast, execute silently, or more. Of course the later characters are more powerful, though they end up surrendering the use of powerup equipment in the process (which honestly isn't too big of a loss).
Not A Hero is a lot of fun to play from beginning to end, despite the aggrivation involving deaths. It's got some awesome varied voice acting too which helps with the constant dying thing. It is a twitch sidescolling shooter though so if you don't have the reflexes or the quick wit you best find something else as the game only gets faster. If you think you're up for the slaughter, then pick up this game whenever you feel like it - on sale or full retail. Hopefully there'll be a rad sequel.

I could not recommend this game less. I have developed a keen sense of loathing for Hollow Knight. I put in a good amount of time with it, and I wanted to enjoy it because the art is amazing and the level design is well done. But there are a number of game mechanics that skyrocket the difficulty into rogue-like territory, and I am NOT a fan of rogue-like games. About halfway through it starts to become ridiculously hard, tampered by the glaringly offensive play mechanics that the developers included to no doubt make the game more difficult then it needed to be. Let me explain.
First of all, save points are few and far between. They are almost never right before a major boss battle. I reached a point in the game that I simply could not surmount. As mentioned above, about halfway through the game the enemy difficulty increases at a ridiculous rate. Enemies begin to teleport all over the place and become very unpredictable, which in a pattern based game is beyond unfair. There is one particular boss fight which is quite far from a save point, and you encounter a number of difficult enemies along the way. Each time you die, you are sent all the way back to the save point and have to face ALL of these enemies once again before taking on the boss. I was rarely able to reach the boss with a full health bar, and during the battle it is almost impossible to heal due to the insane rate of speed and teleporting attacks that the boss assaults you with. All the developers had to do was to put the save point right before the boss battle and there would have been no issue. This is a simple mechanic which is made unnecessarily cruel and difficult.
On top of this, each time you die, you lose all of your currency, and are forced to go back to the point that you died and kill a shadow version of yourself to regain it. EVERY. TIME. YOU. DIE. While the concept is cool (and I suppose very rogue-like), what it means game-wise is that you are punished for exploring. See what looks like a cool area that you wanna check out? Turns out it's beyond your current abilities, which because the map system in the game is also busted (you have to purchase maps as well as the ability to even locate yourself on the current
, you never know what you're getting yourself into when exploring a new area, and then you die, are sent all the way back to a save point, and then have to go back to the super hard area with the over-powered enemies and hope you can avoid them long enough to find your shade and get back your loot. Terrible. Frustrating. Cruel.
It seems to me that apparently everyone on Steam who has showered this game with praise is a hardened gamer who eats rogue-like games for breakfast. That, sadly, is not me. I'm decent, and I love patterned based boss battles, but I'm just not that good. I wish I had known that there were so many rouge-like elements in the game before purchasing otherwise I would have never bothered wasting all this time and frustration. Other reviews mentioned the game being at times very challenging, but none that I read got into the rouge-like aspects (hence my emphasis on pointing them out in this review). I figured if I could handle Ori and the Blind Forest, which IMHO was INSANELY difficult--though it DOES respawn you right before all of the difficult areas in the game--then I'd be able to handle this game. Nope.
Personally, I think adding rouge-like elements to a Metroidvania style game is an awful idea. These games are supposed to encourage exploration and if done well, they balance the difficulty, gradually increase it over time, and don't allow you to progress into areas that are too difficult for you at that time. Hollow Knight does none of this. It throws in horrendous play mechanics to CONSTANTLY punish the player. Team Cherry, I hate you (though you do have some amazing artists).

I was not expecting much of this game ... well, I was pleasantly surprised :)
Sure, it's linear (invisible walls included) and certainly not the game of the century. But the story is interesting, mostly lore-friendly and plausible (so to speak :p), the graphics (though a bit dated) do their job, voice acting is fine, and combat is quite enjoyable (with some nice finish moves). Character customization is interesting too (3 different sets of a skills, and you can't unlock everything in a single playthrough so you'll have to make choices), side quests are well integrated with the main story and not too abundant (I think that's a plus in that case), and achievements flow pretty well (though you'll have to make a second playthrough to get them all, I think). Loot/gear is good too, but getting a full set of armor seems, if not impossible, quite tough.
I only played singleplayer, with a single character, there's a coop mod too (not tested). Your AI sidekicks do their job, most of the time. No bug that I saw, just a few strange checkpoints (for example, if you use fast travel back to a haven while in mission, you might have to start over certain fights when you come back).
To make it short, I enjoyed playing it, and if I did not have a hoard of other games to play :D, I think I'd make a second playthrough on higher difficulty (you keep your stats and skills when doing this). Good game, recommended.

First off, if you do not have a controller to play this game with, you're gonna have a bad time (it is in fact, a fighting game based of competitive super smash brother melee). If you do however, have a controller, love smash brothers, and fighting games in general, you're going to have a blast with this game!
The cast of characters bring some elements from popular characters in smash and combine them with their own unique elements in order to create a solid lineup. Each character offers a diverse range of abilities and playstyles that will keep you on your toes. This game also removes ledge grabbing, grabbing, and shielding in order to speed up gameplay while giving each character a counter used to stun enemies. Wall jumping and wave dashing are made easier to use so that anyone can pick up some of the more advanced methods of play easy. Also there is a larger emphasis on stage control in RoE due to the movesets of the various characters dirrectly affecting the enviornment, something you will thoroughly enjoy.

I was very disapointed by this due to the devs hyping storymode up so much, but nonetheless, you don't buy a fighting game for the campaign (unless that game is brawl) you buy it for the core gameplay. If you keep that in mind Rivals of Aether is worth every penny.
With brilliant retro stylized visuals, and a fantastic soundtrack, Rivals of Aether not only holds up as it's own fighting game when put against smash, but will likely become one of your all time favorite fighting games as a whole.

I didn't know what I was getting into when I decided to purchase this game. I simply bought it because it was on sale and my friend at work had been begging me to start playing it some time.
I must admit, I was reluctant -- after all, it's farming...
So, to start, the game is very inviting once you start it up. The opening sequence is high quality and the starting menu is easy enough to navigate and figure out. Once you start the game you can either follow the tutorial or get to work on your own.
The graphics are very pleasing and can be very detailed at times, from dirt on the tractors to small details like factory decals, nuts and bolts and system lights.
There are some physics in the game play which make driving tricky sometimes and you have to know how to distirbute the weight on your rig. There aren't many maps to choose from, but depending on your game style there are so many different ways to play!
As you progress you can start upgrading your equipment: tractors, harvesters, trucks, trailers, mowers, et cetera. Upgrading and getting new equipment allows you to play with each piece and gets your hands into so many different components and styles of gameplay. Whether walking from tree-to-tree with a chainsaw or pulling your semi-truck to your next delivery you can experience every step of simple farm industry life.
Like I said, I was reluctant, but this game is admitably one of my favorite guilty pleasures now. Whether planting a new crop, driving my tractor trailer, or shearing my sheep I always like to take a step back and admire the hard work I've done on my virtual farm and I appreciate the hard work and effort the company put into assembling such a fun and thorough game.
For anyone who enjoys a game where they can relax and walk away occassionally and enjoy a little micro-managing every once in a while, I strongly recommend this game!

Battlerite is a great arena brawler. Imagine LoL/DotA top down gameplay combined with WoW arenas. That's what Battlerite is. It's rather fast paced and most importantly, fun. Matches aren't 30 minutes of farm this farm that hope your other teammates aren't mouth breathers. Matches are a best of five rounds. Once the gate drops, you have two minutes until sudden death forcing a quicker gameplay. Instead of farming creep or reagents or anything of that nature you have "Battlerites" which are essentially upgraded skills.
The biggest downside to this game seems to be the league system (their competitive ladder). Platinum is oversaturated and for some reason the largest concentration of players though in any normal competitive game, that would never be the case. The league ladder ranks are from 8 to 1 (8 being the lowest) and in terms of worst to best you have Contender, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond, Champion, Grand Champion. Devs, if you read your reviews, people need to fill out your lower ranks, that's why you guys have them.
The game plays very smooth on my personal rig (4770k/1070SC/16GB RAM), load times are very fast. Overall a great game. I was lucky enough to get a beta key albeit on the last day of the beta and loved the game but did truly struggle with the $20 price tag, however the game was recently at ~$13 and for that price I think the game is whole heartedly worth it. After becoming wildly addicted to this game, I'd go back and pay $20 on launch if I could rewind time.

I have to go out on a limb here and say that this is actually one of the best FPS games I ever played, period.
Others may point out the deficiencies, but through the curious way I experienced this game it has ultimately assumed the status of an absolute classic in my eyes.
That experience I mention is this: On my first ever playthrough, my rig was such that the game crashed as soon as I entered the final act - all that water and all those explosions, you dig? - and so I never actually knew that it was the final act. In my mind the game stretched on into inifinity - and what an infinity it was.
The game goes through three distinct phases, each more jaw-droppingly perfect than the last. At first, one is navigating a jungly-coated tropical island world, evading - or annihilating, though this was never as fun for me - conventional, dastardly Korean forces in a manner strongly remeniscent of the original Far Cry (for me at least, Far Cry didn't really have any stealth component, though i did everything i could to force it to play like a stealth shooter nonetheless) In the second phase, all-out conflict has broken out and, while you can continue to play as a phantom if you wish, the stakes and scale soar upwards into 'epic' territory. In the third phase, you discover a vast and fantastic secret lurking within the island, exploring this secret in a state of permawonder, before re-emerging into a drastically altered form of the second phase, to see out the game.
My initial experience was cut short most of the way through the third phase, so in my mind it was, as I've said, neverending, and by jebus that neverending game was FPS fantasy made reality. It really is just an awesome game.
Quite apart form the graphics, which are to this day superior to almost any other offering of comprable setting (visually if not technolgically, though the tech is still close), the gameplay is tight and perfectly polished. This is the kind of game that, while vaguely linear, allows a player to turn 100m of linear progression into around 1km of side-track meandering and sneaking more or less throughout the entire experience. One can craft one's own adventure here, as surely as any of those gimmicky kids books from the '90s, and just as everyone had envisioned in their wildest dreams back then this adventure is lush, endless and full of wonders more wonderous than the last.
The gameplay is consistent and with the possible exception of the final moments of the second phase, in which combat is more or less forced on you and the game literally ejects any background action in an effort - only marginally succesful - to turn your final stage into some kind of arena, it is consistently entertaining.
Why should you buy this game? Because your computer may very well finally be able to run it in something approaching max settings, because it is one of the best FPS experiences you will ever play, and because it is streets, miles ahead of any other
game released in the years before or the years after.

Score: 5/10
Summary: I don’t want to give the impression that I completely hated Gat Out of Hell. Sure, the “story,” which I have put in quotation marks more than once now, only lasts a meager four hours playing at a casual pace, taking time to distract yourself with collecting things, the game is repetitive and easy, there’s no customization, I have zero desire to go back and get the last thirty to forty percent completion, and, despite letting you choose your own ending, you get an anticlimactic ten second clip with one more joke that’s completely unrelated to the ending you chose, the game isn’t completely terrible. It just isn’t substantial enough to really feel that it warranted its own release. I’m not even sure it could have been justified as DLC. Saints Row story DLC is traditionally short but still has a real, full-fledged story behind it. The Loyalty missions in the previous game gave insight into the characters and served a real purpose. You don’t get any of that here. The premise was a promising one but the result is just so half-baked that I can’t really recommend it at the current price. If you got in on the GameStop pricing error, and you’re a Saints Row fan already, you will probably get your money’s worth. I can’t say that many others will, though.

Bertram and his Peruvian cyclops manservant, Gavin, are back to catch the nefarious Geoff the Murderer in the second installment of the Bertram Fiddle Adventuring series. The game is made with lots of love and it shows. It's full of British comedy, wacky characters, and puns, oh the puns!
The Basics:
The game has a point and click interface with inventory, where items can be combined. The game is saved automatically with no manual save slots. You can play as Bertram (for most of the game) as well as control Gavin for heavy lifting tasks or on solo expeditions. You do not need to play episode 1 to play episode 2, but the jokes will make more sense (and why not?). The first episode can be finished within 2 hours, but this game is considerably longer and offers around 6-9 hours of gameplay with more things to do.
The Pros:
The comedy is deadpan and great. It is the main reason to play this game. There is more variety in the puzzles offered- inventory based, number combination, word plays, etc.- than the first game, with no timed puzzles!!! The story is much less linear than the first game too. And there are a lot of dirty jokes (OK for kids, the zingers will fly over their heads).
The Cons:
Some of the puzzle solutions are not intuitive (there is a very strange way to make a paint brush and red paint), but not brain burningly so. The game could benefit from a help feature besides Gavin sometimes saying "hinty" things regarding puzzles. The sound volume was not consistent in the version I played, and there were quite a few glitches and bugs in the graphics- but this was within the first week of release.
Overall, I highly recommend this game if you enjoy irreverent humor and mad-cap adventuring.

The port - is it good enough to play happily (now) ? - Certainly.
Is it perfect? - Absolutely not.
I've just about finished a fairly comprehensive playthrough (after doing everthing several years ago in the PS3 version) running at 4k on a 980Ti and i7 6700k and after 83 hours ingame, have experienced a single CTD.
Yes there was the occasional FPS low, it would dip now and again to the 30s, but for the most part spent its time happily sitting at 60.
Did the occasional frame rate low detract from the game? Not at all.
Whilst the original port was somewhat shoddy, it has been hugely improved and is a very pleasant experience.
Final Fantasy XIII is a curious game. For the first 30+ hours, you are railroaded along with minimal input, occasional fights (auto attack) and a LOT of FMV.
The storyline is a little confusing and even non-sensical (I honestly think its the absolute worst FF storyline, ever, having played everything since 3) but I love the character development.
Forget the l'Cie, forget the Fal'Cie, forget the never ending fight between Cocoon and Gran Pulse, listen to Lightning, Vanille, Fang, Sazh, even Snow and Hope as they grow and realise that the world is a much bigger place than they thought it was and that their own problems are really quite petty in the grand scheme.
Auto Attack really does kill off the majority of fighting, but the paradigm system shines when the going gets tough, being able to switch in healers, buffers and debuffers and swap melee / ranged classes as required was a masterstroke of design, its the single biggest inovation in the FF franchise in a long time, so much so I found the 6 variation limit too... limiting.
The side quests (Ci'eth Stone missions and Choco treasure hunting) do offer some variation, but even when on Gran Pulse, there is quite limited freedom and whilst quite large, there are too many tunnels.
Finishing the game isnt terribly hard, but if you want to level your main teams weapons up, finish the Ci'eth Stones / Titan Missions, then you are going to have to farm a fair bit as you are fairly starved for gil unless you focus on earning it.
Overall, a good port of a somewhat different Final Fantasy game that has garnered a lot of love and hate over the years.

If you missed out on the magic of Rapture back in 2007 there is no better time to jump in. Despite the little bugs, a crash or lack of options in the current version, the additional features make up for the shortcomings, which should be patched in due time. BioShock Remastered is my third time in Rapture and the first time the game opened itself up to me. While the world was always immersive, lousy physics aside, I found the gameplay clunky and repetitive. As an immersive world, Rapture is a joy to explore though, so I was not surprised that this time I had missed only one Audio Diary.
BioShock now has achievements. Thankee-sai! That wasn't the case back in 2007, which was a different time, obviously. As someone who likes achievements in my single player games, they are often the best way to learn about every aspect of a game on your journey to a 100% and this was no different. The Research Camera, for example, was something I didn't fully understand at the time or the various tonics with their bonuses, but now I realize they're an ally for harder difficulty levels. I've only ever played it on Medium.
I haven't tried the Challenge Rooms yet, but one thing I enjoyed immensely and not found in the original, are the developer commentary film reels scattered throughout the game. The video commentary, hosted by Geoff Keighley, gave me a newfound respect for BioShock and what that small team had pulled off almost 10 years ago. BioShock owes so much to its voice acting talent, which I guess is a passive aggressive way of saying the writing wasn't all that compelling, but that's only partly true for me. Another thing that holds back the writing in this case are outdated character models. I mostly attribute the success of the writing to bringing the world to life, than to its twists and turns and conclusion. I can tell you the names of the main characters, but none of them have cemented their presence over the years.
BioShock is an amalgam of genres and with successful results, something I can finally agree with being a modern classic. I often envy the connection fans have with certain games, games I don't click with at all, like F.E.A.R., Far Cry or Crysis, but if BioShock Remastered has taught me anything, it's worth giving a game another shot, especially when so much effort has gone into bringing a game world to life. An art style not found in many games and ultimately it's a period piece with the appropriate music and use of language and all in the form of an FPS. That is rare and something I always respected about BioShock. The terrible physics are still there, but at least it doesn't look as plastic anymore, once the textures have popped into place. I hope a grumpy "BioShock is meh" person is reading this, cos here's to you having a good time.

This game is a must play if you play league of legends.
Battlerite is actually a Moba, fitting the literal definition of the term, in which players battle it out with avatars in a battle arena.
However the actual game is very different to a Moba or Dotaclone game and is more like an original blend of a fighting game with a top down rts game.
The basic mechanics should be familiar to league players, however your hero in this game is maneuvered using WASD and you press left mouse button to launch a skillshot autoattack.
There is no laning phase and teammates cannot ruin a game as easily. The entire game is basically a bo5 teamfight, except instead of the mindless skillshot spam and baiting that happens in league of legends, the skillshot duels in this game require you to land and combo your abilities if you want to have a chance at winning.
They also replace the surrender button with a pause button instead, and got rid of pesky runes. Stunlock studios are doing all the right things and if you don't want to get the game now in early access wait a bit for the f2p and then start playing for free. The grind for new heroes isn't as big in this game as league, so it's much easier to catch up!

Update: I harshed on the game pretty hard, but I also stuck it out and decided to update my review, as well as change my negative to a positive. Let's go!
I really like the new changes a lot. The new UI will certainly have some hate, but I like the direction it brings in organization. It could probably use some tweaks, but I think it will make more sense in the long run. The aesthetic is something that could bother some, but art style isn't something that concerns me as much, though I probably prefer the old one slightly.
I really love the new game mode, Battlegrounds. This feels like a great balance between traditional MOBAs that have tedious skills like last hitting, while having objectives that give you focus besides completely relying on defeating your opponent in direct combat. The nice thing about it, minions won't complete objectives for/against you at all. It's completely dependent on player action still. I hope the game adds a ranked mode for this soon.
Loadouts was a huge bonus for this game. Finishing a match in 3 rounds won't effect the ability to customize your character anymore. You get to have all of the Battlerites you choose for the entirety of every match and you can build multiple loadouts to customize your play based on the team you face. It's a great change of pace. I do want the Loadout UI to change a bit though. In the character select, there are pages of tiles you have to scroll through to select your Battlerites, but in a match, they are all in one screen organized by type and smaller icons. I'd like that to be the way they appear since it's easier to see them all.
Matchmaking is still an issue. After several rounds of Battlegrounds, every match was a complete blowout, whether winning or losing. That takes some fun out of the matches. Also, I really want the days of getting matched with a Plat 1 player, who is trying Jade for the first time, to end. I'd like to see personal rating tied to individual champions. I like being a plat Ruh Kaan player, but I need to work on my Jumong skills. It would be nice to be Bronze or Silver rated with him while I work my skills up. My ranked matches went better, but I could've just gotten lucky as well.
Overall, I highly recommend you give this game a try when it goes FTP. It has quite a bit shorter match times than other PvP games which is great if you can't play as long/often as others. I work 50 hrs a week, yet can comfortably reach a plat rating in a season. It's a fun time!
Old review: "Well, this game completely sucks now. The new matchmaking was "SUPPOSED" to more evenly match things but it's just gotten worse. Raigon is also throwing the matchmaking off. Everyone is playing him but only a few know that you can't just charge in every fight. Somehow, they still get in the gold/plat ranks. Sucks to be a support.
Sadly, it would be really easy to fix too if they would just put your ranking on a per champion basis. Then, you know you wouldn't be playing with a plat who decided to try ashka for the first time and do it in ranked instead of casual. I enjoyed the game at first because the matchups on a whole felt better, but now it's just super frustrating and not worth the price, hardly worth being free.
(On a side note, per champion rating would fix a lot of competitive games in all likelyhood. I'll update if things start looking up again.)"

I have beat the game and put in over 100 hours of active playing (I have a padded time in steam because of leaving the game on while doing other things) so I think I can give this a fair assessment.
This was a bit of a let-down.
The rich world and combat system had amazing potential, which fell woefully short on execution.
Lets start with the world; you are given this great mystery of the remnants and trying to find an answer to their existence, but we are given a short and terrible story to progress through the game with. Towns and surrounding areas are all but-nonexistant because of the way they designed the maps to be enclosed and small. We are given a protagonist who is an utter idiot, and we are supposed to believe all these hyper-competent leaders want to follow this stupid kid who does nothing but mess up and make stupid on-the-fly decisions? The antagonist had potential. in the first disc whenever he shows up he is a pure badass, but then he keeps showing up randomly and leaves randomly. They were stretching it, it seems they just wanted him to do something badass and then disappear again, even though him being at that place and his subsequent actions make no sense. The voice acting is far below par, they have decent VAs but it seems the direction they were given was poor.
The worst of it is the character animations during conversations and cutscenes. I read they had motion capture work done, and it seems ALL of it went into the combat animations which were amazing, but cutscene and conversation animations are so bad it is jarring, and it took me right out of what was happening. This is saying something, I have a high tolerance for mediocre character animation, this game crossed a line somewhere.
Now the combat... Oh the combat, how you had the potential to be a JRPG game changer. "Lets take something tactical and add randomness and take away most of the player control, that would be brilliant!" No SquareEnix, no, stop it, stop... it... stop it. Side tangent; has noone in this world heard of ranged weapons? Are bows and crossbows too complex of an idea, do they have to cast most of their magic in melee range? The combat system of unions and leaders was an amazing idea, but once you get to the actual combat, it becomes garbage. I have 60+ AP to spend, why are all the actions available under 16? The best you can do is remove options you dont want showing up to increase the chance of getting something good, which doesn't work enough to not be very frustrating.
All of your unions will want to bunch up when fighting enemies, only way to stop this is to make them stay back. But as I said, there is a distinct lack of ranged options. Most of the magic in this game does NOT have a ranged option, not even healing. The magic that DOES have a ranged option will greatly limit what that union can do that turn, and the best magic is ALL melee range. Worst of all, you can not then control your union positioning, you can spread out these tightly packed unions all attacking the same thing, which leaves rare monsters and bosses with wide area AoE attacks to really really really suck.
So lets talk about what I did actually like about the game, the things that kept me interested enough to keep playing so long -- All the side things in the game. Hunting down rare monsters, getting my party members stronger, finding new unique leaders, toying with formations and union composition (especially for the really difficult opponents.)
The main quest line might suck, but all the side things to do in this game are what provide content worth experiencing. I absolutely love the SaGa system of character progression, no more grinding out levels to overpower your opponent, you have to be smarter about how you approach bosses. This can be exploited of course, no leveling system is perfect, but for your first play through, you are unlikely to manipulate the system. There is another downside - where SaGa frontier games allow you to build a suitable party early, the unique leaders in Last Remnant are spread out. So, leaders you get early will be a lot stronger than ones you get later, they did not scale recruits to your Battle Rank (your level as it were) they merely gave them starting stats which they think is sufficient for that point in the game.
Hunting down rare monsters and crafting materials... at points frustrating, very frustrating, but that just makes the pay off of getting them all the sweeter. Could have been handled better, sometimes the RNG really kicks you in the mouth.
I can not honestly recommend this game, what it does well, others do it better so you are better off with those. I was strangely compelled to keep playing to the end, but too much was not enjoyable. I will not be coming back to this game at a later time like the vast majority of my other games, I will not feel like playing this game again, it will collect dust in my steam library. Best I can say is that I really got my money's worth, as I bought it during a steam sale.

Though everyone recognizes Crysis as a game that taxes the most impressive spec'd computers, few speak of how great the game is. This is a shame as Crysis is still one of my favorite FPS's of all time, it's an open sandbox with a variety of ways to approach your objective. The physics are a blast to play with, pick up a dumpster and hurl it at an enemy, lure enemies into a building and then literally punch the roof out on top of them. The game has a great campaign with a well paced plot the only notable problem with the game would be the final chapter which plays nothing like the initial campaign.
Enemies are smart and will hunt down your last known area, they can call for reinforcements with flares, and will generally outsmart you if you stay put too long.
The game was simply ahead of its time which is why even today most rigs can't play it maxed at 60 fps, but my point is this game is worth a playthrough even if you have to lower your settings to play well.
I'd give it an 8.5/10 with the only negative notes being the final chapters, poor optimization, and occasional glitches.

You see I've been following the game for an eon essentially so you'd assume I'd be in love with the crisp pixel smash bros game with cool features that make it unique in it's own right to the genre.
However with the more recent updates leading up to the release it seems as if they took drastic turns to create a game too unlike itself. In it's infancy it used to be very melee-esqe which of course was the main wow factor the game had going for it, large amounts of tech skill a skill ceiling that continues to grow higher with each piece of tech that was found. It was at first a more calculated melee, punishes were very crazy and one mess up would cause you to lose a stock if the opponent was good enough. With the lack of shields and the inclusion of parrying the game had less campy play especially with ledges being entirely removed and recovery options based around such fact but they went a bit overboard on how aggro the mentality behind the game.
Newer characters came out to freshen up the game each with their unique gimmicks that promoted vast playstyles per character. As they balanced out the older characters they still felt outdated and not worth playing (save Wrastor, ♥♥♥♥ is he good still) some character's recovery options started to feel almost unstoppable when Etalus came by, the combo game on Maypul and Absa became a bit too insane and the originals mostly sat on the top shelf collecting dust so the game has become a boring heap of what it used to be.
On a side note the servers have a convinient feature in which you can set regions to yourself so others can expect to have a great connection if in the same region however the servers are a bit odd in that they sometimes flat out are garbage beyond belief or people in your region are still showing with 200 ping in a game that relies on the push of a button to finish off a stock.
The game has become a lot worse over time, and don't let my time played I've easily played over 500 hours offline with friends or at events and have slowly been realizing this game was actually fun to play during the middle of the beta stage before all the final changes (up to this point as they are still updating the game for those interested still!). Now you sit around for about 15 minutes to play against the same 1X people who play daily who even if both parties are hooked up to hardwire connection will lag slightly causing the game to lose playability.
I loved this game and I'll say I still do but it's nothing to look forward to anymore unless you're really looking into a game you can play locally with friends or at gaming venues. The online aspect has become a cesspool of issues sadly and since that's a big portion of the gameplay itself, you might want to buy another game with the $15 you have.

A fun FPS with a twist. You play as a futuristic Super-soldier with the ability to turn invisible or turn your Armor on to resist bullets.
This game is semi-open world and gives you the option for multiple ways to take down your enemies. The combat is fun and engaging, and definitely keeps you on your toes. You can only carry a handful of weapons at a time, you constantly need to monitor your suit's energy usage, and you never know when there's a hidden sniper waiting in a tree for you.
The game allows you to roll with your own playstyle if you prefer to run in with Armor and a shotgun or stealth through the bushes with a long range rifle. The weapons are all responsive and unique, and customizable to suit yourself. I found myself struggling to decide which ones I wanted to keep with me.
The environment is beautiful, the entire island is rich and looks like they put a lot of effort into it. The areas where you make enemy contact are designed for fun firefights with lots of movement and interaction with the environment--especially when some of it is destructible.
However, the game is a bit repetitive and there are only like 2 boss fights, so a lot of your time is spent running around the island and dealing with more normal enemies, with a few breaks in the monotony. Also about 2/3 of the way through the game, the focus is shifted more towards fighting aliens instead of the human enemies, which changes the gameplay a little bit.
Still, it was a fun adventure, a good FPS, and interesting story.

Crysis was a very good game and the first in a great series developed by Crytek and published by Electronic Arts in 2007. Crysis is a science-fiction first person shooter. You, the player, play as Nomad, an exceptional and strong-willed character determined to fight to survive. The game is primarily set on a North-Korean controlled island where they are attempting to uncover the mystery of a potential grand discovery. Nomad and his nano-suited military team mates and the United States army intervene, however the reveal of a greater power, named the Ceph, strongly influences and alters the story.
This campaign is excellent. The campaign is a great example of a story that starts slow, but builds to a climax. The setting of being on one island suggests a limited campaign, however, the great areas of on the island and in the island create a nice variety of missions. I adore the fluidity and transition between missions within the campaign. For instance, you complete a mission and run to the extraction point - instead of the game taking you to a loading screen, it immediately starts the next mission, which is a massive positive. The only issue I encountered with the campaign is the mild relevance of the side missions. Nomad would have to gain intel from a North Korean camp, and while it adds some further dialogue in the story, it is not substantial. Also, it is really a standalone player game as your squad-members do not assist you in missions and are very useless.
Gameplay is your standard first person shooter gameplay, The gameplay is fluid and solid. There is nothing more to elaborate on regarding shooting and cover. Driving is a nice feature but clunky as the vehicle is very sensitive to player controls. The issues I encountered within the gameplay section is the lack of ammo for an American gun and the very small variety of overall guns in the game. I had to rely on a North Korean assault rifle because there was no ammo to be found for my American Scar. There are some minor bugs such as the red dot on a red dot sight not appearing and the insane amount of bullets required to kill an armoured North Korean enemy. To kill an enemy would regularly take 75% of a magazine. To kill an Alien would take a larger amount of ammo, which is understandable as they are strong aliens, but for humans, that is very odd. The main disturbance regarding gameplay is the sheer stupidty of AI. Some enemies would run in circles while ally team mates would be useless in completing objectives, as stated prior.
The graphics are incredible for a game developed in 2007. Crytek is known as a high-quality graphical company and they really emphasised that in Crysis. While the recommended settings were a Nvidia GT 8800, I could not play at ultra settings, even with my graphics card, which is odd as I had to play on very high settings with V Sync and Anti Aliasing turned off.
Overall, this game is a good game. I only played the campaign and I can safely say I thoroughly enjoyed the experience. I played this game in around eight hours. It's a solid length of a game. I recommend the game at the Steam price of $19.99. Furthermore, I would strongly suggest buying the Maximum Edition that includes Crysis, Crysis: Warhead, and Crysis II.

Gat out of Hell is an entertaining standalone expansion to Saints Row IV. You play as Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kensington in an entirely new world on a quest to rescue the Boss (your player character in the previous four games.)
A side effect of this is that the game is nowhere near as in-depth as the previous games. You cannot customize your wardrobe or appearance past swapping between Johnny and Kinzie, car customization has been totally removed, there is no radio soundtrack (though there is an original ambient score similar to playing IV with no radio,) and the story mode is very bare-bones. It sort of returns to the form of previous games where you need to cause havoc in order to trigger cut scenes that progress the plot. There are very few actual story missions, as the story is mostly told through these cut scenes.
Instead, the game is mostly progressed by completing the activities scattered through the world. Most of these are classics returning from the previous games with some added twists, but the most fun new one is Salvation, where you must save souls that fall from the sky by flying around to catch them.
What story there is, however, is immensely satisfying. It gave Johnny Gat some much needed character development, some old faces return, and nearly every inch of the script is hilarious. Dane Vogel in particular surprised me, with an immensely witty dry streak that adds tons of character to the world. There are some blemishes, though. The game is very self-aware, almost to a fault. Sometimes it hits it out of the park, but other times it relies on breaking the fourth wall.
The setting is wonderful. Hell is a very interesting environment. There is no time cycle but the map is definitely more interesting than Steelport. Each district is remarkably different, from the slums that look like they were taken straight out of Francis Lawrence’s Constantine to a bustling entertainment district to a dystopian metropolitan city.
The game builds heavily on the super power framework from IV. Some oldies but goodies return such as blast, stomp, and aura. Some have been reworked such as super jump becoming flight. Finally, some are entirely new such as the summon ability. The powers are very similar, but they’re different enough to make the game interesting again. Flight alone is graceful, exhilarating, and immensely fun to use, breathing life into the somewhat dated superpower framework.
The new weapons are very satisfying. A few biblical plagues appear as an explosive frog launcher and a locust swarm launcher. The Seven Deadly Sins appear as the Seven Deadly Weapons, each immensely satisfying to use. The Sloth gun is just a recliner that you drive around with giant miniguns and rocket launchers, and the Greed gun shoots diamons that force enemies to drop more money (which is convenient because the varied weapons will require tons and tons of money to fully upgrade.) Unlike most other open-world sandbox titles, money is actually an important resource to collect and spend.
The graphics are average. The game isn’t ugly, but it’s not amazing either. The game will run fine and the world loading is responsive considering the insane speeds you can achieve, but it won’t be winning any awards either.
The bottom line is that this is more of the same of Saints Row IV with a few added twists. If you’re a fan of IV, Saints Row, or superpower games in general, you will have a good time with this and will see your $20 well spent for the entertainment you will get out of it. If you are somewhat interested but are otherwise bored with IV, you might want to wait for this to go on sale. If you disliked the Third and IV outright, this game will do little to sway you and you should give it a pass.
Note: I got this game for $5 thanks to the Gamestop pricing glitch.

I think I give up. Civ V is better all round, this one is just a series of annoyances. The bugs, the insipid and timid ai from the other nations, and the insanely over powered effects of trade all add up to making this worse than the previous versions. I've played them all, from the original back in about 1990, and this is the first version that I have beaten on every level I've played first try, without understanding what was going on in detail. I can't be bothered to push for the final highest level again, I just started a game to try, it gave me the quest to pick a trade station and then planted it EXACTLY in the right place to JUST prevent me being able to build my second city where I wanted to. Every time that mission appears...
I can't get my head around the fact that the designers have managed to reintroduce one of the biggest flaws in the original versions, the infinite city sprawl. It's not at the start this time, but at the end. With trade vessels flowing everywhere, I have had brand new cities growing every turn, building a building every turn, and health becomes a joke later on. The computer nations don't respond to threats, the ONLY time I have been attacked by anyone was on my first game on the second difficulty level. I've tried to provoke through words, and nothing's happened. I've even gone so far as to start hunting colonists and killing them, wiping out outposts, anything to get a reaction and the most I've seen was a pair of weak ships tamely sailing straight into a small fleet a few turns apart. Until you actually attack their cities directly, you seem to be free to do anything you like without consequences.
The trade stations are poor cousins to the old city states, the victory conditions force you onto certain paths, and while I liked the new tech tree concept, making it far harder to stay ahead on all fronts, and the virtues allowing a nice government design, they just aren't enough. In much the same way as Alpha Centauri, it's far harder to relate to the game because it's speculative, rather than historical, and it struggles to make sense.
I wanted to like it. I have over 1200 hours logged on Civ V alone, I dread to think how many hours have gone to whole series, but no more, I'm uninstalling it now and going off to play the amusing Venetian set up in Civ V once again. That was a new idea that made the game fun, unlike too many of the changes in this one.
Sorry, Sid, need to do better next time.

I decided to buy this seeing as it was only £5 on sale. It's definitely not like the older games in the series, so i can understand why fans were♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when this was first released. Having played FF7 on PS4 as my first introduction into the franchise and then straight after FF6 (said by many to be the best one in the series), i came in knowing it probably wouldn't have the same impact that the other 2 games i played had. Although the game took a very linear approach with exploration, which seems to be everyones main criticism, i still found the game as a whole to be quite enjoyable and i enjoyed playing through the story. The game does open up halfway through so there's that, but the game is extremely linear overall no denying. This didn't bother me too much as it was a change of pace to the others i had played, which in a way i appreciated. The main pull of this game for me was the battle system. People that say you just press one button to win only played the first few hours of the game. It is painfully easy at first and i did question if this was it for combat, but there is alot that goes into the battle system so it makes sense that it adds new mechanics slowly to the combat as you go. Fights become very challenging and you have to set up the right class combinations and shift paridigms often to win. The characters were pretty good overall, Vanille is definitely annoying as hell. Some of the stuff she says... just why. Hope is a complete good for nothing puss at the beginning but he does develop as a character and i ended up liking him, as for the rest of the crew they were all cool in my opinion, love Sazh. The music is really good, love the main battle theme! Visuals are great. Story was meh, you'll be confused as hell with the L'Cie, Fal'Cie and whatever else there are unless you read the journal or search up online which is a massive flaw, as the game should be able to explain the story through the game, not by throwing information logs at you. Overall the battle system and the characters kept me playing as i did want to know what would happen at the end and the combat was really fun. I'd give the game 8/10. I'd say it deserved around 7-8/10 in general.

Gameplay: Poor to non exsistant AI, clumsy and nonsensical tech tree mixed that only exaggerates Civ5's  weaknesses in a game that completely fails to inspire. It is essentially a standalone mod for CIV5 and quite frankly, there are already better. Games degrade into either a haphazard mess or a spammy waste of time as you are forced to click through repetetive trade route actions while the AI either blunders around in circles accomplishing nothing or wins haphazardly without fanfare or notice. The Diplomacy system is basic and simplistic to the extreme; you can quite happily go through the entire game without talking to anyone; expouding Civ 5's weaknesses - and least Civ 5 had the World Council system to make it more interesting. Furthermore, while the espionage system could have worked, it fails to amount to much as lack of feedback or control makes secret missions and the like lacklustre adn ultimately pointless busywork. Having said that, the music is nice and the number of different tile upgrades one can have is a great addition.
Setting and Game Feel: While affinities could been interesting, they ultimately fail to provide any form of narrative. CIV's 'story' came from enacting history 'your way', but the setting and themes discussed are sudden and ultimately lead up to nothing. The Supremacy track can basically be summarised as 'K IMMA ROBUT NAO' as it fails to give any reasoning as to why your civilisation are delving into what by all accounts is a transhumanist system of body horror dominated by transcendent religious ethos. By all accounts, Sid Meier's Alpha Centuri does Sci-Fi better, and with far more personality, not just because factions and leaders have variant playstyles and actual motives and opinions that is expressed in game via lore and tech popups (This game uses a single voice actress for everyone, muddying what little interest you had in each faction and further stripping an ensemblence of individuality), but because its story, lore and hard sci-fi setting is in your face since turn one. Conversely, this game is but a mere reskin of better things that have came before it.

Let me start by saying I love Final Fantasy games. I have played every single one from when Final Fantasy first appeared in Nintendo Power. I watched a friend play through the entirety of "II" (IV) when it came out on SNES. I played VI. I preordered VII for the PSX before preordering was even a thing and got a T-Shirt. I found emulators in the Win 95 era and played fan made translations of the real II, III, and V. I bought IV and After Years on Wii before they upgraded to chibi polygons. I bought the various collections like Anthology and the PSP ports of I and II. I bought II, III, IV, IV After Years, V, and VI for my android phone. I had Tactics, VIII, and IX on PSX. I played Chocobo's Mysterious Dungeon. I bought the original CDROM version of VII for PC. I have X, X-2, and XII for PS2 and the remasters of X and X-2 on PS3. I played XI until the second expansion. So yea, I am sort of a fan.
That being said, I recommend this game, but NOT to fans of the games, gameplay systems, themes and inherint features of the series in general. And certainly not to possible new players of the series because it will ruin Final Fantasy for them forever.  I only recommend this to old school, completionist type fans, hence the non-rec.
Why? Well first, this game was a b**** for me to finally finish. I bought it on PS3 when it first came out. My life went off track for a while and I had to sell my PS3 and games to make rent and when I finally picked it up again last year it was on my brother's Xbox 360 and I remember how much it deviated from every other Final Fantasy. I got pretty far again, then my brother moved away and took his 360. Finally completed it when I bought it on Steam a couple months ago, but only because I felt the need to finish it before XV comes out.
It feels on rails. The linearity is just ridiculous. The other games are also very linear but they mask it with things like optional bosses, an airship you can fly to go where you want, even sometimes completely optional, missable characters like in VI.
They forsake towns and cities and unimportant, but oft times charming NPC interactions. Treasue chests are now these floating spheres. It's just all wrong for a FF game. First ever FF with no airship. Just a lot of bad differences. When you finally get to the point in the game where you can explore on your own, it's mostly post game and limited to a very boring open plains and canyon type setting that will infuriate you because you will be traversing the same humongous expanse, back and forth, back and forth, back and forth, sometimes just running for 30 minutes to kill a certain mob then running back 30 minutes to turn in the quest to a stone, only to do the exact same thing for another stone, over and over for I think 50+ of these side quest stones. No depth, story limited to a paragraph of text explaining why you need to kill a monster. It's really lame.
I can't write anymore because thinking of this abomination of a FF game has now♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. God, I am so glad this game is finally done and behind me.

Now there are a lot of negative review of this game and some of those are reasonable complaints. What you need to understand is that Magic The Gathering is a severly complex game. It's not hearthstone where you OTK your opponent regardless of their preperations. It has a decent amount of cards in game, more than enough to start out with. This isn't paper mtg, it's a free to play game. Don't expect the entire MTG collection in a f2p model at launch. I will agree that the questing is obnoxious because to complete the daily "Blue/Black or Blue/Red" quest you MUST use the assisted deck helper. The joy of MTG is making your own unique deck fit for your playstyle. Variance is a ♥♥♥♥♥, but any tcg will show you that.
One MAJOR Pro about this game is that once you've aquired the card limit you won't see it again in a pack so your collection is going fill in time making it much more f2p friendly. (1 Mythic, 2 Rare, 3 Uncommon, 4 Common)
Fix chatting options for Twin Headed Giant mode.
If an opponent conceeds you should win the match. I'm fine with the AI playing through because it lets the player continue testing a deck, playing out a scenario ect, but at least credit them for the opponent leaving.
Overall I think it's a great game, a lot of potential, and after the bugs are tweaked/fixed it can compete with other popular PC tcg. I can only hope that with each MTG expansion we see them in this game as well.

Now that I finished the game I feel like I have enough knowledge to leave a review here.
This game is incredible.One of the best I've played this year.
A beautiful hand-drawn world that made me like this game from the start.Funny and unforgettable characters,especially Zote.This game,alongside Super Metroid and Castlevania should stand as the best of the best in this genre.Not many people like Metroidvanias,but for an enthusiast like myself this has been a pleasure from start to finish.
Now,I'm not saying this game is perfect.It deffinetly has some flaws:
-It takes way too long to get all the movement upgrades
-The backtracking becomes a bit annoying whenever you die to a boss,considering that benches are placed at a pretty long distance from the boss fight.
-If you are not familiar with this kind of game,it can be a little bit hard to know where to go at first,since there are no obvious guidelines that tell you where should you head next.
-One of the things I noticed as I was close to finishing the game is that sometimes your shade(the thing that spawns after you die,and must kill in order to get your money back)simply dissapears after you die a repeated number of times.This is an irritating bug and should be fixed.
The platforming is very well designed.Air control is great compared to other metroidvanias that have a delay when changing directions in the air or on the ground(such as Shovel Knight,although that game is good too).The movement doesn't feel clunky and it fits into the game perfectly.
Let's talk about music.It fits very well with every level.I personally believe Cristopher Larkin did an amazing job with creating the music for this game(City of Tears music is wonderful).Being such a diverse game,it needs the music to go well with all the exploration and fighting you are doing,and boy did Chris deliver.
Hallownest is huge.For a 15 euro price tag,I felt bad paying so little for so great enjoyment.Every level has a different color pallet(the only exception being Greenpath and Queen's Gardens that share the similar green with a few differences).I did not expect the world to be so big.Honestly I thought this game would have around 8-9 zones,but it has FIFTEEN.some of them having more than one entrance,to reward your exploration with a different introduction to that zone,depending on the choices you make.
To wrap this up,I think Hollow Knight is a must buy for anyone who is interested in something different.For such a great price everyone should have the opportunity to explore and fight their way through the world.

I bought this on launch, have over 100 hours(mostly due to speedrun attempts, steel soul mode attempts and the game save files just breaking apart once the free content packs came out) and I have to say despite a few grievances I would have to say it is the best game to come out in the last 5-10 years.
Even though some updates broke a couple of my save files I still replayed the game because it's just an amazing experience. The non-linearity allows for mixing up of the paths taken in different playthroughs and mixing and matching charms or putting up self imposed challenges really helps keeps the game fresh.
As a kb+m user, the controls are tight and it never feels like the lack of a controller handicaps the player. The platforming and downward attacks take some getting used to with the keyboard but it isn't impossible.
The visual aesthetic is simple and some parts of the world left me awestruck at the design. Enemies are fairly varied with the base game having over 140 bugs as enemies and the content packs maybe adding 10 to 15. Very few of the basic enemies have similar design and they have decent variation in attack patterns. The real show stealers amongst the enemies are the bosses. The boss design is phenomenal and I would give a kidney to just experience them for the first time again, Nightmare King Grimm being one of the most mesmerizing bosses with his design, moveset and the MUSIC.
The artstyle and gameplay are solid but are elevated to a whole new level by the music. It really sets the tone with some really neat ambient tracks during the quieter moments to some great orchestral scores to the boss fights. I still catch myself humming some of the tunes.
The game has some issues. One being the broken saves but like I mentioned it wasn't a deal breaker for me but be warned if you are looking for this game right now. I'd wait till next year once all planned dlcs and content packs are out so that you don't have to deal wiith such an inconvenience or if not be prepared to just backup saves often.
Few other minor nitpicks would be the various 'rooms' that you traverse through are too boxy, for the lack of a better word. It could have been a little better if there were some inclines or just curved surfaces to traverse along but I can see why it wouldn't work with the way movement works in the game. While it is fluid it is no Ori and the Blind Forest when it comes to traversal. It's not a bad thing, just an observation.
The white palace (an end game, super meat boy like platforming challenge) feels out of place with the rest of the world, but it is fun in a challenging way.
A lot of players didn't enjoy the exploration mechanics since the game doesn't have an auto filled map of the regions and requires players to stumble around till the get the map for a new region but I loved the lack of hand holding and it helps set the mood for the game when you enter uncharted territory.
The game is a modern masterpiece and needs to be experienced by all fans of the medium.

The issue with Final Fantasy 13 is the characters. As a story it's kindof interesting in setting up the big plot that is 13-2 and LR(haven't played it yet so don't spoil), but it's also 30 hours too long. It tries really hard to be another Final Fantasy 7, but only what we thought FF7 was. We thought FF7 was a whine fest but on a recent playthrough I found it to be actually quite less so and any "whining" is actually warranted. Nothing teen angst about it!
The characters are all too whiney. Hell, the main character(Lightning) has a line that is "Worst birthday ever." Not even joking. That line is SPOKEN. That's full on teen angst. Hope is absolutely one of the worst characters in any game I have played. I understand he's young, but that doesn't give him the right to be dumb. Snow is full on stubborn, Vanille is annoying, Sazh is all right, and Fang is....okay fine Fang is awesome. But that's one out of like...7 playable characters. That's not good. It's the antithesis of good. It's...not good.
As for the story? Well it's interesting. You have the relationship with the Fal'cie and the L'cie, the war between Pulse and Coccoon, what the Sanctum is actually up to, and vague hints at something bigger going on. And you find out what that bigger thing is in 13-2 and it's actually kindof awesome. But that's 13-2 and this is 13.
Another issue is the script. One of my friends said that he refuses to play a game where you have to read a codex(or in this case, a datalog) about all these things being mentioned to understand what they are, and I can see that. At the same time I will also argue that the characters themselves know what all this is, so why explain it via dialogue? On the otherside, there are ways that you can explain this♥♥♥♥♥♥via dialogue such as little before-chapter things or "last time on blah blah blah" and then you wouldn't need a datalog.
