Black Flag is competing to be the best Assassin's Creed title since Assassin's Creed II.
Not only the story is well written to a point that not only the gamer relates to the main character, a pirate named Edward Kenway, it also creates an emotional tide with the adventure and exploration of sailing the high seas and hunting treasure and other bounties while discovering more about the Assassins, the Templars, and the secrets of both.
Sailing.
Before Black Flag was released there was a game no one heard of called Pirates of The Burning Sea, a F2P MMO that currently had the title for best Sailing experience, Black Flag took that away and better.
With a immerse and easy to understand camera and control mechanics sailing in Black Flag is an amazing time, so much so that the game gives you the option to Fast Travel if needed, and I played for over 50 hours completing the game, without Fast Traveling Once.
With the additions of random AI Ships with Different Random Cargo roaming the seas, special challanges, secrets, and different weather and time conditions, the sailing it self sells the game.
Running.
The main aspect of running and jumping on rooftops and trees to explore ways to complete your objectives still a big thing and very well crafted, the only Con to it is that often you find yourself jumping in Hay Stacks or Trees just by running Aside some, which is a very hard thing to balance, but even tho very frustrating at the time, it goes away as soon as you get done with it.
Storyline.
The main storyline is very interesting to watch read and play, with various famous characters as usual of an Assassin's Creed game, introduced very well in the story.
The ending feels solid, and with enough questions for more story, but not enough to upset anyone.
Multiplayer.
The multiplayer feels more balanced than previous AC titles, with more maps and a more fluid and Skill Based mechanic.
The only bad thing is that as always and sadly gamers would always for some reason find ways to exploit game mechanics for an easy win.
The game introduced GameLabs a feature that allows players to customize Game Modes, everything from what skills can be used, to how much a kill would be worth, and what kind.
The issue currently with GameLabs is that you can only play your custom made Game Modes with your friends, and only find a Random "Approved" Type on the public lobby.
With enough luck, that would be fixed, and a new feature would allow gamers to publicly host GameLab creations for any player to pick and play.
Overall this is the level of detail the so called Next Gen titles should be all about. Great environments graphics, level design, interaction, and details to very small things.
This might be the best AC Title so far, and might also be GOTY.

Battlerite is a great arena brawler. Imagine LoL/DotA top down gameplay combined with WoW arenas. That's what Battlerite is. It's rather fast paced and most importantly, fun. Matches aren't 30 minutes of farm this farm that hope your other teammates aren't mouth breathers. Matches are a best of five rounds. Once the gate drops, you have two minutes until sudden death forcing a quicker gameplay. Instead of farming creep or reagents or anything of that nature you have "Battlerites" which are essentially upgraded skills.
The biggest downside to this game seems to be the league system (their competitive ladder). Platinum is oversaturated and for some reason the largest concentration of players though in any normal competitive game, that would never be the case. The league ladder ranks are from 8 to 1 (8 being the lowest) and in terms of worst to best you have Contender, Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond, Champion, Grand Champion. Devs, if you read your reviews, people need to fill out your lower ranks, that's why you guys have them.
The game plays very smooth on my personal rig (4770k/1070SC/16GB RAM), load times are very fast. Overall a great game. I was lucky enough to get a beta key albeit on the last day of the beta and loved the game but did truly struggle with the $20 price tag, however the game was recently at ~$13 and for that price I think the game is whole heartedly worth it. It's nice to not be in Steelport again, after the Third and IV I never wanted to see it again. The Hell city is small but it's got a lot of cool designs and flying around feels great. It really feels like an open world Ratchet & Clank (PS2 era) with the crazy weapons, high mobility, colourful graphics and decent sense of humour. That's one other thing, the humour is actually decent, not entirely made out of cheap references (mostly just general silliness) and thankfully I didn't see or hear any internet "humour" (Imagine those quotation marks are the size of the planet Jupiter).
The change (first in IV yes I know) to having health pickups instead of pure regenerative health (read: surrounded by enemies in a big open area and getting constantly clipped while trying to hide to get health back) is a welcome one but there is one bad gameplay trope that's pretty prominent throughout Gat out of Hell; filling up meters that get reset every time you get hit. I don't think there's been a single game that doing that has been fun in. There are tons of them in this and yes, it's still irritating. For those that may be unaware of this concept, you have to hold E on something while a bar fills up and you can't attack, while enemies keep spawning in around you. If any of them hit you, you get knocked out of the animation and the bar resets. The only "strategy" for them is to try to get to them before the enemies do/spawn and fill the bar before they can get a shot off.
Graphically, like the Third and IV, Gat out of Hell is a mixed bag. There are a lot of graphical options and the vibrant, colourful style is very pleasing to look at but on the other hand the draw distance is awful. When flying around at full speed (which you will probably be doing a lot of) there's noticeable pop-in and no, there's no setting to fix that. I've got a top of the line gaming pc that can easily handle it on maxed out settings and it was the same in the Third and IV too, especially with traffic and pedestrians. This game was released in 2015, step it up Volition.
The short musical number was nicely done and despite hating musicals, in this it was kind of nice and I enjoyed it. I haven't 100% completed Gat out of Hell yet (10 hrs) but I'm at about 80% and I've had fun so far. As usual, I'll update this review if anything changes to make sure the information stays accurate. I hope it helped your decision.

I hope they come up with some patches to fill in the gaps in this game.

If you've experienced the ending of Saints Row IV in co-op,  then you know what to expect with this game.
Wait. You still can't finish Saints Row IV in co-op without the game entering an infinite loading loop that you have to attempt to find your own workaround for fruitlessly, and end up settling for finishing single player instead.
This game is even more unstable than SR IV. The first Fraud mission cannot be completed in co-op, with 5+ attempts, after a certain amount of time (not enough to actually complete the mission) we would disconnect every time. Regardless of what we did.
While playing in the open world, aside from situations where you're standing in a handful of buildings, there is no music. Nothing. No radio stations for cars, which might have something to do with re-licensing or licensing new songs; but also, no original soundtrack while you're out exploring Hell. None of the character customization has carried over, either, which I guess is to be expected since this is a standalone game rather than DLC. To progress the "story", you complete side-mission after side-mission - side-missions that existed in previous games, SR3 and SR IV, but in Gat Out of Hell, they are forced if you want to progress the story's cutscenes. Side-missions are way more enjoyable for me when they're not forced, and you can do them at your own pace. I also like side-missions in co-op. But unfortunately, it's hit or miss whether or not the game will remain stable enough to let you finish the mission with your partner.
There was also an instance of my co-op partner randomly jumping inside of a wall, and out of bounds, just by attempting to fly. He remained stuck there until I was able to trigger a mission which teleported him elsewhere.
The game's also crashed a couple of times. I have 4 hours on record and I've already encountered enough issues to make me put it down.
I'm very glad I didn't pay for this myself (a friend gifted it to me, and I feel terrible for him for spending the money), because I don't feel like this game is even remotely worth the $20 price. I'd have more faith (or any hope period) for a patch to address these issues if I hadn't experienced Saints Row IV, and its lack of patches to address game-breaking issues that have been present since release.
If you want a fun Saints Row game, I recommend Saints Row: The Third. Even Saints Row IV is alright, if you're okay with some co-op instability every now and then, and being unable to finish the final mission with your partner. Just don't touch this.
That's my recommendation.

There's a huge amount of potential in this game. Lots of good and great ideas that, if they get fleshed out, would make for an excellent Civilization game.
Unfortunately that's all the game is. A gigantic ball of potential that doesn't amount to much of anything. The tech web was a great idea, but its a horribly unbalanced mess that is a chore to even get through. The orbital layer could add a lot of strategic depth to the game, unfortunately all it ends up being is a fancy new way to look at the map. The abundance of aliens could make for a way to break up the monotony that was barbarians in older games, unforunately they're so pathetically useless with the exception of sea based ones (which are so horrifically overpowered that you need end game sea units to even stand a chance) that you can effectively ignore them without cause for concern. The affinity system is a wonderful idea, but the execution just turns it into a pointless slog that, instead of giving you options actually limits your choices. It also makes 0 sense that you can max out all 3 affinities which allows you to be a society that lives in perfect harmony with the world you've both shunned and subjugated all at the same time.
On top of the annoyance of wasted potential is the extreme annoyance with tons of little problems.
Playing island based maps will make you want to punch your computer screen because the only efficient way to get around is to hope there's a source of firaxite around and you have the supremacy affinity level to drop the teleport satellite over them. Why is that? Because there is no such thing as a transport ship in Beyond Earth. Your only way of gettin units across vast oceans is to embark them which gives them a maximum of 2 movement a turn. This number can not be increased by any quests/tech/wonders. Do you know how agonizingly long it takes to move an army across an ocean when you only can move 2 spaces a turn on large maps?
The ocean is, in general, just a giant death trap anyway. Both sea alien units are far stronger than anythin you can field for a very long time meaning the only way to effectively use the ocean to your advantage is to field a disgustingly large navy. The basic sea dragon can, and will, destroy an entire fleet of T1 ships. The Kraken can, and will, destroy T4 ships with ease while you struggle to kill a single 1 and the stupid things swim in packs of 3-4 at times.
The AI has never (and at this point I'm goin to say will never) be remotely up to par. I once got in a war with an enemy that should have been able to wipe my face off the planet. They were ahead in tech, they were ahead in unit size, they were ahead in cities. The only single advantage I had was I held city in a decently strong choke point between our 2 empires. That being said, they had enough firepower to destroy that choke point like paper. The AI never took the city, nor did I ever feel in danger of losing it. At one point I plopped a ranged unit in the middle of their line, expectin it to get a single shot in and damage an attacker just enough for him to back off a bit. This unit was literally surrounded by other enemy ranged units and was in range of bein hit by enemy tanks. It lasted for 5 turns and was allowed to shoot the entire time. In other games I've had the AI declare war on me 3 times in a row. Each time I captured 2-3 cities, sued for peace, then went on my way. Then the AI would denounce me, over and over again. They'd spy on me and I'd capture their spies and ask politely for them to stop while forgiving them in the process. They'd denounce me again before asking for some ridiculous demand. When I denied the demand, war were declared. I'd capture 2-3 cities, sue for peace and it'd start all over again.
The pinnacle that was the stupidity of the AI was when I was in a really good relationship with another Civ. We'd been friends since the start, we had great trade relations, we shared affinities, we shared allies, all was well in the world. Then I declared war a few times for various reasons beyond my control Was forced into a war by my ally once, was forced into a different war due to a protection treaty, the usual. Suddenly my bestest friend in the world turns on me and denounces me as a war monger. Suddenly all our wonderfully mutually beneficial trade agreements aren't mutually beneficial anymore. I still like them so I give them more and more. At one point we had a treaty that was literally just me giving them 10 energy a turn. This deal expired and the trade window pops up with the person saying "I hope we can renew this deal that has somethin somethin somethin." The trade is literally me giving them energy for nothing. I accept and instead of that being it, I get angry faced and now I'm being told that this deal isn't good enough for them.
Its literally a deal to get energy for nothing and its not good enough anymore. Not only is it not good enough anymore, its not good enough literally right after I was told that they hope the deal can be renewed. That's not just dumb AI, that's bad programming.
All in all the game was fun while I played it, but I only enjoyed myself if i I completely ignored every little annoyance with the game. Unfortunately after a certain amount of time, those little annoyances become a big enough problem that I just had to turn off the game.
Hopefully patches and future expansions fix the base game, but I'll definitely be taking a wait and see approach.

Forget the naysayers. Now that the connection issues that have plagued the launch week have been rectified, this is a cracking good game.
It's got a very generous free to play model, which will have you earning cards at a quick pace, and the presentation is slick, if a little bare-bones.
There are, however, a few minor annoyances. Some decks are more potent than others due to the initial size of the card pool, and the AI's inability to deal with certain strategies (I've found quick-firing aggro decks particularly effective, even on hard difficulty).
And speaking of difficulty, the story mode matches, although unusual and exciting to play, have a curve that stretches all the way from cake-walk to rage-quit, depending on your initial hand (hint: "restart" is your friend).
That being said, on the whole, the gameplay is still very satisfying, and the game itself does a great job of teaching not only the basics of Magic, but also the miriad of deck archetypes, play styles and strategies available to a new would-be Planeswalker.
Overall, Magic: Duels is set on solid foundations, and with new card sets planned for release every three months, I can see this game going from strength to strength.
So what are you waiting for? Start your collection today! After all, you wouldn't want to be left behind, would you?
A refreshing take on the previous setting with a few minor hiccups, including an abysmally short story, but serves to immerse the player in the confines of Rapture once again.

This game is really good. So good that I went ahead and bought it despite having it available through Family Share. Because there are so many things this game does right, it will be easier to describe the few glaring annoyances.
Exploring new areas is stressful when it should be exciting.
For a game where exploration plays such a big role, Hollow Knight's map layout and game mechanics punish players for exploring more than it rewards them. Map rooms are placed in the middle of unexplored areas, occasionally behind some barier that requires an ability to pass. I understand that this is par for the course in "metroidvania" games, but the issues here are that 1) it is sometimes unclear whether you are meant to get a new ability an another area or if you are supposed to search for an alternative route in the current area 2) the maps that you buy for a new area are incomplete anyway, and do not show you the location of points of interest (even if you purchase the items that reveal them on the map, you have to find them on your own) 3) Save points are sparse, meaning that if you have not already found a map room for an area, you will likely be stumbling through the dark for quite some time when you die 4) Some rooms have surprise boss battles, which can easily catch you off guard while looking for a map room which can set you back (see point 3) 5) dying, similar to in Dark Souls, causes you to lose all held currency until you find the point where you died to recover it making it difficult to purchase items that would be helpful in the new area. Also like in Dark Souls, dying twice means that the currency is lost forever.
Traveling in the world is annoying.
While I'm on the Dark Souls comparison, I realize that this game is supposed to be difficult. Honestly, I wouldn't have too much of a problem with the difficulty of exploration if it werent for how sparse the world of Hollow Knight is and how excruciatingly slow it is to traverse. In Dark Souls, difficult-to-navigate sections would be rewared by a shortcut to a hub area, so that it is relatively straightforward to jump back to where you left off if you wanted to try a new area. Additionally, most NPCs that you could trade with would also be in this hub. In Hollow Knight, shortcuts are few and far between and rarely connect directly back to the hub. Friendly NPCs are also scattered throughout the world. Because the fast-travel stations are in such awkward locations, I found that even when using these I was taking very long, boring walks to NPCs to buy new items. Whenver a situation arose where I needed a new ability to get through a new area, I would also have to take these same long boring walks to get to where I needed to go.
The good stuff (pretty much everything else):
- Beautiful art style
- Satisfying combat (responsive controls)
- Challenging but fair and rewarding bosses
- Extensive item system that allows for customizing playstyle
Things that would make me stop complaining:
- The option to spend more currency in a map room to buy a map outlining all rooms (except secret rooms) in a new area.
- Additional optional save points (unlockable by killing a mini-boss) so that MOST area entrances and boss rooms have a save nearby.
- A central hub with direct connections to MOST areas, and where all found NPCs gather.

To me, Beyond Earth is a mixture of Good and Bad.
I enjoy the fact that they decided to do something different from their usual historic to future gameplay which we saw in the first 5 and it was nice to see this change and it had lots of potential.
Beyond Earth, to me, has not reached it's full potential and there was a lot more that should of been done before release. I think the one main part that we are missing is the amount of civs that were in civ 5. It gave the game a unique adventure each game where you would have a different set of 12 people and every time you would have to change your plan to work with the resources you have and the others civs around you.
Beyond Earth didn't have that, With only a couple civs, you are playing with them every single time. No fresh faces or anything. I didn't put many hours into it because I lost interest but that's because I preferred Civ 5 over Beyond Earth.
Pros:
Technology web - It allows you to go on a research path that suits you and you don't have to follow the usual line which you see in the other games.
Satellite view - It gives the game a second layer, where you can have units on the field and in the air giving you other bonuses like extra energy.
Space - New land generation compared to the old earth one gave the game a new interesting look, things aren't the same on this planet and they have proven that with nice new lands.
Cons:
Not enough civs - There is just not enough civs to choose from to give each game a different unique adventure which we could get from the other games. Every game you will know who you get and it just gets boring.
Green? - Way too much green in the game. Two civs are green,  Miasma is green, mob icons are green and half the terrain is all the same shade of green. I get it, we are on a new planet, spacy and stuff. There is way too much  of green and green variants on the map. I feel sorry for colourblind people.
Price - For what we got, I don't think it's worth the full price of a AAA game.
If you are new to the Civilization games, I'd recommend trying this game out, it's a great game, but old Civ players, you will probably prefer the older games.

A Metroid-Vania Must Buy!
While it seems the majority of Metroid-Vanias tend to wallow in the Castlevania and particularly the Metroid Series, Hollow Knight stands on its own as a fantastic example of simple mechanics used to their fullest.
+ Excellent Atmosphere
+ Ridiculous Amount of Content for the Price
+ Great, Non-Linear Story with Interesting Characters
+ Great Customisation for Combat
+ Excellent Soundtrack
+ Great Art Style and Variety of Location
Since I’ve made it clear that this is an incredible product and one of my favourite games of 2017, I will attempt to criticise it as art alone without spoiling anything in game.
1. Not Enough Content. This will sound baffling since I just praised it for having a tremendous amount of content for the price. The only way I can describe it is through metaphor: While most Metroid-Vania's content can be compared to a full lake; Hollow Knight's content is an ocean three quarters full. While this is an immense amount of high quality content, it does feel sometimes that there is some content missing. In many areas, you are almost sure that there will be a boss, but there is just nothing and it happens multiple times.
This can be applied to the story too, Team Cherry designed the game before the story and it does show at times since some parts of the story are clearly missing with a handful of locations seeming to have hidden story but there is none to be found. Though the excuse can be made that games that use environmental, Dark Souls like story telling purposely leave gaps for the player to fill in, even the first dark souls had more information in it than hollow knight. It is probably a bit unfair to keep comparing an indie Metroid-Vania to a large developer RPG but it’s the closest equivalent to hollow knight in narrative design I can think of. Team Cherry has added two free DLCs to the game (Hidden Dreams and The Grimm Troupe), with one more definitely planned to come and possibly more after that which do flesh out the lore a bit more. These DLCs might fix this issue in the future.
2. Level and Enemy Design. Though the principle level and enemy design in game is great, it does feel it could be better. I believe a large part of this problem stems from the rate you receive upgrades, in particular, movement based ones. In the very late game, once you have unlocked all of these abilities, it is an immense feeling of liberation with a some late game areas and one boss forcing you to utilise all of these abilities and it is truly some of the most fun I have had in a videogame in years. However, it occurs too late into the game, and as such, only a small handful of areas and combat encounters force you to utilise them and I feel the level design was simplified across most of the game so that players without these abilities could cross them. When I said a handful of areas make use of your movement abilities, I do mean a handful. The vast majority of the game allows you to do without them which I feel may have stymied interesting ideas that could've been applied to the rest of the game. I do understand that Metroid-Vania allow a player to take whatever route they wish, but even many of the very late game areas don't make use of them. I should still note that the combat and level design in this game is great, it’s just that it could've been better if they had utilised the abilities more.
3. Late Game Economy. This is a relatively minor point but in Hollow Knight, you gain a currency called geo, which you can use to buy numerous items across multiple different merchants. This is excellent in the early-mid game but towards the late game, you will be drowning in Geo with nothing to spend it on. They did minorly rectify this with an NPC in the Grimm Troupe DLC though it still could be improved. As of publishing this, it is confirmed that there is at least one more DLC on the way, which will hopefully remedy this minor issue.
There are some other minor issues I could mention but they are so miniscule that I won't bother mentioning them. Do not misunderstand these complaints I have stated that Hollow Knight isn't good. It is my favourite Metroid-Vania game of all time. I believe if Team Cherry is willing to keep adding new content to fill in some of the blank areas of the game, this game could honestly rise to be one of the best games ever made.
Thank you for reading

Is Civ:BE a $50 game? No. Is it a heck of alot of fun to play? Yes, emphatically Y E S (but I'd try to get it at ~$40). Firaxis has streamlined quite a bit of the Civ tech trees, expanded the alien(barbarian) presence and introduced more than a few beginning options that make almost every game feel like it's NOT just a replay on new territory. Make 1 or 2 different choices and you'll find the game to be quite a bit different.
I see alot of people comparing it to Civ5 but it has little to do with Civ5. It shares the same engine and similar mechanics but a different story. If you're old enough to recall the BG and IWD series then you'll see what I mean. Two totally different games that share the same graphics engine, the same mechanics and even the same core concept but told  2 completely different tales. Civ:BE allows you to CHOOSE between activating the fauna's aggression or attempting to work around them. Technically speaking, YOU are the "aliens" and it's up to you as to how you're going to deal with the local wildlife. Trust me, the wildlife you find in the first 50-100 turns is NOT all there is :/
I bought Civ:BE on sale and am LOVING it. I started my first game when I first put my dinner into cook and only realized it was pushing 1:30AM when I got a /tell from a friend. When a game can suck you in like that, it doesn't MATTER that it's "derivative" from the previos Civ games. It only matters that it adheres to the core concepts of the series and offers up 2tons of replay value for the initial cost of $50(or less)

Where to begin with this gem? Actually, not gem, a ♥♥♥♥ing diamond!
This is the most polished metroidvania I've ever been a witness to. Actually, it's the first metroidvania I've ever properly played but this game makes me realise why people love this game genre so much.
The graphics and presentation deliver a unique artstyle that just works its desired atmosphere spectacularly. The game's art inflicts this gloomy, derelict vibe and can be really dark when it needs to be like the tragedy of Myla the crystal miner, the bodies dropping from the Colosseum of Fools, Nosk the creepy spider from Deepnest...
But the game never fully dwells on this forboding feeling. There are cracks of light-hearted playfulness scattered beneath its surface like the Grubs, the map dude, giving a flower to the Elderbug in Dirtmouth. It has this Tim Burton artstyle that I just admire and become fearful of.
Of course, the graphics can only do so much. To get the full atmosphere, you need good sounds and music. This game has both of these as well. The sound effects resonate beautifully and makes you feel some satisfaction in a nail hit on an enemy or sitting on a bench. The music captures the solemnity and the somberness splendidly and really sets the mood for the rest of the game with some truly powerful melodies and themes.
The combat and gameplay is fine-tuned to perfection. There are over 140+ enemies including 30 amazing bosses. All of them have unique designs and distinguishable attacks that are fair enough on the player (except those stupid Primal Aspids that always seem to hit you no matter what). Although the game will be hard for some, that's the beauty of it. It will give you more satisfaction when beating a hard boss and claiming its rewards than an easy boss and I personally think the difficulty is fair and forgiving. Just remember that if you die before destroying your Shade that was left behind when you previously died, you can lose ALL of your money!
Overall, this game is my GOTY for 2017. It is near-flawless and to think only 3 people worked on this game that does better than most AAA companies out there. Kudos to Team Cherry who have made this $15 only masterpeece!

It is redundant to talk about how good this game is, it earned its reputation for a reason. The negative reviews are either players wanting the game to cater to their specific genre, or blowing lesser problems up like they ruin the whole game.
There is no live plot. That did not bother the community when the amateurish Dark Souls tech demos could not bother to add in basic plot. The game is almost definately based off a lot of concepts the Souls tech demos had but the quality difference is not even remotely comparative. This is a game, with a living world. Not a bunch of static assets thrown into a static map with primitive combat mechanics and almost no conventional game design elements.
The game does have a vague idea to the plot, which even that is more meaningful then the Souls tech demos, but the greater weakness is how obscure the actual lore is. There are bits of lore around the game, but a lot of them tell extremely vague and difficult to interpret stories. Which makes it borderline impossible to really develop a grasp of the backstory of the world itself, which is probably the biggest problem with the game. Is that from start to finish the player has almost zero understanding of the world and it really diminishes the potential immersion with the world. The lore telling is very, very poor.
There is also a lot of backtracking and running around in this game. Which is a part of the fact that it is a full scale world and discovering new things in old areas, when you have new abilities to find them, is a part of the experience. But there is a lot of grunt running around, looking at the map, potentially going back to where you died, keeping track of places you have not been. It is tedious but it is an inherent downside to the games design which is a full sprawling world.
The difficulty is quite well balanced up until the point where it becomes completely imbalanced. There are a lot of moments in the game where enemy attacks just are not telegraphed enough for the player to dodge it without being ready ahead of time. There are a lot of moments where enemies will act faster then the player can recover from their actions, so if the players makes one mistake it can lead to them getting chained into being hit once or more because without exact timing the player literally cannot function quickly enough otherwise to respond to some enemy patterns.
Worst of all however are the multiple spots in the game where the developers just decided the game has been too fun and they need to put something unfun into it. There are very specific spots in the game where the developers just decided to start making the player regret having turned the game on. Some of these instances are optional, some are not. But even with the optional ones, the game encourages the player to acquire new things and explore; so the idea of purposely not doing something because it is unfun or unfair goes against what the game has been teaching players. Furthermore, it makes it even harder to walk away from something unenjoyable when the game world is so immersive that the desire to get as much as possible out of it is there.
It is in extremely specific places and it is noticeable almost immediately that the games standards for player performance have suddenly just reached l33t paid-to-do-this levels instantly out of absolutely no where. It is not fun or fair but the game has been relatively nice up until then so you want to do the unfun thing for the sake of unlocking new things and finishing more of the game; so you either have to just do the unfun thing and not have fun for a half hour to an hour multiple times throughout the game. Or give up and feel incomplete.
But the frustrating no fun zones in the game are negligible in the end just like the more tedious running around, map checking, path remembering gameplay. The game does pretty much everything else well, save for the absolutely terrible lore telling. Which is really unfortunate as the game has an interesting story but all the text in game on the lore is cryptic, vague and brief.
Game takes about twenty to thirty hours to complete based on how much players try to acquire as much as possible. Worth far more then the retail price.

Not a Hero brings the devil-may-care Devolver Digital back onto the frontlines of indie domination. They've cranked out so many hits over the last few years, with Hotline Miami and Broforce showcasing a constant desire to edge themselves off their own thrones. But Not a Hero only continues that trend with one of the most frantic games to ever come out of this already rambuctious publishing house.
Bunnylord's future mayorship needs saving, but that requires the time-traveling rabbit to win the election in the present. Of course, in Devolver Digital fashion, this isn't going to go as typically planned. This is a campaign trail of blood. Executing drug dealers, pandering to reporters, and taking out rivals is the name of the game, and you as Bunnylord's vigilante must follow the rabbit's orders to ensure his victory.
Not a Hero is a 2D shooter where stage has multiple floors, with windows to traverse through, stairways to climb, and ledges to tenuously traverse. It's action movie adrenaline at its finest, as your vigilante of choice (each with unique properties and skills) must take out enemies and complete objectives for Bunnylord. It's momentum-driven and will keep your blood pumping as the bodies hit the floor.
With multiple optional objectives in each level, you can take alternative directions to find hidden items, get killstreaks, or dodge damage. Completing optional objectives nets you approval, which can unlock new characters to play as, along with progressing through the story. Approval is forgiving, as not all optional objectives are required to progress in the game, which is good, because some optional objectives are just a pain to complete. The mad dash to find reporters before they are killed is a real pace-breaker, especially when some levels have slow moving obstacles keeping you from victory.
But Not a Hero is just fun to play. Not a trace of seriousness courses through its veins, offering ample opportunity to mix things up with its rag-tag group of not-heroes. There's a solid amount of post-game content beyond a brief story mode, but in quick arcade-y bursts, it's a rush to play. Funny, frantic, and full of panache, Not a Hero is another win for Devolver Digital. All hail, Fork Parker.

I liked it, but there are a few warnings to bear in mind.
It's recommended that you play it with a controller from the start. I don't have a controller compatible with my PC, so I played with a keyboard.
The game is difficult, regardless of the method with which you play. Your attacks are basic and your health pool is small, so winning any fight relies on your ability to outmaneuver enemies and exploit their openings. This starts fairly simply, as enemies either bee-line toward you or have a single attack pattern, but quickly begins to become more complicated. By the third zone enemies will begin to feint, block, and have mixes of close and projectile attacks. Pretty strong difficulty curve, and an absolutely challenging experience.
Bosses are generally fair, with short telegraphs. However, I found that the regenerative ability took too long un-charmed to allow its use in many boss fights, forcing me to practice the same boss fights a dozen times until I could prevent any mis-steps. This became especially frustrating when the nearest 'checkpoint' was several maps away with many enemies in between.
You know how every game claimed to be the "Dark Souls" of something or the other. In this game, death will reduce your 'focus' bar which is used to heal yourself and drop all of the currency that you're carrying. Both your focus and your currency can be reclaimed at the place of your death, assuming you don't die again on the way; a very familiar mechanic to those who played the Souls series.
I do have a few criticisms, and I'll try my best not to let the fact that I played this game on keyboard muddy my opinion.
The movement and attack sets are limited. This game doesn't give you a whole lot of skills that benefit you in combat. The exceptions are the dash and the spells. The former allows you a short-distance teleportation left or right and the latter are strong attacks that deplete your 'focus,' which you also need to heal. The basic attack which you'll use most often is a single sword strike aimed horizontally or vertically. Hitting enemies with the basic attack recharges your focus and, again, allows you to heal or cast spells.
With these qualities in mind, your character never feels more powerful than the enemies you encounter. Outside of charms, he never seems to grow stronger or more manueverable. As the enemies become more challenging, your ability to defeat them stems solely from your ability as the player. This is a double-edged sword, as hard-core players may rise to the challenge while the more casual players become frustrated. Trial and error becomes a necessity, not only for the bosses, but for the more advanced mobs as well.
It's also hard to justify using spells outside of boss fights, since you're likely going to need your focus to heal while exploring or prior to entering boss fights, where you will be hard-pressed to find an opening to heal.
For these reasons, I felt combat could be underwhelming. The options that I have as the player are limited to a sequence of baiting, attacking, and retreating, if not avoiding the fight entirely.
Additionally, it can be difficult to figure out where the next objective is or how to go about it. I've spent many hours backtracking and searching through areas, completing a lot of non-essential puzzles along the way, with no idea what the next major step was. There have been at least two points where I saw a unique object in the game, couldn't figure out how to interact with it, backtracked trying to find some equipment that would allow me to interact with it, and then realized that my approach was wrong and that I had the means to pass it the entire time. I don't like hand-holding, but maybe give me a foothold somewhere along the cliffside.
I've touched on my most important thoughts, but I wanted to add some general thoughts to explain why I recommend the game.
The art style is fantastic, with examples of varied and interesting zones. NPCs have layers of character and feel unique within the world. The player character himself looks very compelling, and I imagine he would make a very attractive bumper sticker. Even if you may not finish it, the game is still very much worth playing.

Ahhh Crysis.
This was one of those games which totally got me back into PC gaming.
Yeah, some years I was actually quite frequently using a console but when this game came out...
DAMN. I loved it. I actually build my first rig back then. Myself, no prebuild crap. 8600GT and a Intel Pentium 4. Back then I wasnt spending much money for hardware. With that specs I was able to play the game on medium settings with playable FPS but that was it pretty much. In 1024x768. Gosh, couldnt even imagine myself playing like this anymore. Back then no hardware could run it playable with 30FPS on Very High. I guess my rig had like 10FPS, haha.
Also I was still using Windows XP so no DX10 for me back then, or 64Bit...
Many years there was the term, "But can it run Crysis". Even today Crysis still serves as Benchmark.
But thats snow from yesterday as we Germans say, so lets get into the review.
The story is about some US soldiers invading a island named Ling Shan. Their mission is to safe some people and uncover the secrets of the island. You are Nomad and belong to those soldiers. The island belongs to the Korean army and General Kyong is the leader of them. The US soldiers dont stay undercover for long and have to deal with the army and... something else. Something else is present on this island and while you do your journey through the island you are going to uncover this entity.
The game is a FPS. You have to pass through very big open world levels to reach your mission goals and progress in this game. While you are doing so, many soldiers and other things will attack you. Luckily you have a bunch of weapons AND the Nanosuit! The Nanosuit pretty much is the reason why this game sets itself apart from other generic FPS shooters. Its a armor with that you can be very strong, fast, armored and even invisible. For a certain time until the energy has to recover. I love this feature about the game. Its so simple, yet addicting. On your way you also often get the possibility of using vehicles. How you do certain goals is up to you. Go in guns blazing or stealth. On higher difficulties you should definitely try to stealth. The difficulty can be quite high at points. Especially when playing on something higher than normal.
The game is made by Crytek. One of my favorite developers of our time.
The game runs on the CryEngine 2 which, similar to Far Cry in 2004, made a revolution in terms of graphics in videogames. Nothing could even mess with the CryEngine 2 back then. Not even the Unreal Engine 3 which came out around the same time and often was praised for its graphics. It even offered DX10 and 64Bit support. But the downside of this was that the engine was extremely taxing on PCs. Even top notch highend rigs couldnt handle the game on very high settings. I really loved the graphics, it was amazing to see what actually was possible. It really looked like RL.
Even today the game still looks stunning and beautiful, even if the CryEngine 3 probably took its place as best looking engine. This was especially noticeable after Crysis 3 came out. Crysis 2 sadly didnt use its full potencial at launch. But this was addressed with patches and even Crysis 2 looked stunning after the patches. Still, Crysis is unmatched for me in terms of gameplay and graphics. Also Crysis was not made for consoles, unlike its other games. Therefore I guess Crysis was not limited to anything like level sizes. But its probably also the memories that I have with this game. Crysis 2 and 3 are also amazing games and I like to replay all of them from time to time, or after I have a new rig. Always when I have a new rig or something about my hardware changed, its time to play Crysis. Its something like a ritual for me, haha.

So, after 90-odd hours in my game save, I managed to all the achievements on Steam. Although I would like to give it a positive review, I feel the game could've been so much more than it was. Some thoughts which I had:
1. Square Enix tried to port the game from the PS to the PC. Apparently they forgot to include more options for graphics settings because there were close to none. My PC (GeForce GTX950, 16 GB RAM, i7) kept dropping frames in hectic fights which had more than 3-4 creatures in the mob. Although Square Enix did patch some of the issues, frame rate was still a problem.
2. I really enjoyed the combat system which they used in FFXII. Its an Active Time Battle(ATB) which uses Paradigms assigning each of the 3 characters you can control in fights. Only qualm which I did have with the system was that once your party leader would die, you would immediately lose the fight (They have apparently changed this in the next game).
3. The first 20 hours of the game is essentially a linear dungeon crawler with no form of resourse management, refilling health bars after every battle, etc. This could probably turn a lot of people to other games which present an open-world. There are games like Mass Effect which a relatively linear storyline but are really good at the same time. This wasn't spectacular in any sense of the word.
4. The bosses were all managable provided you would know which paradigms to use. After the first 20-30 hours of the game, you can no longer make do with just pressing "Auto-Battle" every fight.
5. The story was actually pretty good (I read a lot of fantasy) and I loved exploring the lore which was present in the Datalog. Loved reading about the whole Fal'Cie and L'Cie thing and the way Cocoon and Pulse was presented was visually appeasing.
6. The one thing I absolutely hated about this game is the amount of GIL farming you have to do to get all the Achievements. The last 30-40 hours of the game is literally repeating the same battle over and over again hoping for a platinum ingot to drop. The in-game economy was really messed up. Maxing out the characters was pretty easy and maxing out their weapons took forever. The Treasure Hunter achievement was a literal pain-in-the♥♥♥♥♥ I hope that they have fixed that in the next game.
7. I would honestly recommend this to people who like a relatively easy to play game with a pretty decent story and a great world with amazing scenery.
Game Length: 50-60 hours (90-100 hours to plat)
Game Score: 7.5/10

The storyline takes an abrupt turn from all previous Hitman games. This game takes the "dark and gritty" paint and sloshes it over everything. Almost all the characters are needlessly foul-mouthed and sociopathic. Almost every henchman you meet on every level is some kind of scum--of-the-earth type of guy. In previous Hitman games I've striven to avoid collateral killing in order to obtain the coveted Silent Assassin rating but in this game I got more joy from disregarding the ratings and instead disposing of all humanoid trash by selling buttons on most levels.
As far as game mechanics are concerned, there are a few new things: a directional and individual tension detector per NPC, throwable weapons, throwable distraction items, Instinct power, etc. Altogether, I think these things made this Hitman too easy, even on the hardest modes. I don't mean easy as in easy to get high scores. I mean easy as in easy to survive and assassinate your targets even if you are discovered. This game lost a good deal of the Hitman essence in favor of making it some kind of third-person shooting game with stealth elements added in. Overall, it doesn't suck but it really doesn't inherit a lot of the Hitman spirit.
I greatly appreciate that there are now myriad ways to kill every target. It was a joy just replaying every level solely to discover all the different ways you could whack your hits.

Forget the naysayers. Now that the connection issues that have plagued the launch week have been rectified, this is a cracking good game.
It's got a very generous free to play model, which will have you earning cards at a quick pace, and the presentation is slick, if a little bare-bones.
There are, however, a few minor annoyances. Some decks are more potent than others due to the initial size of the card pool, and the AI's inability to deal with certain strategies (I've found quick-firing aggro decks particularly effective, even on hard difficulty).
And speaking of difficulty, the story mode matches, although unusual and exciting to play, have a curve that stretches all the way from cake-walk to rage-quit, depending on your initial hand (hint: "restart" is your friend).
That being said, on the whole, the gameplay is still very satisfying, and the game itself does a great job of teaching not only the basics of Magic, but also the miriad of deck archetypes, play styles and strategies available to a new would-be Planeswalker.
Overall, Magic: Duels is set on solid foundations, and with new card sets planned for release every three months, I can see this game going from strength to strength.
So what are you waiting for? Start your collection today! After all, you wouldn't want to be left behind, would you?

So as you probably know at this point, this is a standalone expansion for Saints Row 4. As a result, it retains a lot of the things that makes SR great, but it also feels very obviously constrained. I get the impression that this was made because Deep Silver wanted new content for the XBO/PS4 versions of SR4 and gave Volition/High Voltage 10 months and a shoestring budget to do it.
Instead of having set missions, basically the game gives you a new city with a collection of side missions, and once you do enough you trigger events that advance the plot.  This isn't inherently a bad thing, since some of these side missions (like the Hellblazing races and the Torment Fraud minigame) are a lot of fun.  You also get a few new abilities, such as being able to fly (which feels great).  But there isn't enough variety, and by the time you get to the Satan fight you'll be glad it's not dragging itself out any further.
I got this for 5 bucks, and it was definitely worth that price. I'd say it's probably worth $10 or $12 if you're craving more Saints Row. Just don't buy it at full price - wait for a sale.

there are a few funny moments in this and a few badass ones but the amount of "moments" there are is somewhat limited. i can certainly say there was alot of things that caught me off guard during the game and i couldn't help but laugh but then the moment usually went as quickly as it came.

another problem i had was that this game was somewhat short and i had it more or less all finished up in about 4.5 hours. other saints row games have always taken me a fair amount of time and that isn't even including getting collectables. Now, don't let the age or tacky trailers fool you; Crysis, 9 years later, is still a phenomenal game that sent the industry forward. Imagine an FPS that removed most of the stupid cliches of modern FPS games, getting rid of things like "shotguns are short range" and "melee attacks deal 100x damage". When I first hopped into the game, I expected an FPS I would play for 3~ hours and say "eh, it was worth 4 dollars". What I got was a unique experience that left me with a constant desire to replay the game again and again,
GAMEPLAY:
Playing a tad like Far Cry (The developers started the series, featuring huge environment and gameplay similarities) or modern MGS, it allows you to approach enemies with a variety of ways with an INSANE ammount of ways to approach it. It isn't like Dishonored (Which I also highly reccomend) where every option feels forced and in your face; I can switch to Strength mode and knock down a hut, then use the curved roof as a ramp to launch myself out of danger by charging at it in speed mode. Encounter a 3 man patrol? pick up the strongest of the group, switch to strength mode, snap his neck and then toss him at another soldier, before finishing off the last one with a bullet to the head or a punch strong enough to instantly incapitate him. Base surrounded by trip mines? single individual guards out, toss them over the wall, and walk away as his body slides over the mines. Cornered by 4 men and using a box as cover? Switch to Strength mode, smash the box with the butt of a shotgun, then have the now flying box incapitate them all. Small radio station on a hill? lure the opposition into a frail building then smash the roof, causing the building to collapse and kill everyone inside. Taking the high ground to scout is beneficial, as in one situation I spotted a car 'bout half a mile off speeding down the road, allowing me to take the chance to shoot out its tires from a long distance, causing the speeding vehicle to go spiraling into a ditch, killing the crew inside. While scouting, I spotted an attack boat surverying a cargo loading zone. As the boat went further down shore, I dove to the bottom of the seabed. As the boat made its approach, I switched to speed mode and swam upward at superhuman speed, sending me a good 20~ feet out of the water... and allowing me to toss a grenade stright into the boat. Armored patrol of 5 getting out of a car? Strength mode, jump to one side, kill the two koreans and shoot the gunner atop the car, then punch the car hard enough to send it spiraling into the remaining Koreans. Catch a DISGUSTING COMMUNIST taking a leak (Enemies actually do this) at a river? hold him underwater until he drowns.
Needless to say, the game is packed with variety, and even without it, the gunplay, which is phenomenally realistic and enjoyable, would alone make the game worth it.
STORY:
A bit generic on the outside (Crysis 2 and 3 aren't as good but expanded on the story quite well), Crysis' story is quite good, but certainly not the best feature of the game. SPOILERS AHEAD; Technologically advanced Aliens nicknamed the Ceph are advanced to the point of being able to create anything they can think of; so, they turn their minds to things they cannot think of or predict. They send "Colonization pods" to planets that have the potential to host life, with our world being Pod-ed two-million years before Humanity came to exist. In 1912, Richard Hargreave sets out on an expedition with 3 other individuals to Alaska, where there is rumored "riches". What he and his crew discover, however, is a massive ammount of Ceph Technology. Hargreave's two colleagues are heavily injured in the operation, and using alien tech, he saves their lives with reported super-human abilities. Hargreave, being a genius, founds Hargreave Science Corp, and begins to use Ceph technology to create weapontry and amass a fortune. Sometime between 1990 and 2200, Hargreave begins to fear a Ceph awakening and allies Hargreave Science Corp. and the child company Crynet Systems (Hence why "Crysis" is spelt the way it is) with the United States, giving them acess to Nano-Suit technology.  North Korea discovers and alien colonization pod on the Lang Shian Islands and mobilizes the North Korean People's Army to evacuate the island with the intention of utilizing Alien technology to become most advanced civilization and to defeat the United States. However, their intentions are never fufilled, as two elite Nanosuit teams (Team Raptor, Crysis 1, and Team Eagle, Crysis Warhead) defeat massive ammounts of Korean People Army Forces, and combined with the awakening of the Ceph colonization pod, which the main charecter of Crysis 1, Nomad, enters in an attempt to defeat the Ceph. Realizing his efforts are futile, he attempts to escape the pod, only to be met with a Frozen Wasteland created by the Ceph in an attempt to push out human forces. Nomad, Psycho, and Prophet (Nanosuited Individuals) escape the frozen landscape and rejoin eachother on a U.S Battleship, where Nomad is provided an experimental tactical nuke device, and also where the Captain of the ship fails to realize that Ceph absorb energy, foolishly launching a massive nuclear missle into the massive, frozen dome, causing it to massively expand and to trigger the full force of the Ceph invasion. The Ceph assault the ship, and after defeating a massive alien monster called "The Hunter", the ship is attacked by a gigantic alien battleship, witch sinks the ship and is barely defeated by Nomad. This "Victory" is only a small one in a massive war, with more to come in Crysis 2 and 3 (Honestly, just read about the lore. The games are pretty bad and ruined any chance of the series being any good once more)
I hope you've enjoyed my lengthy review. Crysis is easily one of my favorite games of all time, if not THE favorite (Next to New Vegas <3). I'm sure you'll enjoy the game, here are some mods I reccomend;
Blackfire's Mod Ultimate OR CyberAlien's Extreme Immersive mod
Advanced AI
Realistic Enhancement
Rygels HD Texture pack AND HD Crysis Texture Pack 2016
Maximum Immersion
Crysis 2 Nanosuit Voice (Crysis 2 did a lot of things wrong but the suit was awesome)
Enjoy the game!

Recently, there has been a great deal of controversy surrounding "walking simulators", first-person (usually) games with little to no actual interactivity beyond movement. That's about as much as anyone can agree on; people being the opinionated bunch they are, no two people completely agree as to how little interactivity qualifies a "walking simulator", let alone whether such a game is truly a game. I mention this because the debate surrounding "walking simulators" is both extremely important and utterly irrelevant to discussion of The Stanley Parable.
Now, your reaction to that last line was likely something along the lines of: "What do you mean by that, you big old dunce? Either it is relevant or it isn't, you can't have it both ways!", to which I will of course reply by telling you that, as a theoretical reaction, you have no business being so rude. Were I to take such a response seriously, however, I would begin by pointing out the game's official description, which should be listed above. Go on, check. I'll still be here by the time you get back.
Back yet? Good. Now, as even a cursory examination of the "About This Game" section will reveal, this game delights in paradox. The Stanley Parable is, at its core, an examination of choice and linearity in gaming by way of a semi-linear story. Everything about this game is carefully crafted to present possibly the single greatest such examination possible, and yet, in order to do so, the entire game had to be carefully scripted, freed from all but the simplest of needless complications. This is the crucial reason why the game must necessarily be denigrated as a "walking simulator", it is also why it must be glorified for it's self-awareness in willingly imposing the very linearity it mocks. The Stanley Parable is thusly an exemplar and an enemy of its kind, and for its ability to inspire thought and amusement both I implore everyone to experience it. Of course, you don't have to play it. After all, you have free will, don't you, Stanley?
(Also, you totally just read that whole thing in Kevan Brighting's voice, didn't you? Thought so. His narration really is top-notch.)

First off, let me just say that for me Final Fantasy XIII isn't a bad game, but a very disappointing one, and one of the worst main Final Fantasy games. For me, the biggest problem is that the entire game is designed to be a corridor. There's only one big open area, but the rest is just straight pathways, with some minor sideways. There's almost no exploration, which is almost mandatory in an RPG of this caliber. Thankfully, the rest fares a little better, but just by a little. I actually enjoyed the story, but it's a little confusing and most of the characters are uninteresting: both main, side and villains. But i liked how it dealt with human growth and emotions. The voice acting and the character animations are good. The graphics and music are also top-notch, and show it's high production values, especially in the cutscenes. But those aren't the most important things in a game. It's the gameplay. And that's where the game gets divided for me. You may have heard that the game gets good after 20-30 hours. Kinda. After that time, the game introduces it's open area, but if you ignore it, it's more corridors until the end of the game. If you choose to tackle the 64 side missions, prepare to backtrack a lot in corridors. You unlock some fast travel points, but you'll still need to backtrack a lot in boring corridors. And most of the missions aren't interesting. What i'm saying is, the level desing is bad the entire game. What gets good after 20-30 hours is the combat. Until then, you mostly mash the attack button to win. But then, you must truly learn the combat system to defeat the tougher enemies, and then it'll feel more interesting and rewarding. Still, there are more design choices that i don't like: a) the combat is fast paced, so it's hard to control 3 characters at once. But you can't change you main character in battle. b) And if he dies, it's game over. c) There's no penalty for losing a battle, and you can quit and retry if you like. d) Leveling up is simple but you need to manually do it. e) Levelling up weapons and accessories is unnecessarily complicated. f) Summoning is almost pointless. g) There's isn't a replay chapter feature. And it's a shame that the game is purposely designed like this, because there's much potential in here that get's wasted. Despite all this, i enjoyed the game, but less than other Final Fantasy titles. In the end, it's an average game, and i can recommend it for cheap IF this isn't your first Final Fantasy title. Because most of the other titles are way better than this one. I should also mention that this an average PC port. It plays OK, but it could be better optimized.

PROS:

I would compare this game to Hotline Miami like so many other people do, but it's far-off from it.
Not a Hero is a game where you are a amateur campaign manager/assassin tasked with cleaning up crime in the city. Your boss is an anthro rabbit from the future, and he gives you some ridiculous tasks sometimes. In one level you're murdering drug dealers and in the next you're rescuing giant rat heads. Whatever the case, you need to take down crime bosses in the end, specifically a Russian mob boss, a backstreet gang leader, and a triad yakuza boss.
The game is very fast-paced, as I was able to complete the first 2 chapters in only 3 hours. It has the interesting mechanics of ducking for cover and sliding under your enemies to stun them. There are 8 unique characters, each having their own weapon or ability. Cletus wields a shotgun, Ronald uses melee only, ect. One of the more interesting parts of this game is the powerups and usable weapons. With them, you can shoot lasers, explosive rounds, or pretty much anything out of your gun, as well as throw molotovs, ricochet grenades or a cat that explodes near an enemy. There's even secret levels and challenges as you go along, but I could never unlock the secret levels or complete all 3 challenges.
Overall, the game has a nice feel to it, although it would help if the soundtrack was a bit better in some cases. I like the pixel graphics and sidescrolling design of it, and it's always fun to play a political game where you can beat someone's face in with a hammer.
I rate this an 8.5/10. I would reccommend this to my friends.

I really had a lot of expectations, and added it to my wishlist after having watched a trailer and played a demo on the Xbox 360.
Well... after around 35 hours I started wondering how come enemies were becoming stronger and stronger (e.g. 1 hit kill) even though I had a good strategy in place. Let's break the issues down:
- Fighting/Turn based whatever: this is pretty much random. You can attack an enemy, but even though it's your turn sometimes enemies get more turns than you do, and even take your turn! As soon as you reach a level of 25+ and progress through the storyline, then this becomes a problem since you get your a** kicked REALLY badly.
- Grinding: I wandered around a lot in this game, trying to get more XP in order to unlock some magic, special skill, new areas, collectables, and so on, as it is in any RPG. For example, exploring areas around you and encountering enemies is always for the sake of a good battle but.... as you read in my first point, I soon realised that this game is not meant for exploration because exploration means fighting (of course, you meet enemies and even if you try to avoid them, you'll probably end up in a bloody mess with attacks from everywhere), and it's not like the classic role playing gaming you are used to. This game does not want you to explore or fight - which is the main feature of any RPG - , else you end up with a really high level and you are f***ed as every fight will be a disaster and you'll probably end up using a trainer in order to just finish the game and just delete it forever. Ok, you might say that there is a challenge, however there isn't hardly a challenge here; the game is unfair at all levels, the AI will be just concatenating attacks even if it's your turn, and if you want to have great weapons and "hoping" to kick some enemies' a**es , well you can only get those by collecting materials (killing enemies?) and exploring, and then? Ha! Well, then the enemies will level up as well, so it's just a pointless chain.
If you have time to spend, have patience to spend months and months on this game just to reach an ending to a story that is not really that great tbh, and if you don't like classic RPGs, then go ahead. I strongly do not recommend to play this game if you don't want to end up hating RPGs.

TL;DR
Are you looking for a free game that lets you play some simple magic with the new Origins set against a passable AI? Then this game is worth the download.
Are you looking to play some serious MTG? Move along, you're looking for MTGO.
The meaty review.
There's a lot of bad reviews for this game, which all seem to have a few common threads:
1) Poor card selection - It's just the Origins set right now. Yes, the plan is to add more sets as they come out, but that's for the future. I wouldn't bank on it.
2) Server disconnects - Might be a major issue with online play against others, I don't know. I only use this to play against the AI and have had no problems after launch day. If you're looking for online play, do what I do: go play MTGO.
3) Daily quests - The rewards don't scale for the number of wins you need (either 2 or 4 with a specific archetype deck). This is true, but also not really a big deal. Play against the easy AI, it takes about 40 mins to plow through 4 matches. As a side note, these are not bugged. They say "Archetype" deck, which means you have to use the deck builder. The deck builder is garbage. The decks you build will be garbage. Only play against the easy AI and you'll be fine. For the non-win quests (ie Do 30 damage outside of combat quest), it doesn't matter if you win or lose. Build a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ red burn deck with several Into The Maw of Hell cards. Easy to complete in a single match.
4) The AI - Its an AI, it's programattically stupid. If you expect an AI that plays at the same skill as you, you're clearly new to this video game thing.
5) Cost of boosters - They cost 150 coins. That's 30 matches against the easy AI. Or 15 against the medium, or 10 against hard. Not counting the daily quests, which cut that down significantly. And the 5 story campaigns net you about 1100 coins, plus a few free booster packs. So, play the story campaign first, like you're supposed to. That gets you a decent card pool to build a not crappy deck from. Then beat up the AI, get free coins, complete quests, get free coins, buy boosters, improve deck and repeat. Is it going to take you a while to unlock all the cards? It sure is. But when against the AI, who cares? (And if you're looking to compete against other people, again, go play MTGO. If you're willing to drop actual money for cards? Go play MTGO.)
6) This game is really limited and only of value to new players who've never played MTG before - Yes, and? You expected it to be more than that? When the explicitly stated purpose of Duels (both the video games and physical deck versions) is to get new players started on MTG. You seem to be confusing this game with (wait for it).....MTGO.
So, I recommend this game for people who want to play some simple Magic against an AI for free and nothing more.

I loved Saints Row IV. I played the hell out of it, doing every side mission, spending hours upgrading every weapon, customising my character, vehicles and upgrading my abilities and powers. I loved the writing, the antagonist, the loyalty missions and the radio stations. It was one of my most favourite games of the 2013.
Gat Out of Hell is such a disappointment and it left me feeling very sad, with no desire to play on after spending just a couple of hours on the side missions and basically stumbling upon the ending without realising it. It lacks so much of the joy and love that SRIV had. It's stripped of any customisation, the missions are generic and all of the loyalty missions are exactly the same. The writing was a big let down too, with a lot of the comedy hit and miss. The musical was great, but it was a complete contrast to the rest of the game. It didn't feel natural or absurd. It felt more of a sweet release from an otherwise dull atmosphere.
The lazy excuse to "remove all sins" from the citizens of hell, simply so they can get away with using the same model for every pedestrian adds to the feeling of a very unloved game. I feel like the ambition of taking the Saints to hell was let down by either timing issues, budget or just the team wasn't up to it.
It's Saints Row 4 without the customisation, the writing, the diversity of the loyalty missions, the range of assets and the radio. It's Saints Row 4 on a budget, which leaves me asking whether Saints Row is actually any good without those things. Gat Out of Hell answered that for me. It simply left me feeling very disappointed and with just 4 hours of gameplay, I feel like I've done everything I wanted to do in that game and instead would rather go have some more fun in Saints Row 4.

Its likely you may experience three stages of Sid Meiers Civilization: Beyond Earth.
Stage 1: Bewilderment.
With a new tech tree, coupled with a new virtue system and coupled again with an affinity system; the first dozen hours or so of this game is really a feet finding exercise. Its slow and not very exciting. Without its grounding in the real world, like the other CIVs, certain aspects of your development may not make much sense, or, may ultimately be a bit trivial.
Stage 2: Epicness
Once you start experiencing a few different ways to play the game then the next task is to make your way through the different victory types. Completing these for the first time is where the real appeal of this game lies. Domination/Conquest still exists in this game, but alongside this are four new victory types. Three based on advancing through the three different affinities; and a fourth victory unattached to any affinity (or so its designed - I believe you will complete this victory earlier if you follow the Supremacy affinity, but anyway...). These victories are more esoteric than previous CIVs, and along with a quest system,  makes Beyond Earth a more exploratory colonization sim, rather than a combative strategy game. This stage of Beyond Earth may last 15-25 hours depending on which speed/map size you choose
Stage 3: Boredom
Yes, Im afraid so. Once you've learnt the victories and experienced the quests, the game doesnt have the breadth to keep you as occupied ad previous CIVs, particularly CIV 4. It also seems to be lacking in any real motivation to develop strategies, which is probably its main downfall. There is some variety in its maps, but not enough to recommend this as a game to replace whatever CIV it is you're playing at the moment.
Overall, the game is quite pretty and atmospheric and that does make it appealing. However, although superficially the idea to split the tech tree into three components (a smaller tech tree, the affinities and the virtues) seems like an advancement; in fact the idea is a bit tepid because there are no real interesting advancements to make at any point in the game. You advance slowly and uninterestingly. Also note that the update has slowed the game down even more. It takes longer to rank up in affinities, ergo it takes longer to complete the victories. The game isnt awful, but its not massively interesting.

I heard about Hollow Knight through chatter on the internet. "It's the 2D Dark Souls!" was the common theme. It got mentioned often enough that when I saw it on sale for $10 I thought 'Sure, lets see what the fuss is about.' I'm really glad I did. This game is Metroidvania at its finest.
Exploring the world of Hallownest is a pure pleasure. Normally I'm not one for these types of game either, I tend to find the constant backtracking tedious and get frustrated with the Dark Souls level of challenge (I'm not the finest of gamers, fully admit this!) but Hollow Knight enchanted me. The world is lovingly crafted and fit together smartly, you'll constantly find yourself spilling into areas through new paths you didn't know existed. The game is non-linear allowing freedom in what avenues you take, I missed an entire starter area and wondered why I had no where to spend my money for the first eight hours I played...
If you enjoy exploring, atmosphere and, of course, challenge, Hollow Knight is a must buy.

If you are a fighting game enthusiast, then, by all means, you should get this game. The mechanics are solid, the gameplay is unique and tight, and the charcters are fun different from any other fighting game I have played.
However, if you are a casual gamer, then this game simply does not have enough content for you. There are very few things in which you can do -- a very short 30 minute story mode, an online versus mode with very competent players, and a rather dull "Abyss" mode that you can play infinitely -- that would make this game worth it to anyone who does not play games for the competition.
Furthermore, I had purchased this game in early access when it had first come out. For some reason, upon release, I was locked from two of the characters and several of the new stages and had to grind for an in-game currency in order to unlock them. This mechanic is not fun, nor is it needed, as there is not nearly enough content to make this currency remotely useful.
I also had grand hopes for the characters I had grown to love through playing the simple versus modes during early access, but after trudging through the childish writing for the story mode I have become detached. I expected tales of the betrayal between two brothers after one dabbles in forbidden smoke elements, the grand leader of the fire nation to lead conquest upon the lands only to meet head-to-head with the inhabitants of the wild forest, and for every character to be fighting for life and limb. But, instead, my favorite character is reduced to nothing than a pet animal, important characters become meaningless minions to a faceless empire, and everything adds up to an unsatisfyingentity against some god. No opposition whatsoever, and I am not sure "Rivals" is a fitting title for this game.
However, this is a game meant for competitive spirits and seekers of glory. If you do not wish for either of these things and want a game full of story and content, you are best looking elsewhere. If your concern is purely mechanical gameplay, then this game can fulfill that.

Pretty much one of the best platformers I've ever played. It's difficult, challenging - time by time frustrating as hell - but overall addictive and I'm having a lot of fun with it. It's satisfying to see how you get better and better, how the bosses get easier once you understand their pattern and progress in the game. And how much faster you get once you've done something once and start the game all over.
However, there are some bosses and platforming parts that frustrated me so much I had to quit the game and try again some hours later. Still haven't done everything 100%, but I'll get there.
The story is... well, first I was pretty bored by it but once I understood exactly what's going on in the game I noticed how deep, wonderful and also how sad it is. The more you know about it, the better and the more tragic it gets. At some points I had a tear or two in my eyes.
The combat is very simple, but it's great how much was made out of it. A controller is heavily recommended and sometimes I saw exactly why, but a keyboard is fine as well, especially with custom keybindings (which I appreciate a lot).
Also I'm personally a big fan of the graphic style, it's not as grey and monotonous as it might appear at first and I love the effects of attacks, the sparkles and the colors.
A big plus are the DLCs - the new one (Grim Troupe) is very nice, especially considering it's for free.
I'd recommend it to anyone who's not too afraid of challenges (even though that's pretty subjective) and is willing to learn attacks and patterns and improve their own playstyle.
