For me, this is a difficult game to review. This is the closest thing I have to a guilty pleasure as the open world is repetitive and dull, the combat is one-sided and stacked against you and the story makes little sense. And here I am with over 80 hours in it and another 20-30 likely to come soon.
I'll start by stating that I have never played a Final Fantasy game that isn't 13, so if that changes the context of this review, so be it. That said, this game makes me want to and I have already bought 13-2.
Before I talk about the problems with this game, I'll try to explain why I've sunk so much time into it. It is stunningly pretty; just ordinary gameplay is beautiful with a nice variety of colours, tones and eye-catching set pieces. While a lot of the enemies are over-designed so you have no idea if what you're looking at is a head or an arm, the lead characters each have their own aesthetics that speak of the fashion of the FFXIII world. As bizarre as JRPG clothing usually is, I really like the design choices that went into the protagonists.
But where the game comes alive is in the pre-rendered cutscenes. Holy crap, they are stunning. I took 701 screenshots over the course of the main story (admittedly that's kinda par for the course for me), but the majority of them were in cutscenes. I cannot really convey how nice to watch these cutscenes are, so go check out the opening cinematic for the game.
The only downside of the cutscenes is that a couple have SO MUCH going on that it's hard to follow; these were the ones where my screenshots caught only blur and semi-obscured characters. They were so desperate to show activity and movement that they don't linger on anything and that's a shame.
The gameplay of FFXIII is split between 'open world' running and the combat. Neither is perfect. By which I mean that both kinda suck. Aside from the rather petty complaint of all the characters having really loud footfalls (actually, the whole sound balancing was off on this port), the main problem with the 'open world' is how linear it is. You have to run down long corridors formed of walkways, tunnels or just convenient debris. You meet enemies who just stand there and wait for you, staring right at you under six feet away and doing nothing until you take that step too close. And you drift.
I assume it's a problem with the port as I don't recall it on the PS3 version (I played the first 15 hours or so on PS3 before getting bored), but if you press forward you drift to the left or right. Running in a straight line, even down straight corridors, is impossible. You can alter whether you drift left or right, but the little dotted line on the minimap showing where you've been will always be a zigzag. It's not game-breaking, but it's bloody annoying.
I've heard it said that "it gets good 20 hours in"; this is when the tight corridors open up into a large area with side quests, but for me that was 40 hours in. By then I knew I was hooked, but the opening doesn't make as big a change as I thought. It's just one big area with a load of corridors coming off it to any other area. The final 2 chapters just go right back to narrow and confined.
The combat also has a lot to answer for. God, I could write a whole essay on why the FFXIII combat is bad, but I'll give you the brief version. It's real time combat with time-based elements. This means that if you sit there and do nothing, the enemy will keep attacking you. The time-based elements are that it takes time to charge up your attacks; any attacks. Each attack is worth a different quantity of 'attack bars' with more powerful attacks requiring more bars and thus more idle time to use.
The problem with this is that you have no time. A massive focus of the combat is winning as quickly as possible; the combat scoring system that affects item drops requires you to win quicker than a set time. This on its own wouldn't be too bad but, given the range of abilities available, the daunting weakness/strength system and the terrible menu-based combat (the kind that fits perfectly in turn-based combat), it's impossible to fight most enemies with anything other than auto-choose attacks. Luckily the auto-choose AI is pretty good; it always calculates the most effective moves and uses them, taking into account damage, weakness, buffs etc.
But there are other elements to the combat...random elements that you have absolutely no way to control. A number of attacks (both yours and the enemies') are proximity-based; some heal the characters near the medic, some deal massive damage to targets directly in front etc. But you have no way to affect where your characters or the enemies stand. Depending on where the mindless AI decides to let your team charge their attacks, you may be excluded from healing, clumped up to receive a powerful AoE attack or simply ignored.
On top of this is the decision to make your party leader all-important. If either of your two companions are killed, drop a revive on them and boom, right back into the fray. If your leader is killed, sorry that's it. Game Over. Retry?
Who thought that was logical? Yeah, I've heard of FF characters forgetting to revive outside of combat (Sorry, Aeris), but not being able to do it in combat, just because the arbitrary leader was downed? Rubbish.
Oh. And having an unskippable animation for switching character roles mid-battle - WHEN THE ENEMY WILL STILL ATTACK DURING IT - is moronic. I've lost more than once because my leader was killed while the medic was posing.
I've already said that the story doesn't make a lot of sense. That's an understatement. You find out nothing until a good ten hours into the game and then it spoon feeds you a tiny bit at a time and gives you the equivalent of a book to read in the 'Datalog'; a menu with paragraphs of information about the characters, places, concepts and...stuff you encounter. This system is poor storytelling because anyone without the patience to read it all will be lost.
Character motivations are rarely fully explained and this may be because of some translation thing, but most likely it's supposed to make everyone seem that little bit mysterious. It's more annoying than anything. Most motivations come through by the end, but vast portions of the plot are driven by characters doing the exact things they said they wouldn't...so...maybe I just didn't understand.
All that said, I couldn't stop playing until I found out how it all ended. Sometimes it's the lure of 100% completion that keeps me going, sometimes it's gripping gameplay. In this case it was the mysteries of the story and a growing wonder about how the characters' stupid actions would somehow save the day.
From everything I've written, you're probably wondering why this is a positive review. Simply because I still want to play more. Yeah, the open world is a lie and the combat is stacked; I didn't even go into how most of the boss fights are just puzzles on unusual ways to use your combination of character roles. But after all of that I want to return to the bits I missed and finish them.
Some part of me really enjoys this game and, while I'm unlikely to replay it any time soon, I still have a full 24 hours' worth of entertainment to get out of it.

This game brings contradicting feelings. On one side, it is a fabulous incantation of the "metroidvania" genre, of which Super Metroid was my first one, in the SNES console. Hollow Knight is a game that I enjoyed during every minute, in a very consistent way. However, for me it also becomes a frustrating piece of ... when it comes the time to fight some bosses.
The thing is, this game's flow gets totally broken at boss fights: the pace, rhythm and fight skills learned during the normal advancement of the levels is totally different than the skills needed for them. So after enjoying a very pleasant 30 minutes of advancing through unexplored tunnels, you'll encounter another 30 (or much more) of constantly repeating the same fight once and again, and constantly dying against a foe that moves too fast and hits too strong.
Most bosses appear in a moment where they are not really mandatory to fight against, and you can walk around them and come at a later time when your equipment and fighting abilities have been improved. But in my opinion, this is not enough. The playing style that the game teaches you to use goes out of the window when facing bosses: in a closed space, attacking you so intensely that you don't even have time to heal yourself- a game mechanic which is prominent during the rest of the adventure. Yes, if you are stuck I can give you this advice: healing during boss fights is kind of a red herring in this game. Of course, some bosses are so intense that you'll pretty much get hit all the time except if you have perfect reflexes, so good luck with that. It had been a long, really long time since last time I rage-quitted a game, and Hollow Knight made me do it in multiple occasions.
On the other hand, this game is so enjoyable during the rest of the time, that I tend towards recommending it even if the mentioned pain points could ruin the satisfaction for some people.
Exploration is very good, and all unlockables are well disseminated over the whole world map, making it a joy to enter unexplored areas as it will most of the times end up with a power-up or collectionable of some kind. Of course, this game uses the traditional formula of soft-locking different pathways and whole areas behind skill barriers: you'll be able to access whenever you acquire some specific skill. The game also provides a pretty big map with a fast-travel system between areas.
There is a nice game mechanic that gives significance to the fact of dying, as you'll need to get back to where it happened if you want to recover your previous belongings and health capacity. Some people have complained about this, and it is true that it can get a bit bothering if you die a long way from where last saved, but if one is conscious about advancing safely, it shouldn't be too hard to avoid dying a lot.

I tried to love this game, but it's a gigantic mess. You spend most of the game wandering through cartoonishly oversized levels punctuated by arena fights. These fights are usually fun (although an all-orange cast makes identifying your foes a challenge) but the combat system is poorly thought out. You have a variety of moves and weapons but your windup and weapon switch times are too long to do proper combos, with no way to cancel moves together either. This is backed by a gargantuan upgrade tree that's half-full of useless moves, along with a scoring system that never teaches you how to master it. There's a plot, but it's buried under confusing cinematics and an absurd degree of seriousness for a game that bills itself as a campy FPS throwback. Even Lo Wang's character can barely stay consistent in the same cutscene. Next time a game spams "press any key to skip" messages on every single cutscene I'll take it up on the offer. Overall, I like the ideas here, but the execution is abysmal.

Buyer beware! (minor, vague spoilers follow, just thought I'd mention that to those who are.. picky.)
Many people expecting the gameplay of previous games in the series WILL be severely disappointed. X:Rebirth has apparently attempted a new, and poorly informed direction, and no one knows why.
As a first time X series player, with no previous expectations, I am superbly put off by this game, and shocked that they are allowed to charge the price that they do for this amount of low quality.
Let's outline some of the areas where you'll probably be annoyed.
First thing's first, as you take control of your ship, you immediately notice the horrible voice acting and rotten, choppy framerate.
I have an obscenely well built custom computer which i take a bit of pride in, and running the game on maximum graphics causes it to have a choppy, unplayable framerate. Every so often, you notice the graphics engine seems to 'derail' and send you into the abyss of poorly rendered polygon shadows.
Voice clips are often choppy, low quality, and poorly cut. I know quite a bit about remixing music and post processing, and the effort is not to spec at all. By your fifth, 'Now shut up, betty!' you'll understand what I mean.
Repeated, annoying animations, and floating text that will not go away plague you, as you try to understand the complicated nature of the menus which are not logically arranged at all. You feel right away that this game was meant for a console.
Soldiering on, you go to your first station. You are assigned a kill mission, and just as you engage your opponent, the game locks up. Your first crash sets you back about an hour. Mostly due to the painfully slow flight speed of your bucket of bolts called a ship.
You get back to your bounty mission, and your bounty target is now attacking you. You put it down with ease, yet score a plethora of friendly fire hits on the friendly station, which now starts attacking you. Oh yes, some real thought was put into this game.
Reload your save, you restart the bounty mission, which has changed, and start thinking about how you're going to kill a giant freighter with your small peashooter laser.. so you think you need some new guns first. I did.
There are no ship customizations, or upgrades beyond that of 5-6 core weapons (which span from mark 1 to mark 3), 4-5 projectile (missile type) weapons and 3 types of forcefields to choose from. Engines and scanners are upgradeable however this is where you notice the cost..
And start to try to create your own trade empire. Or would, rather, if you could get past the first tutorial mission where you are guided through a 'trade'. Your first freighter seems to get stuck on 'Follow' mode, and will never release.
There is no 'cancel order' or 'cancel last trip' command. So once this happens, you had better have a save or else your game is kaput, as you now have no hope of acquiring currency en masse. Even if you do buy another freighter and get something going, it eventually locks into the 'follow albion skunk' command.
At this point, I became frustrated and tossed in the towel. I'm a guy known for liking complex, absurdly large learning curve games, but this isn't a game.
It's a piece of junk that the developer is scrambling to repair before people turn away from their company, for good.
And because I'm slightly insane, I loaded the game again, jumped into a superhighway, and got randomly dumped into space 1.4M KM away from anywhere, with no jump drive. That's about when I hit my threshold. This apparently 'rare' bug, is just one of many waiting to frustrate you.
People, I implore you. Understand that even a RUDIMENTARY quality control program would have prevented any of these issues from occurring, but this developer seems to be lacking in common sense.
I feel like I've been the victim of a scam, as I paid decent money for what I was to understand was a working product, yet received a game that should still be in alpha, or earlier.
If they had stated 'Well we're doing an alpha early-access' that would have been fine with me. But I would not have paid 40 bucks for it, let me tell you.
Don't make my mistake. Turn your back on this one, and walk away.
Though, there is one thing they got right, naming the first ship you get 'Albion Skunk' cause this game just stinks. (they're not getting a point for that though.)
And I'm afraid no amount of patching is going to erase that stink, since the flaws are on a fundamental, conceptual level.

IGN said it best when they said " 'This War of Mine' might be the war game we need." I will go one step further and say it
the war game we need.
You take the role of citizens of the city of Pogoren, trapped in a bitter feud between militia-rebels and soldiers. Unlike any game I've played or heard of, neither side is "good" nor is either side "bad". Your job is to survive the bloody conflict. Every single day is a struggle to survive. Who gets to eat? Who gets to sleep in a bed? Who has to risk their life at night to go out into the city? And most importantly of all, can we take life of an innocent? All these are questions you'll ask yourself every day.
Before you begin 'This War of Mine' I highly suggest you attempt to get into character. Don't go in thinking "Oh they're just pixels." Put yourself in the shoes of each of your survivors and attempt to think what you would do. You'll find yourself truly asking yourself the tough questions you hoped you'd never have to ask.
I can't recommend "This War of Mine" enough. I will not say I was brought to tears, but this game has made me question what I am capable of. "War is Hell," said Sherman, and he was right. 'This War of Mine' does a better job depicting war than any game to date. There is no glamour, there is no honor. There is survival, and in the end that's all you can ask for.

Like last year's 2015 Duels of the Planeswalkers, Magic Duels seems to be suffering from a serious case of "One step forward, two steps back".
Wizards has taken the brave new step of making the yearly Duels installment into a free-to-play service, that they've promised to continually update. The cost for this, however, is a punishingly slow unlock structure, that is made even more frustrating because of the low power levels they stick you with at the beginning.
As an example of how slow you can expect to unlock things in this game: I've spent 4 hours and have earned enough in-game currency to purchase 3 packs, i.e. 18 cards.
The Story mode is an attempt to fill in some of the back story of the various Planeswalkers, but it is generally an exercise in frustration. You are forced to use deliberately underpowered decks against competent AI with access to far better cards than you, which translates to you praying heavily on RNG for a chance to progress. I hope you enjoy trying to use Lilian's Black Cats to fend off an army of opposing Angels.
All in all, there is very little to recommend for this. I understand that Wizards is reluctant to sacrifice the profitability of their existing Magic Online and paper card game platforms, but Magic Duels is hardly going to put a dent in the online CCG space that Hearthstone dominates.

The story is also worth it, especially if you are invested in the franchise. The President (which, by the way, is your SR4 character if you happened to play it beforehand) is abducted by Satan. Gat and Kinzie goes to hell, literally, and meets Dane and a bunch of other characters. I won't spoil them for you, considering that's half of the fun of discovering them. The ending is the kicker: you get to choose it and you'll get snippets of how some lose ends are tied up. (Loved the first ending with Gat, so heartwarming.)
It will last you a solid 6 hours, more if you want to complete the game.
Should I recommend this game?
YES.
Play it if you want the thrill of open world sims like GTA or Infamous, or are already heavily invested in the Saints Row universe.
Don't play it if: you don't like Saints Row humor, wanted a more solid experience from an open world sim, or comparing it to Saints Row 2/GTA, because there is no comparison to be made.

This is my re-review of Magic Duels after playing it for a few weeks now. I am only comparing this to the former versions of Duels of the Planeswalkers and not to Magic Online or the original paper game.
The Good:
- Actual Deckbuilding with a decent card pool.
- Can actually dictate what lands to tap for mana (I remember earliar versions doing this automatically).
- Getting packs actually doesn't take that long compared to other FTP games.
- Collecting the whole set isn't that hard since packs only give you cards you do not have. After you get a                             playset of everything you will never need to get a new pack until the next set is released.
- While the pool is a bit simple and limited, I still find that there are plenty of decks to build that are both fun and competitve.
- Story mode is interesting and fun for the most part. Some of decks are laughably bad however.
The Bad:
- UI needs some work: Spell lands won't stop glowing red when trying to tap mana so it is hard to tell if you will tap it on accident, selecting cards for spells that are near each other is difficult, selecting cards from draw effects is difficult sometimes since your hand goes away and the board is covered up, and another glaring issue is the deck building screen is atrocious!
- Seriously the Deck Builder is just that bad that I have to talk about it even more now. It is obivously made with consoles in mind but even then it is terrible. Why couldn't they make it a big list instead of some crappy slideshow? Makes it hard to remember what is in your deck even while you are crafting it.
- Don't get me started on their Deck "Wizard" that tries to guide you through the process. It will always choose completely random cards that barely fit theme it wants you to make while bogging it down with overcosted fatties. Forget about it noticing you have no removal and about ten 5 costed creatures!
- Server problems abound! It seems to have stabilzed for now but getting into a game with a real person takes multiple searches and a lot of times lags to high hell.

- If you concede in a player match the match continues! AI takes over! Why? Just end the match who thought this was okay?
I think you may have noticed that my bad list is far more expansive than the good but I still recommend playing! Most of these problems are minor gripes with the only big issues being the AI taking over games and the server issues. I defintely see the conession AI being taken out and the servers will get better over time.
All in all. This is the cheapest way to play Magic, period.
Highly recommend if you are a fan of Civ games.

I've played magic for years.  The experience I've gotten out of this game so far has been dismal at best.
To initially earn some gold to purchase a few card packs a player will naturally start with the story mode.  In story mode there are some instances in which fights at the beginning of a character's story are considerably harder to win than the fights at the end of their story.   You will be completely at the mercy of the RNG gods and they will frown on you numerous times.  Then when you win a particularly difficult battle you may find yourself being told to reconnect which 50% of the time will result in your win not being recorded, you receiving no gold reward, and you having to repeat that battle if you want to progress.
When you move on to playing real people you will be a level 0 player with barely more than the base set of cards and will find yourself being matched up with players as much as (and possibly more than) 15 levels higher than you.  They will have all the advantages you would expect them to have (greater card diversity, better combinations, higher value to mana cost).
You are not able to pre-shuffle sort your deck.  This means you cannot follow the common practice of spacing out your mana across the deck and as a result you will find yourself either drowning in mana but starved for cards to cast with it or drowning in cards to cast but starved for mana more frequently than you would playing the real game.  You will of course also not be able to place relevant cards beside each other in hopes of increasing your chances in getting a good shuffle.
For fans of drafts this game has.... nothing.  There is no drafting at all.  Even if it's implemented in some way in the future consider the following:
The effort and time required to grind the cost of playing will of course be designed to encourage you to pay rather than grind.
If you do decide to but cards then you'll find a 6 pack is $1.99 USD. That makes the per-card cost for these virtual cards more than the per-card cost of real physical cards.  Unlike the real physical cards these ones have absolutely no resale value, no collectors value, and can't be traded with other players.
If you've never played magic before, this can teach you about the basic phases of a turn and about different card abilities.  After which you may as well uninstall it and check online if there are any game stores near you that host Draft nights for the real game because:
It will have a greater return per time invested ratio.
You won't spend 4 hours grinding out the same amount of cards that an hour of going to work can earn you.
Cards you actually pay for will cost you less money.
You will learn more about strategy and deck building from talking to the other players at a draft night than you will from playing this game.
You will be able to trade cards with other players.
And finally....
If you eventually tire of it you will be able to sell your cards and recoup some or all of your investment (if you pull some rare/valuable cards from packs you might even get back more than your initial investment).
Would fight a battle with the odds stacked against, finally win after over an hour, find out I've been DCed and the results weren't saved, and then go play hearthstone again.

Where do you even start... I read, that the whole development of this game was quite a mess with dev team not knowing what they want and how they want to do whatever they do. And you can see the results of that - FFXIII is an expensive mess of good and horrible ideas mixed together and executed mediocre at best.
Story starts horribly, then actually tries to redeem itself with interesting ideas and some character growth that makes unbearable characters interesting... only then to start backtracking on itself and repeating the same lines and silliness over and over and over and l'cie fal'cie enemies of cocoon focus. Which, I guess, perfectly fits the story where characters ultimately don't know what they're doing and why up until the very last cutscene.
Mechanically it's an attempt to fit ideas of FF8, 10 and 12 together with some concepts from The Last Remnant into one thing, but failing spectecularly at doing so. Where FF8 ideas were fresh and concepts interesting (and later evolved further in Parasite Eve and Vagrant Story), here they feel like blind attempts at coping something you don't understand. Where 10 (which, I must add, I don't particularly like and haven't finished yet) tries to make leveling up go interesting ways, here crystalium is just a thing made up to look like it gives you more choice than it really does and surves no real tactical purpose up until the end, where it can, but really doesn't. Where in 12 automating characters in battles was a clever game of making interesting algorithms and made combat fast (as it happened without loadings) but strategic, FFXIII feels like boring battle of attrition with load times for battles (so I got bored and started outright cheating, not because there was any kind of "challenge", but simply because I wanted all of this to end faster). Where Last Remnant actually tried to make some fresh and clever additions to battles with units instead of characters fighting and you having more overall control of the characters, paradigms don't feel all that interesting and fights, despite cool animations and all, don't feel any more epic than they are. Also, corridors up until the very end, where the game "opens up" for one chapter, by which I mean creates few areas specifically for grinding and doing "missions" so the grinding is less boring. It's all optional, thankfully, but still adds up to the annoyance about the overall direction of the game.
Overall, the game feels like a giant time waste built on ruins of amazing ideas that could make FFXIII a very interesting game. Both gameplay-wise and story-wise it shows glimpses of great ideas that got buried under frustrating and ultimately boring and pointless experience. If you want to try it because it's FF... well, you still will, I did after all. If you want to try it because you heard it's bad - don't, it's not entertainingly bad, just boring bad. And if you just want to know the story... I don't think the game does truly know it's story, so playing won't help much.

Final Fantasy XIII is a fun game, and it has it's moments. It helped me relax in a difficult time, so I can't fault the game too much and I'm glad I bought it for just that reason.
==Story== -- Alright.
It's not translated particularly well. The voice actors are LAUGHABLE most of the time. There are some bits where good writing shines through and makes sense. This isn't your childhood Final Fantasy - very much in the style of the sort of emo-hipster Final Fantasy, post-FF9. Still, FFXIII takes itself seriously enough to avoid the travesty of being grouped among titles like FF7: Advent Children or Gynysys. There's some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥izations of the IP, like some strange thing they did with Chocobos halfway through my play time.
I liked enough of what I played, although FFXIII doesn't make a whole lot of sense most of the time, but have little desire to finish this title. I was ready to end the game where I was, but appearently there's another 20-60 hours of game after where I stopped, and thinking about grinding up levels and sitting through a few cringworthy scenes is offputting. I'm thinking about finishing it now, though.
==Gameplay== -- Alright.
FFXIII is emenesely long, too long for me to really care. It reminds me of Final Fantasy 12, except things actually happen between the begining and end of this FF.
The gameplay is samey, but fun enough, and makes you think a little bit. After two months or more of not playing, then coming back to this title, I had NO IDEA how to play it. I quit for a good long while because suddenly I realised I wasn't leveled enough or not using the right strategy to kill a boss.
I do remember that the roll switching mechanic seemed unneeded, but I enjoyed leveling my characters though progression often felt linear and highly prone to min-maxing.
==Tech== -- Meh.
Performance is okay on my PC, and a lot of issues were fixed since launch.. such as resolution and crashes. But there's still weird issues, like the ESC key being bound to crash the game. But they fixed it so a menu pops to ask if you want to quit if that key is pressed. However, this doesn't work well everywhere; for example, using it on the main menu causes performance issues or at least requires a lot of tabbing.
FFXIII takes up way too much space. 50GBs for one game? Is this the Xbox One? This is mostly because cutscenes weren't compressed at all, and each video file is 5gigs. That's more than movies I have saved on my HDD, for one ~14 second clip. I'm not sure how avoidable that is.
It looks impressive enough, and I find it hard to believe this was a PS3 game. Does it look better than PS3, I wonder? If so, I'm a little more impressed with this port, just with the fact that the PC port team tried at all.
==Overall== -- Reasonable.
I enjoyed what I got out of this game, and think it was more or less worth what I paid for it. I find it difficult to find cheap-ish games that give me a solid 20 of play time, and this one boasts quite a bit more than that if one can stand it.
18 hrs and I beat the game. It is an okay game that is a cult classic.

I liked this game a lot, mostly due in part to the amazing soundtrack (Which I have no idea if it is original or not) incredibly smooth controls, and tough but extremely rewarding gameplay.
+The music is fast paced and really goes with the flow of the game.
+The game runs incredibly smooth with no lag on most systems and the controls are extremely responsive.
+The gameplay is extremely rewarding with great animations.
+Has great secret levels and other little things.
+Running through a hallway full of gangsters and killing people while dupstep/chiptune music plays in the background is both horribly immoral and amazing.
+Each of the characters offers a unique experience.
+The breaks from gameplay at the restaurant are a nice touch.
+The story was decent in an exaggerated and somewhat satirical way.
-I felt that a lot of the humor this game has to offer is overshadowed by the fast paced and tough as nails gameplay. Whenever I beat a level I usually skipped most of the restaurant cutscene because I just wanted to play the next level. It was hard to listen to the jokes the game was throwing at me while I was hard-pressed trying not to get shot.
-The gameplay was extremely frustrating to the point of being unfair, mostly due to the fact that I was trying to get Global Megalord on each level. I was experiencing a few cheap deaths and a a lot challenges were enraging to say the least. One checkpoint on each level would have made this more fun and less infuriating.
- I found that either Mike is extremely overpowered, or the others are very underpowered. I was using Mike to beat most of the levels and I wanted a reason to use the other characters.
- The game could get repetitive at times. Most of the side challenges were used on multiple occasions. The challenges were usually something like this: Collect this thing, get a kill streak, kill multiple people in a short amount of time, collect all of the power-ups, kill this dude, kill people using executions or critical hits, etc.
- Little to no replayability once you get Global Megalord on each level.
To summarize it:
Great music
Frustrating, tough, rewarding gameplay
Multiple characters
Sarcastic and humorous storyline
Kinda repetitive
Very small amount of replayability.
Above all, this game deserves way, WAY more attention. I would highly recommend getting this while it is on sale.

I've played magic for years.  The experience I've gotten out of this game so far has been dismal at best.
To initially earn some gold to purchase a few card packs a player will naturally start with the story mode.  In story mode there are some instances in which fights at the beginning of a character's story are considerably harder to win than the fights at the end of their story.   You will be completely at the mercy of the RNG gods and they will frown on you numerous times.  Then when you win a particularly difficult battle you may find yourself being told to reconnect which 50% of the time will result in your win not being recorded, you receiving no gold reward, and you having to repeat that battle if you want to progress.
When you move on to playing real people you will be a level 0 player with barely more than the base set of cards and will find yourself being matched up with players as much as (and possibly more than) 15 levels higher than you.  They will have all the advantages you would expect them to have (greater card diversity, better combinations, higher value to mana cost).
You are not able to pre-shuffle sort your deck.  This means you cannot follow the common practice of spacing out your mana across the deck and as a result you will find yourself either drowning in mana but starved for cards to cast with it or drowning in cards to cast but starved for mana more frequently than you would playing the real game.  You will of course also not be able to place relevant cards beside each other in hopes of increasing your chances in getting a good shuffle.
For fans of drafts this game has.... nothing.  There is no drafting at all.  Even if it's implemented in some way in the future consider the following:
The effort and time required to grind the cost of playing will of course be designed to encourage you to pay rather than grind.
If you do decide to but cards then you'll find a 6 pack is $1.99 USD. That makes the per-card cost for these virtual cards more than the per-card cost of real physical cards.  Unlike the real physical cards these ones have absolutely no resale value, no collectors value, and can't be traded with other players.
If you've never played magic before, this can teach you about the basic phases of a turn and about different card abilities.  After which you may as well uninstall it and check online if there are any game stores near you that host Draft nights for the real game because:
It will have a greater return per time invested ratio.
You won't spend 4 hours grinding out the same amount of cards that an hour of going to work can earn you.
Cards you actually pay for will cost you less money.
You will learn more about strategy and deck building from talking to the other players at a draft night than you will from playing this game.
You will be able to trade cards with other players.
And finally....
If you eventually tire of it you will be able to sell your cards and recoup some or all of your investment (if you pull some rare/valuable cards from packs you might even get back more than your initial investment).
Would fight a battle with the odds stacked against, finally win after over an hour, find out I've been DCed and the results weren't saved, and then go play hearthstone again.

So, overall, this was 12 hours of hilarious fun. I honestly didn't think Volition would be able to top some of the insanity in SR4 but --- well. A musical number. I guess that sums up the crazy in this one.
Gat out of Hell isn't without faults, though. I had a few game crashes, predominantly during survival missions. I also think the flight/sprint mechanic desperately needs a toggle option because you spend twelve f'ing hours holding a button to maintain flight/spring (as you do in SR4, also a mistake) and that's just no fun. Most of the activities are just reskins of previous ones from earlier games, though the Salvation version was a definitely a twist from previous iterations. It would've been nice to have an activity that really keyed into the aspect of "hey, we're in hell!" (though the Fraud activity was in the right spirit, since it involves saving three former characters from previous games). I really missed the radio option too, though the BGM of the game was really good. But imagine (well, if the licensing was worth it, anyway) turning on the classic rock station and hearing "Highway to Hell" or "The Number of the Beast" on the metal station or even the "Devil's Trill" on the classical station (not to mention what sort of weird commercials of dj talk could be used). It's not a huge thing but the lack of the radio (and the in-jokes that could be made) seems a little like a missed opportunity. Finally, even though the game lampshades it, the abitrary nature of when the story missions progress was a bit problematic, as each step (at least until the last mission) would interrupt my progress in activities or diversions.
One thing that I wasn't expecting but really liked is the way Volition stuck to using "they/them" as gender-neutral pronouns when refering to the Boss/President, so as not to break immersion (you know, like when you pick the female PC option and everyone basically refers to you as a dude? That happens in so many games? Yeah, that.). There was one instance I caught with a "he" instead of a "they" but I appreciated the effort.
I definitely recommend this game and DEFINITELY recommend keeping a save right before you go to confront Satan, so you can see all five different endings (the retconed canon one is probably my favorite).

Magic Duels is the first online card game I have ever played. BUT Magic the Gathering I have been playing since 7th edition came out, ( when the thorn elemental holographic was the featured card ) This game introduces the card game of Magic the Gathering through a campign system of story telling of the 5 most famous of planeswalkers. ( epic mages/warriors of their class that can shift into other planes of exhistints.) Each planeswalker has his own color/deck that you use in their campign. You then eventually play as a planeswalker with your own CUSTOM deck. Each color  of cards is to represent your specific magic/spells/summons and your deck is called your library. Each color is known for displaying a certain kind of magic. Using your deck/library of chosen color/colors-magic you  try to eliminate the other planeswalkers life points by playing the card game of Magic the Gathering. Green-Forest is elfs/beasts and mana gaining. Black-Swamp is zombies/vampires and kill/ reseruction. White-Plains is soldiers/angels and life gain/ enchantments. Red-Mountains is goblins/mountain creatures and fire direct fire damage spells. Blue-Island is wizards/water creatures with trickery spells and counters. The first story campign is Gideon the white planeswalker then, Jayce the blue, Lillaina the black, Chandra the red and Nissa the green. After playing these learning campigns with the planeswalkers, you can make your own decks, buy new cards with booster packs with in game coins( witch you earn through the campign, game modes and daily acheivments. ) Also there are Steam acheivments for those out there that enjoy a good challange. Along with collecting cards to make whatever deck to get whatever acheivment daily. The games online rank capability is fun, but can be rather frustrating when against players with superior cards. Dont wory though, you can play against AI and Freinds. Witch is a lot of fun playing 2v2, ( witch is what I did with my bro). It's always great winning a game with your friend where your down to no life losing and come back with one card and an attack phase that one hits em.

The developers offered some coins recently to make up for it and have made some strides to fix the connectivity issues, but they don't make up for the multitude of lost matches, lost coins, lost progressions, and simple inability to play two head giant with your friend.
Second of all, the UI is atrocious for the PC. It's clearly a port from the mobile versions that came out before the PC edition, and there has been little to no attempt to take good advantage of the mouse and keyboard a PC player would use.
Third of all, there are many, many glaring oversights. There have also been countless times where either an oversight or glitch has caused the match. If you didn't turn off easy targeting in the gameplay options, and you're running a deck with black cards or that involve sacrificing, you'll find (at the time of writing) that easy targeting doesn't allow you to attack yourself or heal an opponent (valid strategies for the more advanced players). There would have been no mention of this until you tried it out in mid battle. There have also been countless times where the game has skipped my main phase (usually the second one, but also the first) or my battle phase. I've been unable to choose my blockers after having pressed the pause timer button and resuming.
All the pros to this game are due to the card game itself. There has been no time where I thought to myself, "Wow, that was a really nice implementation of the card game." In case you're wondering about the hours I've put in, keep in mind I've played the physical card game before as well as played the iOS version when it first came out. All of the glitchiness that version had when it came out got ported right to the PC version, and all the complaints I've mentioned have come from the PC version. I was hoping the PC version would have had the time to fix a lot of these issues, but they haven't. It's actually worse off, because at least the UI makes sense for a tablet not a PC game.
The game implements the virtual currency in exchange for real world money or time that all f2p and mobile games use. If you don't like that in mobile games, you won't like it here.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game. It's too buggy with many oversights on the basic fundamentals of the game. The few good times I've had do not make up for the intensity of the frustration of losing a match due to a fault entirely on the game itself and not due to your skills, or going through an annoying campaign mission only to find out that the game lost internet connection (on an always connected PC) and none of your progress will be saved. A lot of people I know have complained about the lack of cards, but I'm more worried and upset about the very bad foundation they've set up to worry about any future card expansions. I would recommend to wait until they fix these fundamental issues.

I'm not gonna lie. While I was young, I played the crap out of Super Smash Brothers Melee. I got very good at it. I couldn't properly master any of those exploits in-game, but I bet my brother almost every time! SSBM was a blast!
When my friend told me about Rivals of Aether, however, I was feeling nostalgic, when I heard that it played like SSBM. So of course, I paid the full price for it, and lemme tell you this. If you're a SSB enthusiast, this is a purchase worth investing in. However, there are a few conditions that must be met to get the full enjoyment.
This game is targeted towards the competitive scene. This is a game that's not for filthy casuals. I'm not particularly "great" at this game myself, I'm still trying to master everything, but I held my own in online. f you are willing to go head-first into online play, you better know what you're getting into. There are people out there who have mastered every aspect of this game, with almost every character, and can use any situation to their advantage. So if you've mastered those techniques in SSBM, and have learned the ins and outs of your main character, then you can put up a good fight online. If you can't manage to muster everything in this game, and if you have Zetterburn as a trigger word, think twice before buying this game.
Naysay all you want that Zetter might need a nerf. Even though a few asked for a nerf, there are gonna be people who "main" Zetter. You just gotta cope with it. HOWEVER, if you're a professional player, you can show Zetter your favorite finger, and combo him to death. It's possbile to defeat a Zetterburn player. I have a few times. There are ways to counter his moves and zone him out. Even though I agree that Zettre might need a small nerf, it might not happen, and I'm okay with that.
To list the basics, you can't edgegrab, the shield is replaced with a parry mechanic. and there is no way to grab your opponent. This might take some time for SSB players to adjust to, but you'll get the hang of it eventually.

At first I thought this game was cute. Then I realized how wonderfully WRONG I was.
Hollow Knight is a beautiful marriage of whimsy and macabre that had me raging, crying, and laughing; sometimes all at once!
The artwork is unique and very well drawn.
The music is BEAUTIFUL and I highly recommend getting the soundtrack (which is on Apple Music if you already have a subscription. You're welcome).
The characters are intersting and most of them have insight into the equally intersting lore of the world.

My only gripes are:
1. Two of the endings are almost identical. Don't get me wrong, they're still worth playing through, but I feel like there could have been a bit more disparity between them.
2. The game ALWAYS crashes whenever I quit or after the credits finish rolling. A quick Ctrl-Alt-Delete > End Task fixes it but it's a bit annoying.
3. I had FPS drops caused by V-Sync, so I have to play without it. Not a huge deal.
4. This one could just be Windows 10 stupidity. Occasionally when dealing or receiving damage the game will minimize itself. It doesn't happen frequently enough to be game-breaking, but adds unnecessary frustration to the game's already challenging battles.
In the end, this is hands-down my new favorite game and I've already recommended the hell out of it to everyone I work with.

If you’ve ever played a Metroidvania before, you’ve essentially already played Hollow Knight. There’s nothing too new in terms of how it actually feels, moves, and flows, but is differentiated from the crowd with its light Soulslike elements, sweet soundtrack, and pretty backgrounds. Sound interesting?
I’d like to think so. I think it’s a decent game, but that’s all it is—decent. For everything I liked about the game and what it offers, there was something that bugged me; whenever I started getting into the groove and beginning to appreciate its more unique facets, something cropped up that dampened my experience or made me feel like I was the one being played.
Most if not all of the issues this game has originally stem from the game developers’ obsessive, intense focus on a non-linear experience that supposedly opens up to player choice. Non-linearity is something I appreciate, choice is always great, and it’s all in good fun, but too much of a good thing really ends up being a bad thing in the case of Hollow Knight. The thing with Metroidvanias is that you can only take your non-linearity too far. A player needs to be strung along in some fashion for all the exploration, platforming, boss battles, and puzzles that the genre incurs to meet their full potential. But this game just drops you in a world and expects you to wander around without motive, without motivation, without purpose. You have no incentive in the early game—you can only explore so much of the game, so when you don’t know what you’re doing, the only visible way to make progress is through buying items from shops and farming monsters, assuming you don’t manage to get lost doing so. Neither of these are supposed to be the focus of a game about a character trying to find his way through a world that is foreign to them, killing things along the way, and ultimately learning more about themselves.
There is so much downtime created by getting lost, getting sidetracked, and generally doing your own thing that it diffuses all intention and excitement the game possesses. Going through an area for the first time feels strange, odd, and nerve-wracking... and yet it’s nowhere near as exciting the next fifty times you go through there, trying to make your way from point A to point B. Once you know what to expect of a screen and have completed its primary content, the only incentive to go back is for 100% completion. And yet it forces you to do that anyway. It’s the same exact thing every time. It’s boring. Hollow Knight wants to be a cool open world game for you to explore, but the game’s content does not match up whatsoever. All that isn’t helped by the fact that you sometimes need to walk twenty seconds back to a boss over multiple screens just because the developer thinks the game is somehow harder or cooler by refusing to put a bench (the game’s version of bonfires) right before a boss fight, unlike in the actual Souls games. That doesn’t change the difficulty whatsoever. It just forces you to play for longer. You are then just creating downtime for absolutely zero reason. It is nothing more than stubborn, pretentious game design which accomplishes nothing other than to further waste your time.
Similarly, the ‘player choice’ aspect falls flat almost immediately for the same reasons. When forcing the player to use a nonlinear playstyle, you are essentially denying them a choice, so there is objectively no true player choice to be had. That’s shooting yourself in the foot on your own terms. Even when you do make your own choices, you’ll probably feel like you’re doing something wrong if you don’t happen to take an optimal or speedrun-optimised route (which will happen to most people). Personally, getting through the game without resorting to using a guide for routing was rough, and figuring things out with old trial-and-error brute force easily accounts for 10 hours of the 24 it took me to beat the main game. It felt like the game was designed with a linear campaign in mind, but was ultimately scrapped and replaced with the vague and half baked format that makes up its open-world ‘exploration’.
I could be repeating myself a little here, but that‘s what the game felt like, too! Sure, you could shrug all criticism of the game off with a simple “git gud”, and that definitely applies to people who are replaying the game, but it is not representative of the horrible, potentially offputting experience that is the first playthrough. That outright denies the experience presented to new players to tout one’s own personal experience and adoration for the game. (It also isn’t all that constructive a response to begin with.)
Not like the difficulty is worth mentioning, either, other than being a little poorly paced. It’s all pretty boring up until a decent and sudden skill spike towards the mid-to-end portion of the main game. Even then it can be a little on the easy side (I beat all of the final bosses on my first try), but maybe my expectations were set too high.
Even what little writing Hollow Knight has through lore tidbits doesn’t actually seem to go anywhere, and its quality begins to dip toward the end of the game. A little disappointing, what with the promising and bold start it makes, and still I find myself wishing there was more. What good is an interesting world and cast of characters if you make nothing of them?
It’s a little, uh, hollow, but I’d say that Hollow Knight is largely a nice and worthy little journey to be had, and an especially alluring title for us completionists. While your first time may be rough, there’s always a second, then a third, then a fourth…

Hollow Knight is very close to being exceptionally good, but unfortunately falls flat in a few, but decidingly critical facets.
Most notably the map system, which is quite possibly one of the (if not THE) worst I've ever seen in a metroidvania game. For starters, being able to map a section at all requires finding an NPC and buying the corresponding map from him. This will reveal some areas in close proximity to where said NPC was found. In combination with the maze-like nature of the game makes it quite possible to miss the map vendor and aimlessly walk around in circles without being able to track your position or progress, which if you possess a poor sense of direction (like me) is quite annoying and frustrating experience. This wouldn't be too bad in and of itself, but when combined with the fact that map progress doesn't automatically update it becomes quite annoying. Only upon DYING or by siting on a bench (which incidentally serve as save points throughout the game) does the map progress update.
Speaking of benches, their numbers are of average distribution (compared to simillar games), although a bit on the low side, but their placements are many times inconvenient, which becomes jarringly obvious when encountering (and dying) against bosses - usually involving an unnecessarily long and tedious climb to get back to said boss. The same can be said about the tram stations, which serve as the fast travel between different regions, which many times are far and few between the main objectives of the sections in which the tram stations are placed.
Another annoyance in regards to the mapping: a room which hasn't been fully explored still shows as fully explored in the map upon sitting on the bench. This means that a room with any kind of hindrance which requires and item to bypass, will not clearly show on the map. Combined with the aforementioned maze-like complexity of the stages requires either 1) above average memorization 2) tedious amounts of blind back tracking or 3) the use of some kind of guide. All of which are unnecessary premisses for a game of this calibre and there's really no excuse for this kind of design decision.
Hollow Knight also suffers from severe pacing problems. The first few hours, until you aquire the first two upgrades, are mind boggingly slow and uninteresting. As new upgrades unlock, you are able to reach previously unreachable places, which as previously mentioned, causes obscene amounts of backtracking.
Another minor disappointment is the music score, which on its own is beautiful, but doesn't pack a punch or have any sort of meaningful impact as I feel it should.
THAT BEING SAID,
the game is still quite stellar overall. The controlls are tight, the customization options plentiful and the bosses and puzzles challenging.
Due to the binary thumb up/down system and the lack of anything in between, I feel forced to give the thumbs down option to hightlight this (otherwise good) game's flaws.

Well overall i did not like it. The game have some good moments. It looks nice and the combat can be enjoyable in a "i am tired from work and want something simple as hell" kind of way. The problem is that you are going to spend a very long time with the combat and it gets repetitive really fast. Most battles can be won by simply spamming the auto attack and changing your role set up every now and then. It is not very interactive and i got very tired of the absurd amount of trash mobs the game kept throwing at me.
But there are times when the combat gets a bit harder and you are required to change your role set up with a pretty high intensity. But since you are limited to only controlling your main character it doesn't really get all that more complex and you are left to hope that your ai companions do their role well enough. Few enemies require any interesting tactics and the combat basically consists of you swaping between offensive, defensive, healing, etc party set ups.
What i found really frustrating is that you lose if you main character dies. Some enemy parties can deal very large amount of damage to a single character if the RNG god dislikes you and i can not begin to describe how frustrating i found it when my main character with 90 % + health died in a couple of seconds. Some boss battles are insanely long and several times i almost decided to uninstall the game when my main character got killed by some super attack 10 minutes into a boss fight.
This game is also very stat heavy and it is certainly possible to grind in it. I tried to stay away from that but after i got my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me by a boss i threw away my pride and grinded a bit. So how is leveling system? Well it is very basic. You get a bunch of skill trees if you can call them that that consists of three attributes and skills. It is very shallow and very much pretend. All roads lead to rome so to say and in most chapters i managed to fill out every skill tree available.
The items are basic as hell and i found it really disappointing that you only get to swap weapon and accessories. I also wish that i would get items that would change the characters apparence but that never happened.
So what do you do in the game? Well you follow a linear as hell level and initiate combat with enemies and loot chests.  There is a chapter with something some may call an open world but there is really not much to it. Yes you get "quests" which consist of initiating combat with certain enemies but that is it. So this is what you get gameplay wise and i do not think that it is all that interesting. The majority of the games gameplay felt like complete filler to me and i kind of expected more.
So what is left is the story. Is it any good? No it is truly awful. A lot of games have awful stories but it is often obvious that they do not really care about it, this game can not get away with that excuse. The plot does an awful job of communicating basic world info to the player and the game keeps on throwing terms at the player. It was really confusing at first but it never became much better when i started to understand what was going on. The overall plot is just completely nonsensical and i did not care about it one bit.
The characters had some good moments here and there even though they certainly are a bit high on the drama. But very little actually happens and even though the games cast is really small for a rpg of this size i never started to care for anyone expect perhaps Sazh. The antagonist of the game is also a joke by the way.
But the thing about the plot is that it is really nonexistand during the majority of the game. This game does not combine gameplay and story and the majority of the game you are simply traveling to a place because the plot tells you so. It is a big roadtrip and i found the story to be a big waste of time and in my opinion the plot did not bring up any topics, themes, details about the setting, characters or whatever that i found remotely interesting.
Overall i did not enjoy the game and i would not recommend it even if the pc version worked fine. Which it does not.

i heard a lot of bad stuff about this game before finally playing it for the first time on steam. but you know haters are gonna hate, and im glad i didnt listen.
first of all, the battle system is fantastic. yes there is an option on your battle menu labeled "autobattle". it feels cheap and boring at the start of the game but you'll understand it once you reach the third area or so and the battlemechanics are expanded a bit. you'll want to use it often and it by no means fights your battles for you. most of your strategy will go into paradigms. and theres plenty of it. later in the game youll also find yourself canceling attacks or attacking early in response to events as battles progress, and youll also find yourself more frequently going into the menues and setting up specific attacks for certain situations. at the very least i found this battle system to be far more engaging than that of titles like FFX or FFIX. its also much faster paced. battles are meant to be fought as quickly as possible and youll actually find yourself taking advantage of and strategizing around the various strengths and weaknesses of each enemy, which is something that provided very little benifit in most games as I usually found most final fantasies became more and more button mashers towards their endgames, whereas this one seems to get more complex as the game goes on. the game rewards you for defeating enemies faster. it also penalizes you with doom if a battle drags on for too long, but ive only very rarely encountered this, and i actually consider this a pro as its usually a good sign that your missing something and forces you to reconsider and improve your strategy. even then, most of the time i still managed to defeat the boss before time ran out. gone are the days of literally wasting an hour on a single boss battle, or even multiple hours on superboss battles, as even most of these will be no more than 10 - 15 minutes.
that said, this brings me to what i consider to be the only major cons to the game as well. first of all, you can only ever control one character in battle. and while you can change who is the lead character, its a long ways into the game before you get that ability, or any control over your party for that matter. this wouldnt be a major issue in my opinion however, if it werent for my next con.
the biggest con in this game is that you cant save your party configurations. this means that anytime you change out party members, you also have to re-setup all your paradigm settings. because of this, i generally found my self sticking with one group configuration whenever possible and continuously refining my paradigms and strategies with that one group rather than trading out characters and playing as all the different characters to take full advantage of their different character strengths and paradigms.
all in all, yes this game is pretty different from the other final fantasies. but not really any more so than they are from each other.
like all final fantasies this game also has a fantastic story. in fact i would rate it among my favorites next to 9 and 10 as far as story goes. and while japanese voices is an option, i actually found the english voice actors to be very good in this one, with no memorable cringeworthy moments. the story is also serious and deals with some pretty down to earth emotions. the characters of lightning, hope, and sahz are some of the deepest and best developed characters in the entire series in my opinion. lightning even beat sqall in becoming my favorite protagonist of the series.
since this is a port, something has to be said for port quality. shortly after release, they released an update to allow higher resolutions. however, there are still some issues, which i dont expect to be fixed at this point, regarding that update, particularily one involving scan notes that keeps me from taking full advantage of it. for some reason, on my machine anyways, any resolution above 1280x800 causes the notes to disappear from the enemy details screen when using libra. this is especially problematic since, as i mentioned before, playing off your enemies strengths and weaknesses is an important part of the battle system in this game. most importantly, the summon battles become practically unwinnable without some critical information that is provided in those notes.
that said, even playing at 1280x720 on my 1080p monitor, the graphics are surprisingly good, impressive even, and the scaling is hardly noticable. even though for me, most other games ive played are almost unbearable at such low resolutions. ive also only very rarely noticed any of the frame rate issues or lag that most other people complain about so excessively. Edit: it occurred to me that since I've discussed performance in this review, I should list my system specs. So those have been added at the bottom of the review.
last but not least, and perhaps most surprising, the mouse and keyboard controls are good. and i dont just mean for a port, but good in general. its unfortunate that they didnt stick with these controls for the pc ports of xiii-2 and LR. i'll probably have to find some way to get a controller working for those before i can get more into them. but as for this game, well, i was fully intending to play this game with a controller like every other final fantasy id ever played, but i started a game without setting it up at first just to see how it ran and try it out really quick and not only was i completely satisfied, i was very impressed with the pc keyboard and mouse control sceme they came up with. in fact, i played the whole game through using mouse and keyboard. its easily the most satisfying ported controls of any ported game ive played on pc. other ports need to take some notes on this one. very dissappointed that xiii-2 and LR didnt follow suit.
overall, this game was very enjoyable for me and i highly recommend it for anyone whos interested in jrpgs.

For fans of the Hitman franchise I would warn you that this game strays too far from the formula that we have known and enjoyed in previous titles. Each game has almost been part of a work in progress that ultimately lead to Hitman Blood Money - which I feel almost perfected the mechanics of a Hitman game.
Essentially I was anticipating Absolution to be "Blood Money 2", using the same mechanics that made Blood Money so replayable and simply improving aspects such as graphics, AI and progressing the story in even larger and more spectacular game levels. Instead Absolution throws what we know almost entirely out the window.
These mechanics that im talking about, if you don't know, are the following:
1) Be presented with information about the targets and level location.
2) Choose and customise your weapon load out as feels suitable for the mission.
3) Be dropped in to an open sandbox level
4) Using your patience and care, figure out where your targets are located and how to take them out subtly
5) Perform the assassination and make your escape unnoticed.
Of course this could (and normally would) not go to plan and you'd end up getting killed or blasting your way through to the target and / or mission exit point. But that was all part of the fun and what made the game so replayable.
The following is how Absolution moves away from the above points:
1) Some levels do not have any kind of target.
2) There is no option to choose and customise your weapons
3) Most levels are linear
4) Again, some levels do not have a target
5) Same as 1) and 4) Instead of assassinating someone, in a lot of levels you just make your way from A to B.
The main fault here is obvious but what also really disappointed me and stops this being a good Hitman title is 3).
Trying to figure out your way around an open map while not raising suspicion is the bread and butter of the series. But linear levels take this away. The aim is still to go unnoticed but without open levels all we now have is a stealth game like Splinter Cell. Just to rub salt in the wound, as you make your way through these levels you will find that they are divided in to sections that are not really connected. The AI will reset if you make your way back to a previous section which completely breaks the immersion.
I understand what the developers set out to do with this game. They wanted to make a spectacle - a flashy journey through the eyes of a modern day assassin, utilising set pieces to do so. But in doing this they really lost sight of the challenge that made the Hitman series unique. It's all style no substance.
Digging a little deeper I discovered that the lead game director for Absolution was previously the lead art director for Blood Money. All style no substance, now I can see why.

IGN said it best when they said " 'This War of Mine' might be the war game we need." I will go one step further and say it
the war game we need.
You take the role of citizens of the city of Pogoren, trapped in a bitter feud between militia-rebels and soldiers. Unlike any game I've played or heard of, neither side is "good" nor is either side "bad". Your job is to survive the bloody conflict. Every single day is a struggle to survive. Who gets to eat? Who gets to sleep in a bed? Who has to risk their life at night to go out into the city? And most importantly of all, can we take life of an innocent? All these are questions you'll ask yourself every day.
Before you begin 'This War of Mine' I highly suggest you attempt to get into character. Don't go in thinking "Oh they're just pixels." Put yourself in the shoes of each of your survivors and attempt to think what you would do. You'll find yourself truly asking yourself the tough questions you hoped you'd never have to ask.
I can't recommend "This War of Mine" enough. I will not say I was brought to tears, but this game has made me question what I am capable of. "War is Hell," said Sherman, and he was right. 'This War of Mine' does a better job depicting war than any game to date. There is no glamour, there is no honor. There is survival, and in the end that's all you can ask for.

I'll start of with the good things about the game, most notably its graphics in space. The game looks really nice when you're flying in space. There's very little to remark about the graphics in general, and the visuals in the game give you the impression that things in space got a bit bigger compared to the other X games.
But sadly, the good news ends there. I've waited until patch 1.19 until writing this, and the game is still a horrible unfinished mess, well after the initial release.
The AI in the game is seriously broken, up to the point where tradeships are stacked on top of eachother like a game of Jenga. While initially this doesn't seem to be that much of a problem, as the game progresses the situation grows to such proportions that almost all trade grinds to a halt. Bugged NPC traders will hinder the construction of stations, and the in-game economy generally will grind to a halt. While capturing a capital ship, the AI will occasionally think that the ships missing fire on me are also hostiles, reducing the capture of capital ships to "Hide behind/inside the ship and wait for the marines while the capital ship takes care of the trash mobs".
The campaign itself is barely playable due to these kinds of bugs, although some people have reported success to a certain degree. I personally have given up on the campaign completely in favour of the "free play" mode. Sadly the bugs do not lend to a wonderful experience in that gamemode either.
The game at some point will require you to walk around in stations, and while this unconventional for an X game, I can see how this can add to the experience to a certain degree if done right. However, the experience itself is horrid, leading me to believe that it was a nice-to-have feature on a wishlist that never was properly finished and shouldn't have become a core mechanic of the game. You get stuck in the terrain, the NPC character models are especially disappointing, and the gameplay of this mode is lackluster, boring and repetetitve. Of all the features in this game this one strikes me as something that was unneeded, and actually serves only as a demerit to the game in every way.
As far as audio is concerned, while the game has fairly decent sound effects, the voice acting used in the game is below all standards putting even Oblivion to shame. The lines in the subtitling are quite often different from what the voice actor is reading. The voice actors often misread words, including the voice-over computer which will occasionally warn you that its "master" is malfunctioning or destroyed instead of its "maser". In previous X games it was less of an issue due to the nature of those games, but in Rebirth it quickly becomes a huge downside due to the amount of time you spend interacting with NPCs. The voice acting itself varies from lacklustre to dreadful, is generally uninspired and repetetive as the protagonist for the 8154th time asks in the exact same tone "Show me your wares", while your plot-device of a useless copilot will feel the need to utter the words "Shut up Betty" every 2 or 3 minutes.
A minor but quickly annoying quirk is in the music. While in general I don't find music to be much of a big deal, there as a small timing error in the music used in the highways and super-highways. The BGM loops in 8 or 16 bars (2 or 3 seconds in this case), but due to the way the game handles these loops there is the shortest pause in between each loop effectively ruining the tempo of the music. While in general this shouldn't bother you too much, the sheer amount of time spent in the highways and super-highways makes this a really obvious issue, and while it is a minor glitch it quickly becomes terribly annoying. This sort of issue just shouldn't be present in a 50 euro game as it's trivial to do properly and should've been fixed very early on in the sound engines development cycle.
All I can say about this game is that it was shipped as a defective product, and after a number of patches the state of the game has hardly improved to anywhere near a playable state. While I have waited a fair amount of time and tried a considerable amount of patches over that time, I feel that I've grown tired of fighting with this game and its broken design and bugs.
Sadly, the game has lost the charm that it's predecessors offered in gameplay as well. It's clear that the game was obviously not intended to be a direct sequel, and while in general I approve of moving away from the tried and tested formula I don't feel the gameplay took a step in the right direction. If you are expecting to build a giant empire and conquer the stars as in the previous installments you're better off reinstalling one of the previous games. There is very little control over the other ships you own, and what little control you do have has been made as tedious as possible by terrible UI design.
After 22 hours of gametime, which is an alltime low for any game in the X series, 2 corrupt batches of savegames, having to manually edit the savegame to fix bugs in the campaign, clipping through stations and getting stuck, a broken price system that miscalculates how a discount works, getting thrown out of a highway into the void and gritting my teeth at the lack of progress in fixing what is obviously a defective product I have decided to uninstall this game and not look back.
The only thing I can recommend about this game is the amount of money you'll save by not buying it.
