The features of this game may sound promising, but that's how the developers tricked us all into buying the game. The game, in it's current state, doesn't even come close to what the developers promised or to previous games of this series. Do not buy this game (yet), it is a fundamentally broken, dumbed-down, bad console port, which will surely take a year or more to get fixed.
Please read on:
Trade:
Trade to me is the most important aspect of such a game. In the previous games, trade was awesome. Not in X:Rebirth, however. There is a trade computer software which you can install to your ship, which shows current trade offers. However, these offers are only stored in your computer when you fly through the actual zone the offering stations are located in. Once you fulfilled a trade offer, it disappears from your software and eventually your trade offer screen will be empty. That means you can't trade unless you fly through all the zones on a regular basis, which is horribly time consuming.
Also, your trade ships have no way to trade autonomously, you always have to command them to take a trade. Additionally, you can only plan three trips for a ship.
Furthermore, the economy is simply broken. While some systems are doing pretty well, your actions don't really influence the economy of a system. So if you think you can lead a system to wealth and prosperity, you are wrong.
There is a mod which tries to fix this whole mess and so far it's ok, but there is no way I can tell if my actions make a difference. The statistics of your stations (production, sales etc.) are non-existent and the only thing that tells you something is going on are annoying messages of the station manager, telling you that he/she made a little fortune and will be transferring it to your account. I currently have two stations built (yeah, I'll get to that too) and these messages are already annoying me to death.
And yes, there's even more. From broken trade ships (simply doing nothing at all, getting stuck everywhere or trading with hostile factions, which will ofcourse get them destroyed (and you don't even get a message)) to station managers throwing their budget you gave them out of the window to buy secondary ressources instead of primary ressources, everything is in it.
Fight:
EPIC FLEET ENCOUNTERS, they said. Sounds awesome, but it's not. You can have as many ships in your fleet as you like, all the enemies will be shooting at you. The coolest part: Your fleet will not do a thing. The combat AI of your fleet is broken, they will neither help you nor fly out of the battle if they somehow manage to get in trouble.
Dogfights are boring. Fly straight up to the enemy vessel, shoot it a bit and turn when they pass you. Most annoying are drones. They attack you from everywhere and you have no idea in what direction to turn, because the HUD is so horrible. There is no "Target next enemy" button whatsoever and finding the red, thin-lined squares on a vibrant background is really eye-straining and sometimes nearly impossible when you are in a zone with a sun and/or orange nebula in the background.
"Choose to fight for someone". No big deal. You wan't to be police? Buy a license, but it doesn't really matter. Other police vessels will still come at you if you do any shooting.
"Take the action right into massive structures". Yeah, attack a station. By the time you are done, your grand children's children will probably be watching you. The puny weapon arsenal at your disposal is just ridiculous. Speaking of which, there are only five weapon types. And one of these is the mining laser, which is completely useless because you can't pick up ores with your ship.
Boarding got improved compared to the previous games, but it still is bad. First, destroy the ship's jumpdrive. It's pointless, because it won't jump to safety anyways. Then, destroy the engines. Now your boarding crew will launch and fly towards the ship. Once they reach the hull, it's up to you to create "distractions". Destroying turrets, shield generators and sadly the drone launch pad. Unless you destroy these things, the boarding crew will take forever to get the job done. The bad thing is: if you destroy the drone launch pad, all the drones on the ship will be destroyed, which also includes cargo and construction drones. So there you are, you captured a ship without drones, destroyed engines and no jump drive. It's basically a floating wreck. Next up, dock on the ship and tell the captain and the engineer you previously hired to work on the ship (yes, you have to board the ship to tell your crew to work there..). The engineer will only fix your ship to 75% hull, you will have to take it to a shipyard if you want to get 100%. Now you still need drones, so either you fly to a shipyard and order the ship to buy drones (you have to fly to the zone and speak with the shipyard guy on the station), which takes a considerable amount of time since you destroyed the engines and the jump drive, or you open a save game editor and manually add them to your captured ship.
Build:
Empire building sounds great. Again, it's not. Station building is so buggy, that I spend more time editing the save games than playing the actual game. Without a certain mod, your station will be built in an ungly, deformed way, with parts of the station all over the zone. The devs thought it would be nice to have little pointless ships flying around your station to make it look like a city. Ironically, these things make it impossible to have a nice station. They obscure the place where the module is to be built in, so the AI moves the module a bit, resulting in stations looking more like a Picasso painting.
During the plot you are given a task to build a station to vitalize a certain factions economy. That station however, doesn't produce anything. Well it does produce something, but it's not a good which is present in the economy. Furthermore, to produce this useless good which noone will buy, you need ressources from other systems. Your station trader however is restricted to the system your station is in.
Think:
Yeah, will have more than enough time to think about everything. Escort plot missions which take 30 minutes, hacking missions which take forever and travelling the universe without SETA or jump drive.

For a diehard Magic: The Gathering Fan I would barely recommend it. For people as a whole, I would not.
I'm a fan of Magic so I personally enjoy it quite a bit. However, there are a few flaws.
- The campaign can be irritating. The decks are pre-assembled and sometimes your opponent's deck is stacked against yours leading to aggrevating matches. A few times I had to play a match over and over and only won because the opponent kept a poor hand.
- The quest feature is thoroughly agonizing. Many of the quests asks you to use the game's deck wizard to build "theme decks." The problem is that as a starter you don't have the right cards to build on the theme they FORCE you to build on. (Even though this is mildly mitigated by the fact that you can complete quests by playing against the computer, you'll have to fight them repeatedly due to losing with your poorly made, frankenstein theme decks.)
- There's still connectivity issues. I got zero credit for winning a duel because I lost connection. (Maybe they gave me credit when I was finally reconnected, but it's still annoying.)
- Crucial moments when you want to really watch the field moves too fast. During combat there's a lot of tense watching. When to attack, when the opposing side blocks, it's hard to tell when you can respond with your instances and abilities. A lot of the time the phase moves too fast and I miss my timing to make counterplays.
Gripes aside it's still Magic game. If you like Magic I'm sure you'll enjoy it on some level. But drawbacks can be tiresome and rage-inducing.

Despite generally disliking metroidvanias I decided to semi-blindly pick this one up during a 33% off sale simply due to it's positive reception and a direct recommendation from a friend.
Considering this was probably one of my better choices on steam, I might aswel try to continue the cycle and recommend others to do the same.
Pro's:
+++ Looks amazing, even breathtaking at times
+++ Same if not more actual worthwhile content than most triple A games these days with even more on the way.
+++ Ambient soundtrack fits extremely well with every area in the game and adjusts accordingly.
+++ Combat and platforming, especially once fully upgraded, feels amazing.
++ Most bosses are great, two of them,
, I might just consider to be among the best I've faced in 2D games.
++ Getting lost still feels great, especially with most upgrades unlocked, due to the crazy amount of secrets hidden between the nooks and crannies.
+ There's a big story going on here, and while I personally didn't get all of it (yet) the side stories the supporting cast has on their own are well written and very memorable.
Cons:
- Starts off rather slow.
- The main path can be surprisingly hard to find from time to time.
- Something like being able to put pins down yourself on the map would've gone a long way, it's very easy to forget why you couldn't progress at a certain point in the first place, making you backtrack after every upgrade just to find out which in most cases just ends up wasting time.
-- Not all bosses are great and there are a certain few (~3) that stand out,
Overall, a very easy recommendation for anyone even slightly interested, even those that despise the genre.
Additional notes:
Difficulty: Medium - High
Main story playtime: ~13 hours.
100% playtime: ~30 hours. (not including speedruns / additional "hardcore mode" runs)

If you are looking for the old FF feel, as in VII and VIII, well too bad it's not here. I am glad that FF took a bit of a leap to do something new, but people hate change. If you are one of those players don't play/buy this game.
Yes the game has issues but so does every game EVER.
The game is very linear, gives you one straight line with no exploration to talk about until you get to a certain point, thats about 10hours into the game. The Graphics is really beautiful, but some people have issues with fps drops and stuttering on the game.
I really am enjoying the Battle System, the way you have to shift your paradigms to fit to your strategy, this also tries to make the game harder in a sense as you have to select "medic" to get someone to use a healing spell. The most fights is really boring at times as you have 10sec of a fight and then 5meters later another 10sec of the same type of fight but for the boss fights you really have to know when to swap your paradigm and this makes it interesting.
The storyline is confusing at first but they kinda try and explain it to you, with flashbacks. Some characters are really irritating and some you really learn to like. (But thats how the real life is, you don't always like everyone)
The upgrading of your gear could have been done differently, it's a bit boring and you don't always know what to do. The same with the leveling up of your crystarium, also they only get you to upgrade to a point every time, but this stops you from becoming overpowering.
As a last note:
This game is fun to play, really spoon feeds you most of the game, and the fights become bland and tedious as they are short and almost always the same. The game does not have any real exploration features and might make this a boring game for some as you only have one option, moving the way the corridor is leading you to. SE really tried to do something different they didn't make a flop neither was it a masterpiece but this is still a game worth playing if you can get past the 10hour tutorial.

HOWEVER, fans of the original SOSE should know that the publisher, StarDock, has made a complete 180 on the subject of DRM and their treatment of customers since they originally published their "Gamer's Bill of Rights." They have made it a requirement now to register a Stardock account to activate the game, and you only get one activation.
TL;DR: If you don't care about DRM, this is a good game if you like the genre. If you do, however, giving stardock your money now, for this, sets a bad example. I wouldn't have bought it if I had known. Now that I have, though, I'm enjoying it.
If you don't want to buy this because of the DRM, look into the original SOSE title, as it was published 100% DRM-free. Buy that instead, as it's really not that different from this expansion.

Shadow Warrior is an interesting game, and I had a tough time deciding on whether to rate it up or down. Overall, it is one which I recommend - with a rather big caveat, however (hence the thumb down).

The first person sword fights are well done (Skyrim could learn a few things from it) - they're dynamic, elegant, and frankly, a lot of FUN.
The dialog in this game is well written, and the voice acting top notch. The witty back and forth between Wang and Hoji, not to mention his enemies, is very entertaining. The game is also peppered with references to games from the 90's, and you'll find many easter eggs as well. This kept me thoroughly entertained.
The story is a little cliche, but with some nice twists, and, when it flows, the game is actually very engaging.
The gunplay is a not as satisfying as the swordplay. The revolver is an awesome weapon, and it was definitely my most used gun. The SMGs were dissapointing - no umph. The shotgun is an ugly contraption that shoots at far too slow a rate. The missile launcher is severely irritating, as it doesn't always fire when you shoot. Weird, and very inconvenient when you're up to your neck in monsters.
And it's this particular game mechanic that really made me resort to using a trainer to simply power through the game about half way through. The developers have artificially lengthened the game by repeatedly locking the player in a room in which tons of monsters then proceed to spwan. And when I say repeatedly, I mean every other time you open a door.
Other games also force the player to endure this sort of grind, but manage to keep things a little more interesting (DOOM did it right). However, in Shadow Warrior you run into the following dillemma: killing your enemies with a sword is fun, and makes you feel like a badass, but isn't feasible when you're surrounded by a million tough enemies. So you resort to guns merely to survive, but that's a LOT less satisfying, and suddenly the grind is almost unbearable.
The level design is intentionally confusing, as the developers were trying to cram as many secrets into each one as possible. At first it's fun to hunt around for that one elusive altar you've missed, but after a while - as the game begins to drag - you simply stop caring.
The scenary also becomes very repetitive at one point, with al ot of the interiors feeling copy pasted. Which is not to say that the  developers did not include some nice views in there, but one cave tunnel / dungeon corridor soon starts looking like all the others. The brief moments when you stop to actually admire an inspiring view are overshadowed by those monotonous interiors.
In conclusion, Shadow Warrior is, I would say, a gem in the rough. I believe that removing some of the filler fights would allow the story and dialog more of a chance to shine instead of serving as brief moments of coherence between endless grinds. I finished the game in 12 hours by using a trainer, but had I had to spend just a couple of more hours wasting my time on endless waves of enemies, I might have given up and not completed it.

Gat out of hell is an stand alone expansion, which throws alreadyfamiliar characters into a literally infernal enviroment. Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kensington find themself from New Hades, on their path to save the president of the United States.
What you can expect from the game is variety of weapons, variety of deamons to use as target practise and of course humor which is at this point more than expected from the series.
As Saints Row IV can be thought as a big expansion to Saints Row: The Third, Gat out of hell is just more compressed version of it. Maybe the most noticeable change is the new enviroment, which includes enough astonishing architechture and designing. For example the Infernal landscape is filled with lava rivers and fires. and that's about it from the changes.
In Gat out of hell, they have drastically cutted down the amount of main missions to a mere handful. And most of the story is proceeded with a cutscene. Though, they do work for the storyline very well, butt still they don't immerse the player as they did In previous versions.
Storyline itself isn't that astonishing, because the main objective is to help citizens of new hades to take power off from the Satan itself. Plot has it's funny moments though, as can be expected from the game. For example, In one part the whole thing turns into a musical, and punchlines are thrown every now and then. Sadly the story can be finished pretty quickly, and after seeing the 'the end'' text, it feels like the stroy was written in a hurry.
Capturing zones frome the grip of infernal demons can be done by doing various missions. Most of the tasks are already familiar from previous Saints Rows, where they acted as optional side-missions. But now, some of these distractions are included in the main missions. new addition to these is a mode called salvation. Where the player has to catch souls falling to the inferno (even though you are ending up in hell, doesn't mean you can't get a soft landing)
On technical point of view Gat out of hell continues with the old scheme, and at least I couldn't see any screen tearing or frame drops. Yet the graphical presentation was quite the same as in Saints Row 3 & 4. And hopefully Saints Row V will offer more eye candy to the players.
But the series have never been a mindblower on visual side, but more built on the good humor and atmosphere which sometimes rises in very absubrd spheres. Dialogue is still fresh and tasty, and guns bring joy and variety to the player. Or what does a armchair-a-geddon sound like.
Johnny and Kinzie learn new skills along the way, so you don't have to play for too long with average joe. Powers are upgradeable the same way as they were in IV, and the basic skills are useable very early in the game, but after few upgrades you noticed your character to be a hulking death machine who eats iron and ♥♥♥♥♥ barbwire, so therefore it is good for more experienced players to start with harder difficulties right off the bat.
Game itself is relatively fast paced and the main storyline can be completed in about 5-7 hours, you can easily double that by hunting for all the collectibles and trinkets around this infernal sandbox.
As a summary, though Gat out of hell has it's pro's and cons, It still can offer entertainement for couple evenings and nicely seems tied to the previous installation.

You're in control of a group of 3 war survivors (that can grow or shrink depending on how you handle things) living in abandonned house. With the help of your mouse (wasn't expecting the game to be 100% mouse controls at first), you must transform that crappy house into an acceptable living area during the days and scavenge the city at night (and decide if you're going to be that♥♥♥♥♥♥ready to steal from/kill anyone) to find food/resources/meds/weapons to survive and thrive.
Gameplay speed is a bit uneven (can feel slow during the day when waiting for a random visit to happen if you're looking for a trader/extra recruit and a bit too fast at night when you start getting in combat) but it plays nicely overall.
The difficulty is there and the randomness (to keep new games somewhat fresh) doesn't feel "all-or-nothing" like in some rogue-like games, even if it's tempting to keep restarting new games to get a starting crew with good traits.
Replayability so far is ok, I'm on my 4th or 5th game which might also be the last since it's going really well and might let me win the game (and I'm not that kind of completionist who'll restart a new game after winning just to try things slightly differently). I'd rate the game at 10-25 hours of fun depending on how fast you discover the good ways of getting things done.

This is not really a bad game, but it has bad things:
- Bad thing number 1: Matchmaking is horrible, personally I think card games don't need matchmaking, the classic host & join is enough, but if you decide to use a matchmaking system at least ensure it's working fine.
- Bad thing number 2: Lack of game modes on the multiplayer, the main difference that has Magic among other TCG games is that it was designed to allow matches of more than 2 players, that's why on some card texts we can read things like "target opponent" or "each opponent". So that means that regardless how the official tournaments work you could play a 6-man Free for all match with your friends, or a 2 vs 1 handicap, 3 vs 3... The possibilities are almost infinite and I think the game should be more flexible to allow that kind of matches.
- Bad thing number 3: The last, but not the least: Surrender = CPU Player Replacement... Ehm... WTF!? In my town, when someone surrenders, the opponent wins by abandon, however on this game the player is replaced by the CPU. This is not a networking/developing issue, this is a f***ing logic problem.
If the devs fix these things I'm sure this will be a great game, until then I can't recommend this game.

While the core mechanisms are the same as Civ V, many mechanics have been adjusted and new ones added. Enough so that it feels like a totally new game. The early phase is far more difficult than previous Civ titles, the Aliens spawn very fast and are quite tough compared to your units. The larger ones like siege worms and leviathans will remain a concern even at the end of the game. The new quest and virtue systems pretty much guarantee that every game will be slightly different by themselves, add in the the new tech web and the 3 affinities and it will be all but impossible to get a play through identical to one you've done before, without trying specifically to get one. All in all I enjoyed this game far more than Civ V due to the changes they made. I was really disappointed in Civ V and thought the franchise had peaked with IV, but BE gives me some hope 2k learned some valuable lessons.
There are points where 2K did get lazy with things or didn't polish parts as well as they should have, but these are fairly minor issues overall that don't drastically detract from the game experience. The biggest disappointment to me were the lame endings, like Civ V they don't even give you a decent ending cinematic, just a very dull, "you win" screen and picture. Similarly when you build wonders you get blah screens that look like sketched blueprints.
Overall a very worthy addition to the franchise and more fun than its predecessor.

Rivals of Aether takes the Super Smash Brothers approach to fighting games in more ways than one. Damage is only dealt to make it easier for you to launch your opponent off the stage and deplete stocks.
The differences from smash are what make this game so interesting though:
-There is no shield, tapping the block button initiates a parry animation making you invincible and opening up your opponent
-There is no ledge grabbing and there is a much heavier focus on wall jumping to get back on the stage.
-From the little I've played all characters feel relatively balanced and competitive in their own ways
-No items are in the game so battles are entirely skill based with very little random elements such as moving platforms on some stages
Rivals of Aether is an excellent platform fighter and is easy to pick up and play for veteran smash players.

It's easy to see that a lot of love and passion was put into this game. The controls are tight, the areas are gorgeously organic and keep you guessing, it's full of tributes to classic games (such as a power that lets you rocket straight ahead, or collecting four pieces to make a new health container), and it's full of little touches that put fun twists on the metroidvania formula (such as having to find the mapmaker NPC when you reach a new area, adding a new sense of tension and the unknown). The art style is also gorgeous, and it's always easy to tell what you're looking at and where everything is, compared to some games that have muddy or busy visuals.
To warn potential buyers, this is not an easy game. It starts out relatively fun and easy, and early bosses should take one or two tries, but there are some mid and late game bosses that are absolutely ruthless. I suspect the developers listened a little too much to the "IT NEEDS TO BE HARDER" d-bag masochists during development, which is to the game's detriment. I was able to get through it and get the true ending and 106% completion without cheating and with minimal use of guides, but there are some challenges (such as the delicate flower) that are frustrating and ludicrous and no fun at all.

This game is amazing.
What I was expecting: a game with satisfying sword combat.
What I got: So so much more...
The sword combat is great, it's incredibly satisfying, but they manage to balance it well with the guns too. You will find yourself switching to the pistol, the SMGs, the crossbow, throughout the entire game thanks to the weapon upgrade system and game design (ex. shoot the giant axe wielding minataurs, don't try to slash at their knees.)
This game is also has some of the best parts of older FPS design. There is no mini-map that you stare at to get to your next objective. You have to figure out where to go on your own. It's not a difficult maze like Doom, but it helps keep you immersed in the world and aware of your surroundings. Plenty of secret areas too if you are observant.
The story and comedy were well written too. Duke Nukem Forever showed us that comedy from old games does not translate well to modern times. I was worried about Shadow Warrior having the same problem but the humor was absolutly delightful. The story too was really good. I wasn't expecting any story to be honest, but as it progressed I cared more and more about everyone (especially Hojo.) It elicited the full range of emotions from me, which is rare in a game, much less a shooter focused on cutting through hordes of demons with a sword.
The music was also enjoyable. Most games I have to turn it off. With Shadow Warrior It never got repetitive and it did a good job of helping set the pace, from intense action to relaxing and calm (before ramping it up again.)
Shadow Warrior was a gem of a game, with great game design and mechanics and a captivating story, all completely unexpected.

tl;dr:

Got Shadow Warrior SE on Humble Bundle when it went free a while back, didn't have particularly high expectations but this game really delivered. I've played the entire campaign on normal difficulty (yes, I'm a wimp), here's what I have to say about it:
Atmosphere (+3):
Very good atmosphere, aesthetic and ambience is great, so this is pretty much perfect in my opinion.
Story (0):
I honestly don't know if there is a story and I don't really care, the game stands up fine as-is and I didn't feel the need for a story.
Gameplay (-1):
Solid gameplay with good feeling, hits a nice blend between traditional FPS games and RPGs. Upgrades aren't excessive but personally I'd prefer more focus on the game and less on upgrades.
Character (-3);
Good voice and style, but has some pretty bland or overused jokes among his voice lines.
Graphics: (-3):
Great graphics, but there should have been options to further reduce graphics and disable a couple unnecessary effects, like bloom and god rays and maybe some other effects that felt a bit unneeded in places.
Gunplay (-3):
Your sword feels really nice to use, especially with upgrades, but the some of the guns feel weak pretty useless in comparison. For example some guns (crossbow, SMG) feel and sound pretty weak, degrading the gunplay a bit.
Enemies (-2):
Enemies in general have pretty unique designs and feel satisfying to fight them, but some are a bit unintuitive to combat at first, or are a bit harder than would be expected at that particular point.
Level design (-3):
Levels are visually very nice and have unique locations, but in a couple places they become harder than normal or just get unintuitive to figure out what you have to do next. I won't give spoilers but some levels/fights took longer than normal because I couldn't figure out what to do/what I was doing wrong.
Soundtrack (+2):
Very atmospheric and fits the mood and theme perfectly.
Interface (-1):
Interface has some pretty slow animations when going between game and menu, and the menu felt lacking in places and it was a bit hard to find what I wanted to change sometimes. Not particularily intuitive to use, but they did the job well. HUD felt good and didn't seem lacking to me.
Verdict:
86/100
Overall a great game, lacking in a couple spots but still great and has quite a long campaign. Definitely worth checking out, but maybe not at the (current) full price of $40 USD, considering it came out in 2013 and the 2016 remake/sequel is the same price.

This game is simply suburb. From the graphics, the level design to the stealth mechanics. Lovers of classic Hitman may find this game dumbed down, however this simplified mechanics makes stealth actions much more intuitive, the streamlined level design easier to navigate.

Preface: Notice my playtime. I have not finished the game yet, so this is based on my initial impressions. I will amend if need be later.
It would not be an unfair comparison to compare this game to Hotline Miami. It is similar in that it can be extremely fast paced and relies almost entirely on your skill and reaction times than anything else, yet it differs simply because a single mistake can be forgiven. Retries are also common per level, particularly if you are going for 100%.
The gameplay itself is very solid and each level has a set of challenges which are in fact challenging - something many games these days fail to offer. At its core I would say it is basically hotline miami as a cover shooter with optional cover and some leniency with getting hit.
It is very fun, and earns a solid A+ in the fun department, however I must say the game's sense of humor is what I would call "borderlands tier" - that is to say if you liked borderlands' sense of humor you will love this game's sense of humor, and if you did not you will seathe with hatred every time BunnyLord opens his mouth.
Pros:
*Fast paced, hectic cover shooter gameplay
*Relies mostly on reaction speed, skill, and planning to do well
*Along with the above, skillful or perhaps cuhrayzee play is rewarded accordingly and allows you to progress much faster than treating the game like a cover shooter with optional objectives
*Excellent sound direction and music
*Nice pixel graphics and animations, simple as they are
*Good variety of characters who all feel, act, and play differently - no one is a direct upgrade to anyone else, and no one is awful
*Good variety of challenges per level which are actually challenging and introduce replay value
*Power-ups are actually very useful and feel powerful!
*Unlike Hotline Miami, the game features more than just "go here and clear out all the dudes" as a map objective
*Fairly clever level design, with a lot of cheekiness evident you won't notice until it's too late
*Escort missions aren't horrible exercises in patience!
*The voice acting is pretty damn good, way better than expected
Contentions:
*"Borderlands tier" sense of humor. That is to say the game's sense of humor revolves around what I'd describe as "lolsorandom", references to pop culture, and memes. If you like that, you'll love it. If not, you'll hate it.
*The enemies are kinda dumb and predictable. While this can be good for planning an optimal route and playstyle, it detracts from keeping the game interesting as they will always act the same and can be defeated via the same tactics every time
Cons:
*If you don't like the game's sense of humor you're going to be aggravated the whole way through
*The game can fall into "distract 'em up" territory when there are numerous enemies present in a single area. That is to say it becomes too difficult to tell what is going on and how to react with so many bullets and debris flying around
*Making contact or even getting near an enemy results in immediate knockback with no windup on the enemy's part. This can also pass through slides or other actions, and is EXTREMELY irritating especially in levels where enemies can throw you off ledges away from missable objectives or to your death. IMO enemies should exibit some sort of windup to give you a chance to react, even if that chance is tiny.
*Player HP is very forgiving. For a good part of the game you could simply sit uncovered in a hallway and spam the fire key until everything is dead. I think the game would benefit from a "Hotline Miami mode" in which 1 hit equals death on both sides - though I haven't finished the game yet so I don't know if this is already a feature.
Final Comments:
I would definitely recommend this game on sale. Despite the fact the game's sense of humor did not stick with me, I found the gameplay extremely fun with mostly small annoyances. Would absolutely recommend if you can find it bundled or cheaper than its retail price.

The game is very fun, very violent, very funny, and has all the ingredients to being an absolutley phenominal game. It is also borderline unplayable from having one of the worst control schemes I've ever encountered in a PC game, with absolutely no ability to rebind the controls at all. Browsing the forum shows that the developers are aware that at least a handful of people want the ability to do this, and have responded by basically saying it's not going to happen.
You have to, and I do mean have to, move your character with the arrow keys. Space reloads, X slides (something you'll be doing absolutely constantly, so why they'd put it on the X key I have no idea), C shoots (seriously, the C button on a keyboard is shooting. In a game that's 100 percent shooting.) and V is your secondary weapon (think grenades, etc.)
Those are all the controls the game has, except for selecting things in the menu, which is done with, you guessed it, the Enter button. I repeat, absolutely none of these controls can be bound to anything else, at all.
Hope you like having your hand in a weird claw shape the whole time you try to play the game, because you're gonna need it. Also hope you're not, I dunno, right handed, because unlike 99.9 percent of all other games on earth, your right hands' on character movement duties in Not A Hero, for some reason!
The developers' solution to this appears to be to have you plug an XBOX controller into your computer. I can't speak for if the game plays better on it, because it seems rather silly to go buy a peripheral for a console so that I can play a PC game. I've never had to use a controller on a game before, as rebinding keys is just kind of something every game ever lets you do. Hotline Miami had a nearly perfect control scheme, and they still bothered giving players the option to change it.
Hell, I can rebind controls in Half Life. You know, that game that came out nearly twenty years ago. Oh, and in games from the freaking PS1. But for a brand-new PC game, there's no ability to do it nor do the devs intend on adding it, so as is the game is, while not unplayable, way clunkier and less pleasant to play than it has any reason to be.
Putting V as the secondary makes the least sense of all, as if your index finger is on C (which it will be, as 99 percent of the game is just mashing the shoot button), you have to move it to hit V, something you will probably not remember to do in the heat of the very, very fast paced combat this game has. Keep in mind, while this sounds like a minor complaint, this game has four total controls, and essentially forces you to use two fingers to use them for no real reason at all.
Also, for anyone that minds, the game has no windowed mode and the forum's pretty well silent in terms of dev participation so I can pretty well assume it never will.
That all said, the writing's very funny, the action's great when you can get it to actually work, and the whole thing is a black as night comedy that is the kind of thing I'd normally love. The game has tons of content. But none of that really matters when it's so clunky and hard to play, and when it would be maybe ten seconds of coding to fix all of it.
I would gladly, gladly retract all this and write a glowing review if the game would just have the ability to rebind controls added, as that's about the only reason I can't recommend this. However, had i known that the controls were so unintuitive and bad prior to buying the game, I would not have bought the game, so I'm hoping maybe this helps someone out there.

If you're looking for a simple, beautiful shooter that's at least mildly engaging, Crysis is good for scratching that itch. Without the flair and drama of the CoD franchise, Crysis is singularly adept at filling a hole shaped for first person shooter.
Though power armor is pretty ubiquitous in gaming nowadays, the nanosuit is still a fun, reasonably unique way to play "super soldier," running around while invisible, sprinting faster than a car, and /punching cars into people/.
Cathartic, would be a way of describing it.
The storyline is pretty simple but that's alright, simple works well for this sort of game. The characters actually manage to get a little depth, even if it's only enough depth to connect them to one another, but hey I'll take it. The visuals are stunning, of course, but everybody already knows that about Crysis.
Summary
If you want a simple, functional, pleasing shooter with incredible graphics, Crysis is the game for you. It won't win any awards for storytelling, but it'll draw you in all the same, even if it's only for a little while.

This game is utterly bewildering, not really sure how else to put it to be honest. Brings a whole new genre to the idea of survival, almost a spin on sims. I very much enjoy 'god' games, as in controlling other peoples lives & making decisions that effect your storyline individually, rather than being set a line you must follow - so this game was perfect for me. Very depressing, quite dark & the music is just chilling right to the bone.
First game i played of it, i became emotionally attached (partially) to the characters in my storymode, & once they'd died, i almost uninstalled. Grasped me from the get go, & i am sure when DLC's are released the game will thrive.
The concept of the game is survival during the war, hence the name "this war of mine". You're in control of 3/4 people from the beginning in a rather large ruined house. Your job is to make sure they survive - heating the place, feeding them, making sure they rest, making sure they're happy, defended, getting in supplies to generally do up the place. During the night phase, you're given the option to go & scavenge other areas on the maps for supplies that can be of use, but this can cause a whole lot of sh*t for you, such as death. Not just death to your character, but killing others can also have a major effect on your characters mentality etc.
I hope the developers decide to expand the map a bit further, give the option to possibly have more than one person scavenging at night, maybe being able to move location, possibly an online feature? But also - i think the idea of having the option to add post-it notes to the map would be great. I mean, you may raid a place & find that you've not got the right tools or enough back pack space to be able to do what you wish, so being able to just put "remember to take saw next time" on the map would be much easier, as my mind is like a siv.
Great game, 9/10, but could use with a few expansions - but the game is newly released so i am very excited :)

This game is such a travesty to the X franchise i had to write my first review (probably only).
If you are new to the X franchise you may actually find the game interesting for awhile before you find out just how shallow it really is. After the campaign there is NOTHING to do. And the campaign itselt is a bugridden nightmare of how not to create an interesting plot.
Lets go through its shortcomings:
1. The trade part of the game is, show stopping bugs aside, shallow. You, the player, are the only one who uses money for an example. Alot of the items being produced are for building ships. Which the shipyards will do regardless of if the NPC or the player orders any. It will simply churn ships out. If there was no need for it, the AI will take the ship out of sight and delete it from the game (literally). So there is no real "supply and demand" in function. If anything, its a plan economy which the soviet union demonstrated never worked. Yet they implement just that in X Rebirth - and oddly enough it doesnt work. How about that! Rating: 1/10
2. Fight... Well if you like fancy graphics and dont really care that your ship is superior in every way and can just "boost" (afterburn) its way out of any fight that starts to become challenging this game may be for you. Unless you play with a joystick - because they made an xbox controller the featured item for this game. (Yes this was supposed to have been an xbox release 3-4 years ago or so but obviously such a poor game that it was never allowed by MS to be released). You have no way of "tab targetting" as they apparantly think chasing icons on the edge of your field of vision is awesome - that apparantly is set to 60 degrees as well. If you are in a system with a red sun its almost impossible to keep track of said icons. You get the idea. And dont get me started on the whole drone thing. Terrible idea with a terrible implementation. Your so called "co-pilot" which was apparantly going to be piloting your ship while youre busy controlling a drone - doesnt. So you get your♥♥♥♥♥blown off. Brilliant. Rating: 2/10
3. Building stations was one of the interesting things in the past, as you could set up your own trade empire and compete over sectors if thats what you wanted. They have actually thought out of the box in a nice way this time, allowing you to make huge complexes. Great idea. But then they couldnt have you build your stations just anywhere. No there will be 2 maybe 3 slots where you can place it. So much for freedom. There is also the part about "why" you would want to build anything as you are the only one who needs money to fund stuff - and making money is extremely (too) easy. Rating: 3/10
4. Thinking about this game makes my heart hurt. I preordered this game because the X series had been a great experience for me in the past. It no longer is. The campaign is long and unrewarding. The economy is fake so there is no incentive to try and corner any part of the market or try to take a competing (enemy) corporation out. They have no money, they need no money, so they can never be "beaten". So what is there left to do? Nothing. Space combat boring and uninspiring. After a few boarding/captures of capital ships that gets boring too. The placefiller/timesink minigames makes you want to scream. About 1/3 of your time will be WASTED in the highways, in the past you could zoom past boring parts of the game with SETA which allowed you to increase time by factors up to 10 so you didnt have to sit and watch paint dry, sorry i mean wait patiently for your ship to arrive at the next destination so you can jump out of the highways. Rating: 2/10
Other parts of the game i will cover here:
Graphics: I will not lie, the new engine makes space look truly awesome. Stations, NPCs and the skunk itself is a whole other story. And you cant look around the cockpit nor look at your ship from the outside. So minus a few points there. It has a few issues (no doubt because it was programmed for the xbox360) where really high end machines run worse than medium/low end machine. But pretty thats for sure. put 1-2 points on when it gets bugfixed. Rating: 6/10
Music: Great as always, that is one of the parts of the game i always enjoyed. The beautiful score. Sound effects and the voice acting? Not so much, but i feel its adequate for this game. Rating: 7/10
Gameplay: It would probably be easier to say whats actually working for this game which is... nothing. Literally. I have sunk about 16 hours into this game and i havent felt like starting it up again for weeks. And i used to love the X series and have sunk hundreds of hours into them. This one was simply a money grab. That they burned any creditability they had with the X community, well thats just too bad. I love Saints Row 3 and 4, that being said, i don't know what to really think about this game. I enjoyed it for the cutscenes and the musical number made me laugh loud because it came so unexpected and was just awesome.
The general gameplay though is simply minigames, some are known from the previous game like Mayhem others have changed a bit like Blazing which is now Hellblazing. There are new wacky weapons in the form of the "7 Deadly Sins" which are lot of fun and the narration and the cutscenes are amazing, even better than in SR4 and meeting old "friends" is always great.
Still, it just feels like there could've been so much more. "Saints Row V - Saints go to Hell" is what comes to my mind. All the Saints in Hell fighting against Satan while meeting evil people from earth's History while pulling one-liners.  Here instead we meet Vlad the Impaler in a Prison that looks like a Kindergarten with children's music and it's fun - especially when you let the music go for a while, with Vlad begging you to stop it. But that's all you get from him. The loyalty mission is just a bunch of mini games stringed together and afterwards, you never see him again. There's a ton of potential in this setting that Volition ignored because it's just a small stand alone expansion.
The biggest minus is the lack of music. You hear music in buildings like the Nightclub with DJ Shakespeare but there are no radio stations and nothing going one while you collect clusters to upgrade your superpowers. Music made that exercise fun in SR4, here it becomes a burden - unless you put on some music outside the game. SR4 music works great, i did a Mayhem mission with Mötley Crüe's Shout at the Devil, which works just great.
All in all i was entertained (so a thumbs up because i knew it would be a short game), the cutscenes are fun and unexpected, the Gat & Kinzie Team works great since they're different character wise and they make that clear in the first few minutes. Still i think the scenario is wasted on such a short (5 hours for me without doing all the same mini games over and over again 20 times) game. I want Saints in Hell with Pierce singing Meat Loafs Bat out of Hell with the player character!

I preordered BE based on my experience with Civ 5 and SMAC hoping for the same enjoyment level.  Sadly, I was disappointed.  For me the game visuals are too dark, the tech web is confusing, and too much depends on a fairly rare mineral that is nothing more than a plug for the publisher (firaxite).  I still haven't been able to build the mind flower.  The game says it is the culmination of several techs but it is not on the tech web.  So what techs does it require?  In one game I had almost every tech researched and still did not have the option to build the mind flower.  A little more indication of what is needed would be nice instead of forcing the human player to stumble around in the dark while the AI knows exactly what to do would be nice.
I have played this game several times and even won one.  As with most (all?) of this type of game the human player isn't even playing in the same physical reality with the AI factions.  The AI can build faster, research faster, and apparently is not encumbered by "fog of war" or economic limitations on the size of their military as the human player is.  I know the devs claim this is because the AI is basically "dumb" and needs these advantages to be challenging but I think it is laziness on the part of developers.  They can program a rover to roam Mars and do detailed scientific studies, they should be able to program a game so the human player can feel like they are playing in the same physical universe.
I am not as enthusiastic about this game but it does offer some different ey candy and is enjoyable to some extent.  Just don't expect the polished experience of the Civ series of SMAC.

Hollow Knight is an example of why the indie gaming scene is gaining so much traction. It blends a lot of ideas that make it an absolutely memorable experience.
Gameplay-wise, it shares a lot with other Metroidvania-style games - heavy exploration, secrets, and a constantly evolving moveset. There a lot of things to find, collectibles and power-ups. The trinkets you find help build a very defined playstyle. The controls are tight and responsive. I don't recall ever having a moment where the controls failed me.
Story-wise, the game reminds me very much of the Dark Souls series. Much of the information available immediately is vague. You are introduced to a complete stranger, in a strange and ruined land. Much of the story exposition is hinted at it character dialogue, or learned by way of the various stones/signs you find through the game. We're unsure of our character's identity and what role they have to play, never really knowing their intentions. What is certain, is that this is a dark and bleak world, and somehow our Knight has a purpose here.
The art of the game is what sets it aside from most. The game is absolutely gorgeous; the hand-drawn characters and world give it a really unique identity. It is simultaneously cute and cartoony while also managing to be dark, bleak and absolutely terrifying. The sound score also helps drive home how incredibly varied the world of Hollownest is. The soundtrack is beautiful, from start to finish.
Highly recommended. Hollow Knight is absolutely everything a video game should be. There is a lot of content, there is a great story, and the amount of polish is incredible.

Sins of a Solar Empire ('Sins') is an interesting and fairly unique RTS (or RT4X, as the developers would say). Though not the first of its kind, Sins blends together real-time combat and unit management with a fairly detailed (for an RTS) empire management system. The scale of the game is impressive, with maps stretching out across numerous planets (or rather, the space around them) and systems, all linked together by a web of hyperspace lanes. For fans of real-time strategy who are looking for something less micro-intensive and grand in scale, Sins is a worthwhile game to look at.

This game is human. It builds upon human strenghts and weaknesses and is not afrait to bring up serious topics like loss, death, trust, sacrifice and to be someone humble. There are several other games that have the same idea, to explore a civilization and to reveal it's secrets. They do this without realizing that the player will see the obvious. Here, this is presented to us as an apocalyptic, underground world, much like the Chozo from the metroid series. Only that your revisiting the city of YOUR kind. Not someone else. Keep this in mind while playing.
Gameplay-wise, well. For the pricetag at almost 15£, you will get what you pay for. Responsive and fast, challenging, and yet, to some degree forgiving controls. All the enemies are unique, and are made with the same simple and responsive controls and mechanics as you have. Strategy is necessary, as this is not really a hack and slash. You need to approach and learn about the enemies. Considering this and diversity, it's really well balanced.
As I said, this game will not hold your hand. You will be tought the controls, but the rest is up to you. The map, and it's secrets are not really limited in terms of exploration. Just make sure to have patience early on as getting the first few abilities felt slow during my first time throught the game. Not too slow, but still, it is. Allthought, the few drawbacks of this game really gets illuminated by it's amazing gameplay, story and world.
Now I'm not going to tell you to buy this straight off. I will consider this game to be quite difficult (by the incresingly sad modern standard as most games play by themselfes). The map is insane, and you will easely, easely spend at least 60 hours to find, explore and achieve all of the obstacles this game puts up for you. Value is off the chart, and with Terraria this has been one of the most valuable game experiences for the pc for a while (fpr years).
So to wrap this up, I will recommend Hollow Knight for anyone intrested in something new, fun and yet punishing, immersive and intresting.

I really like this game. It is challenging, and there is an optional stealth element. You get higher scores when doing stealth actions or "accidental" kills on targets. Additionally, as a fan of duckies, this is an optimal game for duck sightings. You see duckies pop up all over (sadly, the amount of ducks decreases as you progress further in the game).
I noticed a lot of similarities to splinter cell: blacklist, but ultimately how the game works is different. Hitman: Absolution focuses on superhuman abilities (on easy and normal), which disappear at higher difficulties. Splinter cell has the technology readily available, and you can always opt to have a silent gun. Additionally, In splinter cell, you could eliminate everyone without being penalized wheras in Hitman you are penalized if you kill people (without headshotting) and hiding them.
Checkpoints are really bothersome in Hitman however; you cannot close the game or you restart a segment of the level (In the menu there is a "restart level" option which restarts the entire mission, starting at the 1st part. To reset the part of the level, you would need to exit and then continue). The checkpoint system also does not do a proper check for enemies and can reinitialize enemies that you previously subdued (not sure if it's only an issue if you knock them out or not)- It would seem to me that you could theoretically kill every person (except targets) twice as long as there is nothing preventing you from backtracking. I also had some issues where I got stuck in the upstairs of a mission with nothing to throw, reset the checkpoint, and a guard stood at the entrace. I was able to get around this by shooting a bullet, then hiding in a closet until he passed (if the guard doesn't get alerted by a noise, he would stay there).
If you have the time to play this game, It's definitely worth it, it's a very challenging game. If you're going for perfection, keep in mind that there is minimal room for anything but - you generally have to make no errors and can't rely on checkpoints like in other games.

Bright popping colors are left splattered with dark crimson demon blood to further the ultra high contrast theme of the games graphics in an absolutely brilliant way.
Your campaign of scorched earth is filled with subtle nods to the hay day of old school first person shooters, which ties in nicely with the retro setting of the game. Each blasphemous genital euphemism based sound bite from Wang elicits the same through-the-nose chuckle you made when you played Duke Nukem 3D on your 486 driven beige box, and the gameplay, just like then, is just plain fun. There isn't the obnoxious grinding for a side quest, there isn't an open world, you are just an unstoppable force with a sword on a mission to chop things into tiny pieces. The game isn't another challenge to add to your busy life, it's an amazing catharsis of brutal amputations and beheadings.

First off, let me say that
is a direct sequel in the "for the love of Pete, play the original game first or you'll have no clue what's going on" sense, so if you haven't done that, close the window and go do that right now.
OK, with that out of the way: Did you like
? Did you
it? Did you like it but
you had loved it? This game will appeal mainly to people in the third group. I've consistently seen an inverse correlation between people's willingness to ignore the flaws of the first game and whether they liked the sequel, and it's because the sequel has focused almost slavishly on fixing and improving those flaws. Combat is more fun, hacking is less of a chore, NPCs look less like living china dolls, the levels are better-realized... they even made a major mechanic out of adopting and protecting Little Sisters as if to prove they could make it less frustrating than the awful escort mission in the first game. (And then they made an entire DLC — now bundled with the game — based around defending them with a specific array of weapons and plasmids. Even as someone who normally hates mindless-challenge arenas, I found it to be enjoyable.)
The big issue is the PC port, which officially runs on the same engine as the original but was apparently ported from scratch by someone who didn't actually know how. It uses as much of the CPU as Windows will allow and causes texture pop-in unless you have at least a gigabyte of video memory (and even then, you might need to mess around with an INI file to get the game to acknowledge it), the game will crash if you're running AMD's Catalyst Control Center, and the non-speaking vending machines still haven't been fixed after six patches. I'd say it's a toss-up whether you're more or less likely to have game-breaking issues with this game than the first.
In short, if you liked
and wanted to see what it might have been like if they'd had more time to iron out the kinks, or if you just wanted to see more of Rapture, this is the game for you.

I do have some grievances though.
1. The Story Sucks
The story lacks any development. You fight a Rival and see a scene. You do this until you fight YOUR rival with 2 stocks rather than one. The story scenes don't connect to the rivals that you fight until the very end. It's jarring and incoherent.
2. Zetterburn (and also a little bit of Kragg)
This character is far too easy to pick up. I understand that there's a lot of depth to him, but when the entry bar is so low, it discourages experimentation. I would've rather they all be hard to pick up or be like Kragg, where they are easy to pick up but not totally useful in the meta. Without this consistency, Kragg seems useless, and Zetterburn seems stupidly good.
3. Parry on frame 2-5? Too much lag, not enough Time!!
The Parry system is a good idea in theory, but the timing is far too strict for the itty bitty reward that you get from it. A parry should be frame 1-5, so at least you can do reaction based parries. All parries in the current state are far too dificult to pull off without a hard read.
Overall, this game is just very fun. It's ridiculously fast paced, and never makes you wait. The art is well done and the music is catchy. 8/10

This game has surprisingly more going for it than it's Newgrounds appearance may lead you to believe, with some well designed and tricky puzzles inside its disappointingly short playtime.
Gameplay wise this is a pretty simple, but good idea seemingly inspired by Portal, except rather than firing portals connecting to each other, you fire a blue gravity well, which pulls you towards it, and an orange anti-gravity well which pushes you away. Despite the simple controls being basically move, aim, fire, and remove gravity wells, I found this game to play much better when using a controller, so bear that in mind while considering playing it.
Graphics are nothing more than what would be expected of an in-browser flash game, the space-y backgrounds look nice, but the main character is poorly animated and enemies and other platforms are very simple in design. Despite this the music in the game was pretty nice, nothing too special but it fit well and never seemed intrusive.
I managed to get this game really cheap (9p) in a sale, and while I wouldn't say it's worth full price, it would definitely be worth more than that, although from selling cards I managed to make a (very small) profit, so if that's your goal then go for it. Also if achievements are your thing then it's possible to get all eight of them (which are based solely on story progression) in just three hours, and I didn't need to resort to any sort of guides, despite being stuck in places for a while.
Overall this game is good, cheap fun for a slow afternoon, but don't expect a life-changing experience.

Let me start by explaining something, there has been somewhat of a lot of furor over this game being 'just a re-skin' and a tweak here and there. I would like to put this to rest rather quickly, of course it feels a bit like that, in just the same way Civ IV felt a lot like Civ III, and Civ V felt AND LOOKED a lot like Civ IV, this is to be expected with a franchise, but of course this time around it looks rather different indeed. Because it's on an alien planet......I think that's a reasonable excuse to make it look a bit different isn't it....?
Anyhow, the gameplay is pretty much exactly what you expect from a Civ title, it will be instantly recognisable to anyone who's played one before, and is easy to pick up for newcomers too. Thing is, the game itself has expanded it's horizons this time around. Every time you build something for the first time in a game, you get a choice as to what extra bonus that building may have, every time you upgrade a unit you get to choose how the abilities/stats evolve, and the victory conditions are rather more tense than in previous games, since now for many of the victories you must first build a unique tile improvement (built in the city but actually taking up space on the map) and then defend it until you have met the criteria. I will conceed that there appears to be balance issues in the various victories, whereby some are easier to achieve than others, but then again this has been true for every Civ game to date, and I'm pretty sure this is high on the agenda for Firaxis to address.
I have personally enjoyed the game, with all the new ideas merging well with the old familiars, and giving the feel of a real step onwards in the series. There are teething issues, of course there are, but they are being sorted as we speak, and if the community put half as much effort into bug reports and suggestions as they do into complaining bitterly I have a feeling these issues would be dealt with sooner.
Regardless of the above, every game I've played so far, I have experimented with different decisions, and to my surprise they have made a significant difference in the game itself. Beyond Earth offers new levels of customisation and greater choice over many aspects of the game. Some choices are more obvious than others, but none seem superfluous so far, and with the added complexity of Affinities, the variation in builds and ethos are staggering. Moreover, the way it has been made allows for rather more modular DLC options, and I eagerly await the first DLCs to emerge since I believe the game will truly come into it's own as extra content appears.
Overall, it's a definitive thumbs up from me, yes teething problems exist, no they are not a big issue. Is it fun? Yes. Is it still Civ? Yes. Is it different enough to warrant a new title instead of just DLC? Yes. C'mon peoples, what the hell more do you want?!

I was willing to forgive this game's obvious faults, such as the graphical quality (lots of edge tearing on cards, blackboxes where numbers should be), not to mention the bad bad bad bad bad "always online" check that practically holds all of your save progress hostage.
But here we are again, with what appears be Sealed Play from DotP 14 disguised as its own game. When are you guys going to learn this game type sucks? Everything about it just sucks, from the limited card selection that makes building a synergized deck impossible, to forking over obscene amounts of money for randomized booster packs. As in, pay up and you might get some good cards. The whole freemium pricing model in general makes me and my future children's children weep.
Virtual MtG's strength lies in the creativity of its developers, who are at their best when making their own decks for players to use and tweak. If someone wants to build a deck from scratch, chances are they're going to invest in the actual paper cards, instead of this nickle-and-dime operation.
Wizards/Stainless sees the wild success of Hearthstone and thinks "Aha! So that's how we do it! Just charge for everything separately!" And so now we enter a dark age where 'free' content is sold to us through micro charges, subscriptions and payment plans. This will eventually culminate in an Orwellian nightmare-verse, where we are forced to wear bomb collars in the form of license agreements for our games.
Either let players grind out the cards or think of ways around the Pay2win philosophy, like making cards tradeable (other than Infinity Wars, this has yet to be done in any CCG I've played so far). It would enable better in-game and real-world economy, which would then maybe branch into its own card-swapping community. All it would take is some simple software to set up trades between players and might even encounrage them to buy your blasted boosters in case that trend isn't going away anytime soon.

My first review ever.
TL; DR: Yes, the release was horrible. Yes, there are occasional bugs, the cardpool is limited and there are restrictions that some people find annoying. Give the game some time - it will evolve. For something that doesn't require any money, that's the best Magic you can get.
Skip to Pros & Cons in the end if you don't have the time to read all of it ;)
I'll start with describing the technical implementation first, then move on to the game design and finish with thought on how the game will evolve with time.
I've first heard about this game by mere coincidence at an FNM at my local game store. One of the regulars mentioned it coming out in a week. I was excited as I am very passionate about MtG, playing both paper Magic and MtGO.
The release was, however, spoiled by server problems and players couldn't connect. I still played through the first campaign (even though the progress wasn't saved). The next days the servers were falling and getting back up frequently. Overall these few days were horrible but now the worst is over and the servers are almost constantly up.
Other problems include visual bugs. I, for one, am playing without the fancy silver-ish background as it isn't displaying properly. This is most likely due to the fact that my system doesn't really meet the minimum requirements but I've heard it happen to people whose machines do meet them.
Next up are Unknown Errors that seem to be happening to quite a lot of people. I've experienced them myself a couple of times - the game just crashes.
The game mechanics work well and I haven't noticed any mistakes in card interactions (been playing MtG for about 7 years). Due to the limited number of cards currently available in the game the number of mechanics is also limited, which eases the burden somewhat on new players.
The Deck Wizard is a horrible, hideous and disgusting thing. While it can serve to help new players in deck construction it only hinders those, who are more experienced with the game. I wouldn't mind not using it at all but some daily quests require it. My suggestion would be to implement a sort of a "refresh button" to help players cycle through available cards to put in the deck, as the Wizard always seems to recommend the worst possible cards.
2HG is bugged at the moment. While you can easily play against AI with your friend, playing against real opponents is difficult. I've yet to experience it, since whenever we launch the search for opponents it crashes. Playing with random people works perfectly well.
While we're on the topic of multiplayer - the game doesn't have a game chat, or any way to communicate with other players for that matter. Annoying as hell.
AI could use some tweaking for sure. I haven't noticed any difference between easy and hard in terms of how they use cards: it always attacks when there's an opening, it always uses combat tricks when it has them. Someone on the forums mentioned that easy AI prefers hands with more lands. AI can get manascrewed, manaflooded and make mistakes (Animist's Awakening for 5 revealing no lands :D). It also makes it painfully obvious when it has a combat trick in hand. For starters I'd say it's quite fine. I am expecting it to be improved with time, however.
Planeswalker Campains. They are as awesome as they are horrible. While I loved to read on how the most iconic characters of Magic came to be among the most powerful beings in the multiverse, I absolutely hated the decks I had to use while playing their campaigns. Nissa's and Liliana's second mission were among the most horrible experiences. I'm still having nightmares.
This about covers the technical part of the review. Game design is up next.
The model is pretty simple: play games (vs. AI or other players) and earn gold (5-20 per win). Gold cap is set to 400 per day. Gold from daily quests does not count towards daily gold cap. Boosters cost 150 and contain 6 cards: 1 rare or mythic rare, 2 uncommons and 3 commons. While players can't trade cards they also can't get extras of cards: having 4 Elvish Visionaries will make it so that you will never open them again in a booster. Gold can be bought for actual money.
There is also a limit on mythics, rares and uncommons. While in paper Magic and MtGO you're allowed up to 4 copies of a card in your deck, Magic Duels Origins allows 1 mythic, 2 rares and 3 uncommons. You can put any number of different mythics in a deck but only one copy of each mythic card (1 Kytheon, 1 Chandra, 1 Nissa but not 2 Nissas and 2 Chandras). The same applies to rares and uncommons. Hope I made it clear. Whether this limitation is good or not has been a matter of debate since the game's launch. I, for one, don't mind it at all.
Now the base for the game has been the most recent set: Origins. However not all cards from the set have been implemented in this game. Instead, some card from previous sets have been added, namely M15 and Theros block (also guildgates and conditional lands, to make multicolored deck construction easier). These cards are awarded to players for free, after they finish the tutorial campaign. I still can't understand the decision to cut the Origins cards but I most welcome the cards from other sets.
Speaking of tutorials, while a bit tedious for experienced players they are detailed enough for newbies. Anyone who isn't a new players is recommended to go to the Gameplay Options Menu and turn most of them off.
Experienced players will notice that the color themes are not quite prominent but are still there. Blue has a poor selection of counterspells for instanse.
Pros:
+ it's Magic: the Gathering - one of the best TCG there is. (Although the "Trading" part doesn't really apply here).
+ it is not P2W.
+ decent card pool to start with.
+ comfortable (if not generous) gold cap and booster prices.
+ 2-Headed-Giant is a lot of fun.
Cons:
- some bugs have still not been addressed
- no chat
- deck restrictions (I don't mind them at all but most people seem to find it annoying)
- no trading
Overall an okay game that will only get better with time. Right now it doesn't really reach the level of Blizzard's HS but it is already VERY close (despite all the drawbacks it currently has). Imagine what it will become when more stuff gets added and fixed? Have patience.

I'll keep it short.
I thoroughly enjoyed it, as an avid Tolkien fan, it was nice to see some of the places in Middle Earth explored a little more, Such as Sarn Ford, Fornost etc. I've compiled into a list things I enjoyed and didn't enjoy about the game.
Positives:
The world looks pretty good, and has captured I feel how the various places you visit would be, based on the description from the book.
The combat is decent enough, I played as the Ranger and enjoyed rolling underneath trolls or around Orcs and slashing at them whilst they were exposed.
Side quests are a bonus, as in any game as they give you extra things to do, and increase playtime. There are also two 'Survival' type bonus missions.
Whilst the levels are Linear, I did feel like I was exploring Middle Earth, which is obviously a good thing.
Co-Op, in any adventure game is great, and this can be really good fun with a friend or two.
Things I didn't enjoy:
Not much to pick at here really, and a few of these things won't apply to you guys anyway.
The game felt difficult towards the end, I know it's supposed to be Co-Op, but I found it nigh on impossible doing it on Singleplayer, as both the AI companions ran in a straight line to revive me, straight into the path of that Troll guarding my body.
A few of the locations don't feel 'Tolkienesque' to me, such as the Barrow Downs with 'Zombie' like creatures, but this can be overlooked.
I felt the shop system a waste of time, as I was constantly finding good enough Gear to be getting on with, and had no need at all to buy any gear except for early in the game, even then I now realise it wasn't nessecary as I often found something better than what I'd just bought moments later in a chest.
Conclusion:
This review isn't to be taken too serious, a lot of the issues can be overlooked depending on your expectations, but I enjoyed it, and it's a nice little romp through Middle-Earth as you take a different path from the usual main characters during The war of the Ring, And I reccomend this be it to play Solo or Co-op.

Stumbles over its own feet.
The core of the game (minus quirks and bugs) is well-conceived - it has an interesting style, the cover mechanic is neat, and figuring out how the abilities of the characters help or hinder you is fun.
The first few levels are great - you're figuring out the mechanics and trying to figure out how to complete the extra objectives so you can unlock new characters with new abilities.
The problem is that once you get further into the game, these fun mechanics become a weight around your neck. You have to complete all the extra objectives in one run (no going in with one character, getting one, and then bringing another character to get another), so you end up using only one or two. The cover/execution mechanic is nice, until 4 enemies are stacked up so they go wonky.
There are no checkpoints, and many missions have a sudden difficulty spike at the end (usually when SWAT teams start pouring into the level for no real reason). The enemies are not randomized, but the powerups are. So you end up doing the exact same movements for the first 80% of a mission, over and over, so you can get back to the shootout at the end that killed you. When there's no challenge in a section but you're forced to replay it over and over (and with no checkpoints your progress is reset anyway), it's really easy to just go for the quit button instead.
It's not BAD, but Not a Hero 2 has the potential to be GREAT.
Recommendations for the developers (update/sequel):
- Make it more like 10 extra objectives per level, that are harder but require different characters. Encourage and reward replays.
- Add checkpoints, if only at boss battles / cinematic events. Or split them into mission 10-1 / 10-2, etc.
- Get rid of the "2 people are standing next to each other, so sliding just knocks you down because the second one magically punches you" mechanic
- Add a level editor / something to extend the game and let people think of new scenarios
- More characters with more variety (#1 will play into this)
- Fix the bug where Xbox One controllers fire constantly (due to it always thinking RT is held down unless you hold LT down)

overall : Keep in mind I am not being butthurt about my purchase in this game being nulled due to the fact that I can no longer play it, nor get a steam refund. Defy Gravity Extended is a platformer where the primary gimmick is a gun that shoots gravity wells, which draw you and golden objects in, and anti-wells, which do the opposite. The game maintains a mild level of challenge for the most part; at times it feels like the gravity gun mechanic is ignored since the double jump can get the job done as well. I particularly enjoyed the levels where I had to use the gravity gun to move myself around on a golden platform; those were pretty chill. On the other hand, there are a few incredibly frustrating sections — these usually involved a combination of instant-death pits and robots that spit shurikens. Getting through them felt more up to luck than skill, and it didn't help that the hitboxes of enemies are just a bit larger than they look.
The game tries to add a hint of a story by presenting the stages as a Gravitymancer proving ground, but the game abruptly ends with a "You Win!" credits level; it kinda makes you wonder why they bothered. Completing that level begins hard mode, which takes the original 24 levels of the game, removes your anti-well gun, and makes all enemies golden. There's supposed to be additional changes in later levels, and there could be some more story as well, but I haven't gotten that far yet.
As you can probably tell, the game is not very pretty. The graphics are very amateurish — the developers didn't even bother making the backgrounds tile properly. Sound design is equally simple, though I did enjoy the music selection.
Overall, Defy Gravity Extended is alright for a game that looks as cheap as it is, which is $0.14 currently. The 3 trading cards will very likely recoup the cost of the game once sold.

I've been itching to be the badass in the suit for some time, and as our protagonist is an uber-macho ultra-masculine Iron Man, it can be quite entertaining to tromp around in his NanoBoots. However I was disappointed by some of the glaring technical issues which have been left unattended by CryTek since its arrival on Steam.
You wear the NanoSuit in the first iteration of the photorealistic experience, becoming the ultimate soldier. Prepare to Maximum your way through enemy forces, alien strongholds and countless gorgeously rendered trees and foliage.
Crysis was for nearly a decade the gold standard for performance: "Sure the server's fast, but will it run Crysis?" Modern systems can still be tasked by the demanding CryEngine in its earliest release. Unfortunately it has not aged well, and graphical flaws can break the visual flow, such as spawning objects incorrectly and even breaking mission targets.
Electronic Arts and Crytek issued their final patches in 2007, and it has not received any attention since, which casts a shadow on its asking price. Do not pay full price for this game. Instead, buy it as part a bundle or in a sale. It is a satisfying experience for the hardcore, and even casual shooter.
Stone dumb AI amuses more often than frustrate, and once you learn their recognition patterns, you're nearly untouchable. All that said, this is a fun futuristic if somewhat thoughtfless romp.
