I am a huge fan of the Bioshock franchise and I especially adore the first of the series, Bioshock 1. I won't be talking too much about the game itself, however, as I am sure by now great many are aware of its status as an entertaining FPS and a marvellous story (which is of course subjective. At least most KNOW about the game). Instead I will be focusing on the remastering.
Judging from the topmost reviews, many people are suffering from gamebreaking bugs, like saves deleting, crashing and sequence breaks. During my ~17 hours playthrough I encountered none of those, the game never crashed even though I frequently Alt+Tabbed to and fro. I did encounter some performance issues, even though very slight ones. The game would lag horribly on some parts of Apollo Square levels, especially the long corridors between areas. Small graphical issues were also somewhat frequent. Occasionally some effects, especially around Vita-Chambers, caused red-and-blue artifacts to appear. Sometimes dead bodies would start to slide towards one direction, banging against the wall until finally dissappearing. Textures would still sometimes pop-up, as I remember from the original version, where the high-def version of textures will only load when you are very close to an object. A big problem that many people seemed to be facing on the original version, sounds not working from the get go and requiring some fiddling with output settings, was this time NOT present, so at least some technical improvements have been made.
Minor annoyances, such as the semi-unskippable intro splashes when you start up the game, are still there.  The "quicksave" loading screen is too long to be called a "quicksave" which kind of defeats the purpose. Complaints about difficulty are always a matter of taste, but as an avid gamer I felt normal too easy towards the end, especially final boss was too much of a stroll. Conversely some early game enemies, especially Houdini Splicers, felt sometimes even annoyingly powerful. Same goes for the hacking minigame. While I enjoy the concept, the difficulty seems somewhat bipolar. Usually they are too easy, unless you encounter a very hard one that requires pure luck to be solved in time. People new to video games might have different experiences though and I haven't tried harder difficulties (although I have bad experiences - bullet spongy enemies - on that, particularly in Bioshock Infinite).
The game looked quite nice, although not suberb. Weren't it for the bonus features, namely the Making of documentary and some challenge levels, it would not be enough bang for your buck at full price. Owners of the original version received to product for free. I didn't care about the challenge levels so I haven't tried them, but the documentary is extremely interesting! I've always appreciated features like this included in video games and it was one of the biggest reasons I replayed the game. Huge bonus for that one. Ken Levine mentioned on one episode how he got the inspiration for the story from Ayn Rand's book "Fountainhead", although I wonder if he really meant "Atlas Shrugged". At least its plot and setting resemble the game more than Fountainhead. But I digress.
If you didn't like Bioshock before, you won't like it after this product either. Nothing in the core gameplay has changed. If you can manage a playthrough without debilitating performance issues, Bioshock 1 Remastered will be a fine experience for people returning to Rapture!

I went into an apartment complex to loot some stuff, not knowing yet what that meant. It was my first playthrough, and I thought "stealing" stuff was maybe like it was in Fallout or Skyrim. If someone sees me do it, they get hostile, and I kill them. Shouldn't be a big deal.
I was skulking around when I was spotted by a guy who yelled at me to get out. He had a gun, so I thought he was a bad guy. I blew him away with my shotgun. I started to loot his corpse when when voices started shouting upstairs. I quickly hid and waited for the ambush, but what came around the corner weren't more armed guards. No, it was much worse. It was his parents.
They were wailing about their lost son and how they couldn't survive without him. I couldn't speak to them. I wanted so badly to tell them that they could come back to our place, that I had killed him accidentally, something, anything. I walked out without taking what little they had left, in fact leaving my shotgun and rounds in their refrigerator to help them, hoping that maybe I didn't doom them entirely, but what was the point of survival for them anymore? Why would they want to survive in a world without their son who laid his life on the line for their safety?
I never went back there. I was probably as affected as Marko was. He was depressed. I had to atone. I ran to the City Hospital to donate as much of our medical supplies as we could spare. I risked my life to free prisoners held by armed thugs. Night after night, in my attempt to atone, I tried to do as much good as I possibly could manage, if only to mitigate the incredible horror I had performed. We all survived, and I never went back to their apartment. I couldn't face them again. I don't know if they made it or not.
Man, I'm a terrible person.

-Character customization is a neat feature to add, and opens up a wide range of possibilities for creativity. (Can only pick colors though)
Cons:
-The tutorial mode is mostly unforgiving for new players (Hard to pick up the more advanced moves)
-Ranked mode is filled with very skilled players, making it a chore to compete

If you can get past the minor cons like I did, this game is a blast to play with friends or even practising on bots. If you haven't play Smash Bros before picking this up, you might find it a bit difficult as the learning curve is a little steep, but don't let me stop you from playing this great fighting game.

Before i start, i almost always finish games i start, even if they are bad. This game however got to a point that it was unwinable. The console version was apparently too easy so they ramped up the difficulty scaling on the pc version, which they overdid. Im still interested in the story, i just got to the point where i couldnt kill anything, and to fix it i would have to scrap my save and start again. Ill elaborate though... there are no levels in this game, your main character just gets ranks which are like level ups where you get random points based on what you killed. HOWEVER the game tricks you into thinking you can just fight large groups of enemies to get a larger reward, what it really means is to ONLY fight the tough enemies, otherwise when you rank up you get points based on the weak enemies, which is to say you barely get stat increases but the enemies get tougher. Rank up enough this way and the game becomes unwinnable. I only found out what i was doing wrong about half way into the game and the only way to correct it is to start from the beginnning again. I couldnt do any of the sidequests to beat elite enemies because they often just one shotted me. That said the correct way of playing this game is to pick up the strongest allies, avoid every enemy you can and only fight bosses or elite enemies as part of sidequests to keep your rank down as low as it can go. This game greatly discourages revisiting areas and grinding (such as farming the parts to craft a good weapon). I may someday return to this game in an attempt to beat it, but having to restart because i farmed too much seems like a bad gameplay design.

I started playing Rivals of Aether in early access, but after its full release, I've been playing it a lot more.
The game plays a lot like Smash Bros., as that is its main inspiration.  However, what you'll get from Rivals is not a soulless Smash clone.  Instead, you'll get a game filled with its own personality, quirks, and tons of fun gameplay.
A fantastic inclusion is the two modes of stages.  There's an "Aether" mode and a "basic" mode.  This essentially doubles the number of stages in the game.  Aether mode stages have different gimmicks and stage hazards.  They aren't suitable for competitive play, but make for fun casual matches.  The "basic" stages are a bit misleading.  Rather, they're tournament legal versions of all the  stages, made for competitive use in tournaments.  These stages combine familiar layouts (such as Tower of Heaven using the triplatform layout of Battlefield and The Endless Abyss is a long stage with no platforms, similar to Final Destination), while including original stages that make for interesting additions, such as the quadplatforms of Merchant Port and Fire Capital.  The game includes built in striking and banning for stage selection, which should be familiar to fans of competitive Super Smash Bros.
The gameplay structure itself is fantastic, too.  Rivals of Aether puts its own spin on the platform fighter genre by removing shields and grabs and implementing a parry system instead.  This majorly increases the risk:reward factor.  If you successfully parry an attack, your opponent will be stunned, creating an opening for you to attack.  Parrying a projectile will reflect it.  However, if you miss your parry, you yourself are left open for punishment.  The removal of shields requires you to have more of a read on your opponent.  Movement is incredibly fluid as well.  Wavedashing in Rivals of Aether is much more simplified than in Melee, where it was already relatively easy to perform.  Dash dancing is also present.  There is one character with a double jump cancel, I'll get back to that later.  Hitstun is at a perfect balance, in my opinion.  There is incredibly high combo potential in this game, but most of it requires you to read your opponent's DI.
The sound design in this game is fantastic.  Nearly, if not every song is incredibly catchy.  I find myself listening to some of the music in my spare time (my personal favourite is Tempest Peak).  However, an aspect of the sound design that often goes unappreciated in fighting games is the hit sound effects.  All of the sound effects in Rivals of Aether sound incredibly satisfying, especially when you land a sweetspot.  My personal favourites are Wrastor's clap and Absa's sweetspot kicks.
From a graphical standpoint, the game is simple, but beautiful.  It uses charming pixel graphics to represent the environments and fighters.  The stages are all gorgeous and look fantastic.  Graphics accurately represent hitboxes, which is an issue some fighting games tend to run into.  As an added bonus, since the game is in 2D, there is no Z-Axis to mess with hitboxes, like in some other fighting games.
However, the real meat of a fighting game comes in the form of the characters, and in this area, Rivals of Aether does not disappoint.  There's a cast of 8 characters, with a 9th guest character having been teased.  Each character offers a different playstyle and unique options.  Some are more straightforward than others, but all of them reward skill.  The game is balanced incredibly well, thanks to it being in early access for nearly two years.  This allowed the developers to receive input from top players on matchups and characters.  As a result, everyone is viable, and you can play whoever you'd like at a high level of competitive play.
Each character has their own gimmick, with some being more straightforward than others.
Zetterburn can set his opponents on fire to do damage over time and power up his strong attacks.  Forsburn can create smoke on the stage to obscure the opponent's view.  He can also create a clone that is instantly destroyed when hit.  There's more to him, but that's the simplified version of it.  Orcane can create a puddle on the ground, which you can teleport to at any time, or have it bubble up for some interesting combos.  Maypul can "tag" her opponents, which makes her strong attacks wrap them up with vines and also gives her the option to swing over ot them with her up special.  Kragg has the ability to pull rocks from the ground and even create a platform/wall with his up special.  Wrastor has multiple jumps and can use his side special to create a small area that allows him to move more quickly and extend his combos.  Etalus can freeze the ground, which makes him surprisingly mobile for a heavy character.  He can also absorb his ice to become heavier and power up his strong attacks.  Absa can cancel her double jump to perform aerials close to the ground.  Her forward air, back air, and down air all have powerful sweetspots that are hard to land.  However, Absa can place a cloud on the stage.  By kicking this cloud with her aerials mentioned before, she can create a large shockwave that expands the size of her sweetspots.  The cloud can also be popped from a distance to control the stage.  Absa can also place a slow, but powerful attack on the cloud to make it act as a trap or create a thunderbolt between her and it.
I highly recommend this game to anyone looking to play a fun fighting game, whether competitive or casually.

If you like Saints Row IV then this is a great addition to the series. It strips away with any pretense of being a serious game and just allows the player to have a lot of fun. However, you really need to be a fan of SR to get the most from the game. It does seem short but for the asking price that's fine, takes about 3-5 hrs to complete the main quest  and the same again to do all the sidequests, although there are a heap of collectables to find.
The flying mechanic is excellent although it takes a lot of points to get it to a usable level. Once at that level though soaring through hell is a joy to experience.
The writing could be more fleshed out but when it delivers it really delivers. Some moments are laugh out loud funny and the musical segment is astounding.
On the downside, the graphics are decidedly last-gen, playing as Johnny and Kinzie nixes any customisation as well. A lot of time it definitely feels like a mega-DLC adding very little to gunplay and mechanics. Also no music stations, which has always been a high point of previous SR titles. You also really need to play SR:IV first, otherwise a lot of what happens will make no sense.
All-in-all worth buying if you're a fan of the series then this is a must buy. It's short but an absolute blast and is well worth the low asking price.

This may be the slowest pace game I've ever played thats not based off of real time i.e. Animal Crossing. Hell the "tutorial" took me 15 HOURS to complete. I didn't even know I was still in it. IF you have the patience to work through that then the game really opens up beyond that point and the game becomes pretty decent.
For a game that came out 7 years ago it's graphics are stellar, easily amongst the best I've ever seen. Many times throughtout the game I had to stop and simply admire the scenery around me.
Storywise it's about as convoluted as one could get. I think I was in a fever dream when I finally figured out what the story was supposed to be about. Characters are pretty forgettable except for Lightning and that's solely based off her design.
Gameplay wise early on is extremely repetative as you have the characters have so little to play with and the auto battle system is a huge turnoff for most people. Important to note that not using the auto battle function and  selecting abilities and targets for yourself is more rewarding as the system doesn't necessarily choose the most effective tactics.
In summary:      -Story makes little sense
-Forgettable characters
-Combat takes a long time to fully open up but once it does I find it to be fairly enjoyable
-Beautiful graphics that honestly carried me through a lot of the early game
If you have saintly patience and are a sucker for amazing graphics and scenery like me then I recommend it. If you don't stay far away as you'll most likely lose interest within the first hour.

I have been playing MTG on various platforms on and off for about 3 years now.  I never really wrote a review before so bare with me.   I have played the game for about 4 hours and completed the tutorial and have finished the campaign for one of the Wizards (sorry I forgot his name lol).  I love  the new setup because of the way they teach you how to play during the match sequence with tutorial side lessons, then they send you back into battle where you can implement what you just learned or go at it your own way.
The back story for each characters in Origins is perfect because you get to learn more about how they came to be, I can honestly say playing the other Magic games did not interest me one bit about who the characters were and why they were in this mortal battle with one another.   The cinamatics have been tone down for more of a moving still image ordeal, but I can understand they did this because of online data bandwith, it's harder to transfer a graphically rich game online without some latency (I assume, don't qoute me on that.)
I heard people complaining about slow downs, long loading times and other glitches, I honestly have not experienced any of that while playing for 4 hours.  The game ran smooth and I'm running it on a HP Pavillion G4 laptop with 4 GB of ram Dual core 2.74 64 bit AMD A6 - 4400M processor, with Windows 8.1.  I will say this, don't buy this computer because it over heats (even with artic 5 thermal paste on the CPU/GPU) when running games or intense apps, but I digress.
The games has full controller support which is good for when my family or console friends come over they can play with a controller.  I love the achievements because they are not to impossible to aquire,  the driving force that had me playing and wanting to go further than any other game in the series that I have played before, was the back story of the characters and the earning of money to buy  booster cards from the store.  I don't know why but I wanted to keep playing to see how much money I can gain, this aspect of the game reminded me of when I use to play Wagic The Gathering (google it) on PC, PSP and my Android devices.
I didn't play online with other players yet because quite frankly I honestly never had a good experience with playing Magic online multiplayer.  I always get jerks who say rude things, kick me out of the lobby, let me in so they can just have a laugh as they all turn on me in a 4 player match, etc...  After that I pretty much prefer to play offline, with family/friends or the AI.
Overall I have to say this game is terriffic and I will be grinding to get more coins, cards and to learn more about the characters in the near future.  If you love card battling that is simple to pick up and learn, but is deep in strategy and action this is certainly the game for you!!! I highly recommend this game.

Meh
Edit: Allow me to elaborate. While I still maintain my initial one word review is perfectly accurate for how I feel about this game, I should probably add some insight.
Is it the best or worst rpg you'll ever play? Extremely unlikely in both regards. The game is very linear for the longest time and while I personally believe that that's not neccessarily a bad thing in story driven rpgs, there is very little room for exploration within that linearity. It does consist of mostly hallways and if there's a route you don't need to take to get to the next objective which is always marked on the map, Spoiler Alert: 9 times out of 10 there's a treasure sphere there (this games chest equivalent).
Despite it's linear style, I actually liked the story and thought it was well told however it is alittle confusing at first especially with key aspects of it having similar names. The battle system is another thing I liked especially with the depth it gains as you advance further in the game and unlock new characters. Enemies are visable on the world map and you manually engage them (most of the time) allowing you to actually sneak up on them for a pre-emptive attack which nets you a huge starting bonus for the battle.
So with all these seemingly positive things to say about it, why just a "meh"? Well, there are times when the game gets really frustrating. Early on (and for quite sometime after) you deal with split partys of specific characters. While it functions well with the story and it serves a secondary purpose of allowing you to explore how those characters work within the battle system, one character in particular is just outright insufferable.
The segments where you are stuck with him seem to take forever for two reasons: One, terrible character and two, early on he isn't exactly a powerhouse. Near the end game he's not nearly as bad in both regards but you hang in there because it takes QUITE some time for that to be the case.
So a terrible character ruins a lot of the early to mid game and by the time he finally comes around, the damage has already been done. Outside of that though, its not the worst game you'll ever play though it has its fair share of poorly executed aspects.
I intend to play the entire trilogy so I'll be reviewing them all.

I've been itching to be the badass in the suit for some time, and as our protagonist is an uber-macho ultra-masculine Iron Man, it can be quite entertaining to tromp around in his NanoBoots. However I was disappointed by some of the glaring technical issues which have been left unattended by CryTek since its arrival on Steam.
You wear the NanoSuit in the first iteration of the photorealistic experience, becoming the ultimate soldier. Prepare to Maximum your way through enemy forces, alien strongholds and countless gorgeously rendered trees and foliage.
Crysis was for nearly a decade the gold standard for performance: "Sure the server's fast, but will it run Crysis?" Modern systems can still be tasked by the demanding CryEngine in its earliest release. Unfortunately it has not aged well, and graphical flaws can break the visual flow, such as spawning objects incorrectly and even breaking mission targets.
Electronic Arts and Crytek issued their final patches in 2007, and it has not received any attention since, which casts a shadow on its asking price. Do not pay full price for this game. Instead, buy it as part a bundle or in a sale. It is a satisfying experience for the hardcore, and even casual shooter.
Stone dumb AI amuses more often than frustrate, and once you learn their recognition patterns, you're nearly untouchable. All that said, this is a fun futuristic if somewhat thoughtfless romp.

Shadow Warrior is a fun and straight-forward shooter. It nails all the design principles of games of its type. Levels with secrets to discover and good enemy variation as well as great pacing in how they reward you with weapons as you progress, all of which are useful in their own way. The powers provided are all fun to use and you might even feel the need to use the sword alone at some sections just because they really nail the way it feels. It's also pretty damn cool that you can use a weapon in one hand and a power in another. Overall, gameplay is spot on. My only two gripes would be very minor things. First, enemy curation: at times they just throw enemies at you in sections for no reason. It's just a mishmash of enemy types all thrown together with no pattern in mind. More things to kill isn't bad but it's the fact that this cluster of enemies don't play off each other and aren't utilizing the arena to their advantage, more they've just been tossed in for the sake of being there. The second would be the armoured charging enemy with the weakspot on his back. When other games include an enemy of this type they get it right. Here they fumble it to the point of annoyance. Enemies will always automatically turn to face you. Imagine trying to get behind an enemy when that's the case. Now imagine two of them. People who have played the game will get the level I'm referencing. It doesn't make it impossible or even hard it's just a big waste of time trying to beat them in a game that is actually so fast paced. Despite these gripes, I'd say the game is a fun experience regardless.
(Boss fights are meh, they're quite easy and all the same to an extent though the character design is quite nice.)
It's got a sort of 'Kick♥♥♥♥♥ style of progression in regards to the story. It starts off quite light-hearted and insane but it takes a serious turn as the stakes raise. Lo Wang is still a goofball throughout but he's aware of what's at stake as you progress. The story itself really is plain, no surprise, it's just a save the world tale with a few interesting creative choices thrown in for flavour. Hoji and Lo Wang play off each other pretty well and they're the only things that propel the story to the point of interest as their dialogue is quite fun.
Overall, pick this game up, I certainly enjoyed it and even more than it's sequel and for a 20 hour game at such a decent price I'd say it's almost a steal.

Bad news first;
This was more of a letdown than Duke Nukem Forever.  I love the X series.  I've bought the games more than once.  This does not belong in the series.  The only controller that works right is the Xbox 360 controller, and the entire interface is made around being a console game.  The game only uses DirectX 9 (like Xbox 360), and the story line missions are buggy and you can get stuck and have to manually edit your gamesave in order to continue the game to fix things yourself.  This really feels like a failed console game that was ported to PC that was never supposed to be in the X universe.
Industry standard controllers, like the Saitek X52, do not work.  The button mapping is buggy, as well.  It sees everything as an XBox 360 controller stick for some reason.  Also, it won't let you map more functions to a keyboard and mouse than you could to an XBox 360 controller.  This is a PC game that is constrained by a console controller's limitations.
I'm still in the tutorial and it bugged out on me and stopped giving me any story missions or objectives about 10 minutes in.  Now I'm abandoned.
The "universe" is tiny.  There's only one camera view for your ship and only one small ship to fly.  You will not be commanding a large capitol ship yourself into epic battles.
There are maybe 10 different NPCs reused everywhere and only 3 different tiny interiors of space station ports.  Going inside of the space stations is obnoxiously painful, and the NPCs treat you rudely for no reason and repeat the same few phrases over and over.  It is also a pain to find the vendors you trade with and the interface to trade is awful.  It's just like a big F You when I am talking to every NPC to try to get the story to progress and trigger something, and they all end a conversation with something snarky like "Nice chat.  NOT!"
The economy is less advanced than current convenient stores.  It's seriously like each little port is a mostly empty farmer's market with a few NPCs that will trade with you, but you have to find them and sit through their insulting chat.
There is a trading system you can do from your ship, but I cannot figure out for the life of me if I am buying or selling items and where they are going or where the money is going.  I don't know if I'm buying missles or selling them.  What is the difference between To Sales and To Offers?  I have no idea.  I think I accidentally sold all of my missles, which I thought were on my little ship, but maybe my large ship had them?  I couldn't figure it out at all.
There is no radar for space battles.   No radar.  NO RADAR.  How do you dogfight with no radar to track enemies?  All you have is pointers around your view screen for directions.
Oh yeah.  No targetting, either.
The Good:
The art design for the ships and exteriors of the space stations are amazing.  The art direction really is inspiringly beautiful in how they designed things.  You can get a sense for the purpose of various parts of stations and ships just by looking at them.  It is a joy to first explore them.  Even with only DirectX 9, they did an amazing job for how it looks when you fly around.  (the NPCs and interiors of stations are not that inspiring, though.  The NPCs are especially creepy with how their face pops onto your screen first, then body parts appear at different times and they materialize in front of you, due to pop in)
The sound is nice.
One thing the devs did is almost amazing enough to send them a thank you, though.  The save files are .xml files, which means they are human parsable ane plain text, so you can edit them pretty easily when you need to fix things... or give yourself tons of money, because the economy is so painfully implemented that it isn't worth the time to make money legitimately.  Why do I like this so much?  Because it is a single player game and people want to cheat or do fun things with a game to sandbox it when they want to.  Many people will install "trainers" that are loaded with malware in order to cheat, or install other cheat engine programs that will get you blocked by some online games just for being on your computer, or are also fillled with malware.
It's time to bring cheats back to games.  ♥♥♥♥ acchievements and ♥♥♥♥ encrypted save files.  Thanks to the emphasis on acchievements in the game industry, debug modes and cheat codes have disappeared so that people don't cheat to get some virtual trophy.  The result is giant botnets of malware infested users sending spam, helping to DDoS, and make the internet a worse place, because they install some trainer and now their system is compromised.  Kudos to the devs for letting their users do what they want with their own single player games.
What it would take for me to change my mind about this game;
Revamp the interface to make sense for keyboard and mouse.  You can keep the console option for big screen mode people, but give us a choice.
Fix joystick and key mapping support, especially for the X52, wink wink
Let me map to more keys than an Xbox 360 controller can handle.
Put in the traditional targetting and a radar
Remove the interiors of space stations and just give me some giant landing bays that let me add a station to my trade network that I can access forever from my ship.  Look, right now, in real life, I can use this magical internet to buy or sell anything I want, and even more things that I don't want.  THE FUTURE WOULD HAVE SOMETHING BETTER.  STOP TURNING SPACE TRADING INTO FARMER'S MARKETS.  No one would do that with the technology available.  THIS MAKES NO SENSE.
Fix the story mission bugs
Give me fleet management tools that let me make decisions that don't ever involve flying to a ship to talk to someone in person.  I should never have to dock inside one of my ships unless I am delivering a physical person or object.
Awesome game.

First the downsides. A few graphics cards don't work yet but each time one comes up they work on it. As others said the replayability is somewhat limited but since each game has a few random elements (who you start with, weather, what your house has, etc) it is definitely replayable. The length of play is fairly short but not the 3 hours some claim, for me it is closer to 9-12 hours.
Now the good stuff. The graphics style and soundtrack and interesting and lend to the encompassing mood. But the amazing part, the part that makes it worth the money even if you played it through once, is the atmosphere. You aren't playing a band of soldiers, you are playing a hodegpodge group of civilians trying to survive siege, bandits, soldiers, starvation, disease, in fighting, and dispair. It is dismal in a way I've never seen in games and sucks you in. It helps that the stories and characters are influenced by people who were in the Seige of Sarajevo.
My personal favorite part on replaying the game is seeing how the different characters affect game play. A couple characters are downright physical burdens. Some don't play well with others. Some are caring and get depressed if you go against their moral code. Others are selfish and aren't made happy by being charitable. Normally it is the strategy in these types of games that grabs me. While it is good in this game, instead I think about the street tough that ended up at the wrong place at the wrong time, I wonder if the little boy will ever get his toy soldier back, and what ever happened to the man I had to turn away because we didn't even have enough food for ourselves.
;tldr This game is emotionally moving. I didn't think a computer game could do that.

At a very discounted price of $0.14, I'd say I got what I paid for: both good and bad.
As the trailer shows, this game is ugly. The stages look like they came out of a 2005 Newgrounds game, with its bare-bones layout and stock-image-looking backgrounds that, sometimes, have visible edges where the pattern ends. If you were to judge this game based solely on its looks, then it certainly isn't for you, Mr. Overclocked $800 Graphics Card.
Where the game shines is in its gameplay: and at the end of the day, that's all that reallyt matters. The game ain't no Portal slayer but it does use its gravity and anti-gravity in clever ways, like having to cross a gap by switching between the two. They aren't always tight though: I got to the end of a couple based on luck and I doubt I did it the way the developer wanted it.
So sure, this won't be the greatest puzzler you've ever played, but if you got some refund money sitting around like I did (thanks poorly optimized copy of 'Hatred'!) and you're feeling up for some cheap fun, you could do a lot worse; it's decent and worth a risk of whatever you pay for it.

It grows more difficult every day. At first, we struggled to get food. We boarded the windows early, anticipating looters. On the eighth day, a man named Roman arrived. He had run from the military and asked to stay with us. We agreed. We knew supplies were tight, but we figured he could help us defend against looters and raiders. Two nights later, Roman went out to scavenge a grocery store. He saved a girl from a drunken soldier, but was shot multiple times. When he came back, we had no bandages. The following night, Pavel went out to get bandages to save Roman's life. Without them, he would surely die. Pavel never came back. A neighbor said he went into an old school and they soon heard shots from it after. The next morning, Roman died from bloodloss. Bruno is... growing defensive. I sometimes hear him mumbling in his sleep about how he's glad it was them and not him. He's begun eating a strange meat and laughs randomly. I don't think I can trust him. We're running low on supplies and if he feels the need... he'll sacrifice me to save his own life. I still have the pistol that Roman used to save the girl. I think I can hear Roman coming...
This game is amazing. Reading their journals, depending on who is in the party and who does what with certain events, the characters individual reactions can change. This last playthrough, Bruno, who had always been one of the more compassionate characters, was suddenly upset with others helping people, complaining that they must worry about themselves instead of others. Roman began to get adjusted to killing people in those few days before his death, while the others, except Bruno, kept their usual reactions about the situation. Bruno would always say things about it being better they died than Roman. I was fairly surprised at how much some of the environments could change on different playthroughs. This was the first time I encountered soldiers in the school, and while trying to find their trader, I wandered into the wrong room and was threatened. On my way out, five soldiers decided to start shooting and I lost Pavel as well as the assault rifle he was carrying.
I recommend this to anyone who likes survival games. It has a far better storyline than most survival games out there, and there are no second chances for characters. If someone dies, they are dead and the others will feel the effects of their loss. No matter how well you may be doing, there is always that one catalyst that can destine the whole group for destruction if not watched.

To the game itself:
I played this after I played Infinite and I got to say (after everyone told me that this would be the best part of the series) I got to disagree.
The gameplay here is very stale and closer to the end it just gets frustrating because you hardly make any damage with normal ammo. Many of the plasmids are just there to stun enemies wherefore I happened to use Telekinesis a lot because it made (a lot) more damage in the usual encounters than using the Inferno or Shock plasmids for example.
It's just hours of walking around and collecting things for people to get to another place.
In the end there is that iconic boss you have to defeat and after that, there's a very short epilogue (30 seconds maybe) and then the credits roll.
Although the story and the twists are quite interesting, the way of storytelling isn't that good, since there are just thousands of voice memos of people for you to collect and listen to and then you're also talking to others through a walkie talkie, which is basically the same. The physical encounters with these people are better.
The idea of the plasmids itself in combination with normal weapons is just great but since they haven't made the movement, FOV, graphics better with the remastering and you still want to play this kind of game, I simply recommend you to play Bioshock Infinite because it makes up for most of which this part lacks and has a better story.

The Last Remnanat is a turn-based strategy RPG with a diferent kind of combat mechanincs. Each character will be placed in a squad of 5 (max) and will act on a general command, such as attack with magical arts, etc. Usually, the available commands are influenced by the abilities of the squad leader and the condition of the battle (if they're dying or if another squad needs help etc.). However, you will not be able to directly control what type of action each individual will perform. For example, the command is to inflict ailments, but you cannot specify whether to silence them, poison them, etc.
However, sometimes characters may change their actions depending on the situation. This is usually due to a successful quick time event (QTE), high morale, etc. Sometimes characters will perform healing abilities because they just need healing, or the command was to offer support to others (not a direct command to heal) or the character's class is just inclined to healing. This makes battles much more dynamic and unpredictable. This all leads up to one thing.
Satisfying boss fights. I can say without a doubt, the best thing about this game is how challenging and enjoyable the fights that matter can be. It's the strong point of the game. Paired with secret and extra bosses that are even more challenging, this is what truly makes the game shine.
Unfortunately, to get there may take some patience as there are mechanics or stats that are not detailed enough, there is no  way to directly give items to your party members, and getting said items may lead into a dull grind. It should also be noted that to be a perfectionist in this game, it will require you to consult the wiki frequently. But then, every good game deserves a wiki, and the Last Remnant is definitely a good game.

I would recommend Hollow Knight to almost anyone who have the slightest interest in the Platforming genre, and maybe even to those who normally shy away from platformers as it is a near perfect representation of how much fun the genre can be.
Hollow Knight has one of the most tight platforming mechanics I've ever seen and it combines perfectly with its Metroidvania-style open world. The way you traverse the world feels amazing without giving you the feeling of being overpowered. Each of the unlockable platforming mechanics you acquire through the game feels useful and adds something new to your arsenal both in and out of combat. In addition to that, a lot of the platforming mechanics synergize so incredibly well that just the act of backtracking throughout the vast areas feels fresh and fun. It never feels stale revisiting old areas because the last time you were there, you likely faced struggles you can breeze through this time.
For anyone familiar with From Software's Dark Souls, Demon Souls and Bloodborne franchises, Hollow Knight uses a very similar way to tell a story, using the environment and unique characters. As you start your journey you have almost no context at all, but as you traverse Hollownest, you learn more and more about its past and the remaining inhabitants.
While the game takes place almost exclusively in the interior of Hollownest, the areas are incredibly varied spacially, thematically and in mood, ensuring that you never grow bored or feel trapped. A lot of areas are tightly interconnected with each other and filled with all sorts of little details, enhancing the feeling that this is a lived-in world.
If you aren't sold already, the game offers an incredible amount of optional hidden content. The great thing is that a lot of the content is easily accessible and designed in a way that you will often just stumble into them, taking away any feelings of frustration when looking for it but instead enhancing that feeling that you are on an adventure, never knowing what you may encounter next. There is still some content that is more tucked away, but none of it is part of the critical path, so you can still beat the game and still be left with a satisfying feeling in the end.
One of the most amazing parts of the game besides the incredibly atmospheric and beautifully designed spaces is the music. Each of the different locations you explore in the game has a score that suits the mood and atmosphere perfectly. Whether the developers wants you to feel calm, uneasy, melancholic, excited or terrified, the music is right there to support that feeling.
If you like going on an adventure, braving platforming challenges, meet interesting characters and experience amazing atmospheres, this game is definitely for you. If I had to give it a numerical rating, I'd give it a solid 9.5/10 and a definite recommendation for almost anyone!

As a fan of RPGs new and old, I was tempted to purchase this game as I've heard many things about this "hidden gem". Sadly, I was disappointed to find out how big of a let down this game was.
Jumping into the game without knowing anything about it aside from the title, I was pleasantly surprise and confused to see the game in action, jumping straight into the first battle. But seeing the game in action, it caught my interests and I was more than excited to continue and try to figure out how the game worked. Unfortunately, after 12+ hours of playing, the game felt like it was on a constant tutorial, only to find out the game really didn't have much to offer. As interesting as the game looked, the strategy within the game play comes off as extremely shallow, leaving little to no planning even in the most difficult combat situations. The idea behind the game play is extremely interesting and had so much potential, but alas falls short, lacking depth in every aspect behind it. In other words; what you see is what you get.
The story itself is a complete joke, as it feels like it's parody of an old anime that I've never seen before. It makes senses, but the story is laughably lame, as with the behavior the main character is so unpredictable yet very forgivable regardless of the outcome.
The dungeon design are completely lack luster, as it feels like almost every dungeon is design to be shaped like a Y or an L, and copy paste from there. I never felt lost, and had I come across a dead end, I back track over to a fork in the path I missed, pulled a trigger, and the dead end was averted. Funny thing is, that's basically every dungeon in the game.
The Battle music in this game is great, fitting the tone and idle animations of the characters fighting off their opponents as they wait for you to make a decision on their next action. It's a nice touch, as it almost looks like the party members are hyped up with the music, which also gives out a great arcade-ish feel for each battle (which is not a bad thing for me). Sadly, all songs outside the battle tracks are completely forgettable.
All in honestly, I'd say to avoid this title at all cost and play another RPG title instead... literally any other RPG. If you're still curious, I'd say wait for a sale.

Due to the wierd way you upgrade your characters, youll have to spend quite a bit of time farming drops, or at least I did. Luckily the combat system is great. The main problem with farming too much is; youre trying to upgrade your character, and the more you level the more difficult mobs become.
The characters also harass you until you give them what they want, like a drug addict....you got any of that fly oil Rush.??. *sniff*
2) Certain more rare items require magazines, which are dropped from doing guild quests, which arent tracked, so you have to make sure you know what youre doing before you go out.
3)  The max number of units is 18 in a group of 5 (5 per group) WHY in the world they made it 18 characters instead of 25 I cannot fathom.
4) You can miss quests simply because you progressed in the main story, that was just terrible!
5) There is a late spike in difficulty. The game goes from a fun challenge to soul crushingly difficult at a certain point.

Here's the thing with free-to-play games that offer a "buy to get better stuff" option: You *HAVE* to make that stuff available to players who aren't going to spend money on your game, or else your community is solely made up of people who want to pay to win.
"But ELL, you can get coins just from winning matches!"
Right, from winning. Not from losing, which is what you'll spend most of your time doing when you're playing with the starter packs. You get 5 'coins' for a win against the AI, or 20 against a person. If that person spent enough real money to put together a fast, functional deck, you're not going to win, which means you've just wasted ten minutes of your life for nothing. Playing against the AI is about the only hope you have.
You get 5c for a win, and it costs 150c to buy a booster pack of 6 cards, most of which won't help you build whatever deck you're enjoying playing. So you have to win 30 games with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cards to get 6 new cards you don't want, and go on playing with the deck you already had. Each match takes 5-10 minutes, so assuming you won all thirty games in a row, you've been playing for about four hours or so... for -nothing-.
Oh, and you won't win all 30 games in a row. You're going to do a whole lot of conceding, restarting, and eye-rolling in the meanwhile. If you win 50% of your matches, you're at it for 8 hours. How's it feel to waste a whole day playing Magic with a starter deck, with tons of pauses and holdups, nothing but the same droning music, and the knowledge that your opponent just flat-out has a better setup than you do?
This is -terrible- game design. Absolutely insultingly terrible. Game designers, heads up: If you build an economy and then don't encourage me to participate in it, I'm not going to. MtG plays far faster in real life, and I can play with people I actually like, rather than the bank accounts of strangers. If you aren't going to build a system that ensures that losing players are eventually competitive, the losing players are going to stop playing entirely, like I am now.
A word on story mode: The AI always has a better deck than you, the matches take forever to load, and the AI never misses a tactically advantageous move. Ever. This is boring, one-sided gameplay. To win, you have to get lucky on your draw, AND the AI has to be unlucky on theirs.

It's taken me several years to finally try this game out.  I had read all the complaints about it and I am one of those annoying historic fans who is very precious about the turn based system (woe).  With the remake of VII coming out and watching the trailers, I have to accept that turn based is never going to make a come back in this franchise.
So I set out to get used to it.  What I learned, however, is that the Final Fantasy franchise is no longer worth investing in if this is what they come up with these days.
The story is atrocious.  Clumsily told and they must realise this, because they keep a summary of everything in the datalog and also recap what's happened as you load up the game.  It's just mega confusing.  I read everything and played through everything, and yet when it came to the final boss, I had no clue as to what was going on.  Final Fantasy stories are tradtionally a bit complex but this was truly flimsy writing.
The game play - it seemed rather awesome.  For the first 20 minutes.  Then it got tiresome.  You soon learn that battles are rather long and no amount of grinding will shorten them because  a) they cap your development for each chapter and b) you have to "stagger" an enemy before you can really get your teeth in, and for many enemies, this takes a very long time.  I was very resentful battling an ordinary fiend for the same amount of time I would spend on a major boss in previous installments.  It would be okay if the battles were fun, but they aren't.
Side quests.  There's not many - the side quests essentially centres around 64 missions given to my Ci'eth stones, so unless you find that a barrell of joy, you are not going to enjoy this normally fun aspect of a Final Fantasy game.  And it's not enjoyable.  Again, I was getting really annoyed going through these missions where you spent more time hunting down the stone, and then hunting down the mission.  This involves a lot of running.  A lot.  I cannot convey how much running this entails.  This is what makes the missions take so long - not the missions themselves!  WHO THOUGHT THAT WAS FUN?  I challenge anybody to tell me that they honestly enjoyed running around doing those missions.
You basically have to complete the game before the "world" opens up to you and the stat development completely opens up to you.  That is incomprehensible to me.  Why do you have to go through the whole game before you are free to explore with your maximum potential?
I'm a completist.  I'm one of those people that has to stats maxed out, all super bosses completed every item found, every side quest completed... it's this characteristic that made me play on, not the game and I got so fed up with it, I used cheats.  That's right.  For the first time ever in my life, I used cheats, just to get through the battles quicker, just to finish this game.  AND IT WAS STILL A SLOG.
Positives?  Lightning is cool and the game looks pretty.  Was also pleasantly surprised by the music.  I knew Nobuo Uematsu wasn't involved so really wasn't expecting much, but I really enjoyed it and so bought the soundtrack.
I know it's late to say this and nearly everyone who is going to play this has already done so, but if you are on the fence, I do not recommend this, especially if you cherish the golden age of VI-X - it really has nothing in common with them.

For the first hour or so I thought this was a shooter to end all other shooters. The game looks amazing, like it was released only recently. The spaces are relatively large and you can approach a problem in a number of ways. I was sneaking around like a predator in the jungle.
...Then I wondered why some enemies would get alerted without me doing anything, and realised that they were standing next to objects that were freaking out because of buggy collision detection. "Well that is an annoying bug if you are trying to stealth," I thought, "but alright."
Then I was ordered to get into an enemy base. I carefully planned out my infiltration and moved in. Then, as I took out the guards at the entrance quietly from a distance, their places were taken by two more guards. I was upset that I missed those two in my original survey of the site, but I persevered, killing the new guards and then two more came...and then two more. It would appear the guards were spawning out of thin air in a game that clearly isn't made for that mechanic. As I moved into the camp, this was becoming more obvious. Enemies were running out of their houses despite the fact that I had not yet alerted them.This was on its own a betrayal of the way the game seemed to promise to allow me to play it: precicely, carefully and stealthily.
But then something else happened. I went inside a house where the enemies appeared behind the wooden railing upstairs, but I could not shoot them because...because...because the bullets would not go through the (huge) gaps in the railing, getting stopped by a collision object.
I paused the game and stared into the abyss for a while, feeling betrayed and cheated. With weakened hands I then turned off the game and uninstalled it. I wonder if I can ever return.

I picked this product up a while back when it was a free in the humble store, didn't think much of it and after the first time I played it I didn't pick it up again till recently.
I now have some hours into it and almost completed it on insane, so it is safe to say I can write something about all aspects.
Graphics:
The graphics in this game are amazing for a game from '03 the feel of slashing into demons and cutting of limbs is extremely satisfying and the game offers enough opportunity to do so. It gives me a similar feel to Killing Floor 2 gore wise, although I guess KF2 has a couple more ways of losing limbs and cutting Zed's up.
Story:
Suprisingly good, given the first level I wasn't expecting anything amazing but a nice and funny story. They introduce some aspects that really keep this game going. The overall campaign also takes quite some time to fully complete so length is also pretty good.
Variety:
Variety is plenty in this game enough guns, demon and human skills, enemies and upgrades. This keeps the game interesting this also keeps it interesting because the game uses the variety of enemies to give you new combinations of special enemies to fight. This makes every fight different but as the next topic will tell it becomes a little bit boring on higher difficulties because it just takes longer.
Difficulty:
For me the increase in difficulty on the highest was actually not much harder but more boring. The bosses and 'special' demons are just more tedious as it doesn't become harder but it just takes much much more time. Unfortunate as difficulty /= length at least in my opinion.
Achievement wise:
A lot of achievements for the different weapons and abilities this will most definitely take another playthrough to get all of them. Now that doesn't mean it is a bad thing. I actually feel like the game has enough variety in weapons and abilities to keep the second and maybe third playthrough still interesting. I say this without taking into account the Heroic mode achievement. This achievement and evidently also the "Get all achievements" are not for all people. I don't even think I will be attempting it as the increase in damage and health of enemies in combination with the lack of quicksave and hardcore mode (being reset to beginning of chapter) is just not worth the hassle of getting the last 2 in the end.
Buy?:
For the price it is currently, at 34.99, I wouldn't buy it. This is of course given the fact I got it for free and that this game is reasonably old.

First the downsides. A few graphics cards don't work yet but each time one comes up they work on it. As others said the replayability is somewhat limited but since each game has a few random elements (who you start with, weather, what your house has, etc) it is definitely replayable. The length of play is fairly short but not the 3 hours some claim, for me it is closer to 9-12 hours.
Now the good stuff. The graphics style and soundtrack and interesting and lend to the encompassing mood. But the amazing part, the part that makes it worth the money even if you played it through once, is the atmosphere. You aren't playing a band of soldiers, you are playing a hodegpodge group of civilians trying to survive siege, bandits, soldiers, starvation, disease, in fighting, and dispair. It is dismal in a way I've never seen in games and sucks you in. It helps that the stories and characters are influenced by people who were in the Seige of Sarajevo.
My personal favorite part on replaying the game is seeing how the different characters affect game play. A couple characters are downright physical burdens. Some don't play well with others. Some are caring and get depressed if you go against their moral code. Others are selfish and aren't made happy by being charitable. Normally it is the strategy in these types of games that grabs me. While it is good in this game, instead I think about the street tough that ended up at the wrong place at the wrong time, I wonder if the little boy will ever get his toy soldier back, and what ever happened to the man I had to turn away because we didn't even have enough food for ourselves.
;tldr This game is emotionally moving. I didn't think a computer game could do that.

It grows more difficult every day. At first, we struggled to get food. We boarded the windows early, anticipating looters. On the eighth day, a man named Roman arrived. He had run from the military and asked to stay with us. We agreed. We knew supplies were tight, but we figured he could help us defend against looters and raiders. Two nights later, Roman went out to scavenge a grocery store. He saved a girl from a drunken soldier, but was shot multiple times. When he came back, we had no bandages. The following night, Pavel went out to get bandages to save Roman's life. Without them, he would surely die. Pavel never came back. A neighbor said he went into an old school and they soon heard shots from it after. The next morning, Roman died from bloodloss. Bruno is... growing defensive. I sometimes hear him mumbling in his sleep about how he's glad it was them and not him. He's begun eating a strange meat and laughs randomly. I don't think I can trust him. We're running low on supplies and if he feels the need... he'll sacrifice me to save his own life. I still have the pistol that Roman used to save the girl. I think I can hear Roman coming...
This game is amazing. Reading their journals, depending on who is in the party and who does what with certain events, the characters individual reactions can change. This last playthrough, Bruno, who had always been one of the more compassionate characters, was suddenly upset with others helping people, complaining that they must worry about themselves instead of others. Roman began to get adjusted to killing people in those few days before his death, while the others, except Bruno, kept their usual reactions about the situation. Bruno would always say things about it being better they died than Roman. I was fairly surprised at how much some of the environments could change on different playthroughs. This was the first time I encountered soldiers in the school, and while trying to find their trader, I wandered into the wrong room and was threatened. On my way out, five soldiers decided to start shooting and I lost Pavel as well as the assault rifle he was carrying.
I recommend this to anyone who likes survival games. It has a far better storyline than most survival games out there, and there are no second chances for characters. If someone dies, they are dead and the others will feel the effects of their loss. No matter how well you may be doing, there is always that one catalyst that can destine the whole group for destruction if not watched.

Well, I'm sort of conflicted on this one.
On one hand, I am admitidly dissapointed by this latest venture into the over-the-top Saints universe. The game on a whole does feel unfinished. Not down to numerous numbers of bugs, but just a sensation that something was missing from the game. Avoiding any spoilers, information that is presented during the final cutscenes of the game reinforce this, leading me to believe that the guys at Volition may have had far more grandiose plans in mind for Gats trip to New Hades, but I can only imagine time constraints and budget concerns are the true reasons why those plans have not bore fruit.
Despite that niggling feeling that there should be more to the game, what -is- there is unadulterated fun. Well, perhaps a little. This is Saints Row afterall. While perhaps not a match for the powers that The Boss/President gains in the previous title, those abilities that Johnny earns through the use of Lucifers Cracked Halo are interesting non the least. Most enjoyable perhaps just being his flight ability. While not technically true flight (it's like an advanced glide with a boost mechanic thats limited to uses per flight) it still grants you a great deal of mobility and you'll find yourself often forsaking ever using the now redundant vehicles. Throughout my playthrough, the only times I ever used a car for transport were when I was forced to. All other times, I was just flying.
This however does bring me back to that same niggling thought of dissapointment. As this constant need for Volition to crank the Saints up to eleven seems to be sending them further and further away from what originally interested me in the franchise. What had started as a competitor to Grand Theft Auto, offering a tongue in cheek look at the life of crime, has now become a series where familiar characters are thrown into various, outlandish situations and given the tools to cause as much mayhem as they can. Judging it purely as a sandbox for destruction, it's an A+. But my nostalgia over the old Saints Row is what keeps me from turning fan-girl over this one. This is what the new Saints is always going to be now, I fear. The Boss, Johnny, Kinzie, Shaundie, Pierce (who sadly wasn't present here, WHY VOLITION? You have Satan involved in a musical scene but not Pierce?!) and that host of uninteresting paper characters that have been thrown in the last two games, all of them being thrust together into these strange non-sensical situations, all for the purpose of providing a backdrop for the havoc they want you to create.
If you're looking for some mindless violence with some fun toys, definetly pick this one up. Especially if its on sale. However if you were looking for something that expands the Saints universe positively, I'd stop holding your breath now. It's not going to happen, they're heading in a whole different direction now.

A very simple platformer with basic graphics and perhaps slightly-novel ideas.
- Concept & Controls
Defy Gravity is a simple platformer where you use WASD and mouse to interact with various objects, specifically one gravity sphere and one black matter sphere. Using these two spheres, you attempt to navigate through an intially simple terrain, and later challenging jumps that require split-second-reaction-time. There are no background story as to why you need to navigate through them or whatsoever, hence it's just a linear puzzle game. The controls may feel a bit disjointed at times as you have to mash the buttons or else repeat yourself for a few more times.
- Graphics
It's basic, nothing fancy, perhaps except for the cutscene. The menu and text are easy to read but are again, rather simple. The background does not feel play well with the theme at hand, et cetera, as you can probably notice from the game's screenshots itself.
- Music
It's simple audio effects as well. Nothing spectacular, distasteful or annoying, although I do like a particular soundtrack.
- Pricing
It's cheap, in fact the trading cards you get costs more than the game itself. The plenty of reviews helps to concrete this evidence.
There's no reason to not get it, but then there's no reason to get it either. Or maybe you could earn a few cents from selling the trading cards?

Having done almost everything there is to do in the game including achievements (doing my 100% steel soul run now) and the two dlc's currently released (Hidden dreams, grimm troupe), I feel it is time to share my opinion.
This game is fantastic. I believe I spent 15 dollars on the game and I wouldv'e spent double that for a game of this quality. There is so much in this game it is unbelievable it doesn't have more popularity. Wether you are a metroidvania fan, and are looking for a new and difficult challenge, or you have never touched a metroidvania in your like but are still a fan of platformers, I recommend this game. Lets talk specifics
1. Sound design. Everywhere from the music, to the sound effects, to the made up langauge in the game pleases my ears. The music is an original soundtrack composed by the genius that is Christopher Larkin. Every piece in this game is wonderful and as directly stated by Larkin himself "...for this game we are really pushing the piano and the viola as kind of the center point of the score...", and it is beautiful. The sound effects are pleasurable as well, I will listen to the sound track of hollow knight, then wish that I was playing the game so I could get the music and the sound track, I especially get that feeling when listening to boss themes. The tinging of nails clashing when you parry, the sounds and grunts of the bosses, the thwapping of the nail as it hits the wall, the sound of goops flying out of the maws of your enemies and sizzling against your skull, it's all fantastic.
2. The challenge. I would say this is a difficult game, but not frustratingly so. It has challenge in just running around the different areas as well as the boss fights. At first you are carefully jumping from each platform and taking each room slow. You start to get impatient as the game goes on and go a bit faster, and the game knows this. It provides you with new ways, new movement options to get from point A to point B, it gives you second chances if you fail a jump, it gives challenge without fault. The boss fights are all there to challenge your evasive skills as well as your technical skills, where the areas are there to challenge your platforming skills. The boss fights are hard without ever feeling impossible. If you die you feel like you died because of your inability, so you try again. With a bench usually being nearby you get to try and try until you find new ways to dodge attacks, perfect your movement so you can get an extra hit in here and there. Later boss fights feel like a war of attrition, and I love it. Getting hits in whenever you can, but getting greedy will certainly have its negative effects.
3. The content. This game is 15 dollars, and is currently on sale for 9.89... that is insane. My first play through of the game took about 28 hours and that was without any of the dlc which all of the dlc are free by the way. Is it a 60 dollar game, no, but for a quarter of that you get a game that will give you the play time value in just your first play through, and you'll enjoy every second of it. With more dlc's to come and with the achievements and hidden lore pieces and challenge runs, I would say that this game is a definant buy.

Bioshock 2 is the perfect sequel. Improved visuals much better represent the world of Rapture. Better gunplay: faster ammo switching and reloading, the ability to use plasmids and weapons at the same time, new, exciting weapons, better plasmid upgrades. Overall the gameplay is better: interacting with little sisters is more diverse, as you can carry them around and have them harvest adam from dead bodies, which triggers waves of enemies. You also attain the abilities of big daddies from the first game, such as the drill rush, which is pretty awesome. The narrative starts off a bit too obfuscated, but develops soon enough and quickly captures the player's interest. In the sequel a new ideology takes hold over Rapture, which is the exact opposite of what Andrew Ryan crafted Rapture to be. It's quite interesting to hear the two ideologues trade punches on the audio recorders. Bioshock 2 is the perfect complement to the original Bioshock game.

To be honest I was fairly disappointed in how much this game was lacking in. Don't get me wrong I love the Saints Row franchise, especially when they decided to take a turn in how the content was written in a much more humorous and less serious tone that sets the franchise apart in comparison to your regular "let's run a gang and screw the city over while we're at it" open world kind of game (e.g Grand Theft Auto, which was what a lot of people compared it to in SR I, II). I understand that this game was not produced to be the penultimate sequel to be taken as Saints Row V, but it isn't what every fan-boy here is calling an "expansion" either. It's a stand-alone game, using the engine and assets from the previous game, it is NOT an expansion or DLC to Saints Row IV, which is what everyone seems to be using as an excuse for defending the lack of gameplay. For the sake of everyone's personal subjectivity, I'm going to avoid arguing about the price tag altogether in this review because as it stands, it is a very humble asking price for this game.
First of all, I wasn't disappointed in the story at all, oh no, I loved the idea of the Saints actually BEING in hell and wreaking havoc, not a simulation of it gaining sentience (a-la Enter the Dominatrix) which was what I originally thought this was going to be. Overall the story was cool - it wasn't the best thing you could expect from a follow up of the moments after overthrowing the Zin Empire, but it was cool nevertheless. The game uses several sets of loyalty missions in the form of side quests/mini games similar to the ones from the previous games to progress the story line, which is in my opinion was a terrible form of execution. The 7 deadly sin weapons featured in the trailers are not obtained through story progression either (save for one, the other is purchased as any ordinary weapon), but through taking over districts in New Hades and other forms of mini-game completion. There were a decent amount of animated cutscenes (yes, I love the in-game cutscenes, it's a thing I've grown fond of when you can see your own Saint in one) but a lot of them relied on actual cuts in the cutscenes from one scene to another through a story book page reading in between, it's a nice style but it really shows that they opted not to animate these scenes entirely and just went for story book page camera pans. Many interactions with the supporting cast lacked a cutscene altogether except for an introductory cutscene the first time your character meets them.
The final boss battle

One thing I was disappointed about was probably the potential for this game to have replayability: it has close to no replayability, sure there are 5 different endings but you could just revert your save and try again. I think the lack of customization options was one of the biggest problems here in addition to that. I'm fine with not being able to customize the outfits of Johnny and Kinzie, but no other customization options whatsoever? Also besides all of that, my major disappointment is the lack of screen time for Kinzie - she was advertised to have an equivalent role in saving the Boss, but where is Kinzie in the majority of the cutscenes? The cutscenes always show Johnny as the main character taking the reigns and Kinzie will always be the supporting character instead, the whole game is a homage to Johnny Gat's awesomeness (hence the play on words in the title), but could they not have gave Kinzie just the same amount of glory? Yes, you still have the ability to play as Kinzie but the point here is the cutscenes and certain addressings do not acknowledge Kinzie's presence and role in the rescue the same way it does for Johnny.
Now I've had a lot to complain about but let's get to the good parts of this game including improvements on old aspects. First of all, let's bring up the flying mechanics, at first they were a little hard to grasp but after a while of playing the game and gaining upgrades, flying is probably the best part about this game in all honesty. While in Saints Row IV I still liked driving around because the cars looked cool and over long distances driving can be a lot easier not to mention running around gets a little boring after a while, in Gat out of Hell the cars are rust buckets of the cars from SR4 and have no radio or aesthetic modifications. It's pretty obvious that you were probably not expected to pay attention to any of these cars because there are only about 6 different vehicles in this game - a majority of which are reskinned models. It's apparent that you were expected to enjoy the flight mechanics, which I really did! Some of the new superpowers are pretty cool too, though they are a little nerfed down version of their SR4 counterparts, certain base functions of the versions from SR4 need to be unlocked as upgrades instead. The 7 deadly sin weapons are great too, they are all fantastic in their own right, as are some of the new hell-themed weapons included along as part of the base armory, and if you're not comfortable with new weapons, Ultor has supplied you with some guns you are more familiar with.
As I have mentioned earlier, most of the story is great too. What the game lacks in quantity they make up for in quality, in the form of supporting characters, three historical figures who are now residents in hell: (DJ) Shakespeare, Blackbeard the pirate and Vlad the Impaler. Casted along side them are old enemies: Viola(holy♥♥♥♥♥♥I did not know she was voiced by Sasha Grey) and Kiki Dewynter, Dane Vogel of Ultor and Dex from all the way back in the first game, which you kill whenever you see what's left of his body wandering the streets over and over again. The dialogue between all of the characters in this game are golden, Vlad has spent hundreds of years in agony in an asylum using children's music as psychological torture, Blackbeard has been hiding away trying to rebuild his ship, Shakespeare speaks in the 3rd person and is also a DJ at a nightclub in hell, Dane Vogel is still an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who wants to make money no matter what, and the Dewynter sisters are still making enemies. Your interactions with these characters are interesting to say the least, but there was potential for so much more character development among them all, especially for Jezebel, Satan's sweet daughter who refuses to agree to her arranged marriage with the Boss.
I'm gonna close this review with my least favorite and most favorite part of this game: the amount of content presented to further the plot progression AND my favorite part would be the one scene in the game where Satan and Jezebel, Johnny and Kinzie perform a full-on Disney musical duet number with each other which goes on for a little under 5 minutes:

I saw this on sale for 99 cents and when a game is that cheap, unless the offends your ancestors in some deep and unforgivable way, you buy it. I, like many others on steam, bought this simply because it's this cheap. The 90% off sale is the "we're not making any more money from this" sale last ditch attempt to produce some revenue from a title.  Considering I haven't heard of this rather generic looking, what appears to be some sort of RTS game, I wasn't expecting much and I wasn't surprised in so many ways.
Arena Wars 2 is a top down real-time strategy game that pits you against a player or an AI component in what is essentially a match of capture the flag. This is a "first-impression" review as I am honestly unwilling to put more than the hour and 20 minutes I put into this game. The gameplay is very mediocre and the units in the game are fairly uninspired. The game seems to be a "rock paper scissors" game in the sense that one unit is clearly designed to defeat another particular unit. Unfortunately this concept I felt was implented poorly as one unit will do more damage to another unit seemingly abritrarily and it lacks the thougthfulness of a mature RTS game.
There is no tutorial or any intro missions to introduce each of the mechanics so the player is thrown in to engage in a trail and error process of figuring everything out.
To this game's merit, I do like the idea. This game is designed to get he player in the action right away and matches will end quickly whereas a full RTS game might include 2 hours of base-building prior to any combat. A match or two of this game could be played on a lunch break.
This game is an online game but seeing how this game doesn't have a consistent playerbase this is effectively a single player game. There are several difficulty levels and in my first hour and 20 minutes it took getting to the hardest difficulty level to experience any sort of challenge. One very annoying aspect is that these difficulty levels need to be unlocked *per level* and there are five of them. This means that for each level I want to play on, I need to suffer through four matches of boring before I get to the very average gameplay.
I noticed a bug where an area-of-effect ability hits the wreck of a tower it will register damage and repeat "Turret destroyed" - there may be more bugs but finding this so readily underlines this game's overall lack of polish.
The idea has some merit but I cannot recommend this title for any price. The real cost of a game your own freetime anyway.
