I'm going to tell my experience with the game: there's a TLDR at the bottom for a summary :)
I started playing this game when it first came out using a VPN on its Korean server. I have a lot of great memories of making a new family, running through the first missions and recruiting my first NPC characters. At the time it was the first MMO I'd played (not really an MMO person usually) and I loved the experience. Great music, interesting characters, cool themes and design, cool setting...and the combat system (of 3 characters at once) was pretty unique.
After a while the grind (typical to eastern MMOs) started to wear on my teenage brain, and I only ended up playing it for about 5 months. I think my highest level characters were about level 80, because I'd play it for maybe an hour a day and we didn't have good enough internet (or a pc) capable of handling leaving it on all the time to AFK level (although that was also a cool feature).
Skip ahead about 5 years. I rediscovered the game when the American servers came online. Still entranced by the graphics, music, themes, and character system, I downloaded it again (I seem to remember patching it being a ♥♥♥♥♥ and the technical support a nightmare, but I finally got it working) and checked my account. Oh wait, that's right...I'd been playing on the Korean server...so I had to start from scratch. No problem, no problem...I remembered the AFK system and, as I'd now upgraded my pc and net speed, all good!
So I'd leave it on while I went to work and come back in the evening excited to see how far my characters had leveled. I was making progress! I had maybe 12 characters at Master level 1 (131) and all of the recruitable character quests up to Byron completed. So I started researching what I would need to do to acquire my next recruitable characters (the main reason I played the game)...
HOLY F*%&, I have to grind HOW MANY MILLION rare drop resources to get this character?!
WTF, I need how many MILLIONS OF GOLD to get it off the market?!!!
After swallowing the sinking pit in my stomach, I shook my head, cracked my knuckles, and did some research and numbers crunching over the next couple days. With the minimal minimal help of the apparently entirely non-english-speaking members of the forums, I managed to piece together that I really needed to stop trying to get NPCs for now and instead gear up for end level raids. Getting the rare raid drops was going to be the only way to get the money I needed to either buy the NPCs off the market or buy the materials to do their quests.
So how to do end-game raids? Yet another thing I had to research. Apparently I needed better weapons. Some of those I couldn't access until I completed the Byron story missions. Ok, no problem...
Until I ran into one questline. In it your characters go to scout out a castle area and are attacked by one of the recruitable NPCs. I wiped in like 5 seconds. And the next time. And the next time. No matter what combo of characters I brought or how carefully I used my skills or how many health potions I spammed, I wiped. I must have run that stupid mission 30 times before I realized no matter what I WISHED for, my gear wasn't enough to cut it.
So here I found myself in a predicament. To get to the end game characters and content I needed better gear. But, in order to get better gear I needed to run raids. Which required...better gear. So in order to get the minimum gear I needed for those I needed to either spend a f*&@ton of cash and sell cash items on the market, or run low level raids hundreds of times and sell the drops I got.
Which I did. For about a week. At which point I purchased (off the market) my very first 31AR +3AR pistols (was running an Outrage Shot dual-pistol musketeer character for DPS). YAY! I was so happy to go and try him out...
He died. Oops. Need armor too. How much does armor cost? That's right...3 F*@&ING TIMES the cost of the guns :\
No way. No way was I going to sit for 2 months, grinding every day all day, just to get the loot i needed to sell to get the gear I needed JUST TO COMPLETE THE MAIN QUESTS. That's not even considering the actually worthwhile raids, which were what I would need to run to get the highest quality ingredients and weapons (which I'd then sell just to get my DAMN CHARACTERS lol).
So I bit the bullet and caved and bought some cash shop items. Sold those, bought a couple (3? I think?) characters off the market...and was disgusted with myself.
Did the game succeed in making me pay? Yes. Yes it did. I'm sure the devs would have considered this an astounding success story. Except that I do not believe in pay-to-win games. The only kind of cash shop I approve of in a F2P game is one that sells purely cosmetic or pure boost items. I'm not even going to get into the Lydon Box/Gambling-Box-of-Satan item (which is the only way to get some of the rare Characters)... True, the cash shop does sell some boost stuff. But that's not the problem. The problem was I needed gold (vis), and the only way to realistically amass the amount I needed in any reasonable (re: sane) amount of time was to use the cash shop. I couldn't progress in the damn game unless I did.
Disgusted at myself for becoming one of those 'paytards' that I always criticized, I stopped playing. I've barely played the game in the last 5 years. I log on once every couple months to look at my characters, check market prices (just for the hell of it) and reminisce. Because that's all there is for me to do without paying.
TLDR; This game has beautiful artwork, an amazing soundtrack, and an interesting theme (and storyline, if you can get past the atrocious english translation work...did they hire a 5 year old to translate this?!).
It is also a shallow grind-fest, which no meaningful depth to speak of, no good crafting systems or professions, no newbie-friendly guides or help, very few players (in comparison...especially few actual english-speaking players), and end-game content locked behind a paywall. I honestly can't even say that it was ever any better, although probably some would disagree. Either way, what it is NOW is a nonsensical trainwreck.
If you have any interest in the world setting, graphics, or characters, go ahead and play for a bit! I won't say it's fun or enjoyable, but hey, you can walk around and take screenshots right? That's what I did before I stopped playing. Take some screenshots for when it inevitably dies (the game runs primarily on income from pay-to-win players or moneybags (especially in its Asian incarnations). Because that's all its developers see it as: a money machine. Not a game, not a piece of art...MONEY. "We don't believe in customer service...we believe in MONEY. POOLS OF MONEY."
But...if you have any interest in actual exciting combat or gameplay, well-written characters or dialogue, end-game content or raids and don't want to spent 800$ to make that happen, go play just about ANYTHING else. Please. I implore you.
As a bit of reference:
I checked the Market just before posting this. The newest NPC character is currently listed at:
3,500,000,000vis
Yup. That's three BILLION.
That character is a rare character only available from the Lyndon/Satan boxes. So realistically, you'd probably have to spend 100-200$ on buying the boxes to drop one of that character. Which I'd like to say is a direct correlation to the vis (gold) cost, but it's not. That's a ridiculous price. even a number of the older characters are in the billions.
To give some context: currently, AFK farming for 24 hours (a whole day) at Castilla Ruins nets you ~14million vis. A DAY. That's MANY HUNDREDS OF DAYS of grinding to be able to afford a billion-vis character or weapon. And I'd like to say 'throw down a few bucks and it'll be faster!'. Not really. The most market-worthy cash item is the premium area passes which sell for ~120million. For 20$. :\

The game had potential, but at this point in time I wouldn't waste the money on it there are other games that will work far better as a trading/space sim.
Go back to X3 Terran Conflict and Albion Prelude if you want a enjoyable experience.
Sadly as many people expected there are to many bugs and design flaws for this game to be truly enjoyable. The one truly good point about this game is the developers did spend a large amount of time making it stunning visually. The depth of a planet you get close to the stars within the game all the lighting and particle effects are top notch, but the good news stops there.
Unlike the other games in the x series you are limited to one ship with the ability to use drones. The drones themselves have various uses but in the end seem superficial compared to being able to pilot full fighters. The worst part about this feature is your ship many times will get completely destroyed as you try and use the drones even when there was no threats present.
In addition to this the so call "reactive/interactive economy" is anything but either. Most of the ships in game are fluff as bots that have no purpose other than to make the space ports and space station's look busy. The ships you can interact with seem to randomly disappear after leaving/docking with stations or ships on some occasion's. its disappointing that such a huge part of the prior X games is regulated to a unusable mess.
Everything within the game from getting your other ships to do as you want to trading bulk items #i.e. energy cells and such# is nothing but a complicated chore that ruins any hope of you having fun or at least feeling like you accomplishing something. In addition to this many of the in game commands and the very ships which made up such a big part of the other X games will not respond, move, or work in any way no matter what you need them to do.
The ability to move around stations is a bit fun but ultimately pointless. It seems the real reason you go from station to station is to rob the lockers of items and get illegal items in air ducts to supplement your cash flow as you cant get anything else within the game to work for making money properly. Though there are workarounds for these issues you should not need them as you spent money on a game that should of been ready after 7 years.
Lastly we have combat something truly enjoyable within the prior X series. Its sad, boring, dull, uninspired, slow. If you though you would have fun  think again. As stated before you only have one ship. Wanted tons of turrets? Think again. Wanted to be able to use 8 front mounted plasma throwers? Not gonna happen. You can have one of each weapon but that's ONE only. There are no multiple banks of weapons on your ship and no way to add them. The customization you can do to the ship is very shallow when compared to the other games within this series.
The final verdict is i would hope and try to believe that this game will be fixed by the developers. If not them than the gaming community at large through many mods that defined other games in this series. Alas i cannot see this happening as most of the issues seem to stem from core portions of this game not something that can be modded or fixed without major changes to the game it self. We will just have to wait for the next true X series game or perhaps the new Star Citizen that seems to have allot of promise.

Don't knock it until you've tried it. I know there is a LOT of hate for this game, mostly from the self-styled "Real FF fans;" Final Fantasy VII fanboys who think that VII is the pinnacle of every videogame ever made and that Cloud, Tifa et al are the best characters of all time and blah blah blah (I'm not hating on VII by any means, I actually think it's a great game, but the fanboyism can seriously GTFO) or these hipsters who go on about "I used to play on the old Nintendo Final Fantasy games BEFORE it was cool!" Yeah, would you like a pair of ridiculously overpriced NHS glasses to go with that vintage portable record player of yours?
Now that's out of the way; the game. Well by far the most controversial thing was the fact that the open, sidequest-filled world that is usually associated with FF was recplaced by a more story-driven linear type of game. There are actually some open-world elements to the game, with the hunts from FFXII making somewhat of a return, although not quite as extensively, but this isn't a game where you're going to spend hours getting lost in sidequests. As you can see, I managed to get all achievements done and dusted in 140 hours, which is nothing compared to Final Fantasy XII for example; where I'm 130 hours in and still not even at level 70. But if you're into story-based games, then this is a great story.
That's not to say I don't have some problems with the gameplay. I think the paradigm system is very rigid and can be restrictive during battle. Also, the fact that it's game over if your lead character is KO'd when there are 5 other perfectly good people standing around in your battle team is just plain infuriating. A lot of people complained about not being able to level up fully until certain points in the story. Personally, I think it just means that you have to actually play the game like it was intended, rather than just being lazy and EXP grinding on low-level battles all day until you eventually have enough levels to just beat up all the bosses with physical attacks. Where's the fun in that? One other annoying thing is the fact that most of the stats have been removed, including things like vitality, which can make random low-level encounters more annoying not being to increase your characters' innate ability to avoid status attacks, not to mention the death spell on this game is pretty much pointless because it hardly ever works, but these are really minor issues in the scheme of things. I find the battle system overall is pretty intuitive and if you give it time to get over the learning curve, boss battles that onced seemed insurmountable can become not too much of a challenge.
As for the characters, people say all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about Lightning being just like Cloud, which is a bunch of crap. Sure, she has this cold exterior that she wraps around herself like Cloud and Squall, but that's just one aspect of one's personality. Lightning is an extremely smart individual who's able to catch onto ideas quickly and what's more, she has a very quick wit; her tongue being almost as sharp as her gunblade. She's almost never lost for words or in want of a reply to someone, even if that occasionally involves punching Snow in the face (Which is fair enough, because he is a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) And behind the shell of hers, you see the occasional cracks of emotions that remind you that she is a human, and not just some robot, like some of the XIII haters seem to want to paint her as. Lightning is a complete badass who really makes this game what it is. I also love Fang and think Sazh is pretty cool as well, even if he does seem a bit like the token black guy (well seeing as Barret and Kiros were the only other two controllable black characters in FF history, it was about time they had someone else...) But I'm not so keen on Vanille, Hope and Snow. Snow just comes across as being a big over-masculine ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, whereas Hope is a bit of a wimp who doesn't look like he should be anywhere near a battle, and Vanille is just plain annoying. In fact, Her voice sounds like someone put Kylie Minogue on a pitch shifter and shoved it up an octave. But I would say overall the good characters, including side characters like Lebreau, Gadot, Cid, Yaag Rosch, and Barthandelus, (who makes a pretty good villain, if not slightly clichéd...) far outweigh the annoyingness of others.
The soundtrack to this game is AMAZING. It's by far the best soundtrack of any Final Fantasy game since Uematsu quit. The theme song sends chills down my spine every time I hear it, and you've got the beauty of a full orchestra, and not just synthesizers like most of the previous games. It's unfortunate they had to ruin the last FMV with that Leona Lewis♥♥♥♥♥♥for the English dubbed version though.
As for the quality of the port, it certainly looks nice. The initial problems with not being able to scale up the resolution have long since been resolves. However, there is a slightly weird issue where the framerate seems to drop quite a bit if you have any sort of HUD on the screen. But I always managed to get at least 30, sometimes 60FPS on my old graphics card. This one might even do a bit better. It's certainly a hell of a lot nicer than the PS3 version, which I completed the story of as well.
Overall, I would say that if you like a good story, an awesome soundtrack, and some badass characters, you've definitely come to the right place. ♥♥♥♥ the haters.

Assassin's Creed IV Black Flag is one of the most mixed AC games along with AC1. Most people either absolutely love it and consider it the best game since AC2, or you completely despise it. Me? I'm probably one of the few people who are in the middle.
The story starts off with Edward leaving England to go to the Caribbean to be a privateer. A few years later and he comes across an assassin called Duncan Walpole, who is off to Havana to side with the Templars and tell them of a precursor temple, 'the Observatory' and also the sage, a man who is known as the only one able to access the observatory. Edward sees this as an opportunity to become rich as the ancient artifcact is capable of seeing everything anyone is doing, there would be no secrecy among anyone. However Edward is caught and sent to be executed. With the help of a Jamaican pirate, Adewale, Edward steals a ship and sails to Nassau to get help from Ed Thatch, Ben Hornigold and James Kidd. Shorty after, James Kidd reveals to be an assassin and offers Edward the chance to learn to be an assassin, however Edward hates the idea of being part of that sort of religion and wanders off to find the sage and the observatory. After this... you don't really see much of the assassins. That story sits back and in comes a pirates of the caribbean-like story. Edward is looking for the observatory only for himself, while the assassins do it to keep peace and stop the Templars, the usual. After a while, Ben Hornigold betrays Edward and the other pirates to join the Templars. Ed Thatch, also known as Blackbeard is killed and Charles Vane and Jack Rackham become corrupted and eventually get themselves killed too. Eventually after that, James, who reveals herself as Mary Read earlier in the game, dies from an illness. Edward, with pretty much all his friends gone, he joins the assassins. This is where Edward really becomes an interesting character, someone who was once arrogant and wanting treasure and fame, now wanting to right his wrongs and fight for his friends and the assassins who fight for an honourable cause. Unfortunately... this is at the end of the game, so really it just ends after Edward kills Laureano Torres. The story is quite good, I like how it looks at everything from a different view rather than "oh yeah I'm an assassin gotta kill Templars" however... the whole Assassin/Templar thing is non-existent for most of the game, so its really just Pirates of the Caribbean.
The gameplay is an improved version of AC3's gameplay. Which is great. You can hunt, climb trees, pretty much do everything from the previous games except use a bow. However the main focus of this game is the ship battles, which are extremely fun. You can upgrade the Jackdaw over time and its worth it. Taking down Legendary ships or Man O' Wars is amazing. Its a shame that the gameplay ends up being changed in Unity, but at least its copied and pasted into Rogue??? :D
The music is some of the best in the series. It really gives a good Pirates of the Caribbean feel. The music was made by Brian Tyler, who's responsible for some of the Fast and Furious music. Its not on the level of AC2, Brotherhood or AC3, but definitely my 4th or 5th favourite soundtrack.
On the PC this game is terribly optimised. I have a 1060, i7 6700 and 32gb ram and this game, without being modified, runs at 60fps but keeps lowering randomly. There's a guide to make it perform better which I had to use, it allows me to use the highest graphics settings but with some minor things disabled and also framerate locked to 60. If you have a PS3, Xbox 360, PS4, Xbox One, play this game on that. Its not the best on PC. However the added visual effects exclusive to this version are amazing. Like when you're in a ship battle and smoke starts to appear from cannon fire. It makes the game a whole lot immersive.
Overall, I like this game. Its probably the last good AC game before the downfall which is Rogue, Unity and Syndicate. But is this actually one of the best AC games ever? no. Every game prior to this is better and Origins is better. Black Flag is great if you just want to play a fun game, but if you want an Assassin's Creed game... then you should probably play something else. I think this game gets a little bit too much praise, its fun but definitely dated now, plus the previous games are just a whole lot more fun.

Reading through the description of what the game is supposed to do is actually more fun than playing the game. You get more fun counting the lies and laughing about how absolutly untrue the description of the game is. It's like if someone runs up to you and starts telling blatently obvious lies, you smile and probably get a chuckle or two. That is at least enjoyable.
This game is an anomaly in itself. It is broken to the core. It is actually designed wrong, and to work against itself. I have never in my life experienced anything as fustrating as this game, never.
I don't think the developers even know what a video game is, seriously. The absolute basic "unwritten" standards of gaming do not exsist in this game. Simple things like telling the player what things are. Letting you know what to do. Things like pressing I for inventory, or, even the option to map it to a key (Inventory is not mapable to any keys!!!)
No instructions or idea as to how to do things, it just tells you to do them. Many items in game have a description saying "no description". There is a limited 6 button radial in-game menu, where one option is next page..  and sometimes has 4 or so pages worth of options, on a 60+ button controller (The KEYBOARD!!!)
Seven year development time.. What were they doing? Why aren't the most basic standards of gaming in here.
Why did the game have game breaking bugs on mission 1 and 2. How did it get released? Did anyone even try to play the game first? Was there even 1 single game tester? In seven years of development, you never figured out that the first couple missions have game breaking bugs!?!?!?!?
Horrible frame rate unless you own a low end - mid spec PC. That's right, the more powerful your computer / graphics cards are, the worse the game runs.. Wow. Like I said, this game is an anomaly.
Stations are copied and pasted hundreds of times each, with a total variety of maybe 3 or 4 at most. Why not release an editor, and ask people to submit station designs, then you load them into the game for free. Name it after the creator. Why not? People will do it for free for you.
Why are the developers so terrible at what they do? How is it possible. I know I will never ever buy another game before reading a review ever again. I will never buy a pre-order ever again, and I will never ever buy enything from Egosoft again.

This game is my childhood. I played this game even before the release on Steam, along with my older brother. I was in 2nd grade back then, and Granado Espada was probably my first ever MMORPG. I remember I used to have many discs of this game that my brother brought home one day and each disc had a certain amount of play time on it before it expires where thereafter you can't play the game until you use a new disc. I did come back to this game also back in 2013 (where you could actually play for free) in a different server and account, but soon quitted after the game tired out its value. My current account is also different from my past 2 as they belong in different servers. Anyways as you can already tell from my recommendation, I don't support it anymore.
I won't be listing down the strengths of this game as it is rather subjective to one's beliefs so I will be only saying the main issue the game is in its current state (I would cover this whole review more objectively by also mentioning what it did well in, but I would exceed character limit sadly). Two words: Obvious pay2win.
Some things I'd like to mention is that I absolutely abhor pay2win games. They for one, aren't fair to poorer people, ruins the fun of leveling the game, destroys the game's value. I really tried to go into Granado with an open mind, but no matter how much I tried to change my view, the game's mechanics spoke for itself.
My highest characters in the game are currently Master lvl 1, they being Emilia, Bernelli and Lisa, semi decent characters that were very op in the beginning. However overtime I noticed they were getting weaker and weaker. They needed better gears (I had crescementos for them), but these gears (which for your information is not 1 or 2 for each character) are really expensive! I realised that in my past 30 days+ of playing this game, more often than not I had to actually spent time grinding for Vis (Granado's currency), and I am not talking about idle farming (which I do everyday for 6 hours thereabout) because I have to specially dedicate my Fridays to afk farm from the afternoon till the next morning just to earn Vis. This is the funny part though, it barely earns much! The most I could get everyday was a few millions. One decent gear cost at least 250 mil (and on top of that, to make it even better it would cost at least another 100+ mil)! And that is only for one gear, for one character. There are over 80+ (or so they say on their outdated website) characters playable! Like damn this game also actually encourages this (as seen in the pets picking up for you items) and expects you to? I am appalled at the game in its current state because this is my first time taking the time to understand the sophisticated mechanics of this game. Oh right, and how does this lead to pay2win? Growth Stones.
Growth Stone is like the mediator between Vis and Feso (Granado's cash). For every 5 USD spent on this game, you can get 6 Growth Stones which are worth at least 4 mil each (exclusive of market tax and after market tax). And this part is clearly evident to see how much the developers are fat greedy people. It is a scam, yet a boost still regardless. If we do the calculations to achieve 250mil from selling Growth Stones alone, you would require at least 55 USD to buy one decent gear. And there we have it, grind or pay. Either way you still lose out because you would be wasting electricity leaving your computer on if you're planning on grinding.
So my conclusion. Is this game fun? Yes, in the short run. Is it worth investing time on? No, if you plan to play it regularly. Should I try it out? Yes, don't base your judgement off of mine only, decide for yourself if you like it.

Review (no spoilers):
Positives first, cause there are few of them:
+ Nice aesthetics, I really liked the overall style of the game.
+ Kind of interesting and detailed locations, but not as good as in HM Blood Money
+ Lots of secrets to find in the levels (although I did not extensively look for them)
+ very optimized, runs smoothly.
Now the overwhelming negatives, which mainly consist of things that this game did worse than HMBM (its predecessor)
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ soundtrack, which is really important to convey the atmosphere of a stealth game (unlike BM).
- way too small and linear level design on 80% of all levels, which is limiting your actions very much (unlike BM)
- completely unrealistic disguise system, which basically means that you are hugging cover all the time and waiting for guards to turn their back ...
- basically every level consists of memorizing enemy movement patterns exactly so that you can slip through them (boring and frustrating)
- no free savepoints (unlike BM), which makes the last 3 points even more frustrating, because you have to wait for those guards again every time you get spotted (which is a lot)
- NPCs glitch often, which makes them stop their usual route, which makes the level a lot harder if not impossible to complete without getting spotted. (this happens completely randomly and makes the game even more frustrating without free savepoints)
- achievement and score system make this feel like an arcade game (if it isn't already thanks to the dodging guards aspect)
- the entire storyline is completely ridiculous. The script seems to be written by 12 year old kids.
- one example of the bad story is just how many guards/policeman/ bad guys are in the levels. This is especially true for the "escape" missions. "Well it's totally sensible to have 8 police officers search this 15x20m rooftop right?"
- another example: Killer nuns. With SMGs. I won't say any more :/
- Because the entire game is "story driven" (no contracts), you get some weird cutscenes, like after you shoot someone in the head with a revolver, they are suddenly talking to you in a cutscene before they get finished off.
- also: after you sneak up on one specific target, you kill them in a cutscene with dozens of people watching... not very hitman like.
- You don't have to leave the scene undetected for the mission to end like in BM. E.g. one mission ends, when you pick up a phone in the middle of a guard filled area (wtf?).
- the menus seem to be made for consoles.
- I did not play contracts mode, but I doubt it would improve my opinion on the game.
So that's about it, if you buy this game, it's your own fault :/

Fifty hours in, the best way I can describe "This War of Mine" is that it is Excruciatingly Beautiful. Without a doubt, this seemingly simple 2D side-scroller has captivated not only my mind, but my heart as well.
The player is immediately thrust into a searingly bleak landscape in which choices must be made that effect, not only the characters in the game, but the player herself. The beautifully pencil-swept landscapes foster a sense of abstraction while the character models and interior enviornments lend clarity of purpose and direction, be it towards the dark or the light, as the player struggles to find their way through a war-torn appoccalypse.
The combat is (intentionally?) difficult, for in this world, you are not some super soldier; you are only a person. And that is what speaks most directly to the gamer as they experience "This War of Mine". The first time I decided I had to kill in order to survive, I was terrified. And, it didn't end well. Marko's sacrifice eventually led to the downfall of my entire group and it was a miserable experience. An experience I shall never forget.
The User Interface in this game seems a bit wonky at first, at least it did to me. Once you've mastered the UI, however, you become master of your fate and that is something I like in a game. It becomes a question of not "can I kill this person" but, rather: "should I kill this person?" And that is the target the developers were going for, as far as I can tell.
I cannot remember the last time a video game made me question myself in such a profound way. Things like that are usually reserved for the cinema or found in books, I suppose. But as it stands, "This War of Mine" is a deeply moving and enjoyable game that should not be missed by anyone.

This isn't good old classic Hitman, but it sure isn't complete heresy.
+ Nice story: Best plot and storytelling in the series so far.
+ Great optimization: Looks great and runs great even on weaker machines.
+ New-gen improvements: Improved shooting, movement and stealth mechanics.
+ Sandbox levels: Play stealthy, kill no one, kill everyone, snipe your target, poison his lunch. It's your choice.
+ Harder difficulties: To compensate for the easier gameplay, the harder difficulties are really challenging.
+ Replayability: Find all the collectibles, all the guns, all the costumes, perfect every level.
+ Contracts mode: Create missions for other players to complete. Play other people's missions.
- More linear than the older games.
- Weird pre-rendered cutscenes.
- Slightly dumbed down: Everything is easier, some levels are very corridor-y, you have super-powers now, carry more guns, etc...
- Score system: Sometimes you gain points for doing dumb stuff and lose points for doing smart stuff. Very inconsistent, ignore.
If you never played the previous games or if you aren't a purist when it comes to the Hitman series, Hitman Absolution is great game. If you have played previous Hitman games, this one is going to feel a lot less challenging but it's still a great game on it's own.

This game is too good to pass up while it's on sale.
I'm going to start with Pros and Cons first:
+ The game itself is beautiful. The pictures above show what actual gameplay looks like for the most part, and I found myself ooing and ahhing quite often.
+ 3 entire races to choose from, each fundamentally different. Each empire is easy to pick up once you get the hang of the game, but you'll find you prefer one race over the others, depending on your playstyle. In addition, you can pick between "Rebel" and "Loyalist" classes in each race, which have their own perks as well!
+ There are many ways to win the game. Choose to conquer your enemies by destroying and taking over their planets, research technology, form peace treaties, etc...
+ Diplomacy is a fun aspect of the game, and can be quite challenging to manage at times.
+ Once you get the hang of the game, it's very fun and engaging.
+ You get to build MASSIVE fleets and manage planets at a universal level. It's freakin' awesome.
+ You can create and customize your own universe to play on! It's a lot of fun to make your own maps and see how well you do on them. Most of the time you'll play on fair, randomized maps.
+ The game has a speed-up function for offline play (up to 8x speed) so you can shorten a 20 hour experience vs 8 tough AI to maybe 5 (just an example).
- If you don't have a powerful computer, you may not be able to experience the game to its fullest when manning a massive fleet.
- Pretty steep learning curve; you really want to play the tutorials so you have a remote clue as to what to do.
- All undiscovered planets have neutral units that try to kill you so it's tough to colonize. You get used to it.
- Matches can be really, really long. Also, units take a long time to travel. It's as "realistic" as space games can get, however.
The "Gray Area":
This may be different preference for some people, but some matches can potentially last for hours on end. Computer matches can be paused and saved, but human vs. human really can't be. Playing vs AI is still very engaging, and with the many levels of difficulty, you won't be missing out much if you choose not to play vs human players. Either way, it's a satisfying game for the casual weekend gamer all the way to the basement dweller.
Also, pirates. Pirates can be a b*tch. You can pay them to attack other empires, but you are also at risk of being out-bidden and being attacked as well. They add a really cool element to the game, and you have the option to turn them off. I personally turned them off until I learned the game well, then turned them back on for the fun of it.
Final Thoughts/Review:
When I first bought the game, I really wasn't sure what I was getting myself into; the pictures on the store page are a very simplified and zoomed in view of the game. In actuality, you are looking at a planet-by-planet point of view 90% of the time. The user interface isn't shown in the pictures, and when the game first starts, you are pretty much thrown into the game without much mercy. Once you play through all the tutorials and get beaten around by an easy AI the first time, you start to pick up the tricks of the game. Then you develop strategies. Then you start winning. Then it gets really fun. Then you starting adding more players. Then you increase the difficulty. Then you do it again.
With randomized universes, huge options between each type of empire/victory method, scope of the game, level of challenge, I can't say bad things about this game. Once you invest a bit of time, Sins of a Solar Empire is worth every penny you spend on it.

I absolutely love this game!
Ive always been fascinated with MTG when i was a kid but i never understood the actual game since nobody i knew actually played it & like many i just collected the cards for a little while because they were so beautiful and then kinda forgot about it as i grew older. But now there is Origins and to me it is truly a great introduction.
i didnt have any server problems at all, only on the release day wich is basicly standard for any online game, but since then its been working perfectly. (i can imagine that experienced MTG players might run into a few bugs too but for me as a new player i didnt notice anything that actually bothered me just yet)
For a new player it works very smooth, the story mode is entertaining, very challenging IMO and seems to really teach u alot about the lore, tactics and mechanics in this game. Also the skillquests are a very original way to learn about some more advanced techniques in the game + u earn coins for them! I must say im very impressed by the complexity of MTG, i didnt know there were so many different & original playstyles.
The only thing i could remark on this, eventhough the lore itself is quite interesting, is that the cutscenes are a bit boring, just some artwork with a bit of text but hey, it still a cardgame in the end right?
I've seen a lot of experienced MTG players complain about the restrictions in this game but for new players id say it must be more of a relief because i think its already a very complex game as it is.
I also do think it is rewarding enough, i havent been playing all that much but i already had the chance to buy quite a few booster packs and i like the fact that the grind is quite simple, play the game, buy the booster packs and complete your collection. Wich actually seems doable because there is a limit for the amount of cards u can have of each type. In hearthstone u also have to earn acces to certain expansions wich takes a lot of time and u feel quite obliged to do so because u need certain cards to actually be viable and it kinda makes it feel like a drag instead of a rewarding system.
The cards look beautiful, the battlefield is indeed a bit plain, im hoping for some future customization options, but it doesnt bother me all that much since i still really have to focus on the game itself in order to win.
Things i didnt like so much is the lack of an option to skip the timer in some situations, the fact that an attack doesnt end when a player is already dead (u have to wait until every card is played) and ofcourse the lack of a proper chat but i cant imagine they wont implement this in the future, must say i would be dissapointed if they wont.
i can imagine that if i keep playing this game some sort of a leaderboard where u can compare your stats to other players is also something i would desire in time but then again, as a newbie im not missing this yet.
As u can see all the negative things i mentioned are mostly things that more experienced players would be bothered with but i have been having a great experience so far and discovering the world of MTG even if its just the tip of the iceberg is a LOT of fun.

Don't knock it until you've tried it. I know there is a LOT of hate for this game, mostly from the self-styled "Real FF fans;" Final Fantasy VII fanboys who think that VII is the pinnacle of every videogame ever made and that Cloud, Tifa et al are the best characters of all time and blah blah blah (I'm not hating on VII by any means, I actually think it's a great game, but the fanboyism can seriously GTFO) or these hipsters who go on about "I used to play on the old Nintendo Final Fantasy games BEFORE it was cool!" Yeah, would you like a pair of ridiculously overpriced NHS glasses to go with that vintage portable record player of yours?
Now that's out of the way; the game. Well by far the most controversial thing was the fact that the open, sidequest-filled world that is usually associated with FF was recplaced by a more story-driven linear type of game. There are actually some open-world elements to the game, with the hunts from FFXII making somewhat of a return, although not quite as extensively, but this isn't a game where you're going to spend hours getting lost in sidequests. As you can see, I managed to get all achievements done and dusted in 140 hours, which is nothing compared to Final Fantasy XII for example; where I'm 130 hours in and still not even at level 70. But if you're into story-based games, then this is a great story.
That's not to say I don't have some problems with the gameplay. I think the paradigm system is very rigid and can be restrictive during battle. Also, the fact that it's game over if your lead character is KO'd when there are 5 other perfectly good people standing around in your battle team is just plain infuriating. A lot of people complained about not being able to level up fully until certain points in the story. Personally, I think it just means that you have to actually play the game like it was intended, rather than just being lazy and EXP grinding on low-level battles all day until you eventually have enough levels to just beat up all the bosses with physical attacks. Where's the fun in that? One other annoying thing is the fact that most of the stats have been removed, including things like vitality, which can make random low-level encounters more annoying not being to increase your characters' innate ability to avoid status attacks, not to mention the death spell on this game is pretty much pointless because it hardly ever works, but these are really minor issues in the scheme of things. I find the battle system overall is pretty intuitive and if you give it time to get over the learning curve, boss battles that onced seemed insurmountable can become not too much of a challenge.
As for the characters, people say all this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t about Lightning being just like Cloud, which is a bunch of crap. Sure, she has this cold exterior that she wraps around herself like Cloud and Squall, but that's just one aspect of one's personality. Lightning is an extremely smart individual who's able to catch onto ideas quickly and what's more, she has a very quick wit; her tongue being almost as sharp as her gunblade. She's almost never lost for words or in want of a reply to someone, even if that occasionally involves punching Snow in the face (Which is fair enough, because he is a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥) And behind the shell of hers, you see the occasional cracks of emotions that remind you that she is a human, and not just some robot, like some of the XIII haters seem to want to paint her as. Lightning is a complete badass who really makes this game what it is. I also love Fang and think Sazh is pretty cool as well, even if he does seem a bit like the token black guy (well seeing as Barret and Kiros were the only other two controllable black characters in FF history, it was about time they had someone else...) But I'm not so keen on Vanille, Hope and Snow. Snow just comes across as being a big over-masculine ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, whereas Hope is a bit of a wimp who doesn't look like he should be anywhere near a battle, and Vanille is just plain annoying. In fact, Her voice sounds like someone put Kylie Minogue on a pitch shifter and shoved it up an octave. But I would say overall the good characters, including side characters like Lebreau, Gadot, Cid, Yaag Rosch, and Barthandelus, (who makes a pretty good villain, if not slightly clichéd...) far outweigh the annoyingness of others.
The soundtrack to this game is AMAZING. It's by far the best soundtrack of any Final Fantasy game since Uematsu quit. The theme song sends chills down my spine every time I hear it, and you've got the beauty of a full orchestra, and not just synthesizers like most of the previous games. It's unfortunate they had to ruin the last FMV with that Leona Lewis♥♥♥♥♥♥for the English dubbed version though.
As for the quality of the port, it certainly looks nice. The initial problems with not being able to scale up the resolution have long since been resolves. However, there is a slightly weird issue where the framerate seems to drop quite a bit if you have any sort of HUD on the screen. But I always managed to get at least 30, sometimes 60FPS on my old graphics card. This one might even do a bit better. It's certainly a hell of a lot nicer than the PS3 version, which I completed the story of as well.
Overall, I would say that if you like a good story, an awesome soundtrack, and some badass characters, you've definitely come to the right place. ♥♥♥♥ the haters.

FFXIII Has received a lot of criticism from people over being "Too linear" or "not final fantasy enough" - and while i can't disagree with linearity, i can safely state that this is one of the most fun games i've ever had the privilege to play. Whether you're a die hard fan, or someone new to the genre, i bet you will find yourself immersed regardless.
A story that might a bit confusing at times, but puts a lot of effort into character development - this is the ONLY final fantasy in which i cared for the characters. Sure, there is *that one character* who everybody hates (you will know immediately), but other than that, i really enjoyed watching how characters behaved. Not only that, but this game is actually quite long. I am currently on my 7th playthrough, and 16 hours into the game (knowing where to go / what to do / etc) i just reached halfway point marker. The "sandbox endgame" is not as wide as some of the other jrpgs, but it does offer some stuff to do after you "beat the game" - but even if you're just interested in seeing the story, you will have a long journey.
Graphics are absolutely amazing - although you might have difficulty noticing that with how ATROCIOUSLY this game was ported. Honestly, if you own PS3 or Xbox360, do yourself a favor and buy this game for the console. The port is really, really bad. For example, as part of gameplay you can gather data on enemies that shows stuff like resistances, important notes ("Can self-heal"), etc. Only due to some weird bug, this extra data will NOT be visible if you play using a resolution higher than 720p. Yeah, thats right - you have to choose to either get access to full game UI (but run it at 1280x720) or run it at full resolution but not be able to access enemy data. There are workarounds (google for FF13 GeDoSaTo), but overall this port is a massive, massive fail.
Soundtrack is fantastic. Both voices and game sound are very well done and fit properly. I have FF13 soundtrack in a boxed edition, and absolutely love listening to it.
World design and animation quality deserves its own spot. Its very easy not to notice just how realistic characters are animated - how they twist their hands, move their jaws, etc. But when you start paying attention, you realise just how much detail went into getting it to work - and its astounding. The world is just as awe-inspiring, with lots of design and art process clearly involved in its creation. Sure, there are "simple" areas like that green grass field you can see on example screenshots - but there are also places which look damn fabulous, and there are more of those by far.
Overall, i would absolutely hands-down no-discussion recommend this game. I owned it on PS3 back during its original release, and got it on Steam during one of the sales - it is easily my favourite FF game, and one of most favourite games of all time. Don't listen to the haters (if you see any), go and try it for yourself - i promise, you won;t be dissapointed!

Yes, buy and play this game. It goes on sale frequently. You can choose to quickly play through just the main plot or go for a very long, full completion.
While I doubt that it was their intention to write their main character as so annoying as to drag the whole quality of the game down, I feel like the real complaint from detractors of this game is that the main character isn't socially normalized enough. I've met several people like the main character, though: loud, don't think deeply, altruistic, and self-censoring (re: "Let's kick some A!"). I'd rather sit through an awkward character's screen time in the context of an engaging story than have a really targeted and over-designed main character whose only flaw is that they're too awesome for the world they exist in (ugh, it must be so hard for them).
This game has a story that takes you through individual character storylines with quests that help provide cohesion if you let it, but, and this is the uniquely good part, you have the option to skip all of that. Just like you have the option to skip tactics and decision-making in combat, even going so far as to publicly write it off as wholly random or even just containing "too much" randomness. With the exception of the scenario of "I want to choose exactly what every unit of every union in my army does at every moment", other players' experience (first-hand knowledge of how the game's mechanics work together) demonstrates that there is actually a level of control you can achieve that approaches that but ultimately settles on a medium somewhere between the micro-managerial staple of other RPG games and no control. For me, I don't like the part of old-school RPGs where it's basically button mashing through a ton of menus with no risk of losing a fight. I like this game's system so much better because it only ever approaches that if you're fighting enemies that you seriously out-rank, and the game does a great job of providing difficult areas (an unlockable tiered end-game area) and monsters (they scale up).
Furthermore, the main character being annoying has no bearing on the unravelling of the Conqueror's plans (
), the development of Athlum's independence, the fantastic descent into greed-fueled madness of Duke Hermeien, and the tragic storyline of the Conqueror's Seven. And, that's only the content from the non-missable plot in this game. In the missable plot,
.
Now, does the game fall into tons of stereotypical jRPG story elements (re: tropes)? Undeniably. It includes mechas (Hermeien), main character amnesia, direct replacement characters (Emma), an every-man with a super-power (Rush), parents who are completely out of the picture of their young children's lives, a bizarre sense of fashion that tries to differentiate major characters without building towards some larger narrative, and a mascot (re: Mr. Digg) who looks like nothing else in the whole game. Are they really out of place in this game, though? I don't think so. If Rush's Talisman made him transform into a Remnant Monster (reminiscent of something mechanized), I probably would have felt it crossed the line into tripe. Or,
.
The game's best moments for me were near the end of the game when you can hear the many different voices of your characters in battle modified by the barely positive morale of that battle, signifying that you're on par with your enemies, making you realize you've amassed and trained a small army of awesome companions.
In conclusion, if an "Everyone's getting hyped!" is good and a "They caught us with our pants down!" is bad, then I give this game a grade of: "IRIIIIIIIIIIIINAAAAAAAAA!"

I wish I could give this game a recommendation.  It's got a solid foundation, with an interesting game mechanic, and it reminds of classic Final Fantasy games.  However, there are really serious flaws that make a possibly great game almost unplayable.  Unless you are a big nerd for JRPGs, stay away.
Some of the flaws are as follows:
1. This is a port of the XBox game.  They didn't even bother to change the quicktime icons that appear during battle, and they don't tell you what they are, either, but they are in the settings.  Still, it's a lazy job of porting it that undercuts the quality of the game significantly.
2.  The battle mechanic is interesting, but ultimately flawed - it's almost like there wasn't enough playtesting.  Skills that target one enemy are the norm, and what the majority of both your characters and enemy characters use.  Unfortunately, the game is quickly dominated by AoE spells capable of killing multiple units.  Characters are organized into groups, which have a shared HP pool, and if they are hit by an AoE spell, it may just hurt one character, or it may hit them all (including characters in other groups).  Because the shared HP is much less than the sum of each character's HP, a group hit usually results in the group being seriously injured or killed in one shot, and too many enemies cast group attacks.  The group attacks should have been seriously nerfed.  On the bright side, you also get these spells - but then the game simply consists of you figuring out which action choice will lead to your character busting out one of these AoE spells and then doing that over and over.
3.  Speaking of action choices: it's only possible to give up to 5 orders (per enemy) - this means that a unit that desperately needs to perform a certain act might not be able to, for reasons that are never clear.  Additionally, you can only ask for certain classes of actions to be performed, rather than specific abilities.  This is kind of neat, as it leaves only the larger tactics to you, but the problem is that the AI is flaky.  Your units will often do stupid things, like target a single unit with a group spell, or just fail to cast a useful spell because the enemy group has been defeated (but the battle is not over).   Also, you may have a TON of AP, but you may only get options to use a few, and so you waste a turn because of the game, not because of some mistake on your part.
Additionally, the plot is some Square Enix gibberish that is completely unengaging.  Square-Enix used to be one of my favorite publishers, and I would really love a good Final Fantasy style game.  If they would stick with the stuff that worked instead of trying to innovate, they could really make some very good games.

Hitman has always been a franchise that has been close to my heart. So when it was first announced, I was so excited to be able to pick up where I left off in my personal favourite Hitman 'Hitman: Blood Money'. But after my first completion of the game, I found myself not satified at all with what I had just experienced. It was not the game I grew up playing.
The whole tone of the game is completely different from any of the other previous versions in the franchise. The stealth is so frustrating, which is you are still able to be detected while disguised, which in some cases makes sense, e.g. a empty mansion being guarded by a small group of guards, who would all know eachother, so could easily notice you are not one of them. But when it comes to being dressed as a chief in a street parade and being caught out by a 9 till 5 shop keeper resulting in you getting gunned down for being dressed as a chief in a public area makes no sense at all.
The point system in Absolution is no way near as rewarding as Blood Moneys. You get points for killing enemys in creative ways such as dropping a chandelier on a bunch of thugs. But recieving a newspaper describing how much of a bad♥♥♥♥♥you are, I feel is much more rewarding then getting numbers at the end of the round.
Their has never really been a focused story to be anaylsed in the Hitman franchise, but Absolutions attempt on story telling just does not work. It's dull and you just don't care about whats going to happen next. The charcters are obviously made to be creeps as they are given a sort of inbred look like 'The Hills Have Eyes' but just never really makes you feel creeped out and results in you just not really hating the antagonist of the game.
The biggest problem about Absolution is its level design. It gets rid of previous focus on sandbox gameplay by making it a pont to point adventure that leads into a sandbox which all lack in depth and charm. Their is not a certain area of the game I can properly fully remember as they are all kind of the same. Where as again back to Blood Money, all the diffrent levels feel different and much more carefully made than Absolutions levels.
I'm not saying this is a bad game, I'm coming at this as a long time fan and my expectations were just not meet, as I was left feeling I had not played a Hitman game, but just another genetic mediocre nonlinear game that will be forgoten, which it already has.

Ahh Crysis, what a gem it is.
If I look back to the early 2008 this was nearly a bomb for me; always wanted to play it, playing through and again, again, again.
It holds itself up, after so many years, still looking good and still it is great fun. Mostly because of its Sandbox-like Gameplay. Fast first person shooter, or silent stealth game, or BOTH! Improvise or use tactic methods; weapon mods or the abillities of your armor. Get a vehicle, fill it with explosives and drive it into an enemy outpost, no problem. Throw your surrounding objects, like crates, barrels, refrigerators, chickens, at your enemies or destroy little houses. You can play as you like and the game doesn't punish you for it.
I, for my part, didn't like they stealth gameplay though, it's quite hard if you really want to sneak through without an alarm going off. I like it more as an action game where most effort was put in.
Besides your "one man- army" missions, you can take a seat in a tank battle, a helicopter escort mission or survive in an arctic world, fighting from fire to fire to keep yourself warm.
It is great in every aspect of a game, not superior to most games today has to offer, but still...
And a short word to the multiplayer:
Although the GameSpy servers were shut down, it's still possible to play the multiplayer via a Mod created from the community.
Rating: Very Good -> After all a wonderful shooter, varied, good-looking and just fun to play. Get this pearl, the price is just fair!

Fifty hours in, the best way I can describe "This War of Mine" is that it is Excruciatingly Beautiful. Without a doubt, this seemingly simple 2D side-scroller has captivated not only my mind, but my heart as well.
The player is immediately thrust into a searingly bleak landscape in which choices must be made that effect, not only the characters in the game, but the player herself. The beautifully pencil-swept landscapes foster a sense of abstraction while the character models and interior enviornments lend clarity of purpose and direction, be it towards the dark or the light, as the player struggles to find their way through a war-torn appoccalypse.
The combat is (intentionally?) difficult, for in this world, you are not some super soldier; you are only a person. And that is what speaks most directly to the gamer as they experience "This War of Mine". The first time I decided I had to kill in order to survive, I was terrified. And, it didn't end well. Marko's sacrifice eventually led to the downfall of my entire group and it was a miserable experience. An experience I shall never forget.
The User Interface in this game seems a bit wonky at first, at least it did to me. Once you've mastered the UI, however, you become master of your fate and that is something I like in a game. It becomes a question of not "can I kill this person" but, rather: "should I kill this person?" And that is the target the developers were going for, as far as I can tell.
I cannot remember the last time a video game made me question myself in such a profound way. Things like that are usually reserved for the cinema or found in books, I suppose. But as it stands, "This War of Mine" is a deeply moving and enjoyable game that should not be missed by anyone.

Rivals of Aether is a platform fighting game, inspired by Nintendo's Super Smash Brothers series, that you play for the challenge and the competition. It's retro-styled but pretty slick and well made, boasting nearly instant load times and great controller support.
You'll probably like this game if:
- You adore colorful pixel animal people.
- You dig fighters with small casts that give each character their own unique mechanics and tools.
- You prefer simpler control styles over Street Fighter-style motion commands.
- You play Super Smash Brothers and want a similar experience on PC.
- You think Smash is a little slow because of shielding and grabbing, and want to see how things play without them.
- You can get into time attack and co-op survival modes.
- You like to fight other people--there are strong players on netplay!
You might not like this game if:
- You don't use a gamepad. Keyboard controls are supported but they can be uncomfortable.
- You prefer the party chaos of Smash with items enabled. (In this case, play Smash instead.)
- You demand big character rosters, like to play a different character every time, or dislike mirror matchups. (In this case, I recommend Smash 4, or something like BlazBlue: Chronophantasma Extend.)
- You want a wealth of lore and exploration--this isn't that kind of game.
- You want to test your skills against strong AI instead of online play. The AI is somewhat competent, but most of the single player challenge is in winning fights fast while taking minimal damage, rather than fair fights against increasingly clever opponents. (AI is typically a weak point of fighting games, but you might check out the latest Tekken or Virtua Fighter 4 if you're interested in this.)

Rivals of Aether is a homage to what Smash Bros could have been if it catered to high level tournament players.
Fluid, precise combos executed at a feverish pitch. Playing this game takes me back to the furious speed I could only experience in Melee. To complete the likeness, this game comes packaged with wavedashing among other techs for high level play. I adore the speed at which these matches are fought.
For any newcomers, hopping online will absolutely crush you. The game has been in early access since 2015 so you'll be up against people who've been in it for hundreds of hours.
Luckily for those those just starting there's a story mode you can invest your time in, complete with backstories tailored to each character. After clearing campaign you're segued into a survival mode that issues endless waves of different challenges.
Flashy, vibrant pixel art adorns each stage. Characters have a nearly endless number of customizable colors for you to choose from.
Flashygoodness returns as this game's primary composer. If you haven't heard of him before do yourself a favor and check him out.

Actual effort went into the story mode campaign. Capcom could learn a couple things from this indie team. It's nothing spectacular but fleshing out the characters (especially brand new ones) is absolutely worth the effort.
A handful of pleasant surprises await you in solo or co-op play. The real meat and white-knuckle suspense lies in fighting real people.
Applies only to the campaign and co-op modes. A decent challenge to start yourself off. The endless climb online against real people is defined by the massive number of techs and accompanying mind games the game makes available.
Sakurai one stated in an interview "If we direct Smash only at competitive players then it will have no future." Rivals of Aether might prove him wrong.

Rivals of Aether is, for all intents and purposes, a more financially and technically accessible version of Super Smash Bros. Melee. At a more than generous price point, RoA provides a deep metagame of varied and colorful characters similar to that provided by Melee, but with a somewhat relaxed requirement of technical skill.
That being said, make no mistake; the game is still technically difficult and squarely aimed at the competitive audience. There are great casual modes available, but the focus of the game is on hardcore players with a number of features such as visible hitboxes and tournament stage striking built into the game itself.
Those looking for a zany beat-em-up party game to play with their friends will be more than happy with what RoA provides, but don't expect to hold a candle to veteran players before putting your nose to the grindstone. Thankfully, RoA's tutorial provides a thorough explanation to the advanced techniques the game offers, allowing those with the inclination to get acclimated to the water before jumping into the deep end of online play.

A good game hands down. Now while many here are bashing the title based on its predecessors (and it isn't without its flaws) a lot of folks should keep in mind that it is just the first part of a larger whole. Much like Civ V had addons later in its life (GK & BNW) Civ: BE will most likely have improvements and content added later on as well. For now its playable, fun, and if  given time will improve.
I also said that the game is not without its flaws. The Alien AI can be odd at times with the other computer controlled factions following quickly after. Some maps Alien nests are rare while in others they are abundant which can be the source of some early colonization blues. The Sponsers are a little bland and I did honestly expect more than the handfull you get right now. (The modding community though as aleviated that issue somewhat with new sponsers. Still waiting for an official Byzantine(-esque) Sponser though.) Lastly, I also honestly expected a greater variety of alien life.
Though much of what I've stated as "flaws" can be chalked up to expectations and again the game being a new release. I think this is why many were left feeling unfulfilled. I think we all expected more from Civ:BE right out of the gate.
Again, give the game a try if find it interesting. If its fun and thats what a game should have at its core. New content will come, bugs will be crushed, tweaks made, and so on. The game will improve if you let it. Through mods and/or official content.

Bottom line is, if you own an ATI card, don't buy this game.
Even for $5, it's not worth the headache of constant crashes and disconnects. I wish I had scrolled down the reviews more to have seen warnings about ATI cards. It started out as a pretty great co-op game, with slightly jaded graphics and not top level game mechanics, but still playable and enjoyable.
Then chapter 2 hit, and it all went to hell in barrow downs. Missing textures, random disconnects and system crashes at various intervals, especially in the middle of hard fights - problems either for you or friends connected to your game. The first few were just a minor annoyance because the game was quite fun but, when it kept happening, my friends and I just had to give up in frustration. It was a sad thing too, because the game is pretty addictive.
The biggest annoyance for me is how the game's minimum requirements actually state that ATI cards older than those from 2006 will run this game, and how that is basically untrue after the first chapter. I begin wonder if I can get my money back just for that partially false statement.
I don't want to go through the trouble of listing my system specs, but it runs anything recent like DA:I or FC4 on ultra without issues. I use an ATI 290X.

The Last Remnant is a great role-playing game with a unique take on combat mechanics in form of a turn-based, command-based system using symbol encounters. It is definitely the most interesting part of this game providing a lot of fun especially in the larger-scale battles.
Originally released for Xbox 360 the PC version of this game features numerous changes from the console, including enhanced graphical settings, a Turbo Mode that increases battle speed (very practical when farming for weapon components), and a New Game Plus option, that allows the player to start a new game with the gold and unique items from their first play-through.
And for the hardcore gamers among us there are of course challenges like super boss battles and the component farming for the endgame weapons.
On the other hand the sound is a mixed bag of partially epic orchestral music and sorely limited voice-acting. In addition the protagonist Rush is sometimes a little bit uninspiring as a leader figure.
The game has no Steam achievements.

The game tries so hard to be a squd-based strategic rpg. An nearly gets it done at least halfway.
Which basically means that the base system is good - you can find / hire new units, put them in a squad together and then give them positions in different formations depending on their function. You can even costumize the different units pretty well, in regards of abilities and equipment. In combat you then choose overall orders like "attack enemy with magic / physical abilites" etc. Overall the system is a bit similar to Fire Emblem.
But that is where the bad stuff happens. Actually the game never bothers to tell you anything. Not about how the specialization, itemization and development of units works. Not even what the different orders for the combat do. That is where the game just becomes a bad joke. At some point I got three options for hitting the enemies with physical abilities. All costing the same amount of ability points, but I had no clue what order makes what unit use which ability.
For a game that wants you to micro so much of the units, their equipment and their skills, you have practicall NO controll over their behaviour in combat.
Another example: At some point I decided to do a pure healer squad for backing my fighters up, since they got ganged by AoE-attacks during a hard fight. So I put a few magic users in a squad, told them to only use their healing abilities and let them wait in the background to heal the others. Which was utterly useless. Also, of course you don't know what enemies you fight before you encounter them. So in the same area there can be a group of 2 units which you can one-hit. Then the next encounter is a disguised mini-boss, who summons elite squads every round and hit all your squads every time it attacks. No jokes, those monsters stood right next to each other.

Playthrough time: 16 hours 30 min (single player: main story and most side quests, listening to most conversation)
+Good action RPG combat, severing orc limbs is fun
+Lots of well put together LotR story elements/locations for fans to enjoy
+Enough levelling and loot to keep things interesting
-Gameplay can probably get repetitive if you play more than 1-2 hours each time
-Combat system and leveling/skill tree isn't that deep for hardcore players
-Fiddly character change system
-A few glitches may crash the game
The game is great for using the Xbox 360 controller and playing on the TV from the couch.
Graphics performance R9 280X, 1080P max settings: 60 FPS (V-sync) all the time except for a few stutters when loading new textures.
If you will enjoy LotR: War in the North depends on how you're going to play the game, and if you're a fan of the LotR world. The game is best played casually a few hours at the time, If you play it that way, and you're a fan, the game will probably keep you entertained all the way through and has a lot going for it when it comes to the story and locations.
If you're not interested in the Lord of the Rings world, and come just for the action RPG, you'll probably find the game lacking, especially if you put 3-4 or more hours in to the game each go, then the game will probably feel quite repetitive.
The game tells a story of three heroes (man, dwarf, elf) indirectly helping the fellowship during the LotR story. You run in to quite a few characters from the books/movies, and visit familiar locations as Bree and Rivendell. The locations in this game generally look great, and all the characters has quite a lot to say, so the story builds up well with lots of background information available if you like to listen to conversation.
The main part of the game has you battling mostly orcs in a third person action RPG style. The combat style doesn't differ much through the game, you can select any of the three characters (but switching between them is only allowed upon clearing a section of the current chapter, or after visiting towns, and is a bit clunky), use a light or heavy attack, ranged attacks and magic/skills. You level up and unlock/improve skills and get better gear/other loot that improve stats, but the gameplay doesn't change that much. You're still hacking/shooting at orcs most of the time.
I really enjoyed the combat, and the levelling/loot was enough to keep me interested all the way through, and combat is fun. Sometimes after getting the enemy HP down enough you get a prompt to use a heavy attack for a limb severing finish that for me never got old. Just as satisfying every time.
The game has some nice boss battles as well, and every chapter has a few events that mixes things up.
The game also supports online co op (up to 3 players in total). Unfortunately, I haven't been able to try this, but I can image this game can be lots of fun with 1-2 friends.
As for the glitches: At the final chapter, there was a game breaking glitch, for some reason when navigating the tunnels the game got really choppy and crashed when the frame rate got too low. Apparently a common problem, and the solution was to set the graphics to minimum and get through that section with as little on screen as possible (aiming at the floor while moving helped). When out of the tunnels, restart the game and everything is well again.
Apparently the problem is AMD related and another way of fixing it is by installing the 12.6  version of AMD Catalyst,
.

Would a purple homicidal anthropomorphic rabbit from the future be a better ruler than the real ones we have today? Sadly, the answer is: quite possibly. And that’s exactly the premise of Not a Hero from London-based developer Roll7 that already made a name for itself with the acclaimed side-scrolling skateboarding game OlliOlli. The idea presented by BunnyLord is that, for some reason, the world will end unless he gets elected mayor. The polls aren’t in BunnyLord’s favor and apparently the best way to turn voter opinion around is to assemble a crew of misfits who will brutally and mercilessly poke crime in its ugly face. Well, we’ve certainly seen worse election campaigns.
The story is about as preposterous as it sounds. BunnyLord is obsessed with milkshakes, turtles, pandas and murder (oh, and cheese) and will send the player to perform a wide range of tasks through the territory of three stereotypical gangs. However, all of these tasks basically boil down to killing everyone in your path. It’s a good thing then that killing in this game is really well done. Not a Hero is a 2D side-scrolling cover-based shooter on two planes with the second plane acting as cover. It’s an instantly intuitive system as both you and your enemies are slightly shaded upon entering cover. There’s no jumping in the game, but sliding serves as a substitute mechanic and it is pulled off brilliantly. Basically, you can slide to move faster and also to tackle enemies which enables you to execute them point blank. However, there are enemies that cannot be tackled and they have to be avoided and shot from a distance.
The first character you have at your disposal is BunnyLord’s best friend Steve, but as you go through missions and increase BunnyLord’s standing in the polls, more characters will join your cause. Every character has a distinct amusing personality and it is obvious that this is a very British game. I never got tired of hearing Steve shout “fookin’ ‘ell” as he encountered droves of enemies. Then there’s Cletus (“Dressed like a hillbilly, but actually from Scotland”), Samantha from Wales (“Valley girls last longer!”), Jesus from Spain who has formidable hip-thrusting skills and my favorite, Mike from Northern England with a constant eye twitch most likely indicating a murderous sociopath. There are nine characters in total to unlock and more importantly than their personality, each of them has different skills, weapons and abilities which completely changes the way you go through a level. For example, Steve’s specialty is tackling, Mike performs silent executions, Stanley has high rate of fire good for crowd control whereas Jesus is a really fast runner and performs executions while moving.
The map design is good, but rather straightforward. Each level offers some additional objectives that occasionally take you away from the main route, but most of the time there’s just one way to go through a level. Apart from a helicopter encounter, there aren’t any setpieces to mix things up a bit and offer a bit of diversity. Even during the three boss fights, you’re more of a bystander taking care of other enemies while BunnyLord takes care of the boss. The game does throw you in the fire a bit with enemies popping up unexpectedly most notably when the SWAT teams enter the building and start chasing you down. Enemies also drop various power ups for your weapon and secondary weapons such as grenades or turrets are also scattered through each level.
The game uses pixel art for its graphics and while it’s pleasant, the art style isn’t particularly strong. The same can be said for the soundtrack which uses retro 8-bit music. The goal was obviously going for a retro feel in a more modern package, but neither component really stands out. The controls and the mechanics are tight and responsive. The game runs well for the most part, although I did experience some slowdown in certain places. It’s not anything major, but it is noticeable due to the nature of the game which requires pinpoint precision and speed. There’s a bit of trial and error as the game demands you to memorize the level layout and enemies and then perform really well in order to get to the end because you have to start over from the beginning each time you die. This does get just a bit frustrating, however, the mechanics are so well implemented that you’ll definitely want to jump back in and finish the level. It has that addictive element to it and once you master it, the sense of accomplishment is great indeed.
The game’s biggest drawback is its short length and lack of longevity. Once you finish up the 21 levels in the game all of which are very short, there’s little incentive to go on. You can go through levels with different characters to get better results, but it’s not that compelling. It’s a shame that the game doesn’t support Steam achievements as those would possibly facilitate more gameplay experimentation and provide more incentive to re-visit a level, if wisely implemented. I also have one gripe regarding the story. The premise is great, but the game doesn’t really take it anywhere. Sure, there are a lot of jokes here, but a more engaging political satire, which is actually hinted at in the trailers and the advertising but which is not in the actual game, would go a long way to make this game not only more current and relevant, but also more humorous. Based on the pre-release campaign, I expected something like a gaming equivalent of a cross between the senseless slapstick violence of Bottom and the edgy political satire of The New Statesman. Which would have been brilliant. As it is, though, Not a Hero is only half way there in that regard.
Not a Hero is a very enjoyable game thanks to its tight mechanics, exhilarating gameplay and humorous story. There’s definitely room for improvement and seeing as how the ending leaves the door wide open for a sequel, it will be very interesting to see what Roll7 does next as the foundation laid here is strong indeed.
