Let me start this off with a warning for anyone who decides to play this game - use the Japanese dialog. The English VA will probably really hurt your experience with this game. Something about it just kind of ruins your ability to develop any sort of involvement with the characters.
Anyway, I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It has several innovations that solved things I don't like about lots of JRPGs.
One of my favorite features was being able to retry when you lose a battle and being sent to a few seconds before you encountered the enemy, leaving you with the ability to walk away and go do something else or just try again. I've had too many frustrating moments in other JRPGs when I lost a battle only to be sent back to one of the too-sparse save points or losing progress because I hadn't been obsessively saving every few minutes.
I also enjoyed the battle system. In addition to being real time, which adds to the excitement of the battles for me, the paradigm system has some things I liked about it over other JRPG battle systems. Instead of having to pick every command for every character for every battle, you can instruct your characters what to do (heal, build stagger meter, do damage, tank, buff, or debuff) and leave it to them to handle the details. Then the gameplay loop in the battles becomes analyzing the situation and switching paradigms to suit it.
I also liked the absence of random battles. Just being able to see the enemies you might bump into makes things a lot less frustrating and annoying compared to walking along and suddenly having everything freeze and being thrust into a battle.
I liked the story and overall flow of gameplay from the start until about 40 hours in. Then it really started to go downhill for me. It just felt like it was dragging on. Maybe if it was the only game I had to play I would be fine with it, but I found myself wishing it would just be over. It just started to feel like corridor after corridor with little interesting plot development. I've heard people complain that the entirety of the game is just corridors with cutscenes between them, but I honestly enjoyed the earlier parts of the game. Stuff happens, you are still getting the hang of the battle system, you're looking forward to what's going to happen next, and the pace seems fine. After 40 hours I started to just get bored of the whole thing - it didn't "change it up" enough to retain my interest, and the battle system just wasn't enough to keep me entertained.
As someone who isn't a big fan of JRPGs, I weakly reccomend this. I had a lot of fun with it at first but it started to feel like a chore or job towards the end. To be fair, I start to feel this way with most JRPGs. There's something about a lot of JRPGs, particularly their battle systems, that just makes them start to lose their fun after awhile for me, especially compared to more fast paced and action oriented games. I think it's mainly due to the fast-paced feedback loop those games usually have when compared to JRPGs.
And if you do play it, as stated earlier, I recommend choosing Japanese voice acting. Not because it's always better to play games in the language they were written in, but because it means you won't have to listen to the annoying English VA. I suspect that some people who said they hated the characters or found some of them to be annoying or didn't like the story might've felt that way because of the English VA and would've liked those things a bit more had they switched.

I was watching Linus tech tips video, about how new hardware runs original Crysis, so I bought a copy for myself to see how my today’s rig is able to handle this 2007 PC hardware killer and I was disappointed, but not because of my PC.
Game runs on CRYENGINE 2, which for the time could do a lot of amazing things and it shows in the game. Massive vegetation, huge draw distance, great texture detail, stunning shaders and so on. While I was playing this game, it never felt and looked like something from  2007, it felt like it was released about 3 years ago, and probably with some HD textures and improved lightning mods, the  title will look like it was released last year.  Levels are huge and there's a variety of them, you’ll be traveling through beaches, jungle, swamps, caves, alien space ships, frozen forests etc. and because maps are quite big the objectives can be completed in in some variety of ways.
Story takes you on a islands in Pacific ocean where a group of american archaeologists gets into trouble with North-Korea's armed forces. You are member of elite forces group which are dropped on the islands to find out what happen with the archaeologists. You are quipped with so called Nano-suit which have special abilities like boosting up your strength, speed or makes you invisible for several seconds. Also you'll have variety of weapons and vehicles at your disposal. Game starts slow, with you crawling trough the jungle and eventually stepping in to some armed military group, but gradually escalates in to full fledged military conflict involving heavy weapons and machinery. Some call this game spiritual successor to original Far Cry and in some way and form this game definitely is.
Game is fun as hell, story maybe is weak and nothing original, but I had a lot of fun playing this game. So where is my disappointment ?
Well, the game runs terribly on 64-bit systems, it constantly crashes, sometimes I had 2 hours session with no problems what so ever, but than there was sessions were game crushed like each two minutes. Frame rate is all over the place, sometimes you'll have stable 60 fps, and sometimes game drops to 2-3 fps when there is not much happening on the screen. And not to mention that you'll have to do some research and work to make the game work in the first place.
So to sum it up game is beautiful and fun when it runs well, and when it doesn’t it just frustrates you, so ignoring all the technical problems it would probably be something like 8.5, but for what it is now it’s nothing more than 6.5...

Hitman: Absolution has got to be one of the best Stealth/Shooter games ever made.
You play as Agent 47. A Hitman who's the master of stealth and assassination. With each level, you have to kill a target while facing guards and civilians. And in your open environment, you have a bunch of different means of carrying this out. Mostly by making distractions, creating accidents, hiding, silent kills, or just point blank kills.
It was nice to finally get Hitman: Absolution on Steam for only $4.00 this holiday season. I remember watching a trailer for this game on Youtube called, "Run For Your Life" about 2 years ago and was immediately captivated by the game. The gameplay just looked so cool. I had not played earlier Hitman games, so Absolution's story was confusing for me. It's about quitting your Hitman agency and rescuing a teenage girl from a crazy Texas man. However, what a player can do in this game is what I was focused on.
The slow motion shooting ability is what I probably like most about Hitman: Absolution besides changing disguises. Turning around to an enemy from a side view then lifting a pistol up to shoot them always makes you feel like a badass.
I highly recommend Hitman: Absolution for anyone who is fans of Stealth/Shooter games or earlier Hitman games. I believe it's one of the best games of it's kind.

First of all let me start by saying that I have played and finished ALL Hitman games. I really tried to like this game as I have liked Square Enix's latest works including of course the legendary Deus Ex Human Revolution but I am afraid hardcore Hitman fans will be greatly disappointed by Hitman: Absolution.
Remember the cluster ♥♥♥♥ that was Conviction to the Splinter Cell series? Yeah, the exact same thing happened to the HItman franchise. The newest Hitman game is at best a stealth action game comparable to a shooter, although you can still complete objectives "silently". While it maintained some of the features of its predecessor, Blood Money, like accidents it destroyed one of Hitman's signature feats, the disguise. You wanna grab a policeman disguise and sneak past the officers to your objective? Well, too bad because every f**kin policeman in the force know eachother and if you get too close to them, say 30 feet/10 meters they will immediatly blow your cover! Yeah, a big ♥♥♥♥ you to disguises.
You are no longer able to select your starting gear when on a mission (at least in Absolution mode).
A lot of the missions are split into checkpoints where you have to move from zone to zone to get to the next area objective, like a ♥♥♥♥in' CoD mission. You no longer have the freedom to explore the entire mission map and plan your objective as you would like to fulfill them, you are constrained by  the mission zone objectives which comprise mostly of "evade police", "escape the building", "find the exit". And you do this every ♥♥♥♥in' mission.
Luckily there are points in the missions when you are required to actually, you know, ASSASSINATE A ♥♥♥♥IN' TARGET. Some of which can be completed quite nicely.
The controls feel very clumsy and unresponsive, the camera gets in the way of the cover system if you move the mouse to look around. A very bad mechanics port I would say.
Regarding story and atmosphere. A lot of the times you feel more like Jack Bauer than the cool Agent 47 that carefully plans his every hit and objective details in advance. You are constantly on the run. This game simply became an action/adventure with stealth elements.
The scoring system, while interesting, is radically punishing. For example if you approach a restricted area that's guarded by an NPC who sees you, you automatically lose points even though you quickly react and walk away not to alert him to become suspicious. What the ♥♥♥♥ is that?!

Broken By Design - I have been a fan of Egosoft for a long time now.  I love space sims and I loved X2 and the X3 series of games, so despite warning signs that X Rebirth was headed down a bad path during its lengthy development, I gave Egosoft the benefit of the doubt, especially since they repeatedly assured the community that the game would not be dumbed down and would still allow the full breadth of playstyles that earlier games in the series allowed.  Mistake.
First off, the game is chock full of bugs.  This is nothing new for Egosoft games, they've had rocky launches before, practically with every game they've put out.  The bugs and performance issues can be fixed, as they were in the earlier games.
Unfortunately the problems with X Rebirth go MUCH deeper than simple bugs and horrible optimization.  Horrible design decisions were made that extend down to the core of the game itself.  The X series has always been about allowing the players to play anyway the wanted.  Be a pirate, be a protector, lead giant fleets in massive sector-wide wars, set up a giant trading empire, be an explorer, etc.  During development we were assured that this would still be the case with X Rebirth, despite being confined to one ship at all times.  It's not.  While in theory you could still set up a trading empire or command a massive fleet of warships, in practice both of these are neigh impossible because of how poorly designed the game is.  The problem lies in the complete and utter lack of useful fleet commands and robust trading commands.  Leading a fleet or warships or commanding freighters on trading runs means holding their hand through every step of the way, which, with large numbers of vessels is an exercise in futility and pain akin to repeatedly smashing your own hand with a hammer.
Furthermore, all trading must be done in person, face to face.  This means docking with a ship (and playing a weird dry humping docking game since there is no docking computer) or a station, then embarking on foot.  Egosoft shoehorned on-foot station traversal likely as something they can put "on the back of a box" as a feature.  This may sound neat, but I guarantee you will grow to despise it very quickly.  First of all, the stations interiors aren't exactly pretty to look at, and the character models and animations are downright frightening, like something out of Morrowind.  What's worse is that there are 2, maybe 3 total station layouts in the entire game, and every single station is a CARBON COPY of one of those 2 or 3 layouts, right down to the placement of lootable cargo containers, which you can rob right in front of their assumed owners, in old-school jRPG fashion.  It would be one thing if the stations were different and interesting and had characters you cared about in the slightest bit inside them, but they're filled with clones of the same 5 or 6 horrifically ugly character models, that all just repeat the same 4 or 5 phrases.  The characters are so wooden that it makes Bethesda characters look like some of the amazing characters someone on the level of a Chris Avellone has written by comparison.  So now every time you want to trade or recruit someone you have to fly to a station, land, waste a bunch of time walking around a dull, ugly, lifeless station looking for dull lifeless robot-like "people" and talk to them face to face.  The whole on-foot parts add nothing but tedium and frustration to the game.
Beyond that, computer controlled ship AI is horrific, the copilot in your ship is annoying and useless, the game has tons of game breaking bugs (there's an entire community built around providing saved games to people so they can continue broken games of X Rebirth), there is no SETA to speed up travel or any autopilot, but instead we get a horrible highway travel mini-game that's supposed to "eliminate" the need for SETA or autopilot, basic combat commands are flat out missing (there is no select nearest or next target button.  NONE), the user interface is one of the absolute worst and most counterintuitive I have ever had the displeasure of working with ever, and flightstick control is a broken mess at the moment.
In short, the game is a bloody broken horrific mess right down to the core systems, which were clearly designed for consoles, despite Berndt repeatedly denying that.  The proof is in the pudding as the control scheme was obviously created with a gamepad in mind.
X Rebirth was supposed to be more accessible, bringing in new players, yet retain the depth and complexity of the earlier games that the established fanbase loved.  The game failed horribly on both accounts.  The UI is so counterintuitive and frustrating that it's even less accessible than the earlier games' brutal learning curves, and the game is so convoluted and stripped of features that it has completely alienated Egosoft's existing customer base.
Eventually Egosoft will fix the bugs and implement some of the missing features.  The X modding community is really great and they will mod out (already have in some cases) some of the horrible "features" such as on-foot, and mod in some much needed things.  Still, as great as the modding community is, they can, at best, make this into a halfway decent space sim many months from now.  Frankly, you're much better off just playing X3: Terran Conflict or X3: Albion Prelude because I don't see how this game could ever approach either of those games without overhauling the very core of the game, at which point they'd probably be better off scrapping this and just making a whole new game from scratch, one without terrible design decisions.

This one’s pretty special. One of the best platformers I’ve ever played - although occasionally had to play in small bites because of how fiendishly difficult it is in some places. Thankfully the difficulty is down to pure design and the controls are fantastic, which makes you feel like any improvement needed is yours, and not the game’s fault. The animations are smooth, the map is well designed and there’s a decent upgrade path. The only slight downside is the story, which left me feeling completely confused for more or less the whole game.
I started off really liking the feel of the game; the premise being that you were just exploring some old ruins. This held together well enough for quite a while, but when characters, lore and story elements started popping up I felt like they really weren’t tied together very well. It was hinted at that something was expected of me, but I had no idea what or why, and when I beat the final boss (no spoilers), the cutscene following it just left me more confused and with a feeling of “well that was really badly explained”. If we’re honest, this game isn’t about the story, it’s about the tight and really well designed gameplay, but it did disappoint a bit that what story there was, was lacking.
A lot of reviews complained about the amount of backpeddling you had to do to get to other areas. Personally I didn’t see this as an issue - there were loads of areas to explore, and you had to go back to old areas to see everything, which is kind of the whole point in a metroid-type game. The only weak point here was that occasionally I felt lost and had no idea where to go next even after getting an upgrade.
There were a couple of boss fights that I felt were much higher difficulty than the others. That being said, once I went and upgraded my nail, found a new Charm and got another health point, a boss which I had previously made no progress on in an hour went down on my first attempt, so the upgrades do make a huge difference. By the end of the game I felt pretty overpowered and beat the final boss on my second attempt.

I whole heartedly recommend this and am slightly ashamed I haven't gotten around to reviewing it yet. This was one of the earliest games I played (probably second actually) and I had the game of the year edition on disk (so don't let the time counter fool you, I've actually spent a lot more time on sins outside of steam).
Honestly from a space RTS I really couldn't ask for much more. It's a slightly old game so the graphics aren't "next gen" however the interface is very convenient and allows for quick switching between zoomed out tactical views to help manage your fleet battles, and a more up close cinematic view to really engage the player into what's going on. The civilization management aspect is also very indepth and has many different factors which need to be accounted for when making certain decisions. Coupling that with a very indepth research tree (many aspects of which are race specific) and the other deep differences in the entire play style of the three races, there's a lot of varience for enjoyable replayability.
Honestly thought... I'd say the best part is just the scale the battles can get too, and mine haven't even been that grand compared to other's I've seen. It's quite enjoyable to watch a fleet of 100 frigates, and 50 or so cruisers charge into a pirate base, only for their pirate adversaries to just be engulphed and devoured in your swarms of hundreds of fighters and bombers at the ready.
Also... the main difference the rebellion version has over the rest is that it adds two subfactions to eatch race, loyalists and rebels, and each of these subfactions has their own individual titan, which is just awesome. The titans add a new aspect to the combat as they can be the definite deciding factor in many of your future battles, and when you watch one plow through the enemy frigates like a steam roller... well let's just say it's satisfying.
So honestly all in all I think it's worth it and you can get a lot of hours out of it. Of course it's still smart to wait for sales, so if it's on sale for cheap I'd say snatch it up. However that's just me and my experiences, I hope this helped, bye!

The most devestating realization was that diplomacy is LITERALLY THE SAME. The one thing I want Civ to really make amazing is diplomatic interactions to be stellar and the options to be immense. This game is literally Civ 5 with aliens and that's just not enough. If I could return the game, I would have done so.

This isn't the remaster I though it was going to be. If you're looking to buy, or download to replace the original BioShock, that's up to you. Sometimes "free" isn't always "better", in my case.

- Options to tweak the game are stripped.
- Textures don't look any better than the first. For a moment, I thought they were worse.
- It crashes when you least expect it.
- The [added] Art Gallery isn't dynamic. Dead silent and not too much to show.
+ There is no frame cap on the PhysX behind this game. Bodies, objects, and water motion are more fluid.
+ Free if you have the first BioShock.
+ Not my fault if you install/play the Remastered version and don't like it.
Buy, download, and play at your own risk. Best if you wait for a Halloween or 2K Sale Event and opt in for the original.

I was waiting for this game. I enjoyed Alpha Centauri immensely and was hoping this would live up to my hopes. I always enjoyed the late game tech in all the civ games and always wanted to play beyond the space victory which both Alpha Centauri and Beyond Earth let you do.
Sadly, even if Beyond Earth lets you do this it is just boring. The major factor of this is the AI's. Diplomacy has been almost removed compared to previous Civilization games. The only real interaction you have is getting trading routes to other AI's. There is no real resource trading and you can pretty much play the whole game without interacting with the other AI's at all.
The whole city management and buildings also lack any sort of appeal. You don't really care what you build and with wonders especially. Previous Civ games made you feel like you achieved something when you managed to build a certain wonder, this one doesn't.
I do like the ideas in the game though, the tech tree was a bit of a new thing, while complex to learn provided with some interesting ideas.
All in all though, sadly, this game comes short and will require some massive gameplay improvement to be worth it.

A Remasterpiece. The sound and the graphics are top notch and the game runs fluidly. I must be the luckiest guy on steam, because I've experienced none of the crashing that others have reported.
While I can swear the art direction is somewhat different from the original, it actually adds rather than detracts. Rapture feels more full and complete. Floor and ceiling textures show age and wear and there are more buildings and signs . Overall, it feels like a more belieavable version of a city under the sea -- more true to the creator's original vision. As an added bonus, nearly all of the "loading screens" have been eliminated and movement between levels and areas feels more natural and less disjointed.
If you haven't played Bioshock before, I implore you to pick up the remasters. The game holds up really well despite its age. If it's been a while since your last romp through Rapture, you should definitely check out the great work that Blind Squirrel put into the remaster.
The only real shame here is that 2K spent time and money restoring an old game instead of investing in a new Bioshock.

After reading through the reviews given by professionals, I'm convinced none of them actually played the game. This is not a strategy game; it is an extraordinary exercise in nihilism. Throughout the game you will find there is little purpose in your existence beyond its own perpetuation. In this regard, Civilization: Beyond Earth offers an exquisite simulated experience.
If, however, you're looking for a game that offers (among other things):
- challenges and competition
- meaingful interaction with human/AI players
- interesting strategy options
- engaging peacetime and wartime play
- a compelling reason to continue playing the game
I encourage you to wait until Firaxis does one of the following: patches, expands or creates an entirely new iteration that offers the kind of engaging and dynamic gameplay currently exhibited by Civilization V: Brave New World. In the meantime--and barring any genuine interest in nihilistic game play--I encourage you to invest your time elsewhere as this game is still riding with its training wheels on.
Now that the general review is over, here are the details on the good, the bad and a (more) thoughtful examination of the game generally:
The good:
- Nice graphics
- An interesting take on the traditional 'tech tree'
- Affinity structure is a novel idea
- Lots of small options that impact long term outcomes
- A very exciting concept (this is true, but I'm really reaching here)
The Bad:
- Game play does not encourage much interaction among players
- The AI is underdeveloped
- Much of the terrain simply looks like Civ 5 in gamma mode
- There really isn't much to do during peacetime
- Military unit options are few, making tactics uninspired
- Human players do not feel particularly challenged
- Lacking in substantive competitive pressure
- The affinity structure is somewhat obvious, flat, and limiting
- Can feel overwhelmed with options that seem unnecessary
- Technology quotations are uninspiring (and techs feel very disjointed)
- Wonders are underpowered, also lack the videos many players love from Civ
As I (and my wife) played the game together, we felt the game simply 'drifted' into the future without a clear purpose, driving force or compelling challenges. In this way it felt very bland and, sad as it is to say, boring. Upon reflection, the game seems as if it never made it out of alpha testing. It has great potential to be an incredibly engaging game but misses the mark in its current form by a wide margin.
As an additional note--more to Firaxis than to fans or potential buyers--Firaxis needs to make sure its games are ready for prime time before the initial release. Civilizition 5 only truly came of age via its latest expansion (and quite a bit of money), Brave New World--much to the consternation of fans new and old. Beyond Earth is already off to a much rockier start. With this and other above comments in mind, I don't recommend people purchase this game until Firaxis makes BE a truly compelling game, both generally and as a successor to Alpha Centauri.

I previously gave a negative review of the game when it was in its early stages/ Now that the second set has been released and added into the pool of playable cards, this is finally starting to feel like magic, with the kind of complexity and detail that was missing from the origins set.

I can't wait to see what else this game will bring as it develops.
Now is the time to get into this game, while it is still young and you have time to collect all the cards. Once there are a few sets out you will have a much harder time catching up in difficulty, especially versus more experienced players.
The only ongoing issue I think is that the AI is still just creating random deck combinations, in the past they followed the archetypes vaguely, but now with all the new cards available to them they are just playing any random card regardless of whether it works well with other cards. The difficulty levels are also still entirely meaningless.

I've been playing for a couple days now with 15 hours of gameplay and my initial opinion of the game is not that great. The world that is presented to you is interesting but many of the characters are incredibly annoying and story telling isn't particularly good either. The main character is a whiney little brat that makes stupid decisions one after another. The game also has a very deep character development system but it is muddled with hidden stats which make it difficult to tell if you're going the right direction.
The combat system has potential to be great but it is very frustrating. Besides the extremely frustrating battle command system, it's not uncommon to run into battles where you can be instantly wiped out without anything you can do to prevent it so saving is your best friend. 1 union vs 5? Yeah, you don't even get the option to heal and round one you die. Boss fight? He's got an aoe attack that can 1 shot your party and uses it every other turn. Without using a guide, figuring out the battle commands is nearly impossible and even using a guide, it is often quite frustrating. Character development is also annoying because there are many hidden stats that are factoring into character class and development. If these stats were visible, it would make the game much better and if you could always tell your units exactly what to do it would make the game immensely better. But that is not the case so it lends itself to an incredibly frustrating learning curve.
If I had paid full price for this I would have returned it in a heartbeat. At $4 I still feel annoyed that I spent the money on it. I feel like this game had a lot of potential that just wasn't capitalized on.
If you do end up giving it a shot, don't grind early on. It only hurts you. And start reading a guide from the start to save yourself a ragequit. If you're not using a controller, in the game settings on the controller page, there is an option to change which buttons the tooltips show (xbox, ps3, keyboard, etc.). Change this to keyboard. And to skip cutscenes, hit Pause/Break and then S to skip.

Game is, honestly, just not too great!
The game starts you out with horrible cards (unless you're cool with just running elf tribal which is hella strong) and then allows you to purchase Origins packs via coins you gain in game!  Cards from Origins are fine I suppose but the fact of the matter is most magic players buy their cards individually so that they can compose a deck they enjoy while here you must buy packs (which only have six cards because...because they do) and hope to the RNGesus that you acquire good cards/the cards you like to play with!  By the end of the campaign you have enough gold for around 6 packs I believe which sounds great except for the fact that that's only really 36 random cards.  You can then earn more coins via quests (think Hearthstone) which is fine really except for the fact that quests will take far too long for the amount of gold you recieve.
In complete honesty they have seemed to copy Hearthstone a little too much because while HS may ask you to complete 2 or 4 games or so as a certain class that's fine for HS!  Magic Duels does the same thing giving you the same amount of gold as HS but what they apparently don't take into reason is that Magic is Magic and HS is HS.  Magic games take longer to complete most times leaving you burnt out by your second game of four with a deck that you were forced to make by the deck builder that gives you choices for cards and you pick from its choices!  Yes, that's correct, unless specifically told to win games with a deck of your own you instead have to pick a color combination that the game wants you to use and then the deck wizard goes ahead and builds you the crappy deck of your dreams!  This coupled with the fact that you get completely random cards and not enough of them makes for a hell of a time getting colors you actually have good cards for for the quest of the day!
Another thing is, I hope you all hate black and blue especially the two colors together because my god does Magic Duels hate them!  Your starting black kill spell?  A five drop destroy target creature, it can't be regenerated.  Yeah, and your starting blue counter?  Countermand...a four drop counter spell that then mills your opponent for four cards or so which is whatever, you're getting four mill or so for an extra mana?  Well considering you start with no other mill options unless you pull the right cards from your tiny freaking pack you'll be doing no milling I'm afraid!  Which brings me to the color green:  my god did they get everything!  From the beginning you get great elves coupled with some gross one drop buff spells that, with two of in your starting hand or more, you could easily kill your opponent with with just that!  Red gets no starting burn really except for inferno fist if you really want to count it!  If you do then it's a three drop deal two damage to something which if you know anything about magic you know that's terrible! Black has too many high cost kill and graveyard recursion cards to be useful and white just has white weenies which can be very effective except any flying weenies you have will be blown up via jagged scar archers which green begins with, sorry!
On top of everything else this continues to not be very Magic-y in nature due to an odd cap of only getting two of each rare.  What?!  Listen, there are cards that have to be limited in certain formats but only two of each rare?  ANY RARE?!  What in the hell is that all about?!  I honestly do not know but listen everyone unless this game gets upgraded out the♥♥♥♥♥and unless you get better cards to start out with, this game will be a grind.  A HELLOVA GRIND!  Unless RNGesus shines his light upon you giving you every dream card you ever wanted out of the Magic Origins block which, besides the plainswalkers, there aren't that many great cards in this block, then you will continue to take way too long to win your two to four games which means you will take forever to get a single pack with only six random cards in it.
Another thing is the online play and two headed giant mode, which I should point out are the only modes there really are except for play the computer and the campaign.  Anyways, online play is fine I suppose except for the fact that you will likely play against elves which is fine because you'll likely be playing them too if you want to win!  You then only earn coins if you defeat your opponent which means that at the first sign of trouble one side will inevitably quit playing and then if you lose against the computer you get nothing...yay.  The ranking system is not explained and simply has you going up for winning and down for not!  Is there a legendary rank to get to like HS (probably considering the copy and paste job they've done with the rest of the game)?  Do we get anything for ranking up or do we just get a sense of pride for having spent our time battling and defeating our enemies with our elven armies?  Not sure but damn is it nice to see that number go up as you win  games and get your 20 gold per win!  Just a little tid bit of information for you, that's eight wins for a single pack of six random cards, woo!
On to two headed giant, a fun mode if not a little odd really, matches tend to go the same way as your one on ones except you may find your ally getting replaced with a bot pretty often and, oh yeah, you earn no coins for playing it or winning!
Lastly I have to comment on the atrocious layout for the game.  You play on a 3D sort of table which looks hurrendously bland and I'd rather it be 2D and just a little more colorful!  You know, to break up the monotony and completely boring task of winning all of these games for next to no coins.  Also, you'll more than likely get frustrated with the inability to tap your mana how you like by simply selecting them manually.  Instead you can hover over a spell and then press left control over and over again to get to the right combination!  Seems legit.  Oh and after each campaign you get a horrilbly done animation which, while I appreciate the effort Wizards, I think we could have done without to save you guys a little embarrassment!
Well there's my two...okay maybe a little bit more than that, cents.  If I had to give a number rating I'd say about a 4 is good, which this number could change in the future but not until they give this game a huge overhaul!

GooH takes place in a new city called New Hades. The gameplay is mostly the same as in SR4, you have similar super powers like stomp, aura and blast plus a new one where you call minions to aid you in battle. The powers have some new upgrades but nothing really new.
New Hades is dark and dirty, it looks a bit like Stilwater Shivington with occasional lightning crashes and explosios, cars blow up for no reason and all the inhabitans are husks, imitating peoples behaviours like sleeping on benches or standing at publich telephones and digging in trash cans.
The Boss looks just like you left him/her in SR4 and playing as Johnny Gat or Kinzie is really fun.
You cannot change their appearance or clothing.
The enemies are demons wich look a bit like the Zin from SR4, the big ones behave and look like Brutes from SR3. Also theres Minibosses similar to the Wardens from SR4.
The city is fun to explore especially when flying, but it is quickly done because most of the buildings have no insides. The plot is through in about 2 hours, the rest is just challenges (like kill 1000 demons with weapon xy).
There are some funny features like the Rambulance or Barnstorming locations (flying through tight spots) and a huge amout of collectables to find. But since this is just a big dlc and not SR5 it is not too bad, mostly a fan-thing you can play while you wait for the next part of Saints Row.
Sometimes the game stumbles over its own ideas, you hit start and it seems like after a few minutes everything and everyone bombs your picture. I activated three audio files at once accidently, one from Johnny, one from a weapon and one I collected without noticing.But this is not a bad thing, since the audio logs are stored in your menu.
I strongly recommend to play the original SR (or watch a lets play) and SR2 first since there are many cameos you will not understand otherwise.
So, if you're a fan of the series and were happy with that turn SR did starting with part 3, you liked the super powers and silly stuff and you have some money left, go buy it.
If you liked the original Saints Row and SR2 as a GTA styled game better and hated all the new stuff, don't bother and go get GTA5.

I was watching Linus tech tips video, about how new hardware runs original Crysis, so I bought a copy for myself to see how my today’s rig is able to handle this 2007 PC hardware killer and I was disappointed, but not because of my PC.
Game runs on CRYENGINE 2, which for the time could do a lot of amazing things and it shows in the game. Massive vegetation, huge draw distance, great texture detail, stunning shaders and so on. While I was playing this game, it never felt and looked like something from  2007, it felt like it was released about 3 years ago, and probably with some HD textures and improved lightning mods, the  title will look like it was released last year.  Levels are huge and there's a variety of them, you’ll be traveling through beaches, jungle, swamps, caves, alien space ships, frozen forests etc. and because maps are quite big the objectives can be completed in in some variety of ways.
Story takes you on a islands in Pacific ocean where a group of american archaeologists gets into trouble with North-Korea's armed forces. You are member of elite forces group which are dropped on the islands to find out what happen with the archaeologists. You are quipped with so called Nano-suit which have special abilities like boosting up your strength, speed or makes you invisible for several seconds. Also you'll have variety of weapons and vehicles at your disposal. Game starts slow, with you crawling trough the jungle and eventually stepping in to some armed military group, but gradually escalates in to full fledged military conflict involving heavy weapons and machinery. Some call this game spiritual successor to original Far Cry and in some way and form this game definitely is.
Game is fun as hell, story maybe is weak and nothing original, but I had a lot of fun playing this game. So where is my disappointment ?
Well, the game runs terribly on 64-bit systems, it constantly crashes, sometimes I had 2 hours session with no problems what so ever, but than there was sessions were game crushed like each two minutes. Frame rate is all over the place, sometimes you'll have stable 60 fps, and sometimes game drops to 2-3 fps when there is not much happening on the screen. And not to mention that you'll have to do some research and work to make the game work in the first place.
So to sum it up game is beautiful and fun when it runs well, and when it doesn’t it just frustrates you, so ignoring all the technical problems it would probably be something like 8.5, but for what it is now it’s nothing more than 6.5...
Thanks for reading!

Imagine, if you will, any other final fantasy game in the series. Now take out all the towns, world map, conversations, and mini games from them. What you have left is this game . Walking, battles, and cutscenes is all this game has, and it goes on for 50 hours. Maybe you're thinking "So what? as long as the story is good i can deal with that". Well, i hate to be the one to break the news to you, but the story isn't that good, infact it's kinda bad, the worst in the series, and so are the characters. It's not even so much the story that is the bad part, it's the writing and delivery/timing, it's downright awful. This game is a massive chore to play, with no pay off at all. The visuals, combat, and soundtrack are the only things this game has going for it, and those qualities don't make up for the other short comings. For a game to be 50 hours of nothing but walking, turned based combat, and cut scenes, it would need to have an incredible story and characters, but this doesn't have that. It just goes on and on and on and on. This game is nothing but a beautiful mess, a massive waste of time and undeserving of the Final Fantasy name. Oh, and when you hear people say that this game "opens up" towards the end, that is an absolute lie. All they are refering to is a cupple mini-map fields where there are monsters roaming that you can battle. Not open world at all.
And yes, I am aware their are a cupple towns you walk through in the game. Only 2 actually have people in them, and you can't converse with any of them, no shops, inns, nothing(one of those "towns" is just a beach with a building so i'm not even sure that counts.

Lets talk about what this game is and what this game is NOT.
This is a game for people who make games, or review games as a profession. This is NOT a game for people who play games as a hobby or for entertainment.
Let me explain why. The basic premise of the game is a satire of people who play games. For developers and reviewers, this is hilarious, and instructive. For people who play games, it is also hilarious. But also annoying. Because there is no "game" per se, in The Stanley Parable. There is just a neverending pseudo-philosophical analysis on games, game making, and game experiences. For 15 dollars.
And that really is what finally convinced me to not reccomend this game. Because I can't help by compare it to Pony Island, which is a similar concept to The Stanley Parable, and offered for 5 dollars. More to the point though, Pony Island is a GAME. Yes, simplistic, with runny, jumpy, puzzle solvey mechanics, but still, a game with gameplay, interspersed with the head turning and and philosophy. Stanley Parable is just head turning and philosophy. No gameplay beyond rudimentary observation adventure mechanics. Indeed, it actively insults the player for trying to find any meaningful game mechanics.
If that is your cup of tea, then by all means. Pay the 15 dollars. For everyone else, wait for it to be 75% off, or else give it a pass.

If you're looking for a more tongue-and-cheek BroForce with a higher difficulty curve, this is that exactly.
If you're looking for a funny, relaxing and cathartic game, this doesn't quite fit that niche like Broforce does.
And if you're looking for a pulsing moment-to-moment game that pushes you to the edge of your seat, go play Hotline Miami.
I think it's worth buying, but I ran into gameplay issues that struck me as being done better in Devolver's other games;
-The cover system: It's the same button as slide, which sometimes makes it awkward to take cover when an enemy is close.
-The enemies: They are pretty fast to react and move. That's part of the difficulty, which is fine, but it leads me to my next issue;
-The controls: My biggest issue. It's just awkward to play on a keyboard and you can't remap key-bindings to something comfortable. I had to play on a controller and remap to something I liked and it still felt clunky.
Reload is tough to keep track of with fast enemies that only advance when you reload.
Sliding feels ok, until it slows down, but still feels a little wonky to do.
I couldn't remap "shoot" to a trigger on my 360 pad, so I have to use the shoulder buttons.
-There's no way of knowing how much health an enemy has left, and some of them are real bullet sponges
-Your health audio for when you're two "bars" away from death and one bullet away from death is that same.
-Death: It just feels punishing. You usually don't actually know what ultimately killed you unless it's a one-on-one fight.
-Dialog: It's well written and funny, but it's TOO SLOW. It goes past comedic timing and enters exhausting when it's pushing two sentences every 25 seconds and there is a paragraph of stuff to move through. I usually hit the 75% mark and skipped the rest just to get back to the game, and skipped almost all the post-level stuff because of this.
All this said, I like the game. It's fun, it's colorful, it's a laugh and it's violent. It just feels like a mash up of other, more tight, Devolver games without the fine tuning to really slam it home for me.

Speaking as a Hitman fan, I consider this a mostly worthy entry into the series. It modernizes the gameplay big time with new and welcome features as well as vastly improved control. It's more fun to actually play in this respect, whether you're being stealthy or using the game's myriad weapons to take on enemies. It feels refined. Difficulty is very scalable, with five levels that adjust things like situational awareness (i.e limiting utilization of the "Instinct" hint system, which allows you to see through walls, highlights points of interest, and reveals AI paths), number of NPCs to move through and around, enemy capability, and checkpoints. You can make things very, very hard on yourself if you so desire. To play on "Purist", the hardest difficulty, is to know the game by heart.
Though Hitman is really a stealth game, as previously mentioned there are a lot of guns at your disposal. If you ever decide to play this as an action game, there's a measure of fun to be had just blowing everyone away. It's good for goofing off between serious playthroughs.
The gameplay does have some issues. One problem with the game is that the levels are small, with locales being broken up into sections. They would have done well to open things up a bit more. Also, the checkpoint system is awful. You find sparsely scattered checkpoints that you manually activate, and whenever you restart at a checkpoint, everything except target kills, ammo and 47's current disguise reset. It makes failure a dreadful thing indeed when you know you're going to be redoing things you shouldn't have to.
Story wise IO went with a more cinematic approach this time, putting more focus on narrative. The game has a number of very colorful and well acted characters that keep things weird and interesting while it lasts. It's very macabre in places, which I love. But be warned - it's quite daft. It has the presentation down, but it's not memorable as a story.
Visually the game is very impressive. IO's proprietary Glacier 2 engine allows for a stunning amount of detail (and NPCs) to be rendered on-screen, and the art direction is stellar. This is by far their best work since Contracts, which was in its own way visually brilliant.
I think that Hitman has taken a few steps forward and a couple of steps back. On one hand, the presentation is excellent, the control is vastly improved, and the new Instinct system is a great addition. On the other, levels are small and the checkpoint system makes life unnecessarily hard and monotonous. That said, I think it's a really good game that I could see myself playing through again.

This has got to be one of the most overlooked good games in recent history. I say this admitting full well that I was a part of that.
I bought this game during a Steam Christmas sale bonanza back in 2015, probably because it was super cheap and I thought "hey, might as well." I then proceeded to sit on this game for almost 2 years, relegating it to my "incomplete" list of games as newer stuff came out that caught my interest. Finally, a few days ago, I decided to install the game and give it a try, as I've been working more diligently to complete games that I've bought. I had heard that there was some decent humor in this game, and that interested me more than anything initially. Once I started playing it, though, I was hooked.
I had never played the original Shadow Warrior, so I had no idea of what to expect other than what was described and shown on the Steam page. I have since begun describing this game as "a first person Devil May Cry." You play a very smart-aleck character in first person view, using a sword and a selection of guns, many of which you come across later as you play the game, to kill demons in the Japanese traditional sense. Each level primarily consists of running from point A to point B, destroying barriers in your way. Like the original Devil May Cry, the battles are typically more "arena" based rather than a steady stream of guys like in many first person shooters. By this, I mean, you'll find yourself running down a hallway or through a room that has a bunch of loot in it, and after passing this area, you'll typically find yourself in a larger room or area that sees a number of demons spawn multiple times until you've defeated all the "waves" and then you can move on to the next area.
Since I'm mentioning it, I do have to note one of two negatives I have with this game: this combat formula got a little old towards the end of the game. I'd say you encounter nearly every demon you'll face in the game within the first third of the game, barring one or two, so seeing these guys respawn over and over in an arena setting started to wear on me. It would have been alleviated if there were different enemies constantly being introduced, but as it stands, you know exactly what you have to do the minute you see which enemy spawns, and although the game rewards creativity for eliminating demons, there's only so many different ways you can butcher these guys before it's routine, given how many times they show up. But my feelings on this are how they are primarily because I was more interested in advancing the story and/or viewing the next level design. Segue into that...
The story is pretty darn good. Nothing earth shattering, but far more than what you'd expect from a typical first person game. The dialogue is a lot of fun. The main character has a partner that he interacts with for most of the game, and I like their dynamic a lot. In fact, I actually found myself liking the partner the most. No spoilers, but the two of them play off each other almost like a buddy-cop film where neither character is the straight man. The thing that I absolutely loved was the level design - at least, the first third of the game. There are essentially three primary environments that you fight through. The first is easily the best - the design is set up to look like a midsized Japanese town complete with a bamboo forest outside the town and a large shinto shrine. Much of this level reminded me of a trip I took to Japan almost a decade ago. I had visited Kyoto, of which this first part of the game reminded me a lot of, and I absolutely loved the atmosphere. I believe there's a part when you are at the shrine and you can see the town in the background if you pause and appreciate the graphics. The scene takes place at night and it's just gorgeous. The second third of the game takes place in a shipyard in Osaka. I didn't really care for this part of the game - the design was far more like any generic FPS you might play. It wasn't terrible or anything, but I found myself wishing the setting resembled more Japanese city/town archetypes. The third portion of the game is set in a snowy mountain, and as you progress through it, it becomes more and more traditional Japanese and less and less industrial, which I was happy with.
Of course, all of that wouldn't really matter much if the gameplay was crap. Thankfully, it isn't. Using the sword is a blast, and I far preferred it to guns, actually - at least until things got absolutely chaotic, which they do later on. As you play through the game, you gain new abilities and powers, as well as the ability to place add-ons on your guns to help improve them. All of this just simply added to the positives of the game.
I can't recommend this game enough. And the best thing is, it has good sales that pop up often, so even if you're a little hesitant on the game because it may not be your exact cup of tea, you can pick it up for cheap and have little loss to show for it if you end up not liking it.
Towards the end of the game, I went ahead and bought Shadow Warrior 2; I look forward to playing this one soon. I read somewhere that SW2 quadrupled the sales of the first game for a certain time period, and I'm very glad to hear that. When I started playing it, I was a bit disappointed to be back in a Rapture not too different from the first game - just a bit more barnacles on the wall. It was burning and flooding at an alarming rate in the first game, so why is it still so alike 10 years later? After getting over that disappointment though, I started noticing that it improves on a lot from the first (great) game.   The FPS gameplay has improved. The level design is amazing, as is the music and sound effects. The black & white morality of the first game ("You are either Mother Theresa or a love child of Hitler and Satan") is replaced with something a bit more nuanced, and woven into the gameplay. The main villain is a bit weak ("Extreme collectivism is evil too!"), but there are many secondary characters who are arguably even better written than in the first game, and that is saying something.
Don't expect your mind blown, but to be amazed at great craftsmanship and to be highly entertained.

Sins of a Solar Empire has to be one of the most diversified Real Time Strategy Games that I have played within the last Decade of my Life. I have yet to complete very much research into the back story, and lore of each faction, but there is not much of a campaign to speak of either with the Game, so it's up to you to explore which faction you most identify with. There are Three primary Factions which are playable, while each Faction is divided into the primary Faction, and the Extremist Factions each providing their own unique bonuses and strategies. Did I mention there were Pirates in the game, and  they love to collect Bounty. You will have Tons of opportunities to explore the Game during Solo Play with a couple AI Enemies, I would highly encourage this to learn the Ropes of the Game before full immersion into a Multilayer Game. Have you ever felt like creating your own Galaxy, and then try to Conquer it in its entirety? You can do that with a decent Computer and Sins of a Solar Empire. Did I mention how great all the DLC Expansions compliment the Game, and allow for a much more diversified and unique Galaxy each time you begin a new Game? One time I thought it would be Awesome if I could Control an entire Fleet during a space battle after watching Star Wars for the first time in my life, after purchasing Sins of a Solar Empire, my Dreams became a Reality. Would you like your fellow Clan or Guild Members to hail you as the Galactic Emperor? This could be a Reality for you too with this Game, a little practice, and possibly a couple personal pointers from yours truly.. One aspect that I felt was missing from the Game was the ability to Control each Ship yourself, which I think would be fricken Awesome. Ultimately the Game will be as vast as your Imagination, and Free Time will allow; Many games can be finished within Two to Three hours, I also have some on-going Games which might never end. If I were to describe the Game to you from here on through the rest of this Review, I would make sure to include the Fact that you start out with a Home Planet, and through Military Skill, Intelligent Research, swift Expansion to surrounding Planets, dominating your Local Star, Cultural Assimilation, Diplomatic Relations, and Teamwork, you gradually Conquer the Solar System, Planet by Planet. You will eradicate all Competition, punishing Pirates, or placing Bounty on other Players, hiring said Pirates to do your Dirty Work. Did I mention that you can develop each Planet, and harvest the necessary Resources to Build up and Expand your Armada, and Empire? I heard that the Black Market can always provide a quick Economic Stimulus when you're in a Financial Bind, I've never uttered a more true to Life Statement. Don't forget to do your Research, because there are Multiple Tech Trees to Explore and unlock, which provide great Offensive, or Defensive Bonuses, as well as♥♥♥♥♥♥that helps your Empire expand. Your Fleet may consist of a vast array of unique Ships, each with their own Strengths, depending on your Research Levels, you can quickly Constrict your Opponents to close Proximity Conflicts. One other thing I thought to mention would be the great Modding Community, remember when I was so into Star Wars earlier? There's a Mod for that... Yea when I think of the ultimate Futuristic Space Real Time Strategy Game, Sins of A Solar Empire has become my number One, so go ahead and purchase this game next time you see it on sale, because it is a Great Game, which I feel I have gotten the value of what I had paid for it initially, Ten Fold after my First successful Galactic Conquest. Remember Space is Mankind's final Frontier; Look to the Stars for they are the Future.

Even without all the bugs and performance problems, what we have is a very bad game that is poorly designed. It will take you hours upon hours of maneuvering through convoluted gameplay mechanics and glitches just to find out how shallow the game really is.
It has taken them "7" years to shovel this garbage out the door. A space sim(?) in which joystick/HOTAS support are held together with scotch tape, no physics (like all X games, it feels like moving around in spectator mode from Counter-Strike 1.5), no freelook (much less TrackIR), no radar, no target filtering, etc. In short - it is a big mess.
Some might say it was a failed console game, and by Egosofts own admission they had it working on the Xbox 360 and would love nothing more than to have had X Rebirth as a console game. Instead, they vomited this out on to the PC. I suspect even Microsoft didn't want anything to do with it's poor quality and turned them down.
I wouldn't bother waiting for it to get fixed, either. X Rebirth feels like a "last hurrah" to cash out of the business before Star Citizen and Elite Dangerous carry the space sim genre for the next decade. And we will all be better off for it.
TRADE: Broken and cumbersome. Lacks information that should be easily accessible. Fly around convoluted space stations and pick up trade offers that only last an hour. Waterboard yourself as you wait 30 minutes for your transport ship to fly to the station and break while trying to complete an order.
FIGHT: Incredibly shallow. Fixed view to make you nauseous and you're unable to look around. Cockpit takes up 40% of the screen. No radar or target filtering of any kind. Not even going to go into the AI.
BUILD: Broken with an incredible lack of information letting you know wtf is going on or what you're doing wrong/how to do it in the first place. What can you build? AN EMPIRE!? Yeah, sure....some more stations to do more broken trading.
THINK: You got that right. You'll spend a lot of time trying to figure out how to do basic things only to find out that they are convoluted or don't exist in the first place. Scratch your head in wonder while asking yourself how this garbage could make it out to retail. Be in awe with the slapped together design decisions. Dabble into the world of conspiracy theories at X Rebirths suspicious release timing just ahead of Star Citizen and Elite Dangerous.

Rivals of Aether is a Smash Bros inspired fighting game. I say "inspired" because the only real similarity between RoA and SSB is the simple movement. I'll spare the detail and just get roight into it
Rivals of Aether's main drive is competitive, and boy howdy does it nail it well. The skill ceiling is so high that everytime I play I figure out a new combo or a new trick. When you go online, people are pulling off some god-level combos, however this is integral for learning and improving. Playing online is the main reccomended way of playing, because honestly, the CPU are easy, even on the highest setting. Plus, by playing online you learn to adapt, therefore you "git gud"
However, RoA isn't all competitive. There's a story mode, which is kinda like All-Star mode from Smash Bros. Then once you beat that, you unlock Abyss Mode, which is an endless challenge mode where you have to either break some targets, capture a point, or defeat an armored enemy. Normally playing any mode will get you coins, which you can spend to unlock new characters, stages, AND special perks for Abyss Mode, that basically buff your character.
I'm such a slave for customization, and boy howdy, RoA let's you create your own custom skins for your character. On top of that, there are a few DLC skins that are pretty cheap, as well as promotional skins that you can get for participating in tournaments, or special events. Now I know what you're thinking. "Can't I just recreate the DLC skins in the skin creator??"
no
you cant
The DLC and event skins have a special taunt and particle effects that can't be recreated in the skins creator, which makes these event skins seem more precious.
Seriously tho, why haven't you bought this game yet. It's cheap for all the content it gives you, plus new stages and characters are coming in the near future.

A S
Main Pro: Demanding but highly-engaging gameplay
Main Con: Lack of content (particularly single player)
(Opening Note: A lot of my hours on this game comes from listening to that delicious music in the background. Its good, by the way. Just wanted to point that out so we don't mistake my level of fighting dedication for something it isn't!)
Full disclosure: I am not a hardcore fighter-type at all; I went to one local Smash 4 tourney a little under a year ago and essentially went, "Yeah, no." I've had an often hopeless fascination of their complex systems and tactics, but a lack of the mechanical skill and patience required to learn them at a higher level. In short, bear in mind that I'm reviewing this more or less as a "casual," which I'd like to believe will benefit someone out there reading this.
So here I am, once again trying to somehow eke out the technical satisfaction of conquering a fighter despite the stupid amounts of stress they can cause me. Does Rivals of Aether somehow break the mold of my typical fighter experience? Not entirely: this is undoubtedly a high-octane, competitive multiplayer game first and foremost. However, the convention-breaking finesse and quality of this game is enough to make me genuinely beam when things clicks.
Because if anything, RoA is unconvential. This is essentially a Smash Bros. (Melee) clone, but it does several things differently. First, there are no shields! Instead, you must rely on dodging or what is called a "parry", a way of essentially reversing the enemy's offense back on them. This is important, because the concept of "safety" is very fleeting in RoA. Battles happen quickly and often brutally, and the inability to shield can make it hard to get a grasp on your surroundings without getting absolutely slaughtered in the process. This can make for an unforgiving learning curve at the beginning.
The characters in RoA are frequently as unorthodox as the base mechanics, though this leads to some hero-specific mechanics that are incredibly interesting. Specifically, the interactions between different mechanics and hero attacks make for some nifty setups. Zetterburn can light foes on fire, which grants a knockback bonus to his strong (smash) attacks. Etalus can freeze the ground to increase the distance of his dash attack. Even straightforward tweaks--like Wrastor's strong attacks working only in the air instead of on the ground--really shake things up. Its the kind of stuff that sounds really amazing to fool around with... but reconciling all the nuances of a character, especially against high-tier opponents, can feel very daunting.
In short, RoA makes for some very deliberate, demanding gameplay. Its tough. Its crazy. But when you nail it... its quite amazing. RoA is the kind of game that can definitely push you outside of your comfort zone, but in exchange you can have some truly cerebral moments. Yes, you'll probably get your rear handed to you in short order more than once, but piecing together the elements of success and failure can come just as quickly: the game, in a way, demands it of you. If you can harness that intensity and intellect even for a moment, you may be shocked to find that even as a "casual" you can have your moments. Glorious, glorious moments.
Just remember, this is a competitive fighter first. Story mode is pretty standard fare, if not a little short even for this genre. The solo replayability is tied up for the most part in Abyss Mode, yet another unconventional but nice take on the "multi-man" melee modes from Smash Bros. Nonetheless, I wouldn't plan to get much mileage out of the single player content; its essentially a small appetizer compared to the multiplayer's main course. Despite the game's clear priorities, some may be disappointed in the overall lack of content. With a starting roster of only eight characters (perhaps for the sake of balance,) some might struggle to find a rival they really gel with.
I don't think RoA is going to drastically change my contentious, limited relationship with the fighter genre. But its dedication to rich, deep gameplay makes it feel more casual-friendly than one might think. I don't see myself tearing up the ranked leaderboards any time soon, but I may get me some occasional "slam dunk" KO's from Etalus's grab attack. Watch yourself!

This is one of the most underrated JRPGs of all time almost entirely due to the obtuse combat system that injects some random variation amidst its tactics. But if you can look past that, The Last Remnant is one of Square Enix's best titles, incorporating the crafting and scavenging mechanics straight from Monster Hunter, a typical but engaging story with genuine character relationships that never try to oversell it to the audience, a protagonist whose motives are more quaint than "saving the world" and who is as genuinely likeable as he is out of place in a monarchist society, and the single greatest soundtrack ever composed next to Chaos Rings (that alone should be reason enough to buy it). The level up progression is visuably noticable in battle, with low level spells greatly increasing in "oomph" and flair with each upgrade, and the battle chatter really sells the vividity of each battle, especially during huge, multi-squad combat.
Highly recommended.

8 out of 10, and that's me being nitpicky.
Ok, so time for a review of Magic Duels Origins. My first impression of the game was that it looked great, very catchy to the eye, so I decided to give it a try. I am not a Magic the Gathering player, so the tutorial was really detailed and fun in my opinion. I got hooked... I played it for a while, grinded a little for coins, got some nice cards eventually, and made a decent white-green elf deck. Now, the card pool has increased significantly since the game launched, and more importantly, the dedicated people working on this game have solved some of the issues it had in the beggining.
First of all, grinding for coins is not as difficult as when every quest gave the players 40 gold at most and every versus battle only 20 coins back in the early stage of magic duels. That resulted in tedious coin grinding, and made it really hard to complete a collection. Now one can purchase a booster pack by doing a versus battle and completing a 120 quest. Bravo Magic Duels, with the potential to buy at least a booster everyday, you have suaded me into playing everyday. Also, those who have played this game since its inception know that some time ago, quest could only be completed by decks built in the Deck Wizard system. This isn't the case anymore, and now we can use any deck we designed through any method. All these issues were solved within few patches, so that goes to show that people at Wizard of the Coast and Stainless know exactly what is best for their game.
Now that I have properly buttered the creators of the game, it's time for some tought love. The game is an 8 out of 10 for me because of two issues:
1) The game crashes abruptly from time to time. This has happened since the start for me, and I am sure it is not my computer, as I have no problems with more demanding games. This is very uncommon, but I cannot ignore it because it has caused some frustrating situations where I am about to win and suddenly the "unknown error" screen appears. As I said, game is 100% playable, and this is common for games that get patches and updates constantly. I am sure someone is working on it right now.
2) Daily coin limit! If I am not mistanken, the current coin limit is 400 everyday. The limit only applies to versus and solo games, you can still get more money through quests, achievements, tutorials, or story mode. My main issue with it is that it is completely unnecessary at this point. I have only reached the daily coin limit three times, and the same thing happens whenever I do: I don't want to play anymore. I get that the coin limit was necessary when only the Origin's card were available, but with the release of Eldricht Moon, there are 5 card collections. If someone can get all the cards within a week from playing Versus battles, give that kid a medal.
So that's my opinion right now of magic duels. Give it a try, another hobby can't hurt right?

What can I say about Hollow Knight?
I've never played a Metroid title or an old-school Castlevania title, but I absolutely love 2D platformers with a challenge. As an older gamer who grew up playing the classics, as well as the handful of garbage along the way - this game gives me a great sense of nostalgia and an overall wonderful feeling of accomplishment.
Don't get me wrong, this game has its rough edges. Some parts are definitely NOT meant for the casual gamer, or for people with a short temper, but with that being said, most if not all of those harder areas are completely optional and don't effect the outcome in the end.
The boss fights are just good fun, save for a few that really felt cheap as hell and over-the-top (I'm looking at you Nightmare King Grimm). You have no lives, so there's really no excuse to give up when you're challenged with a tough boss fight. All it takes is practice with a little patience, as well as experimenting with your evergrowing charm collection (items that add special effects/abilities to your character).
The combat is extremely basic. Easy to learn, hard to master. Once you gain all of your abilities you can do some pretty crazy combinations with your character. Some people are so good they don't even get hit by the toughest bosses. The controls are some of the best I've ever played with.
The soundtrack for this game is beautiful. The visuals are obviously there. The only thing this game really suffers from is some major difficulty spikes mid-to-late game (especially if you're not rightfully equipped yet), but all that means is that you should retrace your steps and look for anything you missed. There's a lot of backtracking involved due to areas being locked behind abilities earned later in the game, so you're always encouraged to go back at one point.
There are plenty of secrets to find, and lots of lore to invest in. The NPCs are all unique and interesting in their own ways, and some are downright cryptic. There are weapon and health upgrades to strive for, and valuable items to scavenge for and sell. Also, the game has multiple endings, so there's replayability too.
I'm rambling. All in all, a fantastic game. Clearly there was a lot of love and hard work put into it, and they're still working out the kinks here and there. I didn't witness any bugs throughout my 35 hour playthrough, though.
In short - GET. THIS. GAME.

Square did right by attempting to remove the garbage filler from JRPGs, such as persistent health, MP, having to actually choose every battle command, having to control everyone, etc. It's really nice to see a company trying to fix outdated ideas.
Unfortunately they took out so much that there isn't really a game left. It's just hallways, interspersed with rote battles and mind-numbing cut scenes. There's no exploration either, but sometimes the hallway you're in branches and allows you to fight some more enemies in exchange for a treasure chest. The characters are dull tropes and the dialogue is worse than a 4Kids dub. Even the leveling up system feels like it was pared down: it's like FFX's Sphere Grid, but lacking any kind of significant branching. I'm about 14 hours in, and the game is still feeding me a steady drip of new battle mechanics, each more tedious than the last; unfortunately, new mechanics don't make the game more fun or interesting, because battles are still essentially just blocks of time where you mash A for a while. I mean, sometimes the game throws you a single stronger enemy and you need to switch between preset battle styles, but in practice it feels more tedious than exciting or interesting. Battles aren't the only thing that's repetitive: the dialogue gets repeated and rephrased a lot too, so I frequently found myself watching two dimensional characters think out loud at each other over and over.
Of the ~14 hours I've played, I think about half of it has been just watching cut scenes. Some of the sequences are so long there are (sometimes multiple) save points in the middle. Some of the sequences are so long that my Steam Link shuts off because it hasn't received any inputs in a long time.
I want to like this game, and I feel like if I kept at it, by the time I got to the end the battles could be legitimately interesting. But I also feel like it'll still be dripping me new ideas right up to the final boss. I've kind of been playing this in the hopes that at some point, they say, "OK, tutorial over!" but, again, I'm at 14 hours and so far the game has only treated me like a moron and I'm just kind of tired of doing the same♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over to advance characters that I can't force myself to pay attention to.

For what is worth it, I've played this game for almost 2 years back in 2009/2010, but I'm writing this review based on actual gameplay of the game as it is now. TL/DR version at the end.
Going straight to the point, the game's monetization changed for the better over the past few years.
You can now buy character slots with in-game currency and it's actually pretty cheap for the first 30 slots. Some quests' pay walls have been removed, and the new Crescemento items will perform much better than low llvl elite item, for literaly no cost at all, which means you can play the game without giving a damn about the market until lvl 100.
One thing you should know, though, is that the grind is real. It's been there since 2009 and it's not going anywhere anytime soon. There is an AFK tool that makes power leveling those lower level newly-recruited characters a breeze, but still, if not for XP, you'll be grinding for items or cash. Don't get me wrong, grinding in this game is actually fun, but there really is a lot of it.
As for the end game pay wall, while it took me about 3 days to get four character to lvl 103 and collect most of the chraracter cards available (based on my level, an inexperienced player can easily have fun for over 200 hours before even considering buying something from the cash shop. Hell, there's really nothing you need from the cash shop until level 110, and the game gives you a lot of bonus cash items over as your family level increases (as of now I have about 90 days of 50% bonus xp/drop).
Pros:
- Beautiful art style and soundtrack
- Great variety of fighting styles and characters
- Grinding is actually fun
- Many of the cash shop items can be bought from in-game shops, at fixed prices, for in game currency (Feso)
- Lots of content to be played before any form of pay wall.
Cons:
- No room for casual players on PvP these days
- At a certain point, you either have to grind even harder or pay up to get what you need.
- Not a single newbie-friendly guild as far as I can tell
TL/DR: There's a lot of fun to be had before the dreaded pay wall, so you might as well give it a try for a couple hundred hours. Also, any review based on experiences from 4~5 years ago is utterly outdaded and does not reflect the current state of the game - you'd do well to disregard those.

AC:BF is my favorite AC game so far. I loved the pirate aspect of the game. It was such a welcome departure from the Ezio trilogy (the only other AC games I've played), it really breathed fresh air into the series. I felt such a sense of adventure on the open seas with me hearties, singing shanties as I ride into combat. It was a very fun experience. I believe this game not only stands out as an amazing AC game, but also as a pirate game. I really can't think of too many games that do the pirate life justice, but this one comes really close. Sure you can say that its pretty much an AC coat of paint ontop of the 1700s, but what it does, it does really well.
The story I found overall well done. There were some times when it lagged and slowed down, but between the Astergo parts and the pirate parts, I find it really interesting. Also, as most AC games do, much of the history was (loosely) faithful. Seeing real pirates like Ed Thatch (Blackbard) and Mary Read was pretty cool. Its also the small touches, like with Blackbeard ignites fuses in his hat to scare people, that make AC:BF really well researched and a joy to experience. I will say the ending fight was a bit of a letdown (though the ending itself was good), and some of the puzzles (Absergo hacking) was REALLY frustrating.
The controls deserve their own section. In previous AC games I found myself yelling at the screen due to my character pretty much ignoring what I'm telling them to do, all while getting destroyed by 10 guards. This has gradually improved since Revelations, and it is also true here. There were very few times when I "lost control" of Kenway, so it was a delight to move. The combat, less so. I found it really hit or miss. There were times when I could obliterate 20 guards without taking a hit, and there were other times when I had 1 enemy that would just refuse to die, while Kenway just didnt feel like countering anything.
There are some negatives though. I felt that when I invaded pirate ships, combat could become an annoying cluster. Oftentime sthe enemy NPCs would attack me from much further away then they should have, off of my camera, leaving me almost no time to react. Also there was 3 times in the final 1/4th of the game where I had to Alt + F4 due to gamebreaking bugs. Thankfully, reloading the game fixed it, but if it didn't, it would literally be game over.
Overall, this is my favorite AC game so far, and would recommend it to anyone.
