I've spent about 3 hours in the game so far, killed five bosses, and while I know that I've barely scratched the surface of the game, so far I haven't enjoyed anything but game's art style. There are several severe flaws that make me write the negative review:
- There's no sense of story. You have zero idea who you are, what you are doing and why. There are some games that reveal plot to you by small portions and clues, like Souls series, or Salt and Sanctuary. But this game's begining is shining example of how NOT to do it.
- There's no sense of direction or goal. Levels are large and connected, like metroidvania, but most of the passways are closed, and constantly running into a deadends that you will only be able to access later in the game is frustrating as hell, since game gives you zero indication of where do you actually need to go.
- The game is slow. This is a matter of preference, perhaps some people would count this as a plus, but for me movement looks like any other platforming game in slow motion.
- Combat is boring. Protagonist can strike at one of four directions, has a projectile, can dash and can jump. No combos, no special moves. Each battle feels like you're hitting a boxing bag or a training dummy. Probably it has something to do with the fact that I've played Dead Cells prior to Hollow Knight. It's like drinking water after Guinness - seems very bland.
- Level design is boring. It looks interesting, I give it that, but on each screen, there's just very little to do, too few objects of interest. A couple of enemies, elementary platforming, and several exists to different screens.
Any of these flaws are tolerable on their own, but together they form a very bland and boring experience.
Once again, I know that this review is only for the very beginning, and there is a good chance that it gets better later on, but this doesn't changes the fact that a player should experience several hours of boredom to get to the good part. This isn't what I would call a good game.

This War of Mine is a survival-styled game set in a fictional European nation caught up in a civil war. The player takes control of either one (arguably the hardest start) to four civilians with varying degrees of usefulness at the start of the game and must manage to balance out physical health, mental health, exhaustion, hunger, and scavenging until the ceasefire ends the war.
The game is entirely mouse driven with mostly self-explanatory icons (such as an eyeball to peek through something or an upward arrow to upgrade something) appearing above or below objects/people. The game is split up between the day cycle and night cycle period. During the day cycle, the player accommodates their ramshackle shelter with beds, a heater, a stove, and other useful furniture and appliances to better live through the war. Occasionally, there will be a event at the front door of the shelter ranging from a new survivor trying to join your shelter to a trader trying to sell his wares. You can, at any point, end the day cycle early and skip to the night cycle. During the night cycle, the player decides who sleeps, who guards and keep watch over their shelter, and who scavenges at night for materials and equipment. During the scavenge portion (if the player decides to), the player sends one survivor to another part of the city and decides how to handle meeting up with other scavengers, looters, bandits, or military depending on the stage. Note that not all encounters can be resolved peacefully. It is also during this phase of the game that combat can occur, which is a bit hit or miss for my liking. Visual cues in the form of a ping indicate how loud your actions are (using a crowbar to open up a locker is very loud versus using a lockpick) and the presence of movement nearby your survivor. You can perform a stealth kill via from a hiding spot on the stage, perform a backstab to deal most (if not all pending on survivor and their melee item) of the target's health, a regular melee attack, take cover from gunfire, or discharge a firearm with a high or low degree of accuracy. Combat is very intense because your survivor cannot survive multiple blows or shots and your fight or flee instincts must be on point pending on your current situation. At times, it feels like your survivor did not interpret your command as you would have liked; though this can be attributed to game design since your survivor is not a trained combatant. My sole gripe in the game, to be honest. Unlike the day cycle, your survivor must physically leave the stage before time expires or the stage ends prematurely, with your survivor arriving late to the shelter (or worse) before it reverts back to the day cycle. The interface, though simplistic, allows for a wide range of options with it.
The game's narrative is in the game's title. This War of Mine (in my eyes) intentionally refers to your playthrough of the game, since this war is yours. Your starting survivor(s), how you react to events placed throughout the game, whether people die or not; all of it is nicely encapsulated in an epilogue at the end whether you survived through the war or not. I must say,
. Rejecting common gamer knowledge of trying to keep everyone alive
, the game's narrative really shines through when you persevere in the face of a tragic death. In an unique sense of ludonarrative resonance (look at me), the ability to keep striving to live despite the death of a comrade is one of the highest peaks This War of Mine achieves to tie narrative and gameplay. In my first playthrough, everyone but one in my group died and the last one committed suicide since everyone he cared about died before him. I felt more attached to that playthrough than to the next playthrough where I had everyone live from start to end. Perhaps it was because of the unknown that I was attracted to the first playthrough since subsequent ones saw patterns emerging, but the game mixes it up by changing the starting conditions. The subject matter is also a unique selling point of the game, forcing first-time players to think about how they would (re)act if forced into a wartime situation as a civilian because there is no tutorial. The narrative is easily the game's strongest point and would have diminished had the game incorporated a game mode to see how long you can survive a la endless mode.
The first thing that popped out to me was the game's visuals, utilizing a pencilled sketch filled in with a dark color palette. Reminds me of "Take on Me" to be honest. It helps to realize a grim urban setting drenching in bleakness. Character models are decent, though some might not accurately reflect the real-life portraits of the survivors and select NPCs. Animations are wide, with different variations pending on the physical health of the character doing the action. The audio side of the game is also bleak as well, though you can listen to uplifting music via gameplay (another example of ludonarrative resonance). There are no voice actors, so dialogue is delivered through text as well as animations. Sound effects are for the most part recognizable and crisp, so no complaints there as well. Overall, the game sets a good ambience throughout the game but lacks a defining or memorable track to really recommend the audio side.
In conclusion, This War of Mine is a compelling game. Subsequent playthroughs might reveal your gamer logic getting through as you go through the game as optimally as possible, but the first playthrough will always be yours and not getting everything right is okay. The game even links to a real charity, War Child. This is easily the developer's best game to date and as such, deserves a playthrough. Give it a go and then reflect upon your actions, debating with yourself whether what you did was right or the means justified the ends. You might learn something about yourself.

As a person who had known about this game for years and was curious about what it was like, I found The Stanley Parable to be a enjoyable and unique game. The main characteristic of the game is you are able to, at multiple opportunities, be able to either follow the narrator's instructions or defy them and go your own way. With these choices you are able to access many different endings -- I want to say the number is around 17-19, but I can't put my finger on it -- while enjoying the witty dialogue of the narrator. There are also plenty of easter eggs (including extra dialogue as well as other, more physical (in the digital sense) easter eggs) for those of you who are into that sort of thing or for if you have exhausted every ending in the game and are looking for something new in it.
Most of the endings don't take long to get to (the main exception being an ending that takes literally 4 hours), and such you can end up running through most of the endings pretty quickly. Some of the achievements (if you're an achivement hunting kind of gamer) can be REALLY difficult to get, but there should be guides on how to get the more difficult ones in a short amount of time. And for a game that can run out of endings in a short amount of time, it's a bit pricey. Rivals or Aether, or RoA, is an indie platform fighter, meaning it has the samwe basic mechanics as Super Smash Bros. It takes mechanics from melee and more recent smash games, along with making up a lot of its own and put it together under the guise of a pixel retro art style.
The game is specifically designed for competitive play and in my opinion that it the way it is most enjoyable. Having friends to play with, especially local ones is where the game shines. It has a small single player story mode and the new abyss mode which are fun by themselves and definitely add more depth and value to the $15 game, but in the end are just distractions from the main event.
If you're not familiar with competitive smash the next few things I'll be saying probably make no sense but what can you do. RoA takes the combo and movement heavy style of melee with features such as
-dash dancing
-wave dashing
-strong edgeguard focus
-lots of hitstun
however it also adds the good 'comfort' features of the newer games like
-buffering
-not freefalling out of an airdodge
-more forgiving/intuitive controls.
and it gets rid of shields (making offensive play more rewarding) and the ledge, so no edgehogs or planking.
Believe me when I say it all comes together and isn't just a huge mess of different games. it works and makes for some hugely satisfying combos and edgeguards, without it ever feeling to unfair or unbeatable.
You'll notice that at the moment RoA only has 8 playable characters which seems like a very small number, and in terms of modern fighters it definitely is! however this isn't as big of a drawback as you may imagine. if you compare it to smash 4 with over 50 characters, every RoA character feels completely unique and I play and enjoy all of them. they all have unique tech and mechanics for them which you would need to learn in order to master the character. Also the small number of characters means balance is a lot easier to the devs, and every character is kept viable and strong enough to compete.
One important thing to note is that I highly reccomend you make sure you have some kind of game pad or controller before you buy this game. While keyboard controls exist it really doesn't allow the freedom and enjoyment for me and almost all other players. You can use a gamecube controller if you have a usb adaptor.
Overall I highly reccomend this game if you have a friend or two to play with and you want ti get into the competitive scene. as a standalone single player game I can't see you getting a huge amount of value, unless you have good internet to play with people either through steam or through its matchmaking system.

I had heard alot of bad press about this game, about the story line and graphics, but still decided to buy it. I have a few things to say.

After putting nearly 30 hours into Magic Duels, I feel that I can safely conclude that it represents a tremendous step backward from DOTP 2015.
Had the game just featured Magic Origins as the card pool, it would have been decent (if unremarkable). They instead removed most efficient spells at common or uncommon, replacing them with complete duds. I'd like to slap the person who thought Siege Mastodon would be more interesting to include than War Oracle. Ugh.
Had the game given, say, a single card for each victory, then grinding for cards would have been tolerable. Even playing only ranked matches (ignoring quests, which require you to use the incompetant deck wizard to vomit up something for you to try and use) will give you a pack of six cards for every 7.5 victories. Victories. With a 25% loss rate (still decent), that's ten games of Magic for every six cards, which may or may not be of use. Playing against the AI will take ten VICTORIES for a pack of six cards. Again, this grinding might be tollerable if there were anything worth pulling in these packs. There generally isn't.
Had the game even worked as WotC intended, it might have been barely passable. Instead, it's as if Stainless is trying to emulate the stability of MODO servers. Not a good plan.
They even stripped the ability to chat with online opponents, making the distinction between playing against a person or a bot almost meaningless.
It saddens me that, while many of the mechanical aspects of the game itself are decent, and it is still FTP Magic, I can't recommend Magic Duels to anyone other than complete novices (who will find this a decent, if completely patronizing, introduction to the game) or people with far too much free time on their hands. The only reason I've kept with this is that I fall into the latter camp currently.
TL;DR: While this certainly is one of the worst DOTP games in recent memory (even falling short of the 2015 installment due to a completely bland card pool), Magic Duels is still Magic. Magic at its worst is still a decent game, despite Stainless's valiant effort to prove to us otherwise. Take that for what it's worth.

If it's caught your eye, but you're on the fence about The Last Remnant, then you already love JRPGs; as such, I'll make your decision easy for you: Go hit Add to Cart, and kiss several hours goodbye.
As you could probably tell from the videos as well as other reviews, the core of The Last Remnant is a fairly traditional JRPG, though it has a pretty unconventional take on battle and party mechanics. In reality, your success in battle will *largely* depend on what strategies you embrace, and those decisions start well before the battle screen ever initiates. Your Party is made up of all the characters you've picked up or hired, which you then organize into battle groups called Unions. During a fight, each Union is given a set of pseudo-random commands, and you select one of those options for the Union to perform (see the third-from-last screenshot on the store page).
While at first, this system feels like a complete roll of the dice, as you get a few battles under your belt and start developing your characters, there is actually quite a bit you can do to help create conditions that give you favorable battle commands. Moreso, there are actually a number of different schemes you can play with for Union organization. For sake of example, I've had equal success with having one healer in each of my Unions, as well as having a dedicated Union that serves as an all-around party heal/buff squad, backed up with a couple long-range attackers. In fact, range also plays a pretty important role in combat; units can be intercepted en-route to their intended target, granting a damage bonus to the intervening enemy squad.
Graphics are suprisingly top-notch for a game released back in '09. The spell and particle effects have aged well, and in a *shocking* twist, seem to have been ported favorably from the console version. The controls, however, didn't have as much attention paid to them. Check out warutaru's review for some crucially helpful steps in making the controls more PC-friendly!
All things considered, I have had an absolute blast playing TLR, especially for the mere ten bucks I dropped on it. I can honestly say it's one of the most pleasantly surprising games I've bought in a long, long time!

I played this game for 5 years from 2007 to 2012 (I took about 18 months worth of breaks), and I would be lying if I said I didnt enjoy it. However, do I recommend this game? No for the long run. Feel free to check it out, because it is interesting for the earlygame. Just like how most pay2win MMOs work, this is no exception. The end game is one long grind that either costs a fortune in real cash (I was young and naive and spent 800 dollars on it over 5 years), or hundreds upon hundreds of hours of grinding, requiring a clan and high level gear to do many of the endgame content. I'm not quite sure how the community is now, but when I left 4 years ago, it was a wretched hive of scum and villainy. The closer you approach endgame content, the more you encounter drama between many elitist and veteran players and clans. Often time the drama would get out of hand and affect their personal lives such as players holding grudges over each other and sometimes even hurting themselves mentally and physically.
Gameplay wise it was actually fun and unique at the time. You would control 3 different characters at the same time in RTS style click based movement, switching between characters to use their individual skills. You dont really create original characters. Instead, you as the player name your family and then recruit various unique characters into it. Characters have what are called "stances" that when switched to, depending on equipped weapon, give you a different set of skills. One thing that I didnt like is that when using skills on other player's characters it would stop the character in its tracks and play a sort of animation, and they cant move or be attacked by other players until the animation is over.
The music really made the game. It was simply amazing. Many songs range from classical victorian themed music to highspeed electronic techno rave music. The game sports a music player that you can select tracks depending on the area you are in. If youre reading this review I recommend you at least check out the music on youtube. I can't listen to the music anymore, because when I do I suddenly get PTSD flashbacks of some horrid times involving horrible money sink RNG systems in game.

So I'd gotten wind of this game by multiple peers who all claimed it to be the pinnacle of PC RPG's and sadly I have to find myself agreeing with them. Why I say 'sadly' it's due to the fact that The Last Remnant has left a void in me that not even it could fill; only create.
There's really nothing to be said of great deal about the story of TLR. For the most part the entire storyline was rather predictible with some characters showing insight that could've been called character if they'd decided to act more upon it, sadly only a few characters recieve any amount of characterization, but again the entire story is generic to begin with, so it doesn't surprise me in the least.
This leads me to the gameplay which I'm quite sad to say was extremely disappointing. While on the surface, any new player might look at the gameplay and see an extemely complex and quizzling battle system, the verteran would easily deny such. The combat consists of 'squads' in which you assign a formation to the squad and create who is in the squad. Sadly everyone but the main character is entirely uncustomizable and is only upgraded through fulfilling their needs when they ask (which again is out of the players hands). Battles that seemed to have a sort of strategy with positioning will not let the player decide where the squad stands or allow the squad to run backwards from the enemy. Almost every action in the battles is entirely randomly generated and while you can check what actions will take place with each attack, you cannot choose every action for your attack. For example, say you want the main character to use 'Blue Bird', you would have to check each option to see if he even has the CHANCE to use it. Oftentimes my characters obtain a completely game-breaking move but decide to use their weaker ones for no reason in particular. While I understand for the main character Rush, you can disable arts for him, to force him into using the OP skills it's simply not possible for the other NPCs. Oh also QTE's are the entire combat. Everytime you tell a squad to attack it has a chance of doing a critical offense/defense in which you have to press a single button/trigger to initiate a stronger attack/counterattack/dodge.
I had brought up earlier how you couldn't customize your characters for squads and I'd like to reiterate upon that a little bit more. You cannot give them armor/equipment. You cannot choose their name/appearance. You cannot pick anything about them other than whatever preset the game has given you. While you can choose nameless soldiers, it would be silly to choose those over any of the commanders who are able to learn unique abilities and upgrade their weapons to a higher degree.
Lastly many complain of the difficulty that is this game. I can say I breezed through every fight without much struggle. The game is extremely level-dependent and can scale enemies with the characters though not to a noticible degree. I will warn new players of grinding unless they find themselves in a quest to which they cannot complete, I've heard horror stories of those who grinded prior to getting party members and made the game neigh impossible. I will say that grinding/battling is one of the things the game has improved on. Grinding can be sped through, and gaining 10+ levels in 30 minutes is an easy task. Battles are also pretty fun since you can go all out in every battle since the end of every battle results in a completely healed party.
P.S. Looking for quests suck and some quests can be skipped. I used a guide (to find questgivers, not spoil the quest) because I will not, WILL NOT, run around in stupid circles looking for a quest in every single city's five sections. Especially since as I've said certain quests are entirely skippable and certain quests will only unlock after doing certain storyline requirements. This means you can check all fourty areas for quests, do a single storymode quest, and then have to check all fourty areas again just in case. I just don't have that kind of commitment in me, and I don't think anyone else should put up with such shenanigans. All quests should have been found in the guilds at every city, there was no reason to do otherwise other than to♥♥♥♥♥♥people off.
Overall I do recommend anyone looking for an RPG on the PC to check TLR out, sadly don't look forward for this game to fill your lust for customizable team building or strategy.

Defy Gravity was a game I was pleasantly suprised by. I picked it up for about $0.20 on a sale, and overall, it's a good game.  The game revolves around the use of a gun that shoots gravity wells, the blue gravity well, which attracts things, and the orange anti-gravity well, which repels things. This is a quite fun concept, and is used quite well. Now, if a gun that shoots one of each orange and blue glowy vaguely round objects to progress through a series of puzzles in some sort of challenge course sounds familiar to you at all, that's probably because it sounds a lot like Portal. However, it is actually quite different from Portal. No puzzle has one specific solution, and feels more of a skill-based platformer than a puzzle game. The puzzles are fairly loosely designed, so you can solve them in your own particular style. The game also looks nice, and the music is quite amazing. And after you beat the game, it starts Hardmode, which is implemented in a quite interesting way. Instead of just giving you trickier puzzles or a limited number of wells, it gives you the same puzzles, slightly modified, all enemies are affected by gravity, and you can only use regular gravity wells. This really caught me off guard, because for most of the game, I was using tha Anti-Wells in a sort of rocket jump way to clear the levels. I had to change up my playstyle, and it was kind of cool. However, my biggest problem with Defy Gravity is the bugs. These weren't just small things, they happened every single time I played. When I start the game, I always need to close out of it in task manager and start it again before the graphics will work, and on some levels you need to shoot a gravity well off before the graphics will start, which can get very irritating, especially if there's an enemy nearby. But despite these problems, I enjoyed it. It's creative and fun. If you can pick it up for a few bucks, I say get it. And thank me for not using a Wicked joke throughout this whole review.

This War of Mine is a fantastic war game, but it is also much more than that. It is a war game like no other, one set in the desperate struggles of civilian survivors who only want to survive. Yeah I play my Battlefields, my Insurgencys, and my CODs often but as fun as those games are, they are simply  travesties of what real war is. 360 no scoping and headshotting generic bad guys isn't what war is about. War is about the civilians and the communities that are ripped apart by violence. No matter the root cause of any war in history, most of the civilians certainly want to just be left alone, having no allegiances or opinions other than the safety of their family and friends. Warlord's revolutions and corrupt government's ambitions have little meaning when your home is being threatened by marauding forces. That's what this game is really. I beat it in my third play through by just keeping my head down, and only venturing out of my home when absolutely necessary.
This War of Mine has many elements borrowed from other games, such as rogue-likes random nature and basic, but very functional crafting mechanics similar to Don't Starve. The game is split into two main sections, a "daytime" section that plays out almost like a grim Sims. The player has to decide who gets to eat, who gets to sleep, and who needs to make improvements around the house. However the materials required to feed your survivors and improve your house are obtained only by venturing out into various shell shocked neighborhoods to find supplies. This is where the game really shines, as the semi-random nature of the game always leads to unknown encounters and events. Hear some people hiding out in a school talking? They may be refugees like yourself, or they may be bandits. Stealth is encouraged as your characters can't survive any amount of extended combat. Honestly the weakest part of this game is the combat, as it just boils down to clicking repeatedly on the enemy. It is definitely difficult enough though to prompt you to avoid confrontations whenever necessary.
In addition to this, all of your randomly chosen survivor's moods will improve or deteriorate based on what has happened recently. Had to kill someone for their stuff? Don't be surprised if one of your characters sulks around all day in a bout of crippling depression. Managed to pawn up some medicine for a sick mother? Moods will be improved. All of these systems leads to an amazing experience where decisions truly matter. The lack of food or medical supplies will also lead to difficult choices as well, having to decide who gets to eat or get treated for injuries or diseases. That severely sick man will probably die anyway, even if given some medication, but this slightly sick girl may fare better, who do you give the medication to? Most likely, they're both going to die anyway and you'll fail horribly the first few times you play, as everything falls apart.
This War of Mine isn't necessarily a fun game to play, but it is definitely work checking out for survival fans, or people who like bleak environments or stories. The backdrop of the horrors of war is just the dark, rotten cherry on top.

It's weird when I don't like fantasy RPG's, because for the most part I really WANT to love them. And LOTR: WITN wants me to want to love it, but wanting only gets us so far now doesn't it?
To start, I was immediately disappointed by the lack of local co-op. I had assumed that this version, despite being a port, kept the split screen co-op of the console version. I was, in fact, very wrong about this. So when I bought this and had a friend over that same day to play it together, instead I had to sit there awkwardly and submit to either playing solo while my friend sat around like a git or play LEGO Hobbit because it at least kept the basis of the game intact.
And then there's the combat. As far as hacky slashy button mashy games go, it's not the worst around (lookin at you, Two Worlds). It's not good enough to be called good though. Most of the moves are quite slow and don't really feel like they connect all that well. It feels more like you're having a dramatic pool noodle fight with a bunch of people who aren't convinced you really hit them until you've bopped them on the head fifty more times, and even then the point is barely starting to sink in. I've heard of bullet sponges but most of the enemies here are steel sponges. I have the sneaking suspicion this is one of those games that only gets easier as you go, but after a few long and rather boring quests that I've had to solo I realized I had stopped giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥
But the visuals. Dear Gimli the visuals. This felt much more like a Fallout game than a game set in a magical fantasy universe. Many of the characters you interact with stare at you crosseyed like they're trying their damndest to figure out whether the awkward jagged lines on your face are poor polygons or ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shadows. There are a couple hobbits naffing about in the various towns but at first glance I was a bit concerned that goblins were attacking. And the elves, supposedly the most fair race, look like they've been to Sylvester Stalone's house and got roped into re-enacting the fight scenes from "Rocky". It's all just a bit eerie to look at.
In short, there are lots of collectibles, hidden goodies, etc. and I'm sure online multiplayer could be fun but sluggish combat and poor visuals lead to an ultimately dull experience. Time to go play some Dark Eye: Demonicon.

Ironclad Games's first released title, and a decent RTS which I consider to be at the halfway point between traditional RTS and 4X. It might even be safe to call it a real-time 4X.
As gameplay mechanics go, SOASE is sound, if a bit simplistic. Rock-paper-scissors unit relationships abound, and unit spam is unfortunately a viable strategy in some situations. Each of the three factions is specialized to excel in certain capacities, resulting in widely varying overall strategies and battle tactics. SOASE features hero units in the form of capital ships, which again specialize in certain roles and progress in a MOBA-like fashion, gaining experience through combat, leveling up, and gaining or upgrading abilities (culminating in a powerful "ultimate" ability at level 6). Most battles typically hinge on the survival or destruction of one's capital ships, as they become more and more important targets through leveling.
Technically speaking, combat isn't the ONLY way to win a SOASE match. Like your typical 4X game (say, Civ V), victory conditions can be set which allow for several different paths to win through, for example, cultural influence or technological progress. However, again like your typical 4X game, most matches are won by pure conquest anyway. I don't think I've ever turned on those extra victory conditions since I started playing; conquest is good enough for me.
The Rebellion expansion adds factions-within-factions, with each race dividing in half to offer more specialization, as well as faction-specific Titan-class supercapitals, massive investments in time and resources which serve as the nucleus of an effective late-game fleet.
And that's... really about all I can say. I find it quite fun, both alone and with friends, but if I'm honest, there just isn't enough there to be worth the dollar amount Ironclad is asking for. I understand they're still a fledgling studio that needs the sales to improve and progress as developers, but frankly I believe they're only hurting their prospects by charging $40 when there isn't $40 worth of game. It is, however, a good value for $20 which is the price at which I bought it on sale, and of course any sale price lower than that is even better. The game's capacity for randomization can ensure no two matches are the same, so the replay value on Sins is quite high, but replay value based on randomization is not, in my eyes, a good enough substitute for actual content to justify a price tag approaching that of a AAA title.
Final verdict: definitely worth playing, AND worth buying, if on sale. Don't pay full price for this.

Combining existentialism and humour, confusion and wit, surrealism and stark confrontations with an isolated reality, The Stanley Parable serves as one of the most self-aware video games in recent memory. It is definitely a contender for one of the most intertextual video games ever made in its self-referentiality and in the developers' awareness of all the standard tropes that become subverted or distorted. The Stanley Parable is basically played one of two ways: straight through following the proper story or deviating from the normal path, and there are very specific points where you are given a clear choice between the two. However, once you branch from the correct path, you'll find that even if you try to go back to it, it becomes impossible. This game touches briefly on some notions such as narrative and individual autonomy, but unfortunately never does anything more than make you contemplate them briefly. The way it comes together seems to differ each time as it has a number of different endings, and beginning again will offer you yet more choices. However, as self-aware a game though it is, it is rather short as its intertextual premise simply can't sustain itself for very long. The player reaches an ending of one form or another, and then restarts to explore another path, seemingly arbitrarily.
On to the technical aspects. The voice acting for this game is superb, and although there's a lot to listen to, it never comes across as boring. The developers could not have cast better voice actors for this game, and it's clear that in the hands of lesser talents, this game would be nothing.  They
this game. Visually, it's the Source engine, so it predictably looks good, but nothing fantastic. The overall polish is very good and it ends up finding a nice middleground that looks modern but not too sleek. I didn't have any problems running it. There really aren't too many complaints on the technical side of things.
Now, I do have some criticisms for the game. Although it is very good and the concept, design, and voice work are top-notch, there are still a couple of things that I would say are problems. For instance, I don't think there's more than two hours worth of content here. You can beat the main story in less than five minutes (in fact, for one of the achievements, you're encouraged to), and there's only so long you can run around. On top of that, this is still a Source mod, and although it has a large file size, it reuses a lot of assets from other Source games. Lastly, for the few third person scenes that there are, they look quite bad. There's nothing that just screams lazy like a static image with a slow camera pan out. A lot of the reviews I've read highly praise the game, but I don't think it's really THAT worthy a game for all the praise it's received. The developers deftly subvert the average player's expectations and have created a uniquely cerebral game with some creative design choices, but it doesn't hold a lot of replay value or weight. It incorporates humor and is funny in places, but it doesn't feel like there's a whole lot there. Although there are a ton of different legitimate paths you can take, there isn't any actual puzzle-solving or anything that will make you think. It's well-made but it really does feel like a Source mod and it ultimately just ends up being a short game.
It also drops pretty much all tropes from FPP (first-person perspective) video games, in that there's no combat or intricate maneuvering to be had. I applaud this since it distinctly breaks the mold from most FPP games, but it doesn't fill the hole with much else than wandering around barren corridors. Most games either focus on combat, puzzle-solving, platforming, immersing the player in a compelling and interesting world, or if nothing else, appreciating the scenic view, if not a mix of all five. Removing combat, puzzles, platforming (you can't jump at all and never need to crouch), starting the player with a nonsensical premise and boring environment, and keeping interactivity surprisingly low, The Stanley Parable in fact doesn't have
. Rather, the game opts for what are in actual fact simply minor decisions (such as taking a right path instead of a left path), but constantly reminding the player that this decision is incredibly important. Whether or not this subversion of authority and declaration of autonomy is really as significant as all that is up to the player's interpretation, but it leads to my next point.
****MINOR SPOILERS AHEAD****
Mild spoiler warning from here until further indicated. It ultimately turns out that actually the entire point of the game is
to either follow or disregard the game's storyline. By expressing his own volition, he can choose whether or not to either submit to or betray the narrative. That's it. Now, I'm fine with that, but it doesn't really go anywhere with this. Furthermore, as a game, it doesn't do much, if anything, with its medium. For instance, The Stanley Parable could be rendered in first-person perspective in the Source engine, or it could just as easily be rendered in the medium of an eight-bit pixelated platformer. Or it could even be text-based. The reason is because
(i.e., the engine). The Stanley Parable depicts its environments accurately but likewise, there is little reason for it to take place in the environment it does. It looks like an office, and it feels like an office, but it could just as well take place pretty much anywhere else. The game opens up conveniently after everyone has suddenly disappeared, and although while playing the game the player doesn't really question this much, afterwards it made my brain itch, and I just got the sense that this was done so the developers didn't have to animate models, write scripted dialogue, or find more voice actors. Basically all this is to say that the same concept could be done any number of ways, so much so that the storyline that the game (read: Narrator) is trying to tell is rendered completely meaningless. Lastly, the decisions that you do make are possibly only there for comedic value. Nothing really has any reason to be there, which may be the developer's own ironic take on narrative structure. As it stands, there is at least one point where it becomes literally impossible to save yourself from a bad ending in what feels like should be an ultimate confrontation, which is a major disappointment. One can argue that that was the point, to subvert your expectations and force a "Game Over" during what feels like what should be a boss battle or confrontation, but instead it feels more like an unsatisfying psychological experiment that gives a major case of blue balls. It's as though the developers don't realize that these tropes exist and get perpetuated because they're actually emotionally satisfying to actual living people, the kinds of people who bought this game.
****END OF SPOILERS****

Think of this as a fighting or a brawler game, like Smash Bros or PlayStation All Stars. This is definitely not a Dota 2 or LoL kind of Moba, so don't go looking for that experience. Also flexing between different heroes is really difficult, because slight cooldown differences will throw you off. They did their best to put similar skills into same keys, but it's still a bit hard.
Overall, lovely game, I bought early access and got all the current and future heroes, and I don't regret it at all.

I am a big fan of the previous Civ games. I did not enjoy this one since the game simply lacks depth. There are no specialised unit types (ie everything is equal to everything else in terms of relative attack) which leads to dull combat, religions and corporations are missing, no great people and no way to capture land through cultural means. All these things made previous civ games much more involved and interesting - there was simply more to do, think about and achieve.
I find beyond earth tedious too. Many of the win conditions involve extreme dull clicking (ie the purity win of settle 20 colonists is basically click on a portal 20 times then move 20 of the units to some land away from your cities - tedious.) The trade routes are a pain to re-establish - the game is constantly forcing you to have a trade route decision click fest. This also aplies to espionage - it is a click fest. There is no strategy to espionage other then 'keep clicking on a mission to accelarate your civs resource gathering'.
The new features are limited and do not make up for the lack of previous games features. The orbital layer is a small part of the game - you will hardly spend any time in it and strategy is limited to 'if I build x I get y'. You may as well think of satilites as buildings. The aliens are basically barbarians, you can't ask them to do anything for you and their benifits of you befriending them are random and limited. The naval barbarians are deadly limiting early naval combat reducing more startegic appeal of the game.
Also the similarity to Civ 5 is uncanny other than the new features I have talked about above. Civ 5 is a much better game - why did I spend £30 on this?

I should preface this review by stating that this is my third complete playthrough of this game (All achievements, sidequests etc.) having played through the Xbox 360 and PS3 versions. I played through the Xbox 360 when it first released back in 2010 and then once again in 2013 for PS3 and just completed another 100 hour playthrough for the PC, putting my life total at around 300 hours for this game. Quite a lot of time I must admit, but I feel this game's story and gameplay (despite some flaws) has great replay value and totally justifies coming back and revisiting the world of Cocoon and Gran Pulse every 2-4 years.
One of the main points of contention of this game is the 20-25 hours of travelling in corridors until you arrive at Chapter 11 in the story where the game opens up considerably. But I feel the developers made a wise decision in order to get the player to become emotionally invested in the characters. It's my opinion that if the game opened up completely from the outset, the developers would have had a much harder time trying to develop a cohesive narrative. Nonetheless, if you stick with it, the endgame will keep you quite busy with a myriad of freedom and challenges...you just have to endure 10 chapters of running through corridors.
The game truly shines in the combat department and you'll indubitably spend most of your time fighting monsters. It can become quite "grindy" trying to gather gil for your huge expenditures endgame, but unlike the aforementioned PS3 and Xbox360 versions I played through, the game allows you to switch over to an "easy" mode which greatly increases the drop rate from monsters. This helped me shave hours of my completion time versus the previous versions I played. Also, the combat mode (for the most part) requires your full attention and you have to do more than "repeatedly press x" in battles. When I am grinding endgame in other final fantasy titles, I tend to use about 10-20% of my attention in non-boss battles whilst reading or some other non-gaming activity. However, this game will require your full engagement throughout.
Other reviewers have expressed the pros and cons quite well so I don't need to reiterate them here. To succintly put it; if you are willing to invest some time in the more trying sections of the first half of this game, I feel it can be a rewarding experience.
Update: Due to its nature as being quite misunderstood or "polarizing" amongst fans of the Final Fantasy series; I've henceforth nominated as "Most misunderstood game" for the upcoming Steam Game Awards.
Update: For 2017, I have nominated this under the category of "no apologies" as I still believe this was a great addition to the final fantasy series.

I do love me my Saints Row. Do I love Gat Out of Hell? Sort of.
Like many games that seem to be coming along now, developers really seem to like taking shortcuts to maximize profits, while lowering development time. Saints Row 3, Saints Row 4, and Gat Out of Hell, Dead Island, and Dead Island: Riptide, Call of Duty, and pretty much any of EA's sports lineup are examples that come to mind. Not so much sequels, as they are "samequels" - just offering more of the same style of game, with little added or innovated.
This trend is really starting to really turn me off as a gamer. I'd rather pay full price for a good, thoroughly developed franchise game every few years, than get nickeled-and-dimed with mediocre cash-grab rehashes every year. This is fast food gaming at it's worst. I wish it would stop.
Is Gat Out of Hell one of these? I think it teeters a l'il too close.
Here's the breakdown:
PROS:
-More Saints Row!
-A completely new map to explore.
-Return of a few classic Saints Row characters voiced by their original actors.
-Flight! Once upgraded, flight is the cat's pajamas.
-Price. Game's price point is set between full-price and Season Pass.
CONS:
-No music/radio.
-No character creation. You're forced to play as either Gat of Kinzie. Can't even customize them.
-No homies to call on.
-Hardly any vehicles. No way to customize them.
-Denizens of New Hades have no variety.
-City envionment seems really small. Far too easy to traverse with flight.
-Cutscenes are almost entirely storyboarded with narration. Only opening scene, the musical number, and ending scenes are animated in-game.
-Weapon variety is minimal. Same with customization options. Many weapons are functionally identical to weapons from previous games. Many are pointless.
-Assets, animations, textures, etc. are mostly re-used (or retextured) from previous games.
-Powers are mostly re-hashes of the powers from Saint Row 4, but with some different effects.
-Incredibly short. You can finish this in about 4-6 hours.
Final thoughts:
It's fairly cheap, but otherwise not especially remarkable. In fact, at the beginning of this review I realized I didn't like it as much as I thought I did. Probably saw it through nostalgia-colored glasses.
Like Saints Row 4, Gat Out of Hell could've been some form of DLC, rather than a standalone game.
If you're a fan of the franchise, by all means get it - but I'd recommend waiting until the price comes down. It's a fun, but brief, jaunt back into the Saints Row universe.

tl;dr: It's short, it's fun, it's insane. Is it worth your money? That's up to you to decide, because I loved this supernatural, superpowered romp as Kinzie Kensington.
Difficulty
GooH is -really- difficult. You remember SR3 and SR4 where majority of the enemies could be safely dispatched with or without your powers, with just a simple pair of pistols and some aiming? This does not happen in this game.
Hell's Legions offer you know quarter. They will swarm. They will damage you. And they will keep coming unless you upgrade and learn to use your powers to kick some serious supernatural♥♥♥♥♥
Even at the highest level of Health EVERYTHING you might find yourself on a razor's edge between life and death, using all of your powers just to stay alive. And that, my friends, is pretty awesome.
Gameplay
Flight is amazing. Many games can get it wrong or get it right, but GooH gets it oh so very right. After your first set of falls and dives trying to get used to the controls, you're going to find yourself constantly zipping about New Hades on your pair of Fallen Angel wings and loving it. If you found Cluster Collection in SR4 fun, you're going to find Lost Soul collection in GooH even more so.
This is best exemplified by the Salvation Activity, where you zoom around blasting souls and catching people. There is nothing quite like extended, acrobatic flight, and being literally paid to do it.
The new guns are pretty fun and creative. Instead of SR4 where they just have a pedestrian DoT or bonus to basic damage, these ones now have some pretty kickass effects like chain lightning or my personal favourite, "Sweepstakes" shotguns which fire vampire stakes that explode.
The powers, with the exception of the Coldfire Aura with the freeze upgrade and the Tower Summon with the missile upgrade, are pretty well balanced this time around, and are no longer an optional OP strategy. You will find yourself using all four powers constantly, and it's a rather fun romp, as you learn to use them both to survive and cause general chaos.
I love Sin Fraud best of all its incarnations. Instead of just having your character get run over and punched around at the behest of good old Legal Lee, you get to play as past villains/allies like Troy and have them get constantly run over by Hell's traffic. It's especially fun when you get hit by a Comet, a literal flaming death trap that falls apart as you drive it, and amazing when you get your punishment going and start blowing vehicles up -on contact-. The music certainly helps.
Setting
New Hades is beautiful and interesting. Instead of being a slightly wrong Steelport there is a lot of personality to love about each district, unique in its own way. My personal favourite would have to be the Den, because of the hilarious and amusing ads for the sinful pleasures, and Shakespeare, of all people, owning a nightclub there with some rocking music.
The ads and the details are fun to read, as they really ad to the crappiness and the hilarity of the verse, especially the Assquake Grande orders, when you find out who exactly is behind the counter when you go get a taco.
Story
Closure! Those left hanging about what happened to past characters or loved the way past characters came back in SR4 are in for a treat. Though SR3 is left hanging for good old Oleg, people who want to finally kill Dex get the opportunity to do so, and past villains get a hilarious return in the great ending if you manage all Loyalties for your allies.
Your anti-Satan club is also fun and in of themselves. Dane is still a money-grubbing♥♥♥♥♥as usual, the evil Shakespeare is full of fun, and Vlad the impaler and his Frat Boy Demon problem never ceases to amuse. (The minigame associated with them is also by far my favourite; nothing like whacking frat boys into goals with a spiked paddle.)
Jezebel and saving the Boss also unfolds as you'd think it would: it's simple, it's full of violence, and Johnny being Johnny, threatening people with guns, going in to murder people, and planning to harm Satan in the face.
Overall?
It's ridiculous. It's fun. It's the most "crazy" Saints Row of the trio of SR3, SR4, and this. Not as long as 4, but I'll count it as the far superior version simply because of how the gameplay was (mostly) balanced, Flight, and how the activites and the minigames have been changed to be thematically more hilarious now that you're fighting the damned, not alien simulations.

Last Remnant - exactly what the FF series should be like by now. FF XIII? Fal'Cie, L'Cie, and playing dress-ups with Lightning?
Thanks, but no.
The game has it's flaws, no argument here (feeling more like a budget title from Square because of lack of marketing, which is a pity) - and some are more serious than others, I admit. On top of that, it takes a while to get at least a bit familiar with the battle system, but man... is it satisfying when all the pieces come together in a boss fight :) Like a well-thought-through game of chess.
The learning curve is something else alltogether. Want a druid in your group? Too bad, your unit just became a hunter. How about a warlock? Sounds neat, right? Tossing Mystic Arts around and obliterating enemies like nobody's business. Well, tough sh*t, you just got yourself a ninja. This is not a game for control freaks. A lesson I learned all too well with this game. And I'm thankful for that.
There are tens of characters to pick from, across over 50 classes available, who may, or may not listen to what you want them to be. You do the math. With 18 characters on the battlefield, it really feels like you command an army to be reckoned with. And even with that number.... I was left with wanting a little bit more. Last Remnant feels more "alive" than anything I have ever played from Square Enix.
Characters upgrade their weapons based on what they are ordered to do in battle, and just ask you for components. No time to grind for Vulture Rawhide that Nora has been bugging you about? Well, she will be stuck with her inferior hammer for the rest of the game. Your choice. This is how in-game fighting incentive should work. I don't want to fight monsters just to get enough EP to teleport the hell out of a zone... believe you me.
Last Remnant (2009) looks way better than Lightning Returns (2014), and, from what I have seen playing the latter, is definitely more in-depth. Unless you like playing dress-ups, which, truth be told, is not this game's strongest suit. There's so much more to tell about this game, both positive, and negative (more summon options!), and I feel I just scratched the surface.
Buy it, play it, EXPERIENCE it. Or don't, and let the world be swallowed by the misuse of remnants.
Again, your choice.

Prior to playing Final Fantasy XIII, I had almost exclusively heard negative things about it.
The usual criticisms are that the whole game feels like a linear hallway, Lightning’s character feels very similar to Cloud Strife, the combat is too simple, and it’s pacing goes off at certain points. All of these criticisms hold true however as a fan of big stylistic JRPGs I still managed to largely enjoy FF13.
My first playthrough was done on PC so maybe I don’t feel as jaded as those who spent full price for the original console release. Anyways here is what I enjoyed about FF13.
I generally like my rpg’s a little on the easier side when they’re as long as a Final Fantasy game and I found both the Easy and Normal difficulties to provide a fun experience. The combat is very straightforward which could definitely bother some people, however I enjoyed how fast and satisfying battles felt. I loved the sci-fi fantasy aesthetic presented by the game’s world. Enemy and monster designs are great. The world is full of elegant and angelic robotic deities, giant mythical beasts, and the usual mobs associated with the Final Fantasy series. The story felt pretty average by jrpg standards however I thoroughly enjoyed the main cast of characters.
Everyone seems to have a differing opinion of which games in the Final Fantasy series are the best let alone good. So you should consider giving FF13 a try if you simply wrote it off the same way that I did. You might just happen to like it. Catch it on a sale, give it a fair chance, and form your own opinion.

Far Cry is released, made by the same developers i thought i'd give crysis a run, hearing reviews from people saying its fantastic, 97% rated among others, So i thought i'd run Crysis. Even though the game is a 2008 creation it is visually stunning on my 2012 rig.
The year is 2020, You invade a small island in the South China Sea, after US archeologists uncover a mysterious artifact and The North Korean government quickly seizes the area, imprisoning the archeolgists. You start off as a member of Delta Force sent in on a rescue mission and one by one your team is eliminated by some sort of alien force.
Crysis is a next-generation PC first-person shooter from Crytek, the award-winning developers of "Far Cry."
During the siege the true nature of the artifact quickly emerges, pointing to the existence of an alien presence on Earth, and ultimately the trigger for a massive-scale alien invasion.
The battle to save Earth begins...
Despite the realistic near-future setting and familiar arms, Crysis isn't a military simulation. At its heart this is a superhero game, where the main character is armed with the latest in high-tech equipment. Your nanosuit -- the star of the show -- allows you to be invisible, to be super-fast, to be super-strong, or to be virtually bulletproof. Here's the catch: you can only use one power at a time, and they all have limited energy. Choosing which powers to use in every situation is the heart of the gameplay.
For the most part the powers are excellently balanced. Each has its drawbacks and situations where it's appropriate to use (any power, improperly used, will drain your suit's energy and shut off). The only exception is super strength, which isn't terribly useful in most scenarios.
Stealth, on the other hand, is absolutely essential. You are always outnumbered. Fortunately, stealth is brilliantly implemented: While standing still, your suit can stay invisible almost indefinitely. But the moment you start moving, your energy drops... fast. The gameplay that results is absolutely pulse-pounding. You'll dart from cover to cover, stealing moments wherever possible to recharge your suit. While standing still, enemies will walk right past you, unaware you're pointing a shotgun at their head.
Apart from the occasional crashes and then almost at the end of the game it failing to run at all even in compatibility mode then i would still recommend the game.

Egy metroidvania platformer, ami rengeteget merített a Soulsborne játékokból. Megtalálható benne azok atmoszférája, mechanikái és nehézsége egyaránt.
Ami tetszett benne:
-Gyönyörű design
A Dark Souls játékokra is jellemző "pusztuló szépség", mint esztétikai főcsapásirány itt is tetten érhető és erősebb, mint valahai. Az elhanyagolt, burjánzó kertek, a kihalt, monumentális épületek és az értelmes életet leváltó rohadó pusztulás csodás helyszínt biztosítanak ennek a játéknak is.
-Fantasztikus zene
A fent említett látványt gyönyörűen kiegésziti a játék csodálatos soundtrackje, ami helyenként pörgős, de általánosságban véve sejtelmes aláfestést ad felfedezőutunkhoz.
-Az érdekes karakterek
A From Software közkedvelt kínzóeszközéhez hasonlóan itt sem leszünk teljesen magányosak szenvedéseink közepette. Találkozni fogunk egy csomó karakterrel, akik életunt, melankólikus dialógusaikkal ugyan nem segítenek sokat a világ megismerésében, de kétségtelenül remekül passzolnak hozzá. Kellően különbözőek ahhoz kinézetben és jellemben is, hogy érdekeljen a sorsuk és a múltjuk.
-A rengetegféle ellenfél
A játék harcrendszere faék egyszerű. Ha játszottál a Striderrel/Shovel Knighttal/Rogue Legacyval vagy bármilyen olyan platformerrel, amiben a karakterednek van egy közelharci fegyvere, akkor tisztában vagy az alapjaival. Ezt a formulát viszont baromi jól megkeveri, hogy a játékban majdnem hatvan féle ellenséggel találkozhatsz, akik mind különbözően viselkednek. Ráadásul ha használsz egy mentési pontot ők is újjászületnek, mint a Dark Soulshan (jó, persze a bossokat leszámítva)
-A felfedezés
A játék egy metroidvania. Az ilyenekben alapvető elvárás, hogy tele legyenek pakolva titkokkal, alternatív útvonalakkal és hogy az ember ne csak képes legyen bennük a felfedezésre, hanem motivált is legyen rá. Nos, ezeket a játék maximálisan hozza. Ráadásul meg is spékeli azza, hogy:
-A játék nehéz és igazságos
A folyamatosan újjászülető ellenfelek, az, hogy ha meghalunk, elveszítjük az összes addig felhalmozott pénzünket (hacsak jó Dark Soulsosan vissza nem térünk a halálunk színhelyére és agyon nem verjük a saját árnyképünket) és az, hogy alapból nincs térképünk egyetlen zónához sem, a felfedezés izgalmát megspékeli azzal a csodás rettegéssel, amit annyira szeretek a Niohban és a From Software játékaiban.
Ami viszont nem tetszik benne:
-A teljes térképet összességében egy Ori and the Blind Foresthez vagy urambocsá' egy Metroidhoz vagy Castlevaniához képest én kicsinek érzem. Mondjuk cserébe minden egyes helyszínnek lelke van és jól megkülönböztethető az összes többitől.
Aki szereti a metroidvania játékokat, azoknak mindenképpen ajánlom a Hollow Knightot. Külön előnyt jelent, ha közben Dark Souls rajongó is az ember, de ha nem, az se baj. Így legalább akkor sem marad ki a Soulsborne életérzésből, ha azokat a játékokat nem különösen kedveli.

NOT A HERO took Super Meat Boy's approach to fast-paced and infinitely replayable levels and gave it a Saint's Row level of attitude, goofiness, and guns, all wrapped up in a nice, pixelized Brittish package.
The movement in this game is fantastic. If you've ever played Canablat, you know the joy of crashing through a window in the side of a building, and NOT A HERO has that sensation in spades. The slide functions well, and working it into the cover mechanics is smooth as butter. The gunplay is simple, but effective. Each character has different running and firing speeds, but all work on the same principals. Every level is sliding on the ground to shatter some poor fool's kneecaps, plugging a bullet into his head, and slipping into cover to throw a molotov at the heavy with a machine gun who just caught up with you. Tense, but twitchy and fun.
The problems are minor, but worth noting. Bunnylord's voice is funny for two minutes and then annoying for two hours, and his text crawls extremely slow. I spent more time listening to him talk before and after the mission than I did shooting dudes for the first couple levels. Most of his dialogue is repetitive and can be skipped, and while it too is pretty funny for a while, by the time I'd beaten Upgraydd it was a serious case of "yeah I get it." Having no way to re-access hidden levels once you find them other than going to the original stage again is also a bummer, and (while it made me laugh in the trailer) lacking options like a windowed mode isn't great.
These are, however, total nitpicks. The level-to-level game here is solid, and while I haven't finished it quite yet, I know I'm going to. This is for sure a cool game to keep an eye on, and I'm very much enjoying my time with it.

So, I just finished the game with most of the optional stuff and all the characters unlocked, so I think I have  agood basis to give my opinion on this game.
Pro:
+ short levels make for good short sessions. Also doesn't make one feel too bad if you die and have to redo the whole level.
+ quick paced
+ variety of characters you can unlock, all with different playstyles (though that doesn't become that apparent for the first 4 imo, or maybe it's just understanding the game mechanics better that makes you get why and how these character play rather differently)
+ replayability for the optional missions (which are quite hard sometimes)
+ overall good level and enemy design
+ can be quite difficult at some points, especially if you go for all the optional stuff
Cons:
- Level design in terms of presentation. There are 3 worlds with the same basic design, the first two are rather a bit boring and not so nice to look at. Not much detail, mostly in the same color (or shades of the same color)
- Controls can be really annoying sometimes. The slide and cover button are the same, meaning that you'll always slide into cover, which works really nice most of the time, but it will also leave you not being able to take cover if the cover is too close to your position, which usually leads to sliding into the enemies or their firerange. Really annoying.
Also The shoot and execute(when enemies lie on the ground) button is the same, so you can end up wanting to shoot that guy running at you, but you will instead execute the guy on the ground, which (since you can't cancel it and takes quite a few seconds) will usually get you killed.
- Visibility issues sometimes. Powerups are always in the front, so enemies can sometimes "hide" behind them. Same problem if there's too much carnage (though that rarely happens). All in all this is not a big problem and rarely ever happens, but of course IF it happens it sucks hard to be shot at or killed by an enemy you didn't even soo, even though he was right in front of you.
Overall the game was and is a lot of fun and I'm happy I bought it, but be prepared for some frustration every now and again, as a result of control issues.

Sins of a Solar Empire is possiably one of the greatest RTS games there is. I played the Base game, then i bought this, and I must say that there are a BUNCH of improvments. The Graphics are smoother, there are more units, diplomacy has been revamped and new victory conditions have been implimented (Note I said I played the base game and Rebellion, I have not played Diplomacy, Entrenchment, Or Trinity). One of the things i really think Stardock did well with this is the optmization. I have a fairly run-of-the-mill setup, and i can play this game at about 60 FPS (and in Minecraft Vanilla i average about 30) and only expirence frame rate drop during large battles (50 ships vs 50 ships roughly). Also there is Multi-player (in which you need an Ironclad Online account, which is also required on first time start up, a time nuscance but isnt bad other than that first start up), I havent really messed arround with it very much, but I have heared it is pretty good.
I have heared it compared to games like Starcraft, but there are alot of differences.
-Although there are 3 races (TEC[Humans], Advent[Humans aswell, but were cast of as a sect earlier in history], and the Vasari[Only actual aliens, on the run from a force that has decimated their empire, and they have been stuck in this sector for some time], each race has 2 sub factions, the Loyalist and Rebel Factions.
-Starcraft maps span an area up to about 1 km x 1 km (.6 mi x .6 mi), where as SoaSE spans multiple star systems.
-In Starcraft, you NEED to micromanage your troops in order to win battles, In this, when two large fleets duke it out, they just sit there, trading shots between themselves. Corvette-classes do, however, use hit-and-run tactics on other ships (they attack and then pull off, retreat some distance, then go in for another run).
-In Starcraft, Mineral and Gas patches run out after some time. The Metal and Crystal resources don't run out. Getting more extractors just increases the ammount you recieve per second.
There are just some DIFFERENCES, not pros or cons.
THIS is the Pros and Cons List.
Pros:
-RTS, if you like strategy game you are gonna like this.
-VERY large scale. Larger maps have 5 stars and hundreds of planets.
-Very well optimized. Can run on most set ups on medium-low settings.
-Good re-playability. If you get bored of the many single-player maps, play some multi-player or spice up single player with Steam Workshop Mods.
-2 DLCs, fairly cheep. Don't have them, so I dont really know much about them.
Cons:
-If you enjoy giving orders, and micromanaging forces you might find this game a tad boring.
-The games can be VERY long for an RTS. Starcraft games usually run 15-30 mins, where as 3 hours in you could be reaching the halfway point of your game. Not exactaly a Sit and play a few miniutes game.
-Late game, things can get kinda mechanical. I say that as you jump to an enemy planet, take you the defensive structures, orbital bomb it, rinse and repeat. Thankfully, Stardock added a "AI surrender" mechanic. After if is clear they cant make a comeback, they surrender.
All-in-all, a very good game. Gotten quite a few  hours of enjoyment, undoubtaly will get more.

I don't know what I can say that hasn't already been said. It's a truly amazing fighting game and just game in general. How about I just list off some stuff about it and let you decide if it sounds up your alley?
A solid cast of 8 characters currently which is fine even if it isn't as big as Smash's.
Each character is well balanced with a variety of playstyles.
11 stages currently (6 starting, 5 unlockable in game) with two version of each, one with stage hazards and such and one that's fairer for tournaments and such.
An arcade style story mode with some intriguing backstory and stuff on the 6 starting fighters.
An unlockable endless wave mode unlocked after beating story mode that includes fighter leveling and customization (Just in that mode and it's special versus section, not the normal versus) and it has plenty of objectives spread out along it's waves such as target practice, lighting bug chasing and the floor is lava.
Online ranked, casual, 2v2, and more (I think) in case offline bores you at some point.
Tutorials to get you up to speed on everything from the basics like walking and jumping to advanced stuff like wavedashing, DI, and more.
Character specific tutorials that teach you the ins and outs of which ever character you please.
Practice mode to test out combos and such and to practice what you learned from the tutorials.
Customize-able colors for each character so you can make sure you stand out amongst your friends (not online compatible and friends not included).
More updates on the way including (but not limited to) fighters, stages, modes possibly, and likely more.
It's well worth the $15 if you have ever enjoyed a Smash Bros game before, especially Melee. No, it's not Alpha Centauri.
No, it's not as good as the complete edition of Civ V.
That said, it's still an enjoyable, if flawed, turn-based strategy. At the very least, I consider it better than Civ V was on launch. There's no dramatic changes from the formula, although there are plenty of small details that effect gameplay, such having a tech web instead of a tech tree, or the Affinity system, or making Virtues actually useful. These tweaks have enough of an impact that I'd call C:BE more than a reskinned Civ V, but the solidified, tested mechanics of V's complete edition make a solid launching point for the game itself.
With the changes made in the first major patch, it's clear the Firaxis is working to address issues the community has raised. My biggest gripes with C:BE are less simple to address, however. Firstly, more could be done to differentiate factions and leaders from each other. While I understand the game instead focuses on Affinities, rather than factions, to provide much-needed personality, this leads me to my second point. Much like the modern era in V, Affinities really only come into their own as a source of flavour and personality in the later stages of the game.
As I mentioned, I still consider C:BE to be superior to V on launch, and I'm excited to see what I can be with an expansion or two of the same quality as BNW.

This is a Square made Final Fantasy style game that I never even heard about until I saw it on Steam.  Instead of 1-5 party members like most JRPG's, you get to have around 25 in a fight at a time.  Its broken into 5 man teams.  So each team gets a turn in combat each round.

I'm on the fence about the game.  The quality is there because its a typical Final Fantasy world, which I love, but it seems that at a certain point the battles become a flip of a coin to win.  When one of your squads has a turn it has several options it can perform depending on how the party is set up.  Though these options are not stagnant options.  Out of the say 8 things possible that the squad can do only 4 options will randomly be chosen each turn.  This means that if your healer squad doesn't get the healing option for multiple turns it can mean game over.  You can mitigate this by removing options that a team can perform so that they don't clog up the limited action bar.  While that helps, you still often have to rely on luck and a coin flip to get an important action to occur at the right time.  This is the part that I can't get over.  There is little precision to the battles.  In normal fights the chaos can be really fun, but when a boss fight comes it can lead to a large helping of frustration.

It's fun and playable.  If 5 were my recommend mark, it sits at 4.  Very close but with a heavy heart I cannot recommend it.
