With a preview article appearing in free London rag 'The Metro', it seemed that NOT A HERO was destined for great things in May 2015. However, due to a release delay & several unfortunate control related hiccups at launch it seemingly fizzled away without the usual hype you seem to see from the YouTubers let's playing the current indie darling.
This title is a 2.5D (or Iso-slant as they call it) fast paced, pixel art cover shooter. Think Gunpoint mixed with the frantic action of Hotline Miami. You're tasked with helping an anthropomorphic alien known as BUNNYLORD to become mayor. His main strategy which he'll brief you with in hilariously randomized pre-level sequences is to mostly 'kill people very dead awesomely' and also drink milkshakes.
Roll7 are an English studio and it tells through this game with almost all the main characters given regional UK dialects. While it doesn't offer much of anything in the way of story or character development, it's a nice touch to distinguish different skill types on your controllable protagonist.
While getting from one end of a level to the end isn't particularly difficult, each stage will come with several additional challenges. Most are time or kill streak related & nearing the end of the game, these will require almost pin-point reflexes and stratagem to make it through.
While the game itself is a lot of fun, humorous & challenging, the major flaws arrive in that only 1 of the 8 or so unlockable characters (Mike) is actually a viable option to complete the game & all its challenges. While it's still amusing to dabble with the others, more balancing should have been carried out to provide more possiblities in playing the game & using all the characters in a different fashion.
Keeping in mind the scope & budget of the game, it would have also been nice to see a bit more story originating from Bunnylord's FUN CLUB members.
While perhaps not in the upper echelon of the current golden age of indie steam titles, it's still rather good. Hopefully this won't be the last we see of Bunnylord from Roll7. While it's £10 full price might be a hard sell to those who weren't already sold on the trailer (which is still dare I say one of the best on the service), it'd almost be impossible to pick this up during a sale or bundle & not have a good time.

A very long overdue review. And honestly I don't really think words can do the game justice.
Without a doubt my GOTY, or at the very least my Indie GOTY.
There's just no other indie title that can compare to this game. At all. The world is drop-dead beautiful. Top notch level and environment design, coupled with lighting and music and pacing that all really set an atmosphere and tone for each scenario that you really have to PLAY to really experience. Watching a video is not enough. Reading about it is not enough.
Combat in Hollow Knight is treated a bit differently than most Metroidvania titles. A lot of people like to compare it to the Souls' games style of combat. That's because taking your time and waiting for openings in an enemy's attack pattern are pretty key. However of course, things can be pretty hectic, especially when combined with some platforming puzzles that come along with it.
Unlike most indie titles as well, the game is absolutely massive, with so many things to do and explore. There are some things you might not ever even see or know about in your first playthrough. Even really small, cryptic but trivial things that give the game that much more personality (ie;
).
Aside from the game's combat system, there's also Charms, which give you different kinds or perks and augmentations, whether it be something as simple as increasing the range of your nail, to converting your entire healthbar into literally different kinds of health. Some charms boost stats, others change your spells or moves entirely, some charms have interactions with eachother that create almost entirely new abilities. Some charms allow for hidden dialogue from some NPCs even, letting you learn even more about the world. It's actually kind of mindblowing how much is going on with such a seemingly simple mechanic.
Every boss fight is memorable and exciting, providing some heart pumping challenge, some completely taking you by surprise even as per tradition. Be on your toes!
Every location is memorable and breathtaking. The world is alive, it's breathing, it's in pain. Just by looking around you can learn so much about this dying world.
Every character is memorable and endearing. They all have their own motivations and goals they're looking to achieve. You grow to really like them and get attached.
It's just all... so perfect.

That's not to devalue Cuphead in any way, but creating an entire world with tone and atmospheric shifts is not something anyone should scoff at. Worldbuilding is hard. FFXIII has its drawbacks, and I wasn't expecting much from it. To my surprise, I really like the game a lot, actually, although some of the criticisms against it are fair.
You will tend to enjoy it more and get more out of it if you understand (and are able to accept) this going in, though: Chapters 1-10 – or arguably, even the entire first playthrough (13 chapters I believe) – are basically an epic tutorial/pre-game. The first playthrough exists to A) tell you the story, and B) teach you (slowly) all the subtle, elegant, and eventually very rewarding mechanics of the gameplay and combat. Once you’ve completed the main playthrough, you then unlock access to the other, bigger, more free-roaming/monster-hunting part of the game as a reward, and that’s like a whole game unto itself, for which I recommend a decent strategy guide.
That initial game-length tutorial takes quite a while, it’s true (20-40 hrs depending on your gameplay style) but if you sort of accept it for what it is, it doesn’t bother you as much, and there is still a lot to enjoy along the way. Breathtaking visuals and environments. High-budget, exquisitely rendered CGI animations. The casual racial stereotypes and bizarre, vaguely pedo-ish sexual tension that only the Japanese can get away with. And after the first few chapters, the combat starts to come to life a bit (though it won’t get there fully until Ch. 11 or so). It’s actually a GREAT combat system, it just seems lame at first, because you can’t do anything interesting with it at first. Once you are deeper in, there’s a really elegant, intricately crafted ebb and flow to what’s going on that seems uniquely Japanese to me. You’ll constantly notice little subtleties you missed or took for granted in combat, and there are odd little tricks to the timing and switching and how it all weaves together that make it very satisfying once you kind of “get” it (and are allowed to use it all).
As to some of the other things the game got slammed for, well – I mean, it IS a FF game. So of course it has kind of a stupid story and childish, melodramatic characters. That’s nothing new. Honestly, I’d like XIII as much as VII if it just didn’t take so long to set you free (VII, as well as other FF games, take their sweet time with that too, let’s not forget – just not quite as much time as XIII does).
So, general verdict? It’s a great game, if you have the patience to approach the initial playthrough as kind of a pre-game to unlock the (better, more open-worldish) post-game. And the pre-game isn’t actually all that bad – I had fun with it – it’s just not the main thing you’re there for. FFXIII will eventually give you what you want and has a lot of charm and tricks up its sleeves, it’s just slow to show them all to you.
And as to the quality of the port – I know there were a lot of issues with that when it came out, but the major grievances seem to have been addressed and patched. I didn’t have a single issue with stability or gameplay on PC that I can recall.

I have never been so angered by a video game.
Crysis is a beautiful game. That's no secret. Beyond that, the shooting is competent and the nano suit adds a nice flavor to the game. It would be a pretty fun game if not for its glaring flaws. So let's dive into those.
The game is poorly optimized. It looks great, but similarly good looking games run better. I'm using a 4770k @ 4.6 GHz and an overclocked GTX 970. It runs very well on max with 4x AA in most situations, but it occasionally lags, especially against aliens with their numerous projectile effects.
Crysis can't seem to pick a difficulty and stick with it. You'll go fifteen minutes of easy gameplay, and suddenly it's impossibly difficult. The autosaves are few and far between, so you'll need to stay on top of that yourself. Assuming you don't die in a particularly difficult situation, you might die to any of the numerous bugs.
That's right. The game is HORRIBLY buggy. Here is a nice list of terrible deaths and game-breaking bugs I encountered on a single playthrough:
- Bumped into an object that is subject to phsysics. It collided funny and I was instantly killed by it, from full health, with 100% on armor.
- Randomly fell over dead on numerous occasions, no enemies nearby, full health, no mines.
- Vehicle bumps something at an odd angle, explodes.
- Clipped through a floor and into a fire.
- The second-to-last mission finished and crashed the game. Again. And again. I had to use a command console code to advance to the final mission.
- The final mission allows you to progress beyond something that is necessary to finish it, causing you to have to restart the mission.
The list could go on. I'm sure there are plenty I even forgot.
Beyond the bugs, the game itself is just frustrating. The ground shooting segments are usually good, but the vehicle segments are some of the worst I've ever played. The VTOL is unresponsive and clunky, made even worse by tornados that just throw you to the ground. The tank mission is entirely too difficult at times. There is an escort mission where your friendly has to keep warm, and he twice failed to keep up with me and stand near a fire, getting himself killed.
There is a lot of good in this game, but there are a lot of things so poorly executed, it clearly overshadows the good. Unless you're a masochist, do not buy this game.

In the beginning there were 3. Pavle, the ex-footballer. Katia, the journalist. And Bruno, the
professional chef. They came together during the siege purely by chance, and used their collective skills to improve their survival chances. Over the next 2 weeks they struggled to stay fed. Always low on supplies, and usually having one or more go hungry each day. Then Marko arrived, seeking shelter. The survivors knew they would struggle to support a 4th person, but welcomed him anyways. Marko then proved his worth after bringing home more food and medicine in one night than Pavle had managed in a week. Then he managed to bring home enough supplies to build some more furniture, and a radio. He helped the group not only survive, but flourish. He even at one point rescued a girl under the assault of a drunken soldier, earning him the status of "hero" amongst the people of Pogoren. Then one night he went scavenging in a dangerous area, known to be inhabited by brutal bandits. He had done this many times before, and felt safe enough to travel indoors. While searching through a cabinet, he was spotted. While he managed to kill 2 of the bandits, the remaineder proved to be too much for him. The group was devastated by his death. They never really recovered. A little over 2 weeks later, the siege had been lifted. The group had survived, and all went back to try to pick up where they left off before the war.
Except for one. Whose body silently lies in a shallow, unmarked grave.
RIP Marko. You will be missed.

And those you find, you'll find in low quantities if they're not common cards. You thus can't build decks with clear goals. This goes for your opponent too though, so it's only half bad.
I'd suggest not investing any time in this if you have the option of playing irl. But it's okay to spend a bit of time as long as you don't purchase the game.
ps. simple tips: You're capped at 100 tokens, you'll be autoforced to attack if the game notices you're just stalling but could win, you'll not want to drag out a game if you have the option. The client is very crashy, and if it does crash, it'll count as a loss. Even if your opponent already conseded.

Fenimore Fillmore: The Westener:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The lonesome cowboy, Fenimore Fillmore, reached the Bannister farm just before the lovely Stella served dinner to her family. Our cowboy had a peak in one of the windows and saw Joe (Stella’s husband) with his feet on the table, and her son Billy riding his wooden horse across the small room. As Billy reached the opposite window (into which Fillmore was peaking) with his wooden toy, the young fellow noticed three incoming riders passing the entrance.  They had a mission to purchase the farm at all costs. Joe, standing in front of them, bravely refused to leave his property. This is where a cactus needle will dramatically change Fenimore Fillmore’s evening! So to every cowboy out there . . . be careful of cactus needles - they can be a pain in the bum AND put you in all sort of predicaments!
Fenimore Fillmore: The Westerner, is a point and click adventure game where you play a young and daring cowboy (well, he thinks so) who tries to help two farmers save their estate from the evil Mr Starek from Starek City. This is a remastered version of the game which was released in 2004.
Personally, I am thrilled to see this version of the game on Steam. I guess it is a bit of nostalgia on my behalf, but boy am I enjoying the trip memory lane! As I mentioned above, one of Fenimore’s bum cheeks had a close encounter with an unforgiving cactus needle. After facing off Starek’s accomplice and thoroughly enjoying an artichoke soup, he discovered that Starek owns the nearby town and has removed all farmers from their land, with the exception of the Bannister and Jones families, who are standing up to him.
Fenimore will not have access to any hints in this adventure, which can be a bit frustrating at times. As he visits various locations, make sure that Fenimore looks inside all cabinets and closets - you will be surprised at how many one dollar notes you can find inside, and you will need to use a good number of them during the game. If he becomes short on cash, he can always go to the Einstein Fair to make an extra dollar or two. Great humour in this game - I am sure you will have a few giggles here and there.
I enjoyed the graphics and cut-scenes and the pleasant western soundtrack. The camera placement is not the best, in my opinion, and I did experience crashes here and there.

Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Good graphics
-	Fun characters and dialogues
-	Trip down memory lane
-	Good price point
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	The camera placement is not the best
-	Couple of crashes here and there
-	No trading cards
Whether or not you have played the original version, it’s definitely a point and click adventure game to own!
7/10

The Westerner is an adventure point&click in a western/cowboy setting initially released in 2004. This remastered version adds new lighting and post-processing effects. I personally played the original release when I was a kid and thoroughly enjoyed it.
- Steam Achievements
- Cute and awesome aesthetic (kinda reminds of Toy Story)
- Full of innocent humor and funny dialogues
- Simple storyline and loveable characters
- 7-8 hours of gameplay
- Affordable price for a nostalgia fix
- Fully voiced and subtitled in many languages
- Pleasant soundtrack and ambient noises
- Some very bad camera placements
- Uneven difficulty. Sometimes easy, sometimes frustrating when you have no idea of what to do to advance in the story (e.g. a very specific and unique item is required and you need to find it without any hint)
- UI elements (mainly the hand pointer) are too big even at higher resolutions leading to difficulties to accurately interact with the environment
- Game crashes quite often (had at least 10 crashes in my walkthrough in release date build, might be fixed later on). Check the forum as well for performance issues, some people are experiencing some.
It's hard to say that The Westerner aged well. While I personally feel that graphically the game is still enjoyable because of its aesthetic, the gameplay feels dated and can act as a big turnoff. I would personally recommend the game for younger kids although the lack of hints could very well lead them to frustration. I loved replaying through it because of nostalgia but I hardly believe many adults would enjoy it now as many objectively better 3D point&click have been released since. If you're a fan of humor and aesthetic à la Toy Story and are willing to look past gameplay issues, go for it though, you will have a blast with this clumsy cowboy that is Fenimore.

17 December 2014: I would not recommend Civilization: Beyond Earth yet, but that might change in the future. See below for details.
In short: The game as a whole seems LESS than the sum of its parts.
Similar to Civilization V when it came out - Beyond Earth for now is not a good gaming experience. With time Civ V was patched and extended and became one of my favorites. I hope the same will come true for Beyond Earth.
But  what exactly is the problem with the game? For me it's two things.
First of all the different pieces of otherwise very good mechanics don't exactly come together because of the lacking lore  of the game. The story, the different philosophies of the factions and personalities of their leaders and the overall world setting are far from complete, deep or anything but basic. And when inevitably compared to its spiritual predecessor - Alpha Centauri which had epic lore, Beyond Earth seems pretty poor...for now.
As a result the game does not escalate in scope, something that Alpha Centauri did quite well.
The second problem is the "Technoabble" used in Beyond Earth. The naming of technologies, build options etc. is "clever", but really not clear in it intent and purpose. That kind of ruins the atmosphere. It makes you feel at times that you don't know what you are doing and prevents you from clearly setting your goals in game. Going through several replays of the game you will eventually figure it out, but IMHO it should be more universal and less clever to be more enjoyable.
I'm hopeful that beyond Earth will grow with time to be much better.

I was looking for some good RPGs a few weeks ago and I saw someone recommending this game. When I looked at it on Steam I wasn't really sure about buying it... Well, I did and now I must say that you MUST buy it!!!
The Last Remnant is an awesome Strategy / RPG game!
The combat system feels good, making it easy, but also very challenging at some points. It focus a lot on group combat, while you can't choose each character's action, you can order the group to do the same thing in a strategic way. You can split your party members into units that can have up to 5 members, when you choose an action, the whole unit will perform that same action. The game sometimes changes the options you have in battle, for example, if you're in a story related battle, it sometimes changes your combat options, making you trigger an event. The strategy you use is totally up to you to decide, the game gives you a lot of customizable options, you can change an unit's formation, change it's members, and use specific commands in battle, like ordering an unit to heal other unit.
The graphics are also very good, you know, for a 2009 game.. And since it's a Square Enix game, you can expect a lot of amazing cutscenes and a very well written fantasy story.
There's also a few more features included, like crafting and hiring soldiers to your party.
The game only lacks in some things, like the character's level, since there's no level thingy, sometimes when you complete a battle, your characters can get stronger, gaining HP, AP, Attack, and even their weapons can get improved, but you can't see your stats growth 100%, you can only see things like the HP getting bigger. The option to choose each character's equipment would also be very usefull!
So, I would trully recommend this game to anyone who likes JRPGs! The game is also very cheap!!

After 4 years I finally completed the game, not 100% but quite close to it. After having my savegames being corrupted twice, i took my courage with both hands and decided to plunder this game once and for all in a third walkthrough.
I'll start with the cons to put that away swiftly, and they are pretty much the same in every Assassin's Creed. Collision bugs, clipping and pop-ins. That is always what you experience in any open world games nowadays. Performance wise, it could have been better, but it's still far better than AC: Unity, which i think is the worst in that regard. Oh, and the Abstergo part of the game, it's boring and a feeble attempt to follow on the meta story.
Now with the pros. First of all, what hooked me into this game straight away is the piracy. You have your ship, you have all the Carribean to navigate and a lot of activities to get by. Ok some of it are specially here for grinding (and the sake of crafting) like harpooning, exploring wreckages under the sea, stop by a tiny island to get contracts and sometimes items that give you more to the lore. But just being on your own ship, braving storms, gunnering in open sea against 2 or 3 man'o war, having your crew yelling those shanties, it feels pretty cool and get immersed easily into it.
Edward, the protagonist, is meh at first. But he's being more interesting to play on the later stages of the story, on his motives and implication, if you don't mind to dig into some side quests. To be frank, I didn't really play this game for the story, it's leagues behind Assassin's Creed 1 and 2, even if the casting have colorful characters like Black Beard and Captain Kidd (I didn't find any of the Templars really charismatic and that's a shame).
Gameplay wise, you have a lot of ways to act as a shadow (or a sneaky assassin if you prefer). Get by every guard by hiding in vegetations or behind walls, hiring dancers to be incognito in the masses, or let a guard going bersek do half the job for you if you are lucky. I regret the rope dart ability comes way too far in the game thought, really helpful to stay on the higher grounds if you prefer it this way. And if you don't wanna be sneaky, you can just jump on the first guard you see and engage every enemies, thought just like AC III, combat is way too easy and not challenging, 90% of the time you counter and then start your killing combo by simply pressing left click.
To finish, the map. It's huge. Really huge.A lot of islands, and you add to it La Havana, Nassau and Kingston. It will take you time to grind everything, specially if you don't use the fast travel option, and it's as I said previously, lot of acitivities to do. Quest for the mayan and templar treasures, manuscripts, hidden chests for rare crafting plans, even launch your fleet into missions to get rare items and money, it's pretty much accessory thought, but necessary if you want it all like me.
To conclude, i'll say, even if the story is not as engaging as the past titles and you feel more like a pirate than an assassin, it might be my favorite Assassin's Creed gameplay wise. My favorite remains the second one (and yes I include Brotherhood) because it has the best story and character of the franchise in my opinion, but if you're interested into the pirate universe, cruise on the sweet yet deadly Carribean seas, with a story good enough to play through and a lot of side things to do, you might like, even love this game. Specially now since it's the sales and it will cost you less than 10 bucks, not bad for game that can take you 40+ hours of your time if you wanna ace it.

This game will go down as one of my all time favorites.
Beautiful art and music, superb sound design and a haunting story told in a way that really speaks to me. You will have to dig a bit to get what is happening, in the same vein as in the Dark Souls games, but it is so worth it. The way the game progress actually kinda made me stop playing for a while, because I didn't want it to end. But alas, 2017 is nearing its end, so I felt I should see it through. I am so glad I did.
The game is basically a "metroidvania" game, where you start out with a basic moveset, and have to find and earn new abilities to get around. Because of the way the story is told, where you aren't even sure who or what you are yourself, there is rarely any direct direction you know you must go. But you rarely feet lost, because if you don't know what to do you only have to look at the map and see if you can spot locations you haven't gone. Chances are there will be something there.
As I write this I am 92% done, I have seen the ending(s) and have most likely done everything I need to do in order to feel finished. Yet I still want to get back in and find more stuff! Luckily they have released two small addons with more to do, which integrates beautifully in the base game. I also hear rumors of more to come.
If you like platformers, good but kinda dark stories told in a mysterious way, great art and beautiful music, you should get this.
One last small "kudos" to the developers: The way you structured several of the fights, especially the final boss, was so good. The way you made 2D-art of mute bug-creatures convey so much emotion, just by the use of fighting animation and music was brilliant. Thank you.

Hollow Knight is another fantastic rendition of the Metroidvania series. This game definitely should win an award, which it already has. The amount of story, world building and interesting secrets is sure to keep you gripped to your seats. In Hollow Knight, you play as the a bug knight trying to save the city of Hallownest and its inhabitants from the infection.
Gameplay-wise, it's a side scroller with the controller. You move and jump around slashing at enemies, taking the Geo that splashes out when they die to trade for upgrades. You hunt for Charms that will improve your powers, learn Nail Arts from Nailmasters (There's a Sly one here), and pick up special powers from bosses that will unlock different parts of the map (like double jumping, air dash, rocket charge and ground slam). All Castlevania-ish abilities. Hollow Knight is only really missing the imp and flying. You will also use a Dream Nail that will allow you to absorb ghosts and listen to the hearts of people (like Soul Reaper).
Conclusion, you must try this. Hollow Knight is an amazing game with tons of interesting stuff to offer. Kudos to Team Cherry and I hope to see more games from them with the same insanely massive world (with improvements, of course).
Note: Team Cherry an indie game developer in Adelaide, South Australia. The duo of Ari Gibson and William Pellen have definitely got what it takes to make a good game.
1. The World of Hallownest
This is exactly like the Castlevania of old. A world so big, detailed and filled with interesting characters and locations to go to.
2. Secrets, Secrets, Secrets
So many nooks and crannies to find. I love how certain secrets even need the monsters help to unlock. E.g. Sentry Guard breaking the rocks to reveal the hidden path. The secrets within secrets are the best ones. Some secret areas have their own secret area. E.g. Somewhere in the Resting Grounds after you open a special door, don't want to spoil the secret within a secret.
3. Story of Hallownest
While I believe the story is a trope based on a great sacrifice, I love it. How the sacrifice was done, what the sacrifice was for,
4. Unique Creatures
I love how each new stage has at least 1 creature that shows a unique gameplay mechanic. Sure, you'll see massive amounts of repetitive stuff but it's forgiveable compared to other games.
5. Dreamgate
It's basically a town portal but it's so useful. Sometimes, you want to go through a hard jumping puzzle but it's not located near a bench. The Dreamgate allows to go back and save your adventure and Dreamgate to that location later. However, it requires 700 essence to unlock which is slightly problematic.
1. Repetitive Mechanics
I can see the following mechanics being repeated for certain characters
a. Charge attack
b. Swing blade x1 x2
c. Sky drop attack
d. Goo spitter x1 x2 x3
e. Sticky wall creatures
f. Fart monsters
2. Blast Controls
You can easily turn and slash in mid-air. However, firing a blast is a bit weird. Many a time, I've found myself firing a blast facing the wrong direction.

O (PS4) B (XBox) fires a blast when tapped and heals when you hold it down. Can you imagine how silly it is to put a damage spell and healing spell on the same button?
4. AI Perfect Match Attack/False Difficulty
It's a bit strange when the AI is designed to perfectly counter your move regardless of whatever you do. E.g. Spin rolling to wherever you are going to land regardless of how far it is from you. Instant stopping when you land. I get that you want to create a sense of "hardness" but this is a bad method. Intentionally creating unwinnable stages just makes the game look shoddy, like the legendary pirate ships in Assassin's Creed : Black Flag. If you do not get the special items to kill them, they do stupid things like pivot on its rudder. The flying mantis throws discs that deviate from a return trajectory and track you. Don't create fake difficulties that result in absurd behaviours.
5. Minor Bugs on the Map
a. Certain shopkeepers don't show on the map. E.g. Banker Bug
b. Certain chairs don't show on the map E.g. The chair in the Colosseum of Fools
c. Certain level 2 bosses don't appear on the map E.g. Soul Sentry and Lost Kin
6. Unusable Nail Arts
Unusable in boss fights. They have a natural windup time, they can be interrupted and they are all so similar. Spin slash, big slash and dash slash?
7. Dream Nail
You gave it a whole Triangle button but it can't be used in mid-air, requires you to stand still, can be interrupted and all it does is read thoughts? I think this is better as R1, not a Triangle.
8. Similar Creature Mechanics
Fungling = Uoma = Squit = Mossfly = Vengefly
Husk Bully = Wandering Husk = Husk Hornhead
Fungified Husk = Volatile Mosskin
Tiktik = Shadow Creeper = Crawlid
9. The Teacher, Watcher and Hunter
Disappointed. I was hoping for an epic battle with all 3 seals that would culminate into a climax with the Hollow Knight. Instead, I slapped 2 seals with the Dream Nail and then proceeded to hit and absorb them.
10. Descending Dark does not Work In the Air

From its stunning visuals, and art style, to its outstanding music score, Hollow Knight is a game that does a lot of right. One thing I really appreciate this game for is that its way of teaching players new things is amazing. Some might dislike this, however I disagree with those people. Basically, you stumble across an area where you don't know what to do, and you can't do anything in that room, but it looks like you can. So you ignore it and continue on until you get a power, then go back, do that thing you couldn't do, and then get rewarded for it. It's one of my favorite aspects of this game and it truly makes me appreciate the little things this game does.
The boss battles are also a thing I appreciate. Everytime you die to a boss, you get a sense of, "I have to beat this thing," and you keep dying and dying where it bececomes extremely frustrating where you want to bang your head on the keyboard, but, when you do beat said boss you're having trouble on, it's the most satisfying feeling ever, you get the satisfaction that you defeated something you've been working on for a while, and you get rewarded.
Overall this game is a masterpiece and I strongly reccomend that those are debating about buying it, please buy it, it'll be a hella good of a decision.

NOT A HERO is another Retro style shooter that tries a bit too hard to be funny.
I purchased NOT A HERO based on the release trailer, which I did find to be entertaining and humorous. I came in with high expectations. It showed very nice looking pixel style graphics, many unique characters, and exciting mission segments.
Now, I've only played through the first series of levels, but I found myself bored and decided to take a break to write this review. The plot of NOT A HERO involves playing as different characters in order to assist Bunnylord in becoming Mayor. You will do this by assassinating certain people, destroying gang hideouts, and other forms of destroying crime by committing it.
As I mentioned before, I only played through the first section of levels. These first levels appeared extremely bland to me. Colors consisted of Red and Grey, and it didn't feel like I was ever changing levels after moving on. There are windows to jump through, and doors to open, but so far that is the only interaction I've discovered. I understand that there are secret areas, but I've yet to find any.
I was surprised by the bland levels because the diner and office area are very detailed and attractive. I stopped playing when I got to the "Green Levels," which I will call them. They looked almost exactly the same as the "Red Levels." Aside from a few different assets use for cover, which appeared to just be recolored.
I will try to continue playing to see if the levels become more interesting, but so far, they are just boring.

Just another attempt at humor that lacks creativity. They are varied skill-wise, and it's sometimes helpful to try a different one if you are struggling to complete all the bonus objectives in a level. I may add more to this after unlocking a few more.
The main character in this game is Bunnylord. As I spoke of before, he is doing what he can to become mayor of the city. I found myself skipping most of his dialogue because it was so.. puerile.
The humor in NOT A HERO had to have been written by a teenager. A teenager that just discovered balls and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, and cursing without getting in trouble by his parents.

I have been a big fan of the Hitman series ever since Silent Assassin. I have always enjoyed them, but every time I played the newest one, I couldn't go back to the older ones.
Once I played Contracts, Silent Assassin felt far too stretched out and some of the levels were almost impossible to complete with a Silent Assassin rating. When Blood Money came out, I realized how sluggish and clunky the older two games felt like.
So six years after Blood Money, Absolution comes out. While the gameplay, visuals, and level designs are quite different from Blood Money, I can't decide if I like Absolution better or not.
I'm assuming you know the story. If not, here's a quick synopsis:
Agent 47 kills his old mission briefer Diana. As a last wish from her, he has to protect a girl from becoming a cold-blooded assassin like him. He loses her to South Dakotans. He gets her back the only way Agent 47 knows: killing people.
The thing with Absolution is it's more linear than Blood Money. Levels are divided up into sections where you're stuck in a smaller area to complete a certain objective (kill a target, escape, get your Silverballers, etc.). This means that missions are a little more forgiving when you mess up.
However, just because the levels are divided up into smaller segments, that doesn't mean the segments aren't large and expansive. Almost every level has dozens of ways to eliminate your target(s) and/or accomplish your objective(s). Some are your usual "sneaky-chokey-body-hidey" strategies, others are a little unique (e.g. you steal a piece of evidence from a cop who's going to sell it to your target. When the target meets with the cop to buy it, the cop can't find it. The target pulls a gun on the cop, but the cop kills the target before he kills him). This makes you feel like you're
The one thing this game did lose is a bit of the challenge. All of the special and unique ways to eliminate your targets are vaguely described in your "Challenges" menu. This means you don't have to discover the unique ways to kill your targets on your own. When there's a challenge called "Shocking", has a picture of your target taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥beside a power generator, you can assume what you have to do.
You've also got your "instinct" power which highlights important set pieces and allows you to sneak past suspicious NPC's. Again, like the Challenges, it gives you obvious hints as to what you can use the items and set pieces for.
But despite all of that, where the game really shines is in the set design. While each Hitman game has a few missions that are "out there" (e.g. the meat and gimp party in Contracts and the Heaven/Hell level in Blood Money), Absolution's levels are very colourful, very unique, and very engaging.
In one mission, you infiltrate the main antagonist’s factory to look for the girl you need to rescue. However, Agent 47 makes it his duty to kill any and all of the head researchers there so they won’t continue their horrible research. In this mission, there are many ways to kill each of them, including prematurely activating minefields, trapping the researcher in a casing which explodes, and activating a dissecting machine while they’re demonstrating how to strap someone in it. It’s gratuitous and violent, but satisfying.
While I do miss the usual game formula of receiving your orders on a random target, Absolution at least has a solid story to go off of, giving it more structure than any of the other games.
Overall, Absolution is a lot better built, a lot less frustrating, and a lot more satisfying than any of the previous Hitman games.

My previous review for this game sucked, so I'm re-writing it.
I was very excited for this game as I really loved Bioshock, and I couldn't wait to see what this game would deliver. Unfortunately, after playing an 8 hour campaign, despite being somewhat satisfied by it, I felt it was missing a lot in comparison to the original game.
I then later found out that Bioshock 2 was developed by another developer (2K Marin) instead of 2K Boston (aka Irrational Games) which is why the immersive storyline like in the first game wasn't there. The multiplayer was developed by another developer, Digital Extremes.
But despite the really interesting storyline being there, the gameplay for Bioshock 2 is great. You play as a big daddy in the year 1970, a prototype big daddy to be exact, and if I remember correctly
you have to go and rescue this girl (not a little sister) as you are apparently the father of the daughter.
The gameplay is very much similar to the first game, you have your weapons, plasmids, health and EVE, but you also have a drill as well as your melee weapon. It runs and feels very much like the first game, but in its own way so it doesn't feel like a completely different game.
Bioshock 2 also included a multiplayer as well which was, well... Fun, but it could have been a lot better. You had many ways of customising your character, and it also followed a level up system, you could also access your own little apartment to see all your items that you collected too which was cool.
The multiplayer takes place before the fall of rapture, and you could also (the higher you level up) get more backstory for certain characters.
For the most part, the maps were fairly small, and there were many weapons and features to kill your opponents. There were no dedicated servers of course, which meant that everyone had to put up with unreasonable ping.
There were 3 game modes if I remember correctly, team deathmatch, capture the little sister (CTF), and deathmatch?
But unfortunately the multiplayer is now dead as Games For Windows Live is also dead. Not to mention the single player also had GFWL implemented as well. But I think it may have been removed sometime ago. Although it might be alive through programs like Tunngle etc.
So here are two videos if you're curious what the multiplayer was like.
Overall, despite the lackluster storyline in comparison to the first game. It's still worth definitely playing this if you're wanting to see the future of Rapture and to find out a bit more about the Bioshock storyline. (Even though it doesn't have much to do with the first game) it's not a bad game by any means, but it could have been a lot better.

The sound design and graphics are clearly retro-inspired, and this doesn't neccessarily help or hurt the game one way or the other. But they are definitely GOOD retro graphics, with a lot of attention to detail, and the characters are full of personality.
The gameplay is tight. RoA uses Smash mechanics like comboing, smash ("strong") attacks, tilts, aerials, etc., with its own mechanics like parrying. Oh, and you can't grab ledges, so getting back to stage is always fun. Character special moves can effect the stage in really interesting ways, like Kragg's pillar and Maypul's plant. And characters have their own mechanics like Zetterburn's flames and Maypul's mark that you have to watch out for.
If you have a few buddies and spare controllers, definitely check out the local multiplayer. Stages have "Aether" modes with fun gimmicks and insta-deaths, and things get really exciting with 4 Rivals on-screen at once.
You can also customize your character's color, which is super neat. And the best part is, the game isn't even complete yet. Story mode, and other features will be added in the final release.
Fantastic Indie Smash-like game. 10/10 in my book. Keep the quality coming, Dan.

Beyond Earth is stylistically and mechanically a Civilization 5 mod.
Basing the game on Civ5 is a good idea, but the game feels like Civ5 design principles held the game back.
There is a tech tree web, but the freedom this affords is all an illusion because all the victory conditions except total domination (capture all enemy capitals) are technology based.  This means two things: (1) the game is a technology race (2) you don't get to enjoy most of the tech tree, because most decisions are forced in order to win the tech race.
Pre-patch, there actually was a good mid-game military strategy.  But that got nerfed into oblivion.  So military option is a tech race, too.
Sid Meier has long been interviewed about why the Civ series does not continue into the future.  He has said that Civ game concept is to (re)play through world history.  So there is an overarching fear to not to change too much from original.  While I play these games a lot, Beyond Earth promised something fresh.  It isn't.
* Brand new foreign world or Civ 5 resources with different art and icons?  (There's oil and titanium, which serves the same role as aluminum...)  There are 3 faction specific
* Tech tree --> not really innovative for reasons above
* Combat -- this is stuck in Civ embark units mechanic -- it's 2600 and you don't start with hover tanks.
-- there are no melee naval units
-- your units upgrade for free with tech (hurrah ftw) but also your opponents (IMBA ftl)
* There is novel affinity/unit promotion system
On the whole, this game offers very little in the way of a new play experience.  It's mostly cosmetically atttactive TECH RACE.

The game almost forced me to think about where life came from, where it is now, where it is going, where it will end up at and whether it really matters at all.
"When every path you can walk has been created for you long in advance, death becomes meaningless, making life the same. Do you see now? Do you see that Stanley was already dead from the moment he hit start?"
Are we already dead from the moment we were born?
I wouldn't call it a video game. To call it such would be an insult to humanity and science in my opinion. Primal Carnage definitely stands alone -- and ably, at that -- in the world of FPS games. Lukewarm Media's debut comes out of the gates screeching, roaring, and grenade launching as you fight as either an assorted team of humans or an equally varied team of dinosaurs against the opposite team.
Forget the other dinosaur games that came and went -- this is definitely one to have.
Each class, whether human or dinosaur, has its own unique set of skills, abilities, and weaknesses. The Raptor, for example, is your token stealth class -- he's not got a lot of armor or bulk, but he's fast, can pounce in an instant, and leap higher than every other dinosaur. The Commando class, for the humans, is your token heavy class. He's got an assault rifle with a grenade launcher and can melee kill trapped and injured dinosaurs with ease, but with his big gun comes a lot of recoil and relatively low stamina.

A fascinating game. If you like JRPGs this one will most likely not disappoint. Even if the standard Final Fantasy isn't your thing, this game might still be interesting.
The characters are interesting so far, and break some of the old tropes (though some do remain as well).
If I had to compare this game, I would say it has a very similar feel to Final Fantasy Tactics, especially Tactics Advance. It's got similar party managing. That said, it's more classic JRPG combat and not tactical stategy like Tactics. You also don't have much say in other characters than your main one. You can't choose their equipment or what skills they learn and such. This can either be a blessing to some or a con. I would personally like more customizability to the characters, but so far as I've noted and what I predict, the party system is going to become quite deep and involving, if you want.
Combat has a nice element of twitchy QTE put in between the standard turn-based fighting. It can be somewhat challenging to land those criticals, but they are very rewarding (especially later on when you can get insane Teamwork-chains). In case you don't want to sit there with your fingers ready to press the right button all the time, you can also turn the critical QTEs automatic, which probably works similar to how the auto-trigger works in FFVIII.
The story is so far interesting. We'll see how it develops.
Recommended to fans of JRPGs and other turn-based RPGs.

I have never been so angered by a video game.
Crysis is a beautiful game. That's no secret. Beyond that, the shooting is competent and the nano suit adds a nice flavor to the game. It would be a pretty fun game if not for its glaring flaws. So let's dive into those.
The game is poorly optimized. It looks great, but similarly good looking games run better. I'm using a 4770k @ 4.6 GHz and an overclocked GTX 970. It runs very well on max with 4x AA in most situations, but it occasionally lags, especially against aliens with their numerous projectile effects.
Crysis can't seem to pick a difficulty and stick with it. You'll go fifteen minutes of easy gameplay, and suddenly it's impossibly difficult. The autosaves are few and far between, so you'll need to stay on top of that yourself. Assuming you don't die in a particularly difficult situation, you might die to any of the numerous bugs.
That's right. The game is HORRIBLY buggy. Here is a nice list of terrible deaths and game-breaking bugs I encountered on a single playthrough:
- Bumped into an object that is subject to phsysics. It collided funny and I was instantly killed by it, from full health, with 100% on armor.
- Randomly fell over dead on numerous occasions, no enemies nearby, full health, no mines.
- Vehicle bumps something at an odd angle, explodes.
- Clipped through a floor and into a fire.
- The second-to-last mission finished and crashed the game. Again. And again. I had to use a command console code to advance to the final mission.
- The final mission allows you to progress beyond something that is necessary to finish it, causing you to have to restart the mission.
The list could go on. I'm sure there are plenty I even forgot.
Beyond the bugs, the game itself is just frustrating. The ground shooting segments are usually good, but the vehicle segments are some of the worst I've ever played. The VTOL is unresponsive and clunky, made even worse by tornados that just throw you to the ground. The tank mission is entirely too difficult at times. There is an escort mission where your friendly has to keep warm, and he twice failed to keep up with me and stand near a fire, getting himself killed.
There is a lot of good in this game, but there are a lot of things so poorly executed, it clearly overshadows the good. Unless you're a masochist, do not buy this game.

I have only played a little over an hour upon writing this but i believe that is enough to at least recommend it to anyone that may be on the fence on whether or not they should buy this game. I am a fan of retro platforming games so when i saw this game i wanted it right away. For the graphic style this game has it looks really good and the shooting is flashy and satisfying. There is a decent amount of written dialogue before and after missions so if that's your thing then you're in luck. Me personally i just keep on skipping it so i can move along to the next mission. This game is very straight forward so if you get bored easily of doing the same thing over and over again then maybe you shouldn't buy this game. And there lies my only issue with this game is that it lacks content and if they had added more stuff (Weapons, moves, guns, co-op etc) this game could have gone from great to amazing. Like i said there is plenty of reading to do between missions but that will not satisfy everyone and it might annoy others.
There are some things i wish this game had that they have not added, this is not a con at all but more of a few ideas that i think could have made the game a fuller experience. The main thing that would have been great would be character progression. Like an RPG style leveling system where after each level you get a little stronger, faster etc. Also equippable equipment that you find throughout the levels or buy from a shop in between stages. I have not seen anything like this in the game so far which is slightly disappointing because i believe that could have made this game even better than it currently is.
I will have to come back later after playing the game some more and update some stuff but as of right now the bottom line is this. The game is fun, it's not too expensive, shooting/killing is satisfying and if you're into these type of indie games there is no way you won't enjoy this. If they held the game off for a while and added some RPG elements to the game i think it could have been amazing but it's damn good just the way it is. That is just my personal opinion and i'm sure you might feel another way about it and that's fine just don't bash me for having my own take on things.
If i had to rate this game at this very moment i would give it an 7/10. Enjoy your day and keep on gaming!

Taking a break from skateboarding madness, OlliOlli series creators Roll7 have unleashed something new on the gaming world. With a premise which includes time-travel, British politics and an anthropomorphic purple rabbit, welcome to the world of Not a Hero.
The cover-based indie shooter takes place during a mayoral election where BunnyLord, the aforementioned rabbit, has travelled back in time from 2048 to save the world from total destruction and alien invasion. In a bid to become mayor he hires Steve, a professional assassin turned amateur campaign manager, to clean up the city by any means necessary.
With the help of similarly dubious “heroes”, Steve must utilise their unique skill sets and complete his mission, ensure BunnyLord is elected mayor and save the future of the world, so no pressure on Steve then.
Not a Hero‘s story is, quite frankly, insane, but in the best way possible. The narrative is intelligent, witty, incredibly funny and at no stage during your campaign run does it get boring. It tells the tale of a bunny man from the future on a quest to take Boris Johnson’s job in order to save the human race, what is not to love about that?
This bizarre tale plays out in-game through “BunnyLord’s Briefing Room” meetings prior to each level, followed by a post-carnage one to one in the local cafe when the mission is complete. It’s told extremely well with a dialog that you’ll find it hard pressed to make it through without the occasional laugh out loud moment.
The gameplay itself is extremely enjoyable, from the very beginning of the game when Steve is a lone warrior with his handgun, through to the conclusion of the story where nine different heroes are at your disposal, the game never drops in quality. Much like Roll7’s OlliOlli, the control layout is perfect, the mechanics are simple to master and so the game quickly becomes more about tactics and less about what buttons to press.
This intuitive control setup lets you quickly jump into the game and utilize everything on offer. The mixture of rampage and cover-based shootouts mean that sometimes it’s perfectly acceptable to go crazy while other times you’ll need a little tact. You have at your disposal a primary weapon, a collectible secondary weapon – grenades, turrets, that sort of thing – the ability to slide and knock enemies over as well as dodge and cover, all of which makes the gameplay exceptionally versatile.
One of the greatest design decisions in Not a Hero is the mass quantities of ammo, you do not need to go seeking a resupply mid-carnage, just simply reload. At the end of the day, this game isn’t going for total realism in any way and so taking away the distraction of finding ammo is a superb move which leaves you more time to mutilate your enemies.
Another interesting element is the dynamic mission risks, unexpected mid-level events that can beef up the difficulty considerably just when you think you’ve completed your mission with ease. These may be in the form of S.W.A.T. teams, trigger happy seniors, helicopter gunships, the occasional panda, or even a suicidal samurais. This accompanied by the fact that each level plays out slightly different depending on the character you play as means that yet again Roll7 have mastered the art of replayability.
The cast of characters themselves, while all controlled the same way, each have their own unique personalities, weapons and weaknesses. Cletus, for example, is a shotgun-toting hillbilly type who pretends to be Scottish. He will require a lot more reloads then Steve and given the time it takes to reload a weapon, this can be a significant problem when you’ve got a S.W.A.T. team closing in. That said he does have the ability to shoot open doors, which will definitely work in your favour.
Samantha, on the other hand, is a Welsh warrior, fast and agile, she is able to shoot while running and execute bad guys in a flash. As you progress through the game, the personalities and diverse skill sets increase significantly. Once you’ve unlocked them all, you’ll be able to smash bad guys to shreds with the hammer of Ronald, or slice your way through the crowd with Kimmy.
It’s not just the way the cast plays that is unique though, the voice-over work is hilarious, if a little bit adult-only. Our main hero Steve, for example, sounds like he belongs in a Guy Richie movie while Samantha wouldn’t look out of place in a twisted version of Gavin and Stacey. No word of a lie, this is some of the best voice-over work for an indie game I’ve ever had the pleasure of hearing despite the limited vocabulary.
Much like the OlliOlli series, Not a Hero is visually pleasing with a great deal work put into turning what could easily have been a bland simplistic environment into a colourful vibrant one. Roll7 have gone above and beyond in making this game look good. The animation in each of the characters fighting styles, the unique look of every character, good or bad, even the smooth flow of the gameplay, it’s all done to the highest standard.
In addition to the voice-over work which I’ve already praised, the soundtrack is brilliant. From the casual elevator music on the character select screen to the in-level fast pumping, ready for action music, it’s fit for purpose, adds to the overall experience and just works perfectly. Roll7 do of course have a reputation for awesome soundtracks as anyone that has played one of the OlliOlli games will agree.
Overall, I honestly can’t find a significant flaw with Not a Hero, it is a superb game. While the graphics may initially seem primitive, Roll7 have used their brilliant design skills to make every pixel count on screen. The cast of character is as diverse as it is extensive and the dynamic mission surprises mean that you’re never likely to get the same experience twice.
The story is a laugh to say the least and the gameplay is flawless, an all round great game. Long live the BunnyLord.

This one's a toughie.
Let me start it off by saying that I am an MTG player, in real life.
Magic: The Gathering is a wonderful Collectible Card game, one of the best I've ever seen.
That being said, no matter how good the real version is, none of the digital versions are near as good.
I'm totally on the fence for this game, middle of the road. The reason I've voted it as yes is that it is a good way to get into magic, with good tutorials for new players. If you read this, and you're interested in learning Magic, please download this game. It's great to start learning the game, but for a seasoned pro, it's not up to snuff. Actually, scratch that. If you know how to play, are competent, or own your own set of IRL cards, you don't need this game.
My biggest issue is the available cards. They have an extremely limited set of cards available to buy in-game. You can spend 150 in-game coins (Not that easy to get) to get 6 cards. 6. In real life, you spend 5 dollars (Canadian) on 15 cards, in a booster pack. You, of course, get the best bang for your buck buying in bulk, as for everything. The point is, 6 cards is really not a lot for all the grinding to get the coins. Especially when there are so few available cards to get.
Magic has existed since 1993, with new cards being released every 3 months. Cards released over a year ago (Approximately) become nonstandard, meaning they can't be used in the Standard format, which is used in most tournaments. That doesn't stop you from using any of the thousands of cards created in casual games or Modern or Legacy formats. This creates an extreme variety of decks that can be created. In this version, the tiny amount of cards implemented seriously limits that. In addition to that, there are certain cards used in the tutorials that are totally unavailable to the player. They spent the time programming in a card, just so that an NPC Sphinx can use it against you once, then you never see it again. You can't tell me that makes sense.
If you were to try to collect all the cards (Probably the only way to get anywhere near the variety you'd need), it would take either hours of meaningless grinding, or tons of real life purchases. I believe (Not sure, don't quote me on this) the minimum purchase is 40 dollars. That's a lot for not much. The alternative, the grinding, is also very difficult. You only get coins for winning a game. If you lose, you get no money. You can't buy cards. You can't get better. You can't win. A nasty cycle there. You'd think you could try two-headed giant, where you fight two v. two. You could get a good partner and win. And say you do. "Where's my money?" You ask. The answer? No rewards for two-headed giant. There's also the fact that the online servers aren't the best. This means, the game crashes during online duels. This means you don't win. Speaking of being online, the entire game is always online. If your connection goes down, the game doesn't record your gold or any story progress, even in the single player campaign (Which tends to be either ridiculously difficult due to being forced to use awful decks, or ridiculously easy due to dumb AI)
Boy, I just keep going on and on, don't I?
Better end this while I still can.
In conclusion to this essay of a review, Magic is a fantastic game that I advise you all play. Ok, wizards, where's my 20$? Just kidding on that last part. I'm not being paid to advertise magic. It's an awesome game, that is best enjoyed in real life. These online attempts just never turn up as good. I'd advise this game only to people who want to learn how to play the game, or someone who doesn't have any real friends to play with. It's a good learning tool, but if you have the chance to buy and play the physical cards, take that over this.

This game is a prime example of Auto-Battle done RIGHT, unlike your generic mobile game which does indeed play itself without you looking at it. I picked up this game after watching many speedruns of it, because I was intrigued by the amount of depth in an "auto-battle" game. Needless to say, it did not disappoint.
This game unfortunately doesn't have much hand-holding, you have to discover a lot of tricks and details by yourself, which is considered rare for a modern game. (At least it isn't Mario And Luigi: Tutorial Team right?) At no point does the game really go into detail about things like Cut, Keep or Chain duration. If you dislike discovering things for yourself, there are plenty of game mechanic resources online that you can find. All the same, the game is entirely playable without knowing these things.
This game is HARD. It's quite execution heavy, but you shouldn't fall into the trap of setting your ATB speed to slow in options because just about the only thing it does is help you die of boredom faster. It's a lot about finding out how to best prepare for your fights to equip the AI with the right tools to win, especially so if you want to auto-battle all day. You'll find yourself retrying fights a lot, doubly so if you're not looking to run a Sentinel in every single fight and die of old age. In fact, it's often many magnitudes faster to go into a fight, flail around to understand the enenmy, then retry and optimize your setup. This is the reason why "Retry" is a really good mechanic in this game, despite how cheesy and overly forgiving it might seem.
People like to bash this game for being Hallway Simulator. It definitely isn't the strongest part of the game, but I hated the missions a lot more. The missions felt like hallways simulator + unnecessary padding, and I'd rather play a game with a strong main experience than to be shoved a tonne of boring sidequests to inflate play hours and provide artificial "branching".
That being said, the missions are not bad, they've done a very good job with encounter design in this game. You can't always charge headfirst with the same paradigms into every fight unless you're planning to take 20mins to clear by sitting in Solidarity, Combat Clinic and Tortoise all day. The game might feel like "Stagger and win", but it isn't always the case; Sometimes you want to raise the post stagger chain to 999.9% first, other times you want to not cause the enemy to enter another phase by doing too much damage, and occasionally you want to stagger later so that you can set up a 1 stagger kill. The game has constantly encouraged a variety of strategies to efficiently take down each boss.

As it stands right now, I can't recommend this game. I received the game for free, having already owned Bioshock.
Crashes are frequent, and seem to happen when achievements are supposed to be earned. When the game crashes, there is no alt-tabbing out of it. My computer must be restarted. When I do this, all of my settings in game (video, audio, controls, gameplay) are reset.
There is also a glitch, wherein when changing the controls, after saving them, the game thinks a controller is plugged in, and won't allow me to use my keyboard. I have to close the game and reopen it to continue playing.
I am a HUGE bioshock fan. Have been since Bioshock came out when I was in high school. I own all three games. I started waking up earlier so I could play before work.
I was very, very excited for this re-release, but playing on survivor with no vita chambers, having the game hang and having to restart my computer and readjust all my settings is an extremely irritating experience. I understand there is a patch coming soon. I can only hope it will fix all of these issues.
